en: The Revākhaṇḍa of the Vāyupurāṇa, Chapter 1.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. RKV 1.1.
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Puruṣottama; Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Narmadā;
Oṃ, salutations to Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śuka, and Parāśara; salutations to the gurus, cows, and Brahmins.

Oṃ! May the waters of the Narmadā protect you—waters where swarms of bees are intoxicated by the fragrance of the wine-like ichor flowing from the temples of bathing elephants; waters turned tawny by contact with the saffron falling from the breasts of perfected women during their baths; waters whose riverside trees are covered with heaps of flowers gathered by sages morning and evening; and waves upon which swans are overtaken by the trunks of elephants and sea-monsters. 1.2.
May the Narmadā— whose sacred fords on both banks have washed away the flood of all the world’s evils, and who is worthy of worship by gods, sages, and men— ever remove our misfortune.
May the Narmadā, whose waters are meritorious and who purifies all, destroy every sin—past, future, and present—of those born upon this earth. RKV_1.4.
May the Revā river, whose sandy banks even ascetics desire for the sake of Śiva,
and who is served by multitudes of sages, lead to my welfare.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya."
In the sacred abode of Naimiṣa, frequented by various ṛṣis, Śaunaka, seated at a sacrificial session, questioned Sūta in detail: RKV 1.7.
O Sūta, I believe that skill in the Dharma has always been honored within you;
for you alone are the disciple of Vyāsa, the speaker of meritorious nectar-like discourses.
Therefore, O Sage, I question you, who are the refuge of the ford of Dharma;
for there are many sacred fords, and I have heard of them in great numbers.
I have heard of the divine river Brāhmī as well as the Viṣṇunadī;
however, I have never anywhere heard of the third, the excellent river Raudrī.
O one of great wisdom, tell me of that renowned [river] which contains the Vedas within her, who is saluted by hosts of gods, and who is adorned by a multitude of sacred fords.
Upon which region does the Revā depend, and how did she originate from Śrī Rudra? Tell me also of those sacred fords (tīrthas) that are situated there.
Sūta said:
Well asked, O lord of the lineage, is this history centered on the Narmadā; it is wonderful, purifying, and destructive of faults, O best of beings, as has been declared by Śruta.
Having manifested the Vedas, Upavedas, Vedāṅgas, and so forth,
the son of Satyavatī fulfilled [his purpose] as the speaker of the eighteen Purāṇas.
Having paid homage to him, I shall declare the Purāṇas in their proper order,
by the recitation of which there is an increase of merit and long life.
Revelation (Śruti) and Tradition (Smṛti) are proclaimed to be the two eyes of the Brahmins;
one who is deprived of one of them is called one-eyed, while one who lacks both is declared blind.
The Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas are the three eyes of the learned;
he who perceives them with his own three eyes is considered a portion of Maheśvara.
The knowledge of the Vedas pertaining to the Self was created by the Lord,
as were the Śaunakīya, the Paurāṇika, and that which consists of the Dharmaśāstras.
These three are the primary sciences for the definitive determination of all treatises;
"the Purāṇa is the fifth Veda"—such is the instruction of Brahmā.
Indeed, he who does not know the Purāṇa knows nothing at all here;
for what dharma could that be, or what kind of knowledge could it be? (RKV 1.20)
Whatever else is not seen here in this Purāṇa, it is found elsewhere;
for the Vedas were established first within the Purāṇa—of this there is no doubt.
"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me';
this was the conclusion reached long ago through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. (RKV 1.22)
The Self is the ancient [essence] of the Vedas, and those six [limbs] are its distinct members;
for whatever is seen in the Vedas is indeed seen in the Smṛtis as well.
That which is seen by both [the Vedas and the Purāṇas] is indeed proclaimed in the Purāṇas;
the Purāṇa is remembered as the first of all scriptures, originating from Brahmā.
And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths;
O Sage, in this interval between kalpas, there was only a single Purāṇa.
Having recalled that meritorious means of accomplishing the three goals of life, which extends over a hundred crores of verses, the four-faced Lord spoke to the sages.
From that, the manifestation of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa occurred;
then, seeing that the Purāṇa was not being grasped over time, the sage [acted].
Assuming the form of Vyāsa, the omnipresent Lord always withdraws [the Vedas] at the end of every Dvāpara age, when they have reached a measure of eight hundred thousand verses.
Having divided it into eighteen parts, it is proclaimed here in this world of mortals;
even today, in the realm of the gods, it remains with an extent of one billion verses.
Thus, four hundred thousand [verses] have been set down here in brief.
Now, those eighteen Purāṇas are being spoken of;
I shall state them by name, so listen, O best of sages.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
Therein is the primordial *Brahma-purāṇa*, adorned within the *Saṃhitā*,
consisting of ten thousand verses and endowed with various meritorious narratives.
The Pādma is said to consist of fifty-five thousand [verses],
and the third, named Vaiṣṇava, is numbered at twenty-three thousand.
The fourth was proclaimed by Vāyu and is remembered as the Vāyavīya;
because of its union with devotion to Śiva, it is also known by the name Śaiva.
O Śaunaka, the fifth [purāṇa], the Bhaviṣya, is likewise declared to consist of twenty-four thousand verses and four sections.
That [Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa] consists of fourteen thousand and five hundred verses;
the sixth is proclaimed as the Mārkaṇḍeya, consisting of nine thousand verses.
The seventh is declared to be the Āgneya, consisting of sixteen thousand [verses];
the eighth is indeed declared to be the Nāradīya, consisting of twenty-five thousand.
The ninth, O Blessed One, is adorned with two parts;
it is said to consist of eighteen thousand verses by way of the count of its text.
The tenth is said here to be the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa of that same number;
the eleventh is to be known as the Laiṅga, likewise with the number eleven.
O bull among sages, that Liṅga has been divided into two parts;
they know the Vārāha Purāṇa to consist of twenty-four thousand verses as the twelfth.
O best of fortunate ones, the Skanda Purāṇa is divided into seven sections;
it is indeed defined by a number of eighty-one thousand verses.
Then, O Kulapati, the fourteenth [section] known as Vāmana was formerly declared to consist of ten thousand verses in number. (RKV 1.42)
They say the fifteenth is the Kaurma Purāṇa, adorned with two sections;
it consists of seventeen thousand verses, O Lord of Sāṃkhya, in the Kali age.
O best among speakers, that which was proclaimed by Matsya to Manu in sixteen successive stages is fourteen thousand verses in number.
The Gāruḍa is remembered as the seventeenth, and the eighteenth is the Brahmāṇḍa, adorned with two parts; [the total] is nineteen. (RKV 1.45)
And that consists of twelve thousand verses together with one hundred and eight;
likewise are the Upapurāṇas which were spoken by the Creator.
This is the excellent and easily accessible Saura Purāṇa from the Brahmapurāṇa,
consisting of two Saṃhitās, meritorious, and based upon the narratives of Śiva.
The first was spoken by Sanatkumāra, and the second was uttered by Sūrya;
for that [text] is renowned by the name of Sanatkumāra, O great sage.
The second is the Nārasiṃha, found in the Purāṇa known as the Pādma;
and the third is considered to be the Śaukeya in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
The fourth is that of Bṛhaspati, and the Vāyavya is always esteemed;
the fifth is remembered as the Daurvāsasa, which is always included in the Bhāgavata.
The Bhaviṣya, that which was spoken by Nārada, and that formerly declared by the wise; likewise the Kāpila, the Mānava, and that uttered by Uśanas.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, as well as the two Kālikās, the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, the Saura, and the Sarvārthasaṃcaya; RKV_1.52 //
The Pārāśara, Bhāgavata, and Kaurma— the eighteenth in sequence—
these Upapurāṇas have been declared by me in their proper order.
Whoever reads or hears this Purāṇa-saṃhitā shall partake in infinite merit; upon death, he shall go to the city of Brahmā.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Purāṇa-Saṃhitā," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 2.
Sūta said:
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has proclaimed the majesty of the Narmadā;
that which you have asked about, I shall now fully declare to you. (RKV 2.2)
O best of sages, who else indeed is capable of describing the details of the sacred fords along the Narmadā, except for the Lord Brahmā?
In former times, Janamejaya asked this very same question to the disciple of Dvaipāyana known as Vaiśampāyana.
O Śaunaka, I shall tell you that merit residing at Revātīrtha;
formerly, King Pārīkṣita was initiated for the performance of sacrifices.

When the sacrificial materials had been gathered, while the rituals were being performed, when the foremost of the twice-born were seated, and while the oblation was being poured into the fire; (RKV 2.6)
Likewise, while all manner of Dharma discourses were being held, and while the sounds uttered by people were being heard day and night; RKV 2.7.
"O noble householder, let it be given! Let it be eaten!"—thus they spoke on the sacrificial ground while the entertainers provided various diversions.
While such a sacrifice, equal to a session of the dwellers of heaven, was thus proceeding, Janamejaya questioned Vaiśampāyana as he sat.
Janamejaya said:
"O Vaiśampāyana, in my view you possess knowledge through the grace of Dvaipāyana; therefore, I question you in the presence of these sages."
Tell me of the ancient account of the ancestors' pilgrimage to sacred fords;
I have heard that they endured various kinds of hardships there for a long time.
O Brahmin, how was it that my ancestors, the sons of Pṛthā, defeated at dice,
wandered over the earth as far as the ocean out of a longing for sacred fords?
"By whom were they accompanied, dear father, as they wandered through many regions of the earth?
Tell me all of that; for you are considered by me to be omniscient."
Vaiśampāyana said:
O sinless lord of the earth, having paid homage to Virūpākṣa Vedavyāsa, the great poet, I shall relate that which has been asked by you.
But those five grandsons of yours, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā,
dwelt in the excellent Kāmyaka forest along with the brahmins.
O King of kings, there were also the high-minded Kaśyapa at Pradhānoddālaka, as well as Vibhāṇḍaka and the great sage Muru.
Pulastya, Lomaśa, and others who possessed sons and grandsons,
having bathed in all the sacred fords without exception, went to the Vindhya mountain.
And there they saw a holy hermitage, crowded with all kinds of trees:
campakas, karṇakāras, punnāgas, and nāgakesaras.
It was adorned with *bakula*, *kovidāra*, and pomegranate trees,
as well as with blossoming *arjuna*, *bilva*, *pāṭala*, and *ketaka* trees.
With kadamba, mango, and madhūka trees; with nimba, jambīra, and tinduka; with coconut, wood-apple, date-palm, and jackfruit as well.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, covered by diverse climbing vines,
and lovely with flowers and fruit, like the Caitraratha forest.
It was adorned with vast reservoirs of water, embellished by clusters of lotuses,
and covered with white, blue, yellow, white-and-red, and crimson water-lilies.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by ruddy geese,
frequented by *āḍī*, crows, and cranes, and graced by cuckoos and other birds.
With lions, tigers, boars, and exceedingly fierce elephants, with buffaloes of massive body, and with deer, leopards, and hares; RKV_2.25 //
It was filled with gaṇḍakas and rhinoceroses, as well as jackals and deer;
it abounded with antelopes, bears, and both bipeds and quadrupeds.
And so it was, filled with cuckoos, lovely to the mind, and beautifully adorned,
with flocks of jīvañjīvaka birds and joined by various other species of birds.
It is completely free from suffering and grief, delightful and enchanting to sentient beings,
devoid of hunger and thirst, lovely, and entirely free from all diseases.
Here, the deer drink from the lioness’s teat with affection;
both the cat and the mouse lick her face as they look up.
Having seen that delightful forest, the sons of Pāṇḍu entered it, along with five-headed lions, young elephants, serpents, and peacocks.
There he saw Mārkaṇḍeya, who resembled the rising sun and was being attended by sages learned in various scriptures.
By those of noble birth, endowed with goodness, possessed of purity and proper conduct,
joined with wisdom, endowed with forbearance, and devoted to recitation at the three junctions of the day.
Some were devoted to fire-offerings with mantras prescribed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
some remained in the midst of the five fires, while others stayed in solitary retreats.
Others keep their arms raised without support, while others revolve like the sun; some eat only in the evening and morning, and others likewise take but a single meal a day.
Likewise, others eat only once every twelve days; others eat only once every half-month;
others do so at every new moon; and others subsist on water-moss.
Others ate oil-cake; some subsisted on leaves of the *pālāśa* tree;
others were restricted in their food, consuming only air or water.
Thus served by such aged and eminent sages,
the illustrious son of Dharma entered that hermitage.
Having seen the best of sages, peaceful and meditating upon the supreme state,
he suddenly circumambulated him and prostrated himself like a staff before him.
Seeing him following after him with devotion, the wise Dharma finally took his eye and asked this: "Who are you? he inquired.
Having heard those words of his, the boy who was standing near him said:
"This is the King of Dharma; he has arrived for the purpose of seeing you."

Having heard those words spoken by the boy, the Sage, moving slightly from his place, spoke with reverence: "Come, come, my dear child! Having smelled him out of affection, he seated him upon his own seat.
When he had taken his seat in the assembly hall, they performed worship according to the prescribed rites with various kinds of wild grains, fruits, roots, and juices.
The Pāṇḍavas, having been duly honored by the Brāhmaṇas together with them, rested for a moment; then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, arose.
Filled with curiosity, he questioned the best of sages:
"O Blessed One, you are considered by me to be long-lived among all people."
O sinless one, tell me in full about the seven kalpas,
and even about the destruction of a kalpa, regarding both the world of the immobile and the mobile.
"O chief of brahmins, you have not perished; for what reason or by what cause [did this happen]?
O sage, all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as far as the oceans—" [RKV 2.46]
Among them, which ones remain standing and which have gone to destruction?
Which one always possesses meritorious waters, and which one has not met with decay?
Tell this to me, O father, with a gracious heart;
I wish to hear it in its entirety, together with the sages and my kinsmen.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma!
O sinless one, I shall relate to you, according to the truth, that which you ask of me."
Listen to the fruit of merit for that man who hears with devotion this ancient, meritorious [text] spoken by Rudra, which removes all sins. (RKV 2.50)
O King, one obtains that same fruit by means of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter.
The man who is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or a killer of a cow—
such a person is liberated from all sins, according to the word of Rudra.
The Gaṅgā is the best of rivers, as is the Sarasvatī;
likewise the Kāverī, the Devikā, the Sindhu, and the Sālakuṭī.
The Sarayū, the Śatarudrā, the Mahī along with the Carmilā, the holy Godāvarī, and likewise the river Yamunā; RKV 2.54.
The Payoṣṇī, the Śatadru, and likewise the auspicious Dharmanadī—
these and other rivers are remembered as removers of all sins.
"But, my dear, O best of kings, I shall tell you the reason:
in every kalpa, all the oceans and rivers have gone to their destruction."
O Indra among kings, when the destruction of the seven kalpas has been exhausted, Narmadā did not perish; indeed, Narmadā alone, the best of rivers, remains supreme.
O illustrious one, the Gaṅgā and other rivers, filled with water and praised by hosts of sages, have come to destruction in kalpa after kalpa.
"O sinless one, this goddess was seen by him in the past; therefore, I shall describe her to you."

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Revā," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāsāra, Chapter 3.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, you have witnessed the terrible destructions of seven kalpas."
Moreover, O Blessed One, there is no one here who possesses long life.
For by you, while the world was asleep in the single ocean, was seen Padmanābha, the slayer of the enemies of the gods,
possessing a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, and a thousand bellies.

It is said that, through the grace of that high-souled one, you did not meet your destruction even while the world of moving and non-moving beings was being consumed, owing to the granting of a boon by that great soul.
"O sinless one, what wonderful thing have you seen while wandering?
Tell me this, O Blessed One, for my curiosity is great."
And when the great and terrible end of the age, the time of total destruction, had arrived,
the world was struck by drought for more than a hundred years in the past.

When the herbs had perished in that terrible time, when the world was devoid of gods and dānavas, when it was rendered powerless and the *vaṣaṭ*-call had ceased, and it was utterly corrupted by the Kali age; // RKV_3.6 //
O Brahmin, at that time, during the dissolution of the age, the rivers, lakes, ponds, pools, and groves had all dried up and become formless.
When Janaloka was reached, the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and others,
as well as the high-souled sages endowed with divine splendor, [ascended].
Which elements remain, and which have indeed departed, O Great Sage?
O Illustrious One, explain all of this to me individually.
O best of Brahmins, what are the *bhūtas*, and how may one attain perfection when the most terrible time of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra has arrived?
Thus addressed by the wise Dharmarāja,
Mārkaṇḍeya, surrounded by hosts of sages, then replied as follows.
The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O lord of men, let all the sages together with you listen to this great Purāṇa previously spoken by Śambhu to Vāyu, the deity of wind."
This ancient [account] was heard from Vāyu by Skanda;
Vasiṣṭha heard it from him, and Parāśara after that.
From him it was received by Jātūkarṇya, and from him likewise by the great seers;
thus it has been proclaimed in succession by hundreds of the best of the twice-born.
It is said that in the past, Śambhu, having churned all the scriptures for the sake of speaking the truth, proclaimed this *Saṃhitā* consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
Subsequently, that [Dharma] was divided into four parts according to the nature of the ages,
by the great seers, in accordance with the intelligence and capacity of human beings.
"Having previously propitiated Maheśvara, the Lord of Creatures, I heard this Purāṇa; indeed, I shall now recount it to you in its entirety."
O Lord of Men, having heard this, a living being is liberated from all sins—
both those born of the mind and those born of action— accumulated over seven lifetimes.
"By the grace of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, and the Supreme Lord, I have repeatedly witnessed the terrible destructions at the end of seven kalpas."
When the world had been consumed by the twelve suns and turned into a single ocean,
I grew weary from wandering there, swimming across the sea with my arms.
Then, O King, in the waters I formerly beheld a Person whose form was like that of the sun, the Lord who is without beginning or end.
And another second Manu was seen, accompanied by his sons and grandsons, illuminating the ten directions with the peak of the king of mountains.
He too wanders in that fathomless great ocean turned to darkness,
revolving for even a moment without rest as if mounted upon a wheel.
Then, agitated by fear, I was crossing the ocean with my arms;
while staying there, I saw a great fish filled with rut.
Then, O Bhārata, having seen me, that Great Lord Maheśvara, who is the supreme essence of all things, assumed the form of a fish and said to me, "Come, come!"
Then, O lord of men, having gone there in haste, I was utterly exhausted and my knowledge vanished; I fell into a state of supreme despondency at his mouth.
Then, at the edge of the ocean, I beheld [the city] crowded with great whirlpools,
its waters surging with waves, laughing loudly with masses of foam.
There was a holy river that flowed at will, teeming with large fish and small fish;
in the midst of that river stood a woman who could assume any form at will.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, she carries a great surge of agitation;
her limbs are variegated with divine gold, and she is adorned with the brilliance of blazing gold.
Supporting herself with both knees upon the great ship, she stood there;
Manu addressed her thus: "Who are you, O celestial woman of exquisite limbs?"
"For what purpose do you stand here, O beautiful goddess, while the hosts of gods and asuras have perished? You wander playfully upon the ocean."
Rivers, oceans, and mountains have indeed met their destruction many times over;
yet you alone, O virtuous lady, remain. What is the great cause for this?
O Goddess, I wish to hear it; tell me everything without omission.
The woman said:
"Born from the body of the Lord, renowned by the name Amṛtā,
a meritorious river that removes all sins— having taken refuge in me, from where could fear come?"
"O twice-born one, having taken this boat for you, I have indeed come;
for there is no exhaustion of this boat as long as Śaṅkara remains upon it."
O King of kings, having heard those words of hers, my eyes wide with wonder, I then boarded the ship together with Manu.
Having joined my palms in reverence and bowed my head to the Lord,
I praised the all-pervading Supreme Sovereign, the bestower of fearlessness.
Salutation to the god Sadyojāta, and indeed to Vāmadeva;
salutation to you in every existence, and salutation to you who are accessible through devotion.
Salutations to you, Bhūrbhuva; salutations indeed to the one whose eldest is Rāma.
Salutations to you, Bhadrakāla; salutations indeed to the one in the form of Kali.
We know the Great God, the abode, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest;
we know the God of gods—O Rudra, salutations upon salutations to you!
"Salutations again and again to the cause of the creation and destruction of the world!
Thus was Mahādeva praised by me previously at the beginning of creation, O sinless one."
Being pleased, he said to me afterwards: "Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Mārkaṇḍeya’s Ascent onto Half a Boat at the Dissolution of the Kalpa," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Dharmarāja.
RKV, Chapter 4. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having emerged from the ocean, [he saw him] situated on the peak of Trikūṭa.
Possessing a great golden luster, it was strewn with rocks of various colors.
Seated upon Mahāśṛṅga, accompanied by ten million Rudras,
he is Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Lord, unborn and imperishable.
O dear one of noble vows, together with Manu, he who consists of all beings once again paid homage to the feet that are worshipped by all the gods.
At that time, O giver of honor, I remained for a thousand yugas together with Rudra in that terrible single ocean, O descendant of Kuru.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O father, having heard this, a great curiosity has arisen in my heart;
therefore, please tell it to me as I listen along with my kinsmen."
Who is she with eyes like lotus petals, who wanders eternally like a yogi in this great ocean of darkness, and who spoke of herself as the daughter of Rudra?
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "In former times, I myself asked this very same question to Manu;
that very account of the origin of the woman (Abalā) I shall now relate to you."
When the night of the supreme Brahmā had passed, then at the clear dawn, as living beings were being created; RKV_4.8 //
Having bowed my head to Manu, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I ask this:
who is this woman with eyes like lotus petals, dark-complexioned and with a face resembling the moon?
Wandering alone in the single ocean, she says, "I am born of Rudra";
she is Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, or indeed Sarasvatī.
Is she the Mandākinī, the best of rivers; or is she Lakṣmī, or perhaps Umā;
or could she be Kālarātri herself, or even Prakṛti, who is accustomed to bliss?
Tell me this, O Blessed One: who indeed is she born of nectar who wanders through the terrible single ocean where serpents and rākṣasas have perished?
Manu said:
Listen, my child, as I shall explain according to the truth the origin of this woman of excellent complexion, who was born from Rudra.
In ancient times, Śiva, the benefactor of all worlds, performed extensive austerities together with Umā, his form being tranquil, for the sake of the welfare of all beings.
Having ascended Mount Ṛkṣa, he performed most rigorous austerity;
invisible to all beings, he was the self of all beings and possessed of self-mastery.
As that god was performing penance, sweat indeed arose from him;
that sweat, born of Rudra, flooded the mountain.
From that, there arose the most meritorious and best of rivers,
which was seen by you in the ocean, O lady with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
O King, in that first Kṛta Yuga, she assumed the form of a woman and propitiated Rudra for ten thousand years.
Then Mahādeva Śaṅkara, together with Umā, was pleased and said:
"Speak, O highly fortunate one, whatever dwells in your mind."
The River said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, when the dissolution has arrived and all things moving and stationary have perished, may I become imperishable through your grace."
O Lord of Gods, O Master, by your grace may this merit remain inexhaustible in the world, even as rivers, oceans, and mountains themselves perish. (RKV 4.21)
O Śaṅkara, even those who are guilty of minor sins, secondary offenses, or even the great transgressions,
are liberated from all their sins by bathing with devotion.
If I am thus honored by the gods, may I become the destroyer of great sins in the northern region of Jāhnavī, and likewise on the southern path.
O Lord, O Sovereign of the Thirty-three, just as she is renowned on earth as the Gaṅgā after descending from heaven, so may I become known as the Dakṣiṇagaṅgā.
O Maheśvara, whatever fruit a mortal obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords on earth, that same fruit he obtains by bathing with devotion [here]. (RKV 4.25)
O Lord, whatever accumulated sin such as the killing of a Brahmin may exist anywhere,
let it go to destruction in just one month by means of immersion [in this water].
O Śaṅkara, may all the fruit that exists in all the Vedas and in all sacrifices be mine through this immersion; such is my thought. (RKV 4.27)
"O Śaṅkara, may the fruit of all acts of giving, all fasts, and bathing in all sacred fords arise for me through this water."
"Those men who worship Maheśvara on my banks shall go to your world; let this indeed be so, O Śiva."
"O Maheśāna, O Lord of the World, dwell forever upon my shore together with Umā and the gods; this alone is the boon I seek."
Whether he has performed good deeds or evil deeds, may the creature who dies in my waters— peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered his senses— go to Amarāvatī.
O Lord of the gods of gods, if you are pleased and so consider it, may I become renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of great sins.
O best of kings, having been thus petitioned for these and other divine boons,
the bull-vehicled Lord, being pleased, then spoke to Narmadā.
The illustrious Maheśa said:
"So be it, O auspicious one, regarding that which you have spoken, O blameless lady;
there is no other in the worlds worthy of a boon except for you, O lotus-eyed one."
O fair-faced one, at the very moment you were born from my body, you became the liberator from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
At the time when the eon is coming to an end, and especially during that terrible period, those men who dwell taking refuge on the northern shore— RKV_4.36.
O Goddess, even insects, moths, trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like— even they shall go to a happy destination until the falling away of their bodies.
Those twice-born ones who are devoted to dharma and dwell upon the southern bank until death shall go to the abode of the ancestors.
Indeed, at your word, for some other reason,
I shall dwell forever upon your shore together with Umā.
"Thus it is, O Goddess, Great Goddess; it is exactly so, there is no doubt.
[This shall be accomplished] by Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Varuṇa, and the Sādhyas, together with Viṣṇu."
O Goddess, O beautiful one among the gods, by my command they shall dwell on your northern bank,
while others shall dwell on the southern bank together with the ancestors.
"They shall dwell together with me; this is your supreme boon.
Go, go, O highly fortunate one, and liberate mortals from sin! (RKV 4.42)
Accompanied by hosts of ṛṣis, as well as by siddhas, gods, and asuras—
thus addressed by Umā, the omnipresent Mahādeva remained together with her.
Then, being honored by Manu and by me, he vanished from sight;
and because of that, this [river] is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins.
This which you have asked about has been explained; let there be no wonder in you.
This is Gaṅgā, of great merit, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Flooding the ten directions with ten and five streams,
the Śoṇa, the Mahānada, the Narmadā, and the Surasā were created.
The Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, and likewise the Citrakūṭā;
the Tamasā, the Vidiśā, as well as the Karabhā and the Yamunā.
The Citrotpalā, the Vipāśā, the Rañjanā, and the Vāluvāhinī—
these all originate from the foot of the Bear (Ṛkṣa) and are indeed born of Rudra.
"Removers of all sins, meritorious, givers of all auspiciousness, and auspicious"—
by these divine names is [the Goddess] praised by those who have mastered the Vedas.
O best of men, all this great majesty has been recounted by the illustrious knowers of the Purāṇas, as well as by those who drink the clarified butter and those who drink the Soma juice.
In former times, Manu declared to me this auspicious, meritorious, and incomparable origin of Amṛtā, which was sung forth by Rudra.
O Bhārata, those men who, having risen at dawn, shall recite with devotion these fifteen names, or even those who listen to them; RKV_4.52.
Those men shall obtain the full merit born of immersion;
they shall travel in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, resounding with the ringing of a hundred bells.
Having abandoned the human state, they shall go to the supreme destination.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifteen Names of Narmadā," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, all this that has been told is marvelous;
the hosts of sages, along with me, have fallen into a state of supreme wonder. (RKV 5.1)
Oh, how meritorious is this divine Narmadā, born not from a womb,
emerged from the body of Rudra, and the destroyer of great sins!
O you of noble vows, when the destruction of the seven kalpas had arrived, this highly fortunate woman did not die along with you; what greater merit than this could there be?
What are those eons that have been pointed out as the seven eons that bring about destruction?
For this goddess has not died, nor have you yourself, O bull among sages.
When the world, devoid of flocks of birds, had been turned into a single ocean,
what was the form of Mahādeva at the end of the eon?
How does he withdraw the universe, and how does he abide in the great ocean?
How does he emit the universe, and how does he sustain all creatures?
What would be the form of the goddess when the river has been turned into a single ocean?
For what reason is Narmadā so called, and how is Revatī remembered?
For what reason is it called Añjanā, and for what reason Surasā?
For what reason is it Mandākinī, and how does it become Śoṇa?
For what reason is it called Trikūṭā, and for what reason is it the bearer of sands (Aluvāhinī),
since millions upon millions of sacred fords have entered the great ocean?
How many millions of rivers wait upon the Narmadā,
as well as sages with their sacred threads and likewise deities?
O best of sages, for what purpose is this [Purāṇa] heard as being divided?
And why is it called "Vaiṣṇava" here by those who know the Purāṇas?
In which places and at which sacred fords (tīrtha) is this best of rivers to be worshipped? Tell me separately of those sacred fords where Hara is ever present.
What was the extent of that goddess who was created by Rudra,
and what kinds of rites were taught to you by Rudra?
O best of the twice-born, how is this land so crowded with barbarians?
Tell me this, O Brahmin Mārkaṇḍeya of great intelligence.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, all you sages, and you too, my dear Yudhiṣṭhira;
this Purāṇa concerning the Narmadā was narrated by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) in the past.
From Vāyu it was received by me, and from him by Maheśvara;
because it was impossible for human beings [to grasp it all], it was condensed in former times by the ṛṣis.
O dear one, first is that of the peacock, and immediately after that the tortoise;
likewise the city of the owl, the fish, and the elephant.
The Vārāha, which was seen by me, and the supreme eighth Vaiṣṇava,
as well as the one called Nyagrodha— after these, there was again the excellent Ākāṅkṣa.
Those who contemplate the Vedas declare in the Purāṇas that the Padma, the Tāmasa, and the Saṃvarta-udvarta are indeed the Great Dissolution (Mahāpralaya).
All this has been summarized in brief by those great-souled ones,
and it has been divided into four parts by the great seers beginning with Brahmā.
O you who are skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas, I shall now fully declare those seven most terrible kalpas by which this river was not destroyed.
The world of moving beings had become shrouded in darkness, unknowable and devoid of defining characteristics;
the rays of the sun and moon had perished, and it was abandoned by all living creatures.
Therefore, from that Tamas, the Puruṣa named Mahān, the eternal teacher of the world,
who is both manifest and unmanifest, moved about there alone.
That twice-born one, consisting of the syllable *auṃ*, transcended [the previous state] and created the Gāyatrī;
with her, the Lord, the Puruṣa Virāj, sported.
From his own body he created the universe known as the nature of the five elements;
playing, he brought forth the universe known as the nature of the five elements.
Playing, he who is known as Virāṭ created the golden egg with its seed;
that divine egg became like the twelve Ādityas in brilliance.
Having split that [egg], the four-faced Grandfather, the Puruṣa, was born;
he thus created the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans.
Including fish, cattle, and birds— born from sweat, from eggs, and from the womb—
this is proclaimed as the "egg" (aṇḍa) in the Purāṇas, mentioned first [among the five elements].
O best of kings, in a former kalpa, while Rudra was sporting with Umā, the supreme goddess, the ocean was turned into a playground for them.
From joy, an auspicious maiden was born from the sweat of Umā;
Umā was born from the friction of Śarva’s chest.
From his sweat, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was born a great maiden with lotus-like eyes;
she was the second manifestation from the body of Rudra.
Then she wandered through the worlds— including those of the gods, asuras, and humans—
her form then being peerless and capable of inciting madness in the three realms.
Having seen her, the lords of the gods and daityas were bewildered, wondering how she could have been obtained;
O Bhārata, they searched for that maiden here and there.
She deludes the entire world with her gestures, emotions, and amorous charms;
possessing a divine form, she wanders like a flash of lightning.
Standing in the midst of the clouds with her splendors, she was the most excellent of all women;
then all the gods, along with the Daityas and Dānavas, [beheld] Rudra.
Greatly agitated by desire, they sought to choose that maiden;
then Mahādeva spoke to both the gods and the dānavas.
"O best of gods, he who shall be superior in both strength and splendor will obtain this maiden; it cannot be otherwise."
Then all the gods and asuras approached the maiden, saying, "I shall take her! I shall take her! (RKV 5.38).
While everyone was looking on, that maiden vanished;
then they all saw her again, stationed at a distance of one yojana.
They all went in haste to where she was seen,
[reaching her] at three, four, and even ten yojanas away.
They all beheld her standing there, moving with the gait of an elephant,
stationed at a distance of many hundreds and thousands of yojanas.
Likewise, because of its lightness, it appeared as if by the hundreds of thousands—
both in front and behind, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
They behold that woman of excellent limbs both as one and again as many;
indeed, they were previously led astray by her for a thousand divine years.
But that maiden born from the body of Mahādeva was not obtained;
therefore, the god, together with Umā, laughed aloud again and again.
The hosts, filled with joy, were dancing to the rhythmic clapping of their hands;
suddenly, a maiden was seen standing near Śaṅkara.
Seeing her, the gods, filled with wonder, turned their faces away;
then the wielder of the Pināka himself gave her a name.
"And because I grant you this jest, O lady of beautiful hips, through the various actions performed by them, you shall become the most excellent of rivers, Narmadā."
Since the Lord, established in his own essential nature, became an object of laughter on earth,
he therefore spoke this auspicious Narmadā, whose waters are very cool.
O King of kings, because she did not die even when the destruction of the seven kalpas occurred— as was previously declared by Śambhu— Narmadā attained her renown.
Then the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign and Master of all beings, gave that virtuous and most beautiful maiden to the Great Ocean.
Then the goddess Narmadā, laughing loudly like a mass of foam, entered the ocean, the lord of rivers, from the king of mountains, Ṛkṣaśaila.
Thus, in the ancient Brāhma Kalpa, she was produced from the Lord;
in the Mātsya Kalpa she was seen by me and fully described by me—listen!
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of kings, when the third age-end had arrived once again, the Ṛgveda-khaṇḍa, chapter 6.
Having assumed a body consisting of twelve suns, the Blessed One Nīlalohita—
Having become Time (Kāla), Maheśvara consumes the entire earth— bounded by the seven continents and oceans, together with its mountains, forests, and groves— reducing it to ashes.
Then, becoming a massive cloud, he drenched Kṛṣṇa— who was dark-bodied and marked by lightning and the rainbow— with water.
Having flooded the entire world and reduced it to a single ocean,
he withdrew the universe through his power of illusion (*māyā*) and slept upon the pure waters.
Then, while wandering in that great ocean which had become darkness,
I remained for a thousand divine years while Maheśvara existed as mere wind.
O Indra among kings, having first honored the Lord of the gods by whom this world was made profound,
one should then meditate upon that deity while in pure water.
When that terrible great ocean had submerged all things moving and stationary,
I suddenly beheld in the water a peacock, rich with golden feathers,
endowed with variegated eye-spots, blue-throated, and beautiful-eyed.
Then that peacock, having agitated the edge of the great ocean with his mighty cry,
the three-crested, crested god of great majesty, the protector of the three worlds, moved about.
And Śiva, in his fierce form as a peacock, even while that water was being agitated,
beheld from afar the great river’s mighty torrent whirling together with him at the edge of the vast ocean.
Seeing her wandering amidst a multitude of waves, he, in the form of Mahādeva’s peacock, said:
"Who are you, O auspicious one, who have become an eternal body and do not go to destruction even at the end of the great dissolution?"
When the hosts of gods and asuras have perished, and the rivers, lakes, and great oceans [have vanished], who are you that wander here, O lotus-eyed one? And where have you not gone to destruction?
Narmadā said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace death does not exist for me.
O God, create the universe once again; the night has come to its end."
Thus addressed, Mahādeva shook his cage of wings;
at that moment, from within the middle of that cage, [beings] emerged from his feathers.
As many lords of the gods and daityas as there were were born from his two wings;
and in their midst, that river Narmadā flows again.
And beyond that, O bull of the Bharatas, another great mountain is seen, which,
with its three vast peaks, resembles a horned bull.
It was known as Trikūṭa, adorned with all kinds of jewels;
from that Trikūṭa, she flowed forth, flooding the earth.
Therefore, it is renowned as Trikūṭī, the supreme protector of the ancestors;
and from that second [peak], the Gaṅgā flows out, spreading across the surface of the earth.
And then the third peak split into seven fragments;
these became the seven principal mountain ranges born within Jambūdvīpa.
Together with the moon and the stars, the hosts of planets, the rivers, and the streams—
[all these constitute] that which is born from eggs, born from sweat, born from sprouts, and born from a womb.
In this way, O tiger among men, this entire world in its totality originated from the peacock in ancient times, having arisen from Mahādeva.
Then, having divided the rivers and oceans individually, the Lord of Gods said to the Narmadā: "Go you toward the southern direction."
Thus, that Gaṅgā is the destroyer of great sins;
you are the meritorious Jāhnavī in the northern region and the auspicious one in the south.
Just as the Gaṅgā, which possesses great merit, was born from my head, so too are you, O illustrious lady, even more distinguished than she; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of virtuous vows, I shall exist with you through one portion;
you shall become the medicine for those afflicted by great sins.
Thus addressed by the god, she who destroys great sins quickly departed with her strides toward the southern quarter.
Having reached the king of mountains, Ṛkṣa, by the grace of the Moon-crested Lord,
she set forth with floods of water, impelled by Mahādeva.
And because she was raised up with great force,
O lord of the earth, she is therefore called Mahatī (the Great One) after Mahādeva.
As that god was performing austerity, drops fell from the tip of his trident;
by means of them, this [river] received the name Śoṇa, and those [streams] are remembered as being seventeen in number.
The Narmadā is meritorious for all; she has issued from the body of Rudra, and by virtue of the boon granted by the Great-Souled One, she is superior to all other rivers.
Through the grace of Śaṅkara, the goddess, who destroys great sins,
appeared as a vast form within the terrible great ocean.
Because her limbs were so clearly defined, her body was massive, and she was great, she was known as Mahatī;
therefore, even when agitated by the elephants of the quarters who resemble clouds, [she remains unmoved].
In that way, Surasā leads [the world] to turbidity by means of her flavor;
yet she exercises compassion because she bestows fearlessness upon the worlds.
Because of this, compassion is remembered for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
formerly, in the meritorious Kṛta age, she was adorned with divine mandāra flowers.
Abounding with wish-fulfilling trees and crowded with *rohītaka* trees, this river flows slowly; therefore, it is known as the Mandākinī.
Because she swiftly came to this world after piercing the great ocean,
and because she is to be honored by both gods and perfected beings (siddhas), she is therefore called Mahārṇavā.
It was filled with clusters of various lotuses and crowded with bears and elephants.
Having split the vast mountain, she thus proceeds to the great ocean,
whirling all the directions with her mighty roar as of old.
Flooded and shining because of that, she is known as the Revā;
she [delivers] men who are burdened by the great suffering of wives and sons and enveloped by curses.
Because she purifies one from sin, she is remembered as Vipāpā;
she is a terrible place consisting of a mass of feces and urine, with mud made of dust and blood. (RKV 6.39)
Because she constantly and thoroughly releases one from being bound by fetters,
she is called Vipāśā, the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Narmadā possesses pure waters and a face as beautiful as the stainless moon;
for she is of great splendor in this most terrible darkness.
Therefore, O best of kings, that [night] is called *vimalā* (the stainless) by the wise;
it possesses rays resembling those of the moon and a radiance equal to the sunbeams.
It flows and gladdens the entire universe; therefore it is called *karabhā*. Because, O Bhārata, it delights the worlds by its mere sight. (RKV 6.43)
O best of kings, because it causes delight (*rañjana*), it is called *rañjanā* according to the meaning of the verbal root.
Since it leads even grasses, creepers, shrubs, animals, and birds—
which have arisen from that [earth]— to heaven, it is therefore called the "wind-bearer" (*vāyuvāhinī*).
Thus, he who knows these names and their origin in particular, being liberated from sin, goes to the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Mayūra-kalpa," in the description of the majesty of the Narmadā known as Sahetuka-revā, within the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa), in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 7. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Again, when the terrible single ocean had arisen and all moving and non-moving beings had perished;
When the world was submerged by water and enveloped in darkness born of gloom, devoid of light.
Brahmā alone wandered there in that great ocean which had become as darkness,
for a thousand divine years, possessing a form like that of a firefly.
He lies there, immeasurable and unsurpassed, extending for a thousand yojanas;
he resembles twelve suns and possesses a thousand feet and eyes.
He saw him sleeping in the terrible ocean in the form of a tortoise;
seeing him, Brahmā was filled with wonder and gently awakened him.
With hymns of praise and auspicious rites arising from the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences:
"O Lord of Speech, awaken! O Great Being, homage be unto you! (RKV 7.5)
O Supreme Lord, the entire world remains within your belly;
O Great Being, release that which was previously withdrawn by you.
The night of Brahmā has passed and the day now proceeds,
by which the world comes into being, O Lord of all worlds, as you gaze upon it.
Having heard those words of his, the Supreme Lord arose,
emitting the three worlds that had been swallowed up at the end of the kalpa.
The gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, along with yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as all the moons, suns, and planets, emerged from his body.
Then the Supreme Lord, having divided that entire single ocean—
which was filled with vast floods of stones and water and augmented by rivers and lakes— [established the world].
The god beheld the earth with its trees, medicinal herbs, and ponds;
the Himavat, the best of mountains, and the supreme white mountain.
The great mountain Śṛṅgavat, as well as the other principal mountain ranges,
Jambudvīpa, Kuśa, Krauñca, Gomeda, and Śālmala.
The islands ending with Puṣkara, the seven great oceans,
and the great mountain Lokāloka— all stood before him.
Maheśvara beheld the world of mobile and immobile beings, composed of the four primal elements, emerging at the end of the eon.
The Lord beheld the goddess Earth, strewn with a network of rocks,
resting upon the back of a tortoise and situated within the great ocean.
On that shattered mountain peak, devoid of rivers and lakes,
the water was broken by various waves and crowded with eddies and surging whirlpools.
It was illuminated by various medicinal herbs, possessed stone surfaces with diverse blue lotuses,
resounded with the calls of various flocks of birds, and was teeming with fish and turtles.
The Lord of Gods beheld the goddess, composed of divine illusion, resembling an excellent cloud, a river with a reservoir of incomparable waters.
In its center was she who was dark as a rain cloud, with full thighs, hips, and breasts,
adorned with incomparable divine garments and various ornaments.
The goddess Narmadā herself, assuming a female form, was like that— exuberant with the sound of her anklets and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
He beheld the highly fortunate Narmadā, her limbs unmanifest, adorned with various ornaments consisting of the power of her own yoga-māyā.
Then the young woman, her eyes as broad as lotus petals, rose from the water with one arm half-raised, praising the Lord of the gods.
With my heart filled with wonder upon beholding that auspicious woman,
I bathed in her pure water and then prepared to offer praise.
Greatly delighted, he worshipped with mantras originating from the Vedāṅgas;
and, O King, he beheld that which was created in the past, this world with its moving and unmoving beings.
"I see this illustrious lady, together with the gods, asuras, gandharvas, pannagas, and mahoragas; she has certainly not gone to destruction in the past."
And by the grace of Mahādeva, she, who was born from his body, has been seen by me again and again; thus she has been described to you, O best of kings.
Those best of the twice-born who study this manifestation of the Tortoise,
and those wise ones who listen to it, are likewise liberated from their sins.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Origin of the Kūrma Kalpa," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the world had perished and was again enveloped by water,
he stood in the midst of the great ocean and crossed the waters with his two arms.
O best of kings, when a hundred divine years had passed, I became weary and began to meditate upon the God who enables one to cross the great ocean of existence.
Then, meditating at that time, I beheld a supreme bird—
a crane as white as cow’s milk, resembling a pearl necklace, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Then, filled with wonder upon beholding that crane, I thought:
"How can there be the birth of a bird in this terrible great ocean?"
Crossing tirelessly with my arms, I addressed that crane:
"Who are you, assuming the form of a bird, in this world made into a single ocean?"
O Lord, you who are the self of divine yoga, you wander about as if deluding me;
tell me all this—whatever you are, you are indeed that. Salutations be to you!
Mahādeva said to me: "I am Brahmā and I am Viṣṇu as well;
the entire world has been withdrawn by me, my child—do you not understand?"
O great sage, I am indeed your mother and father, as well as [the father] of the universe;
compassion has arisen within me upon seeing you submerged in the great ocean.
"Having assumed the form of a bird, I have therefore come here; for what reason have you become so distressed and are wandering thus in the great ocean?"
"Enter quickly into my wings, O twice-born one, so that you may rest," said that god to me, O lord of men. Thus addressed by him, I then— RKV_8.10.
Then, at the end of his wings, I dissolved into the water,
wandering tirelessly in the midst of the ocean for a period of a thousand yugas.
Then, O observer of noble vows, I suddenly heard in all directions a certain wonderful and supreme sound mingled with the tinkling of anklets.
Then all that water of the ocean suddenly became contracted;
reflecting, "What is this?", he gazed intently at the quarters of the sky.
Then ten maidens arrived from the directions in the great ocean,
adorned with garments and ornaments, coming from the quarters of the sky and decorated with anklets.
Some have a radiance like the moon, some possess a splendor like the sun;
some have the appearance of a heap of collyrium, and some have the luster of a red lotus.
Assuming various forms, gentle, and adorned with diverse ornaments,
those of virtuous vows worshipped Baka with offerings of water for the feet and guest-reception, as well as garlands.
Then the self-ruling Parvata entered that mountain-like, secret, and imperishable bird, which was most terrible, as a mountain enters the ocean.
There are as many thousands and hundreds of yojanas as there are [in the previous count],
up to thirty thousand yojanas for the extent of the earth-mandala.
Then there was a divine ground, strewn with five kinds of jewels,
featuring celestial crystal staircases and beautiful pillars of gold.
It is one thousand yojanas in width and twice that in length;
it is filled with ponds and wells, and surrounded by palaces and watchtowers.
It was filled with wish-fulfilling trees, adorned with sixty banners,
and beautified by various jewels in that delightful, preeminent city.
Likewise, there was another beautiful city with altars radiant with banners,
extending for a hundred yojanas and twice that length in width.
Then, in the middle of that city, there was a most beautiful river,
great with meritorious waters and likewise possessing rocks of various jewels.
On its bank, I beheld [a palace] with a splendor equal to lightning and the sun,
covered on all sides with jewels such as sapphires and great blue gems.
In some places it has a form like fire; in some places it has the luster of a rainbow;
in some places it is smoky, in some yellow, in some red, and in some white.
The Liṅga, endowed with various colors and wonderful to behold,
was surrounded on all sides by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the Sādhyas.
I behold that very same great Liṅga, the Lord Īśāna, surrounded by the leaders of the Gaṇas such as Nandīśvara, as well as by Indra and the Ādityas.
Then, having surrounded them, I saw those gods and dānavas fast asleep with their eyes closed, adorned with divine ornaments.
Then those women, highly esteemed and with eyes like lotus petals,
having bathed in the water of that river, [worshipped] with delightful, divine flowers.
Having duly offered the water for the feet and the guest-offering to the Liṅga together with the bird,
those ten beautiful and excellent women performed the worship.
Then, having worshipped that linga in that very same supreme city,
they all vanished from sight like flashes of lightning among the masses of clouds.
And that king of birds saw neither women nor deities there;
filled with wonder, he remained there alone, worshipping that very linga.
Then, my soul bewildered by suffering, I thought, "This is Rudra";
thereafter, maidens emerged, adorned with divine garments and ornaments.
Illuminating the entire world like flashes of lightning amidst masses of clouds,
those fair-faced women worshipped him with divine, golden lotuses.
Those adorned with excellent ornaments quickly entered that water from all sides;
and others in that best of cities likewise entered it again and again.
For I beheld an immortal maiden worshipping Maheśvara;
then I questioned that lotus-eyed woman of beautiful limbs.
"Who are you, O Goddess, that dwell in this city worshipping Śiva?
Where have all those women come from, and where have those lords of the Gaṇas gone?"
Homage be to you, O highly fortunate one! Speak, O meritorious Maheśvarī!
By your grace, O lady of excellent vows, I desire to understand this.
Having shown compassion, O Great Goddess, tell me, O sinless one.
Śrī said: "O Brahmin, how could I have been forgotten by you upon seeing me in the ancient kalpa?
Let there be no lapse in your memory; for I am that very river who flows through the kalpas."
The one renowned as Narmadā has issued forth from the body of Rudra;
she is those very maidens whom you saw worshipping Maheśvara.
O best of sages, know that all those quarters of space, presided over by all the lords, were brought here together with the king of birds.
In the form of a bird among the animals, the great yogin Maheśvara brought that Maheśvara here from the city of Śiva, O Brahmin.
This very god, Mahādeva, the teacher of the world of gods and asuras, stands established in the form of the Liṅga and is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
Since the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, goes to dissolution therein,
it is for this reason called *liṅga* by the great sages who know the Purāṇas.
By him, O Lord of the World, all the hosts of gods were formerly condensed through his illusory power; they have indeed dissolved and are no longer seen at present.
They shall become visible again, being created by the Self-born One;
and I, devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, shall be known by the name Narmadā.
For a thousand yugas you have been the attendant of Rudra;
by his grace, O bull among the twice-born, you have likewise become an immortal.
"Endowed with truth, uprightness, and compassion, you have attained perfection through the worship of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished right there.
Having heard those words of hers, those women and Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods in the form of a crane, descended into the great river.
"Having bathed, you must indeed worship according to the prescribed rite preceded by mantras";
then, I suddenly emerged from that body of water.
O King, I saw neither that sign nor that river;
at that very moment, the worlds and the earth with its forests came into being.
That very expanse of the sky, spread with stars, moon, and sun,
was made just as it was before, though previously unseen; then,
bowing with my mind, I worshipped the god Maheśvara.
Thus, in a former kalpa, I beheld this imperishable Narmadā, which destroys the great sins of the world of mortals.
Therefore, Brahmins devoted to dharma, as well as Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, Vaiśyas,
and others who seek to increase their own righteousness, should always serve these highly fortunate ones.
Those who, out of devotion, bathe even once in the waters of the Narmadā and worship Maheśvara,
undoubtedly destroy all their sin.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Bakakalpa," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Furthermore, I shall describe to you another end of the age; listen to that.
In ancient times, when the world of moving and unmoving beings was set ablaze by suns, RKV 9.1.

When rivers, lakes, and oceans had entirely gone to destruction, and when the world had become devoid of humans and the sound of the *vaṣaṭ* call, having reached a state beyond all bounds; ||| RKV_9.2 |||
Then the entire sky was filled with clouds of various forms, resplendent with rainbows; and when it was thus filled, torrents of water poured down.
Then, when everything had become a single ocean and was enveloped on all sides by water,
the blessed Lord Hara, having placed the entire world within his belly, fell asleep.
Having established himself in his own nature, that Prajāpati, whose self is yoga,
lies for the duration of a thousand yugas, entering the time when the ocean remains.
There, all the great-souled sages beginning with Bhṛgu who dwell in the world of Brahmā, as well as others such as Sanaka and his brothers, [beheld] him asleep.
They beheld the god whose banner is the bull, lying upon a pure, bright couch strewn with various coverlets, together with his consort.
That woman was indeed Viśvarūpā, and Maheśvara was Viśvarūpa;
having embraced her firmly, he fell asleep, and I beheld that imperishable one.
Then, at his feet, I saw that dark-complexioned girl with the marks of a lotus, possessed of beautiful hips, as she was massaging his feet.
Clad in a stainless garment, wearing a serpent as her sacred thread,
she was dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, and adorned with every ornament.
Knowing that this entire thousand-fold cycle of ages was but a slumber for the Lord of the Gods, this woman of excellent complexion, the Narmadā, waits upon him.
Having received the four Vedas, Brahmā likewise, along with Maheśvara and the mind-born sons beginning with Bhṛgu, praises the imperishable Śaṅkara.
O King, with supreme devotion, they praised the stainless Śambhu,
the Lord of Gods, there with mantras originating from Īśvara.
Approaching to awaken the sleeping Lord Īśāna, he said:
"Arise, O Hara, O tawny-eyed one, O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara! (RKV 9.14)
All my Vedas have been stolen; therefore, I am prepared to offer praise.
The entire universe—divine and non-divine, moving and unmoving—is pervaded by the Vedas.
I remember and I create both the past and the present;
yet without them, I am alone, like one who is mute, blind, and eternally inert.
Movement, vigor, strength, and enthusiasm—without these, nothing arises;
O Lord of the gods, without them I truly remember nothing at all.
O Lord of the gods of gods, you ought to grant those Vedas to me quickly;
for this entire world, both moving and stationary, is dull, blind, and deaf.
O Lord of the Gods, these ten and four [qualities], beginning with steadfastness, do not shine in me;
O Lord of the Gods, I bow down because of my lack of vigor and my being devoid of Vedic knowledge.
O Teacher of the World, all the scriptures shine only so long as everything that exists, moving and unmoving, has arisen from the Vedas.
As long as this eternal treasure of knowledge does not stand forth,
darkness will not go to its destruction by means of the sun as it has been described.
In this way, all sins pass away through the retention of the Veda;
for that which is subtle and secret in the Veda is the eternal Brahman.
"O Lord Śaṅkara, I know that [the Veda] which was within my heart has departed because of the roar of the Vedas as you recite them today before me."
"O Lord, since those Vedas have suddenly departed, I shall not create the world;
they too, O Mahādeva, have all entered the frontal ocean."
O Lord of Gods, being thus entreated, they said: "Let them remain within my memory; this daughter of mine has large eyes, and everyone knows everything. (RKV 9.25)
"A thousand ages pass, yet no other such [woman] shall exist;
and this illustrious sage Mārkaṇḍeya is the foremost among the wise. (RKV 9.26)
O Mahādeva, in age after age he attends upon you;
for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, he practices the supreme vow.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the supreme lord,
the Lord of Gods spoke in gentle words to Narmadā, the best of rivers.
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, as I ask you: by whom were all the Vedas stolen from Brahmā, the creator and teacher of the world?
Thus addressed by Rudra, the deer-eyed woman said:
"O Maheśvara, while you were asleep, Brahmā was reciting the Vedas."
Having found a vulnerability in you within this terrible ocean-enveloped world,
two asuras born in a previous kalpa, who are invincible even to the gods, [will arise].
O Mahādeva, in former times, the two Dānavas Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were difficult even for gods and asuras to conquer, were produced by you through Śrī.
Having become subtle and transformed into wind as they recited from their grandfather,
those two quickly carried off the Vedas and entered the great ocean.
Having heard these words of Amṛtā, the one of great splendor then remembered the Lord of Gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
O great king, that god, the destroyer of the Dānavas and the one worshipped by all the deities, entered the earth together with the foremost of the gods.
The Lord, assuming the form of a fish, churned the ocean;
and there, in Pātāla, the Master beheld the Vedas that had been deposited.
And Madhusūdana beheld those two Daityas of great heroism,
possessing immense speed and mighty arms, and he destroyed them with his splendor.
There, the Teacher of the World, adorned with the discus, brought the Vedas from that place of water and bestowed them upon the four-faced god.
Then, having recovered the Vedas, the blessed Grandfather was filled with joy and once again brought forth the entire universe, both moving and unmoving.
And that divine river, auspicious and an attendant of Rudra,
purifying all beings, then flowed with its waters.
Then, on its bank, the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity worship the three-eyed god with a joyful inner soul.
One form of Maheśa, having entered into other causes,
performs action through the three qualities (guṇas) in the forms of Brahmā, Cakrin, and Īśa.
But for those who, being utterly deluded, create a distinction between these [three],
how can there be success in the Dharma for such evildoers?
In this way, these three great rivers originating from Rudra—
the Gaṅgā, the Revā, and the Sarasvatī— are in truth one single river that has become threefold.
The Gaṅgā is indeed the form of Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all sins;
and the Narmadā likewise originated from the body of Rudra.
The goddess Sarasvatī, the embodiment of Brāhmī, is renowned throughout the three worlds; she is divine, able to go wherever she desires, and is established for the sake of the power of speech.
The Narmadā is a certain supreme, auspicious goddess, a portion of the form of mortals;
she is divine, able to go wherever she desires, and is worshipped by the gods everywhere.
Pervading all beings, she is remembered as subtler than the subtlest;
for she is indeed imperishable and immortal, the supreme staircase to heaven.
Created by Rudra for the sake of the worlds, she is the one who carries beings across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Even those in the world who drink the water of the Śīrī river are liberated from the multitude of various evils;
having abandoned the beginningless state of saṃsāra, they go for long to the pure state of liberation.
As is the Gaṅgā, so is the Revā, and likewise the Sarasvatī;
the fruit of merit is declared to be equal through bathing, beholding, and meditating upon them.
O highly fortunate one, because of her granting of boons, she is indeed said by the wise to be superior;
due to the internal state of compassion, she has arrived here without having died.
O best of kings, those who bow to the Three-eyed One at the Narmadā are liberated from sins merely by the sight of him through those auspicious baths. (RKV 9.53)
Since this great river was born from the bodies of Umā and Rudra,
and since she leads people to heaven, she has attained the state of being meritorious.
Whoever here hears this division of the body of the supreme Lord Īśāna by the Goddess,
he goes to Rudra with a great roar, as if being sung of by Gandharvas and Yakṣas.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the Narmadā and the Fruits of Bathing Therein," in the Narmadā-Māhātmya of the Revā-Khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-Khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the tenth chapter of the *Rukmiṇīkalya*,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, in which kalpa did this highly blessed Narmadā [arise]?"
It has been divided by all the great-souled seers who were devoted to asceticism.
O best among speakers, tell me all of this in detail:
that which will become a misery for the worlds at the end of the eon, and its true nature as well.
"O sinless one, tell us how this world existed in past kalpas,
and describe the arrangement of this final kalpa, O Lord.
Thus addressed in the midst of the assembly, Mārkaṇḍeya spoke these words:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall speak; let it be heard by all, for this story was heard in former times.
This is indeed a great and distinguished narrative concerning what followed after this kalpa;
there was a most terrible and dreadful time that brought about the destruction of the world.
Even in that most terrible state, listen to this story of how she, having died, was divided among those who were well-pleased.
When the end of the age had arrived, during the three days of the Grandfather’s life,
the mind-born sons of Brahmā were present, most excellent ones who were like Brahmā himself.
The high-souled ones beginning with Sanaka, the hosts of celestial beings,
and the world-protectors such as Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa, [are present] during the three days.
Intent upon the affairs of the world, they remain awaiting the proper time;
then, when the end of the kalpa arrives, their unsurpassed knowledge [manifests].
The lifespan of all beings perished in accordance with the nature of the age;
then, abandoning the Bhūrloka, they went to the Bhuvarloka.
Then [he saw] Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapoloka, as well as Satyaloka, the refuge and the unsurpassed of all worlds.
Accompanied by their sons and grandsons, they remain in Satyaloka for a period lasting a thousand yugas, as long as the world continues to be born.
And whatever sons of Brahmā there may be who do not exist at the beginning of the kalpa,
they abandon the three worlds and become supportless.
Together with them were those brahmins, as well as other ascetics rich in austerity,
and yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and other hosts of celestial beings dwelling in aerial chariots.
The highly fortunate rishis, the various other castes,
and those others who dwell upon the earth— all together, they are perishing.
There occurred a great drought lasting for a hundred years,
fierce and destructive to the world, which brought about the ruin of trees and creepers.
Causing the agitation of the three worlds and drying up the seven oceans,
the people thereafter, overcome by hunger, wandered as if through the ten directions.
Extremely distressed, they subsist on bulbs, roots, or even fruits;
they frequent rivers, oceans, wells, and places of purification.
There too, all the oceans along with their rivers dry up;
thereafter, those beings on the surface of the earth that possess little strength [perish].
Those very [rivers] first dissolve away, split apart by the vast waters;
then, as the rivers themselves waste away along with the oceans, [the earth dissolves].
There were sixty thousand sages residing in Kurukṣetra,
as well as Vaikhānasa brahmins and those who used their teeth as mortars.
All those ascetics rich in austerity who dwell in the secret caves of the Himalayas,
afflicted by hunger and thirst, have all approached me.
With palms joined in reverence, they all said: "O great sage, we are perishing;
O twice-born one, the world, including its rivers, oceans, and mountains, is being dried up."
"Where shall we go together until the turn of time?
You are long-lived, O chief of brahmins; you have not died at the end of the eon."
The past, the present, and the future—all this resides within your heart;
therefore, O observer of great vows, you know everything, so please speak.
"O illustrious one, O observer of noble vows, for how long shall we endure this time when everything, including the moving and the unmoving, is perishing, struck by drought? (RKV 10.26)

"Save us, O illustrious one, so that we do not go to our destruction! Then, having reflected in my mind, I spoke hurriedly to the brahmins: RKV 10.27: "Save us, O illustrious one, so that we do not go to our destruction! Then, having reflected in my mind, I spoke hurriedly to the brahmins.
"Abandon Kurukṣetra, you who are accompanied by your sons and wives;
leaving behind the northern direction, let us all go to the unsurpassed southern region."
"Let us go to the banks of the Narmadā, rich with cities, villages, and cowherd settlements, adorned with towns and ports, and frequented by many perfected beings (siddhas)."
We behold that highly fortunate one, the limb of Rudra, who is of great merit and the destroyer of all sins, surrounded by the settlement of Nyagrodha.
Well-served by the Māheśvaras, Bhāgavatas, Sāṃkhyas, and Siddhas,
[the river] was feared on both its banks by those terrified of the danger of drought.
"Having conquered our vows, let us indeed construct divine hermitages within this hermitage.
Thus addressed, they all gathered together with their followers.
Having reached the bank of the Narmadā, they all stood there free from fear from any quarter,
reflecting for a moment on the terrors of former kalpas.
They reached the bank of the Narmadā at the very beginning of the Kali Yuga;
thereafter, they dwelt on the shore of the Revā for a full hundred divine years.
And twenty-six thousand human years passed there,
O King, during which I witnessed a marvel among the sages dwelling in that place.

When the world was struck by drought, when the stationary and moving beings were completely withered, when the calculation of the Yugas and other cycles had broken down, and when all became senseless in a state of "Alas, alas!"— RKV 10.36.

When the four castes have dissolved, when the sequence of fire-offerings and ritual oblations has perished, when there is neither the *svāhā* nor the *vaṣaṭ* call, and when people are devoid of purity and proper conduct; (RKV 10.37)
This is the one supreme river, frequented by ten million sages;
O Lord of Men, there is nothing else anywhere in the three worlds as beautiful as it.
Just as Amarāvatī belongs to Indra, so this city, with its waters of merit,
is filled with bright temples of the gods and well-constructed hermitages.
The goddess Narmadā shines like the Mandākinī in heaven,
as long as there are trees and great mountains, and as long as she originates from the ocean.
Both its banks were adorned with beautiful, sacred shrines,
and it was filled with the smoke of sacrificial offerings from the Agnihotra fires being kindled.
The goddess Narmadā became like a night during the rainy season,
beautified by numerous temples of the gods adorned with offerings and consecrations.
The excellent city of Śakra shines with rivers and the splendor of the sun;
some there perform the austerity of the five fires, while others maintain the sacred fire-sacrifice.
Some, established in fierce austerity, consume smoke;
some are devoted to the sacrifice of the self, while others partake in devotion.
Having attained Vaiṣṇava knowledge, some likewise observe the Śaiva vow;
some fast for one night or two nights, while others eat only on the sixth day.
And by means of the regulations for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, as well as the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra observances—
through such ascetic practices performed on the banks of the Narmadā, which adorn its shores.
Those who worship the god Śaṅkara, Keśava, or Maheśvara— whether in unity or in distinction— shine eternally.
In this most terrible Kali age, those who have attained the unsurpassed perfection—whatever their devotion may be, and whatever their realization may be—[attain it]. (RKV 10.48)
Whichever deity the Lord, the Master, bestowed upon him,
he attains that very deity through devotion rooted in the unity of his own nature and dissolves within it at the end.
Those men who, being seekers of separate things, wander in saṃsāra,
have abandoned the great tree, the Lord, and are clinging to the branches.
Returning again, they are born within the four ages; wandering through the cycle of existence in due order, from the end of the gods to the end of the stationary beings.
For those who are firmly established in devotion to the Lord, the divine Īśāna Bhava, there is rebirth again in heaven and again in the terrible Raurava hell.
Those who sacrifice on the banks of the Narmadā are not born again;
some, worshipping there until the fall of their bodies, have gone to the Supreme.
Some ascetics [attained it] in twelve years, others in six;
some in three years, and some in a single year.
Some sages attained perfection in six months, while others did so in three, by taking refuge in the god and the illustrious Narmadā.
Having severed the defects of saṃsāra, they went to the eternal Brahman;
thus, in this terrible Kali age, by the hundreds and thousands.
Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, the sages entered into Rudra.
Those brahmins who, having approached the banks of the Narmadā, have applied themselves with effort to the Śaiva vow,
enter the water thrice daily and, worshipping the god Śiva with devotion, go to him.
Those who constantly remember Nārāyaṇa through meditations, worship, recitations, and great vows,
cross to the further shore of the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra like royal swans with their wings of washed white cloth.
Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare:
this one thing is perfectly established, that Nārāyaṇa is always to be meditated upon.
O King, he who, having conquered his self, worships Hara and dwells for a month or a fortnight by the Revā river—
that man of great majesty shall become the Pināka-bearing God of gods himself.
Even insects, moths, and ants that die in the waters of the Narmadā are born into noble families with divine forms, and for a hundred years they remain devoted to the Dharma.
In time, even those trees whose roots are severed by the flood of great waves fall;
yet, their sins washed away by the waters of the Narmadā, they go to the third heaven, shining with brilliance.
Those who are free from desire as well as those with desire, having resorted to the banks of the Revā, die upon its shore;
even the dull-witted, the blind, and the mute go to the third heaven—O Brahmins, what then need be said of those endowed with the realization of existence?
Even those whose limbs are withered by month-long fasts and who have cast off their bodies do not attain that goal;
yet those whose bodies are purified by the waters of the Revā, who are intent on the worship of Śiva, and who are endowed with devotion to Keśava, die [attaining it].
With wild rice, śyāmāka, barley, iṅguda, and other such foods, the lords of sages sustain themselves here;
