having reached the bank of the Narmadā, which is sung of by the gods, they do not enter death.
Those who wander along the banks of the Goddess, purified by truth and by the worship of the deities at the three times of day,
shall never again dwell within the womb of a young woman, using excrement, urine, skin, and bone as their pillows.
What is the use of their many sacrifices, gifts, and visits to all the most excellent sacred fords?
They follow the sequence of Rudra’s movements, serving the southern or northern bank of the Revā.

Deceived, those mortals in the worlds who have not taken refuge in the Revā—who has become the very body of Rudra and is a flight of stairs to the third heaven—are as if lame, dull-witted, and blind, equal to mere beasts. (RKV 10.69)

O best of the twice-born, that man who should wish never again to behold this terrible Kali age must approach the banks of the Narmadā and, being entirely liberated from attachment, worship everything there.
Those who, though assailed by many obstacles, do not abandon the banks of the Narmadā—
they alone are the benefactors of all and are worthy of being saluted and honored by all people.

Bhṛgu, Atri, Gārgya, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaṅka, together with hundreds and indeed countless others who were self-restrained, attained supreme perfection after their limbs were drenched in water; they reached the worlds of the Maruts, and no others did.
Those of eternally pure being recite this great knowledge, which is most meritorious and purifying;
these beings of great majesty go to the supreme goal, for the word of Rudra is indeed authoritative.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hearing of the Fruits of Bathing in the Narmadā," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāvalī, Chapter 11.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Oh, how most meritorious and distinguished is this [place], which has not gone to destruction here even at the end of the age!"
Therefore, it should always be served by the lords of sages who are devoted to meditation, worship, and ritual bathing.
Those rules for the sages, fashioned by the Vedas, which were proclaimed by you— relying upon which, the sages who are devoted to dharma have attained liberation.
For those who attain liberation through various kinds of observances—whether by ten, twelve, six, or even eight [rebirths]—[their goal is reached]. (RKV 11.3)
By worshipping the lords of the gods in this manner for three or four years, or likewise for months, people are liberated from the defects of the Kali age.
Whether one worships Brahmā, the best of gods, or Keśava, the teacher of the world, one certainly abandons all evil; of this there is no doubt.
O sinless one, tell me all this in detail:
how did those beings who were submerged in the deep thicket of saṃsāra attain the third heaven? Speak, for this is my doubt.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: After many successive births, one attains human status;
and herein, devotion toward Śaṅkara arises only by some rare chance.

O King, the attainment of the fruits of visiting sacred fords, giving gifts, and observing fasts, as well as through sacrifices and the worship of gods and brahmins, arises for men through supreme faith.
Therefore, faith should be cultivated by men who are devoted to dharma;
for even the Lord is to be accomplished through faith, and thus faith is preeminent.
Otherwise, O Bhārata, everything devoid of faith is fruitless;
therefore, one should take refuge in devotion to Rudra, the Supreme Lord.
For their birth is fruitful indeed for those whose devotion is unwavering;
and that devotion is of three kinds: sāttvika, as well as rājasa, and tāmasa.
One who is characterized by darkness (tāmasī) obtains a threefold fruit for all the world;
through their connection with the fruits of action, they revolve again and again.
Through hundreds of other births, devotion to the triad of gods arises for those knowers who sacrifice to the deities, once their sinful karma has been exhausted.
Furthermore, liberation arises from Īśāna for one whose doubts have been severed;
this applies especially to those bulls among the twice-born who take refuge on the banks of the Narmadā.
Those who, with one-pointed minds, [worship] Śiva, the imperishable Śaṅkara, proceed without doubt along the path of the triple Veda to the supreme goal. (RKV 11.15)
Those people who are devoted to worshipping here attain success quickly;
for embodied beings elsewhere, success arises only after a long time.
Furthermore, on the banks of the Narmadā, success is swiftly attained;
those people who are knowers of Sāṃkhya achieve perfection within six years.
Those Vaiṣṇavas endowed with knowledge also attain success first;
as do those who know all yogas, like rivers reaching the ocean.
At the end of the eon, those who have entered the yoga of Maheśvara become one;
indeed, among all yogas, the yoga of Maheśvara is the most excellent.
Having reached that [state] and having worshipped Śiva on the bank of a river, even those who may be of sinful birth are liberated; they are no longer born within the [various] wombs.
This path is difficult to ascend, yet it brings about the destruction of all evil;
by resorting to the Revā, living beings are swiftly liberated from saṃsāra.
Therefore, one should always bathe and likewise smear oneself with ashes;
having reached the banks of the Narmadā, one shall swiftly attain perfection.
The man who, being tranquil, reverently worships the Liṅga three times a day,
being liberated from all diseases, attains the supreme goal.
Even if one has been a doer of evil, he succeeds in six months;
however, those whose minds are pure are purified in three months.
Just as snow touched by the sun dissolves from the mountain,
even so is evil dissolved when touched by auspicious particles of ash.
Just as serpents flee in terror from the fear of Vainateya,
even so do sins perish when sprinkled with ashes.
Those who smear themselves with ashes purified by the waters of the Narmadā are immediately liberated from the multitude of their sins; of this there is no doubt.
Those who observe the Pāśupata vow with devotion exactly as prescribed,
avoiding the food of Śūdras, attain the supreme goal.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as milk; the food of a Vaiśya is indeed mere food; and the food of a Śūdra is remembered as blood. (RKV 11.29)
Those best of the twice-born who die nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food,
being devoid of austerity and knowledge, become crows and vultures.
For the evil deeds of men persist by depending upon their food;
whoever eats another's food eats that person's guilt.
"Those who, through the practice of extraordinary asceticism, resort to restlessness in their austerities,
go to hell without a doubt"— thus Śaṅkara has spoken.
And those Brahmins of such a form who are established in the Pāśupata [discipline], they surely burn away the entire mass of great sins; of this there is no doubt.
"Joined with hypocrisy and afflicted by greed, they are beyond restraint"—such is the injunction of the Vedas. (RKV 11.34)
Some are ruined by the faults committed by their parents, others by their own karma; some are destroyed by the arrogance of knowledge, and others by egoism.
Those who have set out upon the dharma of Śaṅkara, even if they are excluded from the meaning of the Smṛtis,
attain the supreme goal despite being afflicted by the Kali age.
Lacking faith, foolish men, increased by hypocrisy, and evil-minded, do not achieve success; they proclaim meanings based on false examples.
Even at a most auspicious sacred site, those who have undertaken the vow of Śaṅkara but are possessed by greed will undoubtedly fall into a low birth.
Indeed, evil deeds are not destroyed by visiting sacred fords nor by acts of charity;
rather, the sin committed through ignorance and negligence perishes [only through this].
Having understood this, the twice-born should conduct themselves according to the prescribed rule;
reciting the supreme Brahman, they should practice it again and again.
He who studies the *Ūrdhvarūpa*, the *Virūpākṣa*, and the *Rudra* [sections],
being free from attachment, beholds Īśāna directly within six months.
He who, being well-restrained, performs ten recitations of the *Saṃhitā* while taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, shall be liberated from all sins.
Whoever recites either a Purāṇa-saṃhitā or a Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava text on the bank of the Narmadā in the presence of Śiva becomes one whose very self is Śiva.
He is honored in the heavenly world until the destruction of all beings;
this was previously declared by Nandin for the purpose of abandoning the seat of worldly existence.
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind to this auspicious *Nandigīta* in the abode of Śiva, amidst an assembly of celestial sages, perfected beings, and gandharvas.
It bestows heaven and liberation, is meritorious, and destroys the fear of saṃsāra.
If you, weary from the heat of worldly existence, desire to abandon this cave-like abyss of saṃsāra—
though bound by the many snares of various karmas created by yourselves— then listen for the sake of happiness to this beneficial teaching spoken by me.
O Śakra, do not follow a crooked path; O Yama, do not inflict torment.
O Pracetas, pacify your mind; O Vittapa, abandon greed.
If you are weary of being tossed by the surging waves of the ocean of saṃsāra, renounce all wealth to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished.

The Purifier, the wielder of the Pināka bow, protects the man who is agitated by birth, terrified of death, seized by desire and other passions, and fallen away from self-restraint and the other virtues.
Do not harbor pride, O Kīnāśa; you will become an object of ridicule by afflicting a living being who is the refuge of all. That very being shall be your refuge.
What is the terrible Time? What is Death? Who is the lowest Yama?
For those men who are devoted to Śiva and Viṣṇu, what fear can there be?
For those beings dwelling on the banks of the Revā who are afflicted by the burden of existence,
both Bharga and the Blessed Lord are the destroyers of the fear of worldly existence.
Worship Śiva, meditate on Śiva, praise Śiva, and sacrifice to Śiva;
bow down to Śiva, O wretched one, if you desire knowledge and liberation.
Study the scripture of the Five-Faced One; recite the five-syllabled mantra;
contemplate the reality consisting of the fivefold self; and worship the supreme Five-Faced One.
What is the use of those lamentable collections of karma, characterized by various states of existence,
if the glorious Śiva, the five-faced one, is served in every way?
What is the use of the trumpeting of the intoxicated elephant of saṃsāra, even if it be silent,
if the lion-like Lord is served by the fragrance of one's inner disposition?
O fool, what is the use of despondency after undergoing such torment from your karma?
Recite the mantra of Bhīma, the beloved of Bhavānī, which destroys all fear.
O fool, worship Bharga, the Lord of the Gods, who dwells on the banks of the Narmadā, who causes the dissolution of the flood of suffering, and who bestows heaven and liberation.
Having abandoned the Revā river, which is served by the celestial Ganges, as well as Hara and Hari who reside upon her banks—
where, O fool, are you going to the distant quarters like a madman, devoid of all spiritual feeling?
Revere the meritorious waters of the Revā; worship the eternal Rudra;
mutter the five-syllabled mantra; and go to your desired abode.
What is the use of tormenting your own body with so many means?
Resort to the Revā; having attained Śiva, you will reach the supreme state that is easily achieved.
Having thus reached Kailāsa at the river in the presence of Śiva, he sang that which belongs to the world-protectors; that has now been told to you by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
He who is devoted to bathing and giving gifts, and who constantly follows the dharma,
having taken refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, is liberated from all sins.
Even if one were to recite all the Vedas daily for a hundred years without following the prescribed rules,
it would not equal the merit of the *mṛtyulāṅgala* recitation, nor even exceed it in its qualities.
Just as one who is impure regarding seed and womb does not find Rudra,
so too the mantra of the plowshare does not remain with one whose life has departed.
The self-controlled practitioner who is joined with the recitation of the *gāyatrī* is indeed superior in virtues; he should daily recite "agnim īḷe," "iṣetvo," or "agna āyāhi. (RKV 11.67)
Standing on the bank, one should mutter "śanno devī"; thus one shall be liberated from sins.
Even one who is constantly composed and recites the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs does not obtain that fruit which a self-controlled person attains through the Gāyatrī.
Having recited the Rudrādhyāya even once, a Brahmin endowed with the Veda is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, by the recitation of other [hymns], such as the Sūktas and the Āraṇyakas,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever recitation of mantras is performed and whatever gift is bestowed while relying on the waters of the Narmadā, all that shall become inexhaustible.
Those who constantly take refuge at the Narmadā with such vows as these,
upon death, go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu or the imperishable station of Śiva.
Some men [attain] the world of truth (satyaloka), and others likewise the world of the sun;
clothed by throngs of celestial nymphs (apsaras), they remain there until the dissolution of all beings.
O bull among kings, while this world was thus proceeding,
there were ten koṭis of sages residing in Kurukṣetra.
O illustrious one, taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā with me, they remained there worshipping Śiva, subsisting on a diet of fruits and roots.
And that divine century, according to the calculation of time,
amounts to twenty-six thousand years by human reckoning.
Then, O best of kings, when that twilight had passed,
only one remaining human lifespan remained for him, lasting for a hundred years.
Then there occurred a drought that brought about the destruction of the world,
by which the entire universe once again fell into a terrible ruin.
Through the power of those sages who had previously attained perfection here and were masters of the Vedas, the Blessed One, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, sent down rain.
A great rain, with abundant water, was poured down on all sides;
by that rain, indeed, their sustenance was produced.
Again, when the end of the age had arrived and only a small remnant of the Kali Yuga remained,
everything— both the stationary and the moving— became entirely withered and perished.
And the entire circle of the earth became utterly destitute, devoid of trees, medicinal herbs, and shrubs, and stripped of grasses and creepers, ravaged by drought.
Then, O King, all those sages by the thousands, afflicted by hunger and thirst,
were overcome by the nature of the age and became diminished in strength.
When the end of the age has arrived, where the performance of fire-sacrifices and the utterance of *svadhā* have perished, what is to be done? Where indeed shall we go? Who will be our refuge?
I replied to them thus again and again: "Do not fear;
I have seen many such turnings of time."
Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, they were all led by me there; for this goddess is indeed the sanctuary when the dissolution of the age has arrived.
"O best of the twice-born, no other refuge exists for us here,
especially since she is the mother of all beings, O most excellent of the twice-born."
Those who were grandfathers, those who were fathers, and others who were great-grandfathers—
all of them have gone to heaven by taking refuge in this great river.
The seven who were my ancestors, Bhṛgu and the others,
as well as the highly fortunate Dhaumṛṇī, my wife of pure smiles;
and she who was known as Manasvatī, [the daughters] of Bhārgava and likewise Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Kaśyapa,
as well as other highly fortunate ones who observe rules and vows,
and hundreds of thousands of others, have attained perfection here.
Therefore, this highly fortunate one must never be abandoned;
no other river is capable of bestowing the fruits of the three worlds.
Those men who dwell on the banks of the Narmadā are instantly liberated from many diverse pairs of opposites and from the great terrors such as hunger and thirst.
Therefore, those who desire the highest good in this world and the next should serve this best of rivers with every effort.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Holy Narmadā," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 12. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, having heard these words, the sages became greatly delighted.
With their palms joined in reverence, the twice-born began to offer praise to the Narmadā.
Homage be to you, O one whose waters are merit; homage to you who move upon the sea-monster!
Homage to you, the liberator from evil; homage, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
Homage be to you, the auspicious reservoir of merit, whose essence is pure and who is served by gods and siddhas;
homage be to you, who are frequented by hosts of holy bathing places; homage be to you, the excellent one born from the body of Rudra.
Homage be to you, O Goddess who flows to the ocean; homage be to you, O auspicious Goddess, bestower of boons.
Homage be to you, O sinless one, who grants happiness in both worlds and is the refuge for the multitudes of many beings.
O best of rivers, remover of sins, adorned with variety, whose banks are frequented by gandharvas, yakṣas, and nāgas;
O eternal one, compassionate toward the multitudes of living beings, O Goddess who bestows liberation, grant us prosperity!
O Goddess, who are served by great elephants, buffalo, and boars, and who possess garlands of mighty waves;
we all bow before you, O bestower of boons and giver of happiness—liberate us from the bondage of the fetters of worldly existence!
Bound by many evil and inauspicious deeds, mortals wander in the hells for as long as they do not touch your waters, which have become like waves stirred up by a great wind.
O you whose face is like a lotus, you are the refuge for those afflicted by the fear of many floods of suffering, those enveloped by manifold sins, and those beset by numerous pairs of opposites.
O Goddess, having reached you, rivers become pure and stainless; there is no doubt in this matter.
You grant fearlessness to those afflicted by suffering, and you are worshipped by many who are disciplined.
If even that which is touched by the rays of the moon and the sun bestows the supreme state,
then what wonder is there that stones submerged in those waters of merit attain the nature of Śiva?
Mortals wander in the hells, afflicted by suffering and their bodies overwhelmed by sin, until they take refuge in your waters, which possess waves broken by great winds; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, those Mlecchas, Pulindas, and Yātudhānas who drink your holy water become liberated here from terrible fear; they too undoubtedly attain this—what wonder is there in this?
While lakes and rivers have fallen into decay in this terrible and utterly corrupted age of Kali,
you alone, O Goddess, shine forth filled with a flood of water, like the Gaṅgā in the path of the stars in the sky.
O bestower of boons, most excellent one, having protected us for this period of time through your grace, we shall then go to Rudra; by your great favor, please indeed grant us such grace.
O Mother, you are our refuge; protect us like a father protects his sons until the end of this age, while we endure this most terrible time ravaged by drought through your great grace.
Those best of the twice-born who recite this hymn, and those men who listen to it with tranquility,
go to Rudra in a vehicle yoked with bulls, adorned with divine garments.
Those who, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, constantly recite this hymn— to them,
at the end, this best of rivers swiftly grants a pure destination.
He who, having risen at dawn or while still lying in bed, recites this hymn every day,
becomes freed from sin, his body thoroughly purified, and attains the refuge of Maheśvara.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn to Narmadā," in the *Śrī-Narmadā-Māhātmya*, within the *Revā-Khaṇḍa* of the fifth *Āvantya-Khaṇḍa*, in the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 13. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus was the holy Goddess praised by those foremost of sages.
He reflected: "I shall grant an excellent boon to all of them."
Then, knowing them to be fast asleep at night, the goddess of lovely smiles went to each ṛṣi individually and appeared to him in a dream.
Then, when midnight had arrived, she rose from the midst of the water,
clothed in spotless garments and adorned with divine garlands.
With a parasol of ghee, possessing beautiful hips and adorned with rubies,
she said to each of them individually, "Do not be afraid."
Dwell by my side, having abandoned fear born of hunger and other such needs.
Having spoken thus to those great sages at the end of her dream, the goddess then vanished from sight, entering her own watery form.
Then at dawn, the sages, filled with joy, said to one another:
"In such a manner was the goddess Sudarśanā seen by me in a dream."
"Fearlessness has been granted to us, and success shall indeed come before long;
there is no doubt that the sight of that Narmadā is most auspicious."
Then on another day, O King, they and their attendants saw the most excellent form of fish in the vicinity of their own hermitage.
Seeing those fish there, the great seers were filled with wonder;
they calmly honored the deities with offerings for the gods and the ancestors.
Having obtained those shoals of fish through the grace of the Great Goddess, they—
along with their sons, wives, and servants— subsist separately.
Nevertheless, day after day, the twice-born in the hermitages were filled with wonder upon seeing such a collection of fish.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, at every gate of the hermitages of the ascetics, they saw those very well-nourished dead fish, especially the pāṭhīna.
Then all those sages dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā became joyful and well-nourished; they all abandoned the fear born of hunger and thirst.
Chanting and performing austerities, O bull of the Bharatas, they remain there,
worshipping the ancestors and the gods while dwelling upon the banks of the Narmadā.
Constantly being recited over and warmed by those best of the twice-born,
that most excellent river shone like the sky with its stars and planets.
There, by those numerous, pure Brahmins devoted to the Vedas,
the Narmadā— the giver of dharma— was formerly divided in due order.
Divided by ten crores of sages dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā,
this Narmadā— her limbs divided— bestows happiness upon men.
O Bhārata, with its auspicious sacred threads and rosaries,
the highly meritorious Narmadā flows toward the ocean along both its banks.
That best of rivers shines with its bright, separate embankments made of sand and clay, like the night with its stars.
Thus all those sages, propitiating the gods and the ancestors,
dwelt on the banks of the Narmadā until the dissolution of all beings.
O Bhārata, when some time more than a hundred years had passed from that terrible event, the maiden then emerged from the water at midnight.
Resplendent like a mass of lightning, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
and holding a trident-tipped spear in her hand, the gentle goddess then spoke to those sages.
"Come, O hosts of sages; enter me, who am not born from a womb. United with your sons and wives, you shall then attain perfection."
Whatever desire anyone may have, I grant that very thing to them—
be it Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Īśāna, or any other supreme deity.
There I shall lead you all; for I am gracious and a bestower of boons. Become intent upon breath-control and, with concentrated minds, enter into me.
Together with your sons and wives, and having abandoned your hermitages, you must not waste time; this dissolution has arrived.
I previously existed for a single day during that most terrible destruction of living beings, the world-destroying conflagration at the end of the aeon.
All other rivers and oceans have indeed gone to destruction;
only because of the boon granted by Maheśa have I not gone to destruction.
The immortal, eternal God, the immovable Lord, the ancient one—what would He not grant when worshipped or entreated, O best of the twice-born? (RKV 13.30)
Having spoken thus, that goddess, holding a trident in her hand and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, then entered the waters of the Revā while the sages looked on.
Then, having heard those words, their minds were filled with wonder;
they all paid homage to me and asked for forgiveness again and again.
"May you forgive us for whatever was said while we were dwelling under your protection,
O highly fortunate ones, who have abandoned your homes along with your disciples and kinsmen."
Having recited the single-syllable Brahman and meditated upon Maheśvara in their hearts, they—
whose vows were mastered— then bathed with waters purified by mantras.
They entered the waters of the Narmadā like winged mountains,
illuminating all directions, with kuśa grass in their hands and accompanied by their leaders.
O Indra among kings, when they had departed, I alone remained there,
having reached Amareśa and worshipping the river Narmadā.
O King, descendant of Bharata, by the grace of the Creator, I experienced all seven kalpas beginning with the Māyūra, together with Revā.
From her birth until this day, I have not known her former state.
For this is the power of Śaṅkara, a digit of Śambhu known as Ilā;
she is Narmadā, the destroyer of evil and the savior from worldly existence.
O Pāṇḍava, even when I did not exist in the past kalpas—
during those fourteen kalpas— this [earth] remained established in happiness.
I shall fully recount those fourteen former kalpas in which the Narmadā did not perish, just as the Goddess told them to me.
Know that the first is Kāpila, the second is Prājāpatya;
then Brāhma, Saumya, Sāvitra, Bārhaspatya, and Prabhāsaka.
The Māhendra, the Agnikalpa, the Jayanta, the Māruta,
the Bahurūpa-Vaiṣṇava, and the Jyautiṣa as the fourteenth.
These kalpas have been described by me, in which the Narmadā did not perish;
the fifteenth is the Māyūra, and the sixteenth here is the Kaurma.
The Baka, the Matsya, the Padma, and the Vaṭakalpa, O Bhārata;
this twenty-first is the Vārāha, which is current today.
These seven [rivers] were practiced by me together with Revā for twenty-one kalpas, starting from the auspicious source of the Narmadā.
O best of kings, since she was born, I have indeed seen her many times;
O best of monarchs, I have already told you [of her], so what more shall I say to you?

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narratives of the Twenty-one Kalpas," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāsāra, Chapter 14.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Then all those highly fortunate sages, whose wealth was their asceticism, [spoke].
Having gone to the supreme world, what wonderful thing happened there?
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, after those inhabitants of the banks of the Narmadā had departed,
there occurred a fierce destruction that brought about the end of all beings.
Then Brahmā and the other gods praised the eternal Mahādeva Śiva, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
"O Lord, withdraw this world together with its gods, asuras, and humans;
the time has arrived at the end of a thousand yugas, capable of bringing about dissolution."
Having assumed my own form, this was created by you;
having assumed the form of Viṣṇu, this was protected by you.
O Maheśvara, the one form has become threefold—Brahmī, Śaivī, and Vaiṣṇavī—for the sake of creation, destruction, and protection; it is thus indeed.
Having heard these truthful words of Viṣṇu and Parameṣṭhin, he, together with his attendants and retinue, along with those two and Umā, [departed].
Having pierced these worlds, from the earth up to the world of Brahmā, and having split the cosmic egg beyond it, the Lord Nīlalohita [penetrated] even further.
The omnipresent Lord entered together with them the divine, unborn state of Śiva;
there was neither wind nor space, neither fire nor earth there.
Wherever Śaṅkara dwells together with Umā, O God,
there neither the sun, nor the planets, nor the stars, nor the directions exist.
There are no world-protectors, neither pleasure nor pain, O best of kings.

That which the seers call the state of Brahmā, that which the seers call the state of Śiva, others proclaim as the Kṣetrajña and the Lord, and the Sāṃkhyas indeed sing of as primordial liberation; [all these are this very state]. (RKV 14.12)
That which some proclaim as the primordial Brahman, whom they call the Lord of all, unborn and ancient;
him who is of a single form and yet of manifold forms, the formless, the primordial, the supreme, known as the Imperishable.
The sages speak of that fourth state, which is beyond description, devoid of name and lineage,
consisting of meditation, meaning, and pure consciousness, exceedingly subtle, abiding within the self, the most excellent and supreme Lord.
Then those three, having approached the Blessed Lord Īśa, become one in essence;
yet, through their distinct individual forms, they once again protect the entire world.
As Rudra, the Lord effects the withdrawal of all beings;
as Viṣṇu, he protects the worlds; and as Brahmā, he is the creator of the universe.
Having become Time (Kāla) conjoined with Primordial Nature (Prakṛti), Maheśvara stands;
by his side is situated the illustrious Viśvarūpā.
That which those who know it and are discerning call the "prakṛti" (primordial nature) of all things—
the Supreme Lord is the cause of both its state as puruṣa (spirit) and its state as prakṛti (nature).
Therefore, when the end of the eon has arrived, this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, goes to dissolution in that very [Brahman].
Everything marked with the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* is indeed pervaded by the Supreme Lord;
Viṣṇu takes the form of the *bhaga*, while Maheśvara takes the form of the *liṅga*.
He shines in all the worlds and is sung of in the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and the rest;
because he has entered into all beings, Viṣṇu is remembered as Bhaga.
Because he enters [all things], he is called Viṣṇu, the great one who consists of all the gods; because of his shining and his moving, the name Bhaga is proclaimed.
The wise know that as the *liṅga* because the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, attains dissolution within it and reaches a state of oneness.
Then Mahādeva spoke to the Goddess, who was standing by his side:
"Withdraw the entire world; do not delay, O beautiful one."
Abandon this gentle form, pure as the rays of the white moon;
assuming the form of Rudra, destroy all that is moving and unmoving.
O Goddess, lotus-eyed one, surrounded by fierce and terrible hosts of spirits, devour this entire world of living beings!
Then I shall crush and likewise submerge the world;
having once again made it a single ocean, I shall sleep peacefully with you.
The Goddess said:
"O God of great splendor, I do not destroy this world;
having become its Mother, I do not devour it while it is motionless and deeply distressed."
Out of her feminine nature, she acts with compassion toward my heart;
O Lord of the World, how indeed shall I burn up this world?
"Therefore, O Śaṅkara, you yourself must withdraw this world.
Thus addressed, Dhūrjaṭi Nīlalohita spoke to that goddess.
Enraged, he reviled Maheśvarī with a *huṃ* sound;
then, with eyes possessed by fury, he said, "Oṃ huṃ phaṭ! You are that! (RKV 14.31).
Uttering the sound "huṃ," O Bhārata, the large-eyed woman, with her full thighs and hips, instantly became as fierce as Kālarātri.
Uttering great roars with "huṃ" sounds and making the ten directions resound,
she grew exceedingly fierce like a flash of lightning.
Difficult to behold due to the falling of lightning, as flickering as a mass of lightning,
fierce and filled with flashes of lightning, her eyes resemble the fire of lightning.
With disheveled hair and large eyes, with a slender neck and a thin waist,
she wears a tiger skin as her garment and a serpent as her sacred thread.
Adorned with scorpions as radiant as heaps of fire and with *gonasa* serpents,
it filled the three worlds in both its breadth and its height.
Her limbs became radiant, with a black serpent as her sole earring;
she held a variegated staff aloft in her hand and was clad in a tiger skin.
She grew exceedingly fierce, bringing about the destruction of the world;
licking the corners of her mouth, she uttered cruel hisses.
With her mouth wide open and a gurgling roar, she causes the agitation of the world;
followed by sporting spirits, she is cruel and causes the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
Bursting into a loud, terrifying laugh, with a misshapen nose and eyes like pits of fire, she set the entire world ablaze with her rising cries of "kilakila."
Being scorched there, the gods fall upon the surface of the earth;
yakṣas, gandharvas, along with kinnaras and mahoragas, also fall.
And hosts of beings fall down, crying out "Hā! Hā! Hai! Hai!
with loud outcries, amidst thunderclaps, and with sounds of uttered distress.

At that time, the entire universe, including the three worlds with all things moving and stationary, was pervaded; the earth was covered by hosts of blazing beings as they rushed together and fell upon it.
In that fierce festival, as the mountain ridges fell with crackling sounds,
there arose a scene that increased the joy of Rudra.
Violating living beings and devouring even the moving creatures,
she took on various scents and let out shrieks like those of a jackal.
Facing streams of blood and gore, her body smeared with it,
Caṇḍī became fierce in nature for the task of destroying the world.
Even those great seers such as Bhṛgu and others who have reached Maharloka,
as well as hundreds of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and the rest, perish as well.
The gods and asuras, along with yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas, terrified by fear,
some enter the netherworld while others hide in caves and similar places.
And that goddess, pervading all directions, stood like Death itself,
having been dispatched by the God at the time that brings about the end of the eon.
Though she is one, she has become ninefold, and likewise tenfold and tenfold again;
she possesses sixty-four forms, as well as the hundredfold form of Aṭṭahāsinī.

And Śivā was born with a thousand forms, with bodies numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions; she assumed various shapes and weapons and moved about playing various musical instruments.
O King, by the command of Śiva, the goddess became such as this:
in all directions and in the sky, she took on forms characterized by formidable weapons.
Obstructing those who were perishing, the hosts of Maheśvara stood firm;
with tridents and spears in their hands, they moved about together with her.
Then some of the hosts of Mothers, together with the hosts of Vināyakas,
grew exceedingly fierce, intent upon the destruction of the world.
Then her fangs, resembling jasmine and the moon, grew to thousands,
tens of thousands, and even hundreds of millions of yojanas.
The rows of his fangs, his claws— cruel, sharp, and harsh—
seem to scratch the sky, the quarters of the horizon, and the earth with its seven continents.
By the impact of her fangs, the forest mountains were pulverized;
masses of piled-up rocks shattered into thousands of pieces.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Gandhamādana,
Mālyavat, Nīla, and the great mountain Śveta.
O best of kings, the seat of Ilā centered upon Meru, along with the seven continents and the oceans, together with the Lokāloka mountain, trembled.
Great trees, struck by the thunderbolt-like fangs, were shattered;
and the quarters of the sky were pervaded on all sides by portents of terrible form.
All the stars and hosts of planets, as well as the classes of beings dwelling in celestial palaces,
were crowded with thousands of Śivās and likewise with the great hosts of Mothers.
When the end of the age had arrived, she wandered throughout the entire world,
[surrounded] on all sides by those wandering, speaking, and crying out.
The ten directions were pervaded by fierce, blazing, and crushing [beings],
as they overturned the vast mass of mountains along with their trees.
The gates of the city towers were shattered, the ground was strewn with hair and dry bones,
and the villages and cities were burnt down, shrouded in heaps of ashes.
The entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, was filled with the smoke of funeral pyres;
it was pervaded by cries of "Alas! Alas! and resounded with the sound of loud laughter.
This entire world became without refuge and without support.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the World by Kālarātri," in the *Narmadāmāhātmya* within the *Revākhaṇḍa*, in the fifth *Āvantyakhaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the narrative of the Kalpas.
RKV, Chapter 15. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then she was surrounded by thousands of Mothers and fierce beings.
The Night of Doom, with blazing eyes, seizes the entire world.
Then those terrible Mothers, whose natures are those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, [and who are] the powers of Vāyu, Indra, Agni, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa; 15.2.
Moving about in terrifying forms, they sport with Skanda, Krodha, and Nṛsiṃha,
wielding discs, tridents, maces, swords, vajras, spears, ṛṣṭis, and paṭṭiśas.
Urged on by Umā, all the Mothers roamed through the abode with flaming skull-topped staves and firebrands, rushing in the ten directions.
By the stamping of their feet and the sounds of their uttering the syllable *huṃ*,
this entire triple world was completely consumed by fire on all sides.

With the sounds of "Alas! Alas! and cries of lamentation, and with the city streets, houses, and gates shattered, the earth became terrible on all sides, its surface mottled and strewn with heaps of skulls.
O best of kings, all this Jambūdvīpa, which is said to consist of a hundred thousand [parts], has been utterly destroyed by force.
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Gomeda, and likewise Śālmali,
together with Puṣkara-dvīpa— those who dwell upon these mountains.
They were all devoured by Death, as well as by the *bhūtas*, the hosts of Mothers,
and the great Asuras with skulls, who were fierce with flesh, fat, and marrow.
Her limbs red with the spouting of blood, the most terrifying Mahāmāyā was there drinking blood, she who delights in great flesh and fat.
Holding a skull in her hand, she is hideous as she devours gods and demons;
dancing and laughing, she is perverse and makes a great roar.
Causing terror to the three worlds and laughing with flashes of lightning,
she devoured the earth as far as the seven continents and oceans.
Then he went to his own abode where the god Maheśvara dwells,
taking up residence on the bank of the Narmadā together with the hosts of Mothers.
Dancing on the high hip of the immortals with a smiling face—
the term "immortals" (amarāḥ) refers to the deities, while "hip" (kaṭa) is said to mean the body.
O best of kings, because this mountain is covered with those skulls, along with heaps of severed and shattered bones drenched in marrow, fat, and blood; [it is called Kaṭāhaka].
Thus was it proclaimed by the wise as Amarakaṇṭaka;
created by Śambhu, it is the most purifying in all the worlds.
For Śaṅkara was always present there together with Umā;
therefore, I remained there constantly, stationed at the tips of his feet.
Bowing with a spirit of prostration, I praise that Nīlalohita;
then, together with the hosts of Gaṇas and the Mātṛs, [I praise him] with the rhythmic clapping of palms.
Greatly delighted, Śaṅkara dances together with Death,
brandishing skull-topped staffs, flaming brands, sharp-edged spears, and iron clubs.
With flesh, fat, and marrow in their hands, they dance joyfully in groups;
some are dwarfish, some have matted hair, some are shaven-headed, and others have long necks, lips, and hair.
With great genitals, bellies, and arms, they dance and laugh with hideous,
terrible faces, their mouths and limbs distorted and fierce.
When the reversal of time arrived, they made Amara their thorn—
most terrible among them, the cause of terror for the world.
I see Death dancing, with hair as tawny as lightning;
by his side stands the Goddess, adorned with spotless garments.
Her cheeks were resonant with earrings, she wore a serpent as a sacred thread,
and she was worshipping Maheśvara with various offerings.
There I beheld the Narmadā, my mother, who is adored by the entire universe;
she possessed manifold waves and whirlpools, resembling the ocean at its beautiful shore.
O Bhārata, she was invisible due to the downpour of great lakes and rivers, yet possessed of a visible form, and was being worshipped by gods, siddhas, and throngs of sages.
In the meantime, [the wind] produced a terrible [storm] known as the "seven-sevens," rich with the foam of the flood of Mahāvīci, making the world full of water.
He then beheld the goddess Narmadā again, clad in black antelope skin,
flowing in seven channels with the roar of smoky thunderbolts.
Having thus witnessed that incomparable dissolution, O best of kings,
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings became one in which the rays of both the moon and the sun had vanished.
Then, like a whirling circle of fire, he rapidly caused everything to revolve without exception— producing great portents and causing the entire mandala of the constellations to vanish.
Crowded with tens of millions of celestial palaces and filled with kinnaras and great serpents,
that great wind, accompanied by thunderclaps, caused all things mobile and immobile to tremble.
Born from the mouth of Rudra, the renowned wind named Saṃvarta dried up the seven oceans that had been spread abroad.
With his limbs smeared with dust, his eyes and hair tawny, his head bound by masses of matted locks,
making a great roar and wielding a blazing, massive trident— may that Hara protect you day after day.
Bearing a trident, a bow, armor, and a crown, his entire body was smeared with ashes from the cremation ground;
the hollow of his throat was filled with a garland of skulls, and his head was bound with cords of great serpents.
His limbs were entwined by swarms of hooded serpents; he bore upon his crest the moon, the fire, and the nectar-ocean;
his hand was formidable with the tip of the Pināka bow; he was clothed in an elephant hide and made the sound of the ḍamaru drum.
With his body extending beyond the seven worlds, his entire frame encircled by great arms,
he possessed eyes resembling the rising sun and bellies like the tender sprouts of coral.
At the time of the end of the eon, he sported with his extended phallus and his eye, which was as red as twilight clouds, a red lotus, rubies, vermilion, and a mass of lightning.
Just as the Blessed Lord Sumeru, when casting down his golden staff,
causes the mountains to shatter by the impact of the tips of his feet, he too went there, making the world tremble.
Desirous of destroying the entire triple heaven and emitting a distorted, loud laugh,
that Great-Souled One, the sole Lord of the World, seized all of Tridiva, truly agitating it.
Having beheld that god, the unborn, the most excellent, the Great Lord who effects the dissolution of the world,
that Kālarātri, together with the Mothers and all the Gaṇas, worships Śiva.
Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and the hosts of Gaṇas bow down day and night to that god Hara— the source of all beings, the best in the world, the cause of all people, and the enemy of Smara.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Fervent Activity of Creation and Destruction," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 16. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Surrounded on all sides by his Mothers and by terrible hosts of spirits, the wielder of the trident danced.
Clad in the covering of a lordly elephant's hide, he desires to withdraw the entire universe.

Maheśvara, the lord of all the lords of the gods, his garland bound by manifold celestial mantras, his limbs smeared with fat, marrow, and blood, Śambhu danced during the conflagration of the three worlds.

Accompanied by Kālarātri, that Great Soul, known as Saṃvartaka, together with the splendor of the sun, seized the entire three worlds at the appointed time; he is Śambhu, the Great Soul, the most excellent in the universe.

Then, opening his mouth which resembled the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha), he let out a terrible, loud laugh— a sound like a gale of great meteors, thunderbolts, and lightning, mingled with masses of sparks and smoke.
By that loud laughter, which arose from Hara and resembled a thousand thunderbolts,
the ten directions were filled and all the great oceans were stirred into turmoil.
That sound reached the world of Brahmā, and the entire vessel of the universe trembled; "What is this? they cried, and the sages became agitated in mind and filled with terror.
Having bowed down, all of them, suddenly struck with fear, spoke to Brahmā, the Lord of the Supreme Lord;
and then all those sages, as well as the gods, the asuras, and the great serpents, were likewise terrified.

Who is this whose limbs are terrifyingly radiant with the brilliance of lightning, who sports while standing upon the earth, bearing a body like the fire of cosmic destruction, and by whose loud laughter the world is bewildered? (RKV 16.8)

In an instant, he shone with a form so terrifying that one wondered: "Does he wish to destroy the three worlds, along with you and the seven oceans, as they proceed toward the Janas, Tapas, and Satya realms?"
"O immeasurable Lord, who is this that desires to destroy all this? Tell us, for we have never before seen such a calamity. You know the truth; you are considered by us to be supreme."
Having heard those words, Brahmā then spoke, having comforted the hosts of gods and others.
Śrī Brahmā said:

This very Time, whose nature is imperishable, desiring to withdraw the entire triple heaven and the world, shall lie dormant when the full cycle of years is complete; it is no wonder that he is the sovereign lord of the Ishanas.
This god is the Saṃvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Udvatsara, and this Vatsara;
though seen, he is unseen; he is the offered oblation and the manifest light; he is both gross and subtle, and he is the atom.
"There is nothing further than this in this world; this Lord, the proclaimer of the Self, is both the supreme and the subordinate.
Having spoken thus, "May he be pleased with me, for his form is like Time itself," the Blessed One, the Lord of the Gods, [departed].
Then, having restrained his self, he, together with Sanatkumāra and others, brought [the sage] to satisfaction.
Brahmā said:
Salutations be to the All, whose form is perfectly tranquil; salutations, repeated salutations to you who are not of terrible aspect.
Salutations, repeated salutations to you, the Self of all, O All; salutations to the Great Self, O Lord of Beings.
Obeisance, obeisance to you who are adorned with the syllables *oṃ* and *huṃ*, and who are the essence of *svadhā* and *vaṣaṭ*.
Obeisance to you, the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), the ruler of the three qualities (*guṇas*), who consists of the three Vedas and whose self is the three *guṇas*.
You are indeed Śaṅkara, you are Maheśvara; you have entered into the foremost Pradhāna. You are Viṣṇu, the Lord, and the Great-Grandfather; you are the seven-tongued one and the infinite-tongued one.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone are the creator and the creation; you are the object of knowledge for the universe and the supreme abode.
Those who know the Vedas call you the most excellent among the twice-born; you are higher than the highest, you are beyond the beyond.
They declare that which is subtler than the subtlest, from which speech turns back and from which the mind also turns back.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
"I have been praised by you with various mantras; O Lotus-born one, I bestow peace upon you.
Behold me, blazing with many mouths, violently seizing this world."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World, together with the Goddess,
comforted the Grandfather and vanished right there.
Having heard this most meritorious and supreme hymn, those who are enveloped by many sins attain a destination here; they proceed to Rudra in stainless celestial chariots.
O dear one, those foremost of the twice-born who recite this shall never experience fear—not in battle, from thieves, fire, the forest, or the ocean; Śiva protects them, of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Śiva Performed by Brahmā," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 17. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus being praised by Brahmā and the other eminent sages, [Viṣṇu...]
There, the Lord of the World gathered together those who had gone to the Brahma-world.
That [face] was formidable, most terrible, and imperishable, situated on the right;
it possessed great fangs and a fierce roar, resembling the depths of the netherworld.
With eyes tawny like the flash of lightning, terrifying and hair-raising,
he had a great tongue, large fangs, and a neck that bore the heads of massive serpents.
Wearing a garland of the heads of great asuras, he is the cause of the great dissolution;
he devours the oblation consisting of wind and water cast into the ocean.
He beheld that face of Mahādeva, resembling the mouth of a mare, licking up the entire world with the tip of its tongue.
Extending for thousands and hundreds of thousands of yojanas in the ten directions, they are most terrible, overflowing with flesh, fat, and marrow.
Then his fangs grew by the hundreds and thousands,
[reaching] the asuras, gods, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
The Grandfather beheld him caught upon the tips of his fangs,
his neck crushed and lodged within the mechanism of his teeth.
O Indra among kings, I behold the world entering my wide-open mouth,
like rivers— whose bodies are broken by various waves and which are filled with great masses of foam— going to their destruction upon reaching the ocean with a roar.
In that same way, this entire universe, spread out and as difficult to fathom as an ocean of manifold living beings,
entered the vast mouth of Rudra— blazing, fierce, and as terrible as the roar of a thundercloud.
Then, from his mouth issued forth most terrible flames— abundant, accompanied by sparks and smoke,
manifold in form, and radiant as fire— as if they were setting all the quarters ablaze.

Then the face of Maheśvara, possessing a wondrous form, became garlanded with thousands of solar flames and possessed moving tongues and fangs; at that time, he who was singular became the twelvefold self.
Then those twelve Ādityas emerged from the mouth of Rudra, taking recourse to the southern direction and scorching the earth.
Whatever terrestrial life there was— consisting of various trees and grasses as its dwelling—
had previously withered due to drought, leaving the entire surface of the earth in total turmoil.
Suddenly illuminated by those suns born of Rudra,
everything became filled with smoke, and the planets and stars vanished.
Suddenly, the entire circle of the earth blazed up intensely; this whole world of moving and non-moving beings became filled with garlands of flames.
In the seven continents, the oceans, the rivers, and the lakes, fire consumes the entire world, just as clarified butter is consumed as an oblation in a sacrifice.
Blazing with vast splendor and filled with great flames,
the Ādityas born of Rudra indeed consumed the entire world.
And as the rays of the Ādityas indeed touch one another,
so did the Blessed One burn the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Having become that fire equal in extent to the seven continents, Maheśvara burnt the earth as far as the seven continents and oceans.
Then they burned the earth as far as Mount Sumeru and Mandara;
having pierced the seven netherworlds, they then consumed the realm of the nāgas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the fire, burning the seven netherworlds beneath the earth along with the stars, moved everywhere, indeed consuming everything.
Like a night of iron being heated by glowing coals,
or like a blazing furnace, everything there blazed forth, set ablaze by the fire of universal destruction.
The earth became devoid of trees and grass, stripped of its waterfalls, lakes, and rivers;
with its multitude of mountain peaks shattered, it became like the back of a tortoise.
Having filled the entire world, which consists of pure consciousness, with garlands of flames,
Rudra, the Great Lord, remained there assuming a magnificent form.
Then the goddess Harilocanā, accompanied by a multitude of mothers and joined by yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas, entered Mahādeva.
Having attained the supreme nirvāṇa, she was like the peaceful crest of a flame;
for the entire world, along with the three realms, O sinless one, has been utterly consumed.
"By the grace of Rudra, having been liberated from me and from Narmadā, who was not born of a womb,
the Lord has today been fed by me for ten thousand yugas."
For in the past, the wielder of the trident was propitiated by him; therefore, I am free from old age and death, as well as the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Ghoramantra, the Vāmadeva, and the Tryambaka.
The Ṛṣabha, the Trisuparṇa, the Durgā, the Sāvitra,
as well as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Uttara-Bṛhatsāman.
Having likewise recited the Raudrī, the supreme Gāyatrī, the Śivopaniṣad, as well as the Pratiratha hymn and the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, ||| RKV_17.31 |||
The earth, extending to its rivers and oceans, was reduced to ashes,
with the exception of the illustrious Narmadā, who is like nectar.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Hemakūṭa, Mālyavat,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges.
The mountains, scorched by the twelve suns, were seen with their rocks shattered and reduced to ashes; yet the Narmadā was not destroyed at that time.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Gandhamādana, Mālyavat— the best of mountains— and Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān.
These kings of mountains, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
have all been utterly consumed by the fire at the end of the eon, their great boulders shattered to pieces.
Thus was the destruction of all things at the end of the age seen by me in the past,
O best of kings— with the exception of the highly meritorious Narmadā.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the World by Means of the Twelve Suns," in the Śrī Narmadā-māhātmya, within the Revā-khaṇḍa, the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 18.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, when this world had been completely consumed by the suns born of Īśvara, [the following occurred].
And with the seven oceans dried up, as well as the seven continents themselves.
Then, from his mouth, there issued forth massive and most formidable clouds, resembling the bow of Indra;
impelled by the boon of Īśāna, those terrible clouds made the world dark.

In some places they have the luster of blue lotuses, in others the appearance of collyrium; some resemble cow’s milk, the kunda flower, or the moon; others have the form of the eye-spots on a peacock’s tail, while some possess a radiance like smokeless fire.
Some were like great mountains, some resembled large schools of fish;
some had the beautiful forms of lordly elephants, and some were like clouds with massive peaks.
Some have the appearance of moving waves and ripples, while others resemble great cities;
some look like fortified towns with gate-towers and watchtowers, their borders adorned with lightning, meteors, and thunderbolts.
That god, whose limbs were completely covered, became the host known as Saṃvartaka; that fierce one, raining down, made this entire immeasurable world into a single ocean.

Then, with my limbs overwhelmed by fear and my body covered by the surging waters of the Gaṅgā, I did not see Īśāna, who was increasing in size like a great cloud and whose form was enveloped by Indra’s thunderbolts.
Furthermore, the elephants, repeatedly drinking from the world that was being consumed on all sides, filled the entire world with their spray; and then they themselves vanished from sight.
The seven great oceans, the lakes, the continents, all the rivers, and the worlds of Bhūr and Bhuvar—
being filled by the masses of water-floods, all this became a single ocean.
Alas, nothing at all—whether moving or unmoving—is seen in this world, even though it is devoid of fire, moon, and sun;
for the stars have perished, the blinding darkness prevails, the winds have been stilled, and the single nest of light has set.
O King, at that time, amidst this great flood of water, I offered praise to this Pure Being;
then, reflecting thus, "Where indeed shall I go for refuge to that one who is peaceful?"—RKV 18.11.
Having called the Lord to mind within my heart, I remember the God while stationed in the water;
I bow to the God, I take refuge in Him, and I have performed meditation upon Him.
Having meditated, I then crossed that water with my mind undeluded by his grace;
both my exhaustion and fatigue vanished through the favor of the goddess, O son of a king.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Narmadā," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa), within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 19.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, in that single ocean, I was distressed and desirous of death.
O best of kings, crossing the water with his arms, he made gasping, croaking sounds.
Then, standing in the midst of the ocean, which was silent and still, I heard the incomparable roar of the waters resounding through the ten directions.
Resembling a swan, the moon, or jasmine, white as a pearl necklace or cow’s milk,
her body variegated with various jewels, with golden horns, she was enchanting to the mind.
Adorned with a banner bearing a tail made of coral by the gods,
with a long snout, bellowing, and plunging into the ocean with its hooves.
Agitated, I beheld a cow standing directly facing me,
adorned with clusters of tinkling bells and pearls, and encircled by golden bells.
By the strides of her feet, the entire water of the single ocean,
with its surging masses of scattered foam, seemed as if it were dancing everywhere at once.
Roaring with the tossing of her waters and agitating the great ocean,
she said to me, "O fortunate one," in a voice that was both smooth and profound.
"Do not fear, my child, my child! Death does not exist for you.
By the grace of Mahādeva, there shall be no death for you, nor even for me."
"Take hold of my tail, O Brahmin; I shall rescue you from this terrible danger until the world is submerged."
"Drink from my breasts for the sake of warding off hunger and thirst; having drunk that divine milk which is the source of nectar, may you find peace."
Having heard those words of hers, her breast was drunk by me out of joy;
as soon as the breast was drunk, neither hunger nor thirst remained for me then.
Divine vital strength was born within him, sufficient for crossing the ocean;
then he spoke this to her: "Who are you, now that the world has been turned into a single ocean?"
Tell me the truth, for a great wonder dwells within my heart;
I am wandering here, distressed, on the verge of death, and struck down.
For you have become my refuge through the remainder of my good fortune, O lady of virtuous vows.
Gaurī said:
"Have I been forgotten by you— I, the Great Goddess of universal form,
Narmadā, the bestower of dharma upon men, and the giver of heaven, happiness, and strength?"
"O Noble Lady, seeing you sinking down, I have been sent by Rudra;
rescue that twice-born man, lest he lose his life in the water."
At the command of the Lord, I have come here to your presence in the form of a cow;
I am in haste so that Śambhu’s word may not prove false. (RKV 19.17)
Thus addressed by her, I recognized my auspicious and imperishable tail, which resembled Indra’s bow, and I grasped it with both my arms.
Then, having reached that ocean, this god who has the tail as his banner addressed me, saying, "I am Mahādeva."
Then, for a period of time lasting a thousand yugas, I wandered together with her through that darkness which enveloped everything and was submerged in water.
Then, in that great ocean, wandering and clinging to the tail of a bull, he remained in a windless,
dark, lightless, and painless void.
Suddenly, within that water, there appeared something resembling an *atasī* flower,
like split collyrium, as stainless as the sky.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, clad in yellow garments, and imperishable;
he was adorned with a crown the color of the sun, which caused flashes of lightning to appear.
With his radiant head, he was as if the very sky incarnate;
his cheeks were illuminated by his earrings, and his chest was made to shine by his necklace.
Adorned with divine ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold,
it was a bed with a serpent-cushion, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns.
The hero, possessing many arms and thighs, with many faces, beautiful to behold,
sleeping upon the single ocean while supporting a thousand eyes and heads.
With his great mass of matted hair, whose radiance was like flashing lightning,
the god remained pervading the entire world as a single ocean.
Having swallowed everything— including gods, asuras, and humans— I beheld the Lord Śaṅkara, the Sovereign, sleeping in the single ocean.
[He saw] the all-pervading, unmanifest, infinite one whose faces are on every side;
near the soles of his feet [was a woman] adorned with golden armlets.

To the goddess of auspicious form, who possesses all forms, who is highly fortunate, who sustains the universal illusion, who consists of prosperity, modesty, wisdom, and speech, and who is the source of well-being; RKV_19.30.
I then sought her— who is success, fame, delight, the power of Brahmā, and the Night of Doom born not from a womb—
as she remained in the very presence of the Lord.
I beheld Umā, the moon-faced one, the steadfast mistress of all.

I circumambulate and pay homage to the Blessed Lord Īśa, who is peaceful, asleep, possessing the color of fresh gold, accompanied by Umā, shrouded in darkness, most meritorious, and the foremost of heroes.
Then, having been fast asleep, that best of gods suddenly awoke at the end of the night by his own nature;
agitating the waters of the ocean with his arms, he perceived the world destroyed within the water.
Thinking only, "What must be done?", he assumed the form of a boar with wondrous limbs;
his splendor was like that of a massive rain-cloud, and he wore long garlands, garments, and necklaces of gold coins.

Bearing the conch, discus, and sword, wearing a diadem, composed of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, the Great Soul is the ancient creator of the three worlds, assuming the form of the triad of deities for the sake of his task.
He alone is Rudra; for the sake of creation, that Lord became the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) who devours the world;
for the sake of protecting the world, he alone is Hari, holding the excellent discus, sword, mace, and lotus in his hands.
Indeed, it is not possible to make a distinction among those great-souled ones who share a single body;
he who would attempt to create a division among them by means of critical inquiry, logical reasons, specific meanings, or reasoning is an ignorant person.
That evil-souled person, who creates divisions and possesses a mind of hatred, gradually goes to a terrible hell;
for whatever one's devotion is, by that very devotion one surely attains immortality upon casting off the body.
Deluding the world here with his forms, that god is the creator, the protector, and the bringer of destruction;
therefore, one should not enter into a state of delusion, nor should one harbor hatred toward him who manifests in diverse forms.
Therefore, even he who is the supreme Lord Īśāna, the creator of the world, assuming the form of a boar,
became the inner self within the waters of the ocean when the three worlds had perished and were submerged in a mass of surging waves.
Then, having split the ocean and its waters, he entered the depths of Pātāla in an instant;
he touched the entire earth, submerged in water, she whose eyes are like lotus petals.
When that earth, with its peaks and mountain-summits shattered like stones, was submerged in the dissolution,
the god Viṣṇu himself, possessing incomparable courage, lifted it up with a single tusk.
With her body hanging from the tip of his fang, she shone like moonlight upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa;
she of incomparable form appeared like lightning clinging to the crest of the moon.

With extraordinary courage and incomparable power, he forcibly rescued her from the waters of the ocean— like an elephant pulling a submerged female elephant, or like one lifting a shattered boat from the midst of the water.
Having rescued her from that great flood of water, the Noble One divided the entire ocean;
he deposited the waters of the great ocean back into the great oceans and once again into the rivers.
He restored the shattered mountains once more, as well as all the continents and the oceans;
during that kalpa, he made those mountain ranges covered on all sides with mountain rocks.
Having divided his body into many forms, he created all the hosts of the lords of the gods;
from his mouth came Fire, from his mind the Moon, and from his eye the Sun suddenly appeared.
Then, as he who was the embodiment of the yoga of the Lord meditated, there arose the hosts of the lords of the gods,
as well as the Vedas, the sacrifices, the social classes, and likewise all medicinal herbs and flavors.

The entire world became present to his mind— whatever exists here that is stationary or born from an egg, born from a womb, born from sweat, or born from a sprout, down to even the smallest insects and ants.
Then, in an instant, the Great Lord suddenly understood with his mind that he had assumed many forms;
and having entered there once more, the immutable Self manifested through those eight bodies.
Then, O Brahmins, he of abundant splendor performed his divine play right here while I was looking on;
by me, O King, the entire sight of them was brought to an end within a single moment.

Having indeed accomplished everything without exception as if in mere play, that God of gods, the creator of the worlds, the all-seeing and omnipresent deity, the primordial author, vanished from sight.
Whatever name-and-form exists here for a moment, I behold that very world just as it is:
indeed, it is encircled by continents and oceans, and strewn with celestial chariots such as the constellations and stars.

I do not see that lady of great majesty, the sovereign of all the gods, who has taken the form of a cow, though she is variegated by the circle of the sun and moon in the sky like clouds and surrounded by various multitudes of living beings.
"O King, thinking 'Where is she now?', my mind was instantly bewildered;
I gazed in all directions and their intermediate points, yet how could I find her, whose limbs were like those of a goddess?"
And there I see her again, radiant, with waters pure and bright as a great dark cloud;
her form adorned by many trees, and she is surrounded by elephants, horses, and birds.
Just as I formerly reached the riverbank and took my stand upon Amarakaṇṭaka,
even so do I see myself now, seated at ease, undisturbed and having attained happiness.

In the same way, at the end of the eon, one who is free from disease and sorrow beholds again that auspicious river carrying pure water— untainted, compassionate like a noble mother, and whose waters are inexhaustible.
Those best of the twice-born who read and hear this most meritorious Kalpa concerning the Great Boar, the Supreme Lord, become pure day by day.
Having shaken off hundreds of thousands of impurities, they have reached the third heaven, frequented by immortals and joined by *siddhas* and *gandharvas*;
together with all the *apsarases*, who resemble the stainless moon, they enjoy celestial bliss through various amorous diversions.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Events of the Vārāha Kalpa," in the Śrī Narmadā-māhātmya, within the Revā-khaṇḍa, the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāvalī, Chapter 20.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By your grace, I have heard various duties and methods of withdrawal."
O sinless one, all those whom you have seen were created by every deity.
Now, O best of Brahmins, I wish to hear of the power of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
you should tell me that which was experienced by you.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hereafter I shall describe the characteristics of the destruction of living beings, what signs are seen therein, and how the Kalpa is ordained.
Meteors fall accompanied by thunderclaps, and likewise there is an earthquake;
a rain of dust falls, and there is a terrible roar.
Yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—
all of them go to destruction when the end of the eon has arrived.
Mountains, oceans, rivers, various lakes,
trees, the remainder of all things, as well as the multitude of creepers and grasses, all come together [into Śeṣa].
For when the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, had thus fallen into disorder, abandoned by all medicinal herbs and water, and had become like mere wood; RKV_20.7 //
When the time for bathing had arrived at midday, I beheld the three worlds appearing like a blazing fire, difficult to look upon and difficult to approach.
"O dear one, two suns were seen in the east, and likewise in the west and the north;
similarly, two scorching suns were seen in the south."
Two suns are situated in the world of the Nagas and two in the midst of the sky;
thus these twelve Adityas scorch in every direction.
He burned the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves;
nothing remained unseen by his fire except for Revā and myself.
When the earth is being scorched, the scent of oblation arises;
from that my limbs wither, and thus thirst becomes difficult to overcome.
Indeed, I find no water; it has been dried up by the suns.
As soon as I look into my water-pot, that water there too has become dry.
Then, tormented by grief and especially afflicted by hunger and thirst, I leaped upward from the earth, gazing toward the heavens.
Then, O best of kings, I beheld a house adorned with ornaments in the sky; desiring to know it, I set out from there.
He approached the gateway, which was adorned with various gates and bolts, and possessed a variegated pinnacle, all set within a multicolored wall.
It is eighty-six thousand yojanas in height, and half of that in width; it is made of gold and adorned with jewels.
There, in the center, O best of kings, I saw a supreme bed,
and upon that bed a man with celestial hair lying down.
With the tips of his hair curling upward, his entire body extended for a yojana,
and he was adorned with a variegated crown that was radiant and beautiful.
Dark-complexioned, with the luster of a lotus petal, radiant and possessing a beautiful nose,
he had a lion-like face, long arms, and was distinguished by a fine beard on his cheeks.
Beautiful with the three folds [of his neck], adorned with earrings,
possessing broad eyes and well-filled limbs, and graced by curls on his flanks.
The god was adorned with a well-proportioned waist and divided knees and shanks; his soles were marked with lotuses, and his toes and nails were beautifully copper-colored.
I beheld the God, the Supreme Person, lying upon his bed, possessing a voice as deep as a thundercloud and beautiful in every limb.
With his right hand, he holds a conch, a discus, and a mace while reclining;
with his [other] hand raised holding a rosary, he possesses a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Having seen him, the devotee stood desiring to praise the God:
"Victory to you, O Lord! Victory to you, O Master of Speech! Victory to you, whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments!"
Victory to you, O glorious Lord of gods, the eternal Brahman manifest!
All worlds abide within your body; you are the ultimate goal, O Supreme Lord.
For all the worlds, O Lord of Gods, are established with you as their support;
you are the most excellent of all beings, the creator, and the upholder of the earth.
You are the office of the Hotṛ priest for the Agnihotra sacrifices, and you alone are the Sūtra and the Mantras;
you are Gokarṇa and Bhadrakarṇa, and you are the state of Maheśvara.
You are the glory of all glories, the destroyer of wretchedness and sin;
you are Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and the supreme Viṣṇupada.
O Lord, the earth was traversed by your feet with ease;
O Lord, Bali was bound by you, and the position of Indra was established by you.
O God, you are Kali, Dvāpara, Tretā, and likewise Kṛtayuga;
you are the subduer of Pralamba, you are the creator, and you are the bringer of destruction.
By you indeed are the worlds sustained; you are Time, the destroyer of all.
For by you, O God, were all those divine origins created.
You are the path for all worlds, and you are liberation, the supreme goal.
The eternal god Brahmā, whose nature is passion (rajas), originates from you;
likewise, Rudra, who arises from anger, is also thus, while you are established in goodness (sattva).
"O Lord, this world of moving and non-moving beings was created by you for the sake of sport.
Thus was the Lord, the Master, praised by me with my body thus tormented.
O King, with supreme devotion, I beheld the Lord, the Master of all beings, there praising him while holding jars filled with water.
Then the thirst that I had forgotten increased once more;
I drew near to the side of that man indeed.
Furthermore, when I desired to drink water, I thought again:
"He does not see me; even though he is asleep, he does not wake up."
But he who, deluded by evil, awakens one who is sleeping soundly,
incurs the great fruit of the murder of a Brahmin for that sin.
While he was reflecting thus, a second man indeed arrived; he did not look at her, nor did he say anything, as she sat with a deer-skin over her left shoulder.
Wearing matted hair, carrying a water-pot and a staff, girt with a sacred thread-belt,
his entire body smeared with ashes, he possessed great splendor and had three eyes.
Just as I, desiring to praise him, beheld him with my clear eyes,
so too did I behold him with a magnificent perfection of form, produced from every limb.
I saw a woman veiled, adorned with all her ornaments;
having seen her, I fell to the ground, then saying, "May you be victorious!"
Victory to you, O Rudrāṅgasambhūtā! Victory, O eternal Vāhinī!
Victory to you, O Kaumārī, Māhendrī, Vaiṣṇavī, and likewise Vāruṇī!
Victory to you, Kauberī Sāvitrī! Victory to you, Dhātrī of the beautiful countenance!
Grant protection to this body scorched by thirst throughout the world of the moving and the unmoving.
The Goddess said:
"O tiger among Brahmins, I am pleased by your most beautiful words; O best of the twice-born, that which is in your mind is known by me."
Listen, O Brahmin, I too have undertaken this most formidable vow; out of feminine frailty, it was begun by me, one of dull intellect, though it is difficult to perform. (RKV 20.46)
"If my future son is righteous and world-renowned,
then after giving the breast to the brahmin, I shall give it to the child."
"That son has been born to me, O great sage, exactly as you described. Drink from my breast, O chief of brahmins, if you wish to live. (RKV 20.48)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: This is an improper act for Brahmins: he who drinks from this breast must undergo the initiation ceremony (upanayana) once again, yet he shall not attain perfection in his vows.
O lotus-eyed one, the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain even in the three worlds; hear now those purificatory rites by which a Brahmin, having been consecrated, is born.
And first, among women, there is the sowing of seed by means of purificatory rites;
because of that very casting of the seed, it is called "the casting of the seed" (bījakṣepa).
And at the end of that, O highly fortunate lady, the second rite is the impregnation (garbhādhāna);
the third is the male-making rite (puṃsavana), and the fourth is the parting of the hair (sīmanta).
The fifth [rite] should be the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), while the naming ceremony is said to be the sixth;
the seventh is the going-forth (niṣkrāma), and the eighth is the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana).
The ninth is indeed the rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma), and the tenth is the tying of the girdle of muñja grass (mauñjībandhana);
likewise, there are those pertaining to the iṣīkā reed, the wood (dāru), the Soma sacrifice, and the earth.
Furthermore, there is the rite for joining with a wife, and after that, the divine rite;
the human rite consists of the ancestral rites (śrāddha) performed on the eighth and tenth lunar days, O beautiful one.
Then follow the Bhūta, the Bhavya, the Iṣṭa, and after that, the Pārvaṇa.
The Śrāddha, the Āgrayaṇa on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, and [the sacrifices] on the full moons of Caitra and Āśvayuja—these constitute ten full-moon rites;
as do the Nirūḍhapaśu, the Soma-sacrifices, the Sautrāmaṇī, the Agniṣṭoma, and the Atyagniṣṭoma.
The sixteen [sacrifices] are the Vājapeya, Atirātra, Aptoryāma, and ten Vājapeyas;
forbearance toward all beings, freedom from envy, purity, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of possessiveness.
One who is refined by these forty-eight purificatory rites becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
Knowing this, O illustrious lady, you ought not to let me drink;
O blessed one, how indeed could one such as I drink from a breast intended for an infant?
Having heard these words of mine, the woman spoke this speech.
"If you do not drink the breast milk, the child will die;
this is heard in the three worlds, in the Vedas, and even in the Smṛtis:
one is released from all sins, yet the killing of an embryo does not release itself."
Furthermore, O great devotee of the Lord, you shall incur the sin of killing;
for eight hundred births, you shall suffer on account of that slaughter of an embryo.
Upon death, he attains the state of a dog for three hundred years;
then, when that period has come to an end, he enters the womb of a crow once again.
There too, for eight hundred lifetimes, he suffers for his evil deeds;
