for ten births he is born as a boar, and at the end of that time, he becomes a worm.
Then, O scorcher of foes, having reached Rohiṇī, he is heard of in the Śruti scriptures and the Vedas as one who takes birth among cattle, elephants, horses, and humans.
O best of the twice-born, the killing of a child is a sin greater than all other sins;
a Brahmin who has committed the murder of a child will certainly be cooked in hell.
For eight hundred years one undergoes the torments of Yama;
therefore, the fault of my drinking from your breast is but slight.
In the same way, for one who drinks [the milk], sin arises that lasts for many years;
yet for one who drinks from the breast, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst, as well as merit.
Therefore, you should never entertain any doubt in this matter;
come, O Brahmin, and drink from my breast for the sake of the child, as you desire.
Then, having heard those words, I prepared to drink from the breast;
yet I felt no satiety even as I drank from that excellent breast.
O Bhārata, for thirty thousand years and hundreds more,
I remained thus on the lap of the Awakened One, deluded by the sleep of Māyā.
O Pāṇḍava, as soon as my delusion had vanished upon waking from sleep,
I did not see him asleep, nor, O Lord, did I see that boy.
And there, O Bhārata, I saw four jars, yet I did not see that goddess; she had indeed gone somewhere or other.
As he remained thus reflecting and contemplating,
the goddess spoke these words to him with a gentle smile.
The Goddess said:
"O best of the twice-born, that man who was asleep is Kṛṣṇa; the second who arrived is Hara; and those four jars are the oceans."
The child whom you saw is Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds;
and I am to be known as the entire earth with its seven continents.
O Brahmin, she who departed from you and became firmly established upon the earth— behold her here, Narmadā, the best of rivers.
For the sake of benefiting all beings, she is characterized by vast merit;
thus the river Revā is renowned, and for that reason Narmadā is not dead.
"Knowing this, attain tranquility and be at ease, O great sage.
Having spoken thus to me, the goddess then vanished on the spot.

For in this way the Blessed One, the Great God, who is of the nature of *sattva*, always rests during the dissolution of the world, established in *sattva* upon that foundation whereon the universe is situated.
"Thus have I experienced and seen this supreme marvel; it is meritorious and removes all sins, O best of men, as I have related it to you. (RKV 20.82)
The account of Viṣṇu’s deeds, which was requested by you, has been told;
O mighty-armed one, what else do you wish to hear further?

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Events of the Vārāha Kalpa," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāsāra, Chapter 21.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, by your grace I have heard various wonders."
Furthermore, I wish to hear more; tell that to me, O observer of noble vows.
O sinless one, tell me further how this river named Narmadā is so famous, being meritorious and the most excellent among all rivers.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins;
she delivers all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind as I shall relate to you that greatness of the Narmadā which was previously heard by me. (RKV 21.4)
The Gaṅgā is sacred at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
but the Narmadā is sacred everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest.
The water of the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, that of the Yamunā in seven days, that of the Gaṅgā immediately, and that of the Narmadā by the mere sight of it.
In the western part of the Kaliṅga country, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
there is a sacred place, beautiful at every step, renowned throughout the three worlds.
There, O great king, gods, gandharvas, and seers whose wealth is asceticism, having performed penance, attained supreme perfection.
Having bathed there, O King, a man who is observant of his vows and has conquered his senses,
by fasting for a single night, shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
O dear one, the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka is indeed a supreme field of accomplishment,
for it is the refuge of all the gods and is frequented by the ṛṣis.
O King of kings, perfected Vidyādharas, Bhūtas, and Gandharvas— both visible and invisible— frequent that supreme abode, desiring spiritual accomplishment.
And from that time forth, I have resorted to that supreme abode;
for here, in the form of the *praṇava*, the Lord of Umā indeed dwells in this place.
O King, Śrīkaṇṭha, together with his attendants and served by the hosts of all beings, has departed from this best of mountains; I shall now describe the full extent of that sacred site.
O best of kings, whatever sacred fords exist here, and whatever fords there are on both banks of the Narmadā; RKV_21.14
O Lord of the Earth, even Brahmā would not be able to describe their extent in detail;
it is heard that this supreme river extends for more than a hundred yojanas.
But in detail, O Indra among kings, it is half a yojana in length,
and there are sixty thousand and likewise sixty million sacred fords (tīrtha).
From the mountain to the ocean, both shores [are reached] without a doubt.
The Wind-god declared that there are sixty-seven thousand, sixty-seven hundred,
and sixty-seven million sacred fords (tīrthas).
But in the Kṛtayuga, O King, those [virtues] become manifest; all human beings, whose minds are constantly fixed on dharma, perceive them directly.
O King, to whatever extent the terrible and cruel Kali age prevails,
to that same extent men of inferior character fall into decline.
O lord of men, they say that the holy sites on this mountain, beginning with Jāleśvara,
bestow satisfaction upon the ancestors and grant both heaven and liberation.
The Dāruvana forest there is excellent, where the confluence of the Caru is auspicious;
and to the north of the Narmadā is the supreme Carukeśvara.
And Dārukeśvara-tīrtha, as well as Vyatīpāteśvara;
Pātāleśvara-tīrtha, and likewise Koṭiyajña.
And thus, O best of kings, on the northern bank of the Revā,
by the side of Amareśvara, there are one hundred and eight liṅgas.
And those headed by Varuṇeśvara are removers of all sins.
Near the city of Māndhātṛ are Siddheśvara and Yameśvara;
and to the east of Oṃkāra is Kedāra, the most excellent sacred site (tīrtha).
Near that, O Great King, is the meritorious Svargadvāra, which destroys sins; in front of it is the holy place named Brahmeśvara, known as Saptasārasvata.
The Rudrāṣṭaka, the Sāvitra, and likewise the Somatīrtha—
these, O bull of the Bharatas, are on the southern bank of the Revā.
But on this mountain, my dear, tens of millions of Rudras reside;
they become satisfied by baths, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
O King, there is no doubt that even the Rudras become pleased with one here;
through recitation, there is purification from sin, and through meditation, one attains infinity.
"Through generosity one obtains enjoyments"— thus spoke Śaṅkara himself,
the god Maheśvara, who stands in the region to the west of the mountain as the eternal origin of the universe in the form of the *praṇava*.
Having bathed there, become pure, remaining celibate and with senses subdued,
one should perform the ancestral rites according to the procedure prescribed by the rules.
With water mixed with sesame seeds, one should satisfy the ancestral deities right there;
his lineage up to the seventh generation rejoices in heaven, O Pāṇḍava.
Together with his own self, he, being happy, obtains various enjoyments;
honored by the gods, he sports for sixty thousand years.
Rejoicing for a very long time through the fruit of honoring his ancestors,
he then, having fallen from heaven, is born into a pure family.
Possessing wealth, being of a generous disposition, free from disease, and honored by the world,
he remembers that sacred ford again and makes the journey there once more.
In his second birth, he shall become a fierce attendant of Hradod;
likewise, by means of celibacy, fasting, and mastery over the senses, [he attains this].
But he who abstains from all violence obtains the highest fruit;
likewise, he who would give up his life while practicing such righteous conduct [attains the same].
O lord of men, listen now to the fruit of that merit:
for a hundred thousand years, O Pāṇḍava, he rejoices in heaven.
In that place crowded with throngs of Apsarases and echoing with divine sounds,
his limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments.
Praised by the Siddhas and Gandharvas, he sports together with the gods;
then, having descended from heaven, he becomes a powerful king.
The knower of dharma, devoted to the scriptures, possessed elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles;
he dwelt in a golden house filled with hundreds of pillars and adorned with silver.
At the great gateway of the seven or eight stories, crowded with male and female servants,
it resounded with the exhalations of rutting elephants and the neighing of horses.
That gateway of his trembles like the realm of Indra;
he is the illustrious lord of the kings of kings, beloved by all women.
Having dwelt in that house, endowed with play and enjoyments,
he shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases.
Thus it shall be for all those who have died at Amareśvara;
and whoever should enter the fire with devotion at Amarakaṇṭaka.
Having died, he attains heaven and shall go to the supreme goal;
[for him], bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, or whatever is auspicious or even inauspicious [bears fruit].
O King, it is heard in the Purāṇas that everything [offered] there becomes ten millionfold;
and as for those trees on its banks that have fallen with the passage of time, [they too yield great merit].
Touched by the waters of the Narmadā, they go to the supreme goal;
their course is irreversible, like that of the wind in the sky.
O lord of men, he who performs a ritual immersion at that sacred site becomes the enjoyer of the company of three thousand maidens in the netherworld.
They remain in his palace and wait for his command;
well-endowed with divine enjoyments, he sports there for the duration of time.
Indeed, on this earth as far as the ocean, no one such as this best of men, Parvata Amarakaṇṭaka, has ever been born.
In that place, to the west of the mountain, there is to be known a sacred ford (tīrtha),
a lake named Jāleśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds.
In that regard, by the offering of funeral cakes and by the performance of the twilight worship,
the ancestors indeed remain satisfied for twelve years.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the great river Kapilā,
covered with *sarala* and *arjuna* trees and adorned with *khadira* trees.
It was further adorned with *mādhavī* and *sallakī* creepers,
as well as by roaring beasts of prey, jackals, monkeys, and the like.
O King, it is always filled with various species of birds;
we have heard that there are more than a hundred million sages dwelling there.
Having performed austerities, they have gone to liberation, such that there is neither birth nor return for them;
it was by that high-souled Kapila that austerity was practiced there.
There, O dear one, that sacred ford came into being, frequented by the Siddhas,
which was formerly resorted to by the Kapila sages.
Therefore, that [place] named Kapilā is sung as the destroyer of evil;
there, at Amareśvara, are more than a hundred crores of sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having fasted for a day and night, one is liberated from all sins,
provided that one has given a gift according to the rules and to the best of one's ability to an excellent twice-born man.
Through the grace of the Lord, everything there becomes ten-million-fold superior;
for here on earth, O Bhārata, the form of the Praṇava is beyond syllables.
Then, for one whose nature is Śiva, there arises the syllable consisting of a single mātrā;
this includes animals, beasts, trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth.
They too, having reached their end there, go to heaven without a doubt;
for the river called Viśalyā that is mentioned there is indeed a great river.
Having bathed and given according to the rule, one would become a doer of good even there;
for all the hosts of gods, along with the kinnaras and mahoragas, are present there.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism—
all of them gathered there and beheld her indeed at Amareśvara.
And having all come together, they paid homage to those two auspicious hips in a former age that was most terrible and terrifying to all the worlds.
There, the son of Narmadā was freed from his dart;
because he was made free of the dart by all the gods and sages, that place is known as Viśalyā.

the water that issued forth at that time—

The Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Revā, and likewise the Yamunā;

Seeing her son approaching, mangled by a flood of weapons,
Narmadā, whose waters are meritorious, rose up in great astonishment.
Embracing him with her arms, her breasts pressed by her flowing milk,
she took her son who was pierced by arrows and entered the Kāpila lake.
As soon as he had entered the Kapila lake, which destroys all sins,
she then instantly rendered him free from his thorn, even though he was still pierced by it.
Because he became free from his dart upon reaching her auspicious waters,

Others also who bathe there, being pure and composed, are liberated from the thorns of evil; upon death, they go to the abode of the gods.
O dear lord of men, I have now explained all of this that you previously asked me regarding the cause of Viśalyā’s birth.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Origin of Viśalyā," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 23. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, at that very confluence, those mortals who give up their lives with supreme devotion go to the highest state.

The man who, having reached Śailendra, gives up his life there,
shall go to Amarāvatī in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
Seeing the man falling from Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
all the apsarases cried out, "May he become my husband!"
Those who know the Dharma declare that water is equal; the awakened ones say it is the same whether from the Sarasvatī or the Gaṅgā.

Whatever fruit is obtained through bathing and giving gifts throughout the earth bounded by the oceans,

Thus, O King, this meritorious and purifying [account] has been told to you;

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Confluence of the Viśalyā," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 24. The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At the confluence of the Kara and Narmadā rivers in the city named after Māndhātṛ,
one who goes there, bathes, and offers libations to the ancestors shall lead them to the city of Viṣṇu.
Having first rubbed his hands together with the desire to slay the Daitya, Viṣṇu seized the discus right there; from that very sweat, the best of rivers was born.
Having bathed there at the confluence with the Revā, one is liberated from sins.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Confluence of Kara and Narmadā," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

One shall dwell in the city of Nīlakaṇṭha for sixty thousand years.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Confluence of the Nīlagaṅgā," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

"Let us all go to that very place where the god Maheśvara is;

The gods said:

O God, the fivefold body is celebrated by the Brahmins as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Īśāna, and Tatpuruṣa.
"O Hara, you cry out like a swan within this vast expanse of golden net.

Gold, silver, jewels, pearls,

For the sake of destroying existence and non-existence, O Bhava, I take refuge in you. For what purpose have you been meditated upon, O God? O Lord, let your command be given to me.

With whom shall I join in strife today, O best among victors?
Having heard the words of Nārada, Maheśvara, the God of gods, his eyes wide with wonder, spoke these words:

"Go quickly, Nārada, to where that great Tripura of Bāṇa, the lord of the Dānavas, who brings fear to all the worlds, is located."

"O best of the twice-born, it cannot be divided by any means whatsoever;

Nārada said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your word I shall cause dissension in that supreme city,

Having spoken thus, O King, he went to that preeminent city of Bāṇa, extending for a hundred yojanas and endowed with prosperity and growth.
It was crowded with festive decorations, variegated with various minerals,

Bāṇa’s supreme city was thus filled with a multitude of excellent qualities.
In its center was Bāṇa’s divine palace, of massive proportions, adorned with seven courtyards, most beautiful, and entirely embellished with gold.
Abounding in the splendor of pearl necklaces, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,

Devoted to her husband, of auspicious conduct, and endowed with truthfulness and purity—

Regarding the Lord of the World, the Sun, the God of gods— the merit that has indeed been described for him by the best of the twice-born— [that fruit he obtains].
O Queen, I shall explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind, O virtuous lady:
ringworm, leucoderma, leprosy, circular patches, and scabies.
Nor do the [defects] acquired through previous karma appear here in her limbs,
for that beautiful woman who bestows a black cow on the eighth lunar day.
"If a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtuous conduct is pleased, may Maheśvara be gracious to me;
the sins accumulated by her throughout her births shall perish, and she shall be endowed with prosperity. (RKV 26.116)
There is no doubt that this arises because giving is unsurpassed;
for whatever woman should cause fragrant incense to be given with devotion to a brahmin, [she attains such merit].
Listen to the fruit that accrues from dedicating [a rite] to Kātyāyanī on the ninth day:
her brother, father, son, or husband shall attain the highest victory in battle.
O Goddess, she who offers the juice of the sugarcane stalk on the tenth day attains [this state]; protected by that gift, they do not perish.
Having dedicated [the gift] to the world-protectors (lokapāla) through a Brahmin who is free from physical defects,
she became forever beloved by the entire world because of that gift.
"This shall come to pass; there is no doubt about this," Śaṅkara said thus:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should then offer water on the twelfth."
Aiming for Nārāyaṇa, she should always cause people to melt and be transformed through touch and conversation with a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to Viṣṇu.

For a gift given to a twice-born man with a specific desire for [the attainment of] Maharloka becomes indeed infinite in water; likewise, anointing the feet or anointing the head [given with such intent]. (RKV 26.123)
And on the thirteenth day, a woman gives [this] with supreme devotion;
in whatever womb she may die and be born again in a future birth, [she shall attain that state].

nevertheless, on the fourteenth day, one should likewise give a vessel and sandals.
For one who intends to offer dharma to Brahmā, his worlds are indeed free from affliction;
likewise, at the end of each fortnight, he should gratify the best of the twice-born with a śrāddha.
O Queen, an uninterrupted lineage is always born upon this earth;
thus has the greatness of this lunar day been described to you in connection with the practice of giving.
Likewise, hear now the procedure for propitiating the lords of the forest:
the *jambū*, the *nimba* tree, the *tinduka*, and likewise the *madhuka*.
The mango, the emblic myrobalan, the silk-cotton tree, the banyan and the holy fig, the *śamī*, the *bilva*, the *āmalī* tree, the plantain, and likewise the trumpet-flower tree.
Having approached other most meritorious trees, one shall attain heaven.
Nārada said:
Whatever woman performs this unsurpassed vow in the month of Caitra,
other vows do not equal even a sixteenth part of that vow.
O fortunate one, by means of that sacred learning through which one does not behold misfortune,
it dissolves upon the earth just as snow dissolves upon reaching the sun.
Likewise, suffering and misfortune are dissolved by this vow,
provided that one indeed propitiates Lalitā, who is known as Madhukā.
O fortunate lady, listen to that rite being described, which brings happiness:
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having bathed well and with a pure mind, [one should perform it].
Having had an image of Śaṅkara together with Umā made from a Madhūka tree,
and having had it consecrated according to the rules by the best of the twice-born;
O beautiful woman, she should worship the God according to the prescribed rite with fragrant flowers, incense, camphor, and saffron, accompanied by the mantra.
One should worship the feet with "Obeisance to Śiva," the genitals with "To Manmatha," the belly with "To Kālodara," and the throat with "To Nīlakaṇṭha."
Having worshipped the head for the Universal Self (Sarvātman), one should thereafter worship Umā;
then the belly for Kṣāmodarā, and the throat for Sukandhā.
One should offer the head [of the vessel] to Saubhāgyadāyinī, and thereafter cause the arghya offering to be presented.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Consort of Umā, O Master of the world!

After offering the *arghya*, he should then present a water-pot filled with water,
containing a vessel of *madhūka* flowers, and accompanied by gold according to his ability.

"A water-pot filled with water and endowed with auspiciousness has been given to you, O Lalitā; it increases [your] fortune and other blessings. Thus is the mantra for the gift of the water-pot. (RKV 26.142)
With this mantra, one should give an excellent water-pot to a Brahmin;
one should avoid salt until the next third lunar day of the bright fortnight.
Having asked the queen, the mistress of the gods, for forgiveness, he himself should eat the sacrificial oblation at night;
according to this rule, he should proceed month after month.
It is completed on the third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna;
salt should be given in Vaiśākha, and clarified butter is offered in Jyeṣṭha.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, flat beans and milk should be given; in Śrāvaṇa, mung beans should be given;
and likewise, in Nabhasya and Āśvayuja, śāli rice.
In Kārttika, one should give a vessel of sugar and a water-pot filled with juice;
but in Mārgaśīrṣa, a cotton garment and a water-pot combined with ghee.
In the month of Pauṣa, saffron should be given; in Māgha, a vessel filled with sesame seeds;
and when the month of Phālguna has arrived, a vessel filled with sweetmeats (modaka).
O beloved of the mind, that which is to be given on the third day should be avoided on the preceding day; this is the general rule for all of these [observances].
One should worship that very image of the Madhuvṛkṣa tree;
all of this is then bestowed upon that brahmin who serves as the preceptor.
Then, at the end of the year, hear the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana):
having gone to a honey-tree (madhuvṛkṣa), one should be provided with many ritual materials.
One should bury a Madhūka image in the center of the Madhūka tree;
situated there, one should worship the entire [deity] who bears half of Umā’s body.
With abundant offerings for worship, repeatedly with saffron, with smooth flower garlands, and with safflower and filaments; RKV_26.153 //
Having clothed that image in two bright saffron-colored garments resembling the color of flax flowers, the couple [should offer] [garments] numbering as many as the sun (twelve).
With pairs of sandals, parasols, necklaces together with throat-ornaments, bracelets, finger-rings, and beds covered with beautiful spreads; RKV 26.155.
With their limbs smeared with saffron and honored with many flowers,
one should feed them various foods and jewels while they remain in a dwelling of madhūka trees.
But having risen from the meal and rested upon their beds, one should ask forgiveness;
for everything has its root in the Guru, and the Guru is to be known as Maheśvara.
When the Guru is pleased, then the entire world, including gods and asuras, is pleased;
whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is dear within one's home.
All that should be given to the teacher by one who desires his own welfare;
however, this [gift] is to be given by the wealthy, while others should give as prescribed.
Having duly honored the first couple according to the rules with auspicious observances,
one should honor the second— the Guru’s couple— while avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
Then one should ask forgiveness from the Goddess, the God, the Brahmin, and the Guru, [saying]:
"O Goddess Lalitā, just as you are never separated from Śambhu..."
"In this manner, having performed the third rite known as Madhu, let non-separation from my husband and sons be granted to me."
And Indrāṇī attained the status of Indra’s wife, as well as an excellent son,
good fortune in all the worlds, and the highest happiness of every prosperity.
A maiden who observes this vow according to this rule obtains an excellent husband, just as Śatakratu obtained Indrāṇī.
An unfortunate woman attains good fortune, and a fortunate woman becomes the mother of sons;
one who has sons attains inexhaustible [merit] and never encounters sorrow.
The misfortune born of many lifetimes is certainly destroyed;
having died, she attains the third heaven and rejoices together with Umā.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures for more than a hundred million eons,
she shall again be born in the world and obtain a king as her husband.
Fortunate and endowed with beauty, she shall give birth to a son who is a king.
All this has been told to you, the most excellent of all vows.
Ask something else, O fortunate one, whatever desire resides in your heart.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ritual for the Madhūka-tṛtīyā Vow," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 27.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the queen spoke these words.
"O best of Brahmins, show favor; accept this gift as you desire."
O best of brahmins, I shall give you gold, jewels, gems, and various kinds of garments, as well as whatever else is difficult to obtain.
Having heard the queen's words, Nārada spoke these words:
"O blessed lady, let this be given to others—those twice-born ones whose means of subsistence are exhausted."
"But we are endowed with all perfections and are always worthy of being received with devotion.
Having spoken thus, the queen then [summoned] those who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having summoned the indigent Brahmins,
he began to give whatever Nārada had described as increasing both generosity and good fortune.
"By this gift, may Hari and Śaṅkara be forever pleased with me.
Then that queen spoke to Nārada, the bull among sages.
The queen said:
"O best of the twice-born, that gift which you have spoken of is indeed centered on the duty toward one's husband; therefore, may Bāṇa be my husband throughout all my births from birth until death."
"For there is no other deity, O dear one, O best of the twice-born, except for Bāṇa;
by that truth, may my husband live for a hundred autumns."
For there can be no other deity for women than their husband;
nevertheless, at your word, the gift has been bestowed according to the prescribed rite.
"O giver of honor, O Brahman-sage, we shall perform our own duty toward our husband; you may go now, and let your blessing be bestowed."
Saying "So be it," Nārada took leave of her, O best of kings;
having captivated the minds of them all, his own mind was now fixed elsewhere.
Being honored by the sky-dwellers, the brahmin vanished from sight;
then, O Bhārata, their minds turned away from their husband.
Deprived of their splendor by Nārada, they became pale and bewildered.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Agitating of Tripura," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the twenty-eighth chapter of the Rukmāṅgavadha,
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the meantime, Rudra was stationed on the bank of the Narmadā.
For he was sporting together with Umā when Nārada arrived there.
Having prostrated before Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, together with Umā,
he then informed the God of what had occurred at Tripura.
At my master’s command, I went to where that palace of Bāṇa was;
having seen Bāṇa according to protocol, I entered the great inner apartments.
There, having seen the thousands of wives of the wise Bāṇa,
he entered that city, agitating it according to his desire and as was appropriate.
Having heard Nārada’s words and honoring them by exclaiming, "Excellent!
Excellent!", the Lord of the Gods reflected upon the wandering of Tripura.
Just as the discus released by the powerful Viṣṇu possesses great speed and great extent, so too is this [discus] protected by my own splendor.
And that Bāṇa is devoted to me and renowned in the world;
moreover, the power of speech has been granted by me especially to the Brahmins.
Thus, for a very long time, Maheśvara,
the god of gods and lord of men, reflected upon the matter of the supreme nirvāṇa.
Then the three-eyed god, having meditated upon Mandara, placed it on his bow; having fixed the earth upon the string, he meditated upon the eternal god Viṣṇu as the arrow.
One should visualize the god Hutāśana blazing with faces on all sides at the arrowhead,
Suparṇa between the two feathers, and Vāyu in the flight.
Having fashioned a chariot made of earth, he placed both Aśvins at the yoke,
the Lord of the Gods (Indra) upon the axle, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) on the front pin.
On the right side he placed Yama, and on the left, the most terrible Kāla;
he placed the Sun and Moon upon the wheels, and the Gandharvas among the spokes and other parts.
Having made the Vedas the excellent horses, he made the Charioteer the Eldest of the Gods (Brahmā),
the limbs [of the body] the bits and so forth, and the Vedic meters the reins.
Having made the syllable Oṃ his goad to be held in his mouth, Maheśvara placed Dhātṛ in front and Vidhātṛ behind him.
From the wind [region], from all directions, from above, and likewise from the mechanical devices,
[he drew forth] the great serpents and piśācas, as well as the siddhas and vidyādharas.
And all the hosts of Gaṇas and multitudes of spirits [are located] in all the joints of his limbs;
Mount Meru stands in the middle of his arms, and the great mountain [Mahāmeru] is beneath his arms.
Terrible serpents stationed upon the mechanical device were at the two yoke-pins belonging to Varuṇa and Nairṛti; Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī stood at the two fastenings of the reins.
Having fashioned a divine chariot with truth as its banner, purity, self-restraint, and protection on all sides, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [mounted it].
Girt with armor, bearing a sword, and having fastened his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors,
he tightened his waistband and bound up his mass of matted hair.
Having prepared his divine bow and yoked his excellent chariot,
the god stood in the middle of the chariot and shone resplendently, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
With the resonant sound of his bow, he caused the three worlds to tremble;
then Hara, assuming the vaiśākha stance, stood there motionless.
Having gazed for a very long time with eyes bloodshot with anger,
he meditated upon that supreme mantra and restrained himself.
Desiring the destruction of the city, he suddenly released an arrow when the three [objects] had come together while stationed in the intermediate space.
Then, having observed the convergence of Tripura for half a moment of time,
he destroyed them with his three-jointed, triple-pointed arrow.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the worlds were terrified by fear in Tripura;
appearing in the form of Time, they were terrifying and destined for the destruction of all the asuras.
At that time, men of terrible appearance let out loud bursts of laughter,
and they even perform the act of blinking their eyes as if in paintings.
Mortals have motionless eyes as if painted in a picture;
the gods dwelling in temples laugh and shriek;
and in dreams they see themselves adorned in red garments.
And falling into a muddy pool with their heads adorned with red garlands,
they perceive themselves indeed with their heads smeared with oil.
O best of kings, they see him mounted upon a vehicle drawn by donkeys,
while the great Saṃvartaka wind, like that at the end of an eon, blows fiercely.
He uprooted houses and numerous species of trees;
there were earthquakes accompanied by thunderclaps and thousands of falling meteors.
The god rains down blood mixed with many pebbles,
while the sacrificial fire is properly offered into the fire-pits of the brahmins.
It blazes forth, joined with smoke and accompanied by sparks;
the elephants have become devoid of their rut, and the horses are stripped of their vigor.
Musical instruments, though unplayed, resounded by the thousands; banners that had been motionless fell down, as did various kinds of parasols.
There the trees blazed, and the leaves fell along with the assembly hall;
everything there became utterly chaotic, filled with cries of "Alas! and "Woe!"
The wind-god shattered the various gardens;
impelled by him, all the flames of the arrows blazed forth.
The fire spread everywhere— among the trees, shrubs, creepers, and vines, and even through the houses—
in all directions and quarters.
Everything appeared blazing, resembling the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers;
at that time, it was not even possible to go from house to house because of the smoke.
Burnt by the fire of Hara’s wrath, the people in Tripura cry out;
Tripura itself is utterly consumed, blazing in every direction.
The shattered peaks fall by the thousands;
the fire, mingled with smoke, burns on all sides.
Dancing indeed, pervading all directions and regions, he runs through the forests,
into all the temples of the gods, into houses, and onto watchtowers.
There, impelled by Time and incited by the wrath of Hara, the consumer of oblations (Agni) set forth and burned all the worlds everywhere in that city.
O King, it consumes the triple-world, including the young and the old,
along with its cities, houses, and gates, as well as its vehicles and forests.
Some were addicted to food, others likewise to drink;
and other courtesans were devoted to dancing and singing.
Embracing one another, O best of kings, they all go forth unconscious, being scorched and tormented by the flames of the fire.
Then other Dānavas there were consumed, bewildered by the fire;
with their faces overwhelmed by smoke, they were unable to go elsewhere.
[They resembled] lotus ponds filled with golden lotuses and crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.
O Bhārata, various ponds and wells there are being consumed by fire;
city gardens and oblong lakes are seen burnt by the flames,
yet they remain covered with unfading lotuses and extend for many yojanas.
There, palaces resembling mountain peaks, adorned with jewels,
are seen burnt by fire and shattered upon the surface of the earth.
While men, women, children, and the elderly were being consumed on all sides, the fire blazed mercilessly; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
O best of kings, some woman was sleeping soundly in comfort while others were heedless.
And a certain beautiful woman with large eyes, adorned with strings of pearls, having played and reclined upon a very spacious bed,
fell into the fire, distressed and bewildered by the smoke.
In that blazing city, a certain woman, longing with affection for her son,
embraced him tightly as she was consumed by the fire in Tripura.
A certain woman, possessing a golden complexion and adorned with sapphire ornaments,
seeing her husband fallen, collapsed upon him.
O King, one woman, radiant as the color of the sun, having fallen asleep upon her beloved,
now clings tightly to his neck as if struck by a flame of fire.
Another woman, with a complexion like that of a lotus and wearing a shimmering golden girdle,
fell to the surface of the earth with a white cloth as her upper garment.
A certain woman, with a complexion like that of the kunda flower or the moon and adorned with blue jewels,
stood with her hands joined in reverence at her head and addressed the Fire-god.
O Bhārata, the garments of some women were ablaze, and the hair of others was aflame;
they were joined together with golden ornaments that resembled blazing fire.
A certain noble woman, afflicted by abundant suffering,
lamented upon seeing her husband reduced to ashes, wailing like a female osprey.
Embracing him tightly, another woman, afflicted by great sorrow, suddenly fell upon his head and lamented in her own home.
Seeing [the body] reduced to ashes, one woman wails like a female osprey; another, seeing her mother or father deprived of consciousness, likewise cries out.
A certain beautiful woman, tormented by the fire, fell to the ground trembling like a distressed mare, writhing here and there.
Standing with her face turned away, she did not see the child on her lap;
she saw only the house of Kumbhila, burnt down and fallen upon the surface of the earth.
And of Kūṣmāṇḍa and Dhūmra, of Kuhaka and Baka,
as well as of Virūpanayana and indeed Virūpākṣa.
Śumbha, Ḍimbha, Raudra, and Prahlāda, the best of asuras;
Daṇḍapāṇi, Vipāṇi, and Siṃhavaktra, O sinless one.
Dundubha, Saṃhrāda, Ḍiṇḍi, and likewise Muṇḍi;
Bāṇa’s brother and Bāṇa himself, as well as Kravyāda and Vyāghravaktra.
Likewise, O King, in the houses of any other Dānavas who are arrogant in their strength, fire blazes forth mercilessly; being consumed by the flames, O dear one, the women wail in every house.

O Fire, if you have harbored enmity toward the enemy of the gods, then why have you departed to the auspicious state, uttering words of compassion for the sake of this man? For such speech is without foundation.
What offense do women commit, these cuckoos in the cage of the household?
You are merciless and cruel; why do you harbor such anger toward a woman?
Have you not heard in the world that women are in every way inviolable?
Yet, there is indeed a quality in you that is fanned by the wind when set ablaze.
"You have shown no compassion nor any courtesy toward a woman;
for it is barbarians who show mercy upon seeing the words of women."
O Bhārata, even as those women were thus lamenting right there, a barbarian among barbarians— indeed, one who was senseless and difficult to restrain— arrived.
The fire blazed forth, abounding in masses of flames;
seeing this, Bāṇa, being consumed by the fire, then spoke.
"Having disregarded Hara, I, a wicked soul, have surely perished;
by me, a sinful fool, those worlds have certainly been destroyed."
Cows and Brahmins have been constantly slain here in this world and in the next;
likewise, food and drink have been destroyed, as well as monasteries, groves, and hermitages.
The hermitages of the seers, the groves of the gods, and the abodes of the divine hosts—
all these have been destroyed by that sin of mine, as has my ascetic power and my strength.
What shall I do with wealth, or with sovereignty, or with the inner apartments?
"O dull-witted one, it is better that I take refuge at the feet of Śaṅkara;
neither mother, nor father, nor kinsman, nor any other person [can save me]."
Having abandoned Maheśāna, the supreme remover of the highest affliction,
one must experience by oneself alone the evil deeds committed by oneself.
"But I, on the other hand, am being burned along with all the virtuous ones.
Having spoken thus, he fashioned an auspicious *liṅga* and placed it upon his head.
Enveloped by fire, he quickly emerged from the house;
distressed and with limbs perspiring, he stumbled again and again.
Praising Hara with a faltering voice, he indeed went for refuge, saying:
"O Śaṅkara, if I am to be slain, let me be consumed by the fire of your wrath."
"By your grace, O Mahādeva, let my *liṅga* not perish;
it has been worshipped by me with devotion, O Best of Gods, and meditated upon by me, O All-pervading Lord."
O God, life is most dear to me; therefore, you ought to protect it, whether I am worthy of your favor or deserving of death, O best of gods.
O Mahādeva, may my devotion to you remain unshakable in every birth;
even among animals, insects, birds, and those born of the animal realm,
by virtue of my own karma, O Mahādeva, may my devotion to you remain unshakable.
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, the illustrious Bāṇa, the best among the devoted, gratified the Lord of the gods with this hymn.
Bāṇa said: O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, salutations to the destroyer of all; salutations to the remover of the fear of those afflicted by the dread of worldly existence.
O God who caused the destruction of the body of the flower-armed one (Kāma), and who are beloved by women, salutations to you, the god of desire!
Victory to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, the essence of the supreme truth! Victory to you, who have fashioned a necklace of terrifying serpents!
Victory to you, whose limbs are smeared with pure ashes! Victory to you, the root of all mantras, the sole vessel of the universe!
Victory to you, whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a venomous serpent; victory to you who hold the Pināka bow, O Bhairava!
Victory to you who are liberated from attachment by your three eyes; victory to you, Śaṅkara, who bear the waves of the Ganges!

Victory to you of terrifying form, who hold the khaṭvāṅga staff in hand and wear the moon upon your crest! Victory to you, the most praiseworthy of all worlds! Victory to you, Lord of the source of happiness, the essence of the realm of the gods! Victory to you, the essence that consumes all things!
Victory to you, who are worthy of being celebrated by the worlds and are the purifier; victory to you, whose bull is your emblem and whose deeds are manifold!
Victory to you, who fashioned a garland of skeletons from the corpses of the demons, and who are the Death to the skeletal remains of the demon Aghāsura!
Victory to you, O Blue-throated One, whose gait is like that of a noble bull; victory to you, the pacifier of the misfortunes of all the worlds!
Victory to you, whose feet are bowed to by Siddhas, gods, and asuras; victory to you, O Rudra, who enables one to cross the terrible ocean of worldly existence!
Victory to you, O Lord of the Mountain, who are honored by the lords of the gods! Victory to you, whose subtle form is to be meditated upon!
Victory to you, who burnt the three cities and are the essence of all existence! Victory to you, the ultimate reality of all the scriptures!
Victory to you, O one difficult to comprehend, who delivers us from saṃsāra and ferries us across the terrible great ocean of the impurities of the Kali age!
Victory to you, Lord of the hosts of gods, asuras, and deities; homage to you whose faces are those of a horse, a monkey, a lion, and a lordly elephant!
Even for the gods, it is impossible to perceive Your form as being excessively short, stout, or exceedingly long;
I bow at Your stainless feet. Victory to You, O Sāmba, who steals away the splendor of beautiful eyes!
If you had not attained [this state], would not such extreme exaltation have brought about destruction?
For that great asceticism is exceedingly violent and most terrible.
Neither sons, nor kinsmen, nor wives, nor all one's circle of friends will accompany one when departing; they do not follow when one enters into the crisis of death, for each must travel alone.
Whatever action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— one has performed for the sake of isolation,
that alone becomes meaningful for one as they proceed forward.
For one who wanders about without wealth, no fear exists anywhere;
a wealthy man cannot be freed from fears. Therefore, I renounce wealth.
The greedy commit sins, whereas men of pure nature do not;
having heard the entire essence of Dharma and having understood it through reflection, [one should act accordingly].
You are Viṣṇu, you are the Lord of the World, the eternal embodiment of Brahman;
you are Indra, O Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the Suras—homage be to you!
You are the earth and Varuṇa, you are the wind and the consumer of oblations;
you are the consecration and the sacrificer, as well as space and the moon.
You are the sun, you are the lord of wealth, you are Yama, and you are indeed the preceptor;
by you the entire world and the three realms are pervaded, as if by the radiant light.
Having heard this hymn composed by Bāṇa, the god Maheśvara,
casting off his anger and with a tranquil mind, then spoke these words.
Īśvara said: "Do not fear, do not fear, O Dānava, from this day forward!
Either remain in a golden mansion or stay by my side."
"From this day forward, my child, together with your wife, sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and kinsmen, you shall be invincible against all enemies."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Furthermore, O Bhārata, another boon was granted to him by the God of gods:
"In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, you shall be honored by the gods and the asuras alike."
"Abide here as you please, for you are indeed imperishable and immutable.
Then Rudra restrained that seven-flamed fire.
The third city of his was protected by the god Śambhu;
the other, filled with garlands of flames, fell upon the surface of the earth.
From the point where it had risen halfway upward, its flames ascended to heaven;
there, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! was uttered by the hosts of sages.
And by the highly fortunate deities, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others,
one supreme fragment fell there upon Śrīśaila.
O King, the second fell upon the Amarakaṇṭaka mountain;
because it fell there blazing, it is known as Jvāleśvara.
When Tripura had been burnt, O King, and the supreme fragment had fallen,
the god Rudra remained there, warding off the garlands of flames.
And for the protection of the sages who were crying out in distress,
Maheśāna himself appeared in bodily form, accompanied by Umā and his bull.
Whoever remembers Amarakaṇṭaka even with the mind, out of devotion, shall obtain merit exceeding that of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the Bharatas, because this most meritorious and excellent mountain constantly effects the destruction of all sins, O King, it should always be visited.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with various flowers,
crowded with various shrubs and vines, and covered by various climbing plants.
Teeming with lions and tigers and adorned by herds of deer,
it was ever filled with joy by the roars of wild beasts.
On that mountain, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, is served by thousands of immortals, headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.
O King, he who performs a leap from this mountain Amarakaṇṭaka sports successively through the fourteen worlds.
The [regions] of Indra, Agni, Kubera, Vāyu, Yama,
Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Soma, and likewise of Sūrya.
The Brahma-pada, which is unafflicted, and immediately after that the Vaiṣṇava;
O highly fortunate one, the Umārudra and immediately after that the Aiśvara.
The steadfast one attains dissolution into that supreme Sadāśiva—the peaceful, subtle, and supersensuous light—by means of the prescribed method; of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of sages, some specific rule has been prescribed here regarding falling;
explain all of this to me, O great muni, for I have a doubt."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O son of Pāṇḍu, I shall describe that procedure;
having performed that first rite, the [subsequent] action follows immediately thereafter.

Having first performed three *kṛcchra* penances and recited [the mantra] one million times, O King, he should subsist on vegetables and barley-gruel, remaining pure and bathing at the three periods of the day.
One should worship the Lord, the God of gods, the three-eyed one, at the three times of day;
O King of kings, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) there with a tenth part [of the recitations].
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and worship the deity with perfumes and garlands;
then, one will see him in a dream at night seated upon a celestial chariot, and thereafter one should cast [the ritual materials].
Whoever casts himself down according to this very procedure,
having reached the heavenly world, sports together with the gods.
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures for thirty thousand years and likewise thirty million years, he would then go to the surface of the earth.
Honored by the world, he shall rule the earth under a single umbrella;
freed from disease and sorrow, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
That sacred ford, Jvāleśvara, is renowned throughout the three worlds;
there, O Pārtha, flows the river Jvālā, created by Śiva.
Having extinguished that city of Bāṇa, O great king, she joined with the Revā;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite accompanied by mantras.
One should satisfy the ancestral deities with water mixed with sesame seeds;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, one obtains the fruit of the Paiṇḍarīka sacrifice.
O lord of men, he who practices fasting unto death at that sacred site is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
For he is served by hundreds of immortals, O Lord of the Immortals, and likewise by hosts of sages; therefore, he is the most meritorious and great.
The sacred ford of Amarakaṇṭaka is indeed meritorious for a yojana all around;
because it is attended by ten million Rudras, it is therefore supremely meritorious.
Whoever performs a circumambulation of that king of mountains has, by that act, circumambulated the entire earth; of this there is no doubt.
"Whatever sin there may be—verbal, mental, and indeed physical of three kinds—all that perishes; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
And near Amareśvara, O King, is the Śakreśvara Tīrtha;
it is said that in ancient times, having performed austerities there, Śakra established it.
There is an auspicious sacred ford named Kuśāvarta, created by Brahmā;
it is renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa, and beyond that is Haṃsatīrtha.
There is the Ambarīṣa Tīrtha and likewise Mahākāleśvara;
and on the eastern part of the Kāverī is the Mātṛkeśvara Tīrtha.
O bull of the Bharatas, these [tirthas] on the southern bank of the Revā remove the multitude of sins through visiting them, bathing, and giving gifts.
O great king, on Bhṛgutuṅga resides the renowned Śiva as Bhairava;
and in its southern sector is the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Capaleśvara.
These two, who remove suffering, are situated on the northern bank of the Revā;
by properly worshipping and bowing to them, one shall obtain the full fruit of the pilgrimage.
For if they are not seen and worshipped, they cause obstacles for men.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Jvāleśvara Tīrtha and Amareśvara Tīrtha," within the Tripura-vidhvaṃsana section of the Revā-khaṇḍa, in the fifth book (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 29.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of beings, she who is renowned throughout the three worlds as Kāverī— [what is her merit?]
O Mārkaṇḍeya, I wish to hear the greatness of her in its true essence.
O Lord, O Sage, what kind of vision does she grant, or what is the fruit of her touch? Or [what is the result] of bathing, recitation, giving, or fasting?
O illustrious one, tell me the fruit of the confluence of the Kāverī;
for merit, whether heard, seen, spoken of, or even performed, [yields great results].
O best of Brahmins, I have heard that even one who merely rejoices [in another's merit] is purified;
O Sage, just as in the context of Dharma, Dharma itself is likewise produced.
"Both heaven and hell exist"—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, that I have now been questioned by you!
Listen with a focused mind to the supreme fruit of the Kāverī.
There is a yakṣa, a great being, renowned by the name Kubera; he too, O King, became the lord of yakṣas through the power of the sacred ford.
Listen to that, O King, according to the prescribed rule with supreme devotion;
for by the confluence of the Kāverī, O illustrious one, you shall attain perfection.
At the world-renowned confluence of the Kāverī and the Narmadā,
Kubera, whose valor is truth, bathed there and became pure.
O best of men, having performed the ritual observances according to the rules and in accordance with the scriptures and logic,
he worshipped the eternal Mahādeva with single-minded devotion.
O best of kings, dwelling for a month eating only once a day, likewise fasting for six days at a time, and observing fasts for a fortnight, he lived there for some time.
The wise man passes another period of time with roots, vegetables, and fruits;
dwelling there at that sacred site for some time, he subsists on water-moss.
O giver of honor, he passed some time with the Parāka penance, others with great difficulty through the Kṛcchra, and yet others by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa, subsisting on air and water.
Thus, O best of men, having abandoned sensual desire,
he remained there for more than a hundred years, emaciating his own body.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
being pleased by his supreme devotion, spoke to him as if smiling.
"O Yakṣa, O Great Being, O observer of excellent vows, choose a boon!
I am well-pleased with your devotion; I shall grant you whatever you desire."
The Yakṣa said:
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara together with Umā,
from this day forward, may you be the sovereign of all the Yakṣas."
O Supreme Lord, may he who is preceded by devotion to you be indeed inexhaustible and undecaying; grant me a constant mind fixed upon Dharma.
The Lord said: "Everything that you have requested as the fruit of your dharma shall be exactly so.
Having spoken thus to him there, Hara vanished from sight.
He too, having bathed according to the prescribed rite and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
took leave of that sacred ford and, his purpose fulfilled, went home.
Honored there by the yakṣas and consecrated according to the prescribed rites,
he ruled over that vast, supreme, and desired kingdom.
And there, O sinless one, were other gods, siddhas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, as well as hosts of apsarases and ṛṣis.
Therefore, they know the confluence of the Kāverī to be the remover of all sins;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is the gateway even to all the heavens.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones, whose birth has been well-lived,
by whom water mixed with sesame seeds was offered after bathing at the confluence of the Kāverī.
O dear one, ten ancestors before and ten after, both on the mother’s and the father’s side—
the fathers and grandfathers— have thereby been rescued from the ocean of hell.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should bathe there and worship the Lord God, if they desire the eternal goal.
O King, O best of men, bathing, giving gifts, and performing worship with devotion at the confluence of the Kāverī by men yields a fruit greater than that of a horse sacrifice.
Through fire-offerings, heaven becomes inexhaustible; through recitation, life is increased;
and through meditation, one eternally attains the state whose nature is the digit of Śiva.
O lord of men, whoever should enter the fire at that sacred site shall dwell in the world of Agni for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
O lord of men,
O best of men, listen now to the fruit of the merit that belongs to one who practices fasting unto death at that sacred ford.
In a celestial chariot resembling the sun, crowded with Gandharvas and Apsarases,
he rejoices together with the deities while being fanned by excellent women.
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years he sports while residing in the world of Rudra; at the end of that time, he returns to the earth.
Possessing enjoyments and being inclined toward generosity, he is born as a lord of the earth;
freed from mental anguish and grief, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
O King, thus that river Kāverī, filled with a multitude of virtues,
is eternally renowned throughout the three worlds at its confluence with the Narmadā.
O dear one, those who have conquered speech, body, and mind, and who likewise delight in meditation upon the object of contemplation,
shall attain liberation at the confluence of the Kāverī.
Listen, O best of kings, I shall tell you another marvel:
what other river is seen in the three worlds that is equal to her?
Those by whom the water of the Narmadā has been obtained, those who perform circumambulation of it, and those who drink its water—they are meritorious; of this there is no doubt.
For fifteen births, there shall be no interruption of their lineage;
their evil shall melt away like snow at the rising of the sun.
Whatever fruit a man obtains at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
that same fruit a mortal obtains by performing a ritual bath in the Kāverī.
On a Tuesday coinciding with the Bhūtajā yoga, during Vyatīpāta, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti),
and during the conjunction of Rāhu and the Moon, that same [gift] is declared to be eightfold [in merit].
It is said that at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā there are eighty barley grains;
at the junction of the Kāverī and Narmadā, that same measure is remembered as being eightfold.
The Gaṅgā is worshipped by sixty thousand guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla); other sacred sites are protected by half that number—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, those confluences of rivers that have been proclaimed at Amareśvara are protected by eighty thousand guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapālas).
Likewise, to the south of Amareśvara is the Capaleśvara Liṅga;
and the second, known as Caṇḍahasta—these two Liṅgas are protectors of the Tīrtha.
Formerly established by Śiva and protected by the Kāverī and other rivers,
the goddess Narmadā, who flows through many kalpas, was guarded by a hundred thousand [deities].
The mountain was protected by sixty thousand men appointed by the Lord, who were each capable of discharging a hundred thousand *oṃ* sounds.
Sin committed in another place is destroyed in this field;
however, sin committed at this sacred site (tīrtha) will become as indestructible as adamantine cement.
This Kāverī, the best of rivers, has been described to you, my dear;
she is holy because she was born from the body of Rudra, and thus she is the most excellent of streams.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Confluence with the Kāverī," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 30.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: On the northern bank of the Narmadā, there is the unsurpassed Dāru Tīrtha.
Wherein that illustrious and best of the twice-born attained perfection after performing austerities.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, who was that most excellent of the twice-born who attained perfection there?
Whose son was he known as Dāruka? You ought to tell me this."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: In the great lineage of Bhṛgu, there was the wise Devaśarman;
his son was the highly fortunate Dāru, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
As a celibate student, a householder, and a forest-dweller according to the sequence of rules, he practiced extensive austerity through the prescribed ordinances for the life of an ascetic.
Meditating upon Mahādeva while abstaining from food, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
he dwelt at that sacred ford until the exhaustion of his life-breaths.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) became renowned throughout the three worlds by his name;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the ancestors and the gods.
O King, one who speaks the truth, has conquered anger, and is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
attains all desires right here in this very world.
He who observes the fast, being devoted to truth and purity, undoubtedly attains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
One who recites the Ṛgveda becomes a knower of the Ṛgveda; one who has mastered the Sāman becomes a knower of the Sāman;
and a knower of the Yajus, having recited the Yajus, obtains the supreme fruit. (RKV 30.9)
"Whatever mortal relinquishes their life-breaths at that sacred site according to the prescribed rite,
their destination is from which there is no return"— thus spoke Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Dārutīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 31.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds.
It is renowned as Brahmāvarta, which destroys all sins.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Brahmā, his constant attendant, remained ever-present,
keeping his arms raised and revolving perpetually without support.
Observing the great vow, he remained for twelve years subsisting on a single meal a day,
meditating upon Maheśvara at this sacred ford according to the prescribed rite.
Therefore, O Lord, that merit-bestowing place was called Brahmāvarta;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities.
One should worship the Lord Īśāna or Viṣṇu, the Supreme Sovereign;
[one shall obtain] that fruit which belongs to all sacrifices when they are performed according to rule with ritual fees.
One obtains that fruit through the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha),
in whatever sacred ford a deity, a Dānava, or a twice-born (dvija) resides.
By that very name he became a perfected one (siddha), and it became renowned in the world as a great [place];
for there was neither water nor dry land, nor any field, nor even saline wastes.
These attain purity for men even without [external] human effort;
O King, through capability, resolve, and fortitude, men achieve success.
Through negligence and greed for that [wealth], they certainly fall into hell.
Wherever a sage may dwell, having fully restrained the collection of his senses,
that very place is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Brahmāvarta Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 32. The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go to Pattreśvara, which destroys all sins,
where the illustrious and powerful son of Citrasena attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmin, who was that perfected one (siddha) of great asceticism at that sacred ford (tīrtha) at that time?
Whose son was he, and what was the cause? I wish to know this."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of kings, in former times there was one named Citra, possessed of great splendor and beloved by Indra; his son was known as Pattreśvara.
He was handsome and fortunate, striking fear into all his enemies;
another son was named Jaya, who was exceedingly dear to Indra.
Once, in the midst of the assembly where all the gods had gathered,
he was indeed infatuated for a very long time by the dance and song of Menakā.
Having transgressed the bounds of propriety, he stood for a moment as if his life-breath had departed;
then the god Indra, the lord of the immortals, cursed him for his lack of self-control.
Since you, though established in heaven, have undergone the condition of a mortal,
therefore you will undoubtedly spend a long time among mortals.
Thus addressed by the lord of the gods, the youthful son of Citrasena,
trembling and with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that best of deities.
Pattreśvara said: "O gracious one, you ought to show favor toward me, for such is the fruit that has been obtained by me, a sinner, a fool, whose mind and senses were unsubdued."
Śakra said:
"Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā for twelve years, with your senses subdued, worship the peaceful Śiva; then you shall again attain the good state."
"This world belongs to those who delight in truth and purity, who are most righteous, and who have conquered themselves; it does not belong at all to sinners—such is the certainty of the scripture."
When this had been spoken, O Great King, by the wise thousand-eyed one,
the wise son of the Gandharva bowed down and went to the surface of the earth.
Having bathed in the pure waters of the Revā near Brahmāvarta,
and having recited prayers according to the prescribed rite and worshipped Śaṅkara;
With wind, water, oil-cakes, fruits, flowers, leaves, roots, and barley-gruel, he performed fierce penances involving the five fires; thereupon, that god attained satisfaction.
Having seen the Lord of Umā— who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, who grants boons, who wields the trident, who is the destroyer of Andhaka,
who has the crescent moon upon his crest, and who is clothed in an elephant hide— standing before him, he fell down upon seeing him.
Īśvara said:
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you—for I am the giver of boons to you, O sinless one.
Whatever you desire, I shall grant it today; there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
Pattreśvara said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then,
O Lord, remain forever here at this sacred ford (tīrtha) under my name."
Having heard this, Mahādeva Śaṅkara, with a voice faltering with joy, said "So be it," and departed delighted along with Umā.
He too, having bathed at that sacred ford after the god had departed for heaven,
performed his ablutions according to the rules for recitation and again offered libations to his ancestors.
O descendant of Bharata, he installed the Lord of Gods in that sacred ford according to the prescribed rites; it became renowned throughout the three worlds as Pattreśvara.
O lord of men, having gone to Indra’s world and being liberated from the curse,
he too was joyful and delighted with auspicious sounds such as shouts of victory.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this question which you asked has indeed been explained to you;
by bathing there even once, one is liberated from all sins.
But he who worships Mahādeva at that sacred site, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
having bathed and honored the ancestors and the gods, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having died and played for more than a hundred years in the city of Śiva,
he is subsequently born among mortals as either a king or one equal to a king.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences shall live for a hundred autumns, freed from disease and sorrow; moreover, he remembers that water again.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Patreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Agnitīrtha,
where Agni himself is ever-present, having gone there infatuated by desire.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How is it that the Lord, the sustainer of the world, is defiled by desire?
And how does his dwelling always come to be in single locations?
"This is an incomparable wonder, unsurpassed in all the worlds;
tell it to me, O illustrious one, for my curiosity is great."
The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! You have asked an excellent question.
I shall relate it to you just as it was heard by me in the past from Maheśvara."
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a great king named Duryodhana,
who protected the earth and possessed a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Seeing that lord of the earth, endowed with beauty and youth and possessed of divine enjoyments, Narmadā made her request.
But that king, the lord of Māhiṣmatī, having abandoned all other women, desired that maiden with the highest joy.
O best of kings, he indeed took delight with her in due time;
Narmadā gave birth to a daughter whose eyes were like lotus petals.
Because she was endowed with all major and minor limbs and was renowned throughout the worlds,
both her father and mother formed a bond of affection for her.
After a very long time, O King, that beautiful woman, though standing in her youth and being sought after, did not wish to give herself away.
Then, on another day, Agni, assuming the form of a twice-born brahmin and performing great austerities,
went to the king in private and requested something very gradually.
"O best of the Raghu clan! I am a twice-born man with a failing lineage, poor and without support; I choose her for the sake of a wife."
There is a maiden named Sudarśanā, whose beauty is peerless on earth;
bestow her upon us, O fortunate one, for she is flourishing in your palace.
"Disgusted with the life of celibacy, alone and tormented by desire,
O father, you ought to show favor to me who am entreating you."
The king said:
"I will never give my own bright daughter to one who is devoid of wealth or of a different caste; depart, O bull among the twice-born!"
Thus addressed, the Fire-god then fell into great distress;
without saying anything to the king, he vanished right there.
When the brahmin had departed from sight, the king, having consulted with his ministers and domestic priest at the proper time, stood at the commencement of the sacrifice, feeling satisfied.
And while he was sacrificing with devotion in the ritual together with the Brahmins, O Bhārata,
the fire then vanished from the sight of everyone who was looking on.
Having become dejected in mind, the Brahmins went to the king’s palace;
with troubled hearts, they spoke thus to the king regarding the disappearance of the fire.
The Brahmins said:
"O Great King Duryodhana, listen to this great marvel! O bull among kings, such a wonder has never been heard of nor seen before."
O King, although all were engaged in the fire-ritual according to the rules, for some reason the fire was not seen to blaze. (RKV 33.21)
Having heard that terrible and unpleasant speech falling from the mouth of the Brahmin,
the king fell from his seat to the ground like a tree severed at its roots.
Having recovered his breath after a moment, he then became as if mad;
looking toward all the directions, he spoke these words.
"O best of the twice-born, what is this that is so full of wonder?
Having reflected upon it through the lens of the scriptures, let the entire reason for it be told."
Is it some misdeed of mine, or perhaps of yours here, by which the consumer of oblations has perished in the fire-chamber? For what reason?

Whether there was a lapse in the mantra, or some other defect, or even if it were performed without the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or if it was done devoid of ritual action—who could fail to see the fire? 33.26.
A sacrifice lacking food consumes the kingdom; one lacking mantras consumes the officiating priests;
and one lacking sacrificial fees consumes the donor. There is no enemy equal to such a sacrifice.
The Brahmins said:
"We are not lacking in mantras, nor are we lacking in vows, O King; nor are you lacking in the ritual materials. Think of some other sin."
The king said:
"Nevertheless, you all together should devise a means by which there may be constant welfare in this world and in the next."
Thus addressed, all those brahmins, having made their resolve,
remained without food at the very spot where the sacrificial fire had vanished.
Then, in a dream, the immensely radiant Fire-god spoke to those brahmins:
"Listen all of you to the cause of my destruction."
"O best of the twice-born, this king was requested by me to give his daughter in marriage, but he did not wish to do so; because of that, I fled from the fire-sanctuary."
"If the king gives me his own daughter, who is most highly honored, then I shall remain in his house blazing; otherwise, I will not."
Having heard those words issuing from the mouth of Vaiśvānara, the brahmins, their eyes wide with amazement, spoke thus to the king: RKV_33.34 //
Having understood your intention, we all went to the fire-sanctuary;
fasting throughout the night, we remained there to behold the god of fire.
He said, "O twice-born ones, if the king wishes to give his daughter to me, then I shall blaze up in his house once more; not otherwise."
Knowing this, O Great King, you ought to give away your daughter.
The king said:
"Whether it be your business or his, the word of the god is held in my heart; I desire to establish an unsurpassed agreement regarding the giving of the maiden."
"Let the purifier (fire) remain ever present in my house;
I shall give you this woman of beautiful eyes, for I will certainly not act otherwise."
Having heard this, those brahmins quickly approached Agni and,
having consulted together, swiftly united him with a marriage ceremony.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, being fully satisfied by the acquisition of Sudarśanā, the Fire-god constantly blazes in the vicinity of Māhiṣmatī.
From that time forward, they have called that sacred site Agnitīrtha;
those who, at the junction of the fortnights, are purified there by means of ritual bathing and gifts, [attain the highest state].
O lord of men, those who bestow gold at that sacred site gratify the ancestors and the gods, and they are endowed with the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
The fruit of the gift of the earth arises there; of this there is no doubt, O lord of men, for whoever should practice fasting unto death at that sacred site.
Having died, he indeed sports in the world of Agni, honored by the gods.
Thus, this origin of the Agni-tīrtha has been recounted to you by me.
"O best of men, merely by hearing it, this merit-bestowing [text] removes all sins;
it is auspicious and eternally destroys evil," so Śaṅkara said.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Agnitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 34. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
But in that very place, O best of men, there is another [manifestation] of the high-souled Āditya; I shall proclaim it to you, if your mind is intent on hearing it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of sages, having heard this incomparable marvel issuing from your mouth,
my hair stands on end with wonder.
The thousand-rayed god, the remover and the creator, free from all taint,
is the savior of the worlds through his incarnation on the bank of the Narmadā.
Is the Blessed One a man, or is he the fruit of asceticism? In whose lineage was he born, and under whom did he become a self-controlled deity?
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: A pure and devoted Brāhmaṇa, born of the Kulika lineage,
made an effort to undertake a pilgrimage to that sacred ford (tīrtha), thinking, "I shall behold the Sun there."
Without food and without water, he set out for more than a hundred yojanas, but it is said that at the end of a dream he was stopped by the God of Gods.
"O Sage, O Great Being, enough of such a vow for you!
Behold me, who pervades all and abide in all that is stationary and moving."
I heat [the world], and from that, I withhold and release the rain;
he who perceives neither birth nor death—he truly sees.
Choose a boon, O auspicious one, whatever is desired by you for yourself.
The Brahmin said:
"O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
then remain forever present on the northern bank of the Narmadā."
O God, for those of subdued self who, staying even a hundred yojanas away, shall remember you with supreme devotion, be the granter of boons to them.
To those who are hunchbacked, blind, deaf, mute, or any others with impaired faculties—
grant your favor to them as they bow at your feet.
With their noses shattered and their intellects gone, they remain as nothing but bones and skin;
O Lord, have compassion for them without delay.
O Lord of the World, may you become the granter of boons to those who, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, worship you there day after day.
O Lord Acyuta, to those who shall praise you at dawn with Vedic and worldly hymns,
grant the desired boon, O God.
"O Lord, on this earth men perform the shaving of their heads before you;
O Master, a boon should be granted to them—this is my supreme boon."
Having said "So be it" to that sage out of compassion once more,
O King of kings, he vanished from sight while remaining for a hundredth part of a moment.
Having gone to that sacred ford with devotion, a person should perform a ritual bath;
by offering libations to the ancestors and the gods, he shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O lord of men, he who enters the fire at that sacred ford illuminates all the quarters and goes to the world of Agni.
"He who, having reached that sacred ford, casts off his body here,
goes to the world of Varuṇa"— thus spoke Śaṅkara.
Whoever should cast off their body at that sacred ford by means of renunciation is honored in the heavenly world for sixty thousand years.
Having dwelt in that place crowded with hosts of Apsarases and resounding with divine sounds,
he indeed returns to the mortal world as one who knows the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Freed from disease and sorrow, he shall become the master of ten million pieces of wealth; endowed with sons and wife, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Whoever rises in the morning and then remembers the Sun-god there is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Ravitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Rukmiṇīkalyāṇavilāsa*,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For what reason does Mahādeva remain in the midst of the water?"
O best of the twice-born, having avoided both the northern and southern banks, [one should proceed].
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O dear one, I shall relate to you in its entirety this incomparable and meritorious narrative, which brings joy to the ears, as it was heard by me in the Purāṇa.
In the Tretā Yuga, O highly fortunate one, there was Rāvaṇa, a thorn to the gods;
he was fierce, a conqueror of the three worlds, and a source of terror to both gods and asuras.
Then, unslayable by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism, he wandered the earth in his celestial chariot.
Meanwhile, in the midst of the Vindhya mountains, there was a dānava named Maya, renowned for his pride in strength; dwelling in a cave, he was practicing ascetic penance.
Standing by his side, the Rākṣasa, having humbly descended to the ground,
