was honored with gifts and marks of respect, and spoke these words:
Whose is this woman with eyes like lotus petals and a face resembling the full moon?
What is her name, and why, O Lord, does she perform such fierce asceticism?
Maya said: "I am Maya by name, the most excellent lord of the Dānavas;
my wife is named Tejovatī, and she has a beautiful daughter."
Renowned as Mandodarī, she performed austerities for the sake of her husband,
propitiating the auspicious beloved of Umā.
Having heard those words of his, Rāvaṇa, deluded by intoxication, approached and, having bowed down, spoke these words to Maya.
"Born in the lineage of Paulastya, the destroyer of the pride of gods and demons, O illustrious one, I entreat you: you ought to grant me your daughter."
Having learned of the conduct of his grandfather, the high-souled Maya also honored him according to the prescribed rites and gave his daughter to Rāvaṇa.
Having seized her, that rākṣasa, being honored by the night-stalkers,
then sported with her in the celestial gardens and in celestial chariots.
Then, after some time, O Bhārata, Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, that best among those who possess sons, begot a son.
As soon as he was born, that great-souled one let out a cry;
by it, the worlds were stunned like those by the Saṃvartaka cloud.
Hearing that terrible roar, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
then gave him the name Meghanāda.
Having been given such a name, he too undertook the supreme vow and gratified Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, together with Umā.
By means of vows, restraints, and gifts, and through the performance of fire-offerings and recitations,
he constantly emaciated his body with the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
Thus, O dear one, on another day, having gone to Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth, and taken two liṅgas, he set out facing the south.
O Lord of Men, desiring to bathe while taking refuge on the bank of the Narmadā, the mighty one placed [the image] down, worshipped the deity, and performed his recitations.
There, having bathed at the sacred sites and offered oblations into the fire,
the night-stalker considered himself as one who had accomplished all that was to be done.
O best of kings, desiring to travel upon the supreme path to Laṅkā,
he bowed down while lifting up a single *liṅga* with his right hand.
But with the second offering, the son of Paulastya [Rāvaṇa] likewise caused a great liṅga to fall into the waters of the Narmadā out of devotion.
Having said, "Go, go," he was established in the midst of the water;
the son of Rāvaṇa then bowed down to that supreme deity.
Entering the sky, he departed while being honored by the night-stalkers;
from that time forth, that sacred ford became renowned as Meghanāda.
But previously, O King of kings, at that sacred ford named Garjana, which destroys all sins, whoever performs an ablution— RKV_35.26.
Having fasted for a day and night, one shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
O lord of men, he who performs the offering of funeral cakes at that sacred site [attains the same].
Whatever fruit is obtained from a sacrificial session (sattra), that shall be his; of this there is no doubt.
By him, the ancestors have been fully gratified for twelve years.
But he who feeds a Brahmin with food of six flavors at that sacred ford, O Bhārata, best of men, obtains inexhaustible merit.
But he who, purified by one whose self is purified, should renounce his life,
shall dwell in the world of Śaṅkara until the dissolution of all beings.
O tiger among men, this supreme account of the origin of Garjana has been told to you out of the bond of affection; it brings about the destruction of all sins.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Meghanāda Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 36. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Dārutīrtha,
where in ancient times Dāruka, the beloved of Indra, attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sinless one, O best of the twice-born, how was penance performed by Dāruka in the past? O dear one, I wish to hear the account of his practice from you."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Behold, I shall relate to you that wonderful ancient event which took place in the midst of the assembly of heaven before the sages of purified souls."
The charioteer of Vajradhara, known by the name Mātali,
once cursed his son for a certain reason.
Struck by the curse and trembling, O Bhārata, he pressed his head against the auspicious feet of Indra, the lord of gods, and addressed him.
To him, who was thus cursed and left without a protector, the Lord of the Gods said:
"By what action will there be an end to this terrible curse?"
"Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā and propitiating Maheśvara, remain there until the end of the Yuga; for you shall indeed obtain rebirth."
Having been born again, purified, and renowned by the name Dāruka,
you shall serve the Supreme God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
"Having entered into human existence, you shall then attain perfection.
Thus was he addressed by the wise, thousand-eyed god.
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground, he, indeed unconscious,
arrived at the bank of the Narmadā and began to emaciate his own body.
Wearied by vows and fasts, always devoted to recitation and burnt offerings,
[he beheld] Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the granter of boons, who holds the trident in his hand.
But through supreme devotion, O King, until the dissolution of all beings,
that high-minded one became the Sūta by virtue of being a partial incarnation of Viṣṇu.
Having indeed gratified the Lord of the World, he then attained the state of the righteous.
O dear one of noble vows, this origin of Dārutīrtha has been told by me to you just as Śaṅkara previously spoke it to me.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard this, was filled with the utmost wonder;
his hair standing on end, he looked at his brothers again and again.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:

O lord of men, having bathed in that tīrtha according to the prescribed rites and having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), one who worships Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, [attains the highest state].
But he who, being composed, practices the study of the Vedas in that very place, O King, obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.
But he who, being pure, feeds Brahmins with devotion at that sacred ford,
obtains the supreme fruit of feeding a thousand Brahmins.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, and worship of the deities—
whatever is performed with a pure disposition, all that shall become fruitful.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Dāruka-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 37. The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Devatīrtha,
where the thirty-three gods bathed and attained supreme perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O father, how was it that all the gods were defeated there by the far more powerful Dānavas, and yet,
having bathed at that sacred ford, attained supreme perfection?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, in ancient times, Indra was ousted from his own kingdom by fierce hosts of Daityas who were exceedingly powerful in battle, along with the hosts of gods.
Having crushed the armored host with floods of elephants, horses, and chariots,
the [enemies], shattered by blows and rendered mangled, fled along their paths.
Trembling and tormented by Jambha, Śumbha, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Kuhaka, and the others, they all approached Brahmā.
Having bowed their heads to the god Brahmā, the supreme lord,
the deities, led by Agni, then made this petition.
Behold, behold, O illustrious one! Rendered into fragments by the Dānavas and separated from their sons and wives, they have come to you alone for refuge.
Save me, O Lord of Gods, Grandfather of all the worlds!
O Supreme Lord, Sovereign of the Suras, there is no other refuge for me except you.
Brahmā said:
"For the sake of destroying the Dānavas, remain established on the bank of the Narmadā and perform penance with composure; for penance is indeed the supreme power."
There is no other means, nor indeed any mantra, nor any ritual action for me that exists which,
like the meritorious water of the Revā, brings about the destruction of all sins.
Poverty, disease, death, imprisonment, and misfortunes—these indeed are the fruits of evil; such is my conviction.
Having understood this, you must therefore perform difficult austerities;
and so shall all the gods, the deities led by Agni.
Having heard those truthful words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
all the gods, led by Agni, came to the Narmadā.
Indeed, Cera performed extensive penance there and attained perfection;
from that time forward, that sacred ford became the unsurpassed Devatīrtha.
It is sung throughout the three worlds as that which destroys all sins;
and whatever mortal, with senses restrained, goes there according to the prescribed rule, [attains the fruit].
O lord of men, he who performs his bath with devotion at that sacred site shall obtain the fruit of pearls; and he who feeds the Brahmins there shall likewise attain the same reward.
O King, he shall obtain a thousandfold the fruit of the foremost Brahmins;
there is the delightful Devaśilā, which increases great merit.
For those who die by renouncing the world there, their destination shall be imperishable;
O lord of men, so too for one who enters the fire at that sacred site.
One shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts;
likewise [the merit of] bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, self-study of scripture, and worship of the deity [is likewise eternal].
Whether it be a good deed or an evil one, whatever is performed at that sacred site shall become inexhaustible.
O Bhārata, this ritual procedure for you, as well as its origin, has been declared.
Those who recite this entire account of Devatīrtha, which was heard from Śaṅkara, which removes sin and grants liberation from all suffering, [attain the highest goal].
Those who follow the conduct of Devatīrtha go to the world of the gods.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Devatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 38] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme place called Guhāvāsī,
where the Great God, having become a perfected being (siddha), dwelt in a cave for ten million years.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, for what purpose, O best of the twice-born, did Mahādeva, the teacher of the world, spend such a very long period of time in the cave?"
O sinless one, tell me all of this in detail;
for I wish to hear it, as my curiosity is indeed supreme.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Excellent is the question, O Great King, which you have asked;
indeed, its full detail in the Purāṇa cannot be recounted by me now."
Because of my old age, it is long past and difficult to recount;
therefore, my dear son, I shall tell it to you in brief—listen to me.
O King, in former times, during the Kṛta age, there was a great forest called Dāruvana,
filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse climbing plants.
It was frequented by lions, tigers, boars, elephants, and rhinoceroses,
and filled with many birds— a divine place like the Caitraratha grove.
There dwell certain men of great wisdom who are firm in their vows;
they live with supreme devotion, perfected through the four stages of life.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
all devoted to their own duties and desiring the supreme state.
Then, during the spring season, for a certain reason,
Mahādeva was indeed traveling in his celestial chariot together with Umā.
He beheld that abode in the water, resounding with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses;
its entry and exit were imperceptible, and it was the destroyer of all sins.
Seeing him, the goddess Muditā, with a voice flowing like the Ganges of joy,
questioned the Lord of the Gods, who is adorned by the moon.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, whose hermitage is this, resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
by the sight of which one is freed from hunger, thirst, and other such fatigues?"
Maheśvara said:
"O Goddess, have you not heard of the great Mahādāruvana forest,
where many Brahmins dwell according to the duties of householders?"
In this place, O daughter of the mountain, whatever woman is devoted to serving her husband knows no other deity and recognizes nothing else as dharma. (RKV 38.15)
Having heard these supreme words spoken by the God of gods,
she, filled with curiosity, spoke again to Śaṅkara.
"O Mahādeva, as for what you have said— that women are devoted to the duty toward their husbands—
you should become Madana and disturb their conduct, O Lord."
Īśvara said:
"O beloved, the words you have spoken do not please me at all;
for Brāhmaṇas are a great being, and one should never do anything displeasing to them."
Brahmins have anger as their weapon, while Hari has the discus as his weapon;
yet anger is more cruel than the discus, therefore one should not provoke a Brahmin to wrath.
Neither those gods, nor those worlds, nor those mountains, nor the asuras are seen within the three realms who have not been destroyed by those [beings] once they were beheld.
For those with whom the highly fortunate Brāhmaṇas— the deities of the earth— are pleased, there is liberation as well as heaven, and in this world of mortals, the fruits of the land.
Knowing this, O illustrious lady, abandon your false attachment;
for in that world it is indeed contrary [to dharma], by which the twice-born truly become incensed.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, I am not your beloved, nor am I subject to your will,
for I have not yet performed those rites that are highly honored by the gods."
O Mahādeva, O Lord, there is nothing impossible for you in this world or the next;
O Supreme God, let this one task alone be performed for me.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, Mahādeva, who is devoted to the welfare of her words,
assumed the form of a Kāpālika and went toward the Dāruvana forest.
Having bound his great mass of matted hair for the sake of great benefit, he who is adorned by the moon made his throat the supreme protection and wore earrings.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with a girdle and a necklace,
he made the earth tremble with the resonant sounds of his anklets.
Wearing a great garland of upright matted hair, smeared with animal skins and ashes,
he took in his hand the skull of the high-souled Brahmā.
Making the earth tremble with the sound of his great ḍamaru drum,
he arrived at the great Dāruvana forest at the time of dawn.
Meanwhile, the person of merit, seeking all kinds of flowers, leaves, and fruits,
went out accompanied by many people, blowing [his horn] in every direction.
O Bhārata, having seen that great wonder— the form of the god—
the minds of those young women were clouded by desire.
Upon seeing that beautiful man, all those excellent women of the Dāruvana forest were moved by joy and then experienced a state of moistening [with passion].
O best of men, upon seeing that most wonderful deity, many transformations then arose among those wives of the brahmins.
Seeing [him], some excellent women did not know how to put on their lower garments,
and others, overcome by great delusion, likewise [forgot] their upper garments.
One woman, having risen from her seat with her mass of hair disheveled,
desired to give alms but was unable to move at all.
A certain woman, proud of her beauty and youth, having seen Mahādeva with a child seated on his lap, forgot to suckle him at her breast.
Another, struck by the arrows of desire, pressed her beautiful breasts with both arms and,
sighing hotly, did not say anything at all in reply.
Having thus agitated all those women, the Supreme Lord,
having caused that most wonderful agitation among them, departed from there.
Meanwhile, all those brahmins, having wandered through the great forest,
returned to their own homes and saw their wives with their vitality drained.
Knowing that those women, whose devotion to their husbands in the practice of wifely fidelity had previously been most steadfast, were now wavering, the best of the twice-born quickly departed.
Having established the supreme consciousness and having known the god Maheśvara,
he agitated their minds and then vanished from sight.
A certain brahmin, possessed by anger, runs forward brandishing a staff;
others likewise carry speckled sticks, while still others hold handfuls of darbha grass.
O King, after wandering here and there through the forest, all those great-souled ones gathered together and spoke these words in anger.
If this which has been offered here, and if my gurus have been satisfied,
by that truth may the supreme liṅga of the God fall down!
"We have all passed from one stage of life to the next according to the sequence of the rules;
by that truth, may the deity’s linga fall to the ground! (RKV 38.45)
Thus, by the power of the truth spoken three times by the twice-born,
while Śiva was looking on, his liṅga fell to the surface of the earth.
O Bhārata, when the Liṅga of the God fell and the great destruction of the world occurred, there was a tremendous cry of "Alas! Alas! even in the Lokāloka mountain.
As the *liṅga* was falling, a most dreadful sound arose;
there were falls of meteors, cries of "Alas! Alas! from all directions, and terrible earthquakes.
The mountain peaks fell and the oceans dried up;
when the Liṅga of the God had fallen, the gods became despondent.
Having assembled together, they all approached Brahmā Parameṣṭhin;
with palms joined in reverence, they all praised him with various hymns.
Then the Lord of the World, whose face is a four-petalled lotus, being pleased, spoke to all the distressed gods: "Do not fall into despair."
Overwhelmed by the curse of Brahmā, this three-eyed God of gods shall again attain liberation when he is gratified by those [sages] endowed with ascetic power.
Having heard this, O subduer of enemies, the gods departed as they had come,
and all the sages likewise did so, O Bhārata.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and others, as well as Jābāli and Kaśyapa,
all coming together and assembling, spoke to that Destroyer of Tripura.
For the spiritual luster of the twice-born is indeed powerful, O Lord of the Gods;
by practicing asceticism endowed with patience, you shall become free from all fatigue.
"O Mahādeva, because that supreme *liṅga* fell due to the agitation of the sages, it shall not be worthy of worship."
That supreme good which human beings attain through the worship of the *liṅga* is not obtained by means of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, nor by the *agniṣṭoma*.
By the word of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as by that of the brahmins, this shall become worthy of worship.
This shall be worthy of worship by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Candra;
whatever fruit belongs to your liṅga in this world and in the next.
Thus addressed, the Lord of the World, having prostrated before the best of the twice-born,
spoke with his palms joined in reverence, filled with supreme joy.
Brahmins are a moving sacred ford, waterless yet fulfilling all desires;
by the water of their very words, even defiled people are purified.
Neither that field, nor that sacred ford, nor even the salt-waste or the lotus-pools can purify one who has gone there after having provoked anger toward a Brahmin.
There is no scripture that was not composed by Brahmins; there is no gift that should not be given to Brahmins;
there is no happiness that does not arise from the favor of Brahmins; and there is no suffering that does not arise from the wrath of Brahmins.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, as well as rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single word spoken by a Brahmin.
Having greeted all the twice-born and being permitted by the great seers,
the god then went to the excellent bank of the Narmadā.
Having undertaken the supreme vow, the Blessed One dwelt in a cave for ten million years,
constantly devoted to asceticism, recitation, and ritual bathing.
When the observance was completed, O dear one, the Lord, having established Maheśvara,
went to Kailāsa while being honored by the gods.
The Supreme Lord was established by him on the bank of the Narmadā;
for that very reason, he is called Narmadeśvara.
The ascetic who has conquered his senses, having bathed, should worship Mahādeva, the Lord of the Narmadā; he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O Pāṇḍava, those twenty-one ancestors of his who offer sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and water to the Pitṛs rejoice in heaven.
O lord of men, he who feeds brahmins at that sacred site with milk-rice mixed with ghee shall obtain a merit equal to ten million times that amount.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who gives gold or even silver to Brāhmaṇas while standing in the midst of water obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who, having reached Narmadeśvara, remains without food on either the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, shall obtain the fruit of his birth.
O lord of men, O Bhārata, he who should enter the fire at that sacred site shall have no fear of disease for seven births.
O lord of men, for one who practices fasting unto death at that sacred site,
there shall be a state of non-return in the world of Rudra.
This procedure for him has been indicated to you, O best of men;
its origin was established in the Purāṇa, my dear, and its designation is explained there in detail.
The man who recites this account of the origin of Narmadeśvara,
or listens to it with devotion, shall also obtain the fruit of bathing there.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Narmadeśvara Tīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 39.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Kapilātīrtha.
By merely bathing with devotion, a person is liberated from all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, you have related the greatness of Narmadeśvara, which is a marvel among the worlds; now tell me about the Kapila [tīrtha].
O Lord, at what time and in connection with what event did that supreme, merit-bestowing tīrtha arise, which removes all sins? How was this sacred ford born?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King; today I shall describe to you the supreme Kapilātīrtha, by hearing of which, O Bhārata, all your wonder will pass away.
In the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
having brought forth the entire fourfold collection of living beings, [proceeded].
Devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, he remained for a moment in meditation;
then, from the blazing sacrificial pit, Kapilā arose.
With peaks blazing with flames of fire, she possesses three eyes, is richly milking,
filled with fire, has fire for her mouth, fire for her nose, and fire for her eyes.
Her hooves are like fire, her back is like fire, and the configuration of all her limbs is fire;
she is complete with all auspicious marks and possesses the melodious resonance of a bell.
Having seen that illustrious Kapilā standing in the midst of the pool,
O dear one, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, bowed down and spoke these words.
Salutations to you, O auspicious Kapilā, who are honored by all the worlds; O Goddess, source of blessings, most blessed one, you who are peerless throughout the three realms.
You are Lakṣmī, you are Smṛti, you are Medhā, you are Dhṛti, O lady of beautiful countenance;
you are renowned as the goddess Umā, you are Satī—of this there is no doubt.
You are the Great Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, you are Brahmāṇī, O fair-faced one;
you are Kumārī, O highly fortunate one, as well as devotion and faith.
You are the Night of Doom for all beings, the maiden, the supreme sovereign;
you are the lava, you are the truṭi, as well as the muhūrta and the hundred-thousandth part of a moment.
You are the year, you are the month, and you are time as well as the moment;
there is nothing in the three worlds, including the mobile and immobile, that is devoid of you.
Thus praised with honor by the Supreme Lord, Kapilā,
being greatly delighted, spoke to that illustrious lotus-born one.
I am pleased by your words, O God of gods, Teacher of the World!
Tell me everything, O Grandfather: what pleasing service may I perform for you today?
Brahmā said:
"O Supreme Goddess, you were brought forth by me for the welfare of the world;
therefore, go from heaven to the mortal realm out of a desire for the benefit of all beings."
"You indeed consist of all the gods and likewise consist of all the worlds;
for those who offer you according to the prescribed rite, their dwelling shall be in Triviṣṭapa."
Having spoken thus to Brahmā, the supreme goddess,
while being honored by the gods and the Siddhas, then descended to the surface of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O dear one, when that auspicious woman arrived here at the word of the Brahmin,
how were the gods and the worlds then established within her limbs?

Or how did that Kapilā come to be situated there, O best of the twice-born? Tell me this, O brahmin: is it at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in a saline wasteland (ūṣara)? ||| RKV_39.21 |||The cow Kapila, having arrived, is established here; tell me this, O best of the twice-born: is she at a sacred ford or in a saline field? Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Brahmā, the creator of the world,
she went from the realm of Brahmā to the meritorious Narmadā, the purifier of the worlds.
Having performed extensive austerities on the banks of the Narmadā,
she wandered over the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, this supreme Kapilātīrtha became renowned as the remover of all sins, frequented by hosts of sages.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite at that sacred ford, he who gives a tawny cow (kapilā) has,
by that act, given the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.
But whoever beholds her with devotion as she is being given to the best of the twice-born, his sin for a hundred years is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Satyam, and Tapas—
these worlds are situated resting upon his back.
For the god Agni resides in the mouth, and the serpents in the teeth;
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are in the two lips, while Sarasvatī is in the tongue.
The two gods with a thousand rays, the moon and the sun with beautiful eyes,
and the vital air situated in the middle of the nose, O best of kings.
Mahādeva is indeed on the forehead; the two Aśvins are situated in the ears;
Nara and Nārāyaṇa are at the two horns; and the Grandfather (Brahmā) is in the middle of the horns.
"O dear one, Kambala and Pāśadhṛg Varuṇa have been attained;
and the blessed god Yama has resorted to and taken refuge in my belly."
Likewise, serpents are in her hooves, and the rays of the sun are at the tip of her tail;
for such, O King, is the tawny cow (Kapilā), who embodies all the gods.
Those who keep [this] in their home are fortunate; there is no doubt about this.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, performs a circumambulation of it, [attains merit].
He who bathes Śaṅkara with the five products of a tawny cow has performed a circumambulation of the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves.
O lord of men, he who is devoted to fasting at that sacred site should bathe according to the prescribed rite and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
All those born of his lineage— the ten ancestors and the ten descendants—
ascend to heaven satisfied, meditating upon his noble aspirations.
This procedure for the origin of the sacred ford has been described to you, O best of kings, as well as its meritorious fruit; what else do you wish to ask?
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, the supreme destroyer of all suffering;
having heard it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kapilātīrtha," in the Śrī Narmadāmāhātmya, within the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, in the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 40. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Karañjeśvara.
There, the highly fortunate Daitya, renowned throughout the worlds, attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O illustrious twice-born one, tell me: whose son was that great ascetic who attained perfection at that sacred ford, how did he attain perfection, and at what time?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a mind-born son of Brahmā named Marīci by name, who was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
O sinless one, after a long time, a son was born from that mass of asceticism, a mind-born son who was like another Brahmā in person.
Forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, truthfulness, purity, and uprightness—
O Bhārata, these indeed are the qualities of Marīci and of that [king] as well.
Knowing Kaśyapa, the best of the twice-born, to be thus endowed with a multitude of virtues, Dakṣa Prajāpati gave him his own daughter to be his wife.
Aditi, Diti, and Danu, as well as ten others;
from them, O bull of the Bharatas, sons and grandsons were born.
Aditi gave birth to sons with Indra at their head;
O mighty-armed one, they were born of that Prajāpati Kaśyapa.
By him, the three worlds—the great realm of the stationary and the moving—were pervaded;
likewise, O highly fortunate one, another son was born to Danu.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and known by the name Karañja,
that fortunate one practiced great asceticism even while still a youth.
O King, resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, he performed the most formidable and unsurpassed divine Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances for a thousand years.
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, and devoted to ritual bathing and burnt offerings,
Mahādeva, accompanied by Umā, was indeed pleased with him.
The Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, invited him to choose a boon:
"O Karañja, great being, O sinless one, I am well-pleased with you!"
"Choose a boon; I shall grant it to you, for I grant even immortality, with the sole exception of my own [death]."
Karañja said:
"O Mahādeva, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
then let my sons and grandsons be lovers of righteousness."
Having said, "So be it," Mahādeva, accompanied by Umā and together with his attendants,
mounted his bull and vanished right there.
When the god had departed from sight, that Daitya, filled with joy,
installed Mahādeva there under his own name and went home.
From that time forth, that sacred ford has been the most excellent among all sacred fords;
by merely bathing there, a person is liberated from all sins.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods,
undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O lord of men, he who practices fasting unto death at that sacred site shall attain an irreversible state; he goes to the world of Rudra.
Alternatively, O son of Dharma, one may cast off one's life-breaths into fire or water;
such a person dwells for twenty thousand years in the abode of Śiva.
And then, when that destruction has occurred, he is born into a pure family as one who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and is proficient in all the treatises.
Whether a king or one equal to a king, he shall live for a hundred autumns,
endowed with sons and grandsons, and free from all diseases.
Thus, O sinless one, everything that was asked by you has been related to you;
now, O Bhārata, hear of the fruit of that sacred ford regarding bathing and giving gifts.
This supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrtha-māhātmya) is meritorious, destructive of sin, auspicious, and a destroyer of evil dreams; it belongs to those who read and listen to it.
But he who, devoted to the ancestors, causes this to be heard or recites it at a śrāddha ceremony, his merit becomes inexhaustible; thus spoke Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karañjeśvara Tīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 41. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Kuṇḍaleśvara.
O best of kings, it is there that the great yakṣa Siddha Kuṇḍadhāra resides.
O best of kings, having performed most extensive austerities that struck fear into both gods and asuras, he sported within the palace of Paulastya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
In which age did that high-minded one appear, and whose son was he,
by whom Śaṅkara was gratified after performing very extensive austerities?
O sinless one, tell me this in detail, my dear;
for as I listen to this unsurpassed nectar of a story, I am not yet satiated.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: In the Tretā Yuga, there was one named Viśravas, the son of Bharadvāja, who was equal to Brahmā; having performed very extensive austerities, he became known as Paulastya.
Greatly pleased by his wife’s devotion, he begot a son who was endowed with all auspicious marks and destined to bestow wealth, accompanied by a multitude of grandsons.
But as soon as he was born, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being well-pleased and accompanied by sages and gods, bestowed a name upon him.
"O sinless one, because you were born from Viśravas and have become my grandson, the name Vaiśravaṇa is hereby given to you by me."
In that way, you shall become the protector of the wealth of all the gods,
the fourth among the world-protectors on earth, imperishable and undecaying.
His wife, O Great King, was renowned as Īśvarī;
their son was Kuṇḍa, the most excellent lord of the Yakṣas.
And he, having attained supreme form with the permission of his parents,
practiced extensive austerities, taking refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
In summer he was scorched by five fires; during the rains he slept on the bare ground;
in winter he stayed in the midst of water, subsisting on air for a hundred years.
O King, when a full hundred years had passed in this manner, he became nothing but bone upon one big toe; O dear one, after that, he remained with his arms raised high.
O bull of the Bharatas, the bull-vehicled god was pleased with Atapa, Ghṛtaśvāsa, and Kuṇḍala during their fourth century of years.
"Choose a boon, O child, whatever pleases your mind;
I shall grant it to you, of this there is no doubt, for I am gratified by your asceticism."
Kuṇḍala said:
"By the grace of the Lord of Yakṣas, I wander at will in his very city as his attendant, invincible by all enemies."
Having said, "So be it," Mahādeva, who is honored by all the worlds,
entered the sky and departed for Kailāsa, the mountain that supports the earth.
When the Lord had departed from sight, that yakṣa, filled with joy,
installed the supreme Kuṇḍaleśvara, the Lord of Gods.
Having adorned the Lord of the World with flowers, incense, and ointments,
as well as with celestial chariots, yak-tail whisks, parasols, and indeed with the filling of the linga;
Having properly gratified the twice-born with food, drink, ornaments, and other gifts,
and having pleased Mahādeva, he then departed for his own abode.
From that time forward, that sacred site became renowned throughout the three worlds as the supreme and most meritorious place known by the name Kuṇḍaleśvara.
Whoever at that sacred ford is devoted to fasting and worships the Lord Īśāna is liberated from all sins.
One who gives gold, silver, jewels, or even pearls,
as well as food, to the Brāhmaṇas, rejoices happily in heaven.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, even one who is a singer of the Ṛg, Yajur, or Sāma Vedas,
by chanting a single Ṛc verse, attains the full fruit.
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to the fruit of one who bestows a cow upon Brahmins:
as many hairs as there are on that cow and on the cows born in her lineage, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
For so many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
his residence in heaven shall be accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
For as many years as that, the person of great majesty shall dwell in heaven together with his sons and grandsons;
there, the giver of food goes to the world of Maheśa for incalculable years—of this there is no doubt.
He indeed rejoices happily in the heavenly world, where Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Apsarases sing together;
thus, O son of Dharma, O Pārtha, has the entire power of this sacred ford been described to you.
Having heard it and praising it, one is liberated from all sins; furthermore, by its power, one returns here to the three worlds.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kuṇḍaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 42.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the most excellent Pippaleśvara.
There, the great yogi Pippalāda, a perfected one of great asceticism, resides.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, I desire to hear the life-story of Pippalāda and the greatness of that sacred ford where the great ascetic attained perfection.
Whose son was he, O illustrious one, and for what purpose did he perform penance?
O sinless one, tell me all of this in detail.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O dear one, in former times, the highly fortunate Yājñavalkya, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas while residing in Mithilā, performed extensive austerities."
The sister of that wise Yājñavalkya became an ascetic;
she, too, by the power of fate, entered into widowhood in her seventh year.
Due to the ripening of past karma, she was born from lowly parents; since there was no one even on her husband's side [to support her], she remained all alone.
Wandering upon the earth, she slowly approached her brother;
he, too, practiced austerities out of a desire for happiness in the next world.
Remaining there, she too practiced great austerities while performing service;
then, at a certain time, having bathed on a day when she was in her menses, she [performed her rites].
Having seen him wearing a tattered rag as an undergarment in private,
Yājñavalkya also slept that night where he was well-concealed.
Having seen a dream, he discharged his semen like drops of blood upon his loincloth;
through his radiant asceticism, it became perfected, possessing the brilliance of fire.
As soon as that brahmin woke up and saw that garment soiled by food remnants, he cast it far away, deeming it untouchable, and performed his purification according to the prescribed rules.
Since bathing at night is forbidden, that twice-born man went to sleep;
at midnight, she too used that garment as a covering for her private parts.
In the morning, the sage searched for the garment here and there.
Then that Brahmin woman said: "What are you searching for, O Lord?
What is your purpose? Tell me the truth of it."
Yājñavalkya said:
"O blessed lady, today indeed at night I saw an impure dream;
my garment was soaked there, yet it is no longer to be seen."
O King, having heard those words, the Brahmin woman spoke with great trepidation:
"O Brahmin, after bathing, I indeed placed that great garment inside [my clothing]."
Having heard those words of hers, the great sage cried out "Alas!
and then fell to the ground like a tree cut at its roots.
"What is this? he asked. Then she, having replied "It is she," pure as the sky, spoke these words at that time, consoling the brahmin.
Speak the cause, my dear, if it be even more secret than a secret;
for once it has been deliberated, a remedy for this may be applied with haste.
Then, after meditating for a very long time, he suddenly regained his speech and, with a mind full of trepidation, spoke; listen to what he said, O Lord of Men.
"There is no fault whatsoever in this for you or for me, O lady of auspicious vows;
as for the embryo within your womb, in that matter destiny is the ultimate resort."
You must indeed always protect him in accordance with reality;
he must never be destroyed until the turning of time.
Saying "So be it," that virtuous woman, though ashamed and with a grieving heart,
protected that embryo until a son was born.
And as soon as he was born, that Brahmin woman took the infant, sought out the shade of an aśvattha tree, set him down there, and spoke these words: ||| RKV_42.23 |||
May all those beings in the worlds, whether stationary or moving,
protect this child who has indeed been abandoned by me.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, that brahmin woman departed;
and that infant, remaining there for a moment like the Tathāgata, [continued to gaze].
Having cast down his hands and feet and contracted his beautiful eyes,
he made his face distorted and wept with discordant cries.
Terrified by that sound, all things both stationary and moving trembled, along with the mountains, forests, and groves, as if by great portents.
Then, O Bhārata, having recognized that great being, the bull among the twice-born, who was overcome by hunger,
the mountain did not abandon its shade for his sake; furthermore,
it drank the milk from him and even carried it away.
Thus nurtured there, the prince, feeling confident in his own mind, reflected: "What sphere of influence do the planets have over me?"
Then Śanaiścara, whose conduct in the assembly is cruel, having been gazed upon with a cruel look,
suddenly fell to the ground like Saturn itself.
And then, trembling with fear and with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"O Brahmin Pippalāda, O great sage, what wrong have I committed?"
While he was indeed traveling through the sky, he was cast down to the surface of the earth by Saturn; thus addressed, the great sage Pippalāda—
Assuming a wrathful form, he spoke these words; listen to them, O lord of men:
"O evil-minded son of Sūrya, why do you inflict such suffering upon me, a child deprived of both father and mother? Speak the truth in its entirety."
Śanaiścara said:
"My cruel nature is innate, and my gaze is likewise;
release me, and I shall do exactly as you say, without a doubt."
Pippalāda said:
"From this day forward, you must not cause affliction to children from one year up to sixteen; this is the agreement made with you."
Having said, "So be it," he departed; then, moving slowly along the path of the gods, he returned and paid homage to that best of sages.
And when he had gone out of sight there, that foolish and great demon,
his mind clouded by anger, began to brood over his father.
Having meditated upon the fire-element concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā), he generated fire;
he offered oblations into the fire with ritual mantras (kṛtyā-mantra), saying, "May a magical female spirit (kṛtyā) indeed come into being."
Then, in an instant, that maiden, adorned with garlands of flames and possessing a form like that of the fire-god, said, "What shall I do?"
"Shall I dry up the oceans? Or shall I pulverize the mountains? Shall I envelop the earth? Or shall I cast down the vault of heaven? (RKV 42.40)
"O twice-born one, upon whose head shall I fall, and whom shall I strike?
Let the task be commanded quickly, lest there be a lapse of time for me."

Having heard those words of hers, Pippalāda of great asceticism, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these words: RKV_42.42: Having heard those words of hers, Pippalāda of great asceticism, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these words.
"O auspicious one, driven by a great surge of anger, I thought of you;
you are my father Yājñavalkya's [wife], so fall upon him without delay!"
Having spoken thus, she departed swiftly, rending the firmament;
meanwhile, the highly wise and noble-minded one remained in Mithilā and practiced austerities.
Yājñavalkya, possessed of great splendor, beheld a quarter of the sky blazing with a radiance like that of the sun, where a great being had appeared.
Seeing him approaching so suddenly, the great sage was terrified; then, pursued by the spirit, he went to King Janaka.
"Know, O best of kings, that I have come to you for refuge;
protect me from the fear of this great being, O ruler of the earth, if you are able."
"Born of Brahmanic splendor, this being is irresistible and difficult to approach;
I am not able to protect him," the king spoke these words.
Then, seeking refuge, that man of great asceticism went to another excellent king; having been released by him, he fled in fear to the abode of Indra.
"O King, O Lord of the Gods, homage be unto you! Trembling with fear of the great elements, the brahmin said again and again, "Protect me! (RKV 42.50)
Having heard those words of his, the King of the Gods said this:
"O Sage, I am not able to protect you from the wrath of Brahmā."
Then that Brahmin, the foremost knower of Brahman, went to the abode of Brahmā and to the world of Viṣṇu, having been addressed by him in this very way.
Then, O King, that sage, distressed and despairing of life,
followed by the spirit, went to the abode of Śaṅkara.
O Pāṇḍava, endowed with the power of yoga, he was hidden within the space between the nail and the flesh of that Mahādeva, so that the god did not see him.
At the end of that, there appeared a being with a radiance equal to fire and the sun—a person, the God of gods, Maheśvara—who cried out, "Release! Release! (muñca muñca).
Thus addressed by that being, O Bhārata, Mahādeva then revealed himself as the Lord of Yogins within the space between the nail and the flesh.
Having established the sage who had fallen into supreme distress, the Lord of Beings said:
"Do not fear, O Brahmin; come forth, O great sage!"
Then, having seen that being situated within his extremely subtle body, he said this:
"O great element, tell me, what will you do with him?"
Kṛtyā said:
"O Lord of Gods, I was conceived by Pippalāda when he was possessed by anger; know me, O Master, to be here for the purpose of harming his body. (RKV 42.59)
Having heard this which had fallen from the mouth of the Bhūta, Mahādeva,
the knower of mantras, consulted with Yājñavalkya, who was standing at his side.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having bestowed the name "Yogīśvara" upon the brahmin,
the Lord of Gods dismissed him and vanished right there.
But having dispatched that being, Pippalāda, too, being dejected and distressed by his father and mother, took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
O King, for sixteen years he remained on one big toe and without food,
propitiating Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods, together with Umā.
Then Śaṅkara, pleased by that asceticism, spoke these words:
The Lord said: "I am well-pleased with you, O brahmin of noble vows, because of this austerity.
Choose a boon; I shall grant you that auspicious thing desired by your mind."
Pippalāda said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
O Maheśvara, remain present here at this sacred ford."
Having been addressed thus, the Lord, accompanied by the hosts of beings, said "So be it" to the great sage Pippalāda and vanished from sight.
When the god had departed, Pippalāda bathed there in that great water,
established Mahādeva, and went to the Northern Mountain.
O King, having bathed with devotion at that sacred ford accompanied by mantras, a person should satisfy the ancestors and the gods and worship Maheśvara.
One obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
upon death, one goes to the city of Rudra—of this there is no doubt to be made.
Moreover, O Bhārata, those ancestors for whom one feeds Brahmins are satisfied and rejoice in heaven for twelve years.
But whoever, through renunciation, should cast off their body at that sacred site,
his destination shall never be anything other than the world of Rudra.
O sinless one, all of this that you asked has been fully explained:
the majesty of Pippalāda and the very origin of the sacred ford.
This merit is a destroyer of sin, auspicious, and a dispeller of bad dreams;
for those who read or even hear it, there shall be the destruction of all evil.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Pippalāda Tīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 43.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Vimaleśvara.
There, the delightful Devaśilā was fashioned by the gods themselves.
O King, for one who bathes there and worships the Brahmins with devotion,
there is no end to the merit gained even from a very small gift.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of Brahmins, what gifts are praised on the surface of the earth,
by giving which with devotion a man is liberated from all sins?
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Gold, silver, copper, as well as gems and pearls,
the gift of land, and the gift of cows— these liberate a man from the state of being a beast.
Whoever brings about the end of their life at that sacred ford shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
Thereafter, one should go to the Puṣkariṇī pond, which destroys all sins;
having bathed there, one should worship the Sun-god, the mass of splendor.
By reciting a single Ṛc verse from the Sāman, one obtains the fruit of the Sāmaveda;
likewise, by the recitation of the Yajurveda and the Ṛgveda.
Or one should mutter the syllable mantra while meditating on the sun;
having recited the Ādityahṛdaya, one is liberated from all sins. (RKV 43.8)
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and recites [the mantra] for the twice-born according to the prescribed rite, for him a merit ten million times greater arises; of this there is no doubt.
By fasting, by entering fire, or by casting off the body in water—
at that sacred ford, whoever dies attains the supreme goal.
O best of kings, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra,
one who performs his prescribed duty shall go to the supreme goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, having recognized disease, the loss of vitality, and delusion, by what means are the social classes liberated from sins? Tell me that method.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: A Brāhmaṇa who offers water with sesame seeds, bathes with sesame seeds, is free from desire and anger, and gives up his life through fasting, attains the state of the righteous.
O dear one, in battle a kṣatriya shall attain a good rebirth at death;
in the absence of that [battle], O highly wise one, he shall attain it by serving [the king].
One who is seized by disease or a planetary affliction, or one who is old or has impaired faculties,
shall attain a good rebirth by having himself cremated in the fire according to the prescribed rite.
For even a Vaiśya, by thus abandoning his life-breaths, shall indeed partake in auspiciousness;
or by casting off his life-breaths in water with a pure disposition, he shall become Śiva.
Even a Śūdra, by serving the twice-born and propitiating Maheśvara, is liberated; otherwise, that sinner will certainly fall into hell.
Alternatively, one who is unable to recite the *praṇava* should dry his body in the five fires after having taken leave of the best of the twice-born and his guru.
One should prepare a fire of dried cow dung with the guidance of those who are peaceful, self-controlled, conquerors of anger, learned in the scriptures, and discerning.
Thus, those of the [social] classes, deluded by the false ego regarding their true nature,
fall into a terrible hell, just as a blind man falls into a mountain abyss.
Those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, act according to their own whims, enter the womb of a worm; for them there is neither the funeral cake nor the ritual rites.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who abandon the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti and follow their own whimsical conduct fall into twenty-eight crores of hells.
Or else each of these falls, submerged in the ocean of hell;
O King, a human birth is difficult to obtain and is acquired through much merit.
That man who, having attained [this state], indeed abandons pride and envy,
always restraining his own self— he is truly a man with the eye of knowledge.
For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the ointment-stick of knowledge—
He whose eye has not opened is indeed blind from birth regarding that which is to be known.
All this that was asked by you, O best of kings, has been told to you.
For even more desirable than the words of Rudra is the Narmadā,
the best of rivers, who issued forth from the body of Rudra.
May he, the Great-Souled Lord, the presiding deity over all gods, deliver all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, this [practice] of great merit has been brought down;
through bathing, mental and verbal evil born of karma is destroyed.
Because she emerged from the body of Rudra, she is indeed most meritorious;
he who, having risen every morning, steps upon the ground with devotion—
O dear one, by reciting this mantra, one obtains the fruit of bathing:
"Salutations, O Goddess of meritorious waters; salutations, O you who flow to the ocean."
Homage be to you, the liberator from evil; homage, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
Homage be to you, served by the assembly of the best of sages; homage be to you, who have issued from the body of the Three-eyed One!
Homage be to you, ever the most excellent among those who perform good deeds; homage be to you, the perpetual purifier of the pure!

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Vimalēśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 44. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, listen to that which is the supreme among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
It was established on the southern bank of the Revā by the wielder of the trident.
"O best of kings, it was created for the sake of the liberation of the lords of men.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard of various duties and various sacred fords."
And all the duties of giving have been fulfilled through your grace, O best of the twice-born.
Furthermore, I wish to hear how saṃsāra is severed,
so that there is no returning again and liberation is attained.
Tell me all of this, O best of the twice-born, through your grace.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the great transition from one sacred ford to another;
for by hearing of its power, one is liberated from the sins committed throughout a year.
Whether by means of speech, mind, or especially by bodily acts,
one is liberated from all sins through the glorification of that sacred site.
O Lord of the Earth, that sacred ford (tīrtha) measures five krośas;
it is divine and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon living beings, even those who have committed sinful deeds.
On the southern bank of the Revā is the mountain named Bhṛgu;
and upon its summit, that holy site was established by Śambhu.
O King, it is renowned throughout the three worlds as Śūlabheda;
and there are trees situated there, all around the holy site in the four directions.
Those who have fallen, as well as any creatures on earth or birds that die right there, go to the abode of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
They go to the supreme world at that sacred ford; of this there is no doubt.
The Gaṅgā, having emerged from Pātāla, is known by the name Bhogavatī.
And that other meritorious great river named Gīrvāṇa, which issues forth from Śūlabheda and brings about the destruction of all sins, flows on.
O dear one, she fell into the middle of the pit where it had been pierced by the trident-wielder Śambhu in the past, and there Sarasvatī was produced.
O King, she fell there upon that stone known as Gīrvāṇa, where the three radiant [deities] reside, which liberates one from ancient sins.
Among those sacred fords, that particular ford has never existed, nor will it ever exist—
be they Kedāra, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, or likewise Gayā.
And other excellent holy places do not equal even a sixteenth part of these;
there are five distinct locations that constitute the holy sites.
And I shall speak in brief of each one individually:
how Gayā is meritorious at its navel, and how Cakratīrtha is equal to it.
Just as the well in Dharmāraṇya and Śūlabheda are equal [in merit],
so too is the Brahmayūpa meritorious, as is the Devanadī.
Just as Gayāśiras is meritorious, as is the stone of the gods, and as are the sacred sites of Puṣkara and the lake of Mārkaṇḍa; RKV_44.19 //
Having offered there the funeral rice-balls and water, which likewise render the balls inexhaustible,
whoever performs a *śrāddha* ceremony there shall drink that water constantly;
he is liberated from all sins, just as a serpent is freed from its slough.
One should honor blameless Brahmins who are free from hypocrisy and anger.
A gift given on the thirteenth day shall possess thirteenfold merit,
upon seeing the honored god Gaṇanātha, who has the face of an elephant.
All obstacles perish upon seeing Kambala, the protector of the field.
One should worship Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, with supreme devotion.
To the east of the God, Umā should be worshipped with diligence;
thereafter, one should worship Mārkaṇḍeśa, who dwells in Guha’s abode, with devotion.
They are liberated from all sins, whether accumulated through ignorance or knowledge;
having entered into the midst of the cave, one should mutter the three-syllabled Sūkta.
He shall obtain a sixth part of the merit born of the Blue Mountain (Nīlaparvata).
Three deities reside there together with the Sun and the Maruts.
This supreme site of ten million liṅgas embodies all the gods;
just as all rivers and streams reach their end by merging into the ocean.
In the same way, sins are destroyed by the sight of Śūlabheda;
O Lord of the Earth, this proof is indeed visible even today.
Sparks quiver within the center of the *liṅga* through the practice of bathing;
therein, the second sign of attainment is that a drop of oil does not spread.
For in this way, the condition there arises from the power of piercing with the trident;
one who should constantly remember Śūlabheda at the three times of day.
O King, he becomes truly purified, both internally and externally;
this has not been told by me to anyone, even though I was questioned by the gods themselves.
This sacred site, more secret than the secret, has been made by me to be always concealed;
it removes all sins, is meritorious, and is the supreme destroyer of all defects.
O Lord of Men, Śūlabheda is a sacred ford that embodies all holy fords;
upon hearing of its power, one is liberated from all sins.
O dear one, I have described Śūlabheda to you in brief;
the man who hears this with devotion is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Śūlabheda," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 45.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: This very question was formerly asked of Maheśvara.
And by King Uttānapāda, in the assembly of sages and gods.
Uttānapāda said:
"O Hara, this supreme holy place is immensely meritorious and consists of all the gods; it is a station more secret than the secret, never before seen or heard of."
O Lord, tell me in detail how Śūlabheda came into being, by whom it was produced in the past, and the majesty of that sacred ford.
Īśvara said:
In former times there was a Dānava of great prowess, arrogant in his strength;
in the mortal world, there was no one equal to him in valor or might.
This son of the Son of Brahmā, a wicked and intoxicated man named Andhaka,
dwelt in his own abode, ruling a kingdom free from thorns while remaining a sinner.
Living in the mortal world, joyful and well-nourished, he is not overcome by the gods;
for that sinner’s abode is like a grove of fire.
At that time, O Bhārata, Andhaka reflected:
"I shall propitiate Mahādeva so that he may be gracious toward me."
"Having made a firm resolve, Andhaka went forth from his home, saying: 'I pray for a divine boon that dwells within my mind.'"
Having reached the bank of the Revā, the Dānava remained engaged in asceticism;
he performed fierce, terrible penance that caused the hair to stand on end.
Then he remained without food for a thousand divine years;
for a second thousand, however, he lived subsisting on water alone.
During the third thousand years, he was devoted to the practice of inhaling smoke;
during the fourth thousand years, he remained steadfast in the cultivation of yoga.
O Bhārata, no one here has ever performed such a most dreadful penance as this man, who remains standing with nothing left but skin and bone.
Then, O King, a column of smoke issued forth from his head;
having passed beyond the world of the gods, it reached and pervaded Kailāsa, where it remained.
Then Umā, standing near the God, spoke these words:
"Who is this man in the world of mortals who stands firm through such fierce asceticism?"
Four thousand years passed, O Supreme Lord;
never before has such penance been seen, heard of, or performed by anyone.
O Lord, why do you show contempt for me here, though I am devoted to my vows? O All-pervading One, you grant everything quickly even for a small amount of austerity.
"O Maheśvara, I shall not play with dice with you today,
until this Dānava has been raised up, O you who are kind to your devotees."
Īśvara said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess, you who are endowed with all auspicious marks!
I do not know that lord of the Dānavas who is thus suffering."
"O blessed lady, remaining steadfast in the practice of yoga and meditating upon that supreme state,
come there with me to where he performs his austerities."
Accompanied by Umā, the Lord Maheśvara went there;
he was seen by the divine Śambhu as nothing but skin and bone remaining.
The pleased Maheśvara, the God of gods, replied:
"O, alas! A terrible, cruel, and hair-raising deed has been committed!"
"And why, my child, have you performed such terrible asceticism?
I shall grant you a boon, my child—whatever dwells in your mind."
Andhaka said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and if you are a granter of boons, O Śaṅkara, may I conquer all the gods through your grace, O Maheśvara."
Īśvara said:
"Even in a dream, none of the gods should ever be fought; one should not speak what is impossible, nor that which is displeasing to the mind."
Ask for anything else that dwells in your mind,
whether it be those situated in heaven, or in the mortal world, or even in the nether regions.
Among mortals, you shall enjoy various pleasures as you desire;
rule your kingdom free from thorns, just like the Lord of the Gods in heaven.
Having heard the words of the god, Andhaka stood dejected:
"My suffering has been in vain; nothing at all has been accomplished by me."
Having exhaled his final breath, he fell to the surface of the earth;
like a tree whose roots have been severed, he then became breathless.
Then, seeing him fallen into a swoon, the Goddess spoke these words:
"O Śaṅkara, grant him whatever desire he may wish for."
If you neglect your devotees, ill repute will befall you.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, if I were ever to grant you a boon according to your desire,
then you would hold neither Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā, nor even me in high regard."
O Goddess of the gods, he attains a height that surpasses even other gods and asuras.
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, by resorting to some means or other, cause them to rise up;
grant this boon: 'Conquer all the gods, with the exception of Viṣṇu.'"
Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, there is an excellent means that dwells in my mind;
I shall grant that very boon to him which was mentioned by you."
Then, sprinkled with the nectar of immortality, he became healthy at that very moment;
thus he was born renewed again, with all his limbs beautified.
Listen with a focused mind and accept this supreme boon;
with the exception of Viṣṇu, I shall grant you whatever is desired and dear to you.
"May all this be fruitful for you, and may your dharma not be otherwise;
O Asura, if you so desire, I grant you this boon."
"You shall conquer all the gods except for Viṣṇu, and even me, were it not for me."
Andhaka said:
"So be it," he replied, relying solely on his own strength;
"O Maheśvara, with my own power I shall conquer everyone except Viṣṇu."
Having said, "I have indeed become one who has accomplished his purpose," he prostrated himself and [said]:
"Go, O Goddess, together with Umā, to the excellent peak of Kailāsa."
Having mounted his bull, the preeminent among bulls, that god, together with Umā,
granted him this boon and vanished right there.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Granting of Boons to Andhaka," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 46] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having obtained the boon, that Dānava went toward his own city;
O King, he beheld his city adorned with variegated squares.
And with various gardens adorned with groves of plantains,
as well as breadfruit trees, bakula trees, āmrāta trees, mangoes, and campaka trees.
It was richly adorned with various trees such as *aśoka*, coconut palms, *mātuliṅga* citrons, and pomegranates, and was beautified by ponds.
It resounded with divine shrines for the deities, beautifully adorned with garlands of banners,
and was made resonant by the chanting of the Vedas and auspicious hymns.
He entered the divine golden palace adorned with garlands of gold;
there he saw his sons, his wife, his ministers, and his servants and slaves.
Then, [he saw] all those bestowers of victory running here and there, making their hearts beautiful with loud shouts of "Victory! (jayantī).
Some fastened the archway, some scattered flowers,
and others, with mātuluṅga fruits in their hands, ran toward Andhaka.
Pure people were seen with vessels filled with food;
many people there were seen with their hands full.
There, with vessels filled with unbroken grains of rice, hundreds of thousands of women and Brahmins recite mantras, while the women also chant auspicious verses.
The ministers and servants likewise presented elephants;
all those who were inhabitants of the city offered their congratulations.
Delighted and satisfied, Andhaka dwelt there with his ministers;
he beheld the entire world, as well as the horses and the foot-soldiers.
In that very place, he saw various treasuries filled with gold, as well as female buffaloes, cows, bulls, and many kinds of umbrellas.
Thus Andhaka dwelt there for some time;
living in the mortal world, joyful and contented, he was not surpassed even by the gods.
Having learned that he had obtained the boon, the inhabitants of heaven became apprehensive;
they all united and went to Vāsava for refuge.
Śakra said: "How did you all, even you who dwell in the celestial realms, come to be here? From what has fear arisen for you, that you have come for refuge? How [did this happen]?"
Then all those immortals spoke these words to Śakra:
The gods said:
"O lords of the gods, there is a Daitya named Andhaka, empowered by a boon from Śambhu;
he is invincible to all the gods. What indeed is to be done beyond this?"
"O Lord of Gods, reflect upon the truth; what remedy should be devised?
Thus spoke those gods, intent on consultation before Śakra.
And as soon as they were conversing,
the Dānava, having learned from the reports brought by his spies that the host of gods was there, departed from his home.
O King, mounted alone upon his chariot yet surrounded by many who were devoted to him,
he traversed the inaccessible summit of Mount Meru with effortless ease.
Encircled by a golden wall and adorned with various hermitages,
it was then inaccessible to the host of enemies, O best of kings.
The Asura entered there as if in sport, like one entering his own home;
the slayer of Vṛtra, overcome with fear, offered him his own seat.
Andhaka sat there upon the auspicious throne of Śakra himself and presided over the assembly hall,
which was surrounded on all sides by the gods.
Śakra said:
"What is the reason for your arrival here? Tell me what must be done;
whatever wealth belongs to us, that I shall give to you, O Dānava."
Andhaka said:
"O Lord of the Gods, I do not desire your treasury nor your elephants;
show me today your own [abode], adorned with the splendors of heaven."
O Lord of Cows, show me Airāvata the great elephant, that very horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the jewels such as Urvaśī and the rest.
O Lord of Śacī, display the pārijātaka flowers, various species of trees, and all kinds of musical instruments.
Having heard those words of his, Śakra thought this:
"I do not see anyone at all who can slay this wicked one."
There was no one to provide protection for the suffering world of heaven;
terrified by fear, he gave away everything else, including musical instruments and the hosts of apsarases.
Having ascended the stage, he performed the tāṇḍava dance,
while all the gods, Yama, the Maruts, and the kinnaras sat down as spectators.
O King, all the Apsarases, beginning with Urvaśī, danced one by one before him, employing song and instrumental music.
O King, upon seeing those apsarases at that time, his mind did not grow weary; rather, his heart became filled with desire for Śacī.
Having taken Śakra’s wife, he set out toward his own city;
then a battle commenced between Andhaka and the gods.
By him, O best of kings, all the hosts of gods were destroyed in battle with various dense weapons, such as discuses, thunderbolts, and others.
All the gods were tormented and brought to ruin in great numbers;
indeed, all the Maruts were shattered by him at the forefront of the battle.
Just as a lion, having hunted down all the elephants, roams the forest,
so too were all those gods defeated by him alone and turned away in retreat.

Just as a foolish ruler in a village might oppress the people according to his own whim, freely invading their homes and repeatedly seizing their treasuries and garments; so too does the mind act upon the body.
That best of Dānavas did not see his own self as he departed, tormented by his subjects; having seized the wife of Śakra, he indeed went away.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Abduction of Śacī," in the *Śūlabheda-māhātmya* of the *Revākhaṇḍa*, within the fifth section (*Āvantyakhaṇḍa*) of the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 47.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all the gods went to Brahmā for refuge.
With elephants having the form of great mountains, and with horses resembling elephants;
With chariots shaped like cities yoked with lions and tigers,
and others with tortoises, buffaloes, and likewise with crocodiles.
Having reached the Brahma-world, the gods led by Śakra,
upon seeing the god born from the lotus, prostrated themselves before him with the eight limbs of the body.
The gods said:
"Victory to you, O God, worshiped by the world! Victory to you, the creator of the cycle of existence!
O lotus-born one, best of deities, we have come to you alone for refuge."
Having heard the words spoken with agitation by the gods of purified souls,
he addressed the king of the gods in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"O gods, what is the reason for your arrival here, and why is everyone so pale?
By whom have you all been insulted? Tell me yourselves quickly."
The gods said:
"O Lotus-born One, there is a powerful great Daitya named Andhaka;
by him all the hosts of gods have been deprived of their wealth and jewels."
Having slain the hosts of gods with his sword, discus, and various weapons,
that Dānava forcibly seized Śakra’s wife and departed.
Having heard the words of the gods, O king of kings, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, reflected upon the means for the slaughter of the Dānava.
"The sinful Dānava is invulnerable to all of you gods;
there is no one else anywhere who could be the protector of all the worlds."
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā immediately thereafter, all the gods placed Brahmā at their head and went to where Keśava was;
led by Brahmā, they praised the wielder of the discus with various hymns.
The gods said:
"Victory to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, whose chest is the abode of Lakṣmī!
O Lord of gods, bring about the destruction of the asuras; we have come to you for refuge."
Being praised by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Janārdana,
his mind filled with great joy, spoke to the assembly of deities.
Śrī Vāsudeva said: Welcome to the gods and the brahmins; today the night has dawned with a beautiful morning.
Tell me quickly what must be done; with whom are the dwellers of heaven angry?
"What is the suffering? What is the distress? Or from where has fear come? O highly fortunate ones, tell me the cause that is in your minds."
"Let him by whom this defeat was wrought go today to the abode of Yama!"—
having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, they reported that matter to him.
Displaying their own bodies, they were indeed ashamed with downcast faces;
for, O Lord, having been deprived of their kingdom by Andhaka, they were rendered devoid of splendor.
"O God, protect [us] as a father protects his son; slay the enemy of Indra along with his sons and grandsons.
Having been addressed thus with "So be it" by the lotus-seated Brahmā, he whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods and demons—
Then the Supreme Lord, grasping his conch, discus, mace, and bow,
rose from his couch of serpents in the presence of the gods.
Śrī Vāsudeva said:
Whether he resides in the netherworld, in the mortal realm, or in heaven,
I shall slay that wicked one by whom the gods have been tormented.
"May the gods, satisfied and with their power restored, return to their own abodes.
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the others, along with Indra, [departed].
Having bowed to Hari with their own vehicles and being satisfied in their hearts, they went to heaven.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Gīrvāṇa’s Ascent to Heaven," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 48 Uttānapāda said:
In what place, O Lord, did that Andhaka, the bull among the Daityas, dwell?
Having conquered all the gods, in what location did he establish himself?
The illustrious Maheśa said: O lord of men, I shall tell you where the Dānava has entered;
having taken refuge in the netherworld (pātālaloka), he is destroying the maidens.
Perceiving him stationed there, Keśava took up his bow and discharged the fiery arrow (āgneya), thinking, "Let him be consumed!"
Being scorched by that fire, he too discharged the Vāruṇa weapon;
then, by that great Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya was extinguished.
Then he reflected: "By whom was this arrow discharged?
Whose is this manly power? Who shall go to the abode of Yama?"
Then Andhaka, enraged in battle, emerged along the path of the arrow;
he saw Janārdana with bow in hand following the track of that arrow.
Andhaka said:
"Having been beheld by my gaze, you shall find no peace today;
you will not be able to go away, just as an elephant cannot escape upon seeing a tiger."
Just as a mouse comes before a cat seeking food,
so you are unable to escape while standing here in my presence.
"I shall send you along the most dreadful path of Yama;
I myself will search for you, and indeed, I shall go to your home."
O Keśava, you have been brought by Time into this battle with me—
the very same Dānavas who were previously conquered by you many times over.
O Keśava, they are neither men nor women;
however, I shall not engage in a further battle with weapons against you.
Keśava did not become angry as the lord of the Dānavas spoke; seeing that he was not fighting, the Dānava reflected.
"O King, having resolved, 'I shall engage in a duel,' he fought;
he was then kicked by Kṛṣṇa with his foot and fell upon the surface of the earth."
After a moment, having recovered his breath and risen, he reflected thus: "I am incapable of fighting in hand-to-hand combat. Thereupon, he employed conciliation;
with palms joined in a hollowed cup, pure and prostrate in the eight-limbed gesture of reverence, he bowed down.
Andhaka said:
Victory to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, to Viṣṇu, to the Victorious One! Salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, the Sustainer of the World, to Acyuta, the Great-Souled One.
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the one who wears a garland of lotuses;
to Janārdana, the Lord of Śrī, the Consort of Śrī, the one clad in yellow garments.
Salutation ever to Govinda; salutation to him who reclines upon the ocean;
salutation to the one with the formidable face, to Narasiṃha, the roaring one.
Salutation to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is white in color and bears the conch, discus, and mace;
salutation to you in the form of Vāmana, and salutation to you whose form is the sacrifice.
Homage to the one in the form of a boar, who has traversed the three worlds;
repeated homage to Keśava, who pervades the entirety of the quarters of space.
O Vāsudeva, salutations to you; salutations to the destroyer of Kaiṭabha.
O abode of Lakṣmī, best of gods, salutations to you, O leader of the deities.
I also bow down to those who establish the authority of Viṣṇu, the god above all gods, and of Prajāpati, the creator of the world.
I bow even to those who offer salutation to the wise Vāsudeva, the god of all beings.
I bow even to those who offer salutation to that Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Boar of immeasurable splendor.
Salutations to you again and again, O Lord, who are the treasury of all virtues,
the ocean of compassion, and the one who is dear to all devotees.
The Blessed One said: "O Lord of Dānavas, I am pleased with you; choose a boon as you desire.
I shall surely grant you a boon, even one difficult to obtain in the three worlds."
Andhaka said:
"O God, if you are pleased with me and will grant the desired boon,
then, O God, grant me a most magnificent battle."
Purified by this untainted hand-offering, may I go to the auspicious worlds.
The Blessed One said:
"How can I grant you battle, since I have been further gratified by you?
Anger shall not overcome you; how then, O Andhaka, shall I fight with you?"
If your mind is set upon battle without a doubt,
then go for battle against the god Maheśvara.
Andhaka said:
"In that regard, no purpose directed toward the god Maheśvara can be accomplished."
The Blessed One said:
"Son, go to the peak and shake it with your strength."
O Dānava, when that [tree] is shaken, the Lord of Gods will become extremely fierce with anger;
once Śaṅkara is provoked to wrath, he will give you a terrible battle.
At Viṣṇu’s word, that wicked one went to where Maheśvara was;
having reached the peak of Kailāsa, he shook it again and again.
When that peak was shaken, the three worlds trembled;
