its many mountain summits fell down, quivering repeatedly.
O lord of the earth, the four oceans quickly became one,
meteors fell, and many trees were uprooted.
Accompanied by Umā, the God was filled with supreme wonder;
having embraced the Daughter of the Mountain firmly, he spoke these words.
For what reason does the mountain tremble, and for what reason does the earth tremble? For what reason do the Nāgas, mortals, and even Pātāla tremble?
Or is it the end of the eon, O Lord? You ought to explain this to me.
The Lord said: Whose evil mind has arisen that the hand was thrust into the mouth of a serpent and armor was placed upon the forehead? He shall go to the abode of Yama.
I shall slay him who took refuge on Kailāsa, by whom I was put to sleep and by whom I was awakened; of this there is no doubt, even if he should stand face to face with me.
The Lord of Gods reflected: "This is indeed Andhaka, there is no doubt;
I shall devise a means by which he may be slain in an instant."
And all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, together with the Vasus, arrived,
having fashioned a divine chariot endowed with every auspicious mark.
Some gods were stationed on the wheel, some at the tip and sides of the beak,
some gods were stationed at the hub, and some were stationed upon the yoke-poles.
Some remained motionless upon the yokes, some were stationed at the sacrificial posts;
some were the supports of the chariots, and some were the enclosures of the chariots.
Others were in the *āmalasāraka* pavilion, and others were stationed at the water-jars;
there was a divine banner, terrifying to the enemy, adorned with rows of flags and other ornaments.
Having fashioned a divine chariot and mounted it, the Teacher of the World,
Maheśvara, filled with wrath, set out for where the Dānava was.
"Stay! Stay! he then cried out. "Where will you go, O evil-minded one?
Grasping his bow in hand, he discharged arrows at the Dānava.
While the battle was presided over by Dānava, he cut down the arrows with his own shafts;
thereupon, Andhaka was completely covered by that very bow.
Neither the sun, nor the sky, nor the moon was visible there;
even the Dānava discharged the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra) against Śiva.
Scorched by the embers of the arrows, all the gods took refuge [in him], crying:
"Protect us! Protect us, O Mahādeva, for we are being burned by the Dānavas!"
Then that God of Gods, consisting of the Vāruṇa weapon, conquered;
by the Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya weapon was destroyed in an instant.
Then, O dear one, the Vāyavya weapon released by the Dānava on the field of battle was destroyed by the Vāruṇa weapon.
With a mind possessed by anger, the god released the serpent-weapon;
there is no doubt that the wind was destroyed there by those serpents with their arrows.
Then the Dānava effortlessly discharged the Garuḍa-missile;
and upon seeing that Garuḍa-missile, the serpent-missile was no longer visible at all.
Then, by the God of Gods, the Nārasiṃha [weapon] was discharged;
by that Nārasiṃha weapon-arrow, the Gāruḍa weapon was quelled.
"An arrow should be neutralized by an arrow; they should not harm one another.
A great battle has occurred, O father, which strikes fear into both gods and asuras."
With discuses, hollow arrows, iron shafts, javelins, swords, and mallets;
likewise with calf-toothed arrows, broad-headed shafts, and beautiful *karṇikāra* darts.
Thus, the Dānava could not be slain by various weapons;
then swords, iron arrows, and javelins became terrifying with their blazing flames.
Released by the Bull-bannered Lord in battle against the Dānava,
the weapons do not touch their bodies, just as [the weapons of the enemy] did not touch the women of Gauḍa.
Then, having cast aside their weapons, the two stood ready for hand-to-hand combat;
seizing hand with hand and striking with their own fists,
Śiva and Andhaka fought, contending with various martial maneuvers.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Lord of Gods reflected upon the subjugation of Andhaka:
"I shall slay this evil-souled one; of this there is no doubt, no uncertainty."
O best of kings, when that Dānava was hurled by Śiva, he fell upon the surface of the earth with his arms upraised and his face turned downward.
Overcome by anger, the enemy of the gods seized the Lord of Gods in battle,
cast him into the hollow of his armpits, and, having bound him, tormented him.
The god Maheśvara became motionless and fell into a swoon;
perceiving him to have fallen into a swoon, the Dānava reflected.
"Alas, alas! A grievous evil deed has been committed by me today through my sinful action.
What shall I do? How can I purify this karma? In what place might I find liberation?"
Having taken the god onto his lap, he went to Mount Kailāsa;
then, having laid Śaṅkara upon his bed, the king of the Daityas departed from there.
Then the god, having fallen upon his bed, experienced intense agony;
yet at that moment, he beheld himself situated within his own palace.
"How was this defeat brought about by that evil-souled one?
Overcome by a surge of anger, he set out toward the Dānava."
Taking up an iron club capable of supporting a thousand *bhāras*,
the Lord then beheld the Dānava and hurled it at his head.
The Dānava struck him with a sword while laughing in the battle;
then, in that great conflict, the god remembered the weapon called Kaucchera.
Having cast off that which was blazing within his heart, he was struck in an instant;
then, being struck by him, he vomited forth a gush of blood.
Having fallen, he lay face downwards, then pierced by the trident;
and once more, he was split into two pieces by the trident of the God of gods.
Standing on the tip of the stake, that wicked man then whirled like a wheel;
and from his body, wherever he fell upon the ground, drops of blood [fell].
All those Dānavas rose up, weapons in hand;
then the god was overwhelmed by the swift Dānava.
Then Durgā Cāmuṇḍā, with a terrifying countenance, was summoned by the god;
she arrived with a fearsome form, resplendent with various weapons.
"O Lord, let the command be given: who, possessing great fangs, a massive body, tawny eyes, and long ears, shall go to the abode of Yama?"
Īśvara said:
"O blessed one, drink as much of this Dānava’s blood as you desire;
O Durgā, catch the blood falling upon the ground without delay."
"I shall slay the Dānava; O beautiful one, grant me your assistance.
Having been addressed thus, Durgā then drank the blood.
All the Dānavas were slain by the Lord of the Gods by the thousands;
and Andhaka, seeing those Dānavas fallen to the earth,
then praised Maheśvara, the God of gods, with words.
Andhaka said:
Be victorious, O Lord of the gods of gods, you who bear a body half of which is Umā!
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, to the All, whose self consists of the three qualities.
Mounted upon the bull-throne, with the moon as your crest-ornament, victory to you who hold the skull-topped staff in hand; O bearer of the Gaṅgā, homage be to you!
Homage to the one who holds the hand-drum; homage to the one garlanded with skulls;
homage be to you, Maheśa, the destroyer of Smara’s body.
Homage to you, the Lord of the Gaṇas, for the shattering of Pūṣan’s teeth;
victory to you, who possess a body of your own essential nature, yet are formless and manifold in form!
O Śaṅkara, [salutations] to the one who dwells eternally in the cremation ground, who eternally possesses the form of Bhairava, and who brings about the destruction of even Viriñci’s head.
You are all-pervading; you are the creator and you alone are the destroyer, and there is no other.
You are the earth, you are the directions, and you likewise are the preceptor Bhārgava.
O Lord of the gods of gods, you are indeed Sūrya, and likewise the son of the Earth;
all that is visible, such as the constellations, planets, and so forth, is you alone.
Having thus offered praise to the god at that time,
the Dānava bowed down to Maheśvara with his two hands joined together.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O great being! Ask for a boon, O Dānava.
For I am the giver and you are the supplicant; I shall grant you here whatever you desire."
Andhaka said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then I must be made like yourself; no other boon [is desired]."
He is smeared with ashes, has matted hair, three eyes, and four arms;
he holds a trident and wears a tiger-skin upper garment and a serpent as his sacred thread.
I desire all of this, O Maheśvara, if you are pleased with me.
Īśvara said:
"O sinless one, I grant you today the boon that you have requested;
my son, established among my attendants, you shall become Bhṛṅgīśa."

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Andhaka and the Granting of Boons to Him," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 49.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having slain Andhaka, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [acted].
Accompanied by Umā, Rudra went to Mount Kailāsa.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā and accompanied by Indra, arrived there;
all of them, joyful and satisfied, bowed down to the Lord of Pārvatī.
Īśvara said:
"O Grandfather, let all those who have gathered here sit down; for this Dānava has been slain for the sake of the gods."
"O Brahmin, my pain does not become free from impurity because of his blood; he, who was devoted to auspicious vows, austerity, and recitation, has been slain by me."
"O Four-faced One, I wish to properly undertake a pilgrimage;
let all of you who have assembled here come along with me. (RKV 49.5)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods departed for Prabhāsa,
[visiting] the sacred sites beginning with Prabhāsa that lie between the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
O King, even after bathing in all [the waters], he did not attain purity;
therefore, the Lord, accompanied by the gods, went to the Narmadā.
Priyavrata plunged into the southern shore;
having gone to the southern shore, he reached the mountain named Bhṛgu.
O lord of the earth, having stayed there with the gods and wandered about for a long time until he was weary, Mahādeva sat down in despondency.
Since that place was captivating to all the inhabitants of heaven,
the Lord Maheśvara, considering it to be a distinguished sacred site (tīrtha), remained there.
He pierced the mountain with his trident; by that act, the subterranean realm (rasātala) was split open, yet the trident remained stainless, and no stain was visible anywhere upon it.
Summoned there by the gods, the highly meritorious Bhāratī appeared;
likewise, the highly meritorious Sarasvatī emerged there from the mountains.
The second confluence there is like that of the white and black [streams] in the Veṇī;
there, the god Brahmā himself is present at the supreme Liṅga known as Brahmeśa.
He established that supreme, meritorious shrine which destroys all suffering;
and in the southern direction from it, the Lord Janārdana himself [resides].
And she remains there forever, stationed upon the tip of Viṣṇu’s foot;
for one situated in the middle of the pool, there shall be no path through the water.
O King, a line drawn with the tip of a trident causes water to flow;
that water flows to where the great river Revā is located.
O best of kings, at the Jalaliṅga, which is of great merit, and at Cakratīrtha,
as well as at Śūlabheda, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rite for the Lord of Gods.
He considers himself pure, having committed no sin whatsoever;
at the very culmination of that state, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, [appears].
By his own self, the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the trident, was established;
that sacred ford is supreme, consisting of all the gods among all sacred fords.
Having installed the God of gods at that sacred site, the Teacher of the World [performed] this supreme merit which removes all sins and destroys all suffering.
Then, having released one hundred and eight Vināyakas as guardians,
one hundred and eight Kṣetrapālas protect that [site] with great effort.
Obstacles arise for one who wishes to remain there;
some are distracted by their households, and others by their agricultural labors.
Some establish assemblies, some are intent on the acquisition of wealth;
some engage in backbiting, while others are constantly devoted to violence.
Some are devoted to the wives of others, some are destroyers of their livelihoods, and others say this: "How can one go to the sacred fords? (RKV 49.24)
When his wife, sons, servants, and so forth are afflicted by hunger,
men are likewise cast into the snares of delusion by the hosts of gods.
For those mortals who engage in sinful conduct, bathing there does not take place;
and the hosts of the gods' servants always guard that sacred ford.
Blessed and meritorious are those mortals for whom a bath occurs in the Sarasvatī,
the Bhogavatī, and especially in the celestial river.
But this is a meritorious confluence, like that of the white and black waters at the Veṇī;
having seen that sacred ford, all those gods were delighted in their hearts.
Having come into the presence of the God, they described this supreme sacred site: "O Lord of Gods, this tīrtha is equal to Gayātīrtha for you."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred site more secret than this secret one;
it was worshipped by Śūlapāṇi along with Indra and the hosts of Apsarases.
By yakṣas, kinnaras, and gandharvas, by the guardians of the directions and the world-protectors, as well as by all the gods and asuras with dances, songs, and hymns of praise; RKV 49.31.
While Maheśvara was being honored by all the Gaṇas, Siddhas, and Nāgas,
O lord of men, he was pierced there by the god with the tip of his trident.
O tiger among men, where even today a whirlpool filled with celestial beings is seen in three ways, there is the great triad of pools accompanied by a tumultuous roar.
It causes the destruction of all sins, it is the supreme destroyer of all suffering;
whoever bathes at that sacred ford, being devoted to fasting, [attains this].
Even one devoid of initiation and mantras is liberated from the sin of a year;
moreover, those who bathe according to the rule with the five mantras [attain liberation].
With the five mantras declared in the Vedas, accompanied by auspicious jars containing gold, and with ten syllables, or six, or even three; RKV_49.36 //
O lord of men, the rite at the sacred ford should be performed separately by the twice-born—
namely the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— as well as by women and Śūdras.
Having meditated upon the threefold [Veda] of the Puruṣas, one should perform the bath according to the rule;
those men who drink the water with the ten-syllable mantra, [attain the highest state].
They go to the other world where the god Maheśvara dwells,
just as [the merit gained] at Kedāra and likewise at Rudrakuṇḍa when one has drunk [the water].
The syllable *kṣa*, joined with five *repha*s (the letter *r*), honored by the gods,
and conjoined with the syllable *oṃ*— this is proclaimed as that which is to be known.
He who performs a bath there according to the prescribed rite, with his senses subdued,
should satisfy the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with sesame seeds.
That man who performs a śrāddha at the five sacred sites beginning with Gayā delivers twenty generations of his family— ten preceding and ten succeeding him.
He who, endowed with the prescribed ritual, gives gifts there with devotion, obtains the fruit at Śūlabheda; of this there is no doubt.
In that place, both good and evil deeds bear inexhaustible fruit;
just as Gayāśiras is always meritorious for ancestral rites.
Likewise, at the meritorious Śūlabheda, he who with devotion offers gold, a cow, land, or sesame seeds there through baths, gifts, and libations [attains great merit].
A seat, sandals, a bed, excellent horses, as well as a pair of garments, grain, and a full house— a Kṣatriya should offer these with great care.
One should give a plough with its yoke, as well as tilled land;
he who gives these gifts to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas [attains great merit].
To one who is learned in the Vedas, of noble lineage, pure, self-controlled,
perfected in sacred learning and study, free from hypocrisy, and endowed with ritual action—
one gift given on each of thirteen days shall become thirteenfold in merit.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin and Greatness of Śūlabheda," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 50. Uttānapāda said:
What kind of twice-born men are to be honored, and what kind are traditionally considered unworthy of honor?
Especially at a śrāddha ceremony, a wedding rite, or during the act of giving.
If, by the turn of fate, faith should arise toward rites such as the *śrāddha*, tell me this, O Lord: to whom is a gift not to be given?
Īśvara said:
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
and just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain a fruit,
so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit.

One who is diseased, deficient or redundant in limb, one-eyed, born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, one with black teeth, one who eats all things indiscriminately, and the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
One who betrays friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a reviler of others, one who abandons father, mother, or teacher, and one who constantly reviles Brahmins; RKV 50.7.
O King, that Brahmin who eats the food of a Śūdra while it is accompanied by mantras becomes untouchable— a Cāṇḍāla by his actions— and having touched him, one should perform a ritual bath.
One with deformed nails, one who has married a Śūdra woman, a thief, a usurer, a Kuṇḍa and a Golaka, one who is devoted to great gifts, and one who is intent on self-destruction; RKV 50.9.
A teacher who teaches for wages, a eunuch, one who defiles a maiden, and one who is falsely accused—
these Brahmins should always be avoided with great effort after careful consideration.
If one, having accepted a gift, should engage in trade, no gift should be given to him; for him, that [gift] becomes in vain.
Whatever gift is given to those twice-born ones who are perfected in learning and study, and who are devoted to virtuous conduct, all that shall attain imperishability.
Support the poor, O protector of the earth, but never the wealthy;
medicine is beneficial for the sick, but what use is medicine to one who is healthy?
Uttānapāda said:
"O Śaṅkara, tell me what the ritual procedure there is for the śrāddha at that sacred ford (tīrtha), what the performance of the rite is, and how the gift is to be given."
The Lord said: Having performed the śrāddha at home with devotion, being pure and having conquered the senses,
one should circumambulate the preceptor and then feed [him] at the boundary.
Restraining his speech, he should set forth until he has not yet crossed the boundary;
then, having gone to Śūlabheda, he should perform his bath according to the prescribed rule.

And he who, at the five prescribed places, should perform the ancestral rites in due order with offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) and so forth, as well as the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa-dāna) with milk-rice, honey, and clarified butter; RKV_50.17 //
His ancestors remain satisfied for seventeen years with unbroken rice grains,
jujube fruits, bilva fruits, molasses, honey, and clarified butter.
She too obtains that same fruit at this sacred ford; of this there is no doubt.
And he who diligently gives sandals to Brahmins [obtains the same].
He too, mounted upon a horse, attains heaven; of this there is no doubt—especially he who gives a bed, a horse, or a parasol.
He who gives an excellent house provided with the seven kinds of grain shall go, mounted upon a celestial chariot and surrounded by throngs of apsarases.
Indeed, he who gives a sesame-cow together with its calf and covered with cloth shall dwell at his own will in a golden mansion in this world.
O King, he shall dwell upon the vault of heaven until the dissolution of all beings,
whether in a house, in the forest, or on the path of a sacred ford.
He who gives water and food does not behold the world of Yama;
all gifts are given by him, and their fruit is obtained.
In this situation, one should give water, gifts, and even the gift of fearlessness;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
"He who performs the gift of a daughter in marriage, or he who releases a bull, shall dwell there where I am; it is not otherwise."
Uttānapāda said:
O Lord, how should the gift of a daughter always be performed by the righteous? Likewise, how should her acceptance and maintenance, as well as her marriage, be conducted?
I ask another thing, O Lord of Gods: whose daughter is not to be given away?
To whom, O God, should it be given, and to whom does that which is given become inexhaustible?
O Lord, how might it be superior, middling, or even inferior; or how might it be characterized by passion (rājasa) or darkness (tāmasa), or even lead to the highest good (niḥśreyasa)?
Īśvara said:
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of a daughter is preeminent;
he who, having approached with supreme devotion, gives his own daughter [in marriage].
One should give the daughter, adorned with ornaments, to one who is of noble birth, handsome, a knower of virtues, and wise, at an auspicious conjunction and during a favorable moment.
Whoever gives horses, elephants, cows, and garments here according to their ability,
their dwelling shall be there, in that place which is free from all affliction.
Since he has given here his daughter, who is dearer to him than his own life,
by that act he has given all this triple world, including all things moving and unmoving.
He who, having obtained wealth for the sake of a maiden, begs for that very wealth [himself], becomes a *caṇḍāla* by his actions; dead, he shall become a wooden stake.
If anyone should eat food in his house by any means out of greed for the tongue,
he shall be purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or again by the Taptakṛcchra.
Uttānapāda said: "If one possesses no wealth but has only a daughter in his house,
how can he perform her marriage if he does not resort to begging?"
Īśvara said:
O King, the marriage of a maiden must be performed with her very name;
by pronouncing the name of the maiden, there is never any fault whatsoever.
The supreme gift given by approaching [the recipient], and that gift which is offered unasked— there will come an end to the age, but no end at all to that [gift].
Giving after approaching [the recipient] is considered the highest; calling out to them is middling; giving when being entreated is inferior; and saying "Give! Give! is the lowest.
Just as a stone bound with another stone, when cast into the midst of water,
both of these go to their destruction, so too is food given to an unworthy recipient.
Therefore, a gift should never be given to one who is incapable;
it leads the donor downward, and especially oneself as well.
Just as one capable of rescuing two people with dry wood in the water, or like a boat,
so too the wise man should bring another to the further shore.
He who maintains the sacred fires yet accepts gifts from Śūdras becomes a Śūdra in this very life, and after death, he is reborn as a dog.
Indeed, for a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire, there would arise useless suffering if he were to accept gifts from the wicked—
an act that is secretly censured by the base.
That mortal shall become unfit for company and is consumed by a fire of chaff;
thereafter, he will undoubtedly become a mat-maker for seven births.
That gift which arises from shame, courtesy, greed, or compulsion,
as well as that gift given to one's own servants, shall be in vain and fruitless.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules Regarding the Examination of Worthy and Unworthy Recipients and the Giving of Gifts," in the *Śūlabheda-māhātmya* within the *Revā-khaṇḍa*, the fifth section (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) of the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 51.
Uttānapāda said: "O Lord, at what time is that performed—the śrāddha as well as the gift?"
A journey should be undertaken there; tell me quickly on which lunar day that should be.
Īśvara said:
Just as the Pitṛtīrtha is meritorious, supreme, and fulfills all desires,
so too is this tīrtha meritorious through bathing, giving gifts, and libations.
One should especially perform the śrāddha on all the beginnings of the yugas;
O child, hear now of the fourteen beginnings of the manvantaras.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Aśvayuja, the twelfth day of Kārttika, the third day of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada; RKV 51.4.
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of Māgha,
the eighth dark lunar day of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, as well as the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha; likewise the fifteenth day [of the dark fortnight].
These beginnings of the Manvantaras are recorded as yielding infinite fruit;
O King, one should perform the Śrāddha during both the northern and southern solstices.
Likewise, the full moon of Kārttika, that of Māgha, the third day of Vaiśākha,
and especially the full moon of Caitra and that of Jyeṣṭha.

On the Aṣṭakā days, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), and likewise during the Vyatīpāta yoga—all these are times for Śrāddha; what is given on these occasions is said to be inexhaustible.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Madhu,
one should perform a vigil at night near the feet of Viṣṇu.
Those who perform the worship of Viṣṇu with incense, lamps, food offerings, garlands, agallochum, and sandalwood, and who recite the ancient narrative; ||| RKV_51.11 ||
The twice-born who mutters the hymn (sūkta) declared in the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
One should perform the morning *śrāddha* after diligently honoring the twice-born;
one should give gifts according to one's ability, such as cows, gold, garments, and so forth.
His ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings;
the giver of the śrāddha, moreover, goes to that place where the Lord Janārdana dwells.
Then, on the thirteenth day, one should go to the Linga residing in the cave;
having beheld the Lord Mārkaṇḍeśvara, one is liberated from all sins.
Uttānapāda said: O Mahādeva, you ought to tell me by whom that most beautiful liṅga was installed within the cave.
Īśvara said: The lord of sages, Mārkaṇḍeya, renowned throughout the three worlds,
performed most severe penance for a thousand divine years.
Having entered the middle of the cave and resorted to the practice of yoga,
he installed a linga known by the name Mārkaṇḍeśvara.
Having bathed there with devotion, fasting and with senses subdued,
one who keeps a vigil there should diligently offer a lamp.
One should perform the bathing of the deity with the five products of the cow;
having anointed him according to one's ability, one should perform worship according to the prescribed rule.
The twice-born should perform their recitation with mantras originating from their own Vedic school;
they should recite the Sāvitrī eight thousand times, or else one hundred and eight times.
Having performed this, O best of kings, one shall obtain the fruit of birth;
indeed, having bathed on the fourteenth day and performed worship according to the prescribed rite.
One who desires his own welfare should give after examining the recipient;
his ancestors are satisfied for twelve years without a doubt. (RKV 51.23)
That donor goes to that place where enjoyments are eternal;
having entered into the midst of the cave, he should indeed roll about according to his power.
They obtain all the merit that exists on Mount Nīla;
moreover, whoever performs a Śrāddha at Śūlabheda on every festival day [attains the same].
Listen to the fruit of his merit, which is especially great at the end of the month of Caitra;
it is equal to the merit found at Kedāra and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Whatever merit exists especially at the confluence of the white and black rivers at other holy sites,
that same merit is found at Arbuda and at Mount Amaraparvata.
A person who, endowed with the proper rites and mantras, offers libations to the ancestors and the deities, obtains the fruit of all sacred fords, such as Gayā and others.
Having become pure and composed, one should then [worship] at the southern image; thus one shall deliver twenty families—ten preceding and ten following.
Having performed the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer the eight flowers;
listen now to how these eight flowers are to be offered mentally, as prescribed in the scriptures: RKV_51.30: Listen to them as follows.
The water-born, the lunar, the fiery, the windy, and again the earthly;
the sixth is that of the trees, while the seventh is that of Prajāpati.
The eighth is the Śiva-flower; hear now the determination regarding these:
the water-born is to be known as water, and the gentle [flower] as honey, ghee, and milk.
Incense, lamps, and the like belong to Agni; sandalwood and such belong to Vāyu;
tubers, roots, and the like belong to the Earth; and that which consists of fruits belongs to the Vanaspati.
The first flower is that pertaining to Prajāpati, namely recitation; the flower of latent impression is the flower of Śiva.
Non-violence is the first flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower.
The third flower is compassion, the fourth flower is patience;
the flowers of meditation, austerity, and knowledge are the seventh.
And truth is indeed the eighth flower; by these the deities are satisfied.
O lord of men, ascetics and the wise should be honored with devotion.
One should offer a parasol as a covering, as well as a pair of sandals;
by merely honoring him with these, three generations of ancestors are honored.
Those men who perform the recitation with devotion to the wielder of the trident shall dwell in the heavenly world until the dissolution of all beings.
One should anoint the Lord of Gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), yakṣakardama, saffron, sandalwood from Śrīkhaṇḍa, and aguru.
Those who perform worship of the Wielder of the Trident with various kinds of flowers should keep a vigil at night and diligently offer lamps.
One should offer incense and food offerings and recite the Puranic stories;
those men who remain in that place with devotion and perform *japa* [there].
One should recite the Śrīsūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the Pāvamāna hymn, and the Vṛṣākapi hymn,
as well as the Raudrī or Bahurūpī mantra with mantras declared in the Vedas.
One should worship the Brahmins with devotion, and having worshipped and prostrated before them,
one is glorified in the world of Śiva with various kinds of great enjoyments.
He who, as a follower of the Ṛgveda, recites the prayers beginning with "Agnim," as well as the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Ślokādhyāya, and the Śukriya; RKV 51.44.
The flood of mantras beginning with *iṣe tvā* and the directions, as well as the *Jyotirbrāhmaṇa*,
the *Gāyatrya*, the *Madhu*, and the *Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇas*.
If a follower of the Yajurveda should recite these prayers with devotion— namely the Devavrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Puruṣarṣabha— RKV 51.46.
That man who, devoted with faith, recites the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans],
goes to the abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
Whoever here performs the washing of the feet and likewise anointing with devotion, obtains the merit that comes from the gift of a cow; of this there is no doubt.
One should feed the Brahmins there with honey and milk-rice;
when a single Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
One should devoutly give gold, silver, and clothing to the best of the twice-born;
by that, the gods, humans, and likewise the ancestors shall be gratified.
Those men who, out of devotion, perform ritual bathing during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
and who offer worship to the gods, and especially perform recitation and fire-offerings,
should give gifts according to their ability to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Or he who might give a horse, a chariot, an elephant, a vehicle, or even a "man-on-a-scale" gift, or a cart filled with the seven types of grain.
One should give a plow equipped with a yoke, as well as two young oxen capable of bearing the burden;
cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other such gifts should be offered with honor to a worthy recipient.
A wise person desiring prosperity should not give anything to an unworthy recipient;
for it is said that the earth alone supports all living beings.
Then that land, garlanded with an abundance of all kinds of crops, should be given to a brahmin.
Now listen further, O Indra among kings, to what the fruit of the gift of a cow (godāna) is.
As long as both feet and the face of the calf are visible at the birth canal,
so long is the cow to be known as the Earth, until she releases the fetus.
By whatever means possible, one should bestow her upon a Brahmin;
by that act, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, becomes as if given.
One who gives a milch cow with silver-clad hooves, a bronze milking vessel, and a cloth, certainly delivers twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
I do not know the measure of the merit of those skillful ones who give when the sun or the moon has been eclipsed, even in hundreds of years.
For indeed, O lord of men, there is a calculable number for every gift in this world;
yet during an eclipse of the moon or sun, no such limit can be found for the merit of giving.
O King, wherever a cow is seen, there indeed are all sacred fords; one should know that there is a festival there—no deliberation is required in this matter.
Furthermore, the man who, having remembered that sacred ford, makes the journey there,
or whoever dies there, shall become an attendant of Rudra.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of the Virtue of Giving at Śūlabheda," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 52.
The Lord said: O lord of men, I shall relate another narrative that occurred in the past.
Accompanied by his family, he went to heaven, to where the sage of great asceticism dwells.
Uttānapāda said:
"O Brahmin, how did that great ṛṣi go to heaven together with his family?
O Lord, O God, tell me this, for my curiosity is supreme."
Īśvara said:
In former times, there was a king of Kāśī known as Citrasena;
he was heroic, generous, virtuous in nature, and possessed of the fulfillment of all desires.
That city, crowded with people and adorned with various jewels,
was renowned as Vārāṇasī and was situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Resembling the autumn moon, adorned by learned men,
filled with sacrificial posts, and surrounded by cowherds and herds of cattle.
It was crowded with many banners, resounded with the chanting of the Vedas,
and was filled with various merchants engaged in buying and selling.
It was beautifully adorned with mechanical devices, gateways, and other lofty structures;
it was filled with divine temples and hermitages situated in dense groves.
Delightful with various flowers and fruits, it was adorned with groves of plantains,
as well as with jackfruit, bakula, palmyra, aśoka, and mango trees.
It was adorned with royal *vṛkṣaka* trees, wood-apples, and pomegranates;
its auspiciousness was sanctified by the resonant chanting of the Vedas.
To the north of that place was a most beautiful hermitage,
renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mandāravana.
Because it is joined with many *mandāra* trees, they know it as Mandāraka;
a Brahmin named Dīrghatapas always resides there.
He performs ascetic penance most intensely, and for that reason he is known as Dīrghatapas;
he dwells there together with his wife, his son, and likewise his daughter-in-law.
His five sons always served him with great diligence;
his youngest son, however, was the highly ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga.
One who is perfected in the study of the Vedas, a celibate student endowed with virtues, constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits; RKV 52.14.
At that time, he lived in the form of a deer, roaming with the herd of deer;
and at the end of each day, he would go into the presence of his mother and father.
The devoted son of the sage always pays his respects and then returns once more to that very forest in the mountain cave.
Playing every day with young deer, that son of the sage,
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, once died by the turn of fate.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Sage Dīrghatapas" within the "Life Story of Ṛkṣaśṛṅga," in the "Glorification of Śūlabheda," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the fifty-third chapter of the Ṛgveda-khaṇḍa, Uttānapāda said: While that sage Dīrghatapas was dwelling in his hermitage, [...]
O Lord, how did my youngest son meet his death?
Īśvara said:
Listen with a focused mind, O lord of the earth, to this divine narrative,
by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
The King of Kāśī, possessed of great heroism and great strength and prowess,
was that lord of men known on earth as Citrasena.
In his kingdom, righteousness always prevailed and unrighteousness was never found anywhere;
he constantly delighted in the dharma of the Vedas while protecting his subjects according to dharma.
Devoted to his own duty and always fond of hospitality toward warriors,
he enjoys pleasures at will by relying upon the dharma of the Kṣatriya.
There would be no end to his treasury, which abounded in elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
he held conversations with learned men who were experts in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Speaking thus, the king shone like Śaṅkara on Kailāsa;
while protecting his kingdom in this manner, the king spoke to his minister.
"I shall go hunting; remain here for the protection of the kingdom. When the ministers had spoken thus, that lord of the earth departed.
And kings and provincial governors, mounted on horses and galloping along,
followed toward the forest, their parasols brushing against one another.
The dust raised there from the earth, kicked up by the feet of elephants and horses,
completely covered everything, including the cardinal directions, the sun, and the sky.
Neither the sun nor the cardinal directions nor the moon are seen there;
neither trees nor mountain peaks are visible anywhere.
Just as they do not see one another at midnight during the rainy season,
there a vast herd of deer was observed.
That king ran together with all those princes;
there was a crushing of the crowd among them, and they quickly fled in the ten directions.
King Citrasena, the lord of the earth, set out alone upon a single path;
he went by himself to wherever those deer had gone.
Then he entered that difficult forest, a mountain cave overgrown with creepers and thickets, where he remained unseen.
Thinking the deer had vanished from sight, the king looked toward the quarters:
"In which direction shall I go? Where will my army rejoin me?"
Thus King Citrasena, the lord of men, having fallen into such distress,
took refuge in the shade of a tree and rested there, O King.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, wandering through a difficult forest in a mountain cave,
he then beheld a divine lake adorned with clusters of lotuses.
Then, seeing that lake filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned with *cakravāka* birds, that lord of kings was thrilled, his hair standing on end.
Having taken lotuses, he then performed his bath,
and offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings according to the prescribed rule.
Having covered [the image] with hundred-petaled lotuses, he worshipped Śaṅkara;
then, being fully composed, he went to fetch pure water in the prescribed manner.
Having emerged from the water onto the bank, he saw a tree nearby;
placing his upper garment beneath him, he sat down upon the ground.
Sitting there, he reflected, "What shall I do today?
While seated there, he then beheld many deer in that forest region.
Some there were facing east, others facing south;
some were facing the direction of Varuṇa (the west), and some were facing the direction of Kubera (the north).
Some were intent on sleep, while others stood with their ears pricked up;
in the midst of the deer stood the yogi Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, a man of great asceticism.
Then, having seen the deer, the king thought about food:
"Having killed one of these deer, I shall eat it as I please."
"By eating the flesh of a deer, I shall become healthy;
having diligently sought the way, I shall go toward Kāśī."
Having reflected thus, the king then took refuge at the foot of a tree;
taking his bow with the tip of his hand, he then fixed an arrow to it.
He discharged an arrow toward where those many deer were;
among them, that great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga was indeed pierced.
Terrified, all those forest-dwellers fled while making a great noise;
that sage, having fallen there, cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! O Kṛṣṇa.
Alas, alas! A grievous wrong has been committed by him who has now struck me down.
Whence has this evil intent arisen against me, whose mind is so sinful?
"Standing in the midst of the deer, I do not cause harm to anyone.
Hearing those human words, the king was filled with wonder.
Having gone quickly from there, he then saw a brahmin endowed with the splendor of Brahman, [saying]:
"Alas! Alas! A grievous thing has been done by me today, by which this twice-born man has been slain."
Citrasena said:
"O sinless one, you were struck by me unintentionally, mistaking you for a deer;
taking many logs of wood, I shall cremate my own body."
Whatever there may be, seen or unseen, nothing is equal to the killing of a Brahmin;
otherwise, my purification from the killing of a Brahmin will not come to pass.
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said: "No success whatsoever shall be yours if I meet my death;
there will be many killings upon my destruction at this moment."
"My mother, my aged father, and my ascetic brothers,
as well as my brother's wife, will die when I have met my death."
"These will become murders; how can there be purification for you?
I shall tell you a means, if you think it right to carry it out."
Citrasena said:
"O great sage, let the means that is in your mind be told to me today; I shall perform it all with effort."
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said: "I ask you: how, who, or from where have you come here?
Among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, who are you, or are you born of a Śūdra?"
Citrasena said:
"O dear one, I am not a Śūdra, nor a Vaiśya, nor a Brāhmaṇa;
nor am I an Antyaja, O best of Brahmins, but a Kṣatriya, O great sage."
One who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, and who delights in the welfare of all beings—
how can there be purification when a transgression has occurred unintentionally?
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said:
"Take me to the hermitage where my two parents are;
there, announce yourself as a distressed man who has killed his own son."
Seeing me, they will feel compassion for you and will tell you a means by which peace will be attained.
Having heard those words of his, O best of kings, Citrasena placed that brahmin upon his shoulder and went to the vicinity of the hermitage.
When he was unable to carry it, he rested again and again;
meanwhile, he saw that brahmin unconscious, his senses disordered.
Citrasena released him beneath the shade of a banyan tree;
folding his garment fourfold, he fanned him again and again with it.
O Indra among kings, even as he was looking on, the great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga,
a knower of yoga, quickly attained the state of the five elements through the practice of meditation.
He caused that brahmin to be cremated according to the rites prescribed by rule;
having performed his ablutions, he, afflicted with grief, lamented again and again.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Ṛkṣaśṛṅga’s Ascent to Heaven," in the Śūlabheda-māhātmya of the Revākhaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 54.
The Lord said: Immediately thereafter, the king fell into a state of extreme agitation.
How shall I go home today to Vārāṇasī once again?
"Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, I shall offer my body as an oblation into the fire;
or else, at his word, I shall go toward that hermitage."
"I shall go to that great sage and relate exactly what has occurred.
Having reflected thus, the king went into the vicinity of the hermitage.
Taking the bones of Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, that best of kings stood within the line of sight of that great seer of purified soul.
Dīrghatapas said:
"Come, welcome to you; please sit here on this seat.
I shall offer you the guest-offering (argha), including the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and the sacrificial grass mat (viṣṭara)."
Citrasena said:
"O great seer, I am not worthy of this guest-offering, nor am I fit for conversation;
O Brahmin, your son, who was standing in the midst of the deer, has been killed by me."
"Know me, O Brahmin, as a slayer of sons; punish me with a severe penalty!
Because of the delusion that he was a deer, O Brahmin, the great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga has been killed."
"Thinking thus, O best of sages, do what is appropriate for me.
Having heard those words, the mother, overwhelmed with emotion, went out from the house.
"Alas, I am destroyed! she cried, and fell upon the surface of the earth;
afflicted by grief for her son, she lamented, tormented by intense sorrow.
"Alas, I am destroyed! O son, my son! the mother lamented piteously like a female osprey in distress: "Where have you gone, having indeed abandoned me?
Show me your face; honor me, your mother."
"O son, when shall I see you returned to the door of my home, perfected in sacred learning and study, and devoted to the recitation of mantras and the performance of fire-offerings?"
It is heard as a common saying: "Sandalwood is indeed cool;
yet the embrace of a son's body is cooler even than sandalwood."
What is the use of sandalwood, what use for drops of nectar, and what use for the moon?
If my body were to become the worthy recipient for an embrace from my son's limbs.
"O my beloved son, I wish to embrace you;
deprived of you today, I shall follow you to the state of the five elements in sorrow."
Lamenting thus, wretched and tormented by grief for her son,
she fainted, overwhelmed and miserable, and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing his wife fallen and afflicted by grief for her son,
that sage then became enraged with King Citrasena.
Dīrghatapas said: "Go away, go away, you great sinner! Do not show your face to me!
Why was the brahmin killed by you, and why my son, even though he was unwilling?"
"O lord of the earth, many sins of Brahman-slaughter shall be yours;
for you have arrived here as death unto me and my entire family."
Having spoken thus and then reflecting again and again, the brahmin abandoned his anger and, out of his ascetic nature, spoke:
Dīrghatapas said:
"O child, abandon your agitation; I have spoken ill, overcome by grief for my son and scorched by sorrow, O giver of honor."
What can a wise man do when impelled by his own past actions?
For the intellect of human beings follows the course of their karma from the very beginning.
By this very method, my death has been ordained;
you will incur the sins of slaughter as previously stated—of this there is no doubt.
"Among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, or among the Śūdra and Caṇḍāla castes—who are you? Tell me the truth; and why was this twice-born man slain?"
Citrasena said:
"I inform you, O brahmin-sage; you must forgive me.
I am not indeed a brahmin, my dear, nor a vaiśya, nor one born of a śūdra."
"I am not a hunter nor one born of the lowest caste, O Great Sage; I am a Kṣatriya, the King of Kāśī, who has come to this excellent forest to hunt deer."
For this sage, who had assumed the form of a deer, was struck down through delusion;
now, burdened by his transgression, he has sought refuge at your feet.
"O Brahmin, what must I do? Tell me the means."
Dīrghatapas said: "O Lord, even a single instance of killing a Brahmin cannot be overcome;
how much less so ten and one? Listen, O lord of men, as I explain how they might be."
"O King, my four sons, along with their wives and preceded by their mother,
do not live with me because of the matter of Ṛkṣaśṛṅga."
"O dear one, I shall tell you an excellent means; listen to it.
Even Śakra, O lord of men, would find this easy means difficult to carry out."
O King, having had me cremated along with my entire family in the fire,
cast my bones into the waters of the Narmadā at Śūlabheda.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is indeed the renowned Śūlabheda,
a supreme sacred ford that removes all sins and destroys all sufferings.
Having become pure, cast my bones there at that sacred ford;
by my word, you will be liberated from all sins, of this there is no doubt.
The king said:
"O father, let a command be given; I shall carry it out without a doubt.
Whatever I possess—all my kingdom, my treasury, my friends, and my sons—is yours."
"O great brahmin, I grant this which is at your disposal; be gracious to me.
O King, while the two kings were thus disputing with one another, the brahmin [spoke].
Then, her heart bursting quickly, the sage’s wife died;
overcome with grief for her son, she fell lifeless upon the ground.
And all the sons passed away due to grief for their mother;
likewise, all the daughters-in-law then died together with their husbands.
O best of kings, when all those foremost sages had passed away,
he summoned the brahmins who were residents of that hermitage.
The best of kings reported to them exactly what had occurred;
then, permitted by them, he diligently gathered pieces of wood.
King Citrasena performed the cremation and the collection of the remains,
having diligently gathered the bones of all those beginning with Ṛkṣaśṛṅga.
O lord of the earth, when the king set out for the southern direction on foot and was unable to proceed, he stood taking refuge in the shade.
Having rested, the lord of the earth, burdened by his load, should proceed again;
at every step, he casts down the bones and performs a ritual bath with his clothes on.
Fasting and drinking only water, he proceeded facing south;
in a very short time, he reached the bank of the Narmadā.
Seeing the twice-born ones residing in the hermitage, the lord of the earth questioned them.
Citrasena said:
"O best of the twice-born, O highly fortunate ones, tell me the path to Śūlabheda, by which I may go for the accomplishment of my purpose."
The sages said:
Within a distance of one krośa from here, on the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is an exceedingly beautiful sacred ford; you shall see it from there, and not otherwise.
Following the words of the sage, that king, the lord of men, went quickly and soon beheld [the place] crowded with many twice-born ones.
It was filled with many trees and creepers, adorned with many flowers,
teeming with bears and lions, and graced by auspicious beings observing various vows.
Some stood on one foot, others had their gaze fixed upon the sun;
some stood on a single big toe, while others remained with their arms raised upward.
Some eat only once a day; some subsist on roots and fruits;
some eat only every third night; and others observe the parāka vow.
Some were devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; some observed fasts for a fortnight;
some observed fasts for a month; and some broke their fasts only at the end of the seasons.
Some are devoted to the practice of yoga; some meditate upon that state;
some subsist on withered leaves, and others consume pungent foods.
Some subsisted on water-moss, some subsisted on air;
some remained in the householder stage of life, and some were maintainers of the sacred fire.

O Lord of the Bhojas, perform the breaking of your fast so that your vow is not lost;
you ought to do whatever you desire for Viṣṇu.
Having heard his wife's words, the Śabara then rejoiced; taking a bilva fruit, he quickly performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite.
Having paid homage to all the gods and having eaten together with her, he remained there for three days, knowing that the equinox occurred on the full moon day of Caitra.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Giving and Other Deeds, Preceded by the Instruction on the Words of the Hunter," in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the fifty-seventh chapter of the Rukmiṇī-kalyāṇa-vyākhyāna, the Lord said:
"Bhānumatī, having fed the twice-born, ate what remained after they had eaten."
Having eaten and having established oneself in great happiness, one should digest that food.
Then, having gone on the thirteenth day, which is the lunar day named Madana,
one should bathe in the lake of Mārkaṇḍa and worship the God who dwells in the cave.
Having observed the rules of fasting and bathed Maheśvara with the five nectars and fragrant substances, [they worshipped him] with incense, lamps, and food offerings.
He worshipped with various flowers and most beautiful food offerings;
having kept a vigil throughout the night, he listened to the Puranic narrative.
With dances, songs, and hymns of praise, he meditated upon the god Maheśvara;
all the food was spread out before the god according to the prescribed rite.
All the sons of the four castes, along with their attendants,
were fed until the fourteenth day, after having fully worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord.
Resounding with the sounds of conchs, cymbals, kettledrums, and the noise of drums,
the place was crowded with many people who had kept a vigil throughout the night.
Then, urged by dances, songs, and hymns, that night passed away;
at dawn, the Brahmins were fed with milk-rice, honey, and ghee.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins according to his capacity and in accordance with their worth,
and having honored them with great flowers, fragrant scents, and incense.
The god was worshipped and enveloped with various fine garments,
and with hanging garlands of flowers and many brightly burning lamps.
Then all those brahmins, who were devoted to the study of the Vedas, [were honored] with various kinds of cooked foods, snacks, and well-prepared sweets such as modakas.
They proclaimed that festival by the name of Padmaka;
today is the day of the Sun, and likewise the fifteenth lunar day.
The constellation of Tvaṣṭṛ, the solstice, the equinox, the Vyatīpāta yoga, as well as the Karaṇa and Viṣṭi.
This festival named Padmaka is four times more meritorious than the solstices and other such occasions; whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or recited here becomes entirely inexhaustible.
Then those twice-born ones, having gone with Bhānumatī to Śūlabheda,
saw a Śabara seated with his wife in a pool.
O King, having gone toward the northeastern direction, he ascended a mountain peak at the head of Mount Bhṛgu, intent on throwing himself down together with his wife.
Bhānumatī said:
"Wait, wait, O Great Being! Listen to my words.
For what reason do you abandon your life, when you are still young?"
What is this burning anguish? What is this agitation? What is this suffering and even this illness? You appear still like a child today; let this reason be told.
Śabara said: I have no cause for anything whatsoever, nor do I experience any suffering at all;
yet, terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, no other thought arises in my mind.
Since a human birth is obtained through fortune only with great difficulty,
one who, having attained a human birth, does not practice the Dharma [is truly lost].
"O beautiful one, he would go to a terrible hell because of his own fault;
therefore, I wish to fall into this sacred ford that destroys sin."
The queen said:
"Even now, the time remains for you to acquire merit;
indeed, one who has performed both good and evil deeds is purified by vows and gifts."
"I shall give you grain, or garments, or much wealth;
always practice righteousness, meditating constantly upon Maheśvara."
Śabara said: "I do not desire wealth, nor grain, nor even clothing;
for whoever eats the food of another, he eats that person's sin."
The queen said:
"Subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, and wandering for alms,
one who has bathed in excellent sacred bathing places is liberated from all sins."
Then, being purified of evil and pure, whatever action you perform,
sanctified by that deed, you will certainly attain a good rebirth.
Śabara said:
"Today I have renounced food, which is dearer to me than even my own life.
O Goddess, one should not violate the truth; this is my firm resolve in this matter."
"O Goddess, grant us your favor; forgive us today along with these people.
Having spoken thus, he prepared himself, binding his body with the upper garment folded in half.
Accompanied by his wife, the hunter meditated upon Hari and fell;
O lord of men, as soon as he had fallen from the middle of the mountain, his life departed.
O King, having seen those two reduced to powder upon the sacrificial pit,
after three muhūrtas had passed, the Śabara, together with his wife, [approached].
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he went to the unsurpassed destination.

Thus, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Revā-khaṇḍa, this is the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Hunter’s Ascent to Heaven.
Uttānapāda said:
Now, O Lord of the gods of gods, what did Bhānumatī do?
This is my doubt, O God; please tell me out of your grace.
The Lord said:
Having reflected for a moment, she went to the vicinity of the pool;
seeing the majesty of the pool, the queen was filled with joy.
Having summoned many Brahmins, he honored them at that very moment;
O Prince, having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites.
Having established supreme resolve and remained with a tranquil mind,
O lord of men, she then duly honored the ancestors and the gods.
Having spent one fortnight of the month of Madhu,
the queen then went to the vicinity of the mountain on the new moon day.
Having climbed upon the peak of a mountain and joined his palms in reverence,
he addressed all the brahmins with these words:
Having asked forgiveness from my mother, father, brother, and all others who are my friends and kinsmen, let my words be spoken.
Your daughter, however, having performed penance at Śūlabheda according to her own capacity and having cast off her body in that sacred ford, went to heaven.
The Brahmins said:
"O lady of auspicious vows, we shall deliver the message spoken by you;
O fair-hipped one, let there be no doubt in this matter regarding your parents."
Then, having dismissed those worlds, she stood upon the mountain peak,
binding [her hair] tightly again and again with the upper garment folded in half.
Then, O lord of men, with a single-minded focus, she threw herself down;
just as she fell upon the mountain slope, she beheld the celestial maidens.
"O child, illustrious Bhānumatī, you of great asceticism!
Ascend this divine chariot and proceed toward Kailāsa."
Then, while those people were looking on, she went to the third heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has the entire detailed account of Śūlabheda been told to you,
which was previously heard from Śaṅkara in the assembly of sages and gods.
Whoever recites this with devotion at a sacred ford or even in a temple is liberated from great sins accumulated over hundreds of births.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, the violator of the guru’s bed, the slayer of a cow, the destroyer of women, and the stealer of the property of gods or Brahmins; 58.16.
One who betrays his master, one who slays a friend, likewise one who violates trust, one who misappropriates another's deposit, and one who embezzles another's entrusted property; RKV 58.17.
One who adulterates liquids, one who adulterates scales, as well as a usurer;
one who creates obstacles for a maiden and likewise one who sells her.
One who approaches another's wife, a brother’s wife, a cow, a daughter-in-law, or a maiden; one who hates others, as well as one who corrupts the Dharma.
All of these indeed are liberated through the power of Śūlabheda.
O King, if one causes this to be heard by Brahmins while they are eating at a śrāddha,
his ancestors will all attain joy and be thoroughly delighted.
And whatever self-controlled man should listen with devotion to this as it is being recited,
he shall be liberated from all sins and become a partaker of all auspiciousness.
This [work] brings fame and long life; it is supremely purifying for men who read or hear it, increasing both their lifespan and their renown.
Thus has been told to you this meritorious greatness of Śūlabheda, which, when heard by men accompanied by their sins,
serves as a spade for uprooting the powerful bulbous root of evil karma, as it stands upon the southern bank of the river of Madana’s enemy (the Narmadā).

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śūlabheda Tīrtha," within the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The greatness of Śūlabheda is complete.
RKV, Chapter 59.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Puṣkariṇī, which destroys all sins;
by hearing of its power, one is liberated from all sins.
On the northern bank of the Revā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha),
where the Sun-god, the embodiment of the Vedas, dwells forever.
Just as Kurukṣetra is meritorious, supreme, and the fulfiller of all desires,
so too is this sacred ford (tīrtha) meritorious and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
O Lord of the World, just as a gift yields great increase at Kurukṣetra, so too does a gift given at Puṣkariṇī increase; there is no doubt in this matter.
O King, he who would give even a single gold grain upon the head [of an image] attains a station in Puṣkariṇī that is remembered as equal to the station attained by a man [who gives a vast amount].

But he who, having bathed during a solar eclipse, gives a gift according to the prescribed rule— such as elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, houses, cows, and yoke-bearing oxen— [attains great merit].
Whoever gives gold or even silver to Brahmins for thirteen days, it shall become thirteenfold in merit.
O Lord of the Earth, one should satisfy the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with sesame seeds;
in that sacred place, satisfaction shall endure for twelve years.
Whoever performs a śrāddha there with milk-rice, honey, and ghee,
the giver of the śrāddha attains heaven, and what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
With unbroken grains, jujubes, bilva fruits, or iṅguda fruits, together with sesame seeds, one obtains inexhaustible fruit at that sacred site; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed there, whoever worships the god Divākara,
recites the Ādityahṛdaya, and again honors the Sun,
shall go to the supreme world, which is venerated even by the thirty gods.
O King, he who mutters even a single *ṛc*, or a [single] *yajus*, or likewise a *sāman*,
indeed obtains the fruit of the entire Veda.
He who mutters the three-syllabled mantra while meditating on the Sun,
having recited the *Ādityahṛdaya*, is liberated from all sins.
O best of kings, he who duly gives up his life there shall go to the supreme abode where the god Divākara dwells.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ādityatīrtha at Puṣkariṇī," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 60.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Once again, I shall describe the supreme Ādityeśvara.
O Pārtha, it removes all suffering and destroys all obstacles.
O joy of the Kurus, compared to that sacred site, all other sacred sites always increase longevity and prosperity, grant sons, bestow heaven, and lead to auspiciousness.
Neither in heaven, nor among mortals, nor in the realm of Pātāla, did they obtain such glory as Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Gaṅgā, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara.
O best of kings, [there are] Vārāṇasī, Kedāra, Prayāga, Rudranandana, Mahākāla, Sahasrākṣa, and Śuklatīrtha.
All [other holy places] are not worth even a sixteenth part of Ravitīrtha.
O best of kings, listen to what occurred at Ravitīrtha.
Out of affection for you, I shall speak; I am greatly oppressed by old age.
Let all the sages, who are devoted to austerity and possessed of great power, listen.
I have heard that in the presence of Rudra, Śambhu was questioned by Pārvatī, along with Nandin, Skanda, and the Gaṇas, regarding the fruit of Ravitīrtha.
And whatever was proclaimed by Śambhu to Girijā with great agitation— all that, sung by Rudra, was heard by me with a single-minded focus.
I shall relate that to you; listen with diligence, O Pāṇḍava!
Afflicted by famine, the Brahmins took refuge along the Narmadā.
Uddālaka, Vasiṣṭha, Māṇḍavya, and likewise Gautama;
Yājñavalkya, Garga, Śāṇḍilya, and likewise Gālava.
Nāciketa, Vibhāṇḍaka, the Vālakhilyas and others, as well as Śātātapa, Śaṅkha, Jaimini, and Gobhila; RKV_60.11 //
Jaigīṣavya, Śatānīka, and all the others gathered together;
they performed a pilgrimage to the Narmadā on all its sides.
The preeminent sages arrived at Ādityeśvara by chance;
it was a bright place, covered with trees such as dhava, tinduka, and pāṭala.
In that highly meritorious sacred site, crowded with fragrant flowers, there were jambīras, arjunas, kubjas, śamīs, kesaras, and kiṃśukas.
It was filled with *punnāga* and coconut trees, with *khadira* trees and wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpapādapa*),
teeming with many beasts of prey and crowded with deer and cats.
Crowded with bears and elephants and adorned with leopards,
all the sages entered the forest, which was thick with flowers.
And at the edge of the forest, he saw women who were passionate, clad in red garments,
enriched with the beauty of red garlands, and anointed with red sandalwood paste.
Adorned with red ornaments, holding nooses in their hands, and terrifying,
they were seen standing nearby, resembling dark clouds.
They have massive bodies and terrifying faces; holding nooses in their hands, they are fearsome to behold.
They resemble a drought, appearing distressed with tawny eyes.
O best of the Kurus, another woman was seen by the preeminent sages— one who had a long tongue, a gaping mouth, sharp fangs, and was difficult to approach, appearing as an aged woman.
Then, O Bhārata, those men of evil deeds saw some elderly Brahmins nearby who were devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
They spoke together in a group to the brahmins established in asceticism:
"All our masters are staying in the midst of the sacred fords;
those illustrious ones must be sent forth by all means with great haste."
Having heard those words of theirs, all those best of the twice-born went with great haste to the bank of the Narmadā upon seeing the Revā.
Then some praised her, while others said: "Victory to you, O Goddess! Homage be to you!"
Homage be to you, who are attended by hosts of Siddhas; homage be to you, the most pure and auspicious of all!
Homage be to you, served by thousands of Brahmins; homage be to you, the excellent one born from the body of Rudra!
Homage be to you, the purifier of all that is pure; homage be to you, O Goddess, the auspicious bestower of boons.
I bow to you, O river supreme, who possess cool waters, who grant happiness, who remove sin, and who are wondrously adorned.
O you whose limbs are well-frequented by multitudes of various beings, whose body is purified by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Uragas,
and who are drunk in upon by great herds of elephants, buffaloes, and boars— you who possess garlands of great waves of water!
I bow to you, the bestower of all supreme happiness; deliver us who are bound by the noose of sin.
Mortals wander in the hells as long as they do not take refuge in your waters;
O Goddess, if touched by the rays of the moon or the sun, it bestows the supreme state.
O you whose face is like a lotus, you are the refuge for those tormented by the fears of manifold saṃsāra, those enveloped by numerous sins, and those beset by many pairs of opposites.
O Goddess, having reached you, rivers become pure and stainless; there is no doubt in this matter.
You grant fearlessness to those afflicted by suffering, and you are worshipped by many virtuous ones.
Mortals wander through the hells with their bodies submerged in excrement and urine for as long as they do not touch your water, whose surging waves are shattered by great power.

O Goddess, even the Mlecchas, Pulindas, and Yātudhānas who drink your holy water are liberated from terrible fear; how much more so, then, the Brahmins here who are afraid of the bonds of worldly existence?
In this terrible age unleashed by Kali, when lakes and rivers have fallen into decay,
you alone, O Goddess, shine forth filled with a flood of water, like the Gaṅgā in the path of the stars in the sky.
O Giver of Boons, O Exalted One, by your grace, having protected us through this time, may we attain liberation through your supreme favor; therefore, grant us your grace.
Those who have taken refuge in you and sought shelter in you—you are their refuge, like a mother and like a father to his sons;
protected by you, we shall pass through this most terrible time struck by drought.
Thus praised then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the goddess Narmadā, the best of rivers,
appeared in person as the supreme form before the brahmins.

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O king, those who recite this hymn or listen to it with supreme devotion and tranquility go to Rudra, their bodies adorned with divine garments, by means of a vehicle yoked with a bull.
To those who, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, constantly recite this hymn,
this most excellent of rivers quickly grants a pure state at the time of death.
O one of great majesty, he who, having risen at dawn or while still lying down, recites this king of hymns daily,
offers his own body as a refuge within his own waters.
Freed from evils and rejoicing in heaven, they indeed partake of enjoyments; it is not otherwise.
O Bhārata, by this hymn of praise, the goddess Narmadā became pleased;
flowing through the southern region, she nourished the brahmins with her waters.
"I grant you immortality, which is not attained even by yogis;
that which is difficult for all the gods to obtain, you shall receive through my grace."
Thus, O King, those brahmins, having obtained that unsurpassed boon,
saw a wonderful and marvelous sight as they departed with joyful hearts.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Pārtha, those five men of great strength were seen by them standing on the bank of the Narmadā, intent upon bathing and the worship of the gods.
O Great King, they were seen by all the brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; listen now to how they were questioned by them.
The Brahmins said:
"At the edge of the forest, we saw a pair of women, most fierce and terrifying;
there were also aged men there, holding nooses and inspiring fear."
Difficult to assail and difficult to behold, flickering here and there,
and uttering auspicious words— indeed, there is no way to go there.
"All of you, looking at one another again and again,
let all that was spoken by them be told."
"Five of our most excellent men are stationed there;
those illustrious ones must be dispatched with all possible haste."
Then those five men, having heard these auspicious words,
looked at one another and spoke again and again.
Where are they, whose are they, from where have they come, and what was said by those terrifying ones?
The men said:
"Bathing in the sacred ford was performed with devotion by all those from the east, south, west, and north; yet sin was not removed by them."
Then, by the power of this sacred ford, they became free from sin;
let all the sages, O twice-born ones who are like fire at the end of time, listen!
And there are terrible sins of embodied beings that are inconceivable;
yet by one most wicked man alone, the wife of his guru was violated.
The property of a friend, as well as gold and wealth, was stolen by another;
and another committed the most terrible sin of killing a Brahmin. (RKV 60.56)
Furthermore, the drinking of liquor occurred for another person unintentionally,
and the killing of a cow was committed by a certain sinner unintentionally.
"O Lord of Men, even for all those who act unintentionally, [there are] sins.
Having heard these words from the Brahmins, they were filled with wonder.
At that very moment, those most sinful beings were born free from defilement through the power of this sacred ford and the power of the Narmadā.
"Indeed, no entry for sins whatsoever occurs here.
Having reflected thus, all those most wicked ones [spoke] to one another.
Having meditated upon Hari within their hearts, they were known as Citrabhānus;
having bathed in the holy waters of the Revā, they offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having bowed to the god Bhāskara and meditated upon Janārdana in his heart,
he circumambulated that blazing Jātavedas with devotion.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the earth, having become agitated by sin, they fell;
yet, having cultivated a sāttvika disposition, they abandoned rajas and tamas as well.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, all that was offered by them into the fire on the northern bank of the Revā was then seen by those Brāhmaṇas stationed in celestial chariots.
An incomparable marvel was witnessed by the sages on the bank of the Narmadā;
from that time forward, they were all entirely free from passion and hatred.
O twice-born ones, the delighted people frequent Ravitīrtha out of a desire for liberation;
O lord of men, hear now what the merit of this sacred site is.
O Lord of Men, though oppressed by old age, I am pleased by your devotion;
standing within a distance of two krośas, I shall describe the location.
O lord of men, I have heard that Kurukṣetra is meritorious, and that Ravitīrtha was proclaimed by Īśvara in ancient times to Ṣaṇmukha.
I was present there nearby when all of them heard it from Rudra. The Lord said:
"O Six-faced One, those who go forth when the eclipse of the Sun has arrived—"
One shall obtain a fruit equal to that at Ravitīrtha in Kurukṣetra.
In bathing, giving gifts, as well as in recitation and especially in fire-offerings, the merit is equal to that of Kurukṣetra; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether in a village or in a forest, the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere;
yet at Ravitīrtha, the Revā especially bestows the fruit of merit.

Those who, having conquered their senses, go [to the shrine] with devotion on the sixth lunar day, on a Sunday, during a Vyatīpāta yoga, on the Dhṛti yoga, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), during an eclipse, or on the new moon day; // RKV_60.72 //
And being liberated from lust and anger, as well as from passion and hatred,
O lord of men, they fasted before the God with supreme devotion.
Having kept a vigil at night, O Pārtha, one should illuminate the lamp for the God, recite the Vaiṣṇava narrative, and likewise practice the study of the Vedas.
Whether it be the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, or the Atharvaveda—
one who mutters even a single Ṛc verse shall obtain the fruit of the entire Veda.
By means of the Gāyatrī, a human being obtains the fruit of the four Vedas;
at dawn, one should honor the Brahmins with gifts of food and gold.
O Pāṇḍava, by the gift of land, clothing, and food according to one's ability, and by the gift of umbrellas, shoes, beds, and houses; RKV 60.77.
By the gift of village-bulls, by the gift of female elephants and horses,
and by the gift of a cart for learning, there shall be freedom from fear for all.
An enemy becomes a friend, and even poison becomes nectar;
the planets become well-pleased, and the Sun himself is pleased with him.
All this, O King, has been told to you regarding the fruit of Ravitīrtha;
those men who listen with devotion to the auspicious fruit of Ravitīrtha [attain great merit].
They too, liberated from evil, indeed dwell in the world of Ravi;
for whatever merit there is in the gift of a cow, and whatever merit there is in the sight of Bhṛgu.
By drinking the water of Kedāra, that merit arises for men;
by serving the Aśvattha tree for a year, one becomes a donor of a vessel of sesame seeds.
O Prince, by the glorification of Ādityeśvara, one attains that fruit,
the power of which, once heard, does not fail to arise.
I shall relate all of that to you with devotion, O lord of the earth;
and sins are dissolved like water in a broken vessel.
One is always born facing toward the sacred ford; of this there is no doubt.
O Pāṇḍava, this most secret of secrets regarding the sacred ford has been told to you.
The wise should always conceal this auspicious narrative of the sacred fords from those who are most wicked, ungrateful, and murderers of their masters or friends.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ādityeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 61] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go to the supremely meritorious Śakratīrtha, well-known on the southern bank of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins without exception.
In ancient times, Śakra himself began a most difficult penance right there,
directed toward the god Maheśvara with supreme devotion.
Then, O lord of men, the god who is the consort of Umā, being gratified,
granted him the boon of sovereignty over the gods, a kingdom, and the slaughter of the Dānavas.
O King, it was obtained by Śakra through the power of the Narmadā tīrtha;
consequently, that most meritorious tīrtha came into existence upon the surface of the earth.
Having fasted with devotion on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, a man is indeed liberated from all sins.
O son of Pāṇḍu, one is liberated from sins arising from bad dreams, from the occurrence of ill omens, and from those produced by malevolent planets and *śākinīs*.
O best of kings, those who behold Śakreśvara with devotion—the sin committed by them in this life is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
In approaching those who should not be approached, in driving away those who should not be driven away, and in harming one's own master or friends— that which is lost therein is beyond doubt.
O King, one should perform the auspicious gift of a cow to an eminent Brāhmaṇa;
or else, one should cause a draft ox, beautiful in all its limbs, to be given to him.
