It should be given with supreme devotion by one who desires residence in heaven.
All this, O King, has been told to you regarding the fruit of Śakreśvara.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śakreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Karoḍīśvara,
where indeed, my dear, the Dānavas were slain along with their followers.
By Indra and the other gods, who were constantly delighted and intent on victory, and by their sons and grandsons who remembered former enmity; RKV 62.2.
The hosts of gods, filled with wrath, slew the Dānavas in battle;
taking their heads, all the gods, together with Indra, [departed].
Having cast [the image] into the waters of the Narmadā while recollecting their kinship,
all the gods bathed there and installed the Lord of Umā.
Accompanied by Indra, all the gods, with joyful hearts, honored him for the sake of the world's success and ascended into the expanse of the sky.
O highly fortunate one, ten million of the foremost Dānavas were slain there;
from that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Karoḍī upon the earth.
O son of Pāṇḍu, that [rite] is renowned in the world as a destroyer of sins;
having fasted with devotion on both the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnights,
one should keep a vigil at night before the wielder of the trident.
Engaged in the recitation of sacred stories and devoted to the study of the Vedas,
one should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods when the pure dawn has arrived.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and smeared [him] with sandalwood paste (śrīkhaṇḍa),
one should worship with effort using auspicious sprouts and flowers.
Reciting the Bahurūpa mantra while stationed toward the southern direction,
one should cast [the substance] into water reaching up to the navel according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
Standing toward the southern direction, one who has conquered the senses should offer a handful of sesame seeds to the deceased and perform a śrāddha for a brahmin right there.
And by honoring those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas—even those of irregular birth—with cattle, gold, betel-leaves, and likewise with food; RKV 62.12.
O son of Pāṇḍu, by giving ornaments and sandals to Brāhmaṇas, one's merit becomes ten millionfold; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O lord of men, listen to the merit that accrues to anyone who, at that sacred ford, casts off their body according to the prescribed rite.
As long as the bones of a mortal remain in the waters of the Narmadā,
for that long does that righteous soul dwell in the world of Śiva, which is so difficult to attain.
Then, having passed away from that state, he attains human birth here;
he is born as a glorious lord of ten million in wealth, honored by kings.
Endowed with all dharmas, intelligent, and a son of the lineage,
that man shall become long-lived and renowned upon the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, O best of kings, by going to that sacred ford and worshipping Karoḍeśvara, one remembers it again and attains the supreme goal.
The Lord of the Thirty-three Gods was installed by Indra, Candra, Yama, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as all the Viśvedevas.
On the northern bank of the Revā, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, whoever—endowed with devotion—should cause a temple to be built; ||| RKV_62.20 |||
O best of men, at that sacred ford one shall attain a good state by means of wood,
stone, or brick, using only wealth acquired through righteous means.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women as well— according to their capacity—
those men also go to the world of Śaṅkara, which is worshipped by the gods.
O King, whoever always listens with devotion to this greatness born of the sacred ford,
his sin shall perish within six months.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Karoḍīśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kumāreśvara,
renowned among all sacred fords, located in the vicinity of Agastyeśvara.
O dear one, O lord of men, in ancient times, having propitiated [the deity] with supreme devotion, Ṣaṇmukha attained perfection which destroys all sins.
He has become a commander of the divine army, a destroyer of all enemies;
through his service at sacred fords, that great-souled one has come to possess fierce splendor.
From that time forward, that sacred site was established on the bank of the Narmadā;
and whoever goes to that tīrtha with a single-minded focus and controlled senses—
On the fourteenth and especially on the eighth day of the month of Kārttika,
one should bathe the Lord of Girijā with curd, milk, and clarified butter.

O Pārtha, singing should be performed there, and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be made according to the rules by auspicious Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and devoted to the six duties.
O son of Pāṇḍu, whatever is given there becomes inexhaustible;
O King, this sacred ford, which embodies all holy fords, was created by Śikhin.
All this fruit arising from Kumāreśvara has been told to you;
O son of Pāṇḍu, merit is obtained simply by the sight of Kumāra.
Upon death, one attains heaven; this is the truth spoken by the Lord.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kumāreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 64.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
The supreme Agastyeśvara [is established] for the destruction of the sins of men.
O King, having bathed there, a man is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
this occurs on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Established in meditative concentration and with senses subdued, one should bathe the deity with clarified butter;
thus endowed with twenty-one lineages, one shall not fall from the state of Īśvara.
One should give wealth, sandals, an umbrella, and a woolen blanket with ghee, as well as food for all; thus everything becomes ten millionfold in merit.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Agastyeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 65.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Ānandeśvara.
I shall describe that sacred ford (tīrtha), which brings about the destruction of all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of the twice-born, joy has indeed arisen within Rudra;
let all of that be told to me in brief, along with my kinsmen.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of kings, I shall describe the supreme Ānandeśvara;
after slaying the Dānavas, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [established it].
Honored by all the deities, kinnaras, yakṣas, and pannagas,
the god whose vehicle is the bull danced, filled with joy.
Assuming a terrifying form, he stands with Gaurī occupying half his body;
Bhairava is surrounded by Bhairavas, as well as by spirits, vetālas, and skeletons.
O son of Pāṇḍu, on the southern bank of the Narmadā,
the Lotus-seated Lord was established by all the gratified hosts of Maruts, and he danced there.
From that time forward, O lord of men, that sacred ford has been called Ānandeśvara; [it is especially auspicious] on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day.
One should worship the deity according to the prescribed rites and anoint him with fragrant unguents;
there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability.
There, the gift of a cow should be performed, as well as the gift of clothing which brings auspiciousness;
on the thirteenth day of spring, one should likewise perform a śrāddha ceremony there.
At the excellent Ānandeśvara, one should perform the śrāddha for the departed spirits using iṅguda, badara, and bilva fruits, or with unbroken grains (akṣata), or even with water.
They shall remain joyful until the dissolution of all beings;
indeed, no interruption of their lineage occurs for seven births,
for they experience joy in every birth, O Bhārata.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ānandeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 66.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Mātṛtīrtha.
It is situated near Saṅgama, on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
O Indra among kings, the Mothers were born there on the bank of the Narmadā;
the Lord of the Gods, whose body is half Umā’s, wears a serpent as his sacred thread.
He said to the host of Yoginīs: "Alas, alas!
O Hara, O Maheśvara, by your grace we have become invincible to all the gods."
"A pilgrimage site shall become renowned here on the surface of the earth according to this injunction.
Having said, "So be it, O Yoginī," Śiva vanished.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
His mothers would be pleased, and this one whose vehicle is the bull would be pleased,
O Yudhiṣṭhira— even for a woman who is barren, whose children have died, or who is childless.
There, the most excellent knower of the mantra scriptures should begin the ritual bathing with a water-pot containing gold, endowed with the five jewels and fruits.
The preceptor should bathe her who desires a son using a bronze vessel;
that woman shall obtain a son who is heroic and endowed with virtues.
O King, whatever desire one contemplates, that one obtains from Mātṛtīrtha; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred site superior to this.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mātṛtīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 67] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O dear one, situated in the midst of the water,
is the place renowned as Luṅkeśvara, which is worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
This sacred ford on the surface of the earth is of great merit and possesses manifold wonders;
O Bhārata, hear now the origin and the majesty of this sacred ford.
In ancient times, there was a Dānava of great prowess, arrogant in his strength,
known as Kālapṛṣṭha, who was the son of a son of Brahmā.
Resorting to the bank of the Gaṅgā, he performed extensive austerities;
even while remaining with his face turned downwards, he drank smoke day and night.
Immediately thereafter, the God stood there together with Umā;
having seen him established in fierce asceticism, Pārvatī indeed beheld him.
Behold, behold, O Mahādeva! A man who subsists on smoke stands before you.
Be gracious; grant him favor today, O All-pervading Lord, and bestow a boon upon him quickly.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, my beloved, those words you have spoken do not please me;
one should always attend to one's own affairs and set aside the affairs of others."
He who follows the whims of fools, women, children, and enemies will fall into terrible calamity; this which has been spoken is the truth.
The Goddess said:
"When a husband is entreated by his wife and speaks at great length regarding the reason [for refusal], that woman incurs lightness of status; thus it is recited in the scriptures."
"I shall give up my life if you do not heed me.
Urged by Pārvatī, the Lord went toward that Dānava.
Īśvara said:
For what purpose do you drink smoke? For what purpose do you perform penance?
What is your sorrow, and what is your distress? Tell me the goal you desire to achieve.
"You appear even now as a youth, barely twenty years of age;
therefore, tell me the entire reason for this great asceticism."
The Dānava said:
"Grant me unwavering devotion and steadfastness toward you.
O Lord, another thousand years have passed for me without obstacle."
Two full thousand days have passed for me because of your ascetic penance.
Īśvara said:
"O you of noble vows, ask for whatever task you desire; I am pleased with you.
Having heard the words of the god, the Dānava reflected.
"What shall I ask for today from heaven? Or what today from the entire earth?"—thus he reflected, tormented by the arrows of desire.
The Dānava said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and will grant me a boon, O Lord, I am not satisfied with battles; I possess no strength at all."
O Lord, upon whose head I may touch with my hand,
let that person, along with gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, be reduced to ashes at that very moment.
The Lord said: "Whatever you have thought of, all that shall be fruitful for you. Arise, O Dānava, and go quickly toward your own abode."
The Dānava said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, please wait while I ascertain your boon;
I shall place my hand upon your head so that I may have confidence."
Thereupon, immediately after that, the god Maheśvara reflected:
"Neither Skanda, nor Hari, nor Brahmā is capable of this task at present."
And having recognized that calamity had arrived, the God requested the Bull:
"Fight now for a moment with this wicked one."
The Daitya extended his hand, intending to touch the god on the head;
struck by the tail, the Daitya fell to the ground, dejected.
But the god, having gone toward the southern quarter together with Umā,
looked back again and again, turning his neck in fear.
When the god had departed from sight, he fought with Vṛṣabha;
these two, the best among the strong and possessed of great power, engaged in combat.
With blows like thunderbolts, he raged for three ghaṭikās;
indeed, he did not touch the head of the bull with his hands.
Then, having killed [him] by the falling of his tail, the bull returned;
and that Daitya, having risen up, followed upon the back of the bull.
Having arrived with the speed of the wind at the place where the god Maheśvara was,
the bull, seeing that the Dānava had come, spoke these words.
"O Lord, having mounted my back, let us depart immediately.
Having mounted the bull, the Lord went forth together with Umā.
Having reached heaven, the god then went to the palace of Śakra;
yet the Dānava, arrogant in his strength, did not abandon the god's back.
Then, abandoning the world of Indra, the god went to the world of Brahmā;
wherever the god might go out of fear, he fled there along with the inhabitants of heaven.
He saw the Dānava clinging right there on his back;
having wandered through all the worlds, the god was filled with wonder.
No place whatsoever was found where one might rest for even a moment,
knowing that there, between the gods and the dānavas, a most terrible battle was taking place.
With a joyful soul, the sage Nārada danced there for a long time:
"Blessed am I today! My birth is fruitful, and my life is well-lived."
Seeing that great strife, Nārada felt supreme satisfaction; there, he abandoned the battle between the gods and the dānavas.
Then the brahmin arrived where the god Maheśvara was;
having seen that brahmin, the god then honored him and spoke these words.
"O Nārada, best of sages, do you know where Keśava is? Go there quickly and report this to Keśava."
Nārada said: "The Lord of the Gods surely removes the calamity of all— the gods, dānavas, siddhas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas."
One should not speak of what is impossible, nor should one even conceive of it in the mind; O Lord, I do not perceive such a calamity as this of yours.
The Lord said: "Go quickly, Nārada, to where the god Janārdana is;
you have already learned everything that was done by the Dānava."
"For this Dānava cannot be slain even by the hosts of Maruts led by Indra;
therefore, O great sage, go and inform the god Keśava."
Nārada said:
"O Lord, I am not going, for Keśava is sleeping happily in the Ocean of Milk. O Master, let an order be given for their dispatching."
One should not wake a sleeping king, a lord, or a teacher— beginning with these— nor one's mother, sister, or daughter.
Īśvara said:
If a great fire should break out anywhere within houses, those staying there meet their destruction unless the wise perceive it.
Nārada said:
"Go quickly, O Mahādeva; protect yourself, O illustrious one!
I shall go, without a doubt, to where the Lord Janārdana is."
Then Nandi and Mahākāla, pillar-like in stature and terrifying,
struck the Dānava there with weapons such as mallets and other implements.
And although those three great bodies were each seven palm trees in height,
no peace arose among them as they fought one another.
Immediately thereafter, the brahmin went toward that Keśava;
he saw him sleeping in the Ocean of Milk, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
Having grasped the pair of Lakṣmī’s feet, which were placed upon her thighs, and having bowed with devotion to Keśava while the Apsarases sang his praises; RKV_67.49.
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived;
O Lakṣmī, awaken the Lord of Gods without hesitation.
Having heard Nārada’s words, he pressed down on his big toe:
"Nārada stands at the door; arise, O Madhusūdana! (RKV 67.51).
The god, too, upon seeing Nārada, attained supreme joy and said:
"Welcome, O best of sages; today the night has dawned auspiciously."
Nārada said:
"O Lord, today my dawn has become fruitful through the sight of you. Is all well with the gods? Arise quickly; let us go."
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and those others who are the hosts of Maruts—
you ought to explain the cause of this calamity."
Nārada said: "The Dānava performed most intense and exceedingly terrible austerities, and Rudra granted him the boon he desired in his mind: that he should be reduced to ashes."
"By the very power of his boon, he is capable of slaying the god;
having recognized such an endeavor, the god was led away together with the immortals."
Having heard the words of Nārada, Hari departed with the sages; and the god, seeing that Lord Śiva proceeding toward the northern direction, [followed].
Then, having seen the god, Rudra embraced him again and again;
and Madhusūdana, having paid homage to the god, the Lord of the World, [departed].
Viṣṇu said:
"O God Maheśvara, let the cause of this fear be told to me;
I shall send the gods, dānavas, and yakṣas to the abode of Yama."
O Maheśvara, dharma has been established upon your forehead;
even after cutting off your head and limbs, as well as your sense organs, there is no doubt [of this].
Īśvara said:
There is no happiness among fools, nor is there happiness for those who are diseased; there is no happiness for one who is dependent on others, and especially not for one who is conquered by women.
"O Viṣṇu, being conquered by a woman, I granted a boon to the Dānava:
'He upon whose head she places her hand shall become like a heap of ashes.'"
"O Keśava, he has indeed been declared by me to be invincible and immortal;
yet that wicked one desires to kill me, and a means for this exists for you."
Viṣṇu said:
"O Śaṅkara, let all the immortals go with you;
today I shall devise a means for the sake of slaying Dānava."
"O Lord, stay on the bank of the Revā together with the immortals;
no delay should be made—go quickly, O Master."
Where the Gaṅgā and the great river Revā meet in the south, and wherever the Prācī Sarasvatī is seen; RKV_67.66 //
And a great sacred ford equal to that is not seen even among mortals;
those who perform ablutions there and likewise give gifts with devotion, [attain the highest state].
The sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
This sacred site is of great merit and is the destroyer of all transgressions.
"O Lord of Gods, go there to Luṅkeśa along with the immortals.
At these very words of Viṣṇu, he entered the supreme lake.
He took immense delight there together with the hosts of Maruts;
and immediately thereafter, the god manifested his power in many ways through his illusory transformations.
Having brought together the spring season, adorned with gardens and groves,
and beautified by *aśoka* trees, *bakula* trees, and most splendid *brahmavṛkṣa* trees;
With śrīvṛkṣas and kapitthas, with śirīṣas and rājacampakas, with śrīphalas as well as tālas, and likewise with kadambas and udumbaras; RKV 67.72.
It was filled with many various trees such as the *aśvattha* and others,
abounding in diverse flowers rich in fragrance, and resounded with the humming of bees.
In its center stood a magnificent great tree, a banyan,
frequented by many birds and resounded with the warbling of cuckoos.
And at that very moment, Kṛṣṇa assumed the form of a maiden;
indeed, there was no maiden equal to her in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
And there were seven other maidens, beautiful and with auspicious eyes;
they all possessed divine forms and were adorned with celestial ornaments.
If a single man should desire many women who long for him,
[he may do so] with pearls, gems, rubies, and most beautiful lapis lazuli.
A swing was constructed, bound with bamboo poles that captivated the heart;
then great maidens mounted it and sang with beautiful voices.
A cool breeze blew, having touched the most beautiful forest;
the fragrance wafted by the wind afflicted the Dānava’s sense of smell.
Then, having smelled such a meritorious fragrance of flowers, he was struck with the utmost wonder, thinking, "Never before have I seen or heard of anything like this."
While he was reflecting on something in the forest, a most beautiful sound of singing arose;
and having heard the sound of that song, he was deluded by the illusory power of Hari.
Just as deer fall into the great trap of a hunter,
O lord of men, so too does one touched by Time fall into the dark [hell].
Upon seeing that maiden, the Daitya fell to the ground in a swoon;
however, while he lay fallen, he saw a single maiden standing at the foot of a banyan tree.
But upon seeing the faces of the women, he was again tormented by desire;
seizing his golden staff, he wished to strike her down.
The maiden said:
"Do not touch me, O best of lineages, for I am a virgin!
Ho! Release me, release me quickly, so that I may go home!"
The Dānava said:
"O beautiful one, I desire marriage with you;
thus you shall become the queen over the entire surface of the earth—of this there is no doubt."
The maiden said:
"In childhood, the father protects; in youth, the husband protects;
in old age, the son protects. A woman does not deserve independence."
"I have no independence of my own; I was born into a great family.
Therefore, my father, brother, and likewise my mother must be petitioned."
The Dānava said:
"O fair-eyed one, if you do not desire me today and do not resort to your independence, then the guilt of killing me will also fall upon you; this is the truth."
The maiden said:
"One should never place trust in just any man whatsoever;
for men are diverse toward women—some being lecherous and deluded by passion."
"Indeed, having married me, enjoy pleasures together with me;
thereafter there shall be the end of birth, for neither you nor anyone else shall exist apart from me."
Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, or even a Śūdrī,
as long as there is no second husband, she shall remain alone in this birth.
The Dānava said:
"The words that have been spoken by you have been held in my heart; now grant me proof today, whatever it is that pleases your mind."
The girl said:
"Know me to be a cowherd's daughter; I am playing with my companions.
Perform whatever divine rite is appropriate for our families according to the prescribed rule."
Neither that divine poison, nor that treasury, nor that scale was found among our family;
in all the lineages of the Gopas, the hand is placed upon the head [in token of submission].
O Indra among kings, by one blinded by desire, his hand was placed upon his own head;
at that very moment, he was reduced to ashes, like a heap of straw consumed by fire.
A auspicious shower of flowers was rained down upon Keśava by the gods;
all the gods, joyful and freed from their feverish distress, went to their own abodes.
When Kālapṛṣṭha had been struck down, Keśava went to the Ocean of Milk;
and whoever should hear this account of the Dānava with devotion—
He becomes eternally victorious, according to the word of Śaṅkara;
for this reason, O King, it is known as Liṅgeśvara.
Since even a deeply embedded sin perishes by mere bathing,
so too do skin, bone, blood, flesh, fat, and likewise tendons.
O Great King, the sin accumulated over ten million births residing in the marrow and semen is destroyed for one who drinks the water at Luṅkeśvara with devotion.
By three handfuls [of water], sin is destroyed in a thousand ways;
especially so on the fourteenth day of both fortnights, as well as on the eighth.
O son of Pāṇḍu, that man who observes the fast with devotion for his ancestors has thereby delivered all those grandfathers who were suffering in hell.
And whoever should give even a single kākiṇī to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
by that act he obtains the entire fruit of giving, including that which comes from Kurukṣetra and other such places.
"O King, it cannot be attained otherwise; this is what Śaṅkara declares.
O King, this is the Linga of Touch (sparśaliṅga) fashioned by Śaṅkara himself."
By the mere touch of it, for human beings, the merit of residing in Rudra’s abode is produced;
by that, the entire fruit of giving, as well as that of Kurukṣetra and other such places, is attained.
For this reason, O King, the world-protectors are the guardians,
and the auspicious Durgā, bearing four hands, was created for the purpose of protection.
Dhanada, the lord of the world-protectors and the guardian of Īśvara,
always protects at all times in the form of the activity of the planets.
O Indra among kings, even now the Lord of Laṅkā is not released from those who appear as his sons and brothers, yet take the form of his masters and kinsmen.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Luṅkeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 68.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should then go from there to that sacred ford (tīrtha) of Dhanada.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it brings about the destruction of all sins.
The fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained there; of this there is no doubt.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, one who has conquered his senses [should go].
Having observed the fast with supreme devotion, one should keep a vigil at night;
O King of kings, the wise man should bathe the Giver of Wealth with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should offer a lamp with ghee and have songs and instrumental music performed;
at dawn, one who desires his own welfare should honor the Brahmins.

Those capable of receiving gifts, proponents of knowledge and established doctrines, engaged in the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, and averse to the wives of others; RKV 68.5.
One should worship with cattle, gold, clothing, sandals, and food;
by the gift of an umbrella and a bed, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
By the power of the Giver of Boons, the sin produced through three births is destroyed;
it bestows heaven upon the ill-behaved and liberation upon those who are disciplined.
In birth after birth, he shall be a provider of food for the poor;
in that man, nobility of birth and the destruction of suffering arise by his very nature.
Their diseases shall be destroyed by partaking of the waters of the Narmadā;
and for him who bestows the gift of knowledge at the sacred ford of Dhanada, [the same result follows].
O son of Pāṇḍu, he goes to the world of the Sun, which is free from all diseases, and right there, according to his own capacity, he reaches Devadroṇī.
Those who perform [meritorious acts] in great abundance on the southern bank of the Revā go to the world of Śaṅkara, which is devoid of all suffering.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Dhanadatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the supreme Maṅgaleśvara,
which was established by the Son of the Earth (Mars) out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Pleased by supreme devotion, Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one,
the divine teacher Maṅgaleśvara, became manifest on the fourteenth day.
"Speak, my son, a bright boon; I shall grant it to you, O auspicious one."
Maṅgala said:
"O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, grant me your grace in every birth;
born from the sweat of your body, I dwell in the midst of the planets."
"By your grace, O Īśāna, I am now worshiped by all the deities;
indeed, I have today become one who has achieved his purpose through the sight and conversation with you."
"In this place, O Lord of the gods, Maheśvara shall exist under my name.
Having said, "So be it, my son," he vanished.
The high-souled Maṅgala, having established Maheśvara,
then worshipped the wielder of the trident by the very power of his own yoga.
O King, at that sacred site, the wise man should gratify the Brahmins with the Liṅga named Maṅgaleśvara, which removes all suffering.
O best of kings, on the fourth lunar day falling on a Tuesday, during this vow,
one should honor a learned, Vedic scholar (śrotriya) who is accompanied by his wife— a twice-born man joined with his spouse.
And at the conclusion of the vow, a cow along with draft oxen is given for the sake of Śiva:
"May Mahādeva, the bull-bannered one together with his consort, be pleased with me."
O son of Pāṇḍu, a pair of garments should be given— red,
as well as white and black— and likewise two draft-oxen of red color.
An umbrella, a beautiful bed, and red garlands and ointments should be given with a pure inner self, O best of the Pāṇḍavas.
On the fourth and likewise on the eighth day of both the bright and dark fortnights,
one should perform the śrāddha at that very place, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
O lord of the earth, the deceased ancestors become well-pleased for one eon;
O best of kings, such a mortal is born with a son in every lifetime.
O King, by virtue of that sacred ford, your lineage shall become beautiful in every limb; it shall be auspicious, and no inauspiciousness shall exist anywhere.
Whoever constantly recites this with devotion, their sin is removed.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Maṅgaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 70.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Revā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
O Pārtha, it was created by Ravi; it causes the destruction of all sins.
The Sun-god himself remains there on the northern bank of the Narmadā with a portion of his own self,
established as the remover of all diseases for men.
O best of kings, on every sixth, eighth, and fourteenth lunar day,
whatever mortal performs a ritual bath and offers a śrāddha to the deceased with devotion,
his sins are destroyed, O Pārtha, and he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he is born into a pure family,
wealthy and free from disease, and may he live thus in birth after birth.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ravitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[RKV Chapter 71] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, listen now to another [place], Kāmeśvara,
where the powerful Gaṇādhyakṣa, the son of Gaurī, attained perfection.

At that sacred site, however, one who is endowed with devotion, possessed of piety, and has conquered the senses, having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and through offerings of incense, food, and worship; RKV_71.2 //
Having propitiated the Lord of the worlds on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one is liberated from all sins after bathing there.
Whoever sacrifices with whatever [means] shall obtain that very desire therein.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kāmeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 72.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the auspicious Maṇināgeśvara.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, which causes the destruction of all sins,
it was established by the serpent Maṇi out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was the Lord propitiated by a venomous serpent—
those creatures who are small, yet full of poison and a source of fear for the entire world?
"O father, tell me everything that brings peace to my sin—
the suffering born of my remorse arising from Duryodhana."
The fierce suffering arising from Karṇa and Bhīṣma, and that born of Pāñcālī, has been washed away by the flood from your lotus-like mouth; I have attained peace.
"O twice-born one, having heard this sin-destroying story sung from your own mouth, this [situation] seems improper to us; our suffering does not subside."
Or rather, O dear one, whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of knowledge,
that same fruit is obtained constantly by listening to the stories of Hari.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, the more you speak, the more my speech flows with ease;
nor does my affection for you, my dear one, diminish despite the infirmity brought on by old age.
Therefore, listen together with your kinsmen to this praiseworthy narrative that removes all sins.
I shall relate this ancient history exactly as it occurred.
O Bhārata, this has been told by the ancients through a continuous tradition.
Kaśyapa had two wives, unsurpassed in all the worlds; Vinatā gave birth to Garuḍa, and Kadrū gave birth to the serpents.
And because of their contentment, my dear, you two remained in the house of Kāśyapa;
and the two women named Kadrū and Vinatā were always joyful.
Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, also sported with those two;
then, when a certain day arrived, she of the auspicious countenance remained in the hermitage.
"Behold, behold, O slender-limbed one, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, endowed with the speed of thought and entirely white! (RKV 72.13)

Seeing that horse running without rest, swift as thought, he suddenly spoke to it with a sense of envy: RKV_72.14: "Running without ceasing, equal in speed to the mind—seeing you thus, I have spoken out of a feeling of jealousy."
Kadru said:
"Tell me, O blessed lady, what color might the horse of the thousand-rayed sun be? I say it is black; tell me, what do you say?"
Vinatā said:
"Do you not see with your own eyes that he is black and not white?
O auspicious lady, because of speaking untruth, you shall go to the world of Yama."
Regarding our words, whether true or false, the wager is yours alone:
for a thousand years, I shall serve in your palace.
"O mother of serpents, if my word is untrue, or if Kṛṣṇa is not Uccaiḥśravas, then may I become a slave in your house."
"If Uccaiḥśravas is white, then I am yours, and you are mine as well"—
in this way, this conversation between the two grew.
Having gone to the hermitages, the young woman remained at night lost in thought,
recounting all those actions of hers to her circle of kinsmen.
O Pārtha, I have told my sons and made this wager;
hearing that the mother had made the wager, the snakes raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
She was born as a slave, there is no doubt; Śveta is the one whose vehicle is the sun, the white horse Uccaiḥśravas; a black one does not exist anywhere.
Kadrū said:
"Consider how that may be done so that I shall not become a slave;
indeed, enter into the hair-pores of the horse Uccaiḥśravas."
For as long as that Kṛṣṇa is seen for even a single moment,
in that very instant she becomes my slave.
"Having made that slender Vinatā, who prides herself on her truthfulness, your slave,
you shall all then go to your own abodes as you please."
The serpents said:
"O Mother, just as you and your mother are honored by all on this earth,
so too must she— your own mother— especially not be deceived."
One should practice what is beneficial for one's mother, father, wife, maternal grandmother, and paternal grandmother, through action, mind, and speech.
Then, enraged by those words and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, she said: "Whosoever among the serpents on earth do not carry out my command," RKV_72.28 //
"They shall all go, without hesitation, into the mouth of the fire-carrier.
Having heard those words of their mother, all the serpents [prepared to depart].
Some entered into the pores of the horse Uccaiḥśravas,
while others, out of fear of Kadrū’s curse, vanished into the ten directions.
Some perished in the waters of the Gaṅgā, some perished in the Sarasvatī;
some dissolved into the great ocean, and others entered the caves of the Vindhya mountains.
O King, having resorted to the waters of the Narmadā, Maṇināgottama performed extensive penance on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
O Pārtha, out of fear of his mother’s curse, he meditated upon that which destroys desire,
which is indestructible, inconceivable, and devoid of both birth and destruction.
Subsisting on air for more than a hundred years, or for half that time while gazing at the sun—
for one thus devoted to meditation, the Destroyer of Tripura becomes directly manifest.
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate serpent! You are indeed possessed of great courage. Since I have been seized by you with such devotion, I am pleased with you, O Lord of Serpents.
Quickly ask of me whatever boon resides in your heart."
Maṇināga said:
"O Lord, I have been afflicted on the bank of the Narmadā out of fear of my mother's curse;
by your grace, O Lord, may that curse of my mother become void."
Īśvara said:
"O child, by my command you shall not enter the mouth of the fire;
moreover, O son, you shall have your dwelling in my world."
Maṇināga said:
"O Mahādeva, please remain in this place by means of a portion of your essence;
remain in the waters of the Narmadā by means of a thousandth part."
O Śaṅkara, for the benefit of the worlds, [act] by my name alone.
Īśvara said:
"O serpent, by my command, install the supreme liṅga.
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished and departed together with Umā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Those who go to that sacred ford with pure and restrained minds on the fifth, the fourteenth, or the eighth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight—
They always worship [the ancestors], O Pārtha, and they do not approach Yama;
[they offer] with curd, honey, ghee, and preparations of milk.
They bathe Virūpākṣa, who bears half of Umā’s body,
the god who burned the limbs of Kāma and who is the slayer of the demon Aghāsura.
And those who, with devotion, behold the Supreme Lord while he is being bathed,
they go to the highest world, freed from all sins.
O Pārtha, those who perform the śrāddha for the deceased on the eighth and fifth lunar days,
employing always worthy Brāhmaṇas who are reciters and thinkers of the Vedas— // RKV_72.44 //
O dear one, [they were] devoted to their own wives, gentle, avoiding the wives of others,
intent upon the six duties, and free from employing Śūdras.
O son, those who are lame, frogs, eunuchs, usurers, and farmers, as well as those who cause the breach of established conduct, should never be appointed to office.
O King, that Brahmin who keeps a queen as his mistress in the house of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) should be avoided from afar during religious observances and ancestral rites (śrāddha).
O Pārtha, those twice-born who are one-eyed, stammering, or dull-witted, and who are devoid of the recitation of the Vedas, are not worthy of worship at the auspicious Maṇināgeśvara.
If one desires to go to the higher realms together with one's ancestors,
one should give a cow beautiful in all its limbs to a brahmin.
He goes to the supreme world until the dissolution of all beings;
then, having descended from heaven, he is born again into a pure family.
O King, those who behold Maṇināgeśvara with supreme devotion—
no fear of serpents shall arise in their lineage, O King.
The serpent fears them because of the manifestation of the jewel-snake;
for they indeed appear in the form of Suparṇas within the circle of the Nāgas.
Now listen, O best of kings, to the fruits of gifts:
those supreme men who give food prepared with seasoning.
Water, a bed, as well as an umbrella, a maiden, and a sweet-speaking maidservant— these,
O King, should be given to a worthy recipient if one desires one's own welfare.
One should cause fragrant flowers, scented garments,
a lamp, grain, and a bright house furnished with all necessary utensils to be given.
O best of kings, those who give with supreme devotion go to the third heaven;
and so too does the gift that is bestowed at Maṇināga.
By the power of that gift, residence in heaven will certainly come to pass;
one's sins dissolve like water in an unbaked clay vessel.
The brahmin who gives food prepared with the waters of the Narmadā,
he too, liberated from sins, sports together with the gods.
Next, I shall describe the characteristics of those who have fallen from heaven:
they are long-lived, have living sons, are wealthy, and are very handsome.
Freed from all diseases, accompanied by sons and servants,
they were generous, endowed with enjoyments, and always delighted in the narration of the Dharma.
They are devoted to the gods, the twice-born, and their gurus; they are intent on visiting sacred fords;
they are always obedient to their mother and father, and are free from malice and anger.
O son of Pāṇḍu, those men who are endowed with these very same qualities have truly returned from heaven; they go to dwell in heaven.
O best of kings, this is the Maṇināga, the most excellent of all holy places;
whoever reads or even hears this meritorious account of the sacred site [shall gain great merit].
He too, liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva;
poison does not affect them, and they roam about according to their will.
Whatever merit is gained by beholding the sun on the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada,
one obtains that same fruit simply by listening to this narrative.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Maṇināgeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 73.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
O Pārtha, Gopāreśvara is the supreme remover of all sins;
O King, this meritorious liṅga emerged from the body of a cow upon the surface of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Why did the Liṅga that destroys sins emerge from the body of a cow on the southern bank of the Narmadā, in the vicinity of Maṇināga?
O Brahmin, please tell me in brief about the origin of Gopāreśvara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Pārtha, in ancient times Kāmadhenu performed penance there,
meditating with supreme devotion upon Maheśvara, the God of gods.
O Lord of the World, the Great Lord Maheśvara was pleased with her;
the Supreme Lord, who cannot be cut asunder, emerged from the center of his body.
"O Goddess, Mother of the World, Kapilā, Supreme Sovereign!
Since worship has been performed [by me], tell me quickly, O lady of auspicious countenance, [the result thereof]."
Surabhī said:
"I was created by the Supreme Lord for the benefit of the worlds;
all the affairs of the world are accomplished through my grace."
"O Śaṅkara, by my grace the worlds shall go to heaven;
O Śambhu, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, become a sacred ford (tīrtha) for me."
Saying "So be it," the Blessed One dwelt there at that sacred ford with joy;
from that time forward, that ford became renowned upon the surface of the earth.
O Indra among kings, by a single bath, it removes the entire multitude of sins.
Whoever causes the gift of a cow to Gopāreśvara to be performed with devotion,
a worthy cow together with gold should be given to a worthy and excellent brahmin.
A young, bright-colored cow with her calf, yielding much milk and accompanied by a cloth,
one should cause to be given away on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
In all months indeed, and especially in Kārttika,
one should cause [the gift] to be given with supreme devotion to a twice-born man devoted to the study of the Vedas.
He who gives according to the rule and he who receives according to the rule—
both of them are performers of meritorious deeds, and the observer is a partaker of merit.
O King of kings, those who, filled with devotion, perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased,
cause the departed spirits to attain the supreme goal by means of even a single cake.
For those who perform prostration to Rudra day after day with devotion,
their sin is dissolved like water in a broken vessel.
O King, whoever releases a bull at that sacred ford (tīrtha) has rescued his ancestors and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O dear one, O best of the twice-born, tell me quickly and with effort all that fruit which arises for men when the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) has been performed.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O son of Dharma, listen as I fully describe the fruit that is obtained from a bull endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
O lord of men, on the full moon day of both Kārttika and Vaiśākha,
having become pure, bathed, and mastered his senses, one should remain in the presence of Rudra.
O son, one should cause the release of a bull, saying, "May Hara be pleased"; and in his presence, one should have four auspicious heifers brought forth.
Having given [these] endowed with all auspicious marks to the foremost of Brahmins, [one should say]:
"May Mahādeva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara be pleased."
O lord of men, for as many hairs as there are on all the limbs of the bull,
for that many years he is honored in the world of Śiva.
Having dwelt in the world of Śiva, when he is born among mortals,
his birth occurs in a great family abounding in wealth and grain.
Free from disease, handsome, rich in knowledge, truthful, and pure—
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I have thus declared the majesty of Gopāreśvara,
the Liṅga that emerged from the body of a cow on the southern bank of the Narmadā.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gopāreśvara," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 74. The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Revā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha),
which removes all sins among mortals, known by the name Gautameśvara.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this sacred ford (tīrtha), which serves as a staircase to heaven for men, was established by Gautama himself out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Go there with supreme devotion, where the Lord, the teacher of the world, resides—
he who destroys sin and likewise bestows residence in heaven.
This sacred ford increases good fortune, bestows victory, and destroys suffering;
by offering a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) there, one may uplift three generations of one's lineage.
Whatever is given with devotion, whether it be very little or much,
all of that becomes a hundred thousandfold by the command of Gautama.
The supreme among all sacred fords, as spoken by Rudra himself.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gautameśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Avantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 75.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
It is indeed renowned on the circle of the earth by the name of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
O son of Pāṇḍu, Śaṅkhacūḍa himself was stationed there on the bank of the Narmadā, which grants happiness, O Pārtha, out of fear of Vainateya.
At that sacred site, one who, having become pure and composed with devotion, bathes Śaṅkhacūḍa with milk, honey, and clarified butter; ||| RKV_75.3 |||
O lord of men, one should keep a vigil at night before the deity;
having honored Brahmins who have observed their vows with offerings of curd-rice,
this gift of a cow by the best of the twice-born brings about the destruction of all sins.
O Pārtha, whoever offers libations at that sacred ford for one bitten by a snake goes to the supreme world; such is the word of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkhacūḍa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 76.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Pāreśvara.
The high-souled Parāśara was indeed on the auspicious bank of the Narmadā.
O son of Pāṇḍu, O King, she performed extensive austerities for the sake of a son;
by her [was born] Gaurī, the daughter of Himavat, who is Nārāyaṇī.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, she was gratified by his supreme devotion;
the Great Goddess, who bears half the body of Śaṅkara, was pleased with him.
"O best of excellent sages, I am pleased with your devotion. O wise Brahmin Parāśara, ask a boon of me."
Parāśara said:
"O Goddess, if you are well-pleased with me and a boon is to be granted to me,
O Blessed One, grant me a son endowed with the qualities of truthfulness and purity."
O Goddess, because of his excellence in granting presence, one who is habituated to the study of the Vedas and is proficient in all the scriptures shall indeed be present here at this sacred ford.
And for the sake of benefiting the world, O Daughter of the Mountain,
remain on the southern bank of the Narmadā under the name Parāśara.
The illustrious Goddess said: "O Brahmin, let it be so for you. Having spoken thus, she vanished right there; the high-souled Parāśara then established Pārvatī.
He established Śaṅkara, who is saluted by gods and asuras,
who is indivisible, inconceivable, and difficult for even the gods to approach.
O King, the high-souled Parāśara indeed became one who had accomplished his purpose.
At that sacred ford, whoever— whether a woman or a man— is pure, with a restrained mind, and free from desire and anger, [should worship with devotion].
O prince, [one should always perform this] during the bright fortnights of the months of Māgha, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa,
and Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having gone there to that auspicious place on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
Having fasted with supreme devotion, one should perform this vow;
having kept a vigil at night, one should offer lamps according to one's ability.
Free from desire and anger, one should perform singing, dancing, and instrumental music;
when the clear dawn has arrived, the twice-born should be honored according to one's ability.
O Pārtha, having honored the Brāhmaṇas with gifts of wealth and gold, with clothing, umbrellas, beds, betel, and food; RKV_76.16 //
O best of kings, one should gratify Brahmins of celebrated vows on the banks of the Narmadā; the śrāddha should be performed with raw food, cooked food, and water.
For women and for Śūdras, the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with uncooked food) is recommended;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, four times as much uncooked food should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
O King, the twice-born should be worshipped with diligent effort according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas, using *kuśa* grass a span in length, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains of rice.
The Brahmins should be made to face north, while he himself faces south;
having uttered the words "one should place food upon the Darbha grass," he should set it down before the foremost of the twice-born.
May the hungry ghosts go to the higher world through the power of this sacred ford;
may my evil be pacified, and may the auspicious always increase.
"O best of the twice-born, may the lineage and the circle of kinsmen always prosper.
Having spoken thus, a gift should be given to the brahmin according to one's own capacity.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, cows, land, gold, and so forth, as well as food and clothing according to one's ability, should be given at the excellent hermitage of Pāreśvara.
Those who hear [this] with supreme devotion are liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Pāreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 77.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which causes the destruction of all sins.
It was frequented by hosts of auspicious sages who maintained formidable vows.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, fasting and with senses subdued,
one should mutter the single-syllable mantra with arms raised toward the sun.
The sin accumulated by that person in this life perishes at that very moment;
the sin accumulated over seven lifetimes is certainly destroyed by the Gāyatrī.
The Gāyatrī destroys the sin produced over ten lifetimes, that committed in the past over a hundred, and that arising from three births over a thousand.
O Lord of Men, whether Vedic or worldly, whatever mantra is recited as a prayer is consumed in that very instant, just as fire burns up grass.
One should never commit an evil deed by relying on the power of the gods;
through ignorance it may quickly perish, but never can there be an escape.
O son of Pāṇḍu, whatever gift one may perform at that sacred ford according to one's capacity, all of it results in inexhaustible fruit.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhīmeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 78.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Naradeśvara.
But Nārada created this supreme holy place among all holy places.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of sages, why was this sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Nārada?
Tell me all of this, O most excellent one, if you are pleased with me.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Pārtha, Nārada, the son of Parameṣṭhin and the best of sages,
formerly performed penance on the northern bank of the Revā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by the cessation of the nine channels and by attaining the state of Kaṣṭhāvatī, Nārada indeed gratified the Lord of Creatures.
The Lord said: "I am pleased with you, O best of Brahmins, O lord of yogis, O one not born from a womb!
Ask of me a boon, my child, whatever dwells in your mind."
Nārada said:
"O Śambhu, by your grace may my yoga indeed be perfected;
may my devotion to you alone remain unshakable at all times."

O Lord, may I become one who acts according to my own will, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a knower of the three periods of time, and one who always knows the art of song, O Lord of the World.
O Maheśvara, day after day there was battle between the gods, dānavas, and humans, whether in the netherworld, in the mortal realm, or even in heaven.
By your grace, may I behold you and Pārvatī,
as well as this sacred ford renowned throughout the worlds, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
The Lord said: "O Nārada, everything will indeed happen in this way; there is no doubt.
Whatever is contemplated shall be accomplished through my grace; there is no doubt in this."
"O child, O yogin, wander according to your own will in heaven, in the realm of Pātāla, or in the world of mortals; you shall not be restrained by anyone."
The seven notes, the three scales, the twenty-one melodic modulations,
and the forty-nine intervals— these shall certainly be yours through my grace.
Divine dance and song shall be dear to me,
and you shall constantly behold Kali surrounded by gods, dānavas, and kinnaras.

"By my grace, O Nārada, your sacred ford on earth shall become meritorious; for by my grace you alone shall be one who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, skilled in all branches of knowledge, and free from attachment."
Having spoken thus to the wielder of the trident, the divine Nārada vanished there;
O king of kings, he established [the deity] for the benefit of all living beings.
O best of kings, Nārada created a supreme sacred site upon the earth; he who goes to that sacred site with his senses conquered, [attains great merit].
O Pārtha, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should fast with supreme devotion and perform a vigil at night.
An umbrella should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with auspicious marks.
One should cause the Śrāddha to be offered for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon;
by the power of the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), they go to the supreme world.
"A tawny cow (kapilā) should be given there on behalf of the ancestors, O Bhārata.
Having uttered this, it should be given to a twice-born man [with the words]: "May they go to the supreme goal. (RKV 78.19)
By the power of this *śrāddha*, through the grace of the Brāhmaṇa,
by the nature of the waters of the Narmadā, and by the power of wealth acquired through righteous means—
by the combined influence of all these, may the deceased spirits attain the supreme goal.
Having uttered this, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the twice-born according to one's ability;
and, O large-eyed one, one should cause sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) to be given to the twice-born as well.
One should devoutly offer a lamp and cause dance and song to be performed;
indeed, he who does so in the temple of the Lord attains everything.
"He goes to the presence of Rudra"—thus Rudra himself proclaimed;
and by the single gift of knowledge alone, one shall attain the imperishable state.
O King, oxen capable of bearing burdens should be given there, as well as land rich with crops;
one should propitiate Citrabhānu there with devotion through auspicious mantras.
O Bhārata, those who always worship with great abundance of clarified butter and sacrificial materials, and likewise perform dance at the three times of day with devotion; RKV_78.25 //
At the sacred ford named Nārada, on the northern bank of the Revā,
dwell the gods headed by Citrabhānu and the sage who embodies all the gods.
Because all were gratified by the Rishi, the consumer of oblations (Agni) is therefore called Prītya;
when the bearer of sacrificial offerings is worshipped, poverty never arises.
Through wealth, abundant joy arises in every birth;
moreover, by means of wealth, one is always of noble lineage and well-attired.
The boat is the master of rivers, the husband is the king of women, and the virtuous man is the king of his subjects;
wealth is the treasure of men and the seasons are the treasure of trees—all these bring back youth that has passed away again and again.
Indeed, the status of the Giver of Wealth was acquired by Dhaneśa at that sacred site;
likewise, Yama attained the office of Yama, and the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) attained the status of Indra.
Kingship has been acquired by other rulers as well;
through the majesty of Nāradeśvara, Dhruva attained immovability.

The best of all sacred fords was created by Nārada on the northern bank of the Revā, across the entire earth bounded by the ocean; it is the most excellent of all holy places and the destroyer of great sins.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nāradeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 79.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to two unsurpassed holy places (tīrthas).
Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda, who cause the destruction of all evil.
O Bhārata, that man who bathes at Dadhiskanda and gives curd to a twice-born man shall have [the merit] attend him for seven births.
For him there is no disease, no old age, no sorrow, and no envy;
he is born into a stainless family for as long as a thousand times ten moons.
If one gives sesame seeds mixed with honey even at Madhuskanda,
he shall indeed not behold the god Vaivasvata for seventy births.
He who causes a rice-ball mixed with honey to be offered,
for him poverty shall never arise among his grandsons and great-grandsons.
Having bathed at that sacred site according to the rules while facing south, a man who causes a ball of food mixed with curds to be offered there—
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather remain satisfied for twelve years; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda Tīrthas," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 80.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Nandikeśvara.
I shall tell you all that place where the great Ānandin attained perfection.
In ancient times, Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas, having placed the Revā before him,
performed victorious austerities as he went from one sacred ford to another.

As long as he went on, abandoning Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda, Mahādeva remained pleased and spoke to Nandinātha: RKV_80.3: "As long as he goes on, having abandoned Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda, so long did Mahādeva remain satisfied and speak to Nandinātha."
Īśvara said: "O Nandīśa, I am pleased; choose a boon as you desire.
I am satisfied with that penance performed by you through your pilgrimage to sacred fords."
Nandīśvara said:
I do not desire wealth, nor do I desire the continuation of my lineage;
apart from this, I desire no object of longing other than your lotus feet.
Whether I am among worms, insects, or moths, or have entered the womb of an animal,
may my devotion to you remain unshakable throughout every birth and in every other life.
Having said "So be it," O King, Mahādeva Hara, out of supreme compassion,
took that perfected one by the hand and went to his abode.
But that man who, having bathed at that sacred ford, worships the Three-Eyed One with devotion,
obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
If one bathes at that sacred ford and gives up their life there,
they become an attendant of Śiva and rejoices for an imperishable kalpa.
Then, after a long time, he is born into a pure family;
knowing the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
This supreme majesty of the sacred ford has been told to you, my son;
it is difficult for one known as a mortal to attain, and it brings about the destruction of all sins.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nandikeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O Great King, one should go to the supreme Varuṇeśvara,
where the great god Varuṇa attained perfection, O best of men.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain with oil-cakes, vegetables, leaves, and through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances, he then attained supreme perfection.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford, gratifies the ancestors and the gods,
and worships Śaṅkara with devotion, attains the supreme goal.
O Pārtha, listen to the fruit of his merit when he gives a water-pot, a vardhanī vessel, or even a large water-jar, together with food.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains at a twelve-year sacrificial session (sattra), that same fruit he attains here; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Among all gifts, O best of kings, the gift of food is considered supreme;
both water and food provide immediate satisfaction.
For those men of purified soul who die at that sacred ford,
there is residence in the city of Varuṇa until the dissolution of all beings.
Thereafter, when that time has been fulfilled, he is born in the world of mortals;
as a man who constantly bestows gifts of food, he shall live for a hundred years.

Thus, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Revā-khaṇḍa, this is the eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Varuṇeśvara Tīrtha.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Vahnitīrtha,
where the highly effulgent Agni attained perfection after performing austerities.
That Fire-god who was formerly made an eater of all things by the sage in Daṇḍaka has become purified by resorting to the bank of the Narmadā.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford, worships Maheśvara,
and enters the fire, shall attain equality with fire.
Whoever bathes there with devotion and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Immediately following that, O King, is the supreme Kauvera Tīrtha,
where in ancient times Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas, attained perfection.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and having worshipped with devotion the Teacher of the World together with Umā, a person is liberated from all sins.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and gives gold to a Brahmin while standing in water reaching up to the navel shall obtain a hundred million-fold reward.
O dear one, by bathing at Dadhiskanda, Madhuskanda, Nandīśa, Varuṇālaya,
and Āgneya, one obtains that same fruit.
They are worthy of worship in the world of men, blessed and fulfilled in their desires,
by whom the five most meritorious sacred sites (tīrthas) on the Narmadā have been seen.
They go to the world of Bhāskara, which destroys supreme suffering;
from Bhāskara to the world of Aiśvara, and from Aiśvara to Anivartaka.
He is led to the higher world for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
then, fallen from that heaven, he becomes a righteous king among mortals.
Those who serve the sacred sites of the Narmadā and have Viṣṇu as their deity enjoy the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, liberated from all diseases.
They become possessed of unbroken majesty; of this there is no doubt.
The Gaṅgā is meritorious at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra.
Whether in a village or in a forest, the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere;
one should dwell constantly on the bank of the Revā and always drink the water of the Revā.
He has bathed in all sacred fords and drunk the Soma juice day after day;
yet while all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans and lakes,
go to destruction at the end of a kalpa, the Narmadā has not died by his hand.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Five Tīrthas beginning with Dadhiskanda," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 83.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the most beautiful holy site (tīrtha).
It is declared that taking refuge on the banks of the Revā removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
for here exists the most excellent Liṅga named Hanumat.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me how the one named Hanūmanteśvara came to be—
the sacred ford situated on the southern bank of the Revā, which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one, ornament of the Lunar dynasty!
This sacred site, more secret than the secret, has not been told by me to anyone.
Out of affection for you, yet oppressed by old age, I shall relate how a great battle took place in the past between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Pulastya was the son of Brahmā, and Viśravas was indeed his son;
from him was born the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, a brahmin-rākṣasa.
Through the grace of the wielder of the trident, he became a conqueror of the three worlds;
all the gods were defeated, and the wife of Rāma was carried off.
The wicked one was repeatedly restrained by Kumbhakarṇa, "Release Sītā! Release her! as well as by Vibhīṣaṇa and Mandodarī.
"You were defeated by Kārtavīrya, and he too was defeated by the son of Reiṇuka;
that Rāma was defeated by Rāmabhadra—how, then, can there be victory for him in battle?"
Rāvaṇa said:
"Never have I been conquered by monkeys, men, bears, or boars, nor even by hosts of gods and asuras, all being unarmed."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Rāmacandra was indeed victorious with these companions— Sugrīva, Hanumān, Kumuda, Aṅgada, and others as well.
The immensely powerful descendant of Pulastya was slain in battle by Rāmacandra;
likewise, the forest was shattered and the heroes were killed by the son of the Wind-god.
In the battle, Rāvaṇa’s son Akṣakumāra was slain;
the formidable array of the Rākṣasas was utterly crushed by the monkey.
Thus, when the events of the Rāmāyaṇa had unfolded and Sītā’s liberation was accomplished, Rāma returned to Ayodhyā, and that great monkey Hanumān likewise departed.
Having gone to the mountain named Kailāsa to pay homage to Maheśvara, that best of monkeys was addressed by Nandin: "Stop! Stop! (RKV 83.14).
"O monkey, since you are indeed burdened by ten thousand murders of Brahmins due to the slaughter of the Rākṣasas,
you must certainly not behold the assembly hall of Bhairava."
Hanumān said: "O Nandin, ask Hara for the pacification of my sin,
for I am a sinful monkey born from a particular cause."
Nandi said:
Have you not heard of her who was born from the body of Rudra and resides upon the earth?
By hearing of her, the sins produced by birth are diminished; by reciting her name, they shall depart doubly.
The sin accumulated over thirty lifetimes is destroyed by bathing in the Revā;
therefore, go to the bank of the Narmadā and perform great penance.
Having heard what was said by Nandin, the son of Gandharvāha likewise set out for the bank of the Narmadā, to the southern confluence with the Aurva river.
He meditated upon the god Virūpākṣa, who holds a trident, is adorned with a crown of matted hair, and wears a serpent as his sacred thread— [meditating] upon him in Sudakṣiṇa.
His entire body is covered with ashes, he resounds with the sound of the hand-drum (ḍamaru),
he makes Umā half of his body, he is peaceful, and he is seated upon the bull as his throne.
For very many years he worshipped the Lord; then Mahādeva, being pleased, arrived together with Umā.
He spoke words that were sweet and deep-sounding like a thundercloud;
the Lord said, "Excellent, excellent! Alas, my child, you have performed a difficult task."
"No evil was committed by you previously during the destruction of Rāvaṇa;
for you are devoted to the service of your master, and you have attained success through the sight of me."
And Hanūmān, beholding Hara standing firm with Umā as half of his body, prostrated himself with eight limbs and said: "Victory to you, O Śambhu! Salutations be unto you!
Victory to the destroyer of Andhaka! Victory to the one who bears the Gaṅgā upon his head!"
Thus praised, Mahādeva, the giver of boons, spoke these words:
"Choose a boon from me, my child, O you who are born from the source of life."
The illustrious Hanumān said: "O Maheśvara, the sin of killing has arisen in me from the slaughter of the Brahmarākṣasa;
yet by the mere moment of conversing with you, I shall certainly not remain a sinner."
Īśvara said:
"O son, by the greatness of the Narmadā tīrtha, through the power of dharma and yoga, and from the sight of my form, you are free from sin; of this there is no doubt."
"And I grant you another boon, O bull among monkeys:
for the benefit of the worlds, [I shall declare] your names, O son of the Wind."
Hanumān, the son of Janaka and the son of Vāyu, possessed great strength;
he was dear to Rāma, of the Phālguna lineage, tawny-eyed, and of immeasurable prowess.
He is the foremost in crossing the ocean, the destroyer of the pride of the Ten-necked one,
the giver of life to Lakṣmaṇa, and the dispeller of Sītā’s grief.
Having spoken thus, the god Śaṅkara vanished along with Umā;
there, Hanumān installed the Lord with devotion.
By the power of one's own yoga alone, through the influence of celibacy,
and by the grace of the Lord, that linga indeed grants all desires;
it is indestructible, inconceivable, and devoid of birth or destruction.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O son, O joy of the Pāṇḍus, hear now of the manifest proof at Hanūmanteśvara, which occurred at the end of the Tretā age and the beginning of the Dvāpara age.
There was a king named Suparvan upon the surface of the earth;
under that monarch, men were always happy and always long-lived.
Endowed with sons and wealth, and free from the affliction of thieves,
he had a son named Śatabāhu, who possessed formidable prowess.
O Lord of Men, ever attached to evil ways,
he wandered throughout the entire earth, over mountains and through forests.
He came to the Vindhya mountain for the purpose of slaughtering herds of deer,
to a place thick with various kinds of trees and crowded with herds of elephants.
Having sported in that forest, which was rich with the beauty of lions and leopards and teeming with deer and boars, the king went at length to the banks of the Narmadā.
He arrived at Hanumān’s forest, measuring one hundred krośas in extent,
rich with the beauty of mango groves and crowded with kadamba trees.
It was constantly adorned with *pālāśa*, *jambīra*, *karañja*, and *khadira* trees, as well as *pāṭala*, *badara*, *śamī*, and *tinduka* trees.
It was filled with herds of deer and resounded with the cries of peacocks,
while it was beautified on all sides by the calls of flocks of pigeons.
In the autumn season, during the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the king took his pleasure;
having gone into the middle of the forest, he saw a tawny-colored brahmin wandering about.
And he quickly questioned the twice-born man who was holding the manuscript in his hand.
Śatabāhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, why do you wander alone in the forest carrying a book, looking here and there? Tell me."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, I have come from Kānyakubja, sent by the princess to cast bones into the waters at Hanūmanteśvara."
The King said:
"O twice-born one, why is the throwing of bones into the water performed at Hanumanteśvara?
For what purpose is this done? Tell me, for it is a marvel."
O lord of men, the son of Suparvan, having abandoned his vehicle and prostrated himself upon the ground,
joined his palms in reverence and related his entire ancient history to the brahmin.
The Brahmin said:
"There is a powerful king named Śikhaṇḍin in Kanyakubja;
that protector of the earth was childless, and a daughter was born to him through his long-cherished desires."
Remembering her past lives by the power of the Narmadā, that maiden of beautiful limbs was once addressed by her father regarding her marriage.
"O daughter, since this cycle of existence is impermanent, I shall give you away in marriage.
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what is to be done in the afternoon; for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished. (RKV 83.51)
The maiden said:
"I wish that I might be given by you to my father at whatever time it may be.
At these words of his daughter, the king was amazed and spoke these words.
Śikhaṇḍī said:
"O highly fortunate lady, let that which you have spoken so wonderfully be told to me; for by her father’s word, that most excellent girl indeed came into my presence."
O King, he related what had occurred at Hanumanteśvara:
"O dear one, I was indeed Kalāpinī, and I lived there at that time together with my husband."
At the confluence of the Revā, situated on the southern bank of the river,
I was sporting by chance in the holy Hanumanta forest.
While she was fast asleep on a straight tree at night with her husband,
hunters afflicted by hunger arrived there in that excellent forest.
Joined with my husband by fate, I was seen by those intent on our execution;
having taken up their nooses, they bound me along with my lord.
The hunters, together with her beloved, wrung her neck and plucked out her feathers while she was in the mouth of the fire.
Having roasted and eaten our flesh as they pleased, they slept with their senses restored; thus that night came to its end.
At dawn, the remains of my flesh were devoured by jackals and predatory vultures,
as were the bones produced from my body, still covered with sinew and flesh.
Then, as it was seized by a single predator and fell from the sky,
other birds arrived upon seeing that act of eating flesh.
Having seen the flock of birds, he cast away a piece of bone while all the birds were watching as they ran after it.
O King, my fragment of bone fell into the waters of the Narmadā at Hanumānteśvara; it has fallen into the waters of the Narmadā.
By the merit of that sacred ford, I have been born as your daughter;
I am born as a princess with a face like the full moon.
"O best of kings, those who remember their past lives have been born into your lineage;
therefore, O supreme monarch, I do not desire marriage for myself."
O Indra among kings, even today that species of birds and deer still dwells in the rugged terrain; at that sacred ford, there shall remain only their bones.
O dear one, for the sake of sending him away, dispatch this best of the twice-born today.
O best of kings, I have explained all this reason to you.
"O father, if you send someone to the bank of the Narmadā, where my husband stays in a precarious place among the species of birds and wild animals," RKV 83.68.
O lord of the earth, I shall describe that place to you as it is marked by its locations and signs; for I was summoned there by Śikhaṇḍin.
"I shall give you twenty villages; go to the bank of the Narmadā.
For, being afflicted by misfortune, I have promised to carry out your command."
The maiden said:
"Go to the holy Narmadā, which brings about the destruction of all sins;
to the southeast of Somanātha is the supreme Hanūmanteśvara."
Half a krośa from the Revā stands a wide-spreading banyan tree,
and near that banyan are both a karañja and a kaṭaha tree.
"In the vicinity of the root of the banyan tree, you will see some minute bones;
having gathered and collected them, go to the Revā, O best of the twice-born."
On the [ninth] lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, you should indeed bathe the Trident-bearer with devotion and perform a vigil at night, O Tripurāri.
"O best of the twice-born, having uttered these words, 'At dawn you shall cast them away while standing in water reaching up to your navel,' may his liberation come to pass. (RKV 83.75)
Having cast away the bones, one must perform a bath again for the destruction of sins;
