when this is done, O King of kings, he shall attain a favorable rebirth.
O best of kings, everything that was told by the maiden has been committed to this manuscript; I have come here to this sacred ford that removes all sins.

Then, O lord of men, having seen that recognition and having taken the bones, I cast them into the Narmadā according to the previously mentioned rite; immediately, O Pāṇḍava, a rain of flowers fell from the sky, and cries of "Excellent! Excellent! arose.
Then, O peacock, a divine celestial chariot arrived.
Having assumed a divine form, the peacock went to heaven; O King, having witnessed such a miracle at Hanumanteśvara.
The brahmin and King Śatabāhu both undertook a fast;
devoted to the worship of the Lord, they two withered away their own bodies.
The two best of the twice-born remained meditating upon the God;
after half a month, the high-minded King Śatabāhu died.
A celestial chariot, magnificent with its array of tinkling bells, has arrived there;
"Excellent, excellent, O best of kings! Ascend the celestial chariot."
Śatabāhu said:
"I will not proceed to the summit of the path to heaven until that best of the twice-born,
who is my preceptor in the form of a guru and the giver of instruction to me, has passed away."
The Apsarases said:
"This brahmin is indeed shrouded by greed; from greed comes the accumulation of sin.
O King, those who die at Hanūmanteśvara are established in goodness."
They go to the world of Śaṅkara, which causes the destruction of all sins;
yet, O lord of men, there is no destruction of sin for this Brāhmaṇa.
"The house and the housewife appear in the mind of the brahmin.
Thereupon, Śatabāhu, filled with humility, spoke to the brahmin:
"O best of the twice-born, abandon this greed, the root of all misfortune.
Having spoken thus, the king departed for heaven, surrounded by celestial maidens.
After some days, the brahmin went to heaven surrounded by celestial bards, as did the peacock,
the son of the King of Kāśī, through the power of the sacred ford.
Reflecting on his own previous birth as one given away by a maiden,
and beholding that mature youth, she— having obtained her father’s permission—
chose him as her husband at her *svayaṃvara*, for she was a virtuous princess.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of kings, this account occurred at that sacred ford;
for this reason, O King, this ford is eternally pure.
O Lord of Men, [one should worship] at all times on the eighth or the fourteenth day;
especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina.
One should bathe the Lord with devotion using honey, milk, clarified butter,
curd mixed with sugar, and furthermore with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
One should smear Maheśvara with fragrant sandalwood paste,
and then worship him with fragrant flowers and bilva leaves.
With *mucukunda*, *kadamba*, *jāti*, *kāśa*, and *kuśa* flowers,
and with heaps of *unmatta* and *munipuṣpa* blossoms produced at that time;
One should worship Śiva as Hanūmanteśvara with supreme devotion;
one should offer a lamp with ghee, or, in its absence, with oil.
And one should have a *śrāddha* ceremony performed there by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas,
who are endowed with all auspicious marks, of noble birth, and guardians of the household.
One should satisfy the Brahmins with devotion by means of clothing, food, and gold,
saying, "May those dwelling in hell go to heaven," and then bow down before the twice-born.
One should avoid Brahmins who have fallen from their status, whose wife is a Vṛṣalī,
and who, without abandoning their own bull, act like bulls with other bulls.
The gods know her as a *vṛṣalī*; a Śūdra woman does not become a *vṛṣalī*.
[Yet] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and the pursuit of the teacher’s wife—[these are equal].
"Likewise, the sin arising from stealing gold, misappropriating a deposit, or betraying a friend—all such transgressions perish; thus spoke Śaṅkara."

it is righteous, conducive to fame and long life, leading to heaven, and effecting the complete purification of men.
One who desires a son obtains sons; one free from desire attains heaven;
and by performing this supreme pilgrimage site, O King, one is liberated from all sins.
All this has been told regarding the fruit of Somanātha;
having heard it, one obtains a son, and by bathing there, one obtains eight [sons], of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Somanātha Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 86.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the excellent Piṅgalāvarta.
O Indra among kings, Piṅgaleśvara was established by Havyavāha on the northern bank of the Revā, in the vicinity of Saṅgama.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, how was the Lord established by the bearer of oblations?
You ought to tell me all of this out of your favor."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, the bearer of oblations was satiated by the seed of Śambhu, who,
having attained bliss, was intent on sporting with Gaurī.
Cast into the mouth of the fire-god by Rudra of immeasurable splendor, he was consumed by Rudra’s seed; yet, he remained devoted to his pilgrimage.
Having traveled across the oceans and rivers, the Fire-god eventually reached the Revā; there, with supreme devotion, he performed intense meditation.
While the consumer of oblations performed penance for more than a hundred years subsisting on air alone,
Mahādeva, the granter of boons, became pleased with Jātavedas;
approaching his presence, he then spoke these words.
The Lord said: "Choose a boon, O consumer of oblations, whatever dwells in your mind."
Vahni said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds; salutations be to you, O one of fierce form!
Scorched by your seed, O Maheśvara, I have become afflicted with leprosy."
Have mercy, O Mahādeva; destroy my disease.
Īśvara said:
O Havyavāha, by my grace you shall quickly be free from disease;
having performed your bath here at this sacred ford, you will regain your true form.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right there;
immediately thereafter, the bearer of oblations (Agni) quickly bathed in the waters of the Revā.
At that very moment, he became free from disease and possessed a divine form;
that Vahni then installed the Lord of Gods as Piṅgaleśvara.
He honored him by name and joyfully praised him with hymns;
then the bearer of oblations for the gods departed for his own realm.
O King, thus was Piṅgaleśvara established by Havyavāha;
for he who, having conquered anger, performs a fast there, [attains success].
The fruit of that [gift] exceeds even the Atirātra sacrifice; in the end, one shall attain the state of Rudra.
O Bhārata, one should give a Kapilā cow there to a Brahmin endowed with virtues.
O Indra among kings, he who, having adorned a cow along with her calf according to his means and decorated them with ornaments, bestows them [upon a worthy recipient], shall go to the supreme goal.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Piṅgaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 87.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the most beautiful holy site (tīrtha).
It was established by the assemblies of sages who were born from the lineage of Brahmā.
At the place known as Ṛṇamocana, situated on the bank of the Revā,
a person who for six months with devotion gratifies the ancestors and the gods, [is freed from debt].
A mortal who has bathed in the waters of the Narmadā is instantly liberated from whatever debt he has incurred toward the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
In that place, evil is seen manifest in the form of its fruit;
yet, O King, he who at that sacred ford remains single-minded and has conquered his senses—
Having bathed, one should indeed give gifts and worship the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
liberated from the three debts, he shines like a god in heaven.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ṛṇatrayamocana Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 88.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O Pārtha, one should resort to the Kāpila Tīrtha.
It was established by Kapila himself as the destroyer of all sins.
O Lord of Men, on the eighth and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight,
one should bathe [the deity] with supreme devotion using the milk and ghee of a tawny cow.
One should smear Maheśvara with fragrant sandalwood paste,
and then, O best of kings, with white, fragrant flowers.
Those who, having conquered anger, offer worship do not go to the abode of Yama;
nor do they enter the terrible forest of sword-leaves or the most dreadful cauldron of Yama.
It is not seen by the wise that [this result] comes from the worship of Kapileśvara alone;
rather, having bathed in the meritorious waters of the Revā, one should feed auspicious Brahmins.
O Bhārata, by the gift of a cow, a garment, and sesame seeds,
and by the gift of an umbrella and a bed, one becomes a righteous king.
O son of Pāṇṍu, his enemies shall never possess intense power, nor shall they be fierce; he shall have sons who live long and he shall be sweet-spoken.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kapileśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Pūtikeśvara,
located on the southern bank of the Narmadā, which causes the destruction of all sins.
It was established by Jāmbuvant, seeking the welfare of the worlds;
King Prasenajit, by name, [placed it] upon his chest from that jewel.
But when it was lifted up by him, the wound became putrid;
having performed penance at that sacred ford, he became free from wounds.
O best of the Bharatas, that supreme Liṅga established by him is Pūtikeśvara; whatever man bathes there with devotion, O best of the Bharatas.
Having fully worshipped the Supreme Lord on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, or at any time whatsoever, O lord of men,
those who always honor the God do not go to the abode of Yama.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Pūtikeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 90.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Revā is an excellent Vaiṣṇava tīrtha.
He is indeed renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Jalaśāyin (the Sleeper upon the Waters).
Having slain the Dānavas, Janārdana slept there;
and the Sudarśana discus was cleansed of its sins by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, through contact with the waters of the Revā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me of Cakratīrtha, which is honored by hosts of sages,
as well as the incomparable power of Viṣṇu and the fruit that comes from the Revā.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira! You are truly detached.
This sacred site, more secret than the secret, was created by the Wielder of the Discus himself.
I shall relate to you that story which destroys all sins:
in former times, there was a great Daitya known as Tālamegha.
By him all the gods were defeated and deprived of their kingdom, O lord of men;
I myself, being Viṣṇu, enjoy the sacrificial portions—of this there is no doubt.
The mind of Kubera was stolen, and Indra’s elephant was carried off;
this wicked man even covets Indrāṇī and the sun’s jewel among horses.
O Pārtha, out of fear of Tālamegha, the Sun, Rudra, and Vāsava,
as well as Yama, Skanda, the Lord of Waters, Agni, Vāyu, and Dhaneśvara, [all fled].
And the gods, including Vākpati and Maheśa, having lost their composure, went to the world of Brahmā; having arrived there, they beheld the Grandfather.
The gods, headed by Vāgīśa, praised him with various hymns as he subsequently underwent division for the sake of the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas).
O lord of the earth, seeing the gods dispirited and pale,
the Lord, inclined toward grace, replied to the denizens of heaven:
Brahmā said:
Welcome to the assembly of gods; your former luster has vanished, and your faces are like celestial bodies whose light is obscured by the power of frost.
Due to the subsiding of its flames, this thunderbolt of the slayer of Vṛtra, no longer emitting its divine radiance, appears as if its splendor has been blunted.
Moreover, this noose in the hand of Varuṇa, which was once difficult for enemies to withstand,
has now assumed the wretched state of a serpent whose power has been neutralized by a mantra.
With its course obstructed, the wind— like a tree with broken branches— seemed to proclaim the defeat of Kubera as a thorn in his heart.
Even Yama, scratching the ground with his staff whose luster has faded, treats this world to the lightness of an extinguished firebrand, though he remains unfailing.
And how is it that these suns, whose heat has been cooled by injury,
have become objects of excessive gazing, as if they were figures depicted in a painting?
"Therefore speak, my children: what do you seek by having come here?
O gods, tell me without hesitation what the purpose of your arrival is."
"For the creation of the worlds rests with me, while their protection is established in you.
Then, [he spoke] with a voice as beautiful as a lotus-pond stirred by a gentle breeze:
The slayer of Vṛtra urged his preceptor with a thousand eyes;
that two-eyed eye of Hari was superior even to a thousand eyes.
Vācaspati, with palms joined in reverence, said this to the Lotus-Seated One:
"O Father, the mighty Tālamegha is born of your own lineage."
Like a towering comet, he tormented the gods;
because of that Dānava, all the hosts of deities were filled with suffering.
"The powerful Tālamegha, lord of the Daityas, oppresses us all;
therefore we have come to you for refuge—O Creator, be our protection!"
Then the blessed Creator, being pleased, spoke these words to them.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, among you there is none equal in strength to that Tālamegha;
without Lord Mādhava, that Dānava cannot be subdued by me."
Then, O King, all the hosts of gods, led by Viriñci,
set out for the Ocean of Milk, distressed by that enemy.
The gods set out in haste, desiring to see Keśava;
having gone to the Ocean of Milk, they praised him who reclines upon its waters.
The gods said:
You are the beginning of the world yet without beginning; you are the end of the world yet infinite.
You are the embodiment of the world yet formless; victory to you, O one worshipped by the immortals!
Victory to you who recline upon the ocean of milk! Victory to you who are ever surrounded by Lakṣmī!
Victory for the destruction of the Dānavas! Victory to you, the son of Devakī!
"Victory to you, O wielder of the conch and mace! Victory to you, O Lord who bears the discus!
Having heard this hymn of praise from the gods, the Lord who reclines upon the waters then awoke.
He spoke these sweet words in a voice as deep as the rumbling of a cloud:
"O Brahmin, for what purpose have you been awakened by you and the capable gods and asuras?"
Brahmā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, out of fear of Tālamegha, they have come to your abode.
O Janārdana, the sinful Tālamegha is not to be slain by anyone.
"You alone must slay that wicked one; he will go to his death, and not otherwise."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O gods, go to your own abodes and receive your offspring;
I shall slay the evil-minded and mighty Tālamegha."
"Let the gods tell me his location, where that Dānava dwells."
The gods said:
"That lord of the Dānavas dwells in a cave of the Himālaya mountains,
surrounded by twenty-four thousand maidens."
O Kṛṣṇa, there is no counting his horses and chariots;
O Hari, the various kinds of actors there possess countless qualities.
There dwell elephants resembling mountains and horses like elephants;
there resides one of great strength who strikes fear into the gods.
Having heard the words of those gods who were distressed in spirit, the Lord thought of Garuḍa, the destroyer of hosts of enemies.
Grasping the discus with his hand, the Lord Janārdana, the wielder of the mace and the discus,
took up the Śārṅga bow, the pestle, and the plow with his hands.
Having mounted the king of birds for the sake of slaying the Dānava,
terrible portents fell upon the city of the Dānava.
The jackal entered among the vultures together with the pigeons;
yet, even without a wind, his very flagpole fell down.
There was a battle between snakes and mongooses, as well as between lions and elephants;
rivers flowed there along wrong courses, mixed with blood,
and flowers out of season were seen on all sides.
Then the Lord of the World reached Himavat, the king of mountains;
suddenly, the Pāñcajanya conch was blown in his presence.
At that great sound, the lord of the Dānavas, the exceedingly powerful Tālamegha, mounted [his chariot] and then spoke these words.
Tālamegha said:
"Who is this that, without knowing my prowess, has fallen under the power of death,
acting swiftly at the command of Dhundhumāra while surrounded by his own army?"
"Bring that man, who is so full of pride, bound by force before me!"
Dhundhumāra said: "I shall bring him— whether he be a god, a yakṣa, or a kinnara— without a doubt,
accompanied by a multitude of chariots along with elephants, horses, and soldiers."
Then the mighty source of the world, seated upon Suparṇa, was delighted; he commanded his servants, saying, "Seize him! Seize him! (RKV 90.49).
Running about in all directions, hither and thither everywhere,
they were burned like moths by Suparṇa in the form of fire.
Dhundhumāra, that wicked one, was also struck by Kṛṣṇa with a blow from his arrow;
he was killed in the chest and lay upon his chariot in a state of death.
Then all the distressed Dānavas raised a cry of "Alas!
Alas! Thereupon, the enraged Tālamegha, mounted on his chariot, went forth;
he beheld Keśava, O Pārtha, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Tālamegha said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, those Dānavas who were slain by you in battle are others;
for they were not men like Hiraṇyakaśipu, O Acyuta."
Having spoken thus, O Pārtha, the Dānava showered him with arrows;
Keśava, however, cut down the arrows discharged by the Dānava.
Garuda slew that army which was unslayable by gods or asuras;
yet Kṛṣṇa dispatched at him twice as many arrows as he possessed.
The Dānava sent them forth, doubling their number twice over;
but Kṛṣṇa covered even those with arrows eightfold in number.
Then, by the enraged Daitya, an excellent fiery arrow was indeed discharged.
Then Tālamegha dispatched a Vāruṇa weapon, and after that, he neutralized an Āgneya weapon; with a Vāruṇa weapon, he likewise repelled a Vāyavya weapon.
And for the pacification of the Vāyavya weapon, O Pāṇḍava, Hṛṣīkeśa dispatched the Sārpa weapon, while Nṛsiṃha also dispatched the Nārasiṃha weapon.
Then, seeing the Man-lion, the exceedingly powerful Tālamegha quickly leaped down from his chariot and seized a sword and a shield.
"O Kṛṣṇa, I shall send you along the most dreadful path of Yama," having said this, O Pārtha, the Dānava approached Keśava.
The Daitya struck Janārdana, who held a mace in his hand, with a sword;
then Keśava, with a joyful mind, seized that dagger.
O Pārtha, in that great battle, Janārdana struck the demon on his hips and chest with a palm-tree thunderbolt; then the demon struck Hari in the fray.
Then Janārdana, filled with rage, O Bhārata, took up his infallible discus and hurled it at the head of Tālamegha.
His head fell down, O Pārtha, and the mountains trembled; the oceans were agitated, and the rivers went astray from their courses.
Then the gods released a rain of flowers over Keśava:
"O Keśava, he who was invincible to the hosts of gods has been slain by you!"
Then the gods became healthy once the palm-tree cloud had been struck down;
O son of Kuntī, Janārdana also took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
Perceiving the Kṛṣṇā as the Ocean of Milk upon the serpent Ananta, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī, lay down on its northern bank.
A terrifying discus, wreathed in garlands of flames, fell into the waters of the Narmadā near Jalaśāyin in the mortal world.
O prince, the sin that arose from the slaughter of Tālamegha has been cleansed through contact with the waters of the Narmadā.
O descendant of Bharata, that entire [sin] was instantly washed away in the waters of the Narmadā;
from that time forward in this world, O lord of the earth, he became known as Jalaśāyin.
O lord of the earth, others call it Cakratīrtha, while some call it Kālāghanāśana; it is renowned in the land of Bhārata on the banks of the Narmadā.
O Lord of the Earth, hear now this power of that sacred ford (tīrtha):
just as Ananta is among the Nāgas and Janārdana is among the gods.
Just as Mārgaśīrṣa is among the months and the Narmadā among rivers,
so it is on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O Pārtha.
Having gone there with devotion, free from desire and anger,
and having cultivated a Vaiṣṇava disposition, that person indeed proceeds to Jaleśa.
O King, eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating what is unasked for, fasting, giving gifts, and feeding Brāhmaṇas— [these are the practices].
And he who does so, O best of the Kurus, does not go to the abode of Yama;
for those worlds, O son of Pāṇḍu, are terrified by the fear of the realm of Yama.
May they behold the beloved of Śrī, reclining upon the serpent-couch,
surrounded by the multitude of gopīs, resting in yogic sleep—
the universal form, the Lord of the World, who destroys the fear of saṃsāra.
One should bathe Janārdana, the source of the universe, with supreme devotion using honey, milk, ghee, and sugar mixed with water.
And those people who, free from envy, behold him being bathed,
go to the supreme world that is honored by gods and asuras.
One should awaken the lamp with ghee or filled with oil;
having kept a vigil at night before the deity, free from envy.
O best of kings, those who listen with devotion to the Vaiṣṇava narrative, even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter.
Those mortals who circumambulate the Teacher of the World reclining upon the waters have,
by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
Then, at the clear dawn, O Pāṇḍava, one should satiate the ancestors with water and perform the śrāddha rite there with worthy Brāhmaṇas.
By those who are devoted to their own wives, peaceful, who avoid the wives of others, who are habituated to the study of the Vedas, devoted to their own duties, and auspicious; RKV 90.85.
One who desires his own welfare should perform the śrāddha with faith, employing those who are habitually devoted to sacrifice and who observe the three daily junctures.
Those men who always dwell taking refuge at the lotus feet of Hari are indeed fortunate in the world of men and worthy of worship on earth.
They behold the Lord of the Gods visibly reclining upon the waters,
performing the fortnightly fast, the Pārāka penance, and the auspicious Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One who performs the severe month-long fast (māsopavāsa) or the fifth vow of eating only every sixth meal at that sacred site shall attain an imperishable state.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the fruit that comes from the sesame-cow (tiladhenu), how,
where, and when it should be given, and the auspicious result of that gift.
Indeed, this meritorious discourse was heard many times in the past from the sage Dvaipāyana at the holy site of Naimiṣa by Nārada and others.
The learned man who causes this supreme means of prolonging life, which is auspicious and increases fame,
to be heard by Brahmins, attains infinite fruit.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many;
for these are divided sacrificial fees that do not reach the donor.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this [gift] is to be given to one person, not to many;
and if it falls into the hands of a seller, it consumes the family unto the seventh generation.
However, for all [the cows], it is traditionally taught that there should be four *droṇas* according to what is available;
or, for many [cows], a calf of one *droṇa* may be made according to one's desire.
In whatever region or regarding whatever object a specific measure has been established,
by performing [the ritual] according to that measure, one enjoys inexhaustible fruit.
On a clean ground, preceded by pleasant offerings such as flowers, incense,
and unbroken rice grains, two jewels should be placed upon the ears, and likewise two lamps upon the two eyes.
Sandalwood should be placed upon the chest, and likewise gold by those two; honey and ghee should be applied above, and one should make [the body] covered with mustard seeds as hair.
One should give a blanket for a blanket, and likewise honey and ghee for the hips;
one should give fodder and milk-rice mixed with ghee and honey.
A cow with horns of gold, a silver tail-hair, and a golden tail-tip,
possessing a back of jewels and yielding milk into a bronze vessel, should be given as a gift.
Whatever evil may have been committed in childhood, or whatever was done unknowingly— whether performed by speech, performed through action, or conceived by the mind.
Spitting into water, stepping over a pestle, sexual intercourse with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), and consorting with the wife of one's teacher; 90.102.
Indeed, the Tiladhenu purifies the act of approaching a maiden, the theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, and likewise other such sins.
By fasting for a day and night according to the prescribed rite, one should duly dismiss that river known as Vaitaraṇī which exists in the terrible city of Yama.
Where the evildoer is cooked upon sands and rocky ground,
there is the Avīci hell, and where the twin mountains stand.
Where there are crows with iron beaks, where there are terrifying dogs, where there is the Forest of Sword-leaves, and where that Kūṭaśālmalī tree stands; (there they go).
Having passed beyond those [realms] with ease, one should go to the abode of Dharmarāja;
and upon seeing him, O Bhārata, Dharmarāja speaks words of truth to him.
O best of men, ascend this supreme and worthy celestial chariot, adorned with jewels and gems, and proceed to the highest destination.
Do not give flattery to a soldier, nor indeed give it to a priest; do not give it to one who is one-eyed, deformed, deficient in limb, or a temple-attendant.
One should never [give] to a Brāhmaṇa who is ignorant of the Vedas, to one who sells all things,
to a betrayer of friends, to an ungrateful person, and likewise to one devoid of the sacred mantras.
It should be given to a śrotriya who has mastered the Vedānta and maintains a household;
it should be given to the son of one who has mastered the Vedānta, or to a śrotriya who protects his home.
O Bhārata, [one should give] to a Brahmin who is beautiful in all his limbs, of virtuous conduct, and pleasant of speech,
on the full moon day of Māgha or of Kārttika.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Āṣāḍha, or Caitra; likewise at the solstices, the equinoxes, and always during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
O sinless one, this ritual procedure for the sesame-cow has been told to you by me on the meritorious occasion of the Ṣaḍaśīti, or under the shadow of an elephant.
Having placed their foot upon Yama, they indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu;
after the abandonment of life, they go to the supreme Vaiṣṇava world—of this there is no doubt.
Having swiftly pierced through the sun, they depart; no further deliberation is required here.
All this, O King, has been told to you regarding the fruit of Cakratīrtha;
having heard this with devotion, a human being is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Jalaśāyi Tīrtha," in the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 91.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to that most purifying holy site (tīrtha).
O best of kings, Caṇḍāditya was installed by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
In former times, there were two most terrible great Daityas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;
resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, they performed extensive penance.
As they were meditating upon the divine Sun, the destroyer of darkness in the three worlds,
the thousand-rayed god was pleased by their asceticism and spoke.
"Excellent, excellent! they said, O Pārtha, on the auspicious bank of the Narmadā;
"O heroes, choose a boon according to your desire and as you wish in your hearts."
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa said:
"O Divākara, may we two, being composed, be invincible to all the gods and forever free from all diseases."
"So be it," said Bhāskara, the stealer of the waters;
having spoken thus to the two Daityas, the Sun vanished there from their sight.
Having established [the deity] with supreme devotion, one should go there for the sake of one's own perfection;
there, one should also offer libations to the gods, humans, and ancestors.
O King, he shall dwell in the world of Bhāskara for the duration of a day of Viriñci; and he who lights a lamp with ghee on the sixth lunar day, O lord of men,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the city of the Sun.
O bull among the Bharatas, he who hears of the rising of the fierce-rayed sun shall surely always be victorious, free from mental anguish and physical disease.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Caṇḍāditya Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 92.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Yamahāsya.
This sacred ford, situated on the bank of the Narmadā, removes all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O bull among the twice-born, how did the laughter of Yama come to pass upon the earth?
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great.
The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise son of a king! You have questioned me well.
Long ago, your father came to the holy Narmadā for the purpose of bathing."
Just as a garment washed by a washerman becomes stainless,
so too did that King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, become pure.
Seeing his stainless body, he spoke with a smile, filled with wonder.
Yama said:
How do men burdened by sin come to my city?
By a single bath in the Revā, the station of Viṣṇu is indeed attained.
Those capable individuals who do not behold the auspicious Revā river of meritorious waters should be known as equal to those born blind, or even to the dead and the lame.
"O King, it is for this reason that the Teacher of the World smiled: that those who are capable do not see the river Revā, whose waters are merit."
O King, having installed Yama there, that lord of Yamahāseśvara— having conquered his anger and mastered his senses— departed for heaven.
Furthermore, by fasting with supreme devotion on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina, one is liberated from all sins.
One should keep a vigil at night and illuminate the lamp for the God with ghee; O King of kings, listen now to the fruit that exists therein.
One is liberated from all sins arising from approaching those who should not be approached,
as well as from those produced by eating what should not be eaten and drinking what should not be drunk.
Just as there would be no fault in milking what cannot be milked or in driving away what is not to be driven,
so too, by the mere act of bathing, various kinds of sins are removed.
That man shall never behold the realm of Yama;
O Lord of Men, this is the supreme secret of the ancestors on earth.
There is no doubt that everything given at the Great Festival of Yama becomes inexhaustible for those who,
having conquered anger, honor the twice-born on the new moon day.
By the gift of gold and land, by the abundant gift of sesame seeds,
by the offering of a black antelope skin, and by the gift of a sesame-cow;
Those who shall devoutly bestow upon a preeminent brahmin as prescribed by the rules either a horse, or an elephant, or two draft-oxen yoked to a plough; RKV_92.17 //
O best of kings, those who give away a maiden, the earth, a cow, or a milch buffalo do not approach Yama.
Yama also becomes pleased at every birth, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
his vehicle is a buffalo, and his mothers are the female buffaloes.
By the power of those gifts, Yama will certainly be pleased;
even if one is shrouded in sins, such a person does not encounter Yama.
For this reason, the gift of a buffalo is supreme here;
water should be poured upon its horn, and it should be draped with smoke-colored cloth.
The hooves should be made of iron, with copper backs and well-adorned;
a mountain of salt [should be placed] in the east, and a mountain of jaggery in the southeast.
Cotton should be placed in the southern quarter, fresh butter in the south-west;
seven types of grain in the western quarter, and rice is prescribed for the north-west.
In the north (Saumya), one should give gold, and in the northeast (Īśāna), clarified butter;
one should offer it while uttering: "May King Yama be pleased with me."
Having uttered this before the twice-born, [he described] the world of Yama with its great terrors:
the horrific Forest of Sword-Leaves and the most dreadful Cauldron of Yama.
Raudra, Vaitaraṇī, and the terrifying Kumbhīpāka;
the most fearsome Kālasūtra, as well as the two Yamala mountains.
The saw and the oil-press, the most dreadful dogs and vultures,
the breathless and loud-screaming [hells], and likewise the terrifying Raurava.
O best of the twice-born, these terrors are heard of in the world of Yama;
by your grace, however, they become gentle through the power of this sacred ford.
By the power of this gift and through the grace of Yama,
O twice-born one, I shall not go to hell in birth after birth.
Those men who hear this narrative of Yamahāsya are also liberated from sin and do not see the abode of Yama.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Yamahāsya-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 93.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kalhoḍī Tīrtha.
It is renowned in the world of Bhārata as the destroyer of sins of the Gaṅgā.
O Pārtha, the Ūṣara and Puṣkara [tīrthas] situated on the banks of the Revā are difficult for men to attain; they exist for the destruction of the sins of living beings.
"This is indeed that holy pilgrimage site," said Śūlin;
thus, Jāhnavī arrived there in the form of a cow for the purpose of bathing.
Therefore, that excellent holy site (tīrtha) is renowned in the world as Kalhoḍī;
one should perform a three-night rite there on the full moon day, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O Pārtha, he who abandons passion, darkness, as well as anger, hypocrisy, and envy— he has attained the fruit born of liberation.
One should bathe the deity with milk at the three junctions of the day for three days;
the milk should be from a cow that has recently calved and whose offspring is living.
Having prepared a vessel made of copper and joined with honey, one should perform the bathing of the deity while reciting: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīśivāya."
He who, having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, bestows gifts upon the deceased, goes to the abode of the thirty gods, surrounded by celestial women.
There, one should cause a white cow to be given, [saying]: "May my grandfathers be pleased;
[may this be given] to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with purity, who is always devoted to his own wife."
O King, one who, endowed with goodness, gives away a cow together with her calf, covered with cloth, and placed upon gold,
shall attain the world of Śambhu.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kalhoḍī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 94.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O King, one should go to the auspicious Nanditīrtha,
which removes all sins for men and was established in ancient times by Nandin.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having fasted for a day and night at Nandinātha on the bank of the Narmadā, one grants liberation to living beings struck by the flood of sins.
O delighter of Dharma, one should worship Nandikeśvara with the five-fold offerings of honor, and likewise, one should give jewels to the Brahmins.
He goes to the supreme abode where the wielder of the Pināka bow resides;
endowed with every happiness, he rejoices together with the Apsarases.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Nandikeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 95.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme hermitage of Badarī.
In ancient times, Śambhu declared this most excellent of all sacred sites to be meritorious.
And know that this wearer of the diadem who has achieved success there for the sake of Bhārata— your brother named Phalguna— is a god among men.
O King, those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have arrived at the bank of the Narmadā; he who possesses devotion to Janārdana indeed attains that very knowledge.
He looks with equanimity upon all things, both the stationary and the moving, whether they be a Brahmin or a dog-cooker; therein Janārdana is pleased.
Behold the oneness, O Kaunteya; there is no difference between me and the Self.
For the hermitage of Badarikāśrama was established by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Śaṅkara was established there for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds;
the Liṅga installed by the Trimūrti grants the path to heaven and liberation.
Having gone there and become pure, having observed a fast for one night,
and having likewise abandoned passion and darkness, one should take refuge in the state of goodness (*sattva*).
Having kept a vigil at night on the eighth day of the month of Madhu,
or on the fourteenth day of either fortnight, one should perform [the rite].
O Pāṇḍava, this has been specifically described to you regarding the month of Āśvina;
one should bathe [the deity] with supreme devotion using milk together with honey.
One should bathe the Bull-bannered Lord with this meritorious *pañcāmṛta*, joined with curd and sugar and adorned with clarified butter.
He who, free from envy, gazes with devotion upon Śiva while he is being bathed,
will undoubtedly dwell in the presence of Śiva or in the world of Śakra.
Even a salutation offered with deceit to the wielder of the trident (Śiva) indeed brings about the uncoiling of those who are bound by the root of cyclic existence.
By him everything has been studied, by him everything has been heard, and by him everything has been practiced,
who has made firm the repetition of the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
Furthermore, O Pārtha, I shall describe to you even a fraction of the fruit that belongs to one who, having conquered his senses and eating but one meal a day, bathes with devotion.
Afflicted by old age, I speak out of devotion to you:
they go to the supreme abode, having pierced through the solar orb.
In saṃsāra, they become the abodes of all happiness;
it is a marvel that they are the abodes of the teachings for their circle of kinsmen.
O Lord of the Earth, those who perform a śrāddha there, mixed with the waters of the Narmadā, shall have all their desires fulfilled upon this earth.
And with worthy Brahmins, O King— of noble birth, masters of the Vedas,
handsome, of good character, devoted to their own wives, and auspicious.
One should indeed have the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) performed by those born in the noble lands, who are gentle and handsome, when the sun has reached the Kutapa period.
O delighter of Dharma, if one desires the supreme world of the ancestors,
one should diligently avoid those who are one-eyed, the wicked, and the hypocritical.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a worthy Brahmin;
he can liberate the deceased from hells, foremost among them Kumbhīpāka.
Liberation comes for all the ancestors, O delighter of kings;
one should give gold to the Brahmins, saying, "May my grandfather be pleased."
O Bhārata, one should cause food and clothing to be given there with devotion;
O best of kings, one should also give a cow, a bull, land, and an excellent umbrella.
"Such a man attains heaven," thus Śaṅkara declared;
"he who should perform the renunciation of life by means of fire or water."
Or else, O King, by means of fasting, he shall go to the abode of Śiva on the banks of the Nara-Nārāyaṇī river and in the Devadroṇī.
He shall dwell in the presence of Īśvara for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
then, having fallen from heaven, he too becomes a powerful king.
Endowed with all the qualities of sovereignty and devoted to the protection of his subjects,
he will then remember that sacred ford and shall return there once again.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nārāyaṇī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 96.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the supreme Koṭīśvara Tīrtha.
Ten million sages arrived at that place, O descendant of Kuru.
O bulls among sages, for the sake of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana’s own welfare,
he consulted with all the twice-born who were reciters of the auspicious Vedic hymns.
Śaṅkara was established there as the cause for the destruction of bondage,
the means for severing the cycle of existence, and the destroyer of the suffering of living beings.
O son of a king, O best of monarchs, that which is called Koṭīśvara on earth— whosoever bathes it with devotion on the full moon day, [attains great merit].
Having performed the libation for the ancestors and the offering of funeral cakes according to the rules,
especially on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
There is inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors lasting until the dissolution of all beings;
this supreme secret of the ancestors, situated on the banks of the Revā,
which grants liberation to all living creatures, was established by the best of sages.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭīśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 97.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Vyāsatīrtha.
The merit established in the intermediate space is difficult for humans to attain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Why indeed is that Vyāsa-tīrtha situated in the intermediate space?
Tell me this in brief; abandon the prolixity of the text.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! You are righteous and fond of the virtuous;
you are devoted to your own duty, O Pārtha, and take great care in your pilgrimages.
"O lord of men, Vyāsatīrtha is difficult for all beings to attain;
O prince, I am afflicted by old age and am no longer capable."
Bereft of consciousness, his wealth gone, and deprived of memory, he has become [thus].
This holy site, more secret than the secret, has not been told by me to anyone.
O Indra among kings, Kali did not enter that very place because it was supported by Vyāsa;
however, he took birth in the intermediate space through the power of Revā’s activity.
Even Viriñci is not able to fully extol the virtues of the Revā;
how then, my dear, shall I know the supreme majesty of the Revā? (RKV 97.7)
Therefore, I shall describe Vyāsatīrtha specifically, even though it is but a small fraction [of the whole],
for in this Kali age, direct perception of its efficacy is seen there today.
Even a bird does not pass through by piercing that most terrible stake;
O Prince, I shall describe its origin to you in brief.
O protector of the earth, in former times there was a venerable sage named Parāśara;
by him, most intense penance was performed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, yielding great fruit.
Having entered the waters of the Jahnavī, he remained there established in breath control (prāṇāyāma);
when the twelfth year was complete, he emerged from the midst of the water.
Seeking alms, he wandered through the village; wherever the boat was moored, there he saw another woman, a young girl who was truly captivating.
Seeing her, he, afflicted by desire, then spoke sweetly:
"Take me to the further shore; who are you, O fawn-eyed one?"
"O you who have boarded the boat on the riverbank, you who agitate my heart!"—
having been addressed thus by him, she bowed down to that bull among sages.
And seeing him infatuated by desire, she spoke of herself:
"O best of the twice-born, I am a maiden, a servant girl in the house of fishermen."
"O Lord, I was commanded by my master for the purpose of guarding the ship;
you ought to know the entire account of what occurred as reported by me. (RKV 97.16)
Having been addressed thus by her, he then reflected for a moment and spoke this:
Parāśara said:
"O blessed lady, by the power of my knowledge I know your origin:
you are not the daughter of a fisherman; you are a princess, O beautiful one."
The maiden said: "O Brahmin, let it be told: who is my father, from whose womb was I born, in what lineage was I produced, and how am I the daughter of a fisherman?"
Parāśara said:
I shall relate everything that you have asked in its entirety.
There was a king named Vasu, an ornament of the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa).
O blessed lady, the lord of Jambūdvīpa increased the fear of his enemies;
he had seven hundred wives and ten sons.
He shall protect the worlds according to the Dharma and is always honored like a lord;
even the Mlecchas dwelling in Kṣīradvīpa will become subject to him.
In order to destroy them, he set out, crossing the ocean,
accompanied by his sons and servants who stood firm in great prowess.
A battle was commenced between them and the Mlecchas along with Vasu;
all those Mlecchas were conquered by Vasu, O fawn-eyed one.
They were made to pay tribute by him, along with their sons, armies, and vehicles;
that chief queen of his, O fawn-eyed one, was your mother.
While the protector of the earth was away on a journey, she reached her menses;
for among women, the god of love is indeed ever more powerful.
Especially during the season of spring, they are pierced by the arrows of desire;
tormented by the god of love, that fair-eyed woman reflected thus:
"Indeed, I shall dispatch a messenger today to the presence of King Vasu.
O messenger, being thus summoned, go quickly into the king's presence."
The messenger said:
"O Queen, King Vasu, the subduer of enemies, has gone to the opposite shore;
it is impossible to go there without watercraft, O auspicious lady."
All those vehicles were taken to the opposite shore by the word of the messenger; that queen was despondent and tormented by desire.
Then her friend said to her: "O Queen, why do you grieve?
Let a letter be sent truthfully into the hand of Śuka."
"O beautiful one, birds cross the ocean;
by the words of her friend, that queen became composed once more, O lord of men. (RKV 97.32)
"O scribe, being thus addressed there, write a letter at my command:
'O King Vasu, Satyabhāmā does not live today without you.'"
"Today the fertile season has arrived; therefore, have a scribe write a letter. Once the letter has been written upon birch bark by the scribe," RKV 97.34.
The parrot, who had been brought from afar, was already present within the cage.
Satyabhāmā said:
"Take this letter and go quickly into the presence of King Vasu. Śakuni, having bowed down and taken the excellent letter, departed.
O King, having suddenly flown up, he went into the expanse of the sky;
then the bird quickly reached the presence of King Vasu.
When the letter sent by Satyabhāmā had been delivered by Śuka himself,
King Vasu then took the letter in his hand and read its contents.
Having reflected upon the meaning of the letter, the lord of men took up his semen,
placed it in an infallible casket, and mixed it with a reply letter.
He gave it to Śuka, saying, "Go to the presence of the queen";
having bowed to King Vasu and taken the seed, he flew up into the air.
Having reached the surface of the ocean, Śuka was spotted by a hawk;
perceiving that Śuka possessed meat, the hawk rushed toward him.
O Bhārata, the parrot was struck by the hawk with a blow from its beak;
due to that impact, it fell unconscious, and its seed dropped into the waters of the ocean.
And that seed of Vasu, the lord of the earth, was swallowed by a fish;
O beautiful one, a daughter was born from that seed within the belly of the fish.
That fish was caught by hunters and brought to their home;
when it was then slit open, you were seen within it, O most excellent one.
Resembling the orb of the moon and possessing a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun,
all the fishermen on the bank of the Ganges were filled with joy upon seeing you.
Filled with joy, they all went to the residence of the leader and said,
"Take this jewel among women, who possesses great splendor."
That slender-limbed, deer-eyed woman was indeed taken as a wife by him who was childless;
he said to her, "O slender-limbed one, O deer-eyed one, protect me."
Then, O lord of men, having been told this by him and having surrendered herself to him, she reflected upon those words of Parāśara.
She said, "O Brahmin, it is well; the scent of fish still clings to me.
Thereupon, that young woman was perfumed with a divine fragrance by him.
Having kindled the fire by the power of yoga alone and having performed a circumambulation of the fire, she was then carried away by him out of passion.
In the midst of the boat, O son of Dharma, she perceived that the brahmin was eager for love, as he touched the various parts of her body; realizing this, she became afraid.
Then, laughing, she said to him: "O Lord, O wise one, how are you not ashamed to do what is fit only for a commoner in the presence of the world?"
Then, having meditated for a moment, he called to mind the Tāmasī [Māyā] within his heart;
the Tāmasī Māyā arrived, by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
Then she was amazed by that very deed, and being delighted by his asceticism, she then sported with him in the pleasures of womanhood.
Then, at that very moment, oppressed by the weight of her pregnancy,
she gave birth there to a boy with matted hair who was carrying a staff.
Holding a water-pot, peaceful, adorned with a girdle around his waist,
with his upper garment draped over one shoulder, he was free from the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
Then, O Pārtha, seeing that young elephant calf, the trembling girl became apprehensive and went for refuge to the sage.
Protect, protect me, O best of sages, O high-minded Parāśara!
A most wonderful son has been born to me, wearing an excellent loincloth and a girdle,
with a staff in hand, endowed with matted locks, and adorned with an upper garment.
Parāśara said: "Do not fear; though a son has been born to you, you shall remain a maiden.
You shall be known by the name Yojanagandhā, and Satyavatī shall be your second name."
The king named Śantanu, who will become your husband, shall have you as his first queen— you, the ornament of the Lunar dynasty.
Go back to your own abode, O radiant one, established once more in your former form;
do not give way to despondency here, for you have witnessed the power of my knowledge.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; that young woman, leaning toward her son, bowed with devotion and, prostrating herself in humility, spoke to her mother with the eight-limbed salutation.
"O Mother, may what I have said be forgiven; let favor be granted to me as well.
O Ambikā, I shall make an effort in the propitiation of the Lord."
Then, despondent at her son’s words, she spoke these words:
Yojanagandhā said:
"O child, do not depart today abandoning me, your innocent mother;
by separation from you, my son, death will surely come upon me without a doubt."
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no family equal to one's brothers;
there is no dharma higher than truth; and there is no sin greater than falsehood.
"In my childhood, you were indeed born as my support;
yet now you are neither my husband nor my son—behold this mockery of karma! (RKV 97.67)
Vyāsa said:
Do not despair within yourself; this which I have spoken is the truth. O Goddess, I must be remembered by you in times of calamity for the accomplishment of your purpose.
"I shall deliver you from calamities; please forgive my harsh words.
Having said this, Vyāsa departed, and the maiden also went home.
O lord of men, at the end of the Tretā Yuga and the beginning of the Dvāpara, the son of Parāśara appeared there, distressed in the midst of the forest.
Led by Śakra, the gods pondered the matter of Vyāsa;
it was Nārada himself who had declared that he was the son of Parāśara.
The wise one, born of a fisherwoman’s daughter on the banks of the Jahnu’s daughter (the Gaṅgā), was there;
then, at the word of Nārada, the best of the gods arrived.
Rāma, Pitāmaha, and Śakra, surrounded by hosts of sages, each offered his own mouth and other parts [of their bodies] while exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
The child was indeed consecrated by his grandfather with the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*;
he was Dvaipāyana because of his birth on an island, and Pārāśarya because of [his descent] from Parāśara.
From a portion of Kṛṣṇa, this one named Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa shall divide the Vedas;
he will be consecrated again and again by Virañci and by the hosts of sages.
Having said, "You are Vyāsa in all the worlds," the gods departed;
then Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana commenced his pilgrimage to sacred fords.
By him the Gaṅgā was plunged into, as well as Kedāra with Puṣkara,
Gayā, the sacred site of Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and the Sarasvatī.
Having bathed at Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, at Somanātha, and at Prabhāsa,
the great sage proceeded across the earth as far as the ocean's edge.
Having reached the auspicious Narmadā, the immortal river born from the body of Rudra,
he beheld the Narmadā with joy and attained peace of mind.
Resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, he performed extensive austerities;
in the summer he stood in the midst of five fires, and during the rainy season he lay upon the bare ground.
In the winter, wearing wet clothes, he stood meditating upon Maheśvara;
having established the Supreme Lord within the lotus of his own heart, he contemplated him.
Devoted to meditation, one should worship the eternal Siddheśvara Liṅga— the creator of creation and dissolution, the indivisible, the bestower of boons, and the auspicious.
Through the worship of the Siddhaliṅga and by the power of meditation and yoga,
Śaṅkara became manifest before Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
The Lord said: "I am pleased with you, my child; choose an auspicious boon."
Vyāsa said:
"O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
you yourself shall become manifest on the bank of the Narmadā."
O Lord of Umā, through your grace, I am a knower of the past and the future.
The Lord said: "So be it for you, my son; by my grace, without a doubt, I have been captured by your devotion and am manifest before you on the bank of the Narmadā."
"By means of half of my thousandfold radiance, I have appeared before you in your hermitage";
having said this, the god departed for Kailāsa, the most excellent mountain.
The marriage of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana took place according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, as he likewise protected his wife.
For a son was born to the son of Parāśara, who had been childless;
he was celebrated by all the gods, led by Indra.
Then, upon the birth of the son, the lords of sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha and led by Parāśara, arrived there in the course of their pilgrimage.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras,
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Thousands, hundreds of lakhs,
and crores of such highly fortunate ones, together with their disciples, have taken refuge on the banks of the Narmadā.
O King, they arrived satisfied at the auspicious and beautiful hermitage of Vyāsa; and upon seeing those foremost of brahmins, he too made an effort to rise up to greet them.
Having first bowed down to his father and then to everyone according to the prescribed rite,
he devotedly offered seats and presented water for the feet and the respectful offering.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke these words:
"I have been uplifted, there is no doubt, by the honor of conversing with you."
And wild vegetables and fruits grown in the forest—
these I shall give to all of you with a heart full of affection.
Having prostrated before each of them one by one, he invited them all;
then, seeing the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana bowing down, they [responded].
Having increased [his merit] with blessings for victory and having looked at one another,
Parāśara was gazed upon by all those eminent sages.
"O dear one, let an answer be given to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
Thus addressed by all of them, the blessed Parāśara spoke to his own son Vyāsa regarding what the ṛṣis desired to accomplish.
Śrī Parāśara said: Furthermore, those who desire to eat do not wish to take food on the southern bank for fear of breaking their vows, especially during a śrāddha ceremony.
Vyāsa said:
"I shall do as you have requested; stay right here for a moment while I propitiate the river and perform the supreme rite."
Having spoken thus and having become pure, he stood upon the bank of the Narmadā and suddenly recited a hymn; listen to that, O Lord of Men.
Victory to you, O Blessed Goddess! Homage to you, the Giver of Boons! Victory to you, the Destroyer of Evil who bestows manifold fruits!
Victory to you, the Holder of the Skulls of Śumbha and Niśumbha; I bow down to you, the Remover of the suffering of gods and men!
Victory to you who bear the moon and sun as eyes; victory to you whose excellent face is adorned by fire!
Victory to you who are intent upon being dissolved into the body of Bhairava; victory to you who dry up the blood of the darkness!
Victory to you, O crusher of Mahiṣa, who hold a trident in your hand; victory to you, the remover of all sins of the world!
Victory to you, O Goddess, saluted by Brahmā and Rāma; victory to you, bowed to by the sun and Indra!
Victory to you, praised by Īśa, who possesses the six faces and weapons; victory to you, praised by Śambhu, who flows to the ocean!
Victory to you, the destroyer of suffering and poverty; victory to you, the increaser of sons and wives!
Victory, O Goddess who sustains all bodies! Victory, O revealer of heaven, O remover of suffering!
Victory, O destroyer of disease, O bestower of liberation! Victory, O giver of desires, O supreme among the perfected ones!
Whoever recites this hymn composed by Vyāsa in the presence of Śiva,
or at home with a pure disposition, free from desire and anger;
Vyāsa will be pleased with him, as will the bull-vehicled Lord Śiva;
and the goddess Narmadā, who causes the destruction of all sins, shall be pleased.
Those by whom the Narmadā has been praised on earth do not go to the realm of Yama;
O Goddess, even the Grandfather (Brahmā) would be bewildered by the chanting of your virtues.
O Narmadā, even Vākpati himself does not know your true nature;
O Goddess, how could I venture to know your qualities?
Having thus recognized his pure disposition through the actions of speech, mind, and body,
the goddess Narmadā became pleased and then spoke these words:
"O Vyāsa, great sage! I am pleased by your truthful speech;
whatever boon you desire, I shall grant it all to you."
Vyāsa said:
"O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
you ought to grant hospitality to the sages on the northern bank."
Narmadā said:
"O Vyāsa, what you have requested is improper—the engagement in a wrong path;
even Indra, Candra, and Yama would not be able to set out upon a deviant course."
"Ask for another boon, my son, whatever may be difficult to obtain on earth.
Having heard these words of the goddess, Vyāsa then fell into a swoon.
Thinking, "Today my suffering has become in vain," he fell down;
indeed, the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Then, seeing Vyāsa fallen into a swoon, all the gods, including Indra, came there by the thousands with cries of "Alas! Alas! on their lips.
They raised up Vyāsa, who was devoted to the preservation of the Vedas;
he had exerted himself for the sake of the Brahmins, and not for his own sake, O best of rivers.
"For the sake of cows and for the sake of Brahmins, one should immediately renounce one's life;
thus was Narmadā proclaimed by Brahmā and the other foremost of the gods."
Terrified, Revā sprinkled him with her own water and many very cool breezes;
and Satyavatī’s son, having regained consciousness and bowed to the gods, spoke to the river.
Vyāsa said:
O Goddess, it is said that the fruit of visiting all the sacred fords has been ordained for me, yet due to my misfortune,
my hope for merit has become as fruitless as wild flowers are to common people.
Narmadā said:
"O high-souled one, wherever you wish to lead me here upon the surface of the earth,
I shall today follow behind you, the wielder of the staff, along your path together with the Vindhya."
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī,
caused the best of rivers to move toward the south of his own hermitage.
The sage of great splendor, staff in hand, uttered the syllable *huṃ*;
terrified by Vyāsa’s *huṃ*, Rudra’s daughter trembled.
Showing the way with his staff, the goddess proceeded there;
the goddess, having entered the wide path, was seen by those led by Śakra.
Then the gods, together with their attendants, released a rain of flowers, saying:
"Tell us, O son, what shall we do? We have been delighted by your deed."
Vyāsa said:
Having performed extensive austerity and having given gifts that yield great fruit,
this alone should be done by men— that which brings happiness to the virtuous.
"If you, O illustrious ones, are pleased, and if I am indeed worthy of your favor, then let all of you stay in my hermitage; there is no doubt about this."
This hospitality, consisting of leafy vegetables mixed with *amṛta*,
has been accepted by all of you, headed by Parāśara.
All of you must remain in your own hermitage on the northern bank of the Revā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
After the best of the twice-born had performed their daily rites of bathing and libations,
they proceeded to Vyāsakuṇḍa, where a fire sacrifice was then offered by them all.
Gautama, Bhṛgu, Māṇḍavya, Nārada, and likewise Lomaśa offered oblations into the fire with bilva fruits and bilva leaves.
Parāśara, as well as Śaṅkha, Kauśika, the sage Cyavana, Pippalāda, Vasiṣṭha, and Nāciketa of great austerity; RKV 97.133.
Viśvāmitra and Agastya, as well as Uddālaka and Yama,
Śāṇḍilya, Jaimini, Kaṇva, Yājñavalkya, Aśana, and Aṅgiras.
Śātātapa and Dadhīci, Kapila and likewise Gālava;
Jaigīṣavya as well as Dakṣa, Bharata and likewise Mudgala.
Vātsyāyana of great splendor, Saṃvarta, Śakti,
Jātūkarṇya, Bharadvāja, as well as the Vālakhilyas and Aruṇi.
Thousands such as these offer oblations into the fire,
their fingers marked by rosaries, devoted solely to the yoga of meditation.
Then all the twice-born, with one-pointed minds, performed the rite of oblation;
thereupon, a linga arose that bestows liberation and destroys disease.
Having beheld the supreme, indestructible God, Vyāsa was filled with joy;
the gods rained down flowers, and the best of the twice-born offered their blessings.
Having seen the three-eyed god, Vyāsa prostrated himself with all eight limbs and honored the brahmins with vegetables, roots, and fruits.
O son of Pāṇḍu, all the twice-born were fed, beginning with the ancestors;
then, having bestowed their auspicious blessings, the brahmins departed once more.
From that time onwards, that sacred ford has been called Vyāsa by the wise.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me all the merit of Vyāsatīrtha,
as well as the rules for bathing and giving gifts there, and at what time they yield great fruit.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Pāṇḍava, together with your brothers, I shall tell you everything regarding the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika; one should remain with senses subdued.
The man who, having observed the fast with devotion, keeps a vigil at night,
should devoutly bathe the Lord with honey, milk, and clarified butter.
Furthermore, one should smear the Supreme Lord with curd mixed with sugar, with water infused with *kuśa* grass, and with fragrant sandalwood paste.
Then one should worship with fragrant flowers and bilva leaves,
as well as with mucukunda, kunda, and jasmine blossoms.
One should worship the unsurpassed Lord of the Island with the utmost devotion, using *unmatta* and *munipuṣpa* flowers, as well as others that bloom in their respective seasons.
The Supreme Lord is pleased by the gift of a jar of sugarcane juice;
by the gift of eight jars, even powerful sin is destroyed.
And that which was acquired in a month is destroyed by eight hundred *gaḍukas*;
that of six months by one thousand; and likewise, that of a year by two thousand.
Sins accumulated since birth are destroyed by ten thousand [repetitions];
diseases are destroyed by twice that number; and with three times that number, there shall be the acquisition of wealth.
Through six million [recitations] one becomes eloquent, and likewise through twice that number one becomes perfected;
through ten lakhs, the state of Rudra is attained—of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, on the full moon day one should perform a ritual bath with devotion according to the procedure prescribed by the mantras, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
The wise man should duly offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings with water for Varuṇa, likewise with fire for Agni, and with that which brings about imperishability for Brahmā.
Through the *ṛc* verse one obtains the merit born of the *Ṛgveda*, through the *sāman* chant the fruit of the *Sāmaveda*,
and through the *yajus* formula of the *Yajurveda* or by means of the *Gāyatrī*, one may attain everything.
One should mutter the imperishable mantra, whether it belongs to the Sun, to Śiva,
or the Vaiṣṇava mantra known as the twelve-syllabled one.
One should worship with devotion those brāhmaṇas who are endowed with all auspicious marks,
who are devoted to their own wives, and who are free from hypocrisy and greed.
Those who cause the breaking of conduct, the sinful, the fallen, those who serve Śūdras,
and those associated with taking a Śūdra woman as a wife— [he] in whose house there is a Vṛṣalī...
Those who speak behind one's back, those devoted to reviling corrupt teachers,
those habitually hostile toward the Vedas, the rationalists, and those who act like herons.
One should avoid such persons at a śrāddha, in giving gifts, and in all religious observances; better is a Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if he knows only the essence of the Gāyatrī.
One should honor with gifts of food, alms, and gold such Brahmins as these— even those who, though learned in the four Vedas, are unrestrained, eat all things, and sell all things.
He who gives sandals, garments, a bed, an umbrella, or a seat to a brāhmaṇa with devotion is also honored in heaven.
In that [rite], a fragrant water-cow made of ghee should be offered visibly,
as well as a sesame-cow and likewise buffalo-cows.
He who is a giver of a black antelope skin, a giver of sesame seeds and clarified butter,
or a giver of a maiden and a book, shall attain the imperishable world.
"One who desires heaven should cause to be given two draft oxen, equipped with hooves and provided with grain and household utensils; this is my truthful speech."
One should encircle the island or the auspicious altar with a cord,
or else the temple or the Supreme Lord with supreme devotion.
O King, that person who performs a circumambulation here according to the prescribed rite [attains] the two continents named Jambū and Plakṣa, as well as the other, Śālmali.
Kuśa, Krauñca, as well as Kāśa, and Puṣkara as the seventh—
by these, O Bhārata, [the earth] is surrounded up to the seven oceans.
O Great King, lord of the island, one should perform the rite of releasing a bull;
by means of a reddish-colored bull, one shall attain the world of Maheśvara.
He who indeed has white markings on the face, the forehead, and likewise on the feet,
and whose tail is bright white— he is indeed a beholder of heaven.
O Bhārata, he who would give such a blue bull to the lord of an island-dwelling is said to dwell in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on its body.
O King, by the power of Vyāsatīrtha, he enjoys the worlds of Sūrya, Śaṅkara, Virañci, and Viṣṇu in succession according to his own will.
Then, one should worship the Brahmin there with devotion along with his wife; he who gives white and red garments to the twice-born [should do so].
Having performed a circumambulation of the pair [of deities], may the Teacher of the World be pleased with me;
for there is no kinsman equal to a Brahmin in this world and in the next.
He who protects one who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, whose senses are conquered, as he falls into the most terrible world of Yama; ||| RKV_97.175 |||
One should worship with supreme devotion, especially a singer of the Sāman hymns;
and those who, remaining at home, remember Dvīpeśvara with devotion.
For them, no sorrow arises, nor loss, nor any ill-deed;
there, one should first worship the Liṅga Siddheśvara.
There, the illustrious Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, attained perfection;
and by worshipping this very [liṅga], the high-minded Dhārāsarpa became a perfected one.
O King, he who gives up his life at that sacred ford pierces through the world of the Sun and proceeds into the presence of Śiva.

O Bhārata, one indeed dwells for seven thousand years in water, ten thousand in fire, sixteen in falling [from a height], sixty in a great battle, and eighty in the seizure of cattle; but by fasting unto death, one attains an imperishable state.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
having become wind, behold their own kinsman as he approaches.
"In our lineage, is there any son who would offer us water with sesame seeds,
especially on the full moon of Kārttika or likewise on that of Vaiśākha?"
"And by resorting to that sacred site (tīrtha), we shall attain the heavenly realm;
all this has been told to you regarding the unsurpassed Lord of the Island (Dvīpeśvara)."
O King, he who recites this with supreme devotion or listens to it with his mind fixed upon it,
shall also be liberated from sin and rejoice in the abode of Śiva.
O best of kings, there is no doubt that Vyāsatīrtha, created by the preeminent sages, is the salt-waste of all holy fords and the granter of all desires.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vyāsatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 98] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Prabhāseśvara,
renowned throughout the three worlds as the most excellent staircase to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, tell me about Prabhāsa—how it came to be, how it yields great fruit, and how it serves as a visible staircase to heaven; describe it to me in brief."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The unfortunate wife of the Sun, renowned by the name Prabhā,
formerly propitiated Śambhu with fierce ascetic penance.
Subsisting on air alone, she remained devoted to meditation for year after year;
then, O son of Pāṇḍu, Mahādeva was pleased with Prabhā.
Īśvara said:
"O child, why are you distressed? Tell me what you wish to say;
for I am indeed the one Bhāskara, and no diversity exists at all."
The Lord said: "O Lord Śambhu, there is no other god for women anywhere except their husband—
whether he be possessed of qualities or devoid of them, wealthy or penniless."
Whether beloved or even hated, for women the husband alone is a deity.
O Lord of the Gods, though I am consumed by misfortune in the midst of my friends,
I suffer intensely because of the happiness I have obtained from my husband.
Īśvara said:
"By my grace, you shall indeed become beloved of Bhāskara."
Pārvatī said:
"O Supreme Lord, even the Sun will make your word authoritative; otherwise, this exertion of Prabhā’s would be in vain."
The sun, which destroys the darkness [of ignorance] through meditation upon Maheśāna,
the husband of Umā, has risen from the sky onto the northern bank of the Narmadā.
Bhānu said:
"O Lord, O destroyer of the demon Aghāsura, why have I been summoned?"
Īśvara said:
O Bhānu, protect your radiance with supreme contentment indeed.
Umā said:
"O Destroyer of Cold, remain forever in the palace of Prabhā;
O Ravi, let her be made the foremost wife among all your consorts."
Bhānu said:
"O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall do exactly as you have commanded.
Having heard this, Prabhā, being summoned, replied to Maheśvara.
The Lord said: "O God, O Enemy of Manmatha, O Lord of Umā, remain here with one portion of yourself;
let another portion be established here for the sake of the manifestation of this sacred ford."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Pāṇḍava, a Liṅga consisting of all the gods was established there;
it is renowned as Prabhāseśa and is difficult to find in all the worlds.
Other sacred fords indeed bear fruit in due time, O king of kings; but Prabhāseśa grants the fruits of one's desires immediately.
O King, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, especially at that time, he who should touch the horse there before a Brāhmaṇa as prescribed;
By that [act], one attains the status of Indra or else the station of the Sun;
having bathed with supreme devotion, one should give a gift to a twice-born man.
O Lord of the Best, the giver of a cow shall attain heaven and the world of truth (Satyaloka),
[receiving] a beautiful, radiant, young, and auspicious milch-cow, lovely in every limb.
O best of kings, those who give a cow together with her calf, equipped with a bell and yielding milk into a bronze vessel, do not go to the abode of Yama.
Now, he who causes the bath of the God to be performed with supreme devotion attains the highest world for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
O Pāṇḍava, misfortune comes to an end merely by bathing there;
moreover, he who devoutly bestows the gift of a maiden at that sacred site [attains great merit].
O son of Pāṇḍu, one should cause her to be given to a Brāhmaṇa through the *vivāha* rite;
she should be given to one of equal age who is likewise endowed with noble lineage, good character, and wealth.
O Great King, even those who are joined with sins, when they give gifts,
their evils dissolve just as salt dissolves in water.
The sin committed by betraying one's master, that arising from misappropriating a deposit, and that produced by false testimony belong to the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful person.
The sin arising from the destruction of that village's grove, the sin of consorting with another's wife,
the sin of a usurer, and the sin born of theft— [all these are incurred].

That which arises from breaking a well, that of one who observes the "vow of the cat," that which is hypocritical, that born from cutting down trees, and that produced by the prohibition of marriage; RKV 98.28.
The sin arising from cutting down trees in a grove, from approaching those who should not be approached, from abandoning one's own wife, and from seeking the wives of others; RKV_98.29.
Whatever sin arises from seizing the property of a Brahmin, from administering poison, from killing a cow, from the sale of sacred knowledge, and from association with such outcasts; 98.30.

The terrible sin arising from the killing of a dog or a cat, as well as that produced by a serpent or a Śūdra, and whatever sin belongs to one who seizes land, as well as to the one who causes the seizure of land— [all these are incurred].
O Pāṇḍava, whatever sin there is in saying "Do not give" regarding cows, fire, or Brahmins— that sin goes to dissolution through the gift of a daughter in marriage.
Having gone to the world of Bhāskara, he shall proceed to the auspicious world of Rudra;
residing in the world of Rudra, he sports for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
When all evil has been destroyed,
O son of Pāṇḍu, this meditation arises for one who goes to the auspicious holy site of Prabhāsa.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), he shall attain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
The gift of a cow is of great merit, the supreme destroyer of all sins;
it is indeed praised at all times, and especially on the fourteenth day.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Prabhāsa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O protector of the earth, one should go to the southern bank of the Narmadā to the shrine of Vāsukīśa, which destroys the entire multitude of sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For what reason, O dear one, was Vāsukīśa installed on the southern bank of the Revā? Tell me this in detail, O Teacher."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having established all this, Śambhu indeed performed the dance.
From his exertion, sweat was born; a serpent devours it as it falls, mingled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, having issued from the crest of Hara’s head.
Then, O Bhārata, Mandākinī became enraged at the serpent and said:
"O snake, O lowly creature, you shall indeed become a python! (RKV 99.5)
Vāsuki said:
"I am a sinner and one of wicked conduct who deserves your favor, for there is no one other than Hara [to do so].
You are a river of auspicious characteristics, holy and the purifier of the three worlds."
For you are the one who cuts through saṃsāra and destroys the suffering of the afflicted; you stand at the gateway to heaven—O Goddess, have mercy on me!
Gaṅgā said:
"Perform extensive ascetic penance directed toward Śaṅkara;
then, by my command, you shall regain your own place and your state as a serpent."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that serpent, having quickly gone to the auspicious Vindhya mountain,
began to perform austerities, intent upon the propitiation of Śaṅkara.

He constantly meditated upon Mahādeva, the three-eyed one who holds aloft a hand-drum. Then, when a hundred years were complete, the Teacher of the World, having been restrained, approached him and uttered these gentle words: RKV 99.10: "He constantly meditated upon Mahādeva, the three-eyed one who holds aloft a hand-drum. Then, when a hundred years were complete, the Teacher of the World, having been restrained, approached him and uttered these gentle words."
