"Choose a boon from me, my child, O serpent, for you have shown me honor."
Vāsuki said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and will grant a boon, O Śaṅkara,
then by your grace, O Lord of Gods, may freedom from sin be mine."
Tell me of some sacred ford that destroys all sins.
Īśvara said:
"O mighty-armed serpent, go to the auspicious Revā;
on its meritorious southern bank, perform your ablutions according to the prescribed rite."
Having spoken thus, the god vanished; Vāsuki, filled with haste, entered the waters of the Narmadā in the form of a python.
Along that path, the supreme stream of the Jāhnavī arose;
the serpent, his impurities shaken off, was born in the waters of the Narmadā.
Śaṅkara was established there on the Narmadā, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
thereafter is the famous Liṅga Nāgeśvara, which destroys all sins.
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, one should bathe Śiva with honey;
he immediately becomes freed from all taint—of this there is no doubt.
O Pārtha, those men who are childless but perform their ablutions at the confluence obtain excellent and auspicious sons, equal to Kārtavīrya.
O prince, he who, devoted to fasting, performs a *śrāddha* at that very place,
shall liberate the deceased ancestors from hell by doing so.
No fear of serpents arises within his lineage or circle of kinsmen; by the grace of the Nāgas, his family prospers free from harm.
All this has been told to you out of affection, O best of kings.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nāgeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the most splendid sacred site known as Mārkaṇḍeśa, located on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
O son, this auspicious place, the most excellent of all holy fords, which is worshipped by the gods and is more secret than the secret, has not been told by me to anyone.
Previously, I established a knowledge that was like a staircase to heaven;
and there, by the grace of Śaṅkara, that very knowledge arose within me.
O son of Pāṇḍu, another who goes to that very place and mutters the Drupadā mantra while submerged in the water is liberated from all sins without exception.
Whether by verbal, mental, or even physical sins,
he remained stationed facing the southern direction, leaning against the pedestal.
One should devotedly join with the thirty-two-fold multiformed Śūlin;
upon the fall of the body, one shall go to Śiva—this is my certainty, O King.
"O Bhārata, one should awaken the lamp with clarified butter on the night of the eighth day;
thus Śaṅkara has declared that one attains the heavenly world."
O prince, whoever performs a *śrāddha* there with devotion,
his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
Whoever offers libations there with *iṅguda*, *badara*, or *bilva* fruits, or with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and water, shall obtain for their ancestors the fruit of their birth.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mārkaṇḍeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha) located on the northern bank of the Narmadā, in the midst of the sacrificial enclosure (yajñavāṭa).
O King, that which is renowned on earth as Saṃkarṣaṇa, the destroyer of sins, is indeed where penance was formerly performed by Balabhadra.
O prince, even the gods were present right there;
Śambhu was stationed in that very place together with Umā, as was Keśava.
O king of kings, Balabhadra, out of compassion for living beings,
established Śaṅkara, the destroyer of sins, with supreme devotion.
He who bathes there with devotion, having conquered anger and subdued his senses,
should bathe Śiva with honey on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight.
Whoever, with devotion, causes a *śrāddha* to be offered to the ancestors at that very place,
goes to the supreme abode, according to the word of Balabhadra.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Saṃkarṣaṇa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Markandeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Manmatheśa, who is saluted by all the gods.
O King, by merely bathing, a man does not see the world of Yama.
And whatever woman is childless, O son of Pāṇḍu, she who bathes there shall obtain a son, O Pārtha— one who is true to his word and firm in his vows.
Having bathed there, O King, a man who is pure and of restrained mind,
by fasting for one night, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O King, there shall be no other such king of holy places as Kāmika;
by performing a three-night rite there, one obtains the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows.
There, one should perform a dance; the Supreme Lord is pleased by the sounds of song and instrumental music, as well as by keeping vigil at night.
And at Eraṇḍī, Mahādeva was seen by me as Manmatheśvara;
what can even an enraged Yama do? A fortunate person beholds auspicious things.
O King, because Śambhu was established by Kāma,
this Manmatheśvara is the granter of desires and the staircase to the path of heaven upon the earth.
Moreover, O Bhārata, there is a special distinction here regarding the performance of *śrāddha* at the twilight hours;
O Indra among kings, the supreme fruit of giving food has been proclaimed.
All this has been told to you out of devotion, O Bhārata;
thus is Manmatheśvara renowned throughout the earth bounded by the oceans.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, one who has conquered his senses should go there in the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra and perform the gift of a cow on the thirteenth day.
O best of kings, having kept a vigil at night before the God,
one should devoutly offer a lamp with ghee before the God.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, this fruit is recorded as being equal for both.

and white, or red, or black-colored, or pale-red, or tawny.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a cow together with its calf, provided with a bronze milking vessel, adorned with golden hooves, and having horns tipped with gold.
May the Lords of the World—Hara, Kṛṣṇa, and Pitāmaha—be pleased with me;
may the Goddess Surabhi, the protectress of the world, deliver me.
O King, O Pārtha, those women who, for the sake of obtaining sons, bathe at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī with the Rudra-sūktas and likewise with hymns originating from the four Vedas;
One should have the rite performed by four Brahmins who are praised [for their qualities], and by two who are proficient;
with one [Brahmin] holding a moistened jar, he should consecrate the couple.
Either by a single astrologer or by a singer of the Sāmaveda,
one should have the jar provided with the five jewels placed right there.
Combined with fragrant water and mixed with all medicinal herbs,
it should likewise be joined with mango sprouts, as well as *aśvattha* and *madhuka*.
It should be wrapped in a white cloth, smeared with white sandalwood paste,
covered with white flowers, and have white mustard seeds placed in its center.
Having placed [the image] in a bell-metal vessel, the best of preceptors, seeking a son,
[should offer] whatever garment clings to his body, as well as bracelets and ornaments.
Then, for the sake of one's own accomplishment, all of that should be relinquished within the maṇḍala;
thereafter, one should prostrate to the Sun and to the Preceptor who embodies Rudra.
Then, in that supreme world of the Goddess, he should eat sweet food;
and he should give fruit, an umbrella, and betel-leaf to a brahmin.
He shall possess sandals and a vehicle, and being freed from suffering,
he shall sport in the world of Bhāskara until the dissolution of all beings.
Every gift, whether entirely auspicious or inauspicious, possesses ten millionfold merit;
just as all rivers and streams reach their end by merging into the ocean.
In this way, O King, the sins of men are destroyed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī,
even by the falling of weapons from all sides at that very confluence.
Śaṅkara has declared that the sin equal to the killing of a fetus is destroyed for one who,
out of devotion, causes the sacrifice of life in the sacrificial fire.
O best of kings, immediately thereafter, one may practice fasting in water for five thousand years, or [practice] in the sacrificial fire for five thousand years.
In water there are three thousand; those who do not eat for sixty days are eaten by crows, cranes, pigeons, owls, and likewise by beasts.
Touched by the water from the confluence, they go to the supreme goal;
even the trees, having known that state, go to the same destination as the yogins.
"I have seen Queen Eraṇḍikā; I have seen my Lord of Love.
What can even an enraged Yama accomplish? A noble person beholds only auspicious things."
Those who constantly smear themselves with clay originating from the confluence [of rivers], their sins such as the killing of a fetus are destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter.
O lord of men, a mortal who is robbed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the state free from ailment.
"Those mortals dwelling in hermitages who praise the confluence of the Eraṇḍī become freed from sin; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara."
By seeing the tops of the castor-oil trees, one dispels evil.
Those men who shall read this meritorious account of the sacred fords (tīrtha),
and others who hear it with devotion, become liberated from sin.
All this regarding the confluence of the Eraṇḍī has been told to you, O King;
furthermore, I shall speak of another [place] which causes the destruction of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness and Merit of the Eraṇḍī-saṅgama Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 104.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the excellent Sauvarṇaśila.
It is renowned on the northern bank as that which brings about the destruction of all evils.
In ancient times, a place difficult to attain on the Revā near the confluence was established by hosts of sages through a hundredfold exertion on all sides.
O lord of men, there is a sacred field divided into a space of one cubit;
having bathed at Suvarṇaśilaka and worshipped Maheśvara, [one attains merit].
Having bowed to the god Bhāskara,
one should offer oblations into the fire using either bilva fruit mixed with clarified butter or even with bilva leaves.
May the Lord of the World be pleased with me; may my disease certainly perish.
Listen to me regarding the fruit that is obtained when gold is given to a twice-born man.
Whoever bestows gold obtains all that supreme fruit which has been declared for a sacrifice involving abundant gold.
Purified by that gift, upon death he shall attain heaven and become an attendant of Rudra for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Then, having descended from heaven, he is born into a pure family,
endowed with wealth and grain, and remembers that water once again.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Suvarṇaśilā Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 105.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, having fasted and subdued his senses, one should go to the place known as Karañja.
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from all sins.
Having worshipped Mahādeva and having given gifts with devotion— whether gold, silver, or even jewels, pearls, and coral— RKV 105.2.
Sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a bed, and coverings—all these yield a merit of ten million times ten million; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Karañja Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 106. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the most beautiful tīrtha.
It is divine, a bringer of good fortune, and delightful to both men and women.
In that regard, O best of kings, whatever unfortunate woman or man bathes there and worships Umā and Rudra, good fortune arises for them.
On the third day, having fasted for a full day and night and having subdued his senses,
he should with devotion invite a handsome brahmin together with his wife.
Having adorned [the image] with perfumes and garlands, and having scented it with incense, garments, and other fragrances,
one should then devoutly feed it with milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara).
Having fed them according to the rule, one should perform a circumambulation and say:
"May Mahādeva, together with his consort and bull-bannered, be pleased with me."
"O Lord of the gods, just as you are never separated [from your devotees], so may it be for me as well; having shown compassion, please think thus. (RKV 106.6)
When this has been done, I shall declare to you all that merit which is proclaimed for him, exactly as it was spoken by the Lord.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, misfortune, an evil rebirth, poverty, the bonds of sorrow, and even sterility shall not arise for seven lifetimes.
Especially on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who goes there and then practices the five-fire austerity with devotion; RKV_106.9 //
Even he is liberated from all sins without exception; there is no doubt about this—provided that, free from the two-fold mind, he burns guggulu incense.
If one should cause the body of a person engaged in that rite to break apart in the vicinity of Gaurī, and if the departure of his breath (utkrānti) occurs, [the following happens].
"Upon the fall of the body, one shall go to heaven"—thus Śaṅkara spoke;
likewise, with white, red, yellow, and various auspicious garments.
Having honored both the Brahmin woman and the Brahmin according to the prescribed rite,
with various kinds of flowers and most beautiful perfumes and incenses, ||| RKV_106.13 |||
One should smear [the image] with necklaces, vermilion, and saffron;
one should represent the woman as Gaurī and the Brāhmaṇa as Śiva.
Having fashioned such forms for them, a gift is then bestowed:
a bracelet, an ear-ornament, a necklace, and likewise a seal-ring.
O best of kings, whoever gives the seven kinds of grain as food, as well as other gifts, at that sacred ford (tīrtha), [obtains great merit].
Whatever merit one might obtain through all forms of giving, there is no doubt that [the merit here] is a thousandfold; no deliberation need be made on this point.
Therefore, he enjoys unsurpassed enjoyment together with Śaṅkara;
his good fortune becomes vast—of this there is no doubt.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without wealth shall attain wealth;
O Indra among kings, there is a wish-fulfilling holy site situated upon the Narmadā.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kāmadatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Bhaṇḍārī-tīrtha,
which destroys poverty for nineteen yugas.
When the Lotus-born Lord was pleased by the asceticism performed by Dhanada,
he attained the protection of his wealth right there through even a small gift.
Having gone there and bathed with devotion, whoever bestows wealth [as an offering],
for him there shall never be a depletion of wealth.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhaṇḍārī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 108.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the excellent Rohiṇī-tīrtha.
Renowned throughout the three worlds, it is the supreme remover of all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I desire to hear in truth the majesty of the Rohiṇī-tīrtha, which destroys all sins; you ought to tell that to me.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: When all moving and non-moving beings had perished in that terrible single ocean, while the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, was reclining upon the waters; RKV_108.3 //
A lotus has arisen at the navel, resembling a solar disc,
endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and beautifully adorned with petals.
There, Brahmā was born, possessing four lotus-like faces;
he said, "O Lord of Gods, O Master, let an order be given to me: what shall I do?"
Thus addressed, the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
then spoke these sweet words to the god Pitāmaha.
O mighty-armed one, by my command, create on the Sarasvatī a world for the entire multitude of beings, including their methods of production and their destruction.
Having heard these words of Padmanābha, O Bhārata,
the Blessed One reflected upon the seven sages out of a desire for their welfare.
In due order, those wise ones were conceived: Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Prācetasa, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
O sinless one, at the sacrifice, the highly effulgent Prajāpati Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas,
likewise begot fifty daughters.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and likewise that illustrious one gave twenty-seven to Indu.
O lord of men, among them was one named Rohiṇī,
who was disliked by all the women and especially by her husband.
Then, O best of kings, having developed supreme detachment,
she came to the bank of the Narmadā and performed extensive austerities.
By fasting for one night, three nights, six, or twelve nights, and by observing fasts for a fortnight or a month, they emaciate their bodies.
O dear one, she constantly propitiates the Blessed Goddess, the destroyer of Mahiṣāsura, who wards off all afflictions.
O King, having bathed repeatedly in the waters of the Narmadā, the goddess Nārāyaṇī, who possesses a pure smile and great fortune, became pleased.
"O highly fortunate one, you are pleased by your vow and your self-restraint.
Having heard these words of the Moon, Rohiṇī, his beloved, [replied].
"O Mānadeva, may it be so that I shall become [as you wish] before long.
Having said, "So be it," Bhavānī, who is compassionate toward her devotees, spoke thus.
Being praised by the hosts of sages, she vanished right there;
from that time forward, that sacred ford was known as Rohiṇī, the beloved of the Moon.
O best of kings, she becomes beloved at all times; and whatever woman or man bathes with devotion at that sacred site, [she/he shall likewise become beloved].
She indeed becomes beloved by her husband, just like Rohiṇī;
and whoever indeed gives up their life at that sacred site (tīrtha), [attains the same].
For seven births, there shall never be a separation between husband and wife.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Rohiṇīsomanātha Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 109.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha.
It is renowned as Senāpura, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
And Mahāsena was brought by the gods, led by Indra, for the consecration as commander-in-chief by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
For the sake of slaying the Dānavas and for the victory of the gods,
he gratified the foremost of Brahmins according to the prescribed rite by means of a gift of land.
With the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, and the resonance of drums;
with lutes, flutes, and mṛdaṅgas, and the auspicious tones of jhallarī cymbals.
Then, having let out a terrible roar, the Dānava named Ruru, arrogant in his strength,
arrived for the purpose of obstructing the consecration.
Filling the ten directions with throngs of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry,
O Bhārata, a great battle indeed commenced there with him.

[The field was] crowded with spears, double-edged swords, nooses, and clubs; with scimitars, javelins, and axes; with crescent-headed arrows, barbed shafts, and iron bolts; and filled with headless trunks and fallen garments.

Then, in an instant, that high-souled destroyer of enemy hosts seized his discus, having shattered the army of the foe’s forces with the strikes of arrows released from his bow, leaving their elephants, horses, and chariots destroyed.

Then the blazing, sharp, and terrifying Sudarśana discus, which strikes fear into both gods and asuras in battle, severed the head of the Daitya; it had been released from the hand of the slayer of Madhu.
Seeing that sudden obstacle to his consecration, the six-faced one abandoned his position there and performed extensive austerities.
The discus, released by Hari, the sustainer of the worlds, for the sake of his destruction,
split the Dānava in two and fell into the pure waters.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Cakratīrtha;
it was fashioned by the one whose form is the universe for the destruction of all sins.
But that man who, having bathed at Cakratīrtha, worships the Lord Acyuta,
obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and honors auspicious Brahmins who are peaceful, self-controlled, and have conquered anger, shall obtain the fruit born of ten million [such acts].
Whoever there at that sacred ford casts off their own body with devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu upon death, accompanied by auspicious sounds such as the cry of "Victory! (Jaya).
Having sported as he desired, honored by gods and gandharvas,
he returns here once more and is born again into a noble family.
This merit-bestowing, sin-removing, auspicious account that destroys suffering has been told to you, O highly fortunate one; listen further to another from me.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Cakratīrtha at Senāpura," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 110.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Dhautapāpa, which destroys even the most grievous sins.
It was created by Viṣṇu in ancient times in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha.
When the terrible Dānavas had been slain, Janārdana, the God of gods,
acted for the sake of destroying that sin and for the destruction of the Dānavas who had arisen.
At that sacred ford, having conquered his anger, he practiced extensive austerity,
observing a difficult vow of silence that was impossible even for gods and dānavas.
Having bathed and given various gifts to the twice-born,
that great sinner went at that very moment to that state of Viṣṇu.
Thus, one who has committed a most terrible sin there, being endowed with this [practice],
is liberated from all transgressions by bathing and reciting according to the prescribed rule.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Dhautapāpa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 111.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
Formerly, Skanda performed most severe austerities.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me truly the entire life-story of Skanda from his birth, as well as the meritorious ritual for the sacred ford.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, in former times the God of gods performed austerities;
once he had been entreated by all the deities, he married the goddess Umā.
O best of gods, there is no general whatsoever for the gods;
all the gods, including Vāsava himself, are being led away by the terrible Dānavas.
Just as the night without the moon or the day without the sun does not shine for even a moment, so too an army without a leader.
Knowing this, O Great God, O All-pervading Lord, out of supreme compassion,
let someone renowned throughout the three worlds be appointed as the commander of the army.
Having heard these auspicious words of the gods, the Supreme Lord,
desiring the goddess Umā, remembered Smara in his mind.
With all his limbs overcome by that [passion], the teacher of the world, who can assume any form at will,
it is said, dallied with Rudrāṇī for a hundred divine years.
Then the king of the gods, having learned that Hara was engaged in great sexual union,
consulted with the deities and dispatched Jātavedas.
Having gone there, Mahādeva, who was established in supreme bliss, suddenly saw him and, crying out "Alas! Alas!", rose up.
Then, O great king, the enraged Mahādevī, trembling, spoke these words of a curse: "Listen to what I am telling you."
Since I was entreated by all the gods for the birth of a son,
and my pleasure was rendered fruitless after they had sent forth Jātavedas, [I am now in this state].
"Therefore, all of them shall be childless; of this there is no doubt.
Then Hara said to Agni, "Carry our seed."

"You ought to act in accordance with what occurs in the worlds. O best of gods, my splendor can be taken up by you for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work; no one else in the three worlds is capable of this."
Agni said:
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, what power do you have to sustain my splendor,
which reduces the entire three worlds, with all that is moving and unmoving, to ashes?"
The Lord said: "O Consumer of Oblations, if pain arises for you because of the seed remaining in your belly,
then cast that splendor into the waters of the Gaṅgā."
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva cast all of that supreme, unfailing seed into the mouth of the fire-god and vanished.
When the god had departed from sight, the fire-god, while still burning,
cast [the remains] into the waters of the Gaṅgā and went to his own abode.
But Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, unable to endure that splendor,
cast him into a clump of reeds and departed quickly as she had come.
Seeing that he had been born there, all the gods, including Indra,
then dispatched Kṛttikā to suckle him with breast milk.
Seeing that they had all arrived at the womb of Gaṅgā, Mahāmati became six-faced and, being thirsty, drank from their breasts.

O King of kings, Padmasambhava performed all the purificatory rites, such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others prescribed in the Vedas, according to the rituals seen in the sacred injunctions.
From the six-faced [Agni] he is named Ṣaṇmukha; he is Kārttikeya from the Kṛttikās;
he is Kumāra because of his youthfulness; and he is anotherly known as Gaṅgāgarbha and Agnija.
Thus the prince was born; for even without formal study, he was a knower of the Vedas.
Having mastered many treatises, he practiced extensive austerity.
In all the groves of the gods, in rivers and streams,
in whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, and those which are in the ocean, O Bhārata—
Then, by means of successive stages, having taken refuge on the bank of the Narmadā,
he performed extensive penance on the southern shore of the Narmadā.
Chanting day and night the prayers prescribed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
meditating upon Mahādeva, pure and with his veins clearly visible, he remained steadfast.
Then, at the end of a full thousand years, the god Maheśvara,
accompanied by Umā, spoke these words at that time.
Īśvara said:
"O dear one, I am the giver of boons to you; Gaurī is your mother and I am indeed your father.
Choose a boon, whatever you desire, even if it be difficult to obtain in the three worlds."
Ṣaṇmukha said:
"If you are pleased, O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, together with Umā, I choose my mother and father; I have no other recourse or thought."
Having heard these auspicious words fallen from the mouth of his son, he said,
"So be it," and embraced him with affection and love.
Then, having smelled him on the head, Śaṅkara spoke to both of them.
Īśvara said:
"You shall become the commander-in-chief, indeed imperishable and immutable."
And a peacock of divine form was given by me as your vehicle for battle, O wielder of the spear;
having said, "Conquer the gods, asuras, and others," that high-souled one departed for the excellent Mount Kailāsa.
When the god had departed from sight, Śikhivāhana then established Mahādeva and went into the presence of the gods.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became known as Skanda-tīrtha;
it is meritorious, a remover of all sins, and difficult for mortals to attain on earth.
O King, whoever bathes with devotion at that sacred ford and worships Śiva with perfumes, garlands, and ritual ablutions, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
Now, listen to the meritorious fruit for one who, having bathed at Skanda-tīrtha, worships the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with sesame seeds.
O Bhārata, by a single offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa) performed according to the prescribed rite, the ancestors remain satisfied for twelve years; of this there is no doubt.
O Indra among kings, whatever is done at that sacred ford— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
all of that becomes inexhaustible both in this world and in the next.
Whoever shall give up their life at that sacred ford according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures shall go to the abode of Śiva.
Having dwelt there for one kalpa, honored by gods and gandharvas,
he is born here in Bhāratavarṣa into a stainless family.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, being free from all diseases,
shall live for more than a hundred years, endowed with sons and grandsons.
O King, this origin of Skanda-tīrtha has been told to you;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, the supreme destroyer of all suffering,
meritorious, and the remover of all sins, as spoken by the God of gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Skanda Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 112.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Aṅgiras.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, it is the destroyer of all sins.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Yuga, there was a Brahmin named Aṅgiras who had mastered the Vedas; for the sake of obtaining a son, he performed extensive austerities.
Bathing daily at the three sessions of the day, chanting the eternal God, and worshipping Mahādeva through penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa; 112.3.
Then, when twelve years had passed, the Supreme Lord was pleased and invited the excellent brahmin of the Aṅgiras lineage to choose a boon.
He chose Mahādeva as his son— the best among those who possess sons—
one who had completed his Vedic studies and vows, and was proficient in all the śāstras.
O King, [he begot] a son who was the counselor of the gods, honored in all worlds,
the eternal abode of the splendor of Brahman, and imperishable and undecaying.
"Thus, your desired son shall become proficient in all branches of knowledge;
of this there is no doubt. Having spoken thus, Hara departed.
And from Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati was born as a son chosen by his father's desire, one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
When the son was born, Aṅgiras installed Śaṅkara there and,
with a heart full of joy and contentment, departed for the Northern Mountain.
And whoever, having bathed there at the Aṅgiras Tīrtha, worships Śiva,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Rudra.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without wealth shall attain wealth;
whatever desire a person may wish for, that he shall obtain.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Agnirasa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 113.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Koṭitīrtha.
Ten million sages went there and attained supreme perfection.
Whoever, having bathed at that sacred ford, being pure, feeds the Brahmins—
when one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the ancestors and the gods,
and when Mahādeva has been worshipped, shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 114.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
It is not born from a womb, it is of great merit, and it destroys all sins.
Having bathed at Ayonija, a man should worship the Supreme Lord;
by performing the worship of the ancestors and the gods, he is liberated from all sins.
O Great King, he who gives up his life at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rite never again beholds the gateway to a womb.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ayonisambhava Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 115.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the supreme Aṅgāraka Tīrtha.
Renowned on the banks of the Narmadā, he was the bestower of forms to all the worlds.
O Indra among kings, it is said that in former times Aṅgāraka performed austerities for a number of years amounting to an arbuda, a nikharva, and a prayuta.
Then, O King, the blessed Mahādeva, being pleased by his supreme compassion and appearing before his very eyes, spoke to the son of the Earth.
"I am the granter of boons, O illustrious one—a boon difficult even for the gods to obtain.
I shall grant you a boon, my child; tell me what you wish to say."
Aṅgāraka said:
"By your grace, O Lord of Gods, O Great Lord of all the worlds,
I constantly traverse the vault of the sky situated among the planets."
"As long as the earth-supporter remains in the world, as long as the moon and sun endure,
and as long as the rivers, streams, and oceans exist, may this boon of mine be inexhaustible."
"So be it," said the Lord of Gods, having granted that unsurpassed boon; then, being praised by gods and asuras, he entered the sky and departed.
Then Bhūmiputra established Śaṅkara in that place;
having gone to the abode of the gods, he was installed as a planet in the world.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the Supreme Lord,
having offered oblations and conquered anger, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
O Bhārata, he who bathes on a Thursday that falls on a Tuesday and worships the planet Aṅgāraka according to the prescribed rite shall [attain merit] for seven births.
In a mandala ten yojanas in extent, one becomes beautiful;
there, a living being who dies— whether intentionally or unintentionally—
becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Aṅgāraka Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 116.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should then go to Pāṇḍutīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there, O King, a person is liberated from all sins.
Whoever, being pure, bathes at that sacred ford and gives gold as a gift, their sins such as the killing of a fetus are destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
By the offering of funeral cakes and water, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
the fathers and grandfathers dance, filled with great joy.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Pāṇḍutīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 117.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the meritorious holy site of Trilocana.
There dwells the Lord of Gods, who is worshipped by all the worlds.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships Śaṅkara with devotion goes to the abode of Rudra upon death; of this there is no doubt.
Then, when the end of the eon is complete, having sported there, he returns here and shall remain for a hundred years, honored and never separated [from his kin].

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Trilocana Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 118.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the most beautiful holy site (tīrtha).
It is renowned as Indratīrtha, located on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of Brahmins, how does Indratīrtha exist on the southern bank of the Narmadā? I wish to hear it in detail, from beginning to middle and end.
Having heard these words of the wise son of Dharma,
he related that ancient history in its true form.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having gained the trust of the exceedingly powerful Dharmaśatru Vṛtra for a very long time,
and having then conquered and slain him, the Lord of Śacī was departing.
As he was departing by way of the road, the unassailable sin of Brahmin-slaughter followed him tirelessly through day and night across the three worlds.
Whichever direction a slayer of a Brahmin goes in a splendid vehicle,
even to the very quarters of the world along with the gods, the sin of killing does not leave him.

The destination of those who commit the great sins—killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s bed—is well known; but such a destination is not seen for those who betray trust.
Having seen the gateway to evil karma, one is purified by bathing and giving;
yet neither woman nor man who betrays trust is ever purified.
Having heard these and other such words spoken by those who knew the truth, the King of the Gods fell into the deepest despondency.
Having renounced his kingdom, sons, wife, home, various riches, and all else, he went with the gods to practice supreme austerity.
These fruits of dharma bring splendor to the lord of men;
friends, kinsmen, and relatives enjoy the fruit of his dharma.
While all these people look on, the sin alone is consumed by one who,
casting aside supreme happiness, indeed emaciates his own body.
That king of the gods went to various sacred fords and shrines,
at all the banks of the Gaṅgā as well as those of the Yamunā.
In all the lakes of Sarasvatī, in the various oceans, in rivers, in natural pools, and in tanks and ponds; RKV 118.14.
No one escapes their evil deeds, even later when gathered with the gods,
at the sacred fords originating from the Revā on both its banks.
Worshipping Mahādeva, he approached Skanda-tīrtha;
staying there, he performed fasts such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
Indeed, emaciating his own body, he found no peace anywhere;
in the summer he stood in the midst of five fires, and in the rainy season he slept upon the bare ground.
In the winter, however, he performed extensive austerities while wearing wet clothes;
thus did Indra, the knower of the self, practice penance.
Ten thousand years passed, O Bhārata;
then, O best of kings, when the eleventh year had arrived, [the gods spoke].
Suddenly the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, was gratified;
likewise were the celestial rishis and the Siddhas, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
There all the gods went to where the god Śatakratu was;
seeing that the gods and the sages had assembled, the high-minded one [spoke].
Having bowed down, the priest of all the gods said:
"Everything is known to these [gods] as to how the slaying of Vṛtra was accomplished."
And previously, by your command, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśvara likewise regarded this slayer of a Brahmin as a perpetrator of sin.
Brahmahatyā does not release him as he wanders among all sacred fords; the entire world, the three realms with all things moving and unmoving, finds no joy.
Just as [the world] is without a moon or sun, so is a kingdom without a leader;
therefore, O best of gods, I now have a request to make to you all.
Having heard those auspicious words uttered from the mouth of Bṛhaspati, let all the great ṛṣis likewise render Śakra free from fault.
Then the Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke:
"This sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin is most terrible."
"Then, I cast a fourth part to the deities and to the spirits";
having spoken thus, the high-minded one should cast the sin upon the water.
Then, having immersed himself, water indeed became drinkable and not otherwise;
the Lotus-born One cast the second portion upon the earth.
Because of that, O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the second day, half of the women on earth became forever unfit to be eaten.
Having set her down, the Blessed Lord spoke again:
"She is indeed ungraspable, ungraspable; therefore she has become menstruating."
The Supreme Lord divided that great sin into four parts and assigned them to the wise for four days.
Having thus apportioned the fourth part from it, the Supreme Lord [proceeded].
When the twice-born [Kṣatriya] engaged in agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, and service to Śūdras,
all the gods and great ṛṣis then expressed their disapproval.
With pleasing words, he invited the Lord of the Gods, who was situated in the waters of the Narmadā, to choose a boon; thereupon Maheśvara was gratified.
"I shall grant you a boon, O Lord of Gods; choose a boon according to your desire."
Indra said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, I shall establish [you] here; remain ever present."
Having said to him, "So be it," Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara entered the sky and departed while being praised by the great ṛṣis.
When the gods of gods had departed, Śatakratu, the king of the gods,
established Mahādeva and went to the abode of the thirty [gods].
But he who, having bathed at Indratīrtha, offers libations to the ancestors and the gods,
is liberated from all sins— even if he is burdened with the most grievous crimes.
But he who, having bathed at Indratīrtha, worships the Supreme Lord,
enjoys the abundant fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Thus has all this supreme majesty of the sacred fords been told to you;
by merely hearing it, men are liberated from their sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Indratīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 119.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Kahloḍī-tīrtha.
On the northern bank of the Revā, it is the destroyer of all sins.
For the benefit of all beings, it was established of old by the sages;
having extracted it through ascetic power from the great waters of the Narmadā.
Listen now to the fruit obtained by one who bathes at the Kapilā-tīrtha, bestows a tawny cow, and hears this divine narrative, O Brāhmaṇas.
Of all gifts, the gift of a Kapila cow is the most excellent;
it was sought by the Brahmins in former times during the assembly of sages and gods.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who, fasting and having conquered anger, gives away a beautiful, tawny cow that has recently calved.
O mighty-armed one, by him the earth—with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves—has indeed been given; there is no doubt about this.
O King, verbal and mental sins, as well as those committed through physical action accumulated over seven lifetimes, are destroyed by giving a tawny cow (kapilā).
Gifts of land, wealth, grain, elephants, horses, gold,
and the like do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single gift of a Kapila cow.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, the man who bestows a tawny cow goes to the city of Viṣṇu upon death, being sung of by throngs of apsarases.
O Bhārata, for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on that cow along with her calf, he shall sport for a long time in heaven.
Then, having passed through the state of being scattered [in various realms], one attains human birth here; endowed with wealth and grain, one is born into a vast family.
One who has completed the vows of Vedic learning, is proficient in all the scriptures,
and is liberated from disease and sorrow, shall live for a hundred autumns.
Thus has been fully described to you this supreme Kalhoḍī-tīrtha;
by performing [the rites] here, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kahloḍī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 120.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme Kambukeśvara.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was a Dānava arrogant in his strength.
Invincible to all the worlds and renowned throughout the three realms,
he had a son of great splendor named Prahlāda by name.
By the grace of Viṣṇu and through his devotion, he was established in the kingdom;
Virocana was his son, and Bali was his son as well.
Bali’s son was Bāṇa, and from him came Śambara;
in the lineage of Śambara was born the great asura named Kambu.
Having realized that a terrible and great danger consisting of Viṣṇu had arrived,
there was never any other cause for the destruction of the Dānavas.
Having renounced his sons, wife, friends, kinsmen, and possessions,
the high-minded Kambu practiced austerities while observing a vow of silence.
Having become one who holds a rosary, carrying a staff, shaven-headed, and wearing a girdle;
subsisting on vegetables and barley-gruel, and clothed in bark and deerskin.
Having bathed daily and being devoted to steadfastness, he resorted to the waters of the Narmadā and worshipped Mahādeva for a period numbering one hundred million years.
Then the Blessed One, Maheśvara, the God of gods, was pleased;
at that time, he spoke to the Dānava with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"O Kambo, O highly fortunate one, I am pleased with you, O observer of excellent vows!
Among all vows, silence is the most desired and the supreme means for accomplishing every goal."
And you have performed deeds in the world difficult even for gods and dānavas to accomplish;
choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever is pleasing to your mind.
Kambu said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
may I move about according to my own will, remaining inexhaustible and immutable."
Among the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, she never fled in battles;
nor would any other fear exist, were it not for the Lord who wields the mace.
O Śaṅkara, tell me that boon, which is my constant desire: by what means may I be conquered by him in battle? RKV_120.14
Īśvara said:
"O Dānava, wherever you shall be in my presence, there is no fear of Viṣṇu; dwell here, free from anxiety."
In battle, neither I nor all the gods and asuras are a match for that God of Gods, the one who contains the Vedas within himself and bears the conch and the discus.
How much less so for one who hates Hari, the Lord of the world and the non-world; in my opinion, such a person does not remain happy for even a moment.
"Therefore, devoted with supreme devotion and intent on the welfare of all beings, you shall dwell for a long time"; having said this, he vanished from sight.
When the Lord had departed from sight at that sacred ford, the high-minded one installed there Śiva, the Lord of Gods, who is peaceful and free from ailment.
Having established Mahādeva at that sacred ford (tīrtha), he ascended to heaven;
from that time forth, O Pārtha, it has been known as Kambu-tīrtha,
renowned throughout all the worlds as the destroyer of great sins.
O best of kings, having bathed at Kambu-tīrtha according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped the Sun-god, a man is praised with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The merit of that [act] has been declared by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
listen now, O King, as I recount all of it to you.
Whatever fruit is found in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs,
one who knows even only the Gāyatrī mantra obtains that same fruit.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods,
and worships the Lord Īśāna, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, whoever casts off their body at that sacred ford goes to the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kambukeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 121.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to Candrahāsa.
Where Somarāja, the best of gods, attained supreme perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How did Somanātha, the Lord of the World, attain supreme perfection?
O sinless one, I wish to hear all of that; please tell it to me."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O descendant of Bharata, it is said that in ancient times Dakṣa, the lord of sages, cursed him [Śiva], saying:
"Because you do not attend to your wife, you shall become afflicted with the disease of consumption."
O lord of men, listen to the fate that befalls those men who do not attend to their wedded wives. (RKV 121.4)
"For by serving women during their fertile seasons, a son is born;
from a son come both heaven and liberation—thus has it been declared in the Śruti. (RKV 121.5)
Enveloped by the dharma appropriate to that time, he shall fall into the Raurava hell;
there, that sinner drinks her blood for as long as he desires.
Then, having descended in due course, whichever womb he enters,
in each and every one that wicked-souled one is always born unfortunate.
In women, desire always increases excessively;
especially during the time of their menses, they are tormented by the arrows of love.
Women who are treated with contempt by their husbands and think of another man as their lord give birth to a son who wanders through the most excellent families.
By him, his fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors dwelling in heaven fall as soon as he is born; therefore, he is called a *kulaṭa*.
By the ripening of that karma, the moon, who was afflicted by consumption,
left the world of the lords of the gods and came to the world of mortals.
Then, wandering through many sacred fords and holy shrines, he reached the Narmadā, which destroys all sins.
For twelve years he practiced fasting, acts of charity, vows, and restraints; consequently, he was liberated from his sins.
Having bathed Mahādeva, the destroyer of all sins,
he departed, filled with radiance, to that unsurpassed world.
For as many years as the deity has been installed,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Rudra.
Therefore, men on earth establish the gods according to the prescribed rules,
because human beings enjoy time that is inexhaustible and undecaying.
Having bathed at Somatīrtha, a man should worship the Lord Īśvara;
that man shines in the world, as pleasing to behold as the moon.
But he who goes to Candrahāsa during an eclipse of the moon or sun and performs his ablutions with devotion is liberated from all sins.
O best of excellent kings, whatever bathing, giving, or [actions]— whether auspicious or inauspicious— are performed there at Candrahāsa, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones; their birth is a life well-lived—those men who, having bathed in the Candrahāsa, witness an eclipse.
O King of kings, whatever verbal or mental sin was previously committed through action perishes by merely bathing at that sacred ford.
Many, possessed by great delusion, do not know him who resides within the body of all as the very form of supreme bliss.
Whatever fruit is obtained by going to Somatīrtha in the western ocean, one obtains all of that at Candrahāsa; of this there is no doubt.
At the transit of the sun, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, and likewise at the equinoxes,
as well as at Candrahāsa, a man who bathes is liberated from all sins.
They are deluded, they are of wicked conduct, and their birth is in vain—
those who do not know Candrahāsa situated upon the Revā.
O twice-born one, whatever person performs renunciation at Candrahāsa, his destination is the world of Soma from which there is no return; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Somatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 122.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the place renowned as Kohanasva.
This sacred ford removes all sins, is meritorious, and destroys death.
Long ago, a certain twice-born man there, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
lived devoted to his own duties along with his wife, sons, and circle of friends.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me all of that— the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as the origins of the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
I wish to know the entire supreme method regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; in my opinion, there is no other knower [of this].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Brahmā is proclaimed as the cause of origin, the God of gods,
the first of all beings, and the teacher of the world of moving and unmoving things.
The twice-born were born from the mouth; the Kṣatriyas from the mechanism of the arms;
the Vaiśyas from the region of the thighs; and the Śūdras then arose from the feet.
Then others, belonging to distinct castes, practiced their respective duties;
for they were born in succession, both in the natural and the inverse order.
I shall proclaim their dharma, as enjoined by the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti,
by the proper performance of which all indeed attain the supreme goal.

O King, that goal which is attained by devotees through meditation is attained by Brahmins even without meditation, provided they teach the Vedas or even a single Veda according to the prescribed rule. (RKV 122.9)
Then, with the permission of his preceptor, he should marry a wife who is of noble birth, endowed with beauty, and marked by all the auspicious characteristics.

Then, having become one who has acquired wealth through lawful acceptance of gifts and being free from hypocrisy and greed, he should worship the domestic fire (smārta) or the sacred fire (śrauta) in due order.
One should indeed cause the five great sacrifices to be performed according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, one should go to the forest for the service of the second stage of life.
Having entrusted his wife to his sons and being free from all attachments,
he attains the desired worlds and is not born again in this world.
But a Kṣatriya, established in his kingdom and having protected the earth, with his mind ever fixed on dharma, attains the supreme goal.
There is no doubt that the duty of a Vaiśya consists in devotion to agriculture and cattle-rearing;
endowed with truthfulness and purity, he goes to the highest heaven.
No separate dharma was ordained for the Śūdra by the Supreme Lord;
he has no mantra, no sacramental rite, and no study of sacred knowledge.
Neither the study of grammar nor the rituals for worshipping deities [are required];
rather, one must constantly conduct oneself day and night in the manner of one who has been born [into the spiritual lineage].
That Dharma was created of old for all social classes by the Self-Existent One;
the three classes endowed with the consecration of mantras are the twice-born.
If, disregarding their counsel, he should act according to his own desires, he will indeed be born as a dog after death; no higher destiny exists for him.
One who constantly remembers their intention and does not send them away partakes in fame; established in his own duty, he becomes a partaker of heaven.

Thus, O Bhārata, that brahmin, though filled with a multitude of virtues, dwelt there while hearing such words as, "Kill him! Then he looked upward, downward, and toward the ten directions;
trembling and terrified, he stumbled at every step.
He sees a man mounted upon a buffalo, his face like mine, encircled by hands holding chains as weapons and most dreadful nooses.
Resembling a mass of black collyrium, adorned with black garments,
with red eyes and long arms, he was endowed with all the auspicious marks.
But seeing him approaching and observing himself by means of his own self,
he was reciting the supreme prayer of praise known as the Śatarudrīya.
Then the blessed Yama, the great restrainer, spoke:
"Listen to these words, O Brahmin; I am Yama among all living beings."
"O illustrious one, withdraw this recitation of the Rudra-hymn, which is so difficult to pierce,
by means of which I, free from affliction, shall bind you with the nooses of Time."
Having heard those harsh words issuing from the mouth of Yama,
the brahmin, seized by great terror, fled away.
All the servants of Yama followed him on the path;
shouting "Stop! Stop!", they addressed that brahmin, and he too ran forward.
Hurrying along, utterly exhausted, I cry out: "Alas! I am destroyed by these evil-minded ones! Protect me, protect me, O Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!"
Having spoken thus, O descendant of Bharata, that best of Brahmins, having embraced the *liṅga* and taken refuge in the Lord of the Gods, fell to the ground, deprived of life.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, Maheśvara, the God of gods, then uttered the sound "Huṃ" and said, "Who shall kill you? Do not fear!"
O Bhārata, by that roar of "huṃ," all those servants of his, together with Yama, were scattered like clouds driven by the wind.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became renowned as Kohanasva;
it removes all sins, is meritorious, and is unsurpassed among all sacred fords.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the Supreme Lord obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
"O Indra among kings, he who gives up his life at that sacred ford does not see the god Yama; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
O best of kings, he who enters the fire or [dies] in water shall dwell in the world of Agni for as long as three hundred kalpas.
Having thus dwelt in the world of Varuṇa for his desired length of time,
he will return to this world and become a lord of great wealth.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kohana Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 123.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Karmadītīrtha.
Wherein dwells Vighneśa, the Lord of Gaṇas, possessed of great power.
O Bhārata, having bathed at that sacred ford on the fourth lunar day or having fasted there, no obstacle shall exist for that person throughout seven births.
O best of kings, whatever is given at that sacred ford indeed yields entirely inexhaustible fruit; there is no doubt about this.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Karmadeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the supreme Narmadeśvara;
having bathed at that sacred site, a person is liberated from all sins.
Whether by entering fire, or by death in water, or by fasting unto death, his destination is from which there is no return; so Śaṅkara has told me.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Narmadeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 125.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Ravitīrtha.
Where the thousand-rayed god, having performed austerities, ascended to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How does the Lord of gods, the creator of the world, honored by all the deities, the Sun, the maker of light, perform ascetic penance as an ascetic?
Worthy of being propitiated by all beings and worshipped by all the gods,
he is seen visibly in the world as the agent of creation and destruction.
O sinless one, tell me all this in brief: how was the state of being Āditya attained, and why is he called Bhāskara?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O great king, regarding this great question which you have asked,
I shall explain it all to you after having paid homage to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
This was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without defining marks, beyond the reach of logic, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Then, for the sake of creation, a supreme and divine mass of heated energy fell from the sky like a meteor with its head downward.
From that radiance, the Person was born, adorned with all [attributes];
he is Śiva, without hands or feet, by whom all this is pervaded.
O Bhārata, after that light-form had arisen,
Prajāpati again became Time (Kāla) over the course of time.
Agni was born as the lord of all beings— humans, asuras, and rakshasas—
and because he is the supreme deity among all gods, he is called Āditya.
First, salutation is offered to him, and immediately thereafter to others,
by all the deities and by all the great seers.
The three twilights and the three gods are present within the solar disc;
by bowing to the Sun, all the gods are bowed to.
Without the sun, O King, there would be neither day nor night, nor the six-month period of the southern course, nor even the northern course.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities do not proceed without the sun; therefore, Ravi is most worthy of worship.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are primarily accessible through the sacred word;
yet the Lord, the God who purifies the world, is perceived directly before one's eyes.
The Lord of the World is the sole cause—the source of origination, the place of dissolution, the repository, and the imperishable seed; no other than the Sun-god exists.
Having thus created the self-existence of the world, both stationary and moving,
he should establish the path of Dharma for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Having taken recourse to the bank of the Narmadā and established his own body there, he,
the thousand-rayed one, the treasure of splendors, departed for the imperishable sky.
Having bathed at that sacred site, whoever worships the Supreme Lord,
the thousand-rayed deity, according to the ritual procedure for the name-mantra;
By him [the fire] was kindled, by him the oblation was offered, and by him everything was performed;
through that correct ritual procedure, the supreme state was attained.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones; their birth is a life well-lived, who, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, behold the Sun-god.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, those who constantly perform circumambulation of the Lord with undivided devotion, endowed with the three syllables, [attain the highest state].
Their bodies purified by that mantra, they were freed from their sins;
listen now with a single-minded focus to whatever merit they may have acquired.
By him, the entire earth—with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves—has been circumambulated; of this there is no doubt.
This entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has the mantra as its root;
therefore, no task devoid of mantra succeeds in this world.
Just as a wooden elephant or a leather deer cannot fulfill its intended purpose, so too an action performed without mantras will not achieve its goal.
O Pārtha, just as an oblation poured into ashes is devoid of water,
so too a gift given without mantras becomes fruitless.
In this world, people perform worship with mantras upon pieces of wood, stone, clods of earth, and especially those made of clay, but certainly not without mantras.
Whatever fruit one obtains through twelve years of devoted prostrations,
one obtains that same fruit by performing a single prostration accompanied by the mantra.
And at the transit of the sun, during Vyatīpāta, at the solstices, and likewise at the equinoxes, whoever bathes in the waters of the Narmadā and worships the Sun;
Whatever sin has been accumulated over twelve years, whether through ignorance or knowledge,
all of it is destroyed in an instant, just as chaff is consumed by fire.
Having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, fasting and with senses subdued,
one who beholds the face of the Sun there is liberated from all sins.
O best of kings, when the month of Māgha has arrived, on the seventh day,
having fasted and subdued his anger, he should dwell in the temple of the Sun.
Having bathed at dawn according to the prescribed rule, he who offers the arghya water to the Sun with the ritual accompanied by mantras shall obtain the highest merit.
Having performed the water libation for the ancestors, gods, and humans,
one should then perform worship in the temple of the God of Gods.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World with perfumes, flowers, incense, and beautiful lamps and food offerings, one should then recite the mantra.
Viṣṇu, Śakra, Yama, Dhātṛ, Mitra, and likewise Varuṇa;
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Caṇḍāṃśu, and Bharga as well.
O Pārtha, listen now with a focused mind to the fruit that one obtains by performing a circumambulation while reciting these twelve names.
"One shall not be poor, diseased, mute, deaf, or even dull-witted for seven births; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
Knowing this, the wise person who desires supreme merit should worship the Sun with devotion, reciting the mantra according to the prescribed rite.
But he who, O Bhārata, should practice devotion to the God while devoid of mantra,
he mocks himself like a beast, an insect, or a winged insect.
Whoever casts off their excellent body at that sacred ford goes there, being honored by the gods and the great seers.
By his own will, he shall become a king in this world for a very long time.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, surrounded by elephants, horses, and chariots,
and possessed of hundreds of male and female servants, he is born into a vast family.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ravitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 126.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme holy site called Ayonija.
A man who has merely bathed there shall not behold the confinement of the womb again.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a man should worship the Lord Īśvara, saying:
"O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, just as you are not born from a womb."
"O Lord, likewise deliver me from the peril of birth;
by means of perfumes, flowers, and incense, he shall be liberated from all sins. (RKV 126.3)
Whoever fills the linga of that god with devotion shall dwell in the abode of the God of gods for as many years as there are grains of rice in the filling.
One should bathe Mahādeva, who is not born from a womb, with fragrant water, honey and milk, or curd; such a person shall obtain abundant prosperity.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
having worshipped Mahādeva, one should please him with songs and instrumental music.
And those who perform this which is so enchanting shall dwell in the auspicious world;
they reside in the auspicious world until the dissolution of all beings.
O Bhārata, he who performs circumambulation of that deity with devotion, while constantly making this petition with the following mantra: [RKV 126.8]
Listen with concentration to that fruit which has been declared for men through the lineage of the God of gods.
O Great God, O Supreme Lord, just as you are not born from a womb,
so likewise, O Śarva, deliver me from the peril of birth from a womb.
What is the use of many mantras for him who is intent on parching his throat,
if he has uttered "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" in the presence of the Lord?
By him everything has been studied, by him everything has been heard, and by him everything has been performed,
who has made firm the practice of the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
A twice-born man does not obtain that fruit among all the gods which he obtains from the utterance of the six-syllabled mantra.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships a Śiva-yogin shall obtain the supreme fruit equal to that of ten thousand brahmins.
Alternatively, if one gives alms with devotion to those who are self-controlled and have conquered their senses after having purified them, the fruit of that action is even greater than the former.
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic after giving alms, and water again;
that alms is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is like the ocean.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ayoniprabhava Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 127.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Agnitīrtha.
Having bathed there at the beginning of a lunar fortnight, one is liberated from all sins.
O best of men, listen now to the fruit that is declared for him who gives away a daughter, adorned herself, at that sacred ford.
By giving away a decorated [cow] according to one's ability, a person obtains a hundredfold increase for each hundred times the merit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Whatever number of hairs there may be on her sons and grandsons,
by that same measure he attains the supreme goal in the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Agnitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 128.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Bhṛkuṭeśvara.
Where the highly fortunate Bhṛgu, who was exceedingly prone to anger, attained perfection.
O sinless one, in former times he practiced ascetic penance for more than a hundred years;
that best among those who possess sons chose a son for the sake of obtaining a son.
O highly fortunate one, a boon was granted there by the god who slew Andhaka:
"Whoever bathes in that sacred ford and worships the Supreme Lord," RKV 128.3.
Whoever [worships] Bhṛkuṭeśa with ghee together with honey shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One who desires a son should bathe there with devotion; he shall obtain the desired son.
Furthermore, whoever bathes at that sacred ford and gives gold to a Brahmin, [shall attain his goal].
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who gives a gift of cows or even the earth.
O best of kings, by him the entire earth—with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves—has been given; of this there is no doubt. (RKV 128.7)
Having sported at ease in heaven by virtue of that gift,
he becomes a lord of kings on earth or a highly honored brahmin.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhṛkuṭeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 129.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha.
And it is the great one, far superior even to all other sacred fords.
At that sacred ford, Brahmā, the best of gods and grandfather of the worlds,
took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā for the sake of all four castes.
Whatever verbal or mental sin was previously committed through action,
the Lord of Gods washes away that very transgression by his mere sight alone.
Having bathed there, the best of the twice-born perform those very penances prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; their residence shall be in Triviṣṭapa.
Furthermore, those who, having abandoned the scripture and being tormented by desire and greed,
shall prescribe expiations— they indeed go to hell.
O Brahmin, having first bathed and bowed down, a sinner should confess his transgression;
that [sin] of his perishes quickly, just as darkness [vanishes] at the rising of the sun.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the ancestors and the gods shall obtain the supreme fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whatever gift one bestows at that sacred ford, dedicating it to Brahmā, all of that yields inexhaustible fruit; thus spoke Śaṅkara.
Even if only the essence of the Gāyatrī is recited there as a mantra, it becomes equivalent to the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas combined; of this there is no doubt.
If one should, with devotion, cast off this body so difficult to abandon at that sacred ford (tīrtha), his destination is the world of Brahmā from which there is no return; of this there is no doubt.
As long as the bones of embodied beings remain at the Brahma-tīrtha,
for that many thousands of years they are honored in the world of the gods.
Having thus descended into the world, he is born into a family that knows Brahman;
he is the most excellent among all castes, like a deity among the gods.
He who has mastered the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas knows all branches of knowledge;
he is born honored in the world by kings, of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and freed from all diseases,
one shall live for more than a hundred years through the power of Brahmatīrtha.
Those high-souled ones who behold this meritorious and sin-destroying sacred site, the best among those possessing knowledge, indeed attain immortality.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the unsurpassed Devatīrtha;
there the Supreme Lord was propitiated by the gods who had assembled together.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford, free from desire and anger, shall certainly obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Devatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 131.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the unsurpassed Nāgatīrtha.
O King, when danger arose from that place where the great *nāgas* had attained their powers, they departed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, how did that intense fear arise for the world and for the serpents, who are so greatly afraid, by which they were made to stand firm in asceticism?
"Whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be among gods, asuras, and humans—all that is known to you, my dear; therefore, my curiosity is great."
The sorrow born of my anguish, arising from Duryodhana,
has been washed away by the flood from your lotus-like mouth and has reached a state of peace.
O observer of noble vows, having heard this sin-destroying story uttered from your mouth,
my desire to hear it has arisen again and again.
O twice-born one, it is not fitting that there should be affliction; nor does anyone else perceive the fruit of this great gift of knowledge, which has been proclaimed, and of the son.
Having understood this according to the proper method, O Brahmin, please show compassion toward me and tell the story regarding the question that was asked by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, the more you speak, the more my speech finds ease;
for although I am overcome by old age and physical frailty, my affection for you, dear one, does not diminish at all.
O Bhārata, I shall relate this ancient history exactly as it occurred, as it was told of old by the elders through oral tradition.
Kaśyapa had two wives, unsurpassed in all the worlds: Vinatā, who was the mother of Garuḍa, and Kadrū, the mother of the serpents.
O Indra among kings, due to the sight of the horse, Kali took form before those two at the time of dawn, possessing a splendor like that of the sun.
Seeing that horse entirely white in form, Vinatā then said to Kadrū: "Look, look, O fair-faced one!"
Behold everywhere the resemblance to Uccaiḥśravas, all white,
running without rest with a speed like that of the wind.
Seeing him departing so suddenly, she was deluded by a sense of jealousy;
thinking it was Kṛṣṇa, O best of kings, she spoke thus to her.
"O Vinatā, you are a liar in this world, cruel and a disgrace to your lineage!
And tell him that Kṛṣṇa is white; otherwise, you shall go to the highest hell."
Vinatā said:
"This wager between you and me concerns truthful and false speech:
for a thousand years, I shall become your slave in your house."
Saying "So be it," they both went to their own homes that night and, overcome with rage, abandoned [their children].
Having gone to Bandhugarva, Kadrū related that wager which had occurred with Vinatā in the pleasure-house.
Having heard that, all the kinsmen and likewise the sons of Kadrū did not consider the beneficial task accomplished by their mother to be anything censurable.
"O Mother, how could this best of horses, who is not black, become black?
For you, O lady of noble vows, will indeed fall into slavery by virtue of this wager."
Kadrū said:
"Act quickly so that I shall not be a slave;
it is my intention that you enter into the pores of that horse's skin."
If this task is performed for even a moment, that female servant shall become mine;
thereafter, all you serpents will be restored to health and live as you please.
The serpents said:
"O Goddess, although you are considered on earth to be the mother of the snakes,
nevertheless, she must never, under any circumstances, be deceived."
Kadrū said:
"Whatever serpents on earth do not carry out my command,
they shall all, without hesitation, go into the mouth of the fire."
Having heard these terrible words issuing from the mouths of their mothers,
some entered into the pores of their skin, while others remained within the mountains.
Some have entered the Ganges, while others remain established in austerity.
