Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, the sustainer of the world, was pleased and spoke with a supreme voice: RKV 131.27: "Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, the sustainer of the world, was pleased and spoke with a supreme voice."
"O serpents, desist! This asceticism yields great fruit.
Whatever you desire, I shall grant it today; there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
The serpents said:
"O God of gods, Maheśvara, terrified by the fear of Kadrū’s curse,
we shall dwell at your side until the dissolution of all beings."
The God of gods said:
"This one, the mighty-armed Vāsuki, the best of serpents,
shall dwell constantly by my side as the protector from fear for all."
"And by my command, there shall be no fear for other serpents as well;
having plunged into the waters of the Narmadā, those snakes are protected."
There is no fear of death for you; dwell wherever you desire.
There is no fear of Kadrū’s curse; this is my further promise in detail.
Having thus granted them this boon, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
entered the sky and departed for Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth.
O King, when the god had departed from sight, those led by Vāsuki,
having thus installed Maheśvara, the God of gods, departed.
Whoever worships Śiva at that sacred site on the fifth lunar day,
the eight families of nāgas shall never harm them.
O lord of men, having died at that sacred ford after a long time,
one becomes an attendant of Śiva and dwells there for as long as he desires.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nāgeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 132.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the northern bank of the Narmadā.
The sacred ford named Vārāha is known by that name as the remover of all sins.
There the Lord, the sustainer of the world, having assumed the form of a boar,
stands for the sake of the welfare of the world, as the one who carries beings across the ocean of saṃsāra.

Having bathed at that sacred ford, whoever should worship the Uplifter of the Earth with special perfumes and garlands, and with auspicious sounds such as the cry of "Victory! (jaya), [attains the highest goal].
O best of kings, having become intent on fasting on the twelfth day,
even those of low birth who perform evil deeds, as well as the blind and the Piśācas, [are purified].
Since evil is transmitted through conversation, physical contact, breathing, and eating together, one should therefore avoid such people.
One should worship the Brahmins with devotion, according to one's ability and according to the prescribed rules;
O Bhārata, a vigil should be kept at night there with the recitation of sacred stories.
Those who, having conquered anger, bathe at that sacred ford in the clear dawn and behold the Teacher of the World, are liberated from all sins.
Just as serpents, upon seeing Suparṇa, quickly perish after discharging their poison of fierce power,
even so do all evils perish swiftly upon seeing the face of him who bears the form of a boar.
Just as darkness in the sky perishes upon seeing the sun, the best of gods, even so,
O Pārtha, sins that are otherwise most difficult to overcome perish upon beholding the face of the Mountain-King.
What need has he for many mantras, who possesses devotion to Janārdana?
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" alone accomplishes all goals.
Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices;
one who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but he who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return to existence.
Those great-souled ones who have conquered their senses, meditating upon the form of Nārāyaṇa, the Hari, abandon their own bodies at that sacred ford.
They go to that stainless state, which is difficult even for the gods to attain—
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is liberated from both the perishable and the imperishable.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ādivārāha Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 133.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the supreme group of four holy fords (tīrthas).
By the mere sight of whom all evil is destroyed.
Then there are the regions of Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, and Vāyu,
where the highly wise and mighty world-protectors have attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O sinless one, for what purpose did the world-protectors perform penance in ancient times by resorting to the banks of the Narmadā? You ought to tell this to me.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Indeed, when all beings find the world unstable— like a drop of water on a blade of grass— they seek a firm foundation within this cycle of existence.
In all four classes of living beings, both stationary and moving, which are as essence-less as the core of a plantain tree and as flickering as a mirage, [there is no self].
Dharma is mother, Dharma is father; Dharma is kinsman and likewise friend;
Dharma is the support of all beings in the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile.
Having understood this, all those world-protectors, having found the opportunity, performed incomparable austerity, intent on subsisting only on air.
Then, O Indra among kings, when half of what had been done had passed, Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord, was pleased in accordance with the nature of that age.
He invited the world-protectors of great power to choose a boon, saying:
"Whatever desire each of you wishes for, I shall grant it to him."
Having heard these words of his, the world-protectors, who act for the welfare of the world, requested an unsurpassed boon from the God, the giver of boons.
Kubera said:
"O Mahādeva, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
let me become the lord of the Yakṣas and the giver of wealth."
Then Yama, who is devoted to self-restraint, spoke to the Lord of the Gods:
"May I become the foremost among all living beings there."
Immediately thereafter, Varuṇa, having bowed to Maheśvara, said:
"May I sport in the world of Varuṇa, accompanied by hosts of aquatic creatures."
Then, O Bhārata, Vāyu, having bowed to Maheśvara, quickly spoke and requested pervasiveness throughout the three worlds.
Having granted all those world-protectors whatever they desired, Śaṅkara vanished along with Umā.
When the god Maheśvara had departed, they remained each in their respective places;
and a consecration was performed by all of them, each individually under their own name.
Kubera [worshipped] Kubereśa, Yama [worshipped] Yameśvara,
Varuṇa [worshipped] Varuṇeśa, and Vāta, O King, [worshipped] Vāteśvara.
Having all worshipped the Lord of All according to the prescribed rites, they all performed the libation with various auspicious mantras.
All those lords of all, like the lords of all the worlds, summoned those brahmins who were patient, self-controlled, conquerors of anger, and bestowers of fearlessness upon all beings.
Those who have performed their ablutions after completing the vows of Vedic study, who are experts in all the scriptures,
and who are endowed with the Rig, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as well as adorned by the Atharva Veda.
"We shall give a fourfold gift to all of you; please accept it.
Having spoken thus, he gave the supreme gift to all the brahmins.
In that place, they bestowed upon them the unsurpassed gift of land,
for as long as the moon and the sun endure, and for as long as the earth remains.
For as long as you give, no obstacle whatsoever shall exist for you— not even a king or one equal to a king, nor the world-protectors— regarding this unsurpassed [gift].
The fool who nullifies what has been given—listen now to the rule regarding him:
O Bhārata, the Giver of Wealth shall dry up the riches of that sinner.
The god Varuṇa takes away the body, and Śvasana likewise the lineage;
Yama, the great restrainer, swiftly carries away his life-span.
Having reduced everything to ashes without exception, O Bhārata, the fire-god departs;
therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, with every effort, devotion to the Brāhmaṇas must be practiced by all kings who desire their own welfare.
The king is the tree; the brahmins are its root, the servants are its leaves, and the ministers are its branches.
Therefore, the root must be protected with great effort; when the root is guarded, there is no destruction of the tree.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years;
the one who seizes it and the one who treats it with contempt shall dwell in hell for those same years.
Whether given by oneself or given by another, the earth must be protected;
for whoever possesses the land at any time, to him belongs the fruit thereof.
O King, those rulers who, recollecting the command of the deity,
shall constantly protect it, their residence shall be in Triviṣṭapa.
Whether given by oneself or by another, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the earth must be protected with effort by a ruler; for a king, the preservation of what has been given is always superior to the act of giving.
O King, longevity, fame, strength, wealth, and imperishable progeny will surely belong to those who are devoted to the protection of their subjects.
Having spoken thus to all those world-protectors, O best of the twice-born,
he honored them according to the prescribed rite, prostrated before them, and dismissed them.
When the foremost brahmins had departed, the world-protectors, having bathed and offered oblations into the fire,
wandered about seeking alms for themselves, overcome by hunger.
With their limbs reduced to mere skin and bone, holding skull-bowls in their hands,
and having failed to obtain even half a morsel of food, they went out from the city.
Having then pronounced a curse upon the Brahmin out of anger, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
they departed for their homes, saying, "May they always be poor and foolish."
From that time forward, all those brahmins, deprived of wealth by the fault of the curse, became vessels of suffering in the northern region.
"Neither sons enjoy the paternal wealth in its entirety for all time, nor does a father [enjoy] that which belongs to his sons and grandsons; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
That man who, having bathed at Kubereśa,
worships Śiva with perfumes, incense, and prostrations, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
But he who, having bathed at Yamatīrtha, beholds Yameśvara,
shall be liberated from all sins accumulated over the course of seven births.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, having bathed on the full moon or the new moon day, performs the libation for the ancestors and bathes with sesame seeds.
By that water, the fathers and grandfathers are well-satisfied,
and the great-grandfathers dwelling in heaven sport for twelve years.
Having bathed at Varuṇeśa and having worshipped Maheśvara,
a man obtains the abundant fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
When he dies after a long time, he shall go by means of a celestial vehicle to that world where the Lord of Waters resides, while being sung of by hosts of apsarases.
Having bathed at Vāteśvara and worshipped Maheśvara,
that man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, beholding the guardians of the world.
What need has he for many sacrifices or for gifts accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees?
Having bathed in the four sacred sites of the world, he has attained the fruit of his birth.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones; their birth is a life well-lived, for they dwell eternally in Kaurilyā, having invited the guardians of the world.
This merit is destructive of sin, auspicious, and increases longevity;
for those who read it or even hear it, there shall be the destruction of all evil.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Four Tīrthas Beginning with Kubera," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 134.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the unsurpassed Rāmeśvara.
This sacred ford removes sin, is meritorious, and is the supreme destroyer of all suffering.
Those who, having bathed at that sacred ford, worship Maheśvara,
the great-souled Mahādeva, are liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rāmeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 135.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately following that is another unsurpassed site, Siddheśvara.
This sacred ford is endowed with all virtues and is honored throughout all the worlds.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships Umā-Rudra shall obtain the supreme fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
By that great merit, upon death, he shall attain heaven, surrounded by hosts of apsarases and accompanied by auspicious sounds such as cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Having sported there at his pleasure for a thousand years,
he is born into a great family endowed with wealth and grain.
O best of men, one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, being thus honored,
shall live for a hundred autumns, freed from disease and sorrow.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 136.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the excellent Cāhalyeśvara.
Where in former times the highly fortunate ascetic Ahalyā attained perfection.
There was a Brahmin named Gautama, who was like another Brahmā in person;
he was endowed with truth and righteousness and devoted to the stage of life of a forest-dweller.
His wife was the highly fortunate one named Ahalyā,
renowned throughout the three worlds for her perfection of beauty and youth.
Even Śatakratu, the king of the gods and slayer of Bala, was deluded by her extraordinary beauty and lusted after Ahalyā.
"Devote yourself to me, O lady of excellent hips, O blameless one;
sport with me, honored throughout the three worlds."
"What will you do with this brahmin, O fair-eyed one, who is emaciated by his purity and conduct, and devoted to austerity and sacred study, as if he were merely suffering? (RKV 136.6)
Thus addressed, that woman of noble form, fickle by the very nature of women,
meditated upon Śakra in her mind, being defiled by passion.
Having understood her state of mind, that god Pākaśāsana,
influenced by a wicked intent, deceived Gautama.
Having discerned his absence and assumed his excellent attire,
he took pleasure with Ahalyā while she was unsuspecting in the vicinity of the palace.
O Bhārata, within a mere moment, the best of sages arrived at the palace of the king of the gods with great haste.
Seeing that Gautama had arrived, Purandara was struck with great fear;
thinking, "This must be Śakra," he departed from there.
Then Gautama, overcome with anger, cursed the Lord of the Gods:
"Since you have not conquered your senses, therefore become one who possesses many wives! (RKV 136.12)
O Bhārata, having been addressed thus, the lord of the gods was instantly enveloped at that very moment by a thousand vulvae.
Having abandoned his kingdom, he went away with the gods, his royal splendor departed;
on the surface of the earth, he performed extensive austerities under Gautama.
Ahalyā, too, was then cursed: "Since you, a woman of wicked conduct, took pleasure with Śakra upon seeing me, therefore become made of stone!"
When a thousand years have passed, having seen the illustrious Rāma on the occasion of his pilgrimage to sacred fords, you shall be cleansed of all sin.
When time had passed in this manner, she was seen by the wise Rāma,
who was accompanied by Viśvāmitra, after she had cast off her stony body.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, their sins gone and free from envy,
they arrived at the bank of the Narmadā and bathed in the sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the ritual injunctions.
He performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a month and another Kṛcchra thereafter;
then Mahādeva, being pleased, granted him an unsurpassed boon.
He vanished once more, and the Lord of Umā enjoyed himself for a long time;
but when the god had departed, Ahalyā established the Teacher of the World [in his place].
He returned again to his own home, [visiting] the one named Ahalyeśvara;
and whoever bathes in that sacred ford (tīrtha) and worships the Supreme Lord there, [attains the fruit].
Upon death, that one of great austerity attains heaven, where the god Maheśvara dwells; having sported there according to his desire, he remains in that world.
When a thousand years have passed, he attains human birth once again,
endowed with an abundance of wealth and grain, and accompanied by sons and grandsons.

By resorting to the Ahalyā-tīrtha, a wise man is born into a stainless family, endowed with beauty and good fortune, and free from all diseases; he shall live for more than a hundred years. (RKV 136.24)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ahalyātīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Markaṇḍeya said:
O son of Dharma, one should then go to the excellent Karkaṭeśvara.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, it brings about the destruction of all sins.
Whoever bathes there according to the prescribed rite and worships Śiva,
his destination is undoubtedly the world of Rudra, from which there is no return.
The greatness of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which I have heard in the Purāṇa, cannot be fully described; therefore, I shall speak of it in brief.
O Great King, whatever action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— one performs at that sacred site, whether out of joy or pride, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
Having performed austerities at that sacred ford, the Vālakhilyas and Marīcis still sport today in the worlds according to their own will, O joy of the Kurus.
Those dwelling there, excluded by human ignorance, do not know that [Brahman],
which resides within the body like the self, imperishable and called the light.
O best of kings, at that sacred ford, the goddess Nārāyaṇī performed a terrible penance in ancient times, which she continues to perform even today for as long as Mount Arbuda exists.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods,
his forefathers shall remain satisfied for twelve years.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Karkaṭeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 138.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should go to the unsurpassed Śakra-tīrtha.
Wherein the illustrious Śatakratu, the king of the gods, attained perfection.
Knowing that he had been cursed by Gautama in the past, all the gods led by Brahmā, the lords of the gods, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism approached Sureśvara.
O Lord of Sages, they entreated Gautama with auspicious and conciliatory words regarding Śakra, who had lost his kingdom and his splendor.
O twice-born one, no one—whether a god or even a human—would desire a kingdom bereft of Indra; this is known to you, O Lord. (RKV 138.4)
O best of the twice-born, show compassion for him who is possessed by Bhaga;
Śakra has vanished from sight, defiled by his own sin.
Having heard the words of the gods, Gautama, the foremost knower of the Vedas,
said "So be it" and proceeded to grant a boon to Śakra.
O Śatakratu, this thousandfold portion was indeed born in the past;
by my grace, it shall become that thousandfold eye.
Having been addressed thus, the thousand-eyed one, after bowing to that best of sages,
then departed toward the Narmadā along with those illustrious brahmins.
Having bathed in the pure water and installed the Destroyer of Tripura,
he went to the abode of the gods while being honored by throngs of apsarases.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and worshipped the Supreme Lord,
a man is liberated from the sin of approaching another's wife.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śakratīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 139.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha.
There, Soma, having performed austerities, took his place upon the path of the stars.
Now, listen to the fruit of the merit of one who bathes at that sacred ford, sips water according to the prescribed rite, performs his recitation, and meditates upon the Sun.
O Bhārata, the fruit that is proclaimed for one who recites the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda is the same fruit obtained here through the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
If one who is pure should, with devotion, feed Brahmins at that sacred site according to the proper ritual procedure, it is as if ten million have been fed by him.
Whoever gives sandals, shoes, an umbrella, garments, blankets, or horses to a preeminent Brahmin, that gift for him is equal to ten million.
If one were to feed a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the Rigveda, they would not equal even a sixteenth part of a single person who is endowed with the sacred mantras.
In this manner, one should feed there a master of the Rigveda who has reached the further shore of the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu belonging to another recensional branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the wise from a thousand Agnihotra sacrifices,
that same fruit is attained at the sacred ford of Soma when one knows the Vedas.
The wise know that the fruit obtained by a man who feeds a thousand of those [ordinary guests] is equal to the fruit of feeding a single person who is absorbed in yoga.
Wherever the sage may dwell, having fully restrained the collection of his senses,
that very place is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
Therefore, with every effort, on the occasion of an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), and especially during the Vyatīpāta yoga, a yogin should be fed.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that man who performs the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) at that sacred site goes to the third heaven by means of a celestial chariot, O highly fortunate ones.
Having become an attendant of Soma, one rejoices together with him.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Somatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 140.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the unsurpassed Nandāhrada.
There the highly fortunate goddess Nandā, the bestower of boons, has attained perfection.
Long ago, when the great-bodied Mahiṣāsura, that best of Dānavas who once inspired terror in the gods,
had his limbs pierced by the trident of the Trident-wielder;
By whom the eleven Rudras, the Ādityas together with the hosts of Maruts,
the Vasus along with Vāyu, and the Moon and Sun were [established], O Lord of the Gods.
By him Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were utterly defeated in a most terrible battle that struck fear into the gods.
Because the large-eyed goddess Nandā, the sovereign of the gods, performed that terrible slaughter and then bathed there, it is known as the Nandā-hrada.
O descendant of Bharata, whoever bathes at that sacred ford and gives gifts to the Brahmins for the sake of Nanda shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Bhairava, Kedāra, as well as Rudra and Mahālaya;
Nandāhrada shall be the fourth, and the fifth is difficult to find on earth.
Many people, possessed by sensual desire, do not know that meritorious pool of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the goddess Nandā—
what need has he for traveling to the midst of the Himalayas?
Not having realized the ultimate truth, they wander about enveloped in darkness;
O Pārtha, their coming together results in nothing but sheer exhaustion.
O King, by bathing in the Nandāhrada lake, one obtains that same fruit which is gained through bathing and giving gifts throughout the entire earth bounded by the oceans.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Nandāhrada Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 141.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Tāpeśvara.
O lord of men, it was there that the doe, having attained perfection, remained terrified of the hunter.
Having cast her limbs into the water, she indeed ascended into the sky;
and the hunter, his mind filled with wonder upon beholding that deer, [remained there].
Having cast aside his bow and arrow, he began supreme asceticism;
for a thousand divine years, the hunter practiced penance.
Then, after some time had passed, Maheśvara was well-pleased and said:
"Choose a boon, O great hunter, whatever is pleasing to your heart."
The hunter said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
O Mahādeva, let a dwelling by your side be bestowed upon me."
The Lord said: "O hunter, let it be so for you regarding the boon that you have desired.
Having said, "Mahādeva, the God of gods," he vanished from sight.
And when the god had departed from sight, having established Maheśvara [in his place].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the hunter then went to heaven;
from that time forward, that sacred site became renowned throughout the three worlds.
In that sacred bathing place, it is heard that there is Tāpeśvara, who arose from the remorse of a hunter; whoever bathes there and worships Śaṅkara [shall attain his goal].
"Those men who have bathed in the waters of the Narmadā at the Tāpeśvara Tīrtha attain the world of Śiva; thus Maheśvara said to me."
They are liberated from the threefold suffering; there is no need for deliberation on this matter—especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the third lunar days.
One should perform the ritual bath daily for the pacification of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Tāpeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 142.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the excellent Rukmiṇī-tīrtha.
Whereby, by merely bathing there, one becomes handsome and fortunate.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the third lunar day, one should perform a ritual bath there; by doing so, one is not born again in this world.
That person who, having bathed at Rukmiṇītīrtha, gives a gift of gold,
does not experience sorrow by the power of that sacred site.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O lord of sages, how did such greatness come to this sacred ford?
Tell me why this ford bestows beauty and good fortune.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Bhārata, I shall relate to you this ancient history exactly as it occurred, as it was told of old by the elders through oral tradition.
I shall relate that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind.
There is a city named Kuṇḍina, which Bhīṣmaka indeed protects.
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, wealthy in riches and exceedingly majestic,
he rules a supreme kingdom while standing in the midst of a thousand women.
His wife was a great queen, dearer to him than his own life;
through her he begot a single son named Rukmaka.
A second daughter was born, named Rukmiṇī by name;
then an incorporeal voice spoke to that king.
"O Bhīṣmaka, this maiden should be given on earth to the Four-Armed One.
Having heard these words, he rejoiced together with his beloved.
Accompanied by learned Brahmins, he entered the lying-in chamber;
having caused the auspicious benediction to be recited for her, he gave her the name Rukmiṇī.
Since she was born with a golden tilaka, O Bhārata,
she was then proclaimed by name as Rukmiṇī by the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, in the course of time, she was born as an eight-year-old girl;
and that very same speech uttered previously by the incorporeal voice was repeated.
Reflecting again and again, the king, the lord of the earth, thought:
"To whom should this girl be given by me? Who will become a four-armed being?"
In the meantime, Damaghoṣa, the chief lord of Cedi, arrived there from Raivata, the best of mountains.
He entered the royal palace where King Bhīṣmaka was;
seeing that he had arrived at his home, the king honored him.
Having provided a spacious seat, he was led into the assembly hall and seated; "Is it well with you, O Indra among kings, Damaghoṣa, endowed as you are with glory? RKV 142.17.
"Today an auspicious day has dawned; I have been longing for the sight of you, O Indra among kings. My daughter has indeed given birth to a child eight years of age."
An incorporeal voice was to be given to the four-armed one;
having heard Bhīṣmaka’s words, Damaghoṣa spoke this.
"My son Caturbhuja is renowned throughout the three worlds;
O Bhīṣmaka, let this maiden be given to him, to Śiśupāla."
O King, having heard those words of Damaghoṣa,
Bhīṣmaka then gave Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣmaka then commenced the auspicious ceremony there,
inviting those born of his own lineage who resided in various regions throughout the quarters.
Having been invited, they all arrived in due order;
then came Bala and Keśava, the two ornaments of the Yādava lineage.
Having been invited, those two best of the Yadus arrived at Kuṇḍina, the city of Bhīṣmaka; they were honored by Bhīṣmaka according to the prescribed rites.
Then, at the time of dusk, Rukmiṇī, who was infatuated with desire,
went outside the city together with her female companions to worship Ambikā.
There she beheld Hari, the Lord of Gods, wearing the garb of a cowherd;
seeing him, she fell into a swoon, her heart clouded by passion.
And Keśava, having seen her, said to Saṃkarṣaṇa:
"O dear one, it is my opinion that this most excellent jewel among women must be carried off."
Having heard Keśava’s words, Saṃkarṣaṇa said:
"Go, O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, and let that jewel among women be taken quickly."
And I shall indeed follow behind you along your path,
inflicting great slaughter upon all the Dānavas.
Having received Saṃkarṣaṇa’s counsel, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin,
took the maiden, placed her upon his chariot, and departed in haste.
O King, he suddenly departed with the speed of the wind; then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the city of Bhīṣmaka.
The enraged Dānavas emerged like the tide of the great ocean;
roaring and all armed with weapons, they rushed along the path of the chariot.
Then they encountered Baladeva as he followed along the path of his chariot;
their battle with Bala brought about the destruction of all the worlds.
Just as in the past, during the world-renowned battle at Tārāmaya,
the long-armed one, mace in hand, was peerless in strength throughout the three worlds.
Dragging him away with force, he struck him down with blows from his mace;
the mighty Balabhadra was impossible for the Dānavas to slay.
He shattered all the Dānavas and stood firm like an immovable mountain;
and they beheld that Bala, enraged and invincible even by the gods.
The son of Bhīṣma, the highly energetic and illustrious Rukmin,
accompanied by an akṣauhiṇī, was among the most heroic of men.
Then, bypassing Balabhadra in battle, he repulsed him;
having evaded that combat, he quickly proceeded by way of the chariot path.
Then the god Keśava, the imperishable preceptor of the three worlds, went forth together with Rukmiṇī, having already crossed over the Vindhya mountains.
He reached the bank of the Narmadā where, in former times, a Siddha once again became invincible through the power of this very tīrtha.
For this reason, dear one, it is called Yodhanīpura;
that lord of the Dānavas, Rukma, has also arrived there.
Enraged, he replied to Acyuta: "Stay, stay! Do not go away!
Today, with my sharpened arrows, I shall send you to the abode of Yama."
Thus both heroes roared at one another;
their battle became terrible, resembling that between Tāraka and Agnija.
The Dānava hurled nets of arrows at Keśava,
but Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, paid no heed to those arrows.
Then Viṣṇu himself, enraged, seized the Sudarśana discus and was about to strike him when he was restrained there by Rukmiṇī.
He does not know you, the Lord of Gods, the four-armed Janārdana;
show me your own form, having shown compassion toward me.
Thus addressed by Rukmiṇī, O Bhārata, he revealed it;
and even upon seeing that form, the gods stationed in the sky offered praise.
Then, O Bhārata, the Lord granted divine vision to Rukma.
Rukma said:
"O Keśava, you ought to forgive all that my chest was struck with arrows by me, a sinful and ill-fated man."
O Lord, Janakī was indeed previously given by Janaka himself;
O Keśava, Lord of Gods, Rukmiṇī has been given to you by me.
"Marry her according to the rule, by means of the rite prescribed by the sacred law.
Having heard Rukma's words, the Teacher of the World was then pleased.
The Lord of the gods spoke to Rukmin, the son of Bhīṣmaka:
"Go to your own city; do not fear; rule your kingdom free from all thorns."
Having heard the words of Keśava, Rukma, the foremost of the Dānavas,
bowed down to that Lord of the World and went to his father’s abode.
When the golden vessel had gone, Kṛṣṇa then took leave of the best of the twice-born:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha—these are the seven mind-born [sons];
thus these seven Brāhmaṇas are established as certain in the Purāṇa.
"O Great-Minded One, the sons of Brahmā are thus endowed with patience, possessed of progeny, adorned by great seers, and truthful."
Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, those who have conquered their senses dwell there,
devoted to austerity and sacred study, and dedicated to the recitation of mantras and the performance of fire-sacrifices.
O Indra among kings, having invited them by the high-souled Keśava,
he then performed the śrāddha ceremony according to rule, following the procedure prescribed by Brahmā.
Hari honored those seven preeminent brahmin-sages;
there, Janārdana bestowed twelve villages upon them.
As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains, for that long has this gift been given by me; there is no obstacle whatsoever.
To those kings who are free from sin and shall protect what was given by me, I will grant well-being and bestow the supreme goal.
For as long as the five great elements endure in the worlds,
so long do those who protect what was given by me rejoice in heaven.
But that fool who violates what has been given to you upon the surface of the earth,
his residence shall be in hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
Whether given by oneself or given by another, the earth must be protected;
for whoever possesses the land at any time, to him belongs the fruit thereof at that time.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another,
becomes a worm in excrement and sinks there along with his ancestors.
Land seized by unjust means and land caused to be seized by unjust means—
the one who seizes it and the one who causes it to be seized is born as a worm in excrement.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years;
both the one who seizes it and the one who consents to its seizure shall dwell in hell for that same duration.
What wise person indeed would take back those gifts given here in the past by former kings, which brought about merit, wealth, and fame, and which have now become like withered flower offerings?
Having thus honored them properly and according to rule, O Pāṇḍava,
Madhusūdana took the hand of Rukmiṇī in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Then Muśalī, having conquered all those foremost among the Dānavas and accomplished that most splendid task, returned to his own abode.
Both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa set out for Dvāravatī;
and seeing Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, as he was departing, [the people followed].
The Brahmins, truthful and firm in their praised vows, had gone out;
they saw those two approaching along the path of the chariot.
Having rested there for a moment, Keśava spoke these words:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me everything: what is the purpose of your coming?"
"While they perform their own duties, my task remains.
Having heard the words of the god, the sages spoke these words:
Having been honored for the truth of your being for thousands of millions of eons, you are difficult for humans to encounter; now that you have been attained, why indeed do you abandon us?
Having heard the words of the brahmins, the Blessed One spoke this:
"In Mathurā, in Dvāravatī, and indeed in Yodhanīpura."
"I shall come at the three times of day; this is the truth, the truth, again and again.
Having heard this from him, those brahmins returned to Yodhanīpura.
Having descended in three parts during his manifestation in Mathurā,
all this has been told to you regarding the cause of the origin of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
The past, the present, the future, as well as the current and that which is beyond—having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships Balarāma and Keśava,
by him the Lord, the sustainer of the world, who consists of the three qualities, is worshipped.
The man who, having observed a fast, performs a circumambulation, is liberated from all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Moreover, those men who even merely behold the trees at that sacred ford are liberated from sins, even those equal to the murder of an embryo.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, beholds Balarāma and Keśava,
shall indeed become equal to that wielder of the discus, the God of gods.
They are worthy of worship, they are worthy of salutation, and their birth is a life well-lived—
those who bow before the Lord of the World, the divine Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
"O King, whatever gift, bath, or worship of the gods is performed at that sacred site, all of that becomes inexhaustible for him; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
O best of kings, listen now as I describe in its entirety the fruit that has been proclaimed for those who die by entering the fire.
In that [realm], one rejoices for as long as desired in a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of small bells, belonging to the domain of Agni.
And those who die in water dwell in the world of Varuṇa, in the midst of Yodhanīpura, until the dissolution of all beings.
O lord of men, for those who die at that sacred ford through fasting unto death, the destination of men is from which there is no return; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Now listen to the fruit that belongs even to him who, at that sacred ford, should give the excellent gift of a Kapila cow, performed in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
O Bhārata, as many hairs as there are on her and on her offspring,
for that many years they rejoice in heaven, well-honored with all their desires fulfilled.
For as many hairs as there are on the cow, for that many years he is glorified;
even when fallen from heaven, he shall be reborn in the three worlds into a family possessing cattle.
Whoever should give silver or even gold at that sacred ford (tīrtha) is honored in the world of Viṣṇu by means of a golden celestial chariot (vimāna).
Whoever should give a pair of sandals or even a garment at that sacred ford,
by the power of this gift, he attains his desired heaven.
O King of kings, whatever fruit may arise from the recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, one obtains that same fruit at that sacred ford by means of the Gāyatrī.
O King of kings, whatever merit may be obtained at Prayāga, at Gayā, at Tripuṣkara, or at Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu; [that same merit is attained here].
Whatever merit is obtained at Someśvara during an eclipse of the moon, one obtains that same fruit there simply by bathing; of this there is no doubt.
On the twelfth day, however, a man who bathes and pays homage to Janārdana has rescued his ancestors and attained the fruit of his birth.
At the transit of the sun, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and especially on the twelfth lunar day, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa; it is as if ten million have been fed.
O Pāṇḍava, whatever holy places exist on earth as far as the ocean,
they are all present right there on that twelfth day, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Gifts, sacrifices, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations come to an end;
but, O Great King, that which is performed at that sacred ford (tīrtha) does not perish.

O Bhārata, I have related to you in its entirety, according to their distinct characteristics, the supreme majesty of all sacred fords— both those that have existed in the past and those that will exist in the future.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 143.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the excellent Yojaneśvara.
Where, in a former kalpa, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa attained perfection.
Having performed austerities at that sacred ford in battle against the gods and the dānavas,
both the high-souled Nara and Nārāyaṇa attained victory.
Furthermore, when the Tretā Yuga arrived, those two gods, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
bathed again at that sacred site, and the invincible Rāvaṇa was slain.
Furthermore, O Pārtha, when the Kali age arrived, those two gods, Bala and Keśava,
were born in the family of Vasudeva and performed deeds difficult to accomplish.
Balarāma and Keśava slew Naraka, Kālanemi, Kaṃsa, Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Śiśupāla, and Jarāsaṃdha.
Then, in that battle, that Lord will slay his enemies, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, as well as Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others.
On that field of dharma, Kurukṣetra, they fought for a moment,
making Bhīma and Arjuna their respective adversaries and thus acting as pupils to one another.
Having gone again to that sacred ford and performed most difficult austerities,
and having honored the twice-born with devotion, they two shall return once more to Dvārakā.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships Balarāma and Keśava,
by him the Lord, the sustainer of the world, who possesses the nature of the three qualities, is worshipped.
The man who, having observed a fast,
keeps a vigil while singing its auspicious story, is liberated from all sins.
To whatever extent men behold trees at that sacred ford (tīrtha),
to that same extent their sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, is destroyed.
Whoever rises early in the morning and beholds Balarāma and Keśava shall all become equal to that very God of gods who wields the discus.
They are worthy of worship, they are worthy of salutation, and their birth is a life well-lived—
those who bow before the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari, who is worshipped by the entire world.
O King, whatever gift, bath, or worship of the gods is performed at that sacred site,
all its fruit conduces to imperishability.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu; and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
He who gives gold, a cow, and land has thereby given the three worlds.
Thus has all this supreme majesty of the sacred fords been told to you—
their great power, both past, future, and present.
Having heard this, or having read it, or having caused the righteous to hear it, one is liberated from all sins; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Yojaneśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 144.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the most excellent Dvādaśī-tīrtha.
All gifts, recitations, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations flow away [without result].
O Indra among kings, that which is performed at Cakratīrtha does not perish;
such is the supreme majesty of this sacred site regarding what has been and what is yet to be.
All that has been told by me, O Bhārata, in its distinct details.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Dvādaśī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 145.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Śivatīrtha.
By the mere sight of this deity, one is liberated from all sins.
But he who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, bathes at Śivatīrtha and worships Mahādeva, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whoever worships Śiva with devotion at that sacred site while observing a fast will,
without doubt, attain a state from which there is no return from the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śivatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 146.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go to Asmāhaka, the unsurpassed Tīrtha of the ancestors (Pitṛtīrtha).
Whereby one's ancestors are liberated from the state of being a preta by means of a single funeral ball (piṇḍa).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O sinless one, tell me of the majesty of Asmāhaka,
and the merit that is gained through bathing and giving gifts there, as well as through the offering of funeral cakes and water.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of kings, in a former kalpa, during an assembly of sages and gods,
a question was asked by me, my dear, just as you now ask it.
The seven oceans, together with Prayāga and Puṣkara, all taken together, do not attain equality with this; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
But at the famous Somanātha, which was established by Soma,
a man obtains that same merit which is found during a lunar eclipse.
At the end of the month, the ancestors of men look toward their own progeny, thinking:
"Will someone in our family offer us the funeral cake (piṇḍa) here? (RKV 146.6)
"The great-grandfathers as well as the Ādityas—this is the eternal Vedic revelation;
thus do the gods and the sages rich in asceticism declare."
Listen, O King, to the fruit that comes from even a single offering of a rice-ball and water;
having enjoyed the most auspicious yoga for twelve years, O Indra among kings.
In age after age, O Great King, our grandfathers have always gazed upon the one born of their own lineage as he approached.
"What will become of us on the new-moon day of the month of Āśvayuja?
For those who perform bathing, giving, and the libation of sesame seeds for the ancestors [will find no merit]. (RKV 146.10)
Freed from all sins, they indeed obtain all their desires;
O protector of the earth, the Agnitīrtha also stands here in the midst of the water.
By the mere sight of that sacred ford, O King of kings, a heap of sins dissolves;
by merely bathing there, one casts off even the murder of a Brahmin.
Always wearing white garments, self-restrained and having conquered his senses,
he should eat only once a day for one month in the vicinity of a sacred ford.
One obtains the full fruit arising from the gift of a hundred maidens adorned with gold ornaments; one is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
On this earth, as far as the oceans, he shall become a lord of great enjoyments;
endowed with wealth and grain, he becomes a donor and a righteous person.
Having observed the fast and become pure, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
likewise, whoever should cast off their life-breaths upon reaching Asmāhaka.
He is glorified in the world of Rudra for thousands of crores of years;
thereafter, having fallen from heaven, his karma exhausted, he descends from the celestial realm.
One will be born handsome in a family enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls;
by performing the rite of consecration, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He becomes wealthy, handsome, skillful, generous, and righteous;
he gains the merit found in the four Vedas and the fruit obtained from those who speak the truth.
One certainly obtains that fruit by bathing at that sacred ford;
it is the supreme among all sacred fords, established of old by Śambhu.
Viṣṇu himself, the lord of the heart, should mutter the mantra to the god Maheśvara;
likewise the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Maruts and the Mārutās.
The Viśvedevas and the Pitṛs, together with the Moon and the Sun;
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada,
as well as Cyavana, Gālava, and the great sage Vāmadeva.
The Vālakhilyas, the Gandhāras, Tṛṇabindu, Jājali,
Uddālaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vasiṣṭha, and Sanandana.
Śukra, Bharadvāja, Vātsya, Vātsyāyana, Agasti, Mitrāvaruṇa, and Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages; RKV 146.25.
Gautama, Pulastya, Paulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Sanātana, Kapila, Vāhni, and likewise Pañcaśikha.
There, many other sages of celebrated vows also sport, as do all the deities and the ṛṣis whose wealth is their austerity.
Humans, the lords of yogis, and the ancestors together with their grandfathers—all of them indeed abide here in this Āsmāhaka; of this there is no doubt.
The fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers—
for whom whatever is given, whether merit or even demerit, remains present.
Whatever was performed there in Yodhanīpura became inexhaustible;
[he did so] having abandoned his mother, father, and all his kinsmen and friends.
O best of kings, wealth, grain, beloved sons, and likewise the body,
all go along with him as he becomes like the wind, accompanied by his good and evil deeds.
Invisible to all beings, the Supreme Self is most great;
yet, O King, it attains the states of good and evil through its own karma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By what cause does the good or evil of kinsmen not accrue [to one another]?
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes.
For one alone enjoys the fruit of good deeds, and indeed, one alone [experiences] the fruit of evil deeds.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, this great question which you have asked has been remembered by me.
I shall relate to you that which was sung from the mouth of my grandfather and heard by me,
as it was previously learned from my grandfather in the assembly of sages.
Neither mother nor father is anyone's kinsman, nor is anyone ever a friend; for no one knows the form of an embodied being who has become like the wind.
If it were not so, O dear one, lord of men, the world would surely become lawless, and all that is moving and unmoving would perish.
Knowing this, O King, all the creators of the worlds established boundaries in the world so that dharma would not perish.
When the Dharma has perished among men, unrighteousness will once again prevail; consequently, due to the deviation from one's own duty, descent into hell is certain.
The entire world is unrestrained and delights in transgressing the boundaries;
therefore, the great seers, having examined the scriptures, established the boundaries.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, study of the scriptures, worship of the deities, the offering of funeral cakes and water, and likewise the honoring of guests; 146.42.
The fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers—
these three, my dear, are remembered as the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
When they are honored, all [the ancestors] are honored, as are the three maternal grandfathers;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform those rites enjoined by the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti.
One who constantly practices dharma is not stained by even a fraction of sin;
one should not transgress, even in thought, the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
In this world and in the next, if one desires the highest good for oneself,
father and son should always be as one, like a reflection drawn forth from a mirror.
Whether one is separated from others or not, according to the meaning of Śruti and Smṛti, one should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down.
"O Pārtha, there is no doubt that [liberation] occurs through the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and water;
knowing this, one should diligently become an offerer of the rice-ball and water."
Longevity, dharma, fame, splendor, and progeny indeed increase;
as do all the ancestral fields upon this earth bounded by the oceans.
I shall declare to you those places where a gift yields great fruit:
at Gayā, Puṣkara, Jyeṣṭha, Prayāga, and likewise at Naimiṣa.
O descendant of Kuru, the fruit that has been described by the wise for the offering of funeral cakes and water at Saṃnihati, Kurukṣetra, and Prabhāsa— [that same fruit is obtained here].
One obtains that very merit at the Asmāhaka on the Narmadā, there is no doubt;
for it is there that Brahmā, Murāri, and Rudra together with Umā reside.
All the deities beginning with Indra, the ancestors, and likewise the sages;
the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the clouds.
All the ancestors reside there; therefore, that place is superior to all sacred fords (tīrtha).
O King, the Brahma-stone stands there, resembling the frontal globes of an elephant.
O best of kings, when the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, on the new moon day, that Pradhāna which is Gayāśiras is not visible in the Kali age.
Pervading that sacred site, there stands a stone resembling the frontal globes of an elephant;
indeed, that sacred site is said to extend for the distance of one *gavyūti*.
Whoever goes there on that day and offers a śrāddha,
an inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors arises, lasting for a hundred years.
On any other new moon day as well, that man who, having bathed and with his senses subdued, performs a śrāddha according to the rules accompanied by mantras, [attains great merit].
O lord of men, hear what the fruit of that merit shall be:
it is the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma, the Aśvamedha, and the Vājapeya sacrifices.
One obtains that fruit exactly as Śaṅkara told me:
those who are stationed in all the hells, beginning with Raurava.
The father, the grandfather, and the others— both on the paternal and maternal sides—
are especially satisfied by a single funeral cake (piṇḍa), water, and libation.
Those who abide in the world of the ancestors sport there until the dissolution of all beings—
whether they were established in their duties, those who stood outside the path of duty, or those born with the defilement of being hungry ghosts.
They too are liberated there by means of a single funeral ball (piṇḍa); of this there is no doubt.
At Asmāhaka, a divine stone stands resembling an elephant.
O Bhārata, this [river], which was created by Brahmā in the past and which causes the destruction of all sins,
should be honored according to the rules for the sake of one's ancestors.
Having performed the śrāddha according to the rules by offering food prepared on the ground, the wise man should offer the piṇḍas upon darbha grass with their tips pointing southward.

O Bhārata, for the sake of the ancestors, one should give pairs of garments, umbrellas, sandals, and water-pots, as well as various other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to those who observe the śrāddha rites.
O best of the twice-born, hear the fruit of the merit of him who gives:
for twelve years his ancestors attain satisfaction; of this there is no doubt.
O Great King, our fathers and grandfathers,
having become like the wind, gaze upon their own kinsman as he approaches.
If our son comes to this sacred ford, bathes, and offers water,
or performs a śrāddha ceremony or the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), by that merit we shall attain a happy rebirth.
Whatever drops of water fall from one's garments when a bath has been performed, they gratify those ancestors residing in hell; of this there is no doubt.
The drops of water from his hair, as well as others who partake of the smearings,
satisfy those born of his own lineage who have died without fire or funeral rites.
At that sacred site, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules and recites the Pitṛsaṃhitā quickly delivers their ancestors from hell.
When the day of the moon occurs while the Soma has entered the trees,
a human being obtains imperishable worlds by means of a single funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Everything there indeed becomes inexhaustible; of this there is no doubt.
They quickly deliver [the ancestors] from hell by reciting the Pitṛsaṃhitā.
O Bhārata, on the new moon day at that sacred ford, one who bathes a blue bull, complete in all its limbs, and releases it for the sake of the ancestors, [attains great merit].
Even Vācaspati is not capable of describing the fruit of that merit which is obtained from the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) performed on this day.
O Bhārata, through your service, I shall explain all of that: how those ancestors of yours who are being cooked in the Raurava and other hells [may be liberated].
By the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), one may deliver all those twenty-one generations;
[the bull] which is red in color, yet white in its face and tail.
A bull that is tawny in its hooves and horns but dark blue elsewhere is called *nīla*;
however, one that is tawny in all its limbs but white in its tail and hooves [is also so designated].
They call him Piṅga, the bull who increases the delight of the ancestors;
he is the color of a pigeon and has a mole upon his forehead.
They call that bull "Babhru," which is full-bodied, beautiful in all its limbs,
and of a uniform tawny color throughout its entire body, including its tail and hooves.
They call him Khurapiṅga, who bestows the state of the righteous upon the ancestors;
he is dark blue in his entire body, with deep red eyes and firm [limbs].
They call that very one "blue," and blue is remembered as being of five kinds;
he who is born in the house of a Vaiśya is indeed distinguished as the Blue One.
One should never drive away a calf born in one's own house;
by that very act, during the rite of releasing a bull, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
If a twice-born man drives a calf born in his own house [for profit],
his ancestors fall from their state, even if they have reached the world of Brahmā.
For in whatever manner he drinks, having drunk he shakes his head;
by drinking he gratifies the ancestors, and by shaking [his head] he delivers them from hell.
Just as droplets move toward the shoulder by the impact of the tail,
so too do they swiftly rescue their kinsmen who have fallen from hell.
Roaring during the rainy season and scratching the earth with his two horns,
he should gratify the sages with the mud that is raised from his hooves.
By drinking, he gratifies the ancestors; by eating and scraping [the earth], the gods;
and by roaring, the sages and humans—O son of Dharma, for you are indeed the embodiment of Dharma.
Whether seized by spirits, or by *piśācas*, or by quartan fever, one should go to Asmāhaka, which destroys the affliction of all.
Having bathed in pure water, one should tie a knot of darbha grass upon the head,
at the base of the arm, at the navel, or even on the neck.
Having gone into the presence of the deity and circumambulated Keśava,
he should then recite the Gāyatrī mantra or a Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Homage to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Refuge, who is saluted by all the gods;
homage to you, O you who are born from the limbs of sacrifice, the all-pervading one—homage be to you!
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Gods, O Eternal One whose womb is the lotus!
O Dāmodara, victory to you, O Ananta! Protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
You are the creator and you are the destroyer of the world, both its mobile and immobile beings;
you protect all creatures and you sustain the universe.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; awaken my limbs that have fallen asleep.
O Hari, I am constantly absorbed in meditation upon you and am supremely devoted to you.
Thus praised by me, O Lord, grant me your grace, O Acyuta;
protect me, protect me from evils, and save me who have come to you for refuge.
Having thus praised Hari, the Lord of Gods and the destroyer of the Dānavas,
and having bathed again with the repetition [of the mantra], one should then feed the Brahmins.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas and in accordance with the rules,
and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one should then cause the benediction of "svasti" to be recited.
Having thus praised Hari, the Lord of Gods and the destroyer of the Dānavas,
one should bathe again with the *punarukta* [mantra] and then feed the Brahmins.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas and in accordance with the rules,
and having thus caused those Brahmins to recite [the benedictions], he should then dismiss them.
Whatever has been uttered there, one should offer that to the Brahmins;
having bathed at that sacred ford, a man or a woman intent on devotion should give a sacrificial fee according to their ability, after performing the Śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rule.
At that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), as long as a man bathes according to the prescribed rite with milk, honey, curd, or even cold water; RKV_146.103.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the beginnings of the Yugas, and the sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign, the ancestors drink water from lotus leaves.
He who, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers, causes an offering of food to be presented,
obtains the abundant fruit of the horse sacrifice.
O King, whoever performs a solar eclipse ritual at that sacred site (tīrtha) is honored in the world of Viṣṇu by means of celestial vehicles resembling the splendor of the sun.
Whoever offers a śrāddha to the ancestors at that sacred ford has truly attained the fruit of his birth through that very act as a virtuous son.
Having heard this, all the gods, led by Śakra,
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, then installed the Lord.
It pacifies all diseases and destroys all sins for one who,
being purified in mind, observes [this vow] on the new moon day for a full year.
O King, one should also perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors at Āsmāhaka,
as well as at Tripuṣkara, Gayā, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Naimiṣa.
Whatever merit belongs to those who perform the *śrāddha* shall certainly be attained right here by one who,
facing south, offers water with sesame seeds mixed with *kuśa* grass.

He who makes offerings to his father and mother on the first day of the month, at the beginning of a Yuga, during a Vyatīpāta yoga, or on the day of the sun's turning point, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Any man who, having bathed at this place, should worship Hari, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara with devotion, and perform the rite of keeping vigil; RKV_146.113 //
Freed from all sins, that man who bathes in that sacred ford and beholds Janārdana shall attain the hospitality of Śakra.
Having worshipped according to the specific injunctions and having prostrated again and again,
the father’s destiny was secured by him together with his son.
The three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are a single form;
they are endowed with cause and effect, most subtle, and yield great fruit.
This greatness of Asmāhaka, which destroys great sins, has been told to you, O King; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Asmāhaka Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 147.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Siddheśvara.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the one whose banner is the bull shall be liberated from all sins and attain the destination of those who have performed the horse sacrifice.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and performs a śrāddha ceremony with diligence for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, by him everything has been accomplished.
O best of kings, for those beings who die at that sacred ford,
the thought of dwelling in a womb shall never arise again.
Dwelling in the womb is indeed for suffering and never for happiness;
yet, for one who bathes in the waters of that sacred ford, there is no further occurrence of rebirth.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Siddheśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa), within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 148.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the auspicious Aṅgāraka Tīrtha.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, it causes the destruction of all sins.
Having made a formal resolve on a Tuesday that falls on the fourth lunar day, and having reached a firm determination,
he should bathe after the sun has set, being intent upon the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
One should worship Lohita with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, having established the deity upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) anointed with red sandalwood paste.
One should worship Aṅgāraka with "Homage to Aṅgāraka" in the pericarp; [and worship] Kujā, Bhūmiputra, Raktāṅga, and Suvāsas.
"To him born from the wrath of Hara," "to the sweat-born one," "to the very mighty one," and "to the bestower of all desires"— [these are to be worshipped] in the petals starting from the east.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should offer the *arghya* according to the ritual procedure:
"O Son of the Earth, of great heroism, born from the sweat of the wielder of the Pināka bow!"
O Aṅgāraka of great splendor, O Lohitāṅga, homage be to you!
[I offer] a water-pot joined with water and filled with śāli rice.
Having presented that [image], together with gold and cloth, placed upon a sweetmeat, to a Brāhmaṇa, one should say: "May Kuja be pleased with me."
Having offered the *argha* according to the ritual rule with water scented with red sandalwood,
strewn with red flowers, and mixed with sesame seeds and rice grains;
Having placed it in a copper vessel upon an auspicious, circular mandala,
he rested that vessel upon his head and knelt with both knees upon the ground.
O illustrious one, the wise person should offer the *arghya* purified by mantras;
thereafter, he should eat in silence, avoiding alkaline substances, sesame, and sour items.
O King, when the fourth *caturthī-aṅgāraka* has arrived, one who desires their own welfare should [partake of food] that is unctuous, soft, and sweet. *RKV_148.12*
One should have a beautiful golden image of the deity made according to one's means,
and place it in a copper vessel provided with a pedestal of molasses.
One should worship the deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, established within molasses;
one should place the deity in the northeast, accompanied by molasses and water.
Likewise, one should place the supreme water-pot (karaka) filled with kāśāra in the southeast;
[one filled] with red rice mixed [with other substances] in the southwest and in the northwest.
The wise one should place the fourth water-pot together with sweetmeats,
its neck wrapped with thread and adorned with perfumes and garlands.
With the sounding of conchs and trumpets, and with auspicious cries of "Victory!
and the like, [he saw] a brahmin wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Or else, situated in the middle of the altar, seated upon a great throne,
he is handsome, fortunate, peaceful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

O son of Pāṇḍu, having honored according to the prescribed rule one who has completed his studies with the Vedas and their branches and has bathed after fulfilling his vows— one who is proficient in all the scriptures— you should have him recite it.
Then one should give a red cow together with a red bull, [saying]:
"May the god born of the earth, who is worshipped by all deities, be pleased."
Having circumambulated the brahmin from left to right, accompanied by his wife and sons,
and together with his father, mother, and friends, he should ask for forgiveness and bid him farewell.
Now, I shall tell you all that merit and fruit which is specifically declared for one who has performed such acts at that sacred ford.
O Indra among kings, by the power of this sacred site (tīrtha), one shall be handsome and fortunate for seven births; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, a man who dies at that sacred site goes to the city of Aṅgāraka, honored by gods and gandharvas.
Having enjoyed unsurpassed divine pleasures according to the proper rule,
he indeed becomes a righteous king here in the world of humans.
Handsome and fortunate, free from all diseases,
he shall live for more than a hundred years, honored by all the world.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Maṅgaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 149.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Immediately following that is the holy site (tīrtha) known as Liṅgeśvara.
By the sight of the God of gods, wherever one may be, evil is destroyed.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having wrought a terrible slaughter of the Dānavas,
he assumed the form of a boar and established himself upon the Narmadā.
O best of kings, he who bathes at that sacred ford and bows to the deity is liberated from the great sins committed in the past.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having fasted on the twelfth day of both the dark and the bright fortnights, one should worship the Lord of the World with perfumes and garlands.
O highly fortunate one, one should worship the Brahmins with supreme devotion through gifts, honors, and meals; hear now the fruit of that merit.
A living being obtains the fruit of performing a sacrificial session (sattra) over twelve years;
by feeding Brahmins there, one obtains that very same fruit.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods and having bathed, with his mind fixed upon that,
he should recite the twelve names of the God while standing before him.
Month after month, on the twelfth day, O joy of the Kurus, the wise man, remaining without food,
should constantly worship Keśava during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should worship the god Nārāyaṇa; in the month of Māgha, Mādhava;
in the month of Phālguna, Govinda; and in the month of Caitra, Viṣṇu.
In Vaiśākha, one should remember the slayer of Madhu; in Jyeṣṭha, the god Trivikrama; likewise Vāmana in Āṣāḍha, and Śrīdhara in Śrāvaṇa.
By glorifying Hṛṣīkeśa in Bhādrapada, Padmanābha in Āśvina,
and Dāmodara in Kārttika, one does not come to grief.
Whatever verbal or mental evil was previously committed through action,
that perishes without a doubt by the recitation of the names of the months.
Always purified himself, whether opening or closing his eyes,
he should quickly perceive while eating and utter what is devoid of mantra.
Even for a living being fallen into the greatest adversity, this is the remedy:
the recitation of the names of the months corresponding to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Months.
Those nights, those days, those months,
and those years are fruitful for men, in which the Blessed Lord Hari has been meditated upon.
Even for one who has fallen into the greatest adversity, if Lord Janārdana does not depart from the lotus of his heart, he is a yogi; of this there is no doubt.
Those men who are devoid of fortune are most pitiable; they have descended as a burden upon the earth.
They are insentient and equal to beasts—those who lack devotion toward the infinite Lord.
Those men on earth who have fulfilled their purpose, who purify the world by the falling of their own limbs,
and who are wise ornaments of the universe— they are those endowed with devotion toward the infinite Lord.
He alone is truly fortunate; by him the fruit of the tree of birth has been obtained, in whose mind, speech, and body Lord Janārdana dwells.
This is the most excellent and meritorious holy site where Janārdana exists as a Liṅga;
having become eternal Wrath, he deceived his enemies in battle.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, on the Aṣṭakā days, and during the two solstices,
a self-restrained man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors.

May the Boar-form of Hari grant you peace— He whose nostrils have opened up a multitude of caverns in Mount Meru, who is a raft for those sinking in the ocean of suffering, whose hooves are half-submerged in the thick mud within the belly of the netherworld (rasātala), and whose ears are fixed and motionless as they hear the roar of the elephants of the quarters shattered by the winds driven by the force of His snorting.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Liṅga-Vārāha Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 150.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the excellent Kusumeśvara.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it destroys minor offenses.
Established by Kāma, the god known as Kusumeśvara—
the eternal God of gods— is renowned throughout all the worlds.
Kāma, born of the mind, all-pervading, the wielder of the flower-bow and arrow—
when worshipped, he who has the fish as his emblem grants all desires.
By means of that body consumed by fire, Anaṅga propitiated the Supreme Lord and thus attained the state of being possessed of limbs on the banks of the Narmadā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me of the destruction of one who possesses a body, but not of that which is bodiless;
such a thing has never before been heard by me, nor has it ever been seen.
O best of the twice-born, relate all this exactly as it occurred;
O chief of brahmins, I wish to hear it along with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O dear one, in the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
performed extensive penance while stationed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
By that asceticism, those worlds—including the gods and the asuras—were brought to ruin;
they all went for refuge to the God of Gods, the husband of Śacī.
The Great Lord, the God of gods, who pervades all beings, is scorching the three worlds; O Lord of Rays, restrain him!
Having heard those words of the gods, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra reflected in his mind and commanded [a being] to create an obstacle to their asceticism.
The Apsarases Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, and Tilottamā;
the spring season, the cuckoo, the god of love, and the excellent southern breeze.
"Having gone there, disturb Mahādeva— who dwells at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and is intent on the practice of asceticism— in accordance with what is proper."
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, O Bhārata, all those [gods],
accompanied by the Apsarases, went into the presence of Hara.
In the month of spring, crowded with blossoming flowers and filled with peacocks, water-hens, and sweet cuckoos;
amidst the dancing of celestial nymphs and the resonance of their songs, the wind blows, stirred by Yama and Nairṛta.
By that fragrance of spring and early summer, all those best of birds, along with the kinnaras and great serpents, were completely enchanted through their association.
As soon as he looked, that forest was thrown into turmoil;
he beheld the people possessed by passion, fallen into the ten stages of love-sickness.
O King, even the God of gods has entered into three states among the gods—the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa; hear about them from me.

May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you during his time of meditative absorption—eyes of diverse sentiments: one closed by the power of yoga-samadhi; the second languid with the weight of passion upon the slopes of Pārvatī’s breasts and hips; and the other kindled by the fire of anger at Madana, who had cast his bow far away.
Thus seen by the God, Kāma— along with his arrow and his bow— was reduced to ashes and perished, bringing destruction to all embodied beings.
Having seen Kāma destroyed there, all the hosts of gods and apsarases became terrified and fled back to the ten directions from whence they had come.
Deprived of Kāma, the worlds— including the gods, asuras, and humans—
went for refuge to Brahmā, with the gods led by Indra at their head.
Seeing the world sinking, they said to the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord, you know that the remainder of the world arises from sexual union."
All subjects wither away, O Lord, when deprived of their desire.
Having heard these words of the gods, the Great-Grandfather went together with them to where the god Maheśvara was.
He gratified the Lord of the World, the Great Sovereign of all beings,
with hymns, *taṇḍaka* verses, and praises derived from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Then Mahādeva, the supreme lord of the gods, being pleased,
spoke these sweet words to the gods headed by Brahmā:
"What is the task? What is the cause for distress? Or what is the reason for your coming? Let it be told to me without delay by you gods and sages."
The gods said:
"O Śambhu, through the destruction of desire, this destruction of the world of moving and unmoving beings will come to pass; you ought to create the three worlds anew."
Having heard these words of theirs and reflected upon them, the Supreme Lord pondered how to manifest the form of Kāma, which is difficult to find on earth.
Then, O best of kings, while they were looking on, the bodiless one, who had attained a body and who gives life to all beings, arrived swiftly.
Then, with the sounding of conchs and the roar of kettledrums,
the gods, asuras, and great serpents celebrated the Lord.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods! O subduer of enemies, the best of the gods have achieved their purpose; having been dismissed, they have returned as they came."
When all the gods had departed, O Bhārata, even Kāmadeva,
resorting to the bank of the Narmadā, performed extensive austerities.
It is said that for a hundred divine years, having become emaciated through austerity and recitation,
he was tormented on all sides by the great elements acting as obstacles.
O best of kings, Kuṇḍaleśvara was invoked for the sake of destroying obstacles to his own self,
