and he provided protection everywhere within the range of an arrow's flight.
Then Mahādeva, the granter of boons and destroyer of desire, being pleased by his firm devotion, invited Kāma to choose a boon.
Having perceived that Mahādeva was pleased, he whose banner is the fish, bowing down with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the three-eyed God of gods.
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then,
O Lord of the World, remain forever present at this sacred site.
Having spoken these words, "So be it," Maheśvara, the God of gods,
entered the sky and departed while being praised by hosts of apsarases.
O king of kings, when the Lord had departed from sight, Kāmadeva established the Teacher of the World under the name Kusumeśvara.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, one who is devoted to fasting on the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, or on the day of Madana, [attains the fruit].
When the clear dawn has arrived, having bathed and worshipped the Sun,
one should satisfy the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with sesame seeds.
O King, having performed the ritual bath according to the injunctions and having worshipped him, one should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa); hear now the meritorious fruit thereof.
Whatever fruit one obtains from performing the twelve-year sacrificial session (sattrayājin), that same fruit one obtains from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna); there is no doubt about this.
If one causes a funeral ball (piṇḍa) to be offered at the root of an Aṅkulla tree for the sake of the ancestors,
his grandfathers attain satisfaction for twelve years.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even the worms, insects, and moths that die at that sacred ford attain heaven; how much more so those men who have died?
The man who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, performs renunciation here at Kusumeśa with devotion, shall go to the abode of Śiva.
There, O King, he sports for hundreds of millions of kalpas, being served by divine apsarases and by the celestial gandharvas who sing.
Then, when that time has fully elapsed, he returns here to the human state and is born as a great king, honored by the lords of kings.
Handsome, fortunate, eloquent, valiant, wise, and pure,
he shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases.
This merit, which removes sin and exceeds hundreds of millions of holy fords,
is renowned as Kusumeśa and is saluted by all the gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kusumeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 151.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
The majesty of Jayavārāha destroys all sins.
By him the earth was uplifted, she who is saluted by all the gods;
and with a mind intent on favoring the world, he remained established on the bank of the Narmadā.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and beholds Madhusūdana is liberated from all sins through the recitation [of his name] ten times over ten lifetimes.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and then the Dwarf; Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O dear one, O best of sages, what was done by the Fish, and what by the Tortoise?
What deed was performed by the Boar, and what was done by the Man-Lion?
Tell me, what was done by Vāmana and by Rāma the descendant of Raghu; and what indeed was done by him in the form of Buddha, or by Kalki?
Thus addressed by the wise son of Dharma, the lord of brahmins then spoke these sweet words in reply to the son of Dharma.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: In a former kalpa, the omnipresent Lord, having become a fish, rescued the Vedas from the great ocean and offered them to Brahmā for his pleasure.
O King, at the churning for the nectar of immortality, the Teacher of the World, having become a tortoise,
supported Mount Mandara as well as the goddess Earth.
Assuming the form of a boar, Janārdana, the God of gods, lifted up the earth that had sunk down to dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
Having assumed a body half-human and half-lion,
he tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with his hook-like claws.
Having been praised by the best of the twice-born while in the form of a dwarf with matted hair,
he assumed that divine form and traversed the earth with his strides.
And having subsequently made Bali a dweller in the depths of Pātāla,
Viṣṇu, after establishing all the gods in their places, went to his own city.
Having become Rāma, the son of Jamadagni and the best among those who wield weapons,
he slew the Kṣatriya protectors of the earth, such as the Haihayas and others.
Having given the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and mines, to Kaśyapa,
the Lord of Gods still performs austerities on Mount Mahendra even today, O Bhārata.
Then Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having slain Rāvaṇa— the thorn of the gods— along with his hosts in battle, bestowed the kingdom upon Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having protected the earth with justice and gratified the deities with sacrifices,
the lotus-eyed Rāma of great splendor ascended to heaven.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Lord of the World, Vāsudeva, has descended once more into the house of Vasudeva, accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa.
O Bhārata, by your power, he slew Cāṇūra, Kaṃsa, Keśin, and Jarāsaṃdha for the sake of destroying wicked kings.
O lord of men, having slain the enemies with him as your excellent ally,
you shall enjoy the entire earth, well-gathered together with your brothers.
Likewise, the infallible one, the peaceful Lord of the gods, the slayer of Madhu who is fond of honey, shall attain the other, the ninth state of Buddhahood.
By that god, the Supreme Lord, who is the very nature of a Buddha,
the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, will be deluded.
From that time forth, O Bhārata, sons will not listen to their fathers, nor will disciples listen to their teachers; there will be a reversal of high and low among kinsmen.
For dharma has been conquered by adharma, and truth (ṛta) has been conquered by falsehood;
kings have been conquered by thieves, and men have been conquered by women.
The Agnihotra sacrifices falter, worship of the guru perishes,
and human duties decline when the Kali age has arrived, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
In the twelfth or tenth year, a woman shall become pregnant;
there she gives birth to daughters, and the Brāhmaṇa becomes tawny like a monkey.
Thereafter, the Lord Kalki will appear in his tenth birth.
O King, this has been told to you: the reason for the ten births of the Supreme Lord, which brings about the destruction of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śvetavārāha Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 152.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O protector of the earth, one should then go to the excellent Bhārgaleśvara.
Śaṅkara, the life-breath of the world, who destroys all sins by merely being remembered.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and worshipped the Supreme Lord,
a person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Whoever shall give up their life at that sacred ford will undoubtedly attain a state from which there is no return, from the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhārgaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 153.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately following that is another unsurpassed sacred ford (tīrtha) called Dravi.
By the mere sight of whom men are liberated from their sins.
Listen to that fruit which has been declared by the Lord himself for the man who, having bathed at Ravitīrtha, beholds the Sun.
In his sixteen lifetimes, no one in his family shall be blind, mute, or deaf; nor shall anyone be deformed or have diseased nails. (RKV 153.3)
Ringworm, leprosy, skin spots, circular patches, and eczema are destroyed within six months for one devoted to the Divine; of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, that account of the deeds of that god which I have heard in the Purāṇas cannot be told in brief.
Whatever gift is given at that sacred ford, dedicated to the Sun,
according to the prescribed rite to a worthy Brahmin recipient, for that there is never any end.
At the solstices, at the equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, and likewise at the sacred ford of the Sun (Ravitīrtha), there is the highest fruit for gifts that are bestowed.
O Bhārata, there is no finding the end of those gifts— whether offerings to the gods or the ancestors— made at the time of the sun's transit, just as there is none for the waters of the ocean.

Whatever was given by whomsoever at whatever time, and whatever was offered as an oblation by whomsoever at whatever time— the Sun-god shall be the restorer of that very thing to that very person at that very time.
The Sun bestows those very same seven births again and again;
however, a gift given on the waning of the moon yields a hundredfold merit, while one given at the end of a day yields a thousandfold.
At the transition of the sun (saṃkrānti), [the merit is] one hundred thousandfold; at the vyatīpāta yoga, it is indeed infinite.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, how is it that Ravitīrtha is remembered as more meritorious than the most meritorious?
Tell me in detail, for my ears are eager to hear."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen with focused attention to the supreme Ādityeśvara,
located on the northern bank of the Narmadā, which destroys all diseases.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Jābāli,
born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
His wife was devoted to her husband, virtuous in character, and high-minded;
having approached him during her fertile period, she spoke these words to her husband.
"My fertile season has arrived; I have come to you, my husband.
Out of affection, please accept me, a loving woman who desires a son."
Thus addressed, the twice-born man said: "O beloved, today I am engaged in a vow;
go now, O fair-hipped one, and I shall come again at the next change of the moon."
When the second fertile period arrived once more, she approached him again; but he, O Bhārata, replied to her, "Today I am observing a vow."
Thus, having been entreated by him many times again and again,
that passionate woman became despondent regarding her husband.
Overcome by great suffering and having undertaken a fast unto death,
that twice-born man suddenly [perished] due to that very sin of killing an embryo.
His nose and feet became withered, and all his ascetic merit was destroyed,
when that best of Brahmins saw himself pervaded by leprosy.
Having fallen into extreme despondency, that best of the twice-born took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā and questioned the brahmins about a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) belonging to the Sun.
"Thinking in his mind, 'I shall seek health from the Sun,' [he asked:
'O twice-born ones, tell me, from which holy place of the Sun might that [health] come? (RKV 153.23)"
Having gone to that sacred ford, I shall perform austerities with a well-purified mind.
The twice-born said:
On the northern bank of the Revā, there exists a solar holy site (tīrtha) named Ādityeśvara, which destroys all diseases.
"In that matter, if you are able to go there without external deliberation,"—
having been addressed thus by the twice-born, the brahmin set out to go there.
But when, overcome by a terrible, life-threatening disease, he was no longer able to move, then he thought to himself: ||| RKV_153.27 |||
Indeed, the Brāhmaṇas possess power throughout the three worlds;
for it was by the Brāhmaṇas that the falling of the phallus of the trident-bearing God of gods was brought about.
"The ocean has been dried up by the brahmins and even the Vindhya mountains have been restrained;
I too, remaining right here, shall bring forth the Sun."
"By means of great power of asceticism, [I shall attain] that which is known as Ādityeśvara";
having thus resolved in his mind, he established himself in fierce austerity.
Subsisting on air and taking no food, he stood amidst five fires in the summer;
in the winter he remained in the midst of water, and during the rains his body was uncovered.
When a full century plus one year had passed, the Sun-god, being pleased, spoke this:
Sūrya said:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—what is desired in your heart? I shall grant it even if it is not to be given; speak to me, do not delay."
O Brahmin, what indeed is impossible for you now, as you remain established in asceticism?
Jābāli said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then,
O Lord of Gods, my vow concerns the sight of Ādityeśvara."
"O Lord, being afflicted by disease, I am unable to complete that [task] which has been undertaken;
therefore, remain here at Śuklatīrtha, assuming the form of Ādityeśvara."
When this had been said, the Lord of Gods, the many-formed Divākara,
appeared in an instant on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
From that time forward, O protector of the earth, they have called that place a sacred ford (tīrtha);
it is declared to be the remover of all sins and the destroyer of all suffering.
But he who, having bathed regularly on every Sunday for a full year, performs seven circumambulations and beholds the Sun;
Listen now as I describe the fruit one obtains thereby:
here, the dormant [afflictions] such as ringworm, leprosy, and scabies are eliminated.
O King, wealth, sons, and wives perish quickly like a heap of cotton in a fire; yet one may fulfill [the desires for] them within three years.
But he who bestows gifts of faith there at the transit of the sun, dedicating them to the ancestors, his ancestors are satisfied; for the Sun is indeed the deity of the ancestors.
Thus has all this been told to you concerning the supreme Ādityeśvara—
the divine [deity] who removes all sins and destroys all diseases.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ādityeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 154.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the holy site (tīrtha) Kalakaleśvara.
It is renowned throughout all the worlds, having been created by the God himself.
Having slain Andhaka in battle, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
was accompanied by the gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
With the sounds of conchs and trumpets, with mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas,
and the like, with the sounds of lutes and flutes, and with other abundant hymns of praise.
Some sing the Sāmans and others the Yajus; others utter the Vedic meters (Chandas), while others, possessed of great majesty, praise Maheśvara there with manifold hymns of praise.
Because the *liṅga* was installed amidst the roar of the *pramathas* and the chanting of the bards, it became known by that name.
That man on earth who, having bathed at that sacred ford, beholds Kalakaleśvara, shall obtain a merit greater than that of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Purified by that merit, he shall go to heaven upon the relinquishing of his life,
mounted upon a supreme vehicle and being sung of by hosts of apsarases.
After enjoying great luxuries for a long time,
that high-souled one is then born in the world of mortals into a pure family.
A Brāhmaṇa who is fortunate in this world and has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas shall live for a hundred autumns, free from disease and sorrow.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Fruit of the Kalakaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 155.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hereafter, I shall describe that which is the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas).
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the northern bank of the Narmadā is Śuklatīrtha.
Because of its holiness and its auspicious appearance, all other sacred fords on earth do not equal even a sixteenth part of that ford.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Together with all my brothers and other most excellent brahmins, I desire to hear the greatness of that sacred ford (tīrtha) according to its true nature.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O lord of men, hear now the origin of Śuklatīrtha,
by the mere sight of which even the sin of killing a Brahmin is dissolved.
The Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins;
whatever sin was committed in childhood perishes simply by the sight of her.
O King, there is no place anywhere that bestows liberation except for Śuklatīrtha;
such is the majesty of Śuklatīrtha as I have heard it in the Purāṇa.
O descendant of Bharata, I shall relate to you that which was told by the blue-throated God of gods during the assembly of sages and likewise of the deities on Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Viṣṇu performed intense penance for a thousand years to propitiate the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
subsisting on air and remaining without food, he stayed established at Śuklatīrtha.
Then, O lord of men, Maheśvara, the God of gods, suddenly manifested himself and became visible at that sacred ford.
This [place] extends for two krośas and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
having bathed in that sacred ford (tīrtha), a man is released from all sins.
The Gaṅgā is meritorious at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
but the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest.
Among all medicinal herbs, food is the foremost; among all drinks, water is the foremost;
sleep is the foremost of pleasures; a young woman is the foremost of delights; and among all limbs, the head is the foremost.
O best of kings, O Yudhiṣṭhira, just as the forehead of one who has bathed is meritorious,
so too is Śuklatīrtha on the Narmadā meritorious.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers and Janārdana is among the gods,
so too is the meritorious Śuklatīrtha established upon the Narmadā.
Just as the cow is the best among quadrupeds and the Brāhmaṇa among the castes,
so too, O King, is Śuklatīrtha the foremost among all sacred fords.
Just as the sun is among the planets, as the moon is among the stars,
and as the head is among all the limbs, so is truth held to be the foremost among all dharmas.
In the same way, O Pārtha, among all sacred fords, Śuklatīrtha is unsurpassed;
it is as difficult to comprehend as the eternal Supreme Self in this world.
O King, because of its extreme subtlety, it is indefinable; likewise, Śuklatīrtha is characterized by great delusion when one has fallen into a state of dull intellect.
He does not know Śuklatīrtha situated on the bank of the Narmadā;
what is the use of saying more here, O son of Dharma, again and again?
Having attained the highly meritorious Śuklatīrtha through the destruction of one's sins, whoever, having become pure, offers here even a single handful of water from the Revā, [attains great merit].
By him, his ancestors have been gratified for thousands of millions of eons.
On the surface of the earth, there was a king named Cāṇakya, the sole son who dispelled the suffering of his ancestors; he also knew Śuklatīrtha.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best among the foremost of the twice-born, who was this man known by the name Cāṇakya?
He was the knower of Śuklatīrtha, for indeed no one else was its knower."
By what means was that holy site discovered by him on the surface of the earth?
I wish to hear that, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: A royal sage named Cāṇakya, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and the grandson of Śuddhodana, ruled over this earth.
Valiant, wise, and heroic, the best of kings was deceived by all the world;
yet that supreme monarch was suddenly deceived by two rogue crows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How was that king deceived by the two crows, or for what reason?
Previously, it was promised by that high-souled one who was filled with wisdom.
"I shall not live, deceived by another; I will give up my life, there is no doubt.
Tell me this, O best of Brahmins, for my curiosity is great."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having realized that he had been deceived, he then seized the two crows and dispatched them to the abode of Yama with a severe punishment.
The two crows said:
"We are the sons of Sunda and Upasunda who have attained the state of crows;
do not kill us, O illustrious one, for some other reason."
O giver of honor, having made this resolve, whether we are cast out by you in anger or not cast out, we two shall go to the supreme goal.
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, command us; having performed a great service for you, we two shall be released from the curse, in accordance with the word of Brahmā."
Having heard those words of the crow, Cāṇakya, the best of kings, thought:
"I shall not live once I have realized that I have been deceived by someone at some time."
Therefore, O twice-born ones, understand that sacred ford in the abode of Yama;
having heard it, I shall send [you] there according to the rule, and you will explain it.
Having liberated those two crows, he adorned them with garlands and sandalwood paste and dispatched them swiftly toward the abode of Yama.
The King said:
Having gone there to the City of Dharma and wandering here and there, if the righteous-souled Yama, the great restrainer, should question you: [RKV 155.36]
"Tell me, from where have you two come, or by whom have you both been adorned?
My speech must be addressed to him without hesitation."
The righteous king named Cāṇakya, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
gratified [the deceased] with food and other offerings on the twelfth day after his death.
Having heard those words of the king, the two went to the abode of Yama;
adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, they were playing in his courtyard.
They were seen by Dharmarāja, who questioned the two audacious crows.
Yama said: "From what place have you both come, and by whom were you adorned?
O crows, tell me this account without hesitation."
The two crows said:
"There was a righteous king named Cāṇakya, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
on the twelfth day after his death, we were gratified with food and other offerings."
Having heard those words of theirs, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, always [just], looked toward Citragupta, Kali, and Kāla, and spoke this: RKV 155.42: "Let this be observed."
For all beings born from eggs or from sweat, whether mobile or immobile,
the Creator Brahmā has ordained my presence as the maker of the worlds.
"Where has that man of evil conduct named Cāṇakya gone? Let his destination be sought among the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas."
Then, urged by Dharmarāja, those guardians of dharma observed the course of coming and going born of karma as described in the Purāṇas.
Then Dharma, the best among the upholders of righteousness, spoke these words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud to the guardians of dharma who were listening.
For those who die at Śuklatīrtha in the pure waters of the Narmadā,
even among those born from eggs or sweat, there is no [obstacle] to their reaching my presence.
That sacred ford is righteous in the world, having been created by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara with supreme devotion and a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Those men who, though burdened with major and minor sins, die in the waters of the Narmadā at Śuklatīrtha, become pure; they shall never again come within my domain.
Having heard these words spoken by Yama, O Pārtha, those two crows,
traveling swiftly, arrived and beheld the great city of Yama.
Questioned by the king, O Pārtha, those two Dānavas who had assumed the form of crows bowed down and related everything exactly as it had happened and as they had heard it.
"From this place we have gone to the supreme city of Yama,
having passed through many births on the southern part of the earth."
That divine city, moving at will, had golden ramparts and archways;
it was crowded with many houses and adorned with jewels and gold.
Adorned with crossroads and squares and beautified by roads lined with bells,
it was covered with gardens and groves and graced by clusters of lotus ponds.
Resounding with the cries of swans and cranes, teeming with flocks of cuckoos,
crowded with lions, tigers, and elephants, and frequented by bears and monkeys.
It was crowded with men and women, perpetually adorned with festivals,
and resounded with the blasts of conchs and drums and the melodies of lutes and flutes.
Even on the path of Yama, it was made like another heavenly realm;
yet, having gone there, they were once again led by other messengers of Yama at Yama’s command.
Having been informed, the two were sent to where the Lord, the Master of the World, was;
out of fear for their life, they beheld that Lord seated upon his throne.
He has a massive body, massive shanks, massive shoulders, and a massive belly;
he has a massive chest, massive arms, and massive mouth and eyes—he is truly great.
Mounted upon a great buffalo and adorned with a magnificent crown,
there were also Kali, Kāla, and the highly intelligent Citragupta.
Then those two, who had mastered the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti, were seen meeting in the midst of blazing fires, [weighing] the merits and sins of living beings.
Constantly reflecting thus, the two of them remained there day and night;
then, at the conclusion of our prostrations, we were addressed by Yama, who was himself the very embodiment of Yama.
When asked the reason for his arrival, he spoke; listen to that:
"In Ujjayinī, there was a powerful protector of the earth named Cāṇakya."
Having eaten the food of this man who died on the twelfth day, we arrived at the abode of Yama;
then, having heard our words, Yama shook his head.
He spoke these truthful words in the midst of the assembly, as if smiling:
"There is a reason why that sinful man Cāṇakya [acted as he did]."
But for those who have died at the Śuklatīrtha on the Narmadā, there is no return to my world, which is terrifying with all manner of evils; rather, they attain the supreme state.
It arises for all living beings; there is no doubt about this—whether a being is helpless or self-controlled, within that sacred field-mandala.
"Once dead, he will undoubtedly become an attendant of Rudra.
Having heard those words concerning that dharma, [he] went out from the city.
Beholding the various and terrible torments of hell,
O best of kings, for there are indeed thirty million horrific hells.
They were seen there on that great path, overcome by fear and fallen into supreme agony; there was the Raurava hell, and indeed the Mahāraurava as well.
Peṣaṇa, Śoṣaṇa, Kālasūtra, Asthibhañjana,
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kṛmipūtivaha.
Furthermore, another [hell] was seen there, Mahājvāla, as well as Viṣabhojana;
likewise the two hells Daṃśamaśaka and Yamalaparvata.
The river Vaitaraṇī was seen, which destroys all sins;
there they drink cool water that is like nectar.
That very water turns into the blood of sinners;
moreover, they see another forest with sword-like leaves and a massive boulder.
Another great Śālmalī tree has a form resembling a mass of fire;
likewise, there are others such as these, known by hundreds of thousands of names.
Terrible and most horrific hells are seen, wherein human beings suffer due to various kinds of sins committed through speech, mind, and physical actions.
Through faults committed out of egoism, preceded by deceitful speech,
one harms one's father, mother, teacher, brother, the helpless, and those with impaired faculties.
Those whose [bones] are not extracted wander; indeed, their destination is Raurava.
Having spent twelve years there in Raurava, those base ones—
In this human world, those men of evil deeds who seize the property of the gods and Brahmins become wretched and blind.
Having resorted to the Mahāraurava hell, their dwelling in the abode of Yama is certain;
thereafter, after a long time, those sinners remain enveloped by their evil deeds.
Those who eat meat become like silkworms in their cocoons, born pierced by thorns; they become killers of beasts, birds, and winged creatures.
They go to the hell of grinding and to the hell of drying due to the bondage of living beings;
having endured the terrible torments therein as prescribed by the scriptures, they suffer.
In this world, even those men who have attained human birth as lame, blind, or deaf,
[attain their goal] by speaking untruth here for the sake of cows and for the sake of Brahmins.
The downfall of men occurs into the Kālasūtra hell;
the tortures therein are terrible and have been ordained by the authors of the scriptures.
For those who have gathered here after eating will go to the state of an outcaste;
likewise, those who bind living beings while abandoning the continuity of their own lineage [shall do so].
They fall into the hell Asthibhañjana; of this there is no doubt.
There, at the end of a hundred years, having returned to this human state, they are born as humans.
Those fools who consider themselves wise, yet abandon their own wives, are born as hunchbacks, dwarfs, and evildoers who share in suffering. (RKV 155.87)
They go to the terrible Tāmisra hell; of this there is no doubt.
There, at the end of a hundred years, having returned to this human state, they are born as humans.
Indeed, those men who speak falsely regarding measures, weights, or coins are born with skin diseases and misfortune. (RKV 155.89)
Those lowest of men are cast into the Andhatāmisra hell;
having dwelt there for a period of a hundred thousand years, those men [suffer].
In this house of the enemy, those who eat here without first giving food to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born wander about blind, their forms wretched.
Those who nourish only themselves fall into the hell where one is devoured by worms;
consequently, at the time of birth, they are indeed eaten by worms and covered in sores.
There, one who lives off the fortune of others is born with a foul odor;
these wicked ones have fallen away from their own karma and are devoid of caste and stage of life.
They indeed suffer for ten thousand years in a hell filled with pus;
when that time there is completed, they then attain a human birth.
Enveloped by diseases, they become a source of terror to living beings;
such is the man possessed by greed and delusion, who acts as a arsonist or a poisoner.
The evil-minded one sinks into a hell filled with poison;
there he remains until his emergence after a period of a hundred years.
Having attained human birth on earth, he is born again as a wretched person [deprived of] sandals,
shoes, an umbrella, a bed, and coverings.
Those who take the wealth of their father, who delight in beating and reviling others, and who do not give [to others], will be devoured by gadflies and mosquitoes for seventy births.
They are tormented at those twin mountains where that terrible Vaitaraṇī river flows with a current of blood.
There, those evildoers who approach a woman in her menses drink blood; they are tormented in the terrible Forest of Sword-Leaves.

Those men who constantly cause suffering to others, who have sexual relations with women of the lowest castes, and even those great sinners who take pleasure in the wives of their gurus— [for them...]
For seventy births, they experience the embrace of stones—
a blazing, terrible iron [bed] covered with many thorns.
Those who take pleasure in the wives of others, having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, they plunge into the Śālmalī tree.
In a waterless region of the forest, he shall become a cruel rākṣasa—
he who, out of greed alone, seizes the property of the gods and the property of brahmins.
That evil-souled one lives on the leftovers of vultures in the next world;
such evils as these they experience by the decree of Yama.
But for others, merely by seeing or hearing [them], fear arises;
likewise, others enjoy the fruits of their own giving while in the abode of Yama.
I saw messengers by the command of Yama describing what they had heard,
some surrounded by chariots, others by elephants, and some by horses.
O highly fortunate one, there were seen men established in the accumulation of ascetic merit— givers of cows, givers of gold, and givers of land and jewels.
That world grants the desires of men regarding beds, seats, houses, and so forth;
those humans who give food together with drink here [attain it].
There, satisfied and well-contented, they sport in the abode of Yama;
yet here, even a gift as small as the tip of a hair is given.
O best of kings, all that has been seen and heard is told to you in its entirety; at Śuklatīrtha, all of it yields inexhaustible fruit.
"Do whatever you intend, if you are able; let him be released.
Having heard those words of theirs, Cāṇakya was delighted in his heart.
Having honored the two birds again and again,
O Bhārata, he dismissed them after giving away his entire possessions to the Brahmins once they had departed.
Having abandoned desire and anger, he went to the mountain of the immortals;
there he fastened a boat firmly, supported by a black rope.
Floating swiftly while meditating on the god Janārdana,
one should seek freedom from disease from Bhāskara and wealth indeed from Jātavedas.
From Īśāna one attains knowledge; from Keśava one attains liberation. That thread which was blue and red became dark-blue (mecaka).
Seeing a rope resembling pure crystal, the one of great intelligence leaped into the stainless water and went to the state of Viṣṇu.
The great-souled prince, having cast off his body at the auspicious Śuklatīrtha, attained that eternal Nārāyaṇa known by the name Acyuta, whom those learned in the Vedas sing of as the Ancient One.
This success of King Cāṇakya has been told to you, O King;
likewise, I shall tell you something else—listen with a one-pointed mind.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Siddhi by Cāṇakya," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 156.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, there is no sacred ford on earth in all the worlds that is not [surpassed by this].
It is sung of as being comparable to the Śuklatīrtha by way of analogy.
The great Śuklatīrtha is situated on the Narmadā,
in a region sloping toward the northeast, frequented by hosts of sages.
And likewise, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha,
Śaṅkara himself comes from Kailāsa together with Umā.
Having bathed at the time of midday, he beholds himself by means of the self at Śuklatīrtha, composed in meditation and accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
O best of men, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika and Vaiśākha,
one beholds Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva after bathing on that very day.
The king of the gods, together with the deities, stationed in the path of the wind,
bathes on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and beholds Śaṅkara.
On that day, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas, having beheld the Lord of Gods, likewise release themselves from their sins.
Śuklatīrtha, which is half a yojana in width and half of that in length,
is immensely meritorious and the destroyer of great sins.
Wherever the best of men can see the tops of trees while standing,
there they are liberated from the great sins accumulated in the past.
A man joined with major or minor sins is liberated by bathing;
even the murder of an embryo, though difficult to cast off, perishes once it has been accumulated [through this rite].
Because the Lord of Gods dwells right there together with Umā,
Śaṅkara comes from Kailāsa specifically on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
O King, that sacred ford, which is of great merit and the destroyer of all sins,
was previously described by Brahmā and likewise by me to you.
Just as a garment washed by a washerman becomes stainless,
so too does the bathing of the body there make a person pure.
Having committed grave sins in the earlier part of his life, a person,
by fasting for a day and night, casts them off at Śuklatīrtha.
O great king, by offering a handful of water from the Revā at Śuklatīrtha on the day of the full moon,
one's ancestors shall become auspicious for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Neither mother, nor father, nor kinsman can rescue one from falling into the ocean of hell; only merit, O Lord of Men, can deliver one at Śuklatīrtha.
Neither through austerity nor through celibacy do beings attain that same good destination which a living being attains by casting off the body at Śuklatīrtha.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
a man, having fasted and being self-restrained, should bathe the deity with ghee.
Having bathed in the Revā at dawn, one should offer a blanket with ghee and gold according to one's means, dedicating it to the Lord Śaṅkara.
One should perform the filling of the deity with clarified butter, [offering] a "butter-blanket";
that man, possessed of great splendor, goes to the world of Śiva upon death.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage until the dissolution of all beings, that man who bathes at Śuklatīrtha and worships Umā and Rudra [attains this].
O Lord of Men, he who performs a month-long fast at that sacred site shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice through perfumes, flowers, incense, and the like.
He is liberated from great sins accumulated over seven lifetimes;
[the same applies to consuming] camel’s milk, ewe’s milk, and food at a *navaśrāddha* (a funeral rite for the recently deceased).

Likewise, sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī*, the eating of forbidden food, sin in the case of selling what should not be sold or speaking falsehoods, and [the sin of] officiating at a sacrifice for one who should not be sacrificed for—these are [equivalent to the aforementioned]. (RKV 156.24)
O Bhārata, [these include] usury, being a poisoner of the assembly, and reviling the gods and Brahmins; such sins as these, and others as well.
Sins perish through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at Śuklatīrtha; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, he who bathes at Śuklatīrtha and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods [attains great merit].
For twelve years, those well-satisfied [ancestors] attain satisfaction through his sandals,
shoes, umbrella, bed, and seat.
Those who give gold, wealth, grain, a properly yoked plough, as well as food accompanied by water at that sacred ford (tīrtha)— RKV 156.28.
O Bhārata, those who die at that sacred site with devotion, dedicating it to Śiva, go to the world of Śiva—of this there is no doubt; they depart joyful and nourished.
Even those men who obtain only a mere morsel of alms-food there, as well as those performers of sacrifices, those observing vows, and those dwelling at that sacred ford, indeed go to heaven.
Even that which is given as small as the tip of a hair becomes inexhaustible;
so too for one who, with a concentrated mind, enters the fire at Śuklatīrtha.
Freed from passion and hatred, having meditated upon Janārdana in his heart, he,
with all his desires fully satisfied, shall go to the city of Varuṇa.
There is neither disease nor old age where the Lord of Waters dwells; and whoever should practice fasting unto death at that sacred ford, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [attains liberation].
Whether against his will or by his own volition, there is no doubt that a living being within the circle of that sacred field shall have an irreversible destiny from the world of Rudra.
He who, having died, has no doubt, shall become an attendant of Rudra;
likewise, he who gives away a daughter adorned according to his ability at Śuklatīrtha.
O best of kings, the fruit that is declared in the Purāṇa as spoken by Rudra for one who performs the release of a bull according to the prescribed rite— [that fruit he obtains].
I shall explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind, O King:
as many as there may be individual pores of hair on all the limbs, [so many are the atoms].
For as many thousands of years as there were [units of time] given at Śuklatīrtha during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
For fifteen days, that merit increases for one who,
having become pure, performs circumambulation at Śuklatīrtha.
Whoever worships a beautiful couple with Rudra in mind, that yields the same fruit as the circumambulation of the earth performed by him.
For seven births there shall be no separation from him at all;
this great fruit has been told to you in brief, O King.
Whatever merit belongs to Śuklatīrtha, as I have heard it from the God,
that fruit ordained in the Purāṇa shall belong to whoever hears this with devotion.
He shall obtain it; there is no doubt in this. This is the truth, the truth again and again:
one who desires a son obtains a son, and one who desires wealth obtains wealth.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; the fruit of bathing and giving there is great.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śuklatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 157.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, immediately following that, in the vicinity of Śuklatīrtha, [is another sacred site].
The sacred ford of Vāsudeva, moreover, is honored throughout all the worlds.
For that ancient merit on the Narmadā is well-known,
where by a mere utterance of "huṃ," the Revā traveled for a *krośa*.
O Indra among kings, from the moment the river departed by means of the *huṃ* sound,
from that time forth that lord has been called "Huṅkāra" by the wise.
That man who, having bathed at the Huṅkāra-tīrtha, beholds the imperishable Acyuta,
is liberated from the sins committed even in seven previous births.
For men who have sunk into the ocean of saṃsāra and are performers of evil deeds,
there is no one other than Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who can lift them up.
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to him;
those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform his worship.
At all times and in all undertakings, there is no misfortune for those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed Hari, the abode of auspiciousness.
Whatever fruit a human being obtains from the worship of other deities,
that same fruit one obtains by prostrating before Hari with the eight limbs of the body.
For as many thousands of years as there are particles of dust on his body covered by dust, for that long he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
By sweeping, sprinkling, and smearing the floor of that temple, all evil is destroyed;
likewise, by seeing Revā with supreme devotion, women and men [are purified] before the Best of Men.
The sin accumulated over many births perishes for one by whom the Blessed Vāsudeva has been honored;
with his sins shaken off, he goes to the world of the one whose banner is Garuḍa, to be venerated by the hosts of gods.
Even one who offers salutation to the wielder of the discus with deceit quickly goes to the destruction of the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
Rudra is pleased by worship; Divākara [is pleased] by recitations and fire-offerings;
and the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace is satisfied by prostration.
For men who have entered the ocean of existence, struck by the winds of dualities, oppressed by the burden of protecting sons, daughters, and wives,
and sinking without a raft in the turbulent waters of the sense-objects, the boat of Viṣṇu alone is their refuge.
O Indra among kings, O tiger among men, whatever is done at the Huṅkāra-tīrtha— whether auspicious or inauspicious— it never perishes.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Huṅkārasvāmi Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 158.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to the supreme and most excellent holy site, Saṅgameśvara.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it removes the fear of all sins.
O best of kings, Dhanada, having arrived from the world of the ancestors for Mount Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth, rested there for a moment.
O best of kings, even today on the surface of the earth,
stones that are black in color yet brilliant like crystal are seen as proof of this.
The best of rivers, possessing holy waters, having issued from a cascade of the Vindhya mountains,
has entered the waters of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins.
Whoever bathes there at the confluence and worships Saṅgameśvara undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whoever offers a bell, a banner,
and a canopy at Saṅgameśvara shall dwell in a celestial chariot drawn by swans, surrounded by hundreds of divine women.
He attains the state of Rudra and becomes an attendant of Rudra—
he who fills the linga of the God with curd-rice.
In the world of Śiva, he shall dwell for his desired length of time;
even if he is destitute, he should fill the liṅga of Bhava with bilva fruits.
O Lord of Men, he too attains that fruit upon going to heaven;
his lineage becomes inexhaustible for seven births.
Listen to the meritorious fruit for one who performs the ceremonial bath of the God of gods with curd, honey, or ghee according to the prescribed rite.
Where rivers flow with milk and the trees exude honey,
there those men go when Maheśvara is well-pleased.
Whoever offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water to Maheśvara,
enjoys the inexhaustible fruit of all that for seven births.
Maheśvara is the greatest of all worthy recipients;
therefore, Maheśvara should be worshipped with every effort.
He who, remaining constantly established in the celibate life (brahmacarya), worships Śiva,
lives as a lord of gods in this world and, upon death, shall go to the state free from ailment.
O Pārtha, whatever fruit is obtained by the wise when Śiva is worshipped, that same fruit is obtained, O Pārtha, when the Lord of Yogins is worshipped.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones, whose births have been well-lived,
in whose homes men devoted to the worship of Śiva eat.
Wherever a sage may dwell, having fully restrained the collection of his senses,
that very place is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara.
O Pārtha, the fruit that arises from feeding a hundred who are learned in the Vedas is indeed produced by feeding a single Śiva-yogin.
Wherever one who has smeared his body with ashes eats— whether he be a fool or a scholar—
there the Lord of Gods, whose banner is the bull, eats together with his consort.
Whatever fruit is obtained by feeding ten million Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas,
that same fruit is gained by giving even a mere morsel of alms to Śiva-yogins.
He who, having reached Saṅgameśvara, gives up his life,
shall never again return from the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 159.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the supremely purifying holy site (tīrtha).
On the Narmadā, indeed, Anarakeśvara is perfected, though very difficult to attain.
O Bhārata, having bathed at that tīrtha, even a man of sinful deeds does not behold the most terrible place known as the Gate of Hell.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, O best of beings, tell me of those physical marks by which men are born here having already experienced the fruits of their auspicious and inauspicious deeds."
Just as the living being, when departing, does not perceive the body it has left behind,
so too, when proceeding again toward a body, it is accompanied by the five elements.
In this mass of skin, bone, flesh, fat, blood, hair, hundreds of sinews, feces, urine, and semen, what notion does arise in men? (RKV 159.5)
Thus addressed, Mārkaṇḍeya, the knower of yoga,
having meditated upon the eternal Maheśvara, the God of gods who is all things, spoke.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O Pārtha, to this great question; I shall relate it to you as I heard it formerly from the presence of Brahmā in an assembly of sages and gods.
The teacher is the ruler of those who possess self-control; the king is the ruler of the wicked;
but for those who commit sins in secret, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the ruler in this world.
Indeed, for those who have not performed penance, throughout many successions of lives in the world of Yama,
they are subjected to manifold torments.
Having returned to human existence, they bear the marks of their sins;
I shall describe those to you, O King—listen with a focused mind.
Having endured every form of torment and having gone to the abode of Vaivasvata,
those who have undergone extensive torments return to the world marked by their deeds.
One who speaks falsely becomes stammering, and one who lies regarding a cow becomes mute;
a killer of a Brahmin is born with leprosy, while a drinker of intoxicants has black teeth.

By stealing gold one becomes one with deformed nails; by violating the Guru’s bed, one suffers from skin diseases; by engaging in sexual union with a low-born woman, one is born into a base womb; and by failing to give gifts, one becomes impoverished.
O King, one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice becomes a village pig;
one who performs too many sacrifices becomes a donkey, and from eating at a meal where one has been improperly invited, one becomes a dog.
One who eats without examination is like a monkey in a lonely forest; one who reviles others is like a cat; and one who burns his own armpits is like a firefly.
He who bestows ignorance shall indeed become an ox;
by giving stale food to a Brahmin, one shall fall into impotence.
Furthermore, by stealing a book out of stinginess, one becomes blind from birth;
and for one who steals fruits, a child dies—of this there is no doubt. (RKV 159.17)
Upon death, he becomes a monkey; if released from that state, he then becomes a camel.
Indeed, a man who eats these [fruits] without having given them away shall be childless.

One who steals clothing becomes a monitor lizard; one who administers poison becomes a wind-eater (a snake); and by abandoning the life of a wandering mendicant, O King, one becomes a desert-dwelling piśāca.
A wind-god is a stealer of water, and a mouse is a stealer of grain;
it is said in the sacred tradition that one who approaches a girl who has not yet reached puberty becomes a serpent.
One who lusts after the wife of his guru shall become a chameleon for a long time;
and the man who breaks a flow of water shall become a fish.
By selling items that should not be sold, a man indeed becomes Vikaṭākṣa;
by mating with those who are not his wife, he becomes a wolf, and by deceiving in trade, an owl.
One who eats on the eleventh day after a person has died is reborn as a dog;
one who, having promised wealth to a twice-born man, does not give it, becomes a *madhūka* tree.
From approaching the queen, one becomes a wicked thief or a village pig;
by slandering the twice-born, one obtains the body of a tortoise.
The *devalaka* shall go to the womb of a king known as a *caṇḍāla*;
the unfortunate fruit-seller becomes a scorpion, and the husband of a low-caste woman becomes a scorpion as well.
A cat that touches fire with its paw becomes diseased and an eater of the flesh of others;
from approaching a uterine sister, one becomes impotent, foul-smelling, and a stealer of fragrances.
The village priest Divākīrti shall become a donkey, a fortune-teller a cat,
and both Bhaṣaṇa and Vyāsa shall become poor scholars.
O King, that very person is seen [as the object] by those whose innermost secrets have been revealed;
whether it be something belonging to another, however small or however great it may be.
Having committed [such acts], one indeed enters a womb among animals; of this there is no doubt.
These and other such signs, O best of kings, [are found].
O Bhārata, by those very beings through whom men are seen to be governed by their own past actions, birth and death follow for all living creatures.
There is no doubt that [the child] is born when the auspicious and inauspicious [karmas] have become balanced,
through the union of a woman and a man, and when the semen and blood are pure.
The Supreme Lord is endowed with the five elements as the sixth;
the sense organs, the mind, the vital breaths, knowledge, life-span, happiness, and fortitude [are his].
Retention, impulsion, suffering, desire, and indeed egoism;
effort, form, color, tone, aversion, existence, and non-existence.
For this self of his, who desires a beginning for that which is beginningless,
in the first month he becomes moistened and coagulated with the bodily constituents.
In the second month it becomes an *arbuda*, and in the third month it is endowed with the sense organs.
From space, it acquires lightness, subtlety, sound, and the power of hearing;
from wind, it acquires touch, movement, heat, and dryness.
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, color, and illumination;
from water (salila), taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness.
In the third month, the unborn self first perceives the odor of the earth, as well as its weight and form, and it begins to throb.
By not fulfilling her pregnancy-longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman.
In the fourth month there is stability of the limbs; in the fifth, the production of blood;
in the sixth, strength, complexion, and the growth of nails and hair.
Endowed with mental volition, covered by nails and body hair,
in the seventh and eighth [stages] he possesses skin and is also possessed of memory.
His sin pursues him again toward the embryo and again toward the nurse;
consequently, the embryo born in the eighth month is deprived of life.
In the ninth or even the tenth month, driven by powerful winds of labor,
he emerges like an arrow from the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.
Indeed, endowed with the limbs of the body and joined with major and minor members,
there are one hundred and eight vital points (marmas) therein, while the number of bones is three hundred.
Seven skull-plates were ordained by the Self-Existent One;
and there are thirty-five million hairs upon his limbs, O Bhārata.
Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā issue forth from the heart; among them, the one with the luster of the moon is the central one.
Thus does the wheel turn among the fourfold collection of living beings;
for all embodied beings, there is both birth and destruction.

"O King, through righteousness one attains an upward course, while through unrighteousness one goes to a downward state; for all social classes, birth [in such states] arises from deviating from their own duty."
O Great King, whatever actions such as giving and enjoying are seen in the states of divinity and humanity— all that is the fruit born of karma.
One may sink into a terrible hell earned by one's own fierce deeds, acquired through desire and anger— a hell from which there is no crossing.
Situated on the bank of the Narmadā for the sake of delivering living beings,
such is this supreme great tīrtha, Narakeśvara.
That sacred ford (tīrtha), which wards off hell, bestows great merit, and destroys even the most heinous sins, is the supreme among all holy sites and is difficult to find on earth.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships Maheśvara,
even if burdened by great sins, shall never behold hell.
Whoever gives a beautiful Vaitaraṇī cow at that sacred ford is liberated from the Vaitaraṇī river with ease; of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O twice-born one, what is the form and what is the size of that river Vaitaraṇī at the most terrible gate of Yama, and how does it flow?
How are they liberated from it? For whom does it persist continuously?
And for whom is it favorable? Please explain this in detail.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O son of Dharma, O mighty-armed one, listen to everything spoken by me;
that great river at the gate of Yama which is named Vaitaraṇī.
Fathomless and without a further shore, it brings terror as soon as it is seen;
its waters consist of pus and blood, and it is formed from the mud of flesh.
Then it quickly whirls about in the midst of that heat like clarified butter,
amidst pus teeming with worms that have diamond-hard beaks and iron mouths.
And with crocodiles and sea-monsters equipped with adamantine pincers,
and with other aquatic creatures that were extremely violent and capable of piercing the vital organs.
The twelve Ādityas blaze there like fierce fires at the end of a cosmic dissolution;
indeed, mortals fall into that place, crying out most piteously.
"Alas, brother! Alas, son! Alas, mother! they lament again and again for him who falls into the terrible Forest of Sword-Leaves and protects them.
Living beings cross over it, sink down, and fall into exhaustion;
that great river is to be seen by the fourfold classes of living creatures.
Those who do not respect their mother, nor their teacher, nor their guru, cross over that [river] by means of sounds; otherwise, they fall into it.
Those fools who despise her—
her who is devoted to her husband, of virtuous character, and unwavering in her duties— shall dwell perpetually in hell.
Those wicked ones who constantly abandon those who have placed their trust in them—
their masters, friends, and ascetics— shall dwell [in hell].
Those great sinners who seek out the vulnerabilities of women, children, the elderly,
and the wretched, are indeed cooked there in the midst [of that hell], crying out in distress.
The evil-minded person who obstructs a weary and hungry Brahmin shall be devoured by worms there for as long as three hundred kalpas.
For one who, having promised a gift to a brahmin, does not bestow it;
or for one who, having summoned him, says "it does not exist"—for such a person, there shall be constant dwelling [in hell].

One who sets fire to a house, one who administers poison, one who reports to the king, one who slanders, one who interrupts a conversation, a false witness, and a drinker of intoxicants; // RKV_159.69 //
One who destroys a vajra, one who misappropriates what has been given by oneself,
one who breaks the embankments of a good field, and one who violates another's wife.
A Brahmin who sells liquids, one who is the husband of a Śūdra woman, and one who causes the breach of a dam for a herd of thirsty cattle; (these three are equal).
One who defiles a maiden, one who causes distress after having given a gift, a Śūdra who drinks the milk of a tawny cow, and a Brāhmaṇa who eats meat; RKV_159.72.
"These dwell here constantly; do not entertain doubt about this, O King.
Listen, O lord of men, to that by which they may become favorable."
At the solstices, at the equinoxes, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, on the day of the new moon, and on other meritorious occasions, the most excellent gift is bestowed.
One should fashion the auspicious Vaitaraṇī river, either black or pale-red in color,
with horns of gold, hooves of silver, and a vessel of bell-metal for milking.
One should fashion [the image] covered with a pair of black garments, provided with the seven grains,
and seated upon a copper vessel at the top of a mound of one *droṇa*.
One should fashion an image of Yama out of gold, provided with an iron staff;
having constructed a raft made of sugarcane stalks, it should be bound together with strips of cloth.
Having placed that cow, born from the body of the Sun,
upon a raft, the wise man should provide it with an umbrella and a pair of sandals.
One should present the ring and garments to a Brāhmaṇa, and while grasping her tail, one should recite this mantra: RKV 159.79.
Oṃ! At the gate of Yama, in that most terrible place, there is the river Vaitaraṇī;
desiring to cross it, I give this to you—homage to Vaitaraṇī! This is the mantra for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Oṃ, O you who are the form of Viṣṇu, best of the twice-born, god on earth, purifier of the assembly!
This sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been given by me to you; salutations to Vaitaraṇī!
Thus is the mantra for the gift.
Having circumambulated the Brahmin, the King of Dharma, the cow Vaitaraṇī, and Śiva, one should present everything to the Brahmin.
Having grasped the tail of the cow Surabhi and placed the bird at her head, he then—
"O cow, wait for me at the gate of Yama, which is full of great terror;
O cow, I am about to cross over—you, Vaitaraṇī, be saluted.
This is the mantra for following [the cow].
One should follow him as he goes and lead his entire household home;
when this is done, O protector of the earth, the river will flow with pleasant waters.
By means of that cow, she becomes a river carrying water that delivers [beings across];
one obtains all desires, both those that are divine and those that are human.
The sick shall be freed from disease, and supreme calamities shall be pacified;
[the merit] is a thousandfold when one is healthy, and a hundredfold when one is afflicted.
But that gift which is given for one who has already died, when they are out of sight, is remembered as being equal [to giving while they are present].
Therefore, O Great King, one should give with one's own hand, thinking: "When dead, who will give to whom? Thus, what is given by oneself shall yield great fruit.
Thus has this gift concerning the Vaitaraṇī river been told to you by me, O son of Dharma.
Whoever here hears it with devotion or recites it properly goes to the immeasurable abode of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight arrives in the month of Āśvayuja,
one should bathe, perform a śrāddha ceremony, and then worship Maheśvara.
Gifts should be given to the ancestors by those endowed with devotion and faith;
afterwards, one should perform a vigil through listening to sacred discourses and other such activities.
Then, at the time of dawn, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā and having performed the libations for the ancestors according to the rules, preceded by those for the gods;
One should offer a lamp filled with ghee in a golden vessel to a twice-born man;
thereafter, free from envy, one should feed the Brahmins and eat oneself as well.
When this has been done, O best of men, no living being shall go to hell;
yet the state of hell must inevitably be witnessed by human beings.
By performing [this rite] according to this procedure, O King, a man shall not see the hells;
indeed, for those men who die at that sacred site (tīrtha) according to the prescribed rule.
One dwells for a manvantara in the rare world of Śiva,
traveling in a sun-colored celestial chariot adorned with hundreds of tinkling bells.
That fortunate one goes, being attended by hosts of apsarases, and enjoys various pleasures for the duration stated; of this there is no doubt.
Then, when that time has fully elapsed, he will attain human birth here;
freed from all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
and having fasted for a full day and night and worshipped Maheśvara,
even one joined with great sins is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who are freed from the twenty-eight crores of hells indeed go to the world of Śiva, liberated from the sufferings of hell.
Having there enjoyed great pleasures endowed with divine sovereignty,
those men obtain a human birth, which is difficult to attain on earth.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Anarakeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 160.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should go to the unsurpassed Mokṣatīrtha.
It was frequented by gods, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
Many do not know that place, being deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu;
there dwell the highly fortunate perfected ones (siddhas) and the sages whose wealth is their austerity.
Pulastya, the learned Pulaha, and the high-minded Kratu; Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, and Nārada as well.
These and other highly fortunate ones, numbering seven thousand, attained liberation along with their sons; therefore, that sacred ford bestows liberation.
There, in the midst of the current, that great river falls;
there is the confluence at that sacred ford (tīrtha), which causes the destruction of all sins.

Whatever fruit is obtained from the repeated recitation of those [mantras] known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, one shall obtain that same fruit by properly chanting the Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rule.

Whatever is given there, whatever is offered in sacrifice, whatever is recited, and whatever fruit is earned by visiting sacred fords—all that becomes inexhaustible; it is the supreme means for attaining liberation.
For those twice-born who die at that sacred ford through renunciation, there is no returning; their destination is [liberation] by the power of that holy place of liberation.
O sinless one, this procedure has been indicated by me to you in brief;
it is the great fruit of the sacred ford that is described in the Purāṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mokṣatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 161.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the unsurpassed Sarpa-tīrtha.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is there that the great serpents, having performed austerities, attained perfection.
Vāsuki, the terrible Takṣaka, Airāvata among serpents,
the illustrious Kāliya, as well as Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya.
Śaṅkhacūḍa, Mahātejas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vṛkodara, Kulika, and Vāmana, along with their sons and grandsons.
Having performed extremely difficult austerities at that most meritorious sacred site,
they enjoy various pleasures and sport according to their desire.
In ancient times, Śaṅkara declared that whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods shall obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
O Bhārata, for those men on earth who have bathed at the Sarpa-tīrtha,
there is no fear whatsoever from the species of snakes or scorpions.
Having died, he goes to Bhogavatī and, being honored by the great serpents and surrounded by naga maidens, becomes a lord of great enjoyments.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having become pure and observed a fast, one should fill the liṅga with sesame seeds;
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers according to the extent of one's means.
Having performed this according to the rules and having prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
O Lord of Men, hear now what the fruit of that is said to be.
O King, for as many sesame seeds, leaves, flowers, and fruits as there were in that [offering], for so long shall one rejoice in the city of heaven for the duration of his desire.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he is born into a pure family;
handsome and fortunate, he becomes the master of ten million in wealth.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Sarpa-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 162.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should then go to Gopeśvara immediately after the Sarpakṣetra.
Whereby, by a single bath alone, men are liberated from their sins.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and gives up their life there shall go to the abode of Śiva, even if they are burdened with sin.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the Lord God is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Having sported at will in the world of Rudra, that one of great asceticism,
upon attaining human status here, becomes a righteous king.
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, accompanied by male and female servants,
and honored by lords of men, he shall live happily for a hundred years.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gopeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 163.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the unsurpassed Nāga-tīrtha.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, being self-restrained and pure, one should [perform the rite].
Having kept a vigil at night with offerings of perfumes and incense,
and having bathed at the clear dawn and performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules;
One is liberated from all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point, O King, regarding him who shall give up his life at that sacred ford.
"His destination is irreversible," Śiva himself declared.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nāgatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 164.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, one should go to the excellent Sāṃvaura Tīrtha.
There the sun is present, being worshipped by gods and asuras.
There, those men who had become lame, whose noses and nails were decayed,
whose limbs were broken by patches of ringworm, and who were swarming with flies and worms;
Deprived of mother and father, forsaken by brothers and wives,
they are without protectors, mutilated, and maimed, submerged in the ocean of suffering.
Their protector, the source of the world, has taken refuge on the bank of the Narmadā; he is the Lord of Sāṃvaura, the remover of the afflictions of the worlds and the destroyer of suffering.
Now, listen to the fruit of the merit of one who, having bathed at that sacred ford for one month without interruption, worships the god Bhāskara.
O Pārtha, whatever fruit is obtained at Uttara as well as at the Eastern Ocean,
that same fruit is gained by bathing at those sacred fords in the South and the West.
Whatever sin was accumulated in childhood, youth, or old age, that perishes merely by bathing at Sāṃvaura; of this there is no doubt.
O King of kings, by the practice of the *Sāṃvaura* [mantra], for seven births there shall be neither disease, nor poverty, nor separation from what is beloved.
By fasting on the seventh lunar day and likewise observing a fast on that very day, one obtains that fruit by bathing there; of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, by bathing at that sacred ford, one obtains the same fruit that is said to result from an offering of water mixed with red sandalwood.
The delightful water of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins,
was especially beheld by the high-souled Sāṃvaura.
They are blessed, they are great-souled, and their birth is well-lived,
who, having bathed, behold the supreme Lord of Gods, Sāṃvaureśvara.
One shall dwell in the world of the Sun for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Sāṃvaureśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 165.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is a place renowned as Siddheśvara.
"O Great King, O Lord, this is a supreme sacred site established by the Siddhas."
There, O Great King, is a sacred ford of great merit, the most purifying among all holy sites,
situated on the southern bank of the Narmadā.

Having bathed at that sacred ford, O Bhārata, a man should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods; he who performs a śrāddha ceremony right there for the sake of his ancestors [attains great merit].
The ancestors of one who bathes with devotion at that sacred site and worships Śiva are satisfied for twelve years; of this there is no doubt.
Having kept a vigil at night, one should recite the Puranic stories;
then, at the clear dawn, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
He who beholds the beloved of Girijā shall go to the supreme goal;
in ancient times, the highly fortunate great sages such as Kapila and others [attained it].
Chanting the supreme Brahman, those of great vows who had attained perfection through yoga achieved the highest Siddhi by the power of the Narmadā.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Siddheśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 166.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the goddess Siddheśvarī, the Vaiṣṇavī who destroys all sins, [spoke].
Having seen that most beautiful place, they attained supreme bliss.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a man should worship the ancestors and the gods;
he who beholds the Goddess with devotion is liberated from all sins.
A woman whose children have died, one who is barren, or one who gives birth only to daughters— such a woman obtains a son who is virtuous and endowed with good qualities.
O King, whoever bathes at that sacred ford and beholds the Goddess with true devotion— whether on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, or at any time at all— [attains the supreme goal].
Then, having bathed at the confluence, whether it be a woman or even a man,
the Goddess, being well-pleased, bestows sons as well as wealth.
When seen and well-worshipped, the Goddess protects one's lineage;
and when worshipped, she constantly protects her progeny—of this there is no doubt.
And on the ninth day, O Great King, having bathed and observed a fast, one should worship the Goddess with supreme devotion and a mind purified by faith.
He shall go to the supreme world, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Siddheśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 167.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it is distinguished by your sign.
O great sage, tell me of this sacred ford and its origin.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, on the excellent southern mountain Vindhya,
which is endowed with all virtues, [he dwelt] self-restrained and restricted in his diet.
Having been received as a guest by hosts of sages, I dwelt for a long time in Daṇḍaka;
having lived there happily for a very long period, ten thousand years.
Having taken leave of those sages and followed by his disciples,
O highly fortunate one, he then returned and arrived at the bank of the Narmadā.
Having established there a dwelling place that was meritorious, delightful, and destructive of all evils, I remained joined by a multitude of twice-born brahmins.
It was crowded with celibate students, well-established in the householder stage of life,
and with forest-dwellers and ascetics who were restrained in diet and self-controlled.
There, having performed most severe asceticism for ten thousand years with highly fortunate ascetics who were free from desire and anger, I remained.
Taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, he propitiated the Lord Vāsudeva, the creator and sovereign, chanting prayers and performing austerities and observances.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, those two boon-bestowing gods arrived;
O King, they appeared visibly like two suns, adorned with Umā and Śrī.
Then, having bowed down to the two gods with devotion, I spoke these words:
"I pray to you both, who are auspicious, worthy of boons, and givers of boons."
"O illustrious ones, because of your steadfastness in the Dharma and your unsurpassed devotion,
you shall undoubtedly remain forever in this place together with the gods— free from old age and disease, like those twenty-five years of age."
O Pārtha, O Yudhiṣṭhira, when I had spoken thus, those two gods, Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, being greatly delighted, addressed me regarding my place of residence.
The two gods said:
"Know that we are stationed in this place together with the gods, including Indra.
Having spoken thus, the two gods then vanished right there.
And I, having worshipped those two— Śaṅkara and the imperishable Kṛṣṇa— with great concentration, have since become one who has accomplished his purpose.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a person should worship the Supreme Lord,
Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the three worlds, under the name Mārkaṇḍeśvara.
He shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu or indeed of Śiva,
by means of ghee, milk, curd, or likewise honey.
Then, with the water of the Narmadā, with most beautiful perfumes and incenses,
as well as with offerings of flowers and food oblations, he whose self was disciplined [performed the worship].
In this manner, O King, one who is devoted to bhakti should perform the vigil for Viṣṇu; likewise, being self-restrained and pure-minded, one should perform the ritual bathing and other rites.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, having fasted on the fourteenth day,
a Vaiṣṇava man should perform the worship of the deity on the twelfth day.
Having performed this on the fourteenth or the eleventh day, O best of men,
a person attains the world of Viṣṇu and becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
And in the city of Māheśvara, O king of kings, one rejoices like a member of the Gaṇas;
there, remaining steadfast, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony dedicated to the ancestors.
Having bathed in the Narmadā, a twice-born man who observes silence and maintains a restrained mind attains, without a doubt, inexhaustible satisfaction.
Having performed the twilight devotions there and recited the beautiful japa,
he offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings according to the prescribed rule.
Standing before Kṛṣṇa or again before Mārkaṇḍeśa,
one should here recite the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas with great effort.
Whoever should mutter even a single *ṛc* verse shall obtain the fruit of the *Ṛgveda*;
by means of a *yajus* formula, the fruit of the *Yajurveda*, and by means of a *sāman* chant, the fruit of the *Sāmaveda*.
When one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed;
this applies even to a woman whose children have died, a barren woman, or one who gives birth only to daughters.
Having recited the Rudra mantras according to the prescribed rule, a Brahmin who knows the true essence of the Vedas should place an auspicious water-pot on the right side of the linga.
