O King of kings, by bathing [the child] with the water from the jar while reciting the eleven Rudra mantras, one obtains a son who is long-lived and free from sin.
Whoever beholds the Mārkaṇḍeśvara tree, even from afar, is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; so Śaṅkara has declared.
O best of kings, whoever hears this with devotion or recites it, becomes purified of all sins; of this there is no doubt.
This brings fame, long life, and wealth; it destroys suffering and liberates those who recite or even hear it from all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mārkaṇḍeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 168.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is the excellent Aṅkūreśvara.
A sacred ford endowed with all virtues, renowned throughout the three worlds.
There, O great protector, having propitiated Maheśvara— Śaṅkara, the life-breath of the world who carries away [all things] by mere remembrance— the Siddha attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, what was that Rākṣasa? What was his name, and in whose lineage did he arise?
O sinless one, tell me all of this in detail.
Those men who are blinded by the darkness of ignorance and are doers of evil,
see the world of the moving and the unmoving through those like you who have become lamps.
Having heard the words of the Son of Dharma, Mārkaṇḍeya, the lord of sages,
smiled and spoke that story which destroys all sin.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, there was a mind-born son of Brahmā named Pulastya,
an expounder of the Vedas and Śāstras, who was like a second Creator in person.
Tṛṇabindu’s daughter was the wife of that Parameṣṭhin;
through his devotion to dharma, a high-minded son was born to him.
Because he was granted by Brahmā along with the Vedas and Itihāsas, together with the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Pada and Krama recitations, his name is Viśravas.
Then at a certain time, O King, the great sage Bharadvāja joyfully gave his daughter to Viśravas, O monarch.
O King, that brāhmaṇa, the most learned in the Vedas, took his pleasure with her with supreme joy, just as Maghavan does with Paulomī.
Then, after some time, O King, a son endowed with the qualities of a son was born to Viśravas, renowned by the name Vaiśravaṇa.
Having undertaken a vow of silence out of childishness, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
he too granted fearlessness to all beings and practiced that supreme vow.
Mahādeva, together with Brahmā and the Brahman-sages, was pleased with him;
having granted him friendship, the Lord indeed bestowed upon him the status of the Giver of Wealth.
"You shall become the fourth among Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa";
having spoken thus, Brahmā also departed quickly to his desired status as a world-protector.
Then, immediately thereafter, a rākṣasī named Kaikasī,
having abandoned both the netherworld and the earth's surface, desired Viśravas as her husband.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Rāvaṇa was born as her son,
along with the great rakṣasa Kumbhakarṇa and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa.
Both Kumbha and Vikumbha were the two sons of Kumbhakarṇa;
they were possessed of great strength, great heroism, and were truly great, O Supreme Person.
The great Aṅkūra, the best of Rākṣasas and son of Kumbha,
having thus seen the virtuous Vibhīṣaṇa, [the foremost of Rākṣasas spoke].
Then, having attained youth and learned that his grandfather was a Rākṣasa,
he fell into a state of supreme despondency and performed very great austerities.
Having gone to the southern, western, eastern, and northern oceans,
Aṅkūra, the lord of the Rākṣasas, was encountered by chance at the Narmadā.
It is said that he performed a very great divine penance for a hundred years;
thereupon Mahādeva, the conqueror of the cities of enemies, appeared in person and was pleased with him.
The bull-bannered god invited the Rākṣasa to choose a boon:
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you—and I shall grant it to you, O observer of noble vows."
Seeing the boon-granting Maheśvara, the God of gods, before him, the Rākṣasa bowed down again and again and spoke these words.
If you are pleased, O Mahādeva, you who grant boons, Lord of the Gods,
bestow upon me immortality, which is difficult for all beings to attain.
O Destroyer of Tripura, by this boon, you should remain here in my name and always be present at this sacred ford.
The Lord said: As long as you, firm of soul, act according to the counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa and practice righteousness, so long shall this endure.
Having spoken thus, the god, who is worshipped by all the deities,
departed for Mount Kailāsa, the supporter of the earth, in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
When the Lord had departed from sight, O king of kings, he bathed and sipped water according to the prescribed rites, and then installed the supreme Aṅkūreśvara.
With perfumes, flowers, and incense; with garments, ornaments, and decorations;
with banners, yak-tail whisks, and parasols; and with auspicious sounds such as cries of "Victory!"—[he should worship].
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gods with heart-pleasing and abundant hymns of praise,
the Rākṣasa went to the palace where King Vibhīṣaṇa was.
Honored according to custom with gifts, marks of respect, and reverence,
he was established in the state of brotherhood and dwelt there in supreme joy.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the Supreme Lord named Aṅkūreśvara shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Starting from the Māṇḍavya pit up to the auspicious confluence,
there is the sacred field of the gods, Maheśvara, situated between the Revā and the Āmalakī.
To the west of the Māṇḍavya pit is the sacred site of Aṅkūreśvara;
having bathed at that tīrtha, a man becomes pure with a restrained mind.

Having performed the twilight prayers with diligence and having recited the sacred mantras, O Bhārata, and then having offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, O bull among the Bharatas.
Clad in wet garments along with his lower cloth, observing silence and self-restraint,
a man who has fasted according to the rules on either the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day;
O King, listen to the fruit of the merit of him who performs worship there:
for a full hundred yojanas, all sacred fords and shrines [are present].
When those [shrines] are seen, one is then liberated from sins;
for whatever gift is given at that sacred ford (tīrtha) dedicated to the gods, [it bears great fruit].
Having bathed according to the rules, that [gift] in a vessel is declared to be inexhaustible; the fruit of a burnt offering is said to be tenfold, and that of recitation is even greater than that.
The merit is tripled by fasting and quadrupled by bathing;
this applies to one who undertakes renunciation or who effects the abandonment of life.
There is no doubt that his destination from the world of Rudra is irreversible;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for worms, insects, and moths who die at that sacred ford named Aṅkūreśvara, there shall be a happy rebirth.
O King, this origin of Aṅkūreśvara has been told to you—
a sacred site endowed with all virtues, supreme, and the destroyer of sins.
Those who listen with devotion to this [narrative] of great fruit as it is being recited, they too undoubtedly attain the world of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Aṅkūreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 169.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to the supreme, meritorious tīrtha that destroys all sins.
Where the sage Māṇḍavya attained perfection, as did the sage Nārāyaṇa.
In former times, Nārāyaṇa performed service while fixed upon a stake;
having bathed there, O Great King, one is released from the cloak of evil.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Sage, this which has been told by you is a marvel among the worlds;
O Father, such penance performed while fixed upon a stake has never before been seen or heard."
Out of curiosity, tell all of this to me, together with the sages: the majesty of this sacred ford of Māṇḍavya.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O King, to what happened in the past, in the Tretā Yuga on this earth— of the high-minded King Devapanna, who was like a guardian of the world (Lokapāla).
A knower of dharma, grateful, a performer of sacrifices, and always devoted to giving,
he protected his subjects with effort, just as a father protects his own biological sons.
Dātyāyanī was the beloved wife of that king, obedient to his will;
she resounded with the tinkling of her necklaces and anklets.
O King, the mutual affection between the two of them increased day by day;
established as the pillar of his lineage, that king ruled this earth.
Though he was adorned with all virtues, the king remained childless, despite possessing a realm filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, and endowed with wealth and vehicles.
Overcome by great suffering and tormented without offspring,
O Bhārata, he was constantly devoted to ritual bathing and fire-offerings for twelve years.
Together with his wives, he remained steadfast in vows, fasts, and observances,
worshipping the blessed goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the crusher of the head.
With many hymns, with devotion, and through the meditative absorption of the ritual of worship:
"Victory to you, O Vārāhī! O Cāmuṇḍā! Victory to you, O three-eyed Goddess! (RKV 169.12)
Homage be to you, O Brāhmī, Raudrī, Kaumārī, and Kātyāyanī!
O Pracaṇḍā, Bhairavā, Raudrī, Yoginī, and Ākāśagāminī!
"There is nothing lacking in you within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Praised thus by the king, the goddess was satisfied and spoke these words:
"Choose whatever boon is in your mind according to your desire; I have been propitiated by you through devotion, and being pleased, I shall grant it to you."
Devapanna said:
"If you are pleased, O Goddess of gods, or if I am indeed worthy of a boon,
then deliver me, who am tormented by being destitute of offspring."
Lead my lineage to prosperity and provide protection for my family;
for the homes of those without sons in this world are indeed like cremation grounds.
His ancestors do not eat, nor do the deities along with the sages,
even though the śrāddha is performed day after day— such is the case for my ancestors always.
"They always show me themselves in a dream as being tormented by hunger.
Having heard these words of the king, the queen entered into meditation.

Having beheld the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, with her divine eye, the goddess, her face serene, spoke this to the king: RKV_169.20: "The goddess, her face serene, spoke this to the king."
"O King, there is no lineage for you in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Perform a sacrifice to the Lord of Sacrifice; otherwise, you shall have no offspring."
"O protector of the earth, I have seen the three worlds with my divine eye.
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed, and the king returned to his own home.
She performed sacrifices to the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), and from that, a daughter was born—
radiant, beautiful, and enchanting to all the world.
"Even in the world of the gods and gandharvas, there is no such lovely woman;
her father, out of joy, gave her the name Kāmapramodinī."
Then, in the course of time, she grew; in her beauty she paralyzed the world, with the graceful gait of a swan, beautiful-browed, and bent by the weight of her breasts.
Wearing red garlands and garments, radiant with earrings and ornaments,
and anointed with divine unguents, she was well-guarded by her female companions.
The necklace resting upon the center of her breasts shone like a garland of lightning;
she had hair as lovely as bees, lips like the *bimba* fruit, and a beautiful smile.
With eyes reaching to the tips of her ears, she seemed to drink in her lovers;
with the fragrance of moon-like betel, she seemed to draw toward herself the god of love.
She had a neck like a conch shell, a charming waist, and copper-colored toes, nails, and feet;
she possessed a deep navel, beautiful hips, plantain-like thighs, fine teeth, and was auspicious.
On one day, the young girl, accompanied by a circle of her friends, increased the joy and playfulness of her parents and circle of kinsmen.
Carrying sandalwood, agallochum, betel, incense, and *saumanasa* flowers,
as well as flowers and incense, she went to worship the Goddess.
Having cast their ornaments and garments upon the bank of the pond,
they then entered the midst of the water and engaged in playful sport with joyful cries.
Then, seeing her playing with her companions in the clear water,
a Rākṣasa named Śambara arrived in the form of a hawk.
Having seized her while she stood in the midst of the water, that evil-minded one took her— she who delights in passion— as well as her ornaments, and flew up into the sky.
Then, O Bhārata, having entered the path of the wind together with his beloved,
that great sage fell into the water where his earrings and other ornaments lay.
On the banks of the Narmadā, Māṇḍavya remained with his senses fully restrained like a piece of wood,
absorbed in the supreme state of Maheśvara, the station of Nārāyaṇa.
And his younger brother, devoted to serving his elder brother and emaciated by asceticism and recitation of prayers, meditated upon the god Janārdana.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Abduction of Kāmamodinī," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 170.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
And as she was being led away by him, along with her friends who delighted in fulfilling desires, [she spoke].
Having seen them, they all emerged from the midst of the water and cried out.
Having all gone to Rājagṛha, they spoke in great distress:
"O King, Kāmapramodinī has been carried off by a hawk, a bird!"
"And while she is playing in the water at the pond in the presence of the god,
O King, you must seek her out, knowing her path."
Having heard those words of theirs, Devapanna was deeply distressed; crying out "Alas! Alas! he rose from his excellent seat, weeping.
Accompanied by his ministers, at that lake in the vicinity of the water,
he neither saw a sign nor a path, and he fainted from grief.
The citizens were distressed by the king's distress;
yet in an instant, the king was consoled by his ministers together with the family priest.
"What shall we do? he said; "at this time, let this be ordained.
Having reached an agreement on that with everyone, [he prepared] a fourfold army.
I shall dispatch [armies] into all directions, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots;
and musical instruments shall be sounded amidst the chaotic turmoil.
Armed with iron arrows, javelins, spears, swords, axes, and other weapons,
the king stood clad in armor, as if he were about to devour the entire host.
Neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor a daitya, nor a rākṣasa—what can the king do today? I know not how his wrath will be appeased.
The city folk there, their minds struck with wonder upon seeing fourteen thousand elephants with goads held by their riders, were filled with amazement.
There were eighty thousand horsemen with weapons in their hands,
and three thousand and twenty chariots, O bull of the Bharatas.
In the meantime, O dear one, the dust from their hooves rose into the sky along with the sounds of the battle drums;
for indeed, the protector of the city was there.
Having taken her ornaments for the limbs and minor parts of the body—namely the earrings, armlets, bracelets, necklaces, anklets, and waist-bands; ||| RKV_170.14 |||
Having reported this, he said to the king: "By your grace, I have seen it at the hermitage of the ascetics where Māṇḍavya resides."
There, surrounded by ascetics, he was seen in their presence;
having heard the words of the magistrate, he was visibly adorned with ornaments upon his limbs.
With eyes red with anger, he looked at the ministers and the merchants:
"A brahmin of such conduct as this in my city!"
Disguised by a vow while practicing the life of a thief, he is a stealer of others' property;
by that evildoer, who is a mere ascetic in name, my daughter has been abducted today.
Assuming the form of a bird, he who dwelt in the water rose into the sky;
[he departed] from those heretics, those engaged in improper acts, those following the "cat-vow," and the deceitful.
One may slay flatterers, thieves, and those of evil conduct; there is no sin in this.
"I must not look upon this sinner, this thief, this abductor of maidens"—[such a thought does not apply here].
"Let him be impaled on a stake immediately; there must be no deliberation regarding him.
That wicked one, who has the form of a Rākṣasa though he is rich in asceticism, deserves to be put to death by me."
Speaking thus and moving out of anger, he commanded the village headman;
failing to distinguish between what ought and ought not to be done, he caused the twice-born man to be impaled upon a stake.
Then all the citizens and countryfolk, their faces filled with tears, cried out "Alas! Alas! while others wept and spoke various words.
A despicable deed has been committed by the king who acts like a Caṇḍāla;
for a Brāhmaṇa must never be killed, especially one who is devoted to asceticism.
If one whose conduct is characterized by anger is to be banished outside the city,
one must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin.

O King, they should banish him from the kingdom with all his wealth intact and unharmed; yet the fire of the city-dwellers does not consume his house, for everyone there has become anxious in mind, fearing that their own homes might be overtaken by it.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Māṇḍavya’s Impalement on the Stake," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 171.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
It has been told how that Brāhmaṇa was impaled upon a stake by those whose wealth is their asceticism.
Then all the great seers went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada, Devala, Raibhya, Yama, Śātātapa, Aṅgiras,
Vasiṣṭha, Jamadagni, Yājñavalkya, and Bṛhaspati.
Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, the sage Aruṇi,
the Vālakhilyas, and others— all those belonging to the lineages of the hosts of ṛṣis.
The preeminent sages beheld Māṇḍavya impaled upon a stake;
they said to the brahmin Nārāyaṇa, "What desired service may we perform for you?"
Due to the presence there of the great-souled Māṇḍavya, they all arrived in a state of agitation and asked, "Is he dead? Or does he live?"
Seeing his condition, all those twice-born ones fell into a state of extreme despondency; yet, unable to endure that suffering, they remained so in their minds.
"If you think it right, let the king be asked: 'Reduce him to ashes!
Having heard those words of theirs, Nārāyaṇa spoke these words.
"While I am alive, my brother has fallen into such a state; fie upon my life! Yet, there must be some fruit of my asceticism."
Seeing my eldest son impaled upon the stake, my heart seems to rend asunder;
yet what else shall I do, so that the kingdom along with the king may be preserved?
"And today I shall reduce you to ashes; may this be forgiven by you here.
Having spoken thus, he should take [the object] held in his hand and consecrate it with mantras.
As soon as he looked with anger, he became the utterer of the syllable *huṃ*;
by that sound of *huṃ*, the sages were then struck with amazement.
Then those best of the twice-born asked Māṇḍavya:
"O Brahmin, why do you restrain the curse intended for the destruction of the king?"
Having heard the words of the sages, Māṇḍavyaka spoke with great difficulty regarding this man who, though sinless, had been subjected to an attempt on his life here.
I salute you with my head bowed; welcome always, O sages! You are all worthy of the guest-offering, honor, and worship; please be seated here.
With his mind focused on a single point, Māṇḍavyaka spoke to them all.
"I have experienced this terrible suffering, the fruit of what was earned in previous births.
Do not despair, sirs; for that which was committed as sin must be experienced."
The sages said:
By what ripening of karma does one go to another birth in this world?
And by what fruit of the practice of giving does one go to heaven?
Māṇḍavya said:
Those who have not given gifts are born to live off the fortune of others;
for them there is no ritual bathing, no recitation of mantras, no burnt offerings, no hospitality, and no worship of the gods.
O best of the twice-born, those who do not perform the ancestral śrāddha on the sacred festival days nor give gifts go to a terrible hell; they go to the state of the lowest castes.
Again they are poor, again they are sinful; by the power of their sins they dwell in hell.
For that very reason, in this mortal world of cyclic existence, they become worms and moths among living beings.
Those who are habituated to bathing, devoted to the twice-born and the gods, masters of their senses, and practitioners of compassion for living beings;
those who are virtuous in character and have conquered pride and anger—they dwell joyfully in the worlds of the gods.
Those disciplined by knowledge do not oppress others; they are content with their own wives and avoid the wives of others.
For them, there is no fear whatsoever in this world, for they are pure by nature and free from defilement.
The sages said:
O best of Brahmins, what evil deed was committed by you in a previous birth,
by which this painful state has been reached— a union censured as a stake?
Indeed, seeing you fixed upon the stake, everyone has come here;
we behold you still alive as they lower you into the fire.
Though enduring the suffering born of the agony and heat of the flames, you remain free from pain.
Māṇḍavya said: One experiences for oneself alone the karma that one has performed; whether good or evil, it was done by oneself in the past, and never do others experience it.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does previously committed karma find its doer.

Neither mother, nor father, nor brother, nor wife, nor sons, nor friends can share in one's karma; no one is tainted by another's actions, for each person experiences the results of their own deeds alone.
Listen to my words, for I have been questioned by you;
O Brahmins, in my former youth, I made it my practice to bathe after becoming soiled with dirt.
Out of ignorance and in my childish state, a louse was placed upon my neck; though my head and limbs were anointed with oil, I did not apply oil to the louse. (RKV 171.29)
Having fastened a comb into her hair, she was impaled upon a stake;
the evil committed against them has now borne this fruit for me immediately.
"After spending a short time, I shall attain the stainless liberation;
therefore, O great sages, do not feel distress on my account here."
Having experienced this state, I shall not utter any curse; rather, I will spend some days in agony, exhausting my sin.
"O twice-born ones, I am experiencing the fruit of past karma that was accumulated by me;
therefore, this king should be forgiven, and his anger must be relinquished."
Having heard those words of Māṇḍavya, the great ṛṣis attained incomparable joy and honored him, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Nārāyaṇa said:
"In what place shall I cast this water purified by mantras,
so that the king, along with his kingdom and his domestic priest, may be reduced to ashes?"
Māṇḍavya said:
"Guard this water, which is like the Kālakūṭa poison;
I shall cast it into the ocean, for a task for the gods has arisen."
Then all those sages, having prostrated before Māṇḍavya and taken their leave with joy, Kaśyapa and the others departed for their homes.
As they were departing, those ascetics were told: "You must come into my presence on the fifth day, so you promise."
"So be it," having thus promised, Nārada and the others vanished from sight;
and when those foremost of Brahmins had departed, Śāṇḍilī, whose wealth was her asceticism, remained.
On the second day, she arrived without having learned of that seer;
carrying her husband on her head, she wandered about during the night.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that brahmin was not seen on the stake because he was weighed down by his burden;
the devoted wife fell from her knees as he remained fixed upon the stake.
Pain arose in all her limbs due to the stumbling of the sage; for such was the condition she had been experiencing since the time of her previous destiny.
Furthermore, some painful fruit of my evil deed still remains;
I am tormented by you, O sinful one—why [did you do this] in the act of slaughtering animals?
"I see you as a wanton woman; are you a Rakshasi or perhaps a thief?
Having spoken thus, he cried out again and again for a moment out of delusion.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, all those ascetics and sages, their minds filled with terror at witnessing the sage’s distress, questioned him.

"For what purpose do you wander at night? What indeed is this vehicle? Why have you cast off the burden of your basket? And what is the reason for your coming, O you who revel in sorrow after sorrow, having caused distress to the sage?"
Śāṇḍilī said: "Let everyone know me as one devoted to my husband, established in asceticism— not an Asurī, nor a Gandharvī, nor a Piśācī, nor a Rākṣasī."
I have no desire, no anger, no enmity, and no envy;
you should forgive any lapse on my part arising from ignorance and the dimness of my vision.
The vehicle is afflicted by pain during the day for the sake of the husband's happiness;
know that this husband is always situated within the small basket.
"I provide sustenance, drink, and clothing for this sick man;
know me to be Śāṇḍilī, the foremost among the Ṛṣis, headed by Śaunaka."
Do not be angry with one who follows the dharma of her own husband; treat me as a guest.
Since I have arrived in the presence of the virtuous, you ought to forgive me everything.
The sages said:
"Wandering about at will, you do not understand the suffering of others:
when the sun has risen in the morning, your husband shall die."
"O lowest of your lineage, you do not recognize that the suffering of another is greater than your own suffering!
At those terrible words, Śāṇḍilī became despondent.
Having fallen into great despair and reflected for a moment, she spoke these words,
her eyes bloodshot with anger as she then glared at the sages.

"Indeed, she has arrived at the house of the virtuous and has acted as an offender toward you; yet, when a guest has arrived, one should honor them with hospitality, even if they have come to the home of a refined person. (RKV 171.55)
"You have indeed offered me such hospitality as this,
yet you have not considered the dharma that leads to heaven and liberation."
"Having seen me, who am of Prajāpati's lineage, just as ordinary women [behave],
may you gods today behold my feminine power in heaven."
"My husband will die, for the sun will not rise;
the entire world is shrouded in darkness, yet this night does not wane."
When these words were spoken by her, the sun was paralyzed and enveloped in darkness;
nothing at all could be produced, and the performance of sacrifices with the *vaṣaṭ* call ceased.

O Pārtha, for six months there was no utterance of *svāhā* or *svadhā*, nor the performance of the five great sacrifices; there was no bathing, giving of gifts, or recitation of mantras, and the neglect of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) was transgressed; furthermore, the rites of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water were abandoned.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Śāṇḍilī and the Sages," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 172.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all those sages and the gods, led by Indra, [approached].
They gathered at the holy hermitage of Māṇḍavya on the bank of the Narmadā.
To the sound of conchs and drums, and with the blazing of lamps,
the courtesans danced to the sound of the singing of the *apsarases*.
While he was impaled upon the tip of the stake, eighty-eight thousand ascetic *snātaka* brahmins praised him with sacred narratives.
In that assembly, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, together with the thirty gods, arrived there out of joy and a desire to behold him.
The Mothers, Mallikā and the others; the Kṣetrapālas and Vināyakas; the Dikpālas and Lokapālas; and the best of rivers, Gaṅgā and the others.
In that assembly of sages and gods, which was always filled with joy and delight,
the king arrived together with the people of the city and the countryside.
Seeing that curiosity there had agitated their minds,
they all remained composed out of fear, their hearts filled with terror.
In that divine assembly, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa said to him:
"O Māṇḍavya, O being of great courage, the gods together with us have come to grant you a boon."
Through manifold hardships and austerities, success shall be yours;
ask for whatever you desire that pleases your mind.
"Know this world to be devoid of the sun, lacking the *vaṣaṭ* call, and thrown into chaos, with its dharma destroyed; yet restore it to its natural state.
O best of the twice-born, we pray for the favor of Śāṇḍilī."
"This king, who brings you hardship, has arrived before you;
O brahmin-sage, prepare yourself for the assembly of gods and asuras."
Māṇḍavya said:
"If the gods, having arrived here together with the deities, are pleased with me,
then you must remain at this sacred ford at the three times of day along with the sages."
"By your grace, may my pain be forever stilled.
"So be it," O son of Pāṇḍu, replied the lords of the gods as they spoke.
Then the Rākṣasa, taking the maiden Kāmapramodinī before him, said: "O Blessed One, in the past Urvaśī pronounced a curse upon me."
"When you take the maiden, O Rākṣasa, your curse shall come to an end;
by that curse, my censurable deed was committed while my mind was unawakened."
Having said, "You must forgive me," he then vanished from sight;
and when he had gone, that lotus-eyed maiden looked about.
Having consulted with all the gods, they gave that iron stake to the wise Māṇḍavya after bathing it in the purifying waters of the Narmadā.
Having raised up the sage Māṇḍavya amidst auspicious sounds such as cries of victory,
that bull among sages, Māṇḍavya, married that maiden.
Having honored them all with gifts, hospitality, and respect,
the king, standing nearby, [honored them] also with various kinds of jewels.
Reproached by all those people with words of condemnation,
he was once again honored by the king and by all the brahmins with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Having satisfied them by giving ten million gold pieces and obtained their forgiveness,
he summoned Śāṇḍilī once the wedding was over and spoke to her.
"Honor these brahmins and release the sun,
by which, having dispelled the darkness, compassion may immediately arise."
Having heard the words of the sages, the sorrowful Śāṇḍilī said:
"O twice-born ones, when the sun has risen, my husband will meet his death."
"How then shall I release him here, for it would result in my own misfortune?
O great sages, what should I do now, given that he has set out on this course of action?"
"According to your view, I am a woman without a man and truly without a protector;
therefore, remain in darkness, for I do not desire the rising of the sun."
At those words, all those gods, asuras, and great seers shook their heads and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"O faithful wife, O highly fortunate one, rich in ascetic merit, listen to our words;
if you hold us all in high regard, then carry out what we say."
Śāṇḍilī said:
"Do you quickly deliberate upon that by which my husband shall not die, by which the word of the sage may become true, and by which happiness may increase."
Having heard those words of hers, Hṛṣīka, who had been in a state of sleep,
vanished for a moment and beheld Śāṇḍilī once more.
Taking him up once more, they all restored his body to a state free of wounds; he was bathed in the waters of the Narmadā and entrusted to Śāṇḍilī.
Then, seeing her husband radiant with splendor, she, with a joyful heart,
bowed down to those sages, the gods, and the stainless sun who sustains the world.
All the gods, gandharvas, and humans, impelled by their respective duties,
departed joyful and contented, each to his own great hermitage.
That devoted wife, having stayed for exactly one month in the hermitage with her husband, was permitted by Māṇḍavya to depart; she bowed and went to her own hermitage.
When they had all departed, he installed Acyuta,
who is remembered as Nārāyaṇa, under the name Māṇḍavyeśvara.
O descendant of Bharata, he worshipped [him] for a thousand divine years;
then he went to the mountain of the immortals accompanied by hosts of sages.
O Bhārata, it is said that even today those two brothers, having restrained their selves and performing penance there, meditate upon the supreme state.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods,
his ancestors remain satisfied for ten years by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).

The fruit that one obtains by giving a hundred thousand gifts of cows is the same as that which belongs to one who applies ointment in a temple at the beginning of a fortnight and other such occasions.
Through smearing [with unguents], the merit is doubled; through worship, it is fourfold;
and when a lamp is lit, the merit is proclaimed to be eightfold.
Having become possessed of divine vision throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile,
[one should worship] the Lord with curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, and the waters of the Narmadā.
Those who perform the ceremonial bath with flower garlands and ointments, and those who worship the three-eyed god, Nārāyaṇa Hari; RKV 172.41.
They too shall sport in celestial palaces for the duration of an eon,
he who offers eight lamps on the eighth and fourteenth days.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, those who perform the filling of the Liṅga with various auspicious fruits do not behold Yama.
They too travel by means of a celestial chariot attended by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*;
upon that chariot are bells, banners, and garlands of flowers.
Musical instruments appropriate for the occasion bring auspiciousness at the conclusion;
and he who builds a Vaiṣṇava temple dedicated to Māṇḍaveśvara, [attains the highest goal].
The righteous-souled one dwells in heaven until the dissolution of all beings;
he feeds the Brahmins first at the place known as Māṇḍavyanārāyaṇa.
When the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight arrives in the month of Āśvina, by feeding a single Brahmin, it is as if ten million have been fed. (RKV 172.47)
Having undertaken the vow of fasting and keeping a vigil at night,
one should offer worship according to one's ability with a garland of lamps in the four directions.
O King, whether it be a woman or a man, having performed the rites of bathing and so forth at dawn when the sun is bright, amidst dancing, singing, and instrumental music; RKV_172.49.
Having brought this about through silence, one beholds such a God;
liberated from all evil, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Alternatively, O Great King, it may be performed in Mārgaśīrṣa, or in Caitra and Vaiśākha, or in Śrāvaṇa, or indeed at any time whatsoever.
"The merit is equal to that of Śivarātri"—thus was it spoken by Śiva;
the fruit is the same as that of the Vājapeya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and not otherwise.
A woman who is unfortunate, suffering, barren, poor, or whose children have died— any woman who bathes with the jars of Rudra shall obtain all her desires.
O King, all those worms, insects, and moths that die at that sacred ford go to heaven, assuming divine forms.
Those who, afflicted by disease, die through fasting, in water, or in fire, go without return to the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
O King, he who constantly bows down to both Śiva and Nārāyaṇa obtains the fruit of gifting a cow through the power of that sacred ford.
O king of kings, he who performs a circumambulation in a temple has,
by that act, circumambulated the entire earth together with its oceans.
There are one hundred and fifty sacred fords outside Mallikā’s palace;
such is the extent and width of those fords, O best of kings.
One should wrap a sacred field, or a temple of Śiva, or a Śivaliṅga with a thread; hear now the fruit of that merit.
Jambūdvīpa, Kṛtasna, Śālmalī, Kuśa, Krauñcaka,
along with Śāka, Puṣkara, and Gomedaka— these are the seven islands of the earth.
O Indra among kings, by him this land, including its mountains, forests, and groves,
was adorned on the southern bank of the Revā, in the vicinity of the sacred field of Śiva.
The Devakhāta is a place of great merit, fashioned even by the thirty gods;
whoever performs a bath therein is liberated from all sins.

On the full moon day, on the new moon day, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, at the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), and during the conjunction of planets (*saṃgraha*), one should perform the *śrāddha*; he shall go to the supreme goal.
In Devakhāta dwell the three gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— together with the ṛṣis and the hosts of ancestors and deities.
At that sacred ford, specifically on the fourteenth day of the month of Āśvina,
Śakra, stationed on the path of the wind, remains together with the deities.
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, and oceans exist upon the earth—
all those twenty are equal to two days spent at Devakhāta.
Whatever merit is found at Gayāśira, at Makarakaṇṭaka in Prayāga,
and at Somatīrtha in Prayāga— that same merit is found at Māṇḍaveśvara.
Whatever merit is gained by the binding of the turban at Lakuleśvara on the full moon day of Āśvina,
that same merit is obtained at Māṇḍaveśvara during the conjunction of the Aśvinī nakṣatra in the month of Āśvina.
At Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, at Tripuṣkara in Vārāṇasī,
and at Saṃnihatyā when the sun is eclipsed, one should worship the Eternal One at the place called Māṇḍavya.
Knowing this, O Great King, as the most excellent of all sacred bathing places (tīrthas),
one should worship the ancestors and the gods with baths, gifts, and other forms of veneration.
Having remained without food on the fourteenth day and being established in pure vows,
one should worship Śiva with supreme devotion during the night vigil.
And with various baths, O Lord, with flowers and ointments of agaru,
on the morning of the full moon, one should perform the rites of bathing and libations.
By means of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*), the worship and adoration of Śiva,
and sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma* performed according to rule with the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
One whose sins have been washed away and whose self is purified reaps the highest fruit;
O Bhārata, it becomes as if the gift of a thousand cows has been bestowed.
On that day, having performed the ritual ablutions and other rites according to the rules in the presence of Śiva,
one should give gold, a bull, a cow, land, a pair of cattle, and a horse.
One should indeed offer a pair of garments to a handsome man for the sake of Śiva,
as well as sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, and two red cloths.
Homa, recitation, and likewise charity—all that becomes entirely inexhaustible;
even a single *ṛc* verse in the *Ṛgveda*, or likewise a *yajus* formula in the *Yajurveda*.
Standing before the gods, one should recite the *Sāma* alone from the *Sāmaveda*;
he shall indeed obtain the full fruit of the Veda—of this there is no doubt.
By merely reciting the Gāyatrī, one obtains the fruit of the three Vedas;
and by worshipping Śiva, one attains more than a hundred crores of one's lineage.
Whether at a ritual bath, a gift-giving, a śrāddha ceremony, a vigil, or the performance of song and instrumental music,
his destination shall never be anything other than the world of Śiva.
After a long time, one who has entered [this practice] shall enter the world of mortals;
he becomes a wise king, free from all diseases.
Endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, he shall live for more than a hundred years;
and by remembering that sacred ford once again, he becomes absorbed in Maheśvara.
He who indeed worships during the twilight at that sacred ford on a festival day obtains the supreme fruit through the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs.
There, O lord of men, the murder of a Brahmin, agitated by fear, did not move at all within a distance of an arrow-shot in every direction from the sacred field of Śiva.
Wherever he may stand, one who is devoted to sacred fords beholds the trees;
liberated from various sins, he is released—of this there is no doubt.
O Great King, there a chasm is seen in the midst of the water;
this is the story told in the Purāṇas concerning the female monkey who attained liberation through visiting that sacred ford.
There, O Great King, stands a well fashioned by the gods,
in the western part of Śiva, that unsurpassed sacred field of Śiva.
O lord of men, those ancestors of one who performs the rite of releasing a bull at that sacred ford sport at their pleasure in the heavenly world.
The sin incurred by approaching those who should not be approached, the sin committed by officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice,
the sin of theft, the killing of a Brahmin or a cow, and the murder of a guru—
all that sin indeed perishes when the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) is performed.
Whoever listens with concentrated attention to the greatness of Māṇḍavyatīrtha is liberated from all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Māṇḍavyatīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 173.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it is the destroyer of all sins.
It is renowned as Siddheśvara, the destroyer of great sins,
where Maheśvara, the God of gods, attained supreme purity;
formerly, O Pārtha, the trident-bearing God of gods was possessed by ten thousand killings.
In ancient times, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, had five heads;
on account of a certain circumstance, he spoke a false word.
Hearing that, the Supreme Lord suddenly became enraged at him;
the Blessed One then cut off his head with his fingernails.
That [mark] adhered to his hand never fell away;
for it was because of that that the Lord of the Gods wandered over this earth.
Then he reached Vārāṇasī, and there his head fell;
yet even when the skull had fallen, the murder of a Brahmin did not release him.
Then, O Pārtha, having gone to the ocean in the east, as well as in the south, the west, and the north, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [is present].
While wandering through all the sacred fords, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter did not leave him;
however, the Lord reached Sutīrtha on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
Having approached a lineage of preceptors, the self-possessed one requested an expiation;
then, having performed that rite, he became cleansed of his taints.
Then Maheśvara, the God of gods, became free from all taint;
having seized that place from the gods, the Lord then vanished.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been celebrated as Śuddharudra;
it is renowned throughout the three worlds as the supreme remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Month after month, O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the new moon day during the bright fortnight,
one should bathe there according to the prescribed rite and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to the ancestors with a purified inner self;
O King, for twelve years those ancestors will remain well-satisfied by that act.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord, known by the name Śuddheśvara, with perfumes, incense, lamps, and other offerings, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
This unsurpassed Śuddharudra has been told to you, O King,
just as it was heard by me from the presence of the trident-bearing God;
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śuddheśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 174.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should then go to Gopeśvara on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
Whereby, by a single bath, men are liberated from their sins.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and brings about the end of their life there shall go to the abode of Śiva by means of a vehicle yoked with peacocks.
O lord of men, after sporting for a very long time in the world of Śiva,
one attains human status here and becomes a valiant king.
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, accompanied by male and female servants,
and honored by lords of men, that man shall live for a hundred years.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight,
one should, having become pure and observed a fast, cause lamps to be offered there.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should keep a vigil at night;
O lord of men, hear now the fruit that is declared for that act.
For as many thousands of eons as there is a numerical measure of the merit and fruit of those lamps, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
O Indra among kings, at that sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform the ritual of filling the liṅga with lotuses as well as with curd-rice (dadhibhakta).
O best of men, listen to the fruit of merit for him who should perform this:
as many as are the number of sesame seeds, and likewise of curd-rice.
O King of kings, O ruler, whatever is given at that sacred ford in the world of Śiva, one rejoices there for a period of time equal to the number of lotuses for as long as one desires.
All of that cannot be calculated even by multiplying it ten million times;
thus has all this been told to you, the unsurpassed teaching of all the Tīrthas.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gopeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 175.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, in the middle of Bhṛgukṣetra, [is a certain place].
But Kapileśvara is renowned as being especially destructive of sins.
That eternal deity who is proclaimed in the Purāṇas as Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, has assumed the state of Kapila.
Below that is Pātāla, named Sutala, and indeed Nitala is beneath it; below that is Gabhastiga, and Andhatāmisra as well.
And as for the great seventh netherworld (pātāla) situated below,
there indeed dwells the ancient God, the Supreme Lord.
He is Brahmā, he is Mahādeva, he is the god whose banner is Garuḍa;
being worshipped by gods, Siddhas, and those who discourse on Brahman, he remains present.
O Indra among kings, while that Kapila, the teacher of the world, was dwelling there,
the sons of Sagara met their destruction before him in an instant.
Seeing them reduced to ashes, Kapila, the best of sages,
fell into profound grief as he reflected upon their sin.
When all attachments have been abandoned and the mind has been rendered free from objects,
it was improper for sixty thousand [demons] to attempt my destruction.
There is no undoing of what has been done; therefore, by going to the Kāpila tīrtha, I shall liberate myself from my own sin.
Then, having released Pātāla, Kapila, the best of sages,
established himself on the bank of the Narmadā and performed very great austerities.
By means of various vows and fasts, as well as ritual bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth,
he attained supreme nirvāṇa while worshipping the imperishable Rudra.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the Supreme Lord obtains the fruit of a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
When the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight has arrived in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one who bathes there according to the prescribed rite and offers a gift with devotion [attains great merit].
Whether it be very little or even much, that which is given to a brahmin who is a worthy recipient is declared by Śiva, the Supreme Lord, to yield inexhaustible fruit.
When Tuesday arrives on the fourth or ninth lunar days,
a man or an excellent woman, having fasted with devotion, performs a ritual bath.
For seven births, one constantly and repeatedly obtains incomparable beauty, sovereignty, good fortune, and excellent progeny.
Having bathed on the full moon or the new moon day, he offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa);
for him, those [ancestors] remain satisfied for twelve years and go to the abode of the gods.
O King of kings, whoever offers a beautiful lamp with devotion at that sacred ford shall possess great bodily radiance born of his own person.
Indeed, for those creatures who die at that sacred ford,
their departure from the abode of Śiva shall always be one from which there is no return.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kapileśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 176.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the excellent Piṅgalāvarta.
This sacred ford (tīrtha), endowed with all virtues and fulfilling all desires, is difficult to find on earth.
Whatever verbal or mental sin was previously committed through action,
all of that shall go to dissolution upon reaching Piṅgaleśvara.
O King, Śaṅkara has declared that whatever bathing and giving is performed there at Devakhāta shall all become inexhaustible.
Having drawn auspicious water from all the sacred fords on earth and released it there after digging, it became known as Devakhāta (the God-dug) because of that.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, how did that Devakhāta come into being,
and how did all the gods release there the water born of the sacred fords?
Tell me everything, O Brahmin; my mind is eager to hear.

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Rudra, carrying his auspicious water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), wandered over the entire earth together with the hosts of gods for the purpose of purifying the trident, [he came to this place].
Then the gods performed ablutions at the sacred fords beginning with Prabhāsa;
they indeed placed in a vessel water that had arisen from all those sacred fords.
Having reached Śūlabheda, they took the pure water of the Trident-bearer that arose there, and returned to Bhṛgukacchaka.
There he saw Agni, who had yellowish-red eyes and was afflicted by disease,
intent upon fierce asceticism and meditating upon Maheśvara.

Seeing that Agni, the mouth of the gods, was afflicted by many diseases due to the sacrificial portions of the Brahmins and the kings suffering from ailments, the gods, having assembled together, spoke to the god Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
The gods said:
"O Śambhu, let favor be shown to Piṅgala, who is afflicted by disease,
so that his body may become free from ailment and capable of receiving the oblations."
Furthermore, he becomes tawny; act accordingly, O Maheśvara!
Īśvara said: "O gods, I am indeed pleased with your asceticism, and especially because of your words; I grant you your desired boon."
Piṅgala said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, O God, let that which is desired be granted;
having made the moon and the sun your two eyes, remain here established by a portion of yourself."
O Śaṅkara, may my body thus become renewed;
O Virūpākṣa, act accordingly! Homage to you again and again!
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the blessed Śambhu, having assumed a form in the likeness of the Sun,
Śaṅkara removed that disease of his.
Then, having been restored to youth, he spoke again to Śaṅkara:
"O Śambhu, let you remain right here, just as Bhāskara himself does."
For the benefit of living beings, for the pacification of diseases,
for the destruction of evils, and for the increase of auspicious things.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Piṅgala, the Blessed One manifested his descent and spoke this to the gods:
Īśvara said:
"O gods, release the water that has been collected from the sacred fords;
and having dug a beautiful pit to the north of me, make it consist of the gods."
Let the divine water, which destroys all diseases, removes all sins, and is [revered] by all the gods and others, be poured there.
Thus addressed, all the gods dug a trench to the north and released the water born of that sacred site through their throngs numbering thirty-three crores.
All of them together, with Virūpākṣa at their head, [said]:
"Whoever, after first touching the earth in this Devakhāta pond..."
Having performed his bath on a Sunday, having bathed thoroughly in the waters of the Narmadā,
and having performed the śrāddha for the ancestors and given gifts according to his ability;
"He who worships Piṅgeśa shall have his residence in Triviṣṭapa;
this was declared by the gods, and the entire world hears it."
On earth, there are ailments of mortals such as consumption, scabies,
and other diseases of deformed appearance arising from coughs, asthma, and fevers.
Those fevers arising from spirits that recur on the first, second, third, or fourth day,
as well as other morbid humors, ringworm, and jaundice— [may they all be pacified].
Those various types of leprosy, divided into a hundred varieties, go to destruction in seven days by means of baths on the day of the Sun.
He who bathes one hundred and eight times on Sundays,
having worshipped Śaṅkara, should give a vessel of sesame seeds to a twice-born man.
His leprosy shall perish, just as serpents are destroyed by Garuḍa;
having spoken thus, all the gods departed for the abode of the thirty-three.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: A man who regularly performs his ablutions in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, and in streams, is liberated from all sins.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing and giving gifts at sixty thousand holy sites and sixty hundred holy sites, that fruit is even greater at Devakhāta.
O King, he who bathes in the divine pools, gratifies the ancestors, and worships the supreme Piṅgaleśvara, the Lord of the God of Gods; ||| RKV_176.32 |||
O Bhārata, he obtains the merit of both the Aśvamedha and the Vājapeya sacrifices; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Piṅgaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 177.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should then go to Bhūtīśvara, the most excellent among all holy places (tīrthas).
O Indra among kings, by the mere sight of him, one's sin is utterly destroyed.
In that place, O Pārtha, the trident-bearing God of gods formerly smeared his body with ashes; therefore, it is called Bhūtīśvara.
On the Puṣya asterism, on one's birth star, or especially on the new moon day,
a man who bathes at Bhūtīśvara shall deliver ten million members of his lineage.
O lord of men, listen now to the fruit that is declared for one who, with devotion, performs the smearing of the limbs at that sacred place.
For as many particles of dust as adhere to one's body in the temple of Śiva,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Among all forms of bathing, the ash-bath is remembered as supreme;
it has been proclaimed by the ancient seers as unsurpassed in all the scriptures.
Whoever always performs the fire-purification bath once, twice, or even thrice a day, their sin is utterly destroyed.
O bull among the Bharatas, bathing with wind (vāyavya) is superior to bathing with celestial waters;
bathing with the water of Brahmā (brāhmya) is the best after that of the wind, while bathing with the water of Varuṇa (vāruṇa) is superior even to that of Brahmā.
Since the fire-rite (āgneya) is declared by the Self-born One to be superior to the water-rite (vāruṇa),
one should therefore perform the fire-rite bath with every effort.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The fire-weapon, the water-weapon, the Brahma-weapon, the wind-weapon, and the divine weapon—what has been said regarding these? I wish to hear it, for my curiosity is great."

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having immersed oneself in water, one performs the Varuṇa bath; with ashes, the Āgneya bath; with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the Brāhma bath; and the dust raised by cows is known as the Vāyavya bath.
The bath taken when the sun is seen is equal to bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
that is declared to be the fifth divine bath, O best of the Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore, whoever bathes with every effort and worships the Lord Īśāna at Bhūtīśvara is pure both externally and internally.
Those who constantly meditate upon that supreme state—which is subtle, beyond the senses, and eternal—in that place are truly blessed; of this there is no doubt.
That sacred ford is indeed Muktitīrtha, the most excellent among all sacred fords;
by the mere sight of it, even great sin goes to destruction.
Through worship one obtains a kingdom; by praising Maheśvara there, one attains purification from sin through recitation, and through meditation, one enjoys infinity.
Oṃ! You are the very nature of light, without beginning or middle, neither produced nor uttered as a syllable;
you abide within all beings, the auspicious one, the Lord of all yogis, the Lord of all worlds, free from delusion and sorrow, and attainable through supreme knowledge.
O lord of men, that man who goes to that sacred ford and performs an ablution obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice;
yet men who seek liberation do not recognize it as being such.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhūtīśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 178.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the excellent Gaṅgāvāhaka.
On the Narmadā, near Bhṛgutīrtha, there is a place of great merit.
There, the highly meritorious Gaṅgā performed extensive austerities in the past, observing a supreme vow for more than a hundred years.
Having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the stainless source of the universe,
the supreme abode of the Self, that river [flowed forth], O Lord of the World.
Then the god Janārdana, having arrived, spoke this.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Goddess born from the lotus of my feet, I am pleased with your ascetic penance. What do you desire from me? Speak, O Queen; what shall I do for you?"
Gaṅgā said:
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the three worlds, Gaṅgā has fallen from your lotus feet; by chance, she is now being honored by the inhabitants of heaven as her companion."
Therefore, King Bhagīratha, having performed extremely difficult austerities and having propitiated Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World who brings welfare to the world, [attained his goal].
O Upholder of the Earth, you indeed caused me to descend to the earth;
for at your word, I have truly brought about this incarnation upon the world.
Thinking of me as Vaiṣṇavī, people have immersed themselves entirely in me;
indeed, those who belong to the world of Brahmā and those who violate the bed of their guru—[all have been purified].
Those men who abandon their father and mother, those who steal gold, those in the world who kill cows, as well as those who harm living beings; RKV 178.10.
Those who approach women who should not be approached, those who eat what is unfit to be eaten, those who speak falsehoods, and those who are betrayers of trust; // RKV_178.11 //
Those lowest of men who seize the wealth of the gods, of brahmins, or of others;
and those men who utter insults against the gods, brahmins, gurus, or women.
Those twice-born who are consumed by the curse of a Brahmin, those who are self-destroyers, and those who have fallen away from fasting, renunciation, and the observance of fixed vows; 178.13.
Likewise, those who drink what should not be drunk, those who revile their own gurus, those who prohibit acts of giving, and those who are averse to giving to worthy recipients; ||| RKV_178.14 |||
Those who destroy the seasons for their own wives, who are not devoted to their parents, and who indeed have no compassion for distressed kinsmen; (such a person is a killer of the *ṛtu*). 178.15.
One who destroys the boundaries of fields, one who ruins the ancient paths, an atheist, a Brahmin devoid of sacred learning, and one who neglects the twilight prayers; // RKV_178.16 //
Those twice-born who do not offer oblations, who are dissatisfied, who eat all things, who sell all things, who are miserly, atheistic, cruel, and ungrateful; (these are excluded).

Those lowest of the twice-born who consume food from their own kin or from others' kin— men who are slanderers, sellers of liquids, and separated from all [virtuous] times— are excluded at all seasons.
Having reached me, they are liberated from their well-accumulated masses of evil;
yet, because of that evil which scorches me like salt, no peace is found for me.
"O Lord of the World, act in such a way that I may obtain peace.
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods, being pleased, spoke to Jāhnavī.
Viṣṇu said:
"I shall dwell here, accompanied by Gaṅgādhara;
you too, always enter the Revā right here in this very form."
O you who flow through three paths, carry me having reached the soles of my feet,
when the time of abundant water arrives and you are filled with the waters of the Narmadā.
Having reached the rainy season, the goddess will become flooded with water; having inundated both banks, she will reach me as I stand upon the northern shore.
When he shall wash with water the conch held in his hand,
then that which is called the Vaiṣṇava festival, prepared for hundreds of festivals, will be accomplished.
There is nothing comparable to it, such as the transit of Vyatīpāta and other conjunctions, nor even the two solstices; for there is no merit more meritorious than this.
O Goddess of the gods, on that festival day, a person who touches a conch shell and performs a bath in the waters mingled from the Gaṅgā and the Narmadā, [attains great merit].
But merit is the most auspicious of all merits and auspicious things;
since it was upheld by Viṣṇu, peace proceeded from it.
There, at Śaṅkhoddhāra, a person who bathes and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods certainly attains the end of the multitude of evils.
They shall remain satisfied for twelve years and attain the fulfillment of all desires;
this applies to whoever offers a śrāddha at Śaṅkhoddhāra on the Gaṅgāvahe.
By that offering of alms-food, the ancestors likewise dance;
having bathed at Śaṅkhoddhāra, a man should worship Bala and Keśava.
O Jāhnavī, by keeping a vigil at night one becomes pure;
for you consider whatever action is committed by people on earth to be unbearable.
"O best of men, having bathed there on that sacred occasion, you shall cast all that away. Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished.
From that time forward, O dear one, that supreme sacred ford known as Gaṅgāvāhaka has been visited by Brahmā and other sages who have come down through the line of tradition.
O Bhārata, whoever bathes at that sacred ford with a spirit of devotion has,
without a doubt, bathed at all the sacred fords along the banks of the Gaṅgā.
For those men of purified soul who die at that sacred ford,
their departure to the world of Viṣṇu shall never be subject to return.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gaṅgāvahaka Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 179.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Gautameśvara.
This sacred ford, renowned throughout the three worlds, removes all sins.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Gautama performed austerities at that sacred ford for a thousand divine years; thereupon Maheśvara was pleased with him.
Having prostrated with his head there, the Supreme Lord was installed;
because the Lord was installed by Gautama, he is called Gautameśvara.
There, indeed, the gods, Gandharvas, sages,
and ancestral deities attained supreme perfection by propitiating the Supreme Lord.
Whoever bathes at that sacred ford and worships the ancestors and the gods,
and worships the Supreme Lord, is liberated from all sins.
Many do not know this, being deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu;
[namely,] that the god Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, is present there.
But he who, having become a celibate student (brahmacārī), bathes at that sacred ford (tīrtha) and worships Mahādeva, O lord of men, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
But he who, having become a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), gratifies the ancestors and deities and worships the Supreme Lord (*paramīśāna*), is liberated from all sins.
Whoever gives a gift with devotion to a twice-born man at that sacred ford, all of that yields inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O King, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one should offer a hundred lamps.
Having worshipped Mahādeva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
a person is liberated from all sins and, upon death, shall go to the city of Śiva.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and especially on the full moon day of Kārttika,
one should fast, become purified, and bathe Śiva with clarified butter.
Whether with the five products of the cow, honey, curd, or cold water,
that person obtains the fruit of every sacrifice.
Afterwards, one should worship with devotion; by means of unbroken bilva leaves and flowers produced from the unmattaka plant, he shall obtain the supreme fruit.
With kuśa grass and apāmārga, as well as those grown from kadamba and droṇa trees,
and with mallikā and karavīra flowers— red, yellow, white, and black.
The man who worships Śiva with whatever other flowers are available,
or who worships Gautameśvara continuously for six months,
attains all his desires and, upon death, shall go to the city of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gautameśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 180.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the supreme Daśāśvamedhika.
This sacred ford is endowed with all virtues and is the destroyer of great sins.
O Great King, having gone there, bathed, and worshipped Īśvara,
a person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Aśvamedha is a great sacrifice requiring many materials and sacrificial fees; it is impossible for ordinary people to perform. How, then, might they obtain its fruit?"
This reality you have spoken, being a virtuous one, is most wonderful; O long-lived one, speak further in such a way that faith may arise within me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Indeed, this which is truly wonderful was asked of the Three-eyed One by Gaurī;
that I shall now relate to you, who are indeed an inquisitive and discerning listener."
Formerly, O Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, seated upon his bull together with Umā,
once while wandering the earth took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
Having beheld the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha,
the three-eyed Lord Maheśvara joined his palms in reverence toward the sacred site and paid homage.
Seeing the god with his hands joined in a gesture of reverence, the goddess spoke this to him.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, who are saluted by all that is moving and unmoving, why is this?
[Tell me] with supreme devotion, having joined my palms in reverence and bowing low."
O Lord, tell me all of this incomparable marvel.
The Lord said: Behold directly the fruit of the sacred ford; do not be astonished.
O Goddess, remain steady for a moment while I, who stand upon the earth, am situated in the sky.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods became a fair-complexioned brahmin,
his throat emaciated by hunger, with matted hair, withered, and covered with visible veins.
Seated upon the surface of the earth, uttering the mantra in a melodious voice,
Mahādeva, who is fond of the Krama system, gladdened them with his sweetness.
Having heard that sweet voice uttered by the Lord himself,
all the brahmins who had come there to bathe were filled with wonder.
And the daily rites of all were forgotten due to the confusion of the Vedas; yet, seeing him reciting while tormented by hunger and thirst, [they were restored].
Another twice-born man invited him with devotion for a meal, saying:
"O Brahmin, please show me favor by taking a meal at my home."
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my actions have indeed borne fruit.
Today my ancestors, being pleased, will grant all my desires.
"O best of the twice-born, since you have eaten, may you be gracious toward me forever.
Thus addressed, Mahādeva, who was then assuming the form of a brahmin, [replied].
Laughing, he replied to the brahmin with gentle words:
"For a thousand years, I have performed austerities without food."
But now, O best of the twice-born, I shall perform in his house ten horse-sacrifices, by which he has desired the fulfillment of his vow.
Thus addressed by the God of gods, the brahmin, filled with wonder,
shook his head and went toward his own home.
Thus, when their invitations were declined, many of those brahmins—
who did not understand the meaning of the Purāṇas— departed, being for the most part nihilists.
Then a certain learned brahmin, who knew the true meaning of the Purāṇas,
invited the god Śiva, who was assuming the form of a brahmin.
In that very same manner, having been addressed by the god, that best of the twice-born reflected in his mind upon what was declared in the Purāṇas and spoke to him again.
"Whatever has been stated in the Smṛtis, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas shall come to pass exactly so.
Having thus resolved, he spoke to that brahmin as if laughing.
"O Brahmin, wait until my return," having said this,
the twice-born man went to the supreme site of the ten horse-sacrifices (Daśāśvamedhika).
That twice-born man performed his ablutions, the great anointing, and so forth;
having likewise performed recitation, the ancestral rites, and giving in accordance with the Dharma.
Having mentally resolved there regarding a tawny cow according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas,
he quickly arrived at that place where the brahmin was staying.
Then, having arrived, he said to the twice-born man: "The horse sacrifice has been performed by me;
arise, let us go to my delightful home for the sake of a meal."
Thus addressed by that brahmin, Śaṅkara was greatly amazed;
the god said to the brahmin, "Now you have departed from here."
O best of the twice-born, how were those ten great and costly sacrifices performed?
The twice-born said: "You should not entertain doubt; sacrifices have been performed by you, there is no uncertainty.
If the Vedas are authoritative, then so too are the gods and the twice-born on this earth."
O best of the twice-born, if the statement spoken in the Vedas and Purāṇas were beyond doubt, then the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha would likewise be real. (RKV 180.33)
"Then everything was obtained by me; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, [he perceived] the faithfulness of his mind.
Having reflected deeply, he could find no further reply;
he went to that beautiful house, reciting the eternal Brahman.
When that twice-born man arrived, he honored him with devotion by offering water for his feet and the arghya oblation;
thereafter, he gave him food of six flavors according to the prescribed rite.
Then, when Śiva, the Great God who embodies all the gods, had finished his meal,
a rain of flowers fell swiftly from the sky upon his head.
Observing her devotion, the gratified Śaṅkara spoke:
Īśvara said:
"Tell me, O best of the twice-born, what may be done for you today? I am the granter of boons;
I shall certainly give even that which is not to be given to you who are single-minded."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then,
O Mahādeva, you must indeed remain forever at this sacred ford."
"O Lord of Gods, this is my supreme boon for your assistance.
Having been addressed thus by the God, the best of the twice-born ascended.
Honored there, he went to that celestial palace which fulfills all desires and is crowded with Gandharvas and Apsarases, where the worlds are free from affliction.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having seen this incomparable marvel, the Goddess was greatly amazed;
with eyes wide open in wonder, she questioned Śaṅkara once again.
Pārvatī said:
How can this be true, O Maheśvara, since this is inconsistent— that many people indeed perform their ablutions here?
But how did they attain the way to heaven, just as this man has gone to the celestial realm? Explain this to me, for it is a source of supreme wonder to me.
Having heard this, the Lord of Gods, smiling, replied to her regarding the words of the Vedas,
the meaning of the Purāṇas, the meaning of the Smṛtis, and that which was spoken by the twice-born.
Indeed, one should not feel astonishment, for that is merely inference;
for what is proclaimed in the Purāṇas is considered impossible by the people of the world.
O Pārvatī, if people act while placing their own partisan bias at the forefront,
it is no wonder that they achieve no success whatsoever.
For those who are nihilists, who have transgressed the boundaries of conduct, and who are excluded from certainty, no success is found; it arises with certainty only from faith.
Having heard this narrative, the queen paid homage to that supreme holy site situated on the Narmadā, which is meritorious and removes all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Indra among kings, Daśāśvamedha is the most excellent of all excellent holy places;
it is a sacred site endowed with every virtue and the destroyer of great sins.
The highly fortunate Sarasvatī, the most meritorious of all meritorious things and the supreme among rivers, arrived there desiring to bathe.
By the mere name of which one is liberated from all sins;
those who bathe there go to heaven, and those who die there are not subject to rebirth.
O King, having disciplined herself as a celibate student at Daśāśvamedha and having propitiated the Lord of Gods, she attained supreme liberation.
Born from Brahmā, she comes on the tenth day of the month of Āśvina to wash away the turbidity that arises over the course of a year.
Having fasted through that night and worshipped the Destroyer of Tripura,
O King, they go, free from all taint, to the eternal state on the following day.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Sarasvatī is a most meritorious river, the best among rivers.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, on the tenth day of the month of Āśvayuja, that [pilgrimage] is especially distinguished;
there is no doubt that it is so among all earthly sacred sites (tīrthas).
O King, at Daśāśvamedhika, the tenth lunar day (daśamī) is always auspicious;
it is especially so during the bright fortnight of Āśvina, for it destroys even the greatest sins.
Without having bathed, one devoted to fasting should worship the gods;
after performing the śrāddha according to the rules, one should thereafter fully worship Śiva.
One should worship the Goddess Sarasvatī, who resides there and desires to bathe:
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Mistress of Gods, born from the body of Brahmā! (RKV 180.59)
O Goddess, effect the destruction of my evil; deliver me from saṃsāra, having worshipped me repeatedly with perfumes and incense and having honored me again and again.
Having performed ten circumambulations, one should encircle it with thread;
then, O Brahmin, free from envy, one should give a tawny cow as a gift.
Having given a tawny cow, endowed with all auspicious marks and provided with every necessary utensil, to a Brahmin, one does not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
Afterwards, one should keep a vigil, having lit a lamp with ghee,
by means of reciting the Purāṇas and through dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
And one should worship the Moon-crested Lord with those [rites] prescribed in the Vedas;
thereafter, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā at the clear dawn.
One should feed Brahmins with devotion, as well as Śiva-devotees and yogins;
when this is done, O King, one will then properly obtain the fruit of the sacred ford.
If a person bathes at that sacred ford and worships Śaṅkara,
he obtains the supreme merit of the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices.
Purified in soul by that merit, he goes to the world of Rudra,
having ascended a most beautiful supreme vehicle that moves at will.
There, being fanned with yak-tail whisks by divine apsarases, he sports for a very long time amidst auspicious sounds such as cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Then, descending in due time, he will certainly become a king here,
endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, possessing great wealth, and a scorcher of his enemies.
Whatever gift is given at Daśāśvamedha to Śiva-yogins becomes equal to ten horse-sacrifices; there is no doubt about this.
Of all sacrifices, the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is preeminent;
it is difficult for those with meager wealth to perform, and even more so for those who have committed many evil deeds.
"O Indra among kings, at that sacred ford, even that which is difficult for gods and asuras to attain is obtained through bathing and giving gifts; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
O Lord of Men, whether he dies there without desire or with desire, he shall attain divinity; no deliberation need be made on this point.
O best of men, he who should enter the fire at that sacred site shall dwell in the world of Agni until the dissolution of all beings.
O lord of men, he who enters the water at that sacred ford while meditating upon Mahādeva shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
"Whoever should cast off their body at Daśāśvamedha by means of a heroic act, his destination shall indeed be imperishable"— such is the injunction of the Śruti.
Neither those who throw themselves from mountain precipices, nor those who carry staffs, nor even the practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
attain that destination which those who die in a great battle— crowded with banners and resounding with the blasts of drums and conchs— attain in an instant.
Wherever a hero is slain while surrounded by enemies,
