he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not utter words of cowardice.
For one who performs renunciation at Daśāśvamedha according to the prescribed rite,
there is never a return from the world of Rudra.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that merit which is obtained at Daśāśvamedha has been briefly described with supreme devotion; it is the destroyer of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 181.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe in detail the Bhṛgutīrtha.
Having heard which, even a killer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins.
In that sacred place, O king of kings, there is a famous site known as Vṛṣakhāta, where it is said that Bhṛgu performed austerities in ancient times.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For what reason did that best of brahmins, while dwelling at Bhṛgukaccha,
perform such extensive penance and attain supreme perfection?
Who indeed is called Vṛṣa, and by whom was that pit excavated?
O sinless one, tell me all this according to the truth.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O great king, this very question which you have asked—I shall relate all of that; listen with a one-pointed mind, O monarch.
The sixth, however, was the mind-born son of Brahmā, the most excellent of the Bhṛgus;
he performed intense penance in the supreme sacred field graced by Śrī.
For a thousand divine years, that best of sages remained completely withered,
without food and without joy, standing like a piece of wood or a stone.
Then, on one occasion, the glorious Lord of the Gods, accompanied by Umā, arrived by that path, seated upon his excellent celestial chariot.
Having seen the highly fortunate Bhṛgu situated there like an anthill, the Goddess said to the Lord of Gods: "O Lord, what is this that is being seen?"
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, one named Bhṛgu, having performed most severe penance for a thousand divine years, remained solely intent on meditation upon me.
O fair-faced one, he who drinks a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month remains for more than a hundred years.
Having heard those words, Gaurī, her eyes rolling with rage,
spoke to Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the trident.
It is true, O Bull-bannered One, that you are proclaimed in the world as fierce,
merciless, difficult to propitiate, and a source of terror to all beings.
Tell me this: why do you not grant a boon to the brahmin who has been meditating upon Śaṅkara for a thousand divine years?
Thus addressed, O tiger among men, the Lord of the Gods laughed and spoke to Girinandinī in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
A woman perishes through pride; asceticism perishes through anger; cattle perish by wandering too far; and the best of the twice-born perish by eating the food of a Śūdra.
A twice-born man filled with anger [toward Gaurī]—by him no success is attained;
even in tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of years, there is no cause for it whatsoever, O Dear One.
"Even for one such as he, the conduct of anger is great.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu then meditated upon his bull at that very moment.
For, O Blessed One, Brahmā is indeed a bull, and Maheśvara is in the form of a bull;
having attained meditative absorption, he roared repeatedly in an instant.
"What shall I do, O best of gods, and for what reason have I been meditated upon? Whose death shall I bring about prematurely, O Supreme Lord?"
Īśvara said:
"Go, O best of the twice-born, and provoke that most excellent descendant of Bhṛgu,
so that this Gaurī, the peerless beauty of the world, may place her trust in me."
Having heard this, Vṛṣa went to the excellent twice-born Bhṛgu on the delightful bank of the Narmadā, near his hermitage, in order to assault him.
Then, having been seized by the horns, he was cast into the waters of the Narmadā;
thereupon the great sage Bhṛgu became enraged, staff in hand.
Like an animal, I shall strike him on the head with a blow of my staff,
and [seize] his topknot, his sacrificial thread, his lower garment, and his excellent seat.
Having run up from behind, he said to him who was well-restrained: "What have you done? (RKV 181.25)
Bhṛgu said: "O performer of evil deeds, O one of wicked conduct, how will you go away from me, O bull,
after having caused such humiliation and having dug a pit with your hooves?"
Having let out a great roar, he then struck down the Brahmin;
knowing himself to have been struck down by the bull Parameṣṭhin, [he fell].
Bhṛgu blazed with anger like a fire fed by oblations;
grasping a great staff in his hand, it was like a second staff of Brahmā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Brahmin, desiring to kill him, ran after the bull;
seeing him running, that bull [vanished] into the eastern ocean.
Having reached Jambūdvīpa, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Śāka, Gomeda, and Puṣkara, he proceeded from the east toward the southern region.
O Lord of Men, from one island to another, he went to the north and the west,
and then to Pātāla, Sutala, Vitala, and Talātala.
He went to Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, and the seventh netherworld, Pātāla;
from there, seeking his life, that best of bulls proceeded to the world of mortals, Bhūrloka.
Followed by the Brahmin through Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahas, Tapas, Satya, and Janas, he finds no peace anywhere.
Having indeed committed evil, a man oppressed by the power of desire and anger then went for refuge to Brahmā and Viṣṇu as well.
When he was thus abandoned by Indra, Candra, the Ādityas, the Yāmas, Vāruṇas, and Mārutas— by all those lords of the gods and the guardians of the worlds.
Then, as he was being struck by Bhṛgu, the supreme lord Mahādeva, having paid homage to the god, said: "Protect me! Protect me! (RKV 181.36).
O Lord, seeing that bull abandoned by all the worlds like one who is helpless, exhausted, and fallen at his own feet, the God [spoke].
Then the Blessed One spoke these words, preceded by a smile.
Īśvara said:
Behold, O illustrious goddess, O beautiful one, the tranquility of the brahmin.
Pārvatī said: "O Supreme Lord, if you desire to do what is pleasing to me, grant me this boon quickly, before the Brahmin becomes angry with us."
Then the Blessed One, having become one with ashes on his body, matted hair, and a trident, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and Umā as half of his body, spoke to the Brahmin.
"O best of the foremost of the twice-born, since your anger has not been pacified,
therefore, dear one, this place shall become known as Krodhasthāna."
Then, having seen that Śambhu, the three-eyed one, the most excellent Bhṛgu knelt upon the ground and uttered this hymn of praise.
Bhṛgu said:
Having prostrated before the Lord of Beings, the source of existence, the bestower of prosperity, who is beyond fear—
O Lord of the World, being afraid of worldly existence, I desire to make a certain request.
What power does this mortal man have to describe the multitude of your virtues? Even Vāsuki would not suffice, were he not to possess a thousand mouths.

Nevertheless, O Śaṅkara, bearer of the moon, you who have whitened all things with the network of your rays, O Maheśvara, be gracious to me who am vocal in praise and devoted to your feet through devotion.
O Lord, you are the essence of goodness, passion, and darkness, the cause of stability, origination, and destruction;
O Lord of the world, O Master of the universe, [be the refuge] for me who am terrified of worldly existence and devoted to seeking shelter.
Restraints, observances, sacrifice, charity, the study of the Vedas, and the yoga of concentration—
all these together are not worth even a thousandth part of devotion to you.
The perfection of the most excellent elixirs, mercury, and the sword, as well as the success of the cave-dwelling and the sandals—
these signs of those who have bowed to you are clearly visible here in this very life.
O Lord, if one bows with deceit, you still bestow prosperity upon him out of your desire for their welfare;
O Protector, devotion fashioned for the sake of liberation becomes the destroyer of worldly existence.
O Supreme Lord, protect me, who am devoted to the wives and wealth of others, tormented by the pain and grief of being humiliated by others, and intent on gazing upon the faces of others.

O Śaṅkara, protect me who have come to you for refuge— me, whose pride has arisen from excessive conceit, who revels in a fortune that is momentary and fragile, and who am cruel and intent upon the wrong path.
This wretched twice-born man has had his hope for a boon utterly frustrated by his own kinsmen;
O Maheśvara, cut away my thirst! Why do you mock me, a fool?
Swiftly take away my thirst; grant me the Fortune that dwells eternally within the heart.
Cut the noose of pride and delusion, and deliver me from worldly existence, O Lord of Gods!
This divine hymn named *Karuṇābhyudaya*, which bestows all accomplishments, belongs to Bhṛgu; whoever recites it and remembers it goes to the world of Śiva at the end of the body.
Having heard this hymn spoken by Bhṛgu, Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, said, "I am the giver of boons; choose an excellent boon."
Bhṛgu said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, if you are pleased and a boon is to be granted to me,
let this entire field of spiritual attainment (siddhikṣetra) become known by my name."
"You must indeed remain present here together with Umā,
for this is a holy field of the gods by which everything will come to pass."
O Lord of the World, O Lord of Gods, by your grace I shall establish a great shrine at this spot; may my heart's desires be fulfilled.
Īśvara said:
"O twice-born one, was it not known by you previously that this was done by Śrī?
If you consider her to be such, then show due respect to the goddess Śrī."
"Do what you intend; otherwise, that which was done by you for us will be in vain.
Having spoken thus, when the god had departed, Bhṛgu went to Śrī after bathing.
Having broken his fast there and dwelling with her, the brahmin,
accompanied by Śrī, spoke these words at that time:
Bhṛgu said:
"If it pleases you, O blessed lady, and if you are weary from sitting in distress,
then upon your choice, I shall make my own abode in this great field."
Śrī said:
"O brahmin-sage, establish a beautiful place according to my name and according to your own name; it shall be as you intend, for my mind is in agreement."
Bhṛgu said:
"This world is indeed supported by a tortoise; you, O Rame, are situated upon its back.
Having consulted with him, perform what is auspicious together with him."

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Bhṛgukaccha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 182.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Bhṛgu, accompanied by Śrī, went to the tortoise.
Having greeted him according to custom, he spoke these auspicious words.
By you the entire earth is supported, as well as all the worlds with their moving and non-moving beings;
likewise, O Great-minded One, you remain there by virtue of your meritorious nature.
"I shall establish the fourfold system together with Ramā;
if you agree, O Lord, then command me, O All-pervading One."
The tortoise said:
"In this very way, O best of the twice-born, my city shall remain well-established upon me for a long time, marked with my name."
"It is immovable and very firm, dear one; you need have no fear, O fair-eyed one," she said, having heard these auspicious words falling from the mouth of the tortoise.
Delighted and satisfied, Bhṛgu, the son of the Lotus-born Brahmā, together with Śrī,
performed the auspicious rites of consecration once the rising of the Abhijit constellation had arrived.
O bull among the Bharatas, in the year Nandana, on the fifth day of the month of Māgha,
under the auspicious Uttarā constellation, while the lunar orb was situated in Aquarius.
On the northern bank of the Revā, in the deep region of Ābhivāruṇi,
in a place sloping toward the northeast, there is Koṭitīrtha.
That field, measuring one *krośa* and crowded with hundreds of palaces,
was constructed by that best of the Bhṛgus, endowed with the power of asceticism, after he had summoned Viśvakarman in a very short time.
There, the Brāhmaṇas were knowers of the Vedas, the Kṣatriyas were protectors of the kingdom, the Vaiśyas were devoted to their livelihoods, and the Śūdras were servants to the other three.
"Thus, O dear one, this field, surrounded by splendor and gladdened by supreme bliss, was created by Bhṛgu; it is the destroyer of all sins. Thus ends the origin of Bhṛgukaccha.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, after a long time, on account of a certain other cause,
Lakṣmī quickly went to the world of the gods at an assembly of sages.
Having handed over the watchtower and its keys to Bhṛgu, the expounder of Brahman,
protect my station according to its true purpose, O you of noble vows.
Having performed all her divine duties without exception, Śrī returned;
the goddess Ramā arrived at Bhṛgukaccha with great haste.
O Pārtha, when Bhṛgu requested his own house along with its surroundings—the watchtower and the key—then tell me, was that not false? (RKV 182.15)
Thus, O Lord of Men, a very great dispute arose when they met one another, each saying, "It is mine" and "It is mine."
Then, after a long time, the great seer Bhṛgu established a grand system for the purpose of defining the authority of the four Vedas.
O deer-eyed one, O beautiful lady, all the twice-born masters of the four Vedas know our entire city exactly as it is.
Śrī said:
"O best of Brahmins, let there be no doubt; the four castes are my authority.
O most excellent of the twice-born, let them declare whether [the truth] belongs to me or to you."
Then, after all the gods had deliberated among themselves,
they saw that the site of the speech was divided into two parts, with the Brahmins on one side and the king on the other.
The eighteen thousand did not say anything in reply;
O King, because of the fear of Bhṛgu’s wrath, they said:
"This answer belongs to whoever has the *tālaka* in his hand. (RKV 182.21)
Having heard this declaration made by the merchants, that goddess,
overcome with great anger, cursed the foremost of the twice-born.
The Goddess said:
"Since my station has been usurped by those whose minds are afflicted by greed, having utterly abandoned truth, therefore listen to my words."
O twice-born ones, your knowledge may extend through three generations, but wealth shall not last for three generations; nor has a second Veda been studied by you.
O twice-born ones, your houses are not two-storied, nor is your prosperity stable; your dharma proceeds from partiality, and not from the state of ultimate liberation.
A certain beloved kinsman, whose mind is shrouded by greed, will not abandon his duplicity; indeed, there shall be no single truth.
From this day forward, for all twice-born men, there shall be no more egoism:
neither a father in obedience to his son’s word, nor a son in performing his father’s duties.
"All will be brought about by egoism; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus uttered this curse, the goddess Ramā departed for heaven at that very moment.
Then, when Lakṣmī had indeed departed, the gods and the stainless brahman-sages,
having declared this place to be characterized by anger and greed, also went to heaven.
Then, seeing that the goddess had departed as well as the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
Bhrigu, the supreme lord, fell into great despondency;
he then once more sought to propitiate Shankara, the destroyer of Tripura.
O Pārtha, then Maheśvara, gratified by that great austerity,
spoke these words at the proper time, gladdening the best of the Bhṛgus.
"O best of Brahmins, why are you despondent, or what is the cause of your distress?
Even though I am well-disposed toward you, tell me this, O sinless one."
Bhṛgu said:
"In ancient times, after having cursed all the twice-born, Lakṣmī departed;
and having declared, 'This is impure,' the gods then departed as well."
Īśvara said:
What was previously declared by me is exactly so and not otherwise;
there is no doubt that this is a cause for anger, and listen now to another such instance as well.
There, by my grace, the Brahmins shall be born in noble stations and freed from great fear; of this there is no doubt.
Those who have bathed after completing their vows of Vedic learning, who are experts in all the scriptures—
even those hundreds of thousands of them have indeed arrived here in haste.
O best of the Bhrigus, even for one who is unlearned, a fool, and fallen into every possible state of distress, Śakra is able to provide answer after answer; but not so for you.
"O best of Brahmins, from this day forward, this place shall be known as Koṭitīrtha, the destroyer of all sins; of this there is no doubt."
And by my grace, it shall be served by the hosts of gods;
even those worms, insects, and moths who die in Bhṛgukṣetra [shall attain this].
By my grace, they shall dwell in the auspicious world;
a man who bathes in Vṛṣakhāta and worships Maheśvara [shall attain this].
Having bathed at Bhṛgutīrtha and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, a man undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
For twelve years, those ancestors of yours will go to peace, being satiated with curd, milk, water, clarified butter, and honey.
O best of the twice-born, by my grace, those who bathe Virūpākṣa shall dwell in Triviṣṭapa, a place frequented by all the gods.
When a solar eclipse occurs, Bhṛgukṣetra will become equal to Kurukṣetra and other such sacred sites; one should fashion a golden barley-corn [as an offering].
O best of the twice-born, know that he who bathes at Bhṛgukṣetra after giving [gifts] upon his head has, without doubt, performed his ablutions at Kurujāṅgala.
I myself shall dwell here, as will my beloved Ambikā,
the goddess who removes all suffering, known by the name Saubhāgyasundarī.
"I shall dwell together with that goddess at Bhṛgukacchaka.
Having spoken thus, the God remained in Bhṛgukaccha, and Ambikā likewise.
Bhṛgu, however, went to his own city, which resounded with the chanting of the Vedas—
resonant with the sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and filled with the recitation of the Atharvaveda.
"O man, whoever bathes at that sacred ford and releases a bull shall attain union with Śiva; thus spoke Śaṅkara."
Having bathed at that sacred ford in the month of Caitra, one should perform the rites,
and having honored the Saubhāgyasundarī [image], one should give salt to a Brahmin.
May cows, land, and gold be given to the Brahmins; may Lalitā and Śiva be pleased;
and may there be no sorrow, misfortune, or separation from one's husband.
O Indra among kings, a woman obtains [this merit] by bathing at Bhṛgutīrtha;
and he who constantly beholds the god Bhṛgu, O son of Pāṇḍu, [obtains it as well].
O best of kings, hear now what fruit one obtains together with the deities residing there, as far as the abode of Brahmā.

Having given to a twice-born man who is endowed with all vows a tawny cow that has golden horns, yields milk, is virtuous, well-behaved, young, and accompanied by her calf— the fruit that results from this will surely be obtained right here in this world.

O lord of men, one who dies in the water for seven thousand years shall attain the state of twelve fires; and by casting off the body through the conduct of a hero, a mortal of such dharma indeed goes to the hospitality of Śakra.
This narrative is always conducive to fame, leading to heaven, bringing prosperity, granting sons, and bestowing long life;
for by listening with devotion on every sacred festival day, O descendant of Ajamīḍha, one shall indeed obtain all of this.
He who performs renunciation at Bhṛgutīrtha according to the prescribed rite shall,
upon death, go to that supreme state which is indeed difficult to attain.
Having heard this spoken by the God of gods, that best of the Bhṛgus,
the twice-born one, became joyful of countenance and remained right there.
When the Lord had vanished, Bhṛgu, the most excellent of the best of the twice-born,
left his form there and departed for the world of Brahmā.
The origin of Bhṛgukaccha has also been told to you in brief, O Pāṇḍava, O great king; it is the destroyer of all sins.
This holy field, which destroys sins, has been glorified by the Lord;
it is remembered that a day of the Grandfather (Brahmā) consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas.
"O Brahmins, when the day of Brahmā arrives, the birth of the Yugas occurs;
yet Rudra himself declared, 'I do not see this sacred field.'"
"Whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever hears this with devotion goes to the supreme world"— thus Rudra himself proclaimed.
O best of kings, whatever meritorious rites a man performs, such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), after bathing in Devakhāta, they know those acts to yield inexhaustible fruit.
Whoever should listen with devotion to this detailed account of Bhṛgukaccha shall indeed obtain the fruit of ten million holy fords; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Bhṛgukaccha Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 183.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beyond this, O Great King, one should go to the place known as Kedāra.
O Great King, having gone there and performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha), one who drinks the water after worshipping the Lord of the Gods shall obtain the fruit arising from Kedāra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of gods, how is it that he who is himself named Kedāra resides here on the northern bank of the Narmadā? Tell me this in detail.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Maheśvara Śaṅkara was propitiated by Bhṛgu and cursed by Śrī at Bhṛgukacchaka.
"O best of kings, this field shall become impure and devoid of all the Vedas once the beloved of Hari has departed," she said. (RKV 183.4)
Bhṛgu performed extensive austerity for a thousand years;
subsisting on air and taking no food, he remained for a long time with his veins prominently visible.
Then Maheśvara, having become the inferential mark, appeared directly before his eyes;
he suddenly manifested, piercing through the seven netherworlds.
Then Bhṛgu beheld the god like the playful lotus-stalk;
he offered praise to the god Sthāṇu, calling him "Tryambaka."
Thus praised, the Blessed One spoke as if laughing, addressing Bhṛgu again and again: "O sage, what do you pray for from me?"
Bhṛgu said:
"O Lord, this sacred field extending five krośas was cursed by Padmā;
this field is impure and devoid of all the Vedas."
Having said, "It shall come to pass," the goddess departed toward Vidarbha.
O Maheśāna, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased, act in such a way that this supreme field may once again attain purity.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahman, this first liṅga shall be known as Kedāra;
having established this, there will indeed be ten primordial liṅgas."
Indeed, the eleventh [incarnation] shall be invisible within the midst of that field;
the omnipresent Lord himself, as the eleventh, will purify that field.
Likewise, by my grace, the twelve Ādityas shall dwell in person in Bhṛgukṣetra, destroying disease and suffering.
Indeed, eighteen Durgās, sixteen Kṣetrapālas,
Vīrabhadras, and the Mātṛs will appear in Bhṛgukṣetra.
For this sacred field shall indeed be eternally purified;
for by bathing at dawn during the month of Māgha, one who has conquered the senses [attains this].

He who worships Kedāra shall go to the abode of Śiva. Having bathed at that sacred ford, O Bhārata, if a man offers a śrāddha ceremony according to the rules for the sake of his ancestors, his grandfathers become pleased with him.
Thus has the sacred site named Kedāra been fully described to you in detail;
it is meritorious, a remover of all sins, and a destroyer of all suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kedāreśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 184.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Dhautapāpa, which is in the vicinity of Bhṛgutīrtha.
Then Bhṛgu was shaken again and again there by Vṛṣa.
Because of that, it became renowned in the worlds by the name Dhautapāpa;
Mahādeva resides there for the sake of pleasing the best of the Bhṛgus.
O Lord of Men, whoever bathes at that sacred ford, even if out of deceit, is liberated from all sins; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
But he who, having bathed there according to the proper rite, worships Śiva and duly honors the gods and the ancestors, is liberated from all sins.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, at that sacred ford, the murder of a Brahmin and the slaughter of cows shall always enter in fear; even if they have entered, they shall go to their destruction.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me of that which is a marvel in this world—
how it is that the sin of killing a Brahmin does not enter Dhautapāpman.
"There is no sin whatsoever here equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
O twice-born one, how is it that once it has entered Dhautapāpa, it perishes?
I ask all this in detail; tell me out of curiosity."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the beginning of creation, Śambhu formerly beheld the fifth transformation of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, which was shaped like the head of a horse.
By joining the thumb and the finger, he severed that head;
as soon as the head was cut off, the sin of killing a Brahmin departed.
And he was burdened by the sin of killing a Brahmin on the northern bank of the Narmadā,
O King, from which it was shaken off by Vṛṣa, the embodiment of Dharma.
There, the Blessed Lord Śambhu beheld the goddess Dhauteśvarī, who had been established by Vṛṣabha and was worshipped by all the deities.
Having beheld Dhauteśvarī Durgā, the destroyer of the sin of killing a Brahmin,
Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura, rested there.

Śaṅkara, the most excellent God of gods, being greatly amazed, considered himself freed from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter due to the power of that sacred ford, having seen the Brahmin-slaughter far away from the tīrtha.
May the goddess Hatyā, terrified by the fear of the Goddess, enter that place which has been washed of sin and honored by the power of Dharma—
she who is dressed in red garments, adorned with red garlands, dark-complexioned, and bound with red cords.
Desiring me for her shoulder even in private, she stood at a distance by the power of that preeminent sacred site;
then the Lord, the enemy of Smara, reflected in his mind and resolved to dwell in that very tīrtha.
Having reflected at length, the Lord himself, renowned on earth as one whose sins were washed away,
remained there and made his dwelling in that very place, the region known as Vidhūtapāpa.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, that tirtha on the Narmadā, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin and washes away all evil, has remained established there.

O King of kings, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja is especially distinguished at that sacred site; indeed, it is particularly significant for three days beginning with the seventh.
He who, having observed the fast on the eighth day with devotion, recites the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs—the portions known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—in a single day and night; RKV_184.19 //
By practicing this, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
This applies equally to approaching a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) and approaching the wife of one's teacher.
Having bathed in the supreme essence of Brahman with a water-pot, one is completely liberated;
even a woman who is barren, one who gives birth only to daughters, one who is a "crow-barren" woman, or one whose children have died [is purified].

She too, having bathed with water from jars, became a mother of living sons; but a man who has not studied [the Vedas], having fasted, [attains this] through that which originates from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
O King, a Brahmin who recites even a single Ṛgvedic verse on a festival day,
or one who is not learned in the Ṛgveda, should fast and recite the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas.
Reciting [this] on the ninth day, the best of Brahmins is liberated from the accumulation of sins;
thus, my dear, has this been declared by the great seers as stated in the Purāṇas.
This "Washing Away of Evil," which yields great merit, was told to me by Śiva:
whoever should perform the renunciation of life in water, in fire, or even on land.
He travels by means of a celestial chariot, possessing a radiance equal to blazing fire or the sun,
drawn by swans and peacocks, and attended by hosts of apsarases.
In that supreme abode of Śiva, which is difficult even for the gods to attain,
he sports according to his own will as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
But that woman who, O Pārtha, brings about the end of her life at Dhautapāpa, attains manhood at that very moment.
Now, O King, what is the use of saying more? Whatever is done for one whose sins have been washed away—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—all of that yields inexhaustible fruit.
One should renounce food according to the rule; one should renounce sense objects and the like, as well as fruits, roots, and so forth; however, one should not abandon water alone.
O Pārtha, he who acts in this manner goes to the world of Rudra;
having enjoyed all pleasures there, he is born on earth as a sovereign king.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Dhautapāpa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 185.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the excellent Eraṇḍī-tīrtha.
Merely by bathing there, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
In the month of Āśvayuja, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight,
having fasted and bathed with self-restraint, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities.
Endowed with sons, prosperity, and beauty, he shall live for a hundred autumns;
upon death, he goes to the world of Śiva—of this there is no doubt to be made.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Eraṇḍī-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 186.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the most excellent holy site of Kanakhala.
Garuḍa performed austerities after having worshipped Maheśvara.
O Bhārata, as soon as he was born, he remained for a hundred divine years;
having become emaciated through austerities and recitations, he was seen by the god Śambhu.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, spoke these supreme words to Vainateya, who is as swift as thought and the increaser of Vinatā’s joy: RKV_186.3 //
"O illustrious one of noble vows, you have pleased me; choose a boon, O traveler of the sky! I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult to obtain within the three worlds."
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of the gods, I desire to be the vehicle of Viṣṇu and to attain the status of the king of birds;
since you are pleased with me, may all this come to pass—this is my thought."
The illustrious Maheśa said:
"O sinless one, dear child, that boon which you have requested is difficult for living beings to obtain;
to become the vehicle of the God of gods and to attain the status of the lord of the twice-born is exceedingly rare."
The entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, resides within the belly of Nārāyaṇa;
how could you possibly carry him, the God of gods and the Teacher of the World?
By him alone was Indra established as the lord over the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
how then could the status of Indra belong to another? That is extremely difficult to achieve.
Nevertheless, by my word, you shall become a vehicle even for him who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and who sustains the three worlds.
"You shall become Indra among birds; of this there is no doubt.
Having granted him this boon, Hara vanished from that place.
Then, O King, after Mahādeva had departed, the younger brother of Uruṇa propitiated Cāmuṇḍā, who was adorned with severed heads.
The goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, accompanied by many spirits,
a yoginī perfected through yoga, who delights in fat, flesh, and spirituous liquor.
As soon as he meditated upon her, she indeed became manifest before him;
she who is the accomplishment in Jālandhara, in Kaulīna, and in the supreme Uḍḍīśa.
That complete [power] is established in Bhṛgukṣetra, the field of the perfected ones;
there, that goddess Cāmuṇḍā resides in the field of the perfected ones.

O King, for the sake of accomplishing his welfare and security, he— whose birth brought joy to Vinatā— propitiated that Yoginī there with devotion through Vedic and worldly hymns praised by sages and gods.

Garuḍa said: Om! May the goddess Śrīvīramātā, who resembles the stainless moon, protect you—she whose throat is parched with hunger, whose mouth is filled with fresh blood, who sits upon a lotus-throne of corpses, who sports in the cremation ground with throngs upon throngs of spirits, who holds a trident in her hand, who wears a garland of skulls dripping with the blood of multitudes of great heroes destroyed by weapons as an upper garment, and who is clad in skin and carries a severed head. RKV 186.16.

May that Carcāmuṇḍā protect you—she whose throat is parched with hunger, who is deformed, terrifying, and strikes fear into evildoers; she who devours the flesh of the deceased with rows of flaming fangs as sharp as razors;
she who, the Mother of Spirits, dances with her fierce staff-like arms and the clanging of her hand-drum and bells, which sound like the sharp drums of the cataclysmic winds at the end of an aeon;
she who, emaciated by hunger and with a withered belly, gnaws upon the flesh of the dead along with the finest of men, letting out a loud, boisterous laugh amidst a gurgling roar.

May Carmamuṇḍā protect you—she who has a sunken belly, who terrifies those afraid of the fears of existence, who holds a trident in her hand, who is Cāmuṇḍā, the slayer of the headless, who is delightful with the clanging sounds of war-drums and cymbals; she who, dwelling in the cremation ground, dances in the midst of the Mothers, terrifying the three worlds with many terrible roars of "ka-ka-ka-ka."
May Kanakeśvarī protect me— she who, blazing with great splendor, sustains the entire universe through her own portion, and who is merged within the golden blossom.
May the goddess Kanakeśvarī— born from the Himālaya mountains, who has manifested her form out of compassion, the beloved of Śiva, and who is devoted to Śiva— protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī— Padmā, who is the beginningless origin of the world, whose womb is a treasure, who is beloved of wealth, and who holds the discus in her hand— protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī protect me— she who is Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Mṛḍānī, Vāk, and Indirā, and who bestows happiness upon those who remember her.
May Kanakeśvarī— the supreme power, the supreme intellect, who always creates and protects the world through both gentle and fierce forms— protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī protect me— she who, at the time of Brahmā’s creation, is the supreme power of emanation, the illusion of the world, and the sustainer of the universe.
May Kanakeśvarī, the primary power of Viṣṇu for the protection of the universe who brings about the intoxication of Madana, protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī— the primary Raudrī Śakti who is resorted to by Rudra at the dissolution of the universe, who is auspicious and infinite— protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī, who formerly dwelt within golden blossoms grown upon the peaks of Kailāsa and was carried away by Bhasmaka, protect me.
May Kanakeśvarī protect me— she who desires her husband’s splendor, who trembles without her lord, and who, though weak, remains single-mindedly devoted.
May Kanakeśvarī, who is intent on the protection of the universe, who was protected by Kanaka, and who is the mother of all from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, protect me.
May the primordial Śakti, Kanakeśvarī, who by her power caused Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara to assume their bodies, protect me.
Having heard the four verses concerning the Goddess spoken by Garuḍa,
she became gracious, appeared before him, and spoke these words.
Śrī Cāmuṇḍā said: "I am pleased with you, O great being; choose a boon that you desire.
I shall grant it to you, O best of the twice-born, whatever is pleasing to your mind."
Garuḍa said: "By your grace alone, may I become undecaying, immortal, invincible by gods and asuras, and unconquerable by any others."
"And you, O Goddess, must always remain here in the vicinity of this sacred ford.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, "So shall it be," the Goddess was praised by the gods.
O best of kings, when Lakṣmī had established that supreme city, she entered the sky and departed accompanied by a multitude of beings.
Having then obtained the permission of the Goddess, he offered it to her.
Lakṣmī said:
"O Goddess, for the sake of protection and for the accomplishment of well-being and prosperity, I have [accepted this]."
"O Goddess, my city must always be protected by you as if you were a mother.
Then Garuḍa also bathed and worshipped Kanakeśvarī.
Having established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) right there, he departed for the highest realm of space.
Whoever bathes in that tīrtha and worships the ancestors and the gods—
He who worships Kanakeśvara with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
For him, the perfection of mastery over yoga arises in the seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas).
Upon death, accompanied by auspicious sounds such as shouts of victory, he goes to the world of the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara), joined by the host of Yoginīs; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Kanakhaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 187.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go to Jāleśvara, the primordial liṅga of the Self-born (Svayambhū).
The renowned Kālāgnirudra is established at Bhṛgukaccha.
It pacifies all evils, destroys all calamities,
and has arisen out of compassion for the destruction of the sins of the field.
In a former eon, when the three worlds were overrun by hosts of asuras,
when the rites prescribed in the Vedas were destroyed, and when dharma had gone to ruin;
Among the gods, seers, sages, and perfected ones who were supremely full of faith,
smoke arose from Kālāgnirudra, born from the source of Time.
The linga that had arisen from smoke, having pierced the seven netherworlds (pātāla),
remains right there after creating a pit to its south.
O best of kings, at that sacred ford is the pool born of the flame,
where that flame of Śiva fell as he was burning the city.
There, a pit appeared, and from it arose a whirlpool of smoke;
indeed, whoever performs a bath in that pool within the waters of the Narmadā, [attains the highest state].
One should indeed perform a śrāddha for the ancestors and worship the Three-eyed One;
by reciting the names beginning with Kālāgnirudra, he shall go to the supreme goal.

Whatever rite one performs here at this sacred ford— whether it be for the fulfillment of desires, or indeed for malevolent purposes, or even for the destruction of enemies, or likewise for the continuity of one's lineage— all of it, O King, is accomplished without delay.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kālāgnirudra Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 188.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O great king, at a distance of forty steps, [is the next site].
Thereafter, one should go to Śālagrāma, which is worshipped by all the deities.
There dwells in person the primordial god, the blessed Vāsudeva Trivikrama, the soul of the world, out of a desire for the welfare of all.
Having himself performed austerities and recognized Bhṛgukṣetra on the bank of the Revā as a field of spiritual perfection (siddhikṣetra), Nārada established a hall for the twice-born.
The deity known as Śālagrāma is the one who has taken up residence among the Brahmins;
Vāsudeva is established there for the benefit of the virtuous.
For the benefit of yogins, Janārdana, who is the object of meditation for yogins, took refuge on the bank of the Narmadā under the very name Śālagrāma.
When the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight occurs in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should bathe in the holy waters of the Revā and fast on that day.
One should keep a vigil at night after worshipping Janārdana,
and again at the time of dawn on the twelfth day, in the waters of the Narmadā.
Having bathed and offered libations to the gods, as well as to the fathers and mothers, he should thereafter perform the śrāddha for the ancestors according to the prescribed rule.

Having honored the Brahmins according to one's ability by giving gifts of gold, clothing, and food, and having asked those Brahmins as well as the Lord whose banner is the bird for forgiveness; 188.9.
O Great King, O best of monarchs, listen attentively to the merit that shall accrue to men when this is performed. RKV_188.10
He shall not encounter sorrow or suffering here; like one who is dead while yet living, he attains equality with Murāri.
Having cast off great sins, he never again drinks from his mother’s breast, even when it is raised for him.
Whoever, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā which destroy the flood of sins, constantly beholds the Śālagrāma,
is liberated from the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such crimes by that very remembrance of Nārāyaṇa.
Those who, having renounced the world, dwell there having subdued their sufferings and are liberated from attachments,
meditating indeed by means of the Sāṃkhya method upon the fourth state of Murāri— they too go to that very place.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śālagrāma Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 189.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
Wherein the Boar, the upholder of the earth, indeed arose in his exalted form.
Bearing this earth with his bow and his terrible-tipped tusks,
he is proclaimed as the fifth [incarnation], Vārāha, the bestower of liberation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How did the upholder of the earth become one of such exalted form?
By what means did he attain the state of a boar, and by whom was he designated as the fifth?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, in the primordial kalpa of old, the Blessed Lord Hari lay upon the ocean of milk on his serpent-couch, deluded by yogic sleep.
O best of kings, having gone into the presence of the gods, she said: "I am oppressed by this burden; I shall go to the netherworld."
Seeing this, the gods became deeply distressed and went to where Janārdana was;
there they praised Keśava, the Lord of the World, with pleasing words.
The gods said:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Gods, remover of the afflictions of the deities, omnipresent one!
O you whose form is the universe, homage to you; protect us all from great fear!"
Thus addressed by the deities, the Lord said: "What has arisen?
O gods, tell me my task; whatever must be done, do not delay."
The gods said:
"Dharā, the supporter of beings, is sinking down, distressed by her burden.
Lift her up, O Hṛṣīkeśa, and establish the worlds in their proper state."
Thus addressed by all the gods, the omnipresent Keśava, the Supreme Lord,
assumed the form of a boar, which consists of all sacrifices.
Having made Ananta his footstool, he raised up the earth with the tip of his fang, appearing formidable with his fangs, tawny-eyed, and with his hair matted and curled.
Having lifted up the earth, together with its mountains and forests and girdled by the ocean,
the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu arose in his exalted form.
Manifesting his self in five ways on the northern bank of the Narmadā—
thus the first at Koralā and the second at Yodhanīpura.
In the place named Jayakṣetra, it is proclaimed as "Jaya";
the third is proclaimed as the Liṅga that deludes the Asuras.
Since he who possesses the luster of the moon stands for the sake of purifying the world,
therefore, O tiger among kings, he is called Śveta.
Having uplifted the Goddess of the worlds at Bhṛgukacchaka, he rose up;
thereafter, the fifth incarnation arose, known by the name Varāha.
Thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, those five Varāhas have been described to you;
their simultaneous vision removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Especially on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should go to Ādivarāha when the tenth day has arrived.
One should eat sacrificial food at a light meal when the sun has set;
indeed, one should keep a vigil at night during the [festival] known as Ādi-vārāha.
Then, at the break of dawn, having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods with sesame seeds mixed with barley;
One should give a cow adorned with all ornaments to a worthy twice-born;
free from possessiveness and free from ego, one should bestow this gift upon the twice-born.
Having gone there, one should worship the god known as Vārāha, the Primordial One;
having worshipped according to this rite, one should thereafter proceed swiftly toward victory.
Having quickly gone to the place of victory, one should perform the preliminary rite;
one should give a horse that has emerged victorious to the foremost of the twice-born.
In the case of the *liṅga* [defilement], sesame seeds should be given; in the case of the *śveta*, gold alone;
and in the case of the *udīrṇa*, one should give land and perform the previously mentioned rite.
O Pārtha, listen now with a single-minded focus to the fruit that one obtains by beholding five boars before the sun has set. RKV_189.25 //
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife, associating with those who commit these acts, and the deception of those who trust one; 189.26.

O best of the Bharatas, from birth until death, whatever sin one commits through the gratification of one's sisters, daughters, female siblings, or the wives of one's kinsmen— [all that is destroyed by this].
For a Vaiṣṇava, especially one purified by the five sacred fords (tīrthapañcaka),
[all sins] would perish simultaneously like a heap of cotton from fire.
Through the recollection of Nārāyaṇa, and especially through the practice of recitation and meditation,
even sins as massive as mountain peaks are utterly destroyed.
Having seen five boars while standing in great manliness,
he bathed in the waters of the Narmadā after having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rite.
"Whoever beholds Loṭaṇeśvara before sunrise and sunset shall be liberated from the body;
thus spoke Śaṅkara."
He attains suddenly liberation from the Supreme Goddess, who is otherwise difficult to reach;
even when human effort is exerted, if success does not arise, [liberation is still attained].
They even speak of the going to heaven for one who is possessed of sin;
yet wherever such a person may go, there indeed shall be the state of a *pañcavarāhikī*.
On the eleventh lunar day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a man shall certainly dwell there;
[he should visit] Ādi, Jaya, Śveta, and likewise the Liṅga Udīrṇa.
One should observe the boars here and there by relying upon her,
on the eleventh lunar day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, by Viṣṇu, the Lord Viṣṇu.
O Lord, having assumed the form of a boar, the Earth was uplifted by him;
she is more meritorious than merit itself, for she destroys the entire flood of sins.
Having seen the five boars and the Boar of uplifted form,
one should worship them according to the prescribed rite and thereafter perform the ritual vigil.
Having devoutly lit lamps with five wicks using clarified butter,
[one should worship] with the listening to Purāṇas, dances, songs, and most auspicious instrumental music.
O descendant of Ajamīḍha, listen now to the merit that a mortal obtains after spending the night in the recitation of the Vedas and other purifying prayers.
O King, the water of the Revā is the most meritorious on earth, and likewise is Lord Hari, the master of the worlds;
the Ekādaśī, which removes the sins of men, is attained only through great exertion.
O King, each one individually is capable of destroying the multitude of sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin;
yet all these together, even when assembled simultaneously, are not capable of destroying it—why is that, tell me, O King?
O son of Dharma, having heard what has been spoken here by you and what was heard from Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one—
by hearing this, one desiring liberation is freed from all sins, and by reciting it, one indeed goes to the abode of the enemy of Vṛtra.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Udīrṇavarāha Tīrtha," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 190.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha.
It is renowned as Candrahāsa, worshipped by all the deities.
Where King Soma, the best of gods, attained supreme perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How did King Soma, the lord of the world, attain perfection?
O sinless one, I wish to hear all of that; please tell it to me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O descendant of Bharata, it is said that in former times Dakṣa, the lord of sages, cursed him [Dhruva], saying:
"Because of your failure to attend to your wife, you shall become afflicted with the disease of consumption."
O best of men, hear now what the ultimate fate becomes for those who do not attend to their wedded wives.
"By serving women during their fertile period, a son is born;
from a son come both heaven and liberation—such indeed is the injunction of the Vedas. (RKV 190.6)
Those men who do not serve her with the dharma appropriate for that time incur the sin born of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Enveloped by that terrible sin, he shall fall into the Raurava hell;
there, wicked beings drink his blood for as long as time permits.
Then, at the time of his descent, whichever womb he enters,
in each and every one of them that evil-minded one is always born unfortunate.
In women, desire indeed always increases;
it especially breaks forth with the arrows of passion at the time of the menses.
For she, being treated with contempt by her husband, meditated upon another man as her spouse;
consequently, a son was born to her, and he wanders through an excellent family.
O lord of the earth, by that [act], even the ancestors who were previously established in heaven fall as soon as he is born; therefore, he is called a *kulaṭa*.
By the ripening of that karma, the Moon indeed became afflicted with consumption;
having abandoned the world of the lords of the gods, he came to the mortal realm.
Having wandered there among many sacred fords and holy shrines, he reached the Narmadā river, which destroys all sins.
He practiced fasts, gifts, vows, and restraints for twelve years; consequently, he was liberated from all sins.
Having established Mahādeva, the destroyer of all sins,
he went, filled with radiance, to the unsurpassed world of Soma.
For as many years as the deity established by him is worshipped,
for that many thousands of yugas he enjoys the world.
Therefore, men establish on earth the deities as prescribed by the rules;
for in this way, the fruit becomes inexhaustible and imperishable, and not otherwise.
But that man who, having bathed at Somatīrtha, worships the Lord Īśvara,
becomes a beloved sight to the knowers of Soma.
Whoever goes to Candraprabhāsa and performs the ritual bath according to the rules shall not be overcome by disease, nor shall they be afflicted with consumption.
O Lord of Men, having bathed at Candrahāsya on the twelfth lunar day,
one should fast on the fourteenth day and offer an oblation of milk-rice (caru) into the fire.
With the five mantras, one should worship Īśāna, Puruṣa, and Tryambaka;
having personally consumed the remainder of the oblation, one should gaze upon the Lord Candrahāsyeśa.
O King, by this method, the Lord Maheśvara is pleased;
through this ritual application of the sacred ford, one is liberated from the disease of consumption.
Whoever performs a ritual bath there on seven Mondays,
worshipping Śiva, is indeed liberated from diseases caused by the ears.
Likewise, O King, eye disease perishes at Candrahāsya; moreover,
he who goes to Candrahāsya during an eclipse of the moon or sun and performs a bath with devotion is liberated from all sins.
O best of excellent kings, whatever bathing or giving— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is performed there at Candrahāsya, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones; their birth is a life well-lived—those men who, having bathed in Candrahāsya, witness an eclipse.
Whatever verbal or mental sin was previously committed through action,
O Indra among kings, it perishes at that sacred site by the mere act of bathing.
Many, possessed by great delusion, do not know that [Self] which resides within the body of all beings like the Supreme Self.
Whatever fruit is obtained by going to Somatīrtha in the western ocean, one obtains all of that at Candrahāsya; of this there is no doubt.
By bathing at the Saṃkrānti, the Vyatīpāta, the Viṣuva, the Ayana, and likewise at Candrahāsya, a man is liberated from all sins.
They are deluded, they are of evil conduct, and their birth is fruitless;
for they do not know the Candrahāsya situated upon the Narmadā.
O King, whoever undertakes renunciation at Candrahāsya shall never again return from the world of Soma; such is his destination.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Candrahāsya Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 191.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should then go to Siddheśvara, which is in the very vicinity of that [place].
That primordial Liṅga, the Svāyambhuva, likewise flows with nectar.
By merely seeing it here, a man becomes free from his debt to the ancestors,
even after having propitiated the Supreme Lord for more than a hundred years in the past.
The twelve Ādityas themselves shall attain supreme perfection;
therefore, he is proclaimed as Siddheśvara, the bestower of success upon those who desire it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, how did the gods attain perfection at Siddheśvara?
That which was mentioned regarding the Ādityas has caused me great wonder."
O best of the twice-born, for what reason did the Ādityas resolve upon fierce austerity, and how did they attain their desired perfection?
"But I have asked you only in brief; O twice-born one, tell it to me in detail."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From Aditi were born the twelve Ādityas, headed by Śakra:
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu—
these are the twelve Ādityas who desire the station of Bhāskara.
O great king, having taken refuge on the bank of the Narmadā at Siddheśvara, those high-souled descendants of Kaśyapa were established in fierce asceticism.
The supreme perfection was attained by those known as the twelve Ādityas,
and Divākara, the sustainer of the world, was established at that sacred ford.
O King, from that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) became renowned on earth by the name of the Twelve Ādityas, due to the division of their own portions [by the Sun].
O King, when the dissolution has arrived at the end of the age, those twelve Ādityas indeed arise from the Twelve Ādityas.
Indra blazes in the east, and Dhātṛ likewise in the region of Agni;
Gabhastipati is in the south, and Tvaṣṭṛ faces the direction of Nairṛta.
Varuṇa is in the western quarter, while Mitra is likewise in the northwest;
Viṣṇu is in the northern direction, and Vivasvat is in the domain of Īśa (the northeast).
Savitar indeed [shines] above, while Pūṣan dries up [the world] from below;
likewise, the radiant Viṣṇu is the world that has issued forth from his mouth.
Scorching everything, O best of men, they wandered here and there, O great king, just as they consume the entire world.
In the same way, the twelve Ādityas are the means for accomplishing the spiritual disposition of devotees;
he who, having risen early in the morning and bathed, [worships] that which is known as the Twelve Ādityas—
Listen to the fruit that belongs to him who beholds the Lord of the gods:
whatever verbal, mental, or physical sin was previously committed.
O Bhārata, for one who performs a circumambulation of that deity, [any evil] perishes at that very moment, as if by beholding twelve suns.
By him the entire earth has been circumambulated; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, the fruit that is obtained by fasting on the seventh lunar day at that sacred site— RKV_191.20.
Except on the seventh of the seventh [lunar day], they obtain [the fruit] and yet do not obtain it;
however, on the sixth day of the week, by beholding twelve suns during the daytime, they obtain it.
Whoever performs a circumambulation, his sin is destroyed;
he shall indeed be free from disease for seven births—of this there is no doubt.
But he who, with devotion, performs a hundred circumambulations day after day [shall be freed from] ringworm,
pustules, leprosy, circular skin lesions, and eczema.
All diseases perish like serpents before Garuḍa;
by practicing this for sixty days, he shall obtain a son.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Dvādaśāditya Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 192.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O dear one, is the unsurpassed Devatīrtha.
Upon seeing the Lord of Śrī, a human being on earth is liberated from sins.
The divine Janārdana was the son-in-law of that great seer Bhṛgu.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Sage, who is this lord of Śrī, the god who is the sovereign and all-pervading ruler of the gods? How did his birth come to be among the three deities?"
And how did Keśava become a relative of Bhṛgu?
O Brahmin, descendant of Bhṛgu, you ought to tell this to me in detail.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall relate the great life-story of Sādhya in brief;
indeed, all the great ṛṣis are not able to tell it in full detail.
O King, the four-faced god was born from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa; Dakṣa was his son, born from his right thumb.
O bull of the Bharatas, it is said that Dharma was born from between his breasts, and he became the son of that [Manu]; even though he was unborn (aja), he had Nārāyaṇa as his companion.
Marutvatī, Vasu, Jñānā, Lambā, Bhānumatī,
Satī, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, Viśvāvatī, and Kakup.
These ten highly resplendent daughters of Dakṣa were his lawful wives;
from them, O King, the illustrious Sādhyas begot sons.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa—
these four sons of Dharma are indeed portions of portions of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Nārāyaṇa and Nara performed supreme austerity on Mount Gandhamādana, having established the self within the self.
Meditating upon his own cause, which is incomparable, causeless,
indefinable, inconceivable, and without interval— Vāsudeva.
Those two great-souled ones, established in yoga and performing intense austerities,
caused the sun not to scorch them by the power of their penance.
The wind blew hesitantly, yet with a pleasant touch;
though the fire was blazing, it became exceedingly cold.
Lions, tigers, and other beasts roamed peacefully on the mountain together with deer;
O Lord of the Earth, the earth was as if oppressed by their weight, like a cow.
The mountains trembled and the great ocean was agitated;
and the gods, their splendor struck down, became lusterless in their own celestial abodes, O protector of the earth, having fallen into a state of supreme agitation.
Then Śakra, the king of the gods, being distressed by their asceticism,
dispatched apsarases there with the desire to create obstacles for the two of them.
Indra said:
"O Rambhā, O Tilottamā, O Kubjā, O Ghṛtācī, O beautiful Lalitā,
O Pramlocā, O fair-browed Sumlocā, O Saurabheyī, O highly haughty one!"
O Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā, and Varūthinī,
she bore a body worthy of being gazed upon, awakening the god of love.
Having reached Gandhamādana, carry out my command;
there dwell the two brahmins Nara and Nārāyaṇa, engaged in the initiation of ascetic penance.
Those two sons of the Dharma are performing a most difficult penance; while they are performing that supreme austerity, our beautiful women [are left behind].
"Since these two bring about the destruction of future suffering caused by the excess of karma, you should go; no fear should be felt by you regarding this word."
Smara shall be his ally, as will spring and beautiful women;
for upon beholding beauty and youth, which are the supreme excitants of passion,
what man does not fall helpless under the sway of Kandarpa?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, O lord of the earth, all the Apsarases, together with Madana and Vasanta, then departed along with the king of the gods.
Having reached Gandhamādana, which was filled with flocks of male cuckoos and possessed lovely forest trees in full bloom, Mādhava wandered there.
A breeze, following from the Malaya mountains, blew toward the southern quarter;
the forest became delightful with the humming sounds of swarms of bees.
And immediately, a fragrant scent arising from the rows of forest trees became a gratification to the olfactory senses of the kinnaras, uragas, and yakṣas.
And all those beautiful women began to entice the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa with their speech, graceful gestures, and smiles.
One Apsaras sang a captivating song, another danced there,
and yet another played most enchanting music, O King.
With gestures, expressions, glances, laughter, and likewise with other charming words,
the slender-limbed women made an effort to disturb the two of them.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Earth, not the slightest mental transformation occurred in those two, whose minds had reached the further shore of the inner self.
O King, just as two lamps standing in a windless place remain motionless,
even so did the minds of those two abide, established in the state of being offered to Vāsudeva.
Just as the great ocean, even when being filled with waters from another land, does not undergo agitation, so too his mind remains unperturbed at any time.
Regarding Brahman— the supreme Vāsudeva who is the welfare of all beings—
as their very self, they did not fall under the sway of passion or hatred.
Then even Smara was unable to enter the hearts of those two, just as darkness cannot enter a dwelling filled with light through the power of a spell.
The great sage beheld the excellent trees radiant with flowers, the spring season, the southern breeze,
all those celestial nymphs, and Kandarpa as well.
And as they performed that austerity, O bull among men, they beheld their own Gandhamādana mountain in its entirety as the form of Brahmā.
Indeed, fire does not burn itself, nor do waters moisten themselves;
for that very substance cannot be the cause of a transformation in that same substance.
Then, having repeatedly realized the Supreme Brahman in its true nature,
no transformation occurred in those two toward Madhu, Kandarpa, or the women.
Then, O King, Vasanta and Madana exerted even greater effort again and again to agitate those slender-limbed women.
Then Nārāyaṇa, summoning his fortitude with an exalted mind, produced from his thigh a beautiful-limbed woman at that time.
O Lord of the Earth, the entire jewel-like beauty of the three worlds attains insignificance in its qualities immediately upon the sight of her.
Upon beholding her, O protector of the earth, the wind trembled in his mind;
Spring was filled with wonder, and Smara remembered something.
O protector of the earth, Rambhā, Tilottamā, and the other celestial women were filled with embarrassment; their hearts and glances were fixed upon him, and they no longer shone.
Then Kāma, Vasanta, and those celestial nymphs of the king,
having bowed down to those two blessed ones, praised the two best of sages.
The Apsarases, longing for spring, said:
"May the Sustainer of the World be gracious; deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of that God, we do not perceive the distinction between the two."
May that God be gracious to you both, whose form is twofold,
who is the abode of the worlds, beginningless, and without support.
May both the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who bear the conch and the discus as their weapons,
look upon us offenders with faces brightened by grace.
The storehouse of all sciences, the fire that consumes the forest of all evils—
may the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, therefore, dispel every sin.
The glorious Nara, whose weapon bears the mark of the Śārṅga bow, who consists of self-knowledge, and who is sinless,
has destroyed all the sins of every embodied being.
This one, with his mass of matted locks bound together, has gentle faces and eyes; may he indeed destroy the sins accumulated over lifetimes by us two who are patient.
Likewise, through the fault of ignorance regarding the Self, a great offense was committed by those who came to seduce the two Lords, who are worthy of veneration in the three worlds.
Be gracious, O Lord, whose wealth is wisdom; for the virtuous are always protectors of their own duty, even toward those of deluded vision.
Having seen this, it has arisen in us that just as an excellent jewel among women has appeared, so too,
O Nārāyaṇa, has the most supreme and far-reaching wisdom been born within you.
By that truth, O Truth-Self, O Supreme Self, O Eternal One,
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord, refuge of all the worlds, be gracious!
O you of serene intellect, peaceful soul, with a gracious countenance and eyes—
be gracious, O Lord of yogis, O Man, O All-pervading One, O Imperishable One!
We pay homage to the divine Man, as well as to Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
salutations to Nara, who is worthy of being bowed to, and salutations to Nārāyaṇa as well.
O Lord, may that Man grant welfare to us who are serene, who are without a protector, and likewise those who have a protector; O Nārāyaṇa, bestow welfare upon us!
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus honored with hymns of praise, O King, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all beings and free from passion, hatred, and the like, spoke from their midst.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Welcome, O Mādhava, O Kāma, and also to you, O Apsarases!
Let that purpose for which you have come here be stated by us."
"Surely you have been sent by Balaripu for our complete destruction;
therefore, this display of dancing, yoga, and so forth before us."
We are not indeed lured by song and dance, nor by bodily gestures and speech;
I consider sense-objects to be of a terrible nature.
O auspicious ones, when our senses are not corrupted by attachment to sound and other objects,
how could states such as dancing and the like be provocative of greed?
We have indeed attained our goal; we are no longer to be won over by you, nor by Smara, nor even by Mādhava.
Let Śakra also attain his composure, free from all apprehension.
He who is that other, the supreme Person, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self of all that is stationary and moving; RKV 192.65.
He is the cause of their origination and that in which everything is dissolved;
because he is the abode of all and possesses divinity, he is proclaimed as Vāsudeva.
We are portions of portions of that venerable one who possesses the fourfold manifestation; following the path ordained by him, we exist for the awakening of embodied beings in the world.
Seeing Him as the Self of all beings, the Lord of all, and perceiving Him with equanimity everywhere— how could we, who see thus, harbor distinctions such as passion and the like?
When that very self of all beings exists within me, within Indra, within you ladies, and likewise within the God of Love, how then can there be hatred and the like?
Since Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, is identical with and undivided from all living beings, how then could there be passion and the like?
Brahmā, Indra, Īśāna, all the Ādityas and Maruts,
the Viśvedevas, the Ṛṣis, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, and likewise the hosts of Pitṛs.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and the like; nāgas, serpents, and reptiles; those in the form of humans, birds, cattle, elephants, lions, and aquatic creatures.
Flies, mosquitoes, gadflies, locusts, and aquatic insects;
worms; and among the species of shrubs, trees, creepers, climbing plants, bast fibers, and grasses— RKV_192.73.
O celestial nymphs, whatever is either invisible or visible,
consider all that to have been born from the one Supreme Self.
O celestial women, how could one who is being born, or even Viṣṇu himself, or that which is supreme, ever give rise to passion, hatred, and likewise greed?
Since Viṣṇu consists of all beings, is omnipresent, and is the sustainer of all,
how could qualities such as passion exist once he has been separated from them?
Thus, since we, you, and all beings are powerless,
and have become one with that [reality], how can there be any occasion for passion and the like?
This is declared to be right view, which perceives the unity of all things;
it is merely a distinct cognition, like the conventional dealings of the world.
Since this entire world consists of the elements, the senses, the internal organs, primordial matter (pradhāna), and the spirit (puruṣa), what indeed could constitute its differentiation?
The waves of the ocean's waters undergo subsidence and arise;
they are not divided by a division of the water, and likewise this world exists through its unity.
Just as the flames of a fire— whether yellow, tawny, reddish, or grey—
are not distinct from the fire itself, so too is this world not distinct from Brahman.
And as for that agitation which Purandara causes us,
you ladies are inflicting what is improper upon those whose minds are fixed on discernment and right conduct.
These ladies, that lord of the gods, and the worlds together with the Suras and Asuras,
including the oceans, mountains, and forests, all come within the range of my body.
Just as this woman, beautiful in all her limbs, has been shown by me before you,
so too shall I show the entire world.
Let Śakra depart; do not be proud, for whose sovereignty over Indrahood is truly stable?
And you, do not succumb to arrogance, for there are women endowed with beauty.
When no distinction is perceived, how can there be "beautiful" or "ugly"?
For gradations in beauty are always observed through the perception of difference.
Perceiving your pride born from the excellence of your beauty and noble qualities, I have displayed this slender form; through this, you shall attain tranquility.
"Since this auspicious woman with eyes like blue lotuses has been produced from my thigh, she shall become a supreme Apsaras named Urvaśī."
Therefore, let this woman of excellent complexion be led to the King of the Gods;
for he, desiring our pleasure, has sent you to us.

And the Thousand-eyed One should be told: "Our practice of austerity is not for the sake of enjoyment, nor is it performed by one who desires to obtain a fruit that has not yet been reached. (RKV 192.90)
I shall show the true path to this world;
together with Nara, I am intent upon the protection of the world.
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, if anyone should cause you harm, I shall ward him off; turn back, O Vāsava!"
If you are the one who inflicts harm upon no wicked person here,
then I too shall undoubtedly act as his teacher.
Knowing this, O Vāsava, you should not feel distress toward me; for I have descended for the benefit of the worlds.
And this Urvaśī, who has arisen from me, O Purandara, shall become the cause for the three sacred fires (tretāgni) once she has been obtained in this manner.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śrīpati," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 193.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When this had been spoken, all the Apsarases prostrated themselves again and again.
They spoke to the god Nārāyaṇa with the desire for a vision of him.
The Apsarases, longing for spring, said:
"O Blessed One, this instruction which has been spoken by you, who seek our welfare—
this has all been understood, and your greatness is known."
As for that which was spoken by you with a serene inner soul—"This large-eyed lady has been shown; I shall show the world to you"—[so it shall be].
O Lord of the World, reveal Your entire self to those who have surrendered with their whole being for that purpose, just as this Urvaśī has been revealed.
If you are not angry with us despite the offense of the gods, then homage to you, O Lord of the worlds; reveal yourself by yourself.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O celestial maidens, behold here within my body all the worlds,
Madhu, Madana, myself, and whatever else you wish to see.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa then laughed aloud with a resonant sound, and the entire world was filled with that sound.
Brahmā, Prajāpati, Śakra, along with the Rudras and the wielder of the Pināka bow; the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the great ṛṣis.
The Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, Anila, and likewise all the Agnis;
the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Kinnaras.
All the Apsarases, the sciences, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and their expositions, as well as humans, animals, insects, birds, and trees; 193.10.
Reptiles, subtle beings, and whatever else is designated as living,
as well as all the oceans, mountains, rivers, and forests.
O Lord of the Earth, all the continents without exception, as well as all the lakes and the earth filled with cities and villages,
were seen by the gods within the body of that high-souled deity.
Those women of beautiful limbs beheld the vault of heaven, perfectly filled with constellations, planets, and stars, within that one who possesses the form of the universe.
When no end of him could be seen— neither above, nor across, nor below— they then praised that Lord, who is infinite and without beginning.
Together with Madana and Madhu, all those excellent women were filled with trepidation, devoted in their worship, and struck with supreme wonder.
The Apsarases, Vasantakāmā, said:
"O Lord, we see neither your beginning, nor your end, nor your middle, nor the limit of your unmanifest form.
We bow to you, Nārāyaṇa, the infinite refuge of the worlds, who has become the Self."
You are the earth, space, wind, water, and fire; you are the nature of sound and the rest, O Soul of the high and the low.
From you, O Acyuta, all this comes into being; you are the Lord, O Self, whose form consists of diversity and the like.
O Hari, you alone are the seer of the supreme form, the knower, and the hearer of sound;
you are the creator of all, omnipresent, the perceiver of fragrance, and the distinct embodied soul.
O God of gods, there is no one among all the gods, there is no one in the worlds of men,
and there is no one among the classes of animals who is not a portion of you.
O gentle one, your supreme forms are those of Brahmā, the ocean, the moon, and so forth, as well as Śakra and others;
your form is that of the ocean among the steadfast, and likewise the sun and fire among those whose nature is brilliance.
Among those whose wealth is forbearance, you are the foremost earth; among the powerful, you are the swift wind;
in human form, you wear the garb of a king; yet among the deluded, O Lord of All, you are a tree.

O Acyuta, among all principles you are the Dānava; among those possessed of discernment, you are Sanatsujāta. You abide in water as the essence of taste, and your nature as fragrance resides in the earth.
O Lord, you are fire whose nature is visibility; you are wind whose nature is touch;
in the ether, sound and other qualities are your nature; and in the mind, you are of the nature of that which is to be thought.
O Lord of all, O Soul of all beings, you alone are considered the very nature of consciousness everywhere;
I behold Brahmā in the midst of your navel-lotus, and Īśa and Hara upon your brow.
The Aśvins are situated in your ears; all the world-protectors reside in your arms;
the wind is your sense of smell; the sun and moon are in your eyes; and this Sarasvatī, O Lord, is your tongue.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, we behold Your feet as the earth, Your belly as all the worlds;
while we ourselves, along with the hosts of Piśācas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Siddhas, are but the calves, the soles, and the toes.
O Lord, Prajāpati is established in Your masculinity; all the sacrificial rites reside in Your pair of lips;
we all are in Your teeth, O God, for the gods indeed became Your tusks.
O Lord, the entire hosts of gods are your body hairs; O Protector, the Vidyādharas are the lines upon your feet;
O God, all the Vedas with their auxiliary branches are established within you, existing as your joints and your arms.
We behold you as the Boar who upholds the earth, and your ever-terrible form as Nṛsiṃha;
likewise, we behold your lofty horse-head and that immeasurable form during the three strides.
O Lord, these oceans are within Your body; likewise, these mountain-bearers are the abodes of the bowstring;
and these rivers headed by the Gaṅgā, all the continents without exception, and the regions such as the forests [are likewise contained therein].
And these sages, remaining within Your body, O Lord, praise Your supreme majesty;
indeed, these performers of sacrifice worship You, the infinite sovereign of the worlds, with their sacrifices.
O you whose form is everything, there is nothing gentle in this world other than you, nor is anything fierce apart from you;
there is nothing cold and nothing hot other than you—you alone transcend all forms.

Be gracious, O Lord of all, O Being of all beings, O Eternal Self, O Supreme Lord of lords! Forgive this offense which has been committed against You by us, whose minds have been deluded by Your Māyā.
Or what offense have we committed against you, O God of gods, that even your heart is affected by our illusion?
For our minds, though we bow to you as the destroyer of the suffering of those who fear illusion, fall into a state of agitation.
