It is not your fault if we, who have wandered onto the wrong path, have offended you;
let that be forgiven. O God, the fault lies with you alone as the Creator, for you created us without discrimination.
Homage, homage to you, O Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana!
By the remembrance of your name, may all our sin without exception be destroyed.
Homage to you, O Infinite One; homage to you, the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe!
By the remembrance of your name, may all our sin without exception perish.
O most excellent one, O Lord of Sacrifice, O Vāmana who protects all creatures!
By the mere remembrance of your name, may all our sin without exception perish.
Homage be to you, O Hara, whose navel is like a lotus and who was created by Prajāpati;
by the mere remembrance of your name, may all our sin perish without remainder.
O Adhokṣaja, salutations to you, the boat for the ocean of saṃsāra;
by the mere remembrance of your name, may all our sin without exception be destroyed.
Salutation to the Supreme, the illustrious Lord Vāsudeva, the Creator,
who by his own will is endowed with the qualities (guṇas) and brings about creation, preservation, and destruction.
O Soul of the Universe, withdraw this eternal form;
O Lord, our eyes are not capable of beholding it as it continues to expand.
O Acyuta, your radiance is equal to a thousand fires of universal dissolution;
in extent, you pervade the quarters, the earth, and the sky.
We do not know where we are; only you, O Lord, are perceived. We perceive the entire world as gathered together in a single mass.
O Hari, what can we describe of your form, and what is this measure of yours?
O God, what indeed is your majesty, which does not fall within the range of the tongue?
O Lord, even with tens of millions of speakers, and with tens of millions upon tens of millions of intellects,
it is impossible to fully describe your virtues.
This form which has been shown is a supreme grace;
O Lord of the worlds, withdraw it at your will.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus praised by those Apsarases, the Lord Janārdana appeared visibly before them, who were endowed with divine knowledge.
The creator of all beings entered into all creatures by means of his own portions;
seeing Adhokṣaja thus dissolving into all beings, [he was amazed].
All the celestial women were filled with supreme wonder,
as was he, the Lord of All, [who beheld] the mountains, the trees, the oceans, and the earth.
He entered the water, fire, wind, and space; at the proper time, he entered the quarters of the sky as the self of all, and also otherwise as the individual self.
Perceiving the world as abiding within his own form through his own majesty—
[he beheld] gods, dānavas, rākṣasas, yakṣīs, vidyādharas, and uragas.

Humans, cattle, insects, and other such creatures; those moving on land, those dwelling in the air, those in the sky, as well as those on earth, in heaven, and those whose abode is the water—[all these are included].
O subduer of enemies, the Soul of the Universe, having assumed that same form once again, entered into them together with Nara, just as he had been seen by them before.
All those celestial women were filled with supreme wonder;
O best of kings, with pale faces, they bowed down out of awe.
The Blessed One Nārāyaṇa also spoke to those women of the thirty-three gods.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Let the auspicious Urvaśī be led to where that Lord of the Thirty-three resides,
for the sake of your welfare, as he is [the protector] among all beings."
Knowledge has been produced by me once again, effecting the dissolution of beings;
therefore, depart, for this entire multitude of beings is a portion of myself.
Today I have become one with the yogi Vāsudeva, beyond whom there is nothing else; he who is proclaimed as the infinite.
Know that unborn one, the Lord of all beings, to be the supreme state.
I, you goddesses, the gods, humans, and animals—
all this has indeed been created by the infinite Vāsudeva.
Knowing this, O celestial maidens, all things— including gods, asuras, and humans, as well as animals and their qualities— must be viewed with equanimity.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, having been addressed thus by that god, all those celestial women, filled with passion and accompanied by Spring, bowed down to the two of them.
Having taken Urvaśī back, they returned once more to the king of the gods and reported to him exactly what had occurred, just as it happened.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"In the same way, O Indra among kings, you too, by contemplating Keśava within all beings, shall attain equanimity; for equanimity alone leads to liberation."
O King, since you thus perceive the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva as specially present within all beings, how will you not abandon faults such as greed and the like?
O King, when all beings are not other than Govinda,
then let states such as enmity and the like no longer be entertained, my son.
Thus behold, O King, the entire world as having Vāsudeva as its essence;
for this very form has been manifested by Kṛṣṇa, O King.
That form which belongs to the Supreme Lord has thus been described to you;
it is the supreme state of Viṣṇu, devoid of birth and all other states of existence.
Now, O protector of the earth, listen briefly to what I shall tell you— that doctrine which,
once a person has adopted it, leads to supreme nirvāṇa.
For everything is indeed contained within Viṣṇu, and both existence and non-existence consist of him;
this Lord, Mahādeva, is all that is existent and non-existent, the supreme state.
For those who have entered the ocean of existence, struck by the winds of dualities, oppressed by the burden of protecting sons, daughters, and wives,
and sinking without a raft in the turbulent waters of the sense-objects— Vishnu alone is the boat that serves as a refuge for men.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śrīpati," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 194.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard that which was uttered by Anantadeva in his universal form (viśvarūpa),...
The king of the gods and the other gods were likewise struck with supreme wonder.
And having seen the auspicious Apsaras Urvaśī, whose face was like a lotus,
Indra— though surrounded by royal splendor— became both terrified and struck with wonder.
He did not utter any further word, but remained silent;
for such was the account of the deeds performed by Nārāyaṇa.
O King, having heard of the supreme universal form, Lakṣmī, who was born from the womb of Bhṛgu under the asterism Khāti, was then struck with wonder and reflected upon it.
"By what means— whether by a vow, by austerity, by charity, or by a religious observance— may that Lord Nārāyaṇa become my husband?"
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, Satī, having realized that the maiden was thus intent on her thoughts— either through serving the elders or through the propitiation of the gods— "
She said, "Indeed, Śaṅkara has been obtained by me as a husband through ascetic penance;
Prajāpati was obtained by Gāyatrī, and others were desired by different women."
For it is indeed through austerity alone that you must attain it; therefore, practice that, O lady of excellent vows.
For austerity is great and fierce, bestowing all that is desired.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O conqueror of enemy cities, having reached the edge of the ocean, Lakṣmī performed for a vast period of time a most difficult austerity.
She remained standing like a pillar for a thousand divine years;
then Indra and the other gods, bearing conchs, discs, and maces, [appeared].
Having become so, they went for that purpose; she, however, asked the gods:
"Show me without delay that universal form of Viṣṇu."
Then the gods, embarrassed and ashamed, went to Nārāyaṇa and said, "We are not able to display the universal form (vaiśvarūpa) to us."
Then they departed as they pleased, and Viṣṇu reflected:
"The goddess Bhārgavī, standing here in her fierce form, is consuming my body."
Therefore, having gone there and granted her that desired boon,
I shall once again perform penance, or else I shall manifest my Vaiṣṇava universal form (viśvarūpa), which is difficult even for gods and demons to behold.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having gone to Śrī who was situated at the edge of the ocean, Hṛṣīkeśa said, "O Goddess, I am pleased with you; choose a boon as you desire."
Śrī said:
"O Lord Janārdana, if you are pleased with me who have sought refuge in you,
then show me, O Sinless One, that which was seen by the Apsarases."
O Keśava, O creator of beings, you performed penance after reaching Gandhamādana— that which is universal in form and infinite.
Tell me that, O Lord Viṣṇu, if it is not false, O Keśava;
for I have no faith whatsoever in this form of yours.
Many yakṣas and rākṣasas, who move about practicing illusion,
entreated me, knowing my inner disposition toward Hari.
Having become the very form of Viṣṇu, four-armed and bearing discuses,
they all departed with great modesty along with Viśvarūpa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having been thus addressed by her, abandoned that form which is worshipped by the gods and bore the conch, discus, and mace.
He indeed displayed his supreme form as the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) as previously described;
having shown it, he spoke these words according to the ritual procedure of the Pañcarātra.
Whoever shall worship me constantly is himself worthy of honor and is honored;
he shall be endowed with wealth and grain, and possessed of all enjoyments.
For celibacy is the root of all dharmas and the supreme austerity;
therefore, I shall remain there, known by the name Mūlaśrīpati.
The primordial Śrī is proclaimed as Brāhmī, whose very nature is celibacy (brahmacarya);
she consists of all yoga, is meritorious, auspicious, and the remover of all sins.
"O beloved, I am her lord and the bestower of boons upon living beings;
that man who, having bathed in the waters of the Revā, worships me while restrained by his vows," [shall obtain his desires].
One shall obtain the desired fruit from the one named Mūlaśrīpati;
O beloved, whoever gives gifts there, even great gifts (mahādāna), [shall attain that fruit].
A thousandfold merit is obtained compared to other places;
you have seen that in that region and have correctly ascertained it.
By worshipping there, you will attain supreme desires; of this there is no doubt.
Choose a boon, O Goddess of gods, whatever is desired, even if difficult for the gods to attain, O Supreme Sovereign, by those fallen into the wilderness of this miserable saṃsāra.
Śrī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, sustainer of the world; O Nārāyaṇa, lord of the world;
O Nārāyaṇa, supreme Brahman; O Nārāyaṇa, whose ultimate goal is Nārāyaṇa!
Be gracious and protect me; through my devotion, properly employ me in creation.
For you are dear to me and I am dear to you; act in such a way that this may be so.
"O Lord, the household is traditionally held to be the means for attaining dharma, artha, and kāma;
therefore, having established yourself in that meritorious stage of life (āśrama), employ me in what is most beneficial."
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Goddess, since I have been addressed by you with the word 'Nārāyaṇa,' therefore my name here shall be Nārāyaṇagiri."
In the recollection of Nārāyaṇa, the evil born of ten million lifetimes perishes;
because he swallows it, he is therefore called "Giri."
Therefore, O Goddess, this mountain, the king of mountains, shall be the refuge for all— just as I am the refuge for gods, asuras, and humans.

O lady of auspicious gaze, those who shall worship this supreme form of mine, Nārāyaṇagiri by name, which possesses a divine appearance while situated within the mandala— [they shall attain my state].
Endowed with divine knowledge, possessing divine bodies and divine movements,
they shall attain the divine world, fully provided with divine enjoyments.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While the two of them were thus conversing, the gods led by Indra and the great ṛṣis arrived at that forest region on the shore of the ocean.
Then the King of the Gods, knowing that Bhṛgu had been meditated upon by Nārāyaṇa, chose him; and that righteous-souled one gave his daughter to him.
O child, Dharma also, being composed and for the sake of the deity, duly performed the marriage of the royal sage, the god among gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Regarding that which you have stated— that Dharma performed the marriage according to the prescribed rule—
what was the procedure there, and what sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) was given by Bhṛgu as well?

O best of the twice-born, who was it that handled the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles during the marriage sacrifice, and who were the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) for him?
What was his final ablution? Tell me all that in detail;
by drinking the nectar of your words, my satisfaction knows no end.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, [this is the account] of the marriage of Nārāyaṇa, of the sacrifice, of that god’s asceticism, and of his perfect performance [of religious duties].
Even Brahmā, the supreme lord, is not capable of describing his virtues;
nevertheless, I shall speak of them by way of brief indication—listen, becoming composed in mind.

O King, Brahmā and the seven ṛṣis were intent on taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; they offered oblations into the fires, while the earth, together with the oceans, served as the sacrificial altar.
O best of kings, the oceans gave jewels to the brahmin-sages,
and even Dhanada gave wealth desired by all the brāhmaṇas.
O scorcher of foes, Viśvakarman also [constructed] for the gods and the brahmin-sages dwellings that were most wonderful and composed entirely of every kind of gem.
Having done so, he presented it to the illustrious Lord of the Gods;
then Śatakratu [presented] the brahmins, led by Kāpiṣṭhala.
And he questioned Śaunaka and the others, as well as the Baṣkalas and the Chāgalas, and the Ātreyas, O king of kings: "Choose what you desire."
Having seen those variegated jewels, they all addressed the Lord of All Lords:
"This assembly of gods and sages is a source of great merit."
"O Lord of the Gods, we desire to dwell forever in this meritorious place. Śatakratu replied, "Your residence here shall continue for as long as you remain devoted to truth and righteousness."
Mārkaṇḵeya said:
O tiger among kings, listen now with a concentrated mind as I explain who were the officiating priests (hotṛs) at that sacrifice, concerning which you have asked.
Sanatkumāra and others were his members of the assembly;
Atri, Aṅgiras, and Marīci performed the office of the Udgātṛ priest.
Dharmavasiṣṭha performed the office of the *hautra*, and the sage Sanaka performed the office of the *brahman*;
Śatakratu bestowed upon them thirty-six thousand villages.
The Lord brought about that by which Lakṣmī was reunited with her husband while the gods remained in their respective places as Brahmā was offering oblations into the fire.
The forehead was seen; that region is known by the name "Lalāṭa.
That region is a meritorious field of Śrīpati, frequented by gods and sages.
Then she prepared to seat the row of Brahmins, which was divine, filled with all wonders, and endowed with celestial perfections.
Then Lakṣmī spoke these words to the Lord named Śrīpati.
Śrī said: "These Brahmins who are the disciples of Bhṛgu and others, firm in their vows—" (RKV 194.59)
O Adhokṣaja, O Garuḍadhvaja, I desire to establish them through your grace, just as Marīci and the others were established by the Lord of the Gods.
"O Adhokṣaja, there are many Brahmins here who are lifelong celibates and firm in their vows;
some among them are established in the Prājāpatya vow and others in the Brāhma vow. By your grace, O Lord, I shall establish them [in their respective duties]."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the Blessed One, whose banner bears the bull, filled with curiosity,
questioned all those observers of vows who were established in various modes of conduct.
Nārada, too, having approached Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, who was wearing a black antelope skin, said: "These Brāhmaṇas are indeed lifelong celibates."
O lord of men, these twenty-four thousand Prājāpatya Brahmins, the best of the twice-born, should have their private parts covered with fine cloth.
O Bull-bannered One, there are indeed twelve thousand of those established in the vow of celibacy, who contemplate the vow and Brahman.
Having heard the words of Nārada, the gods and the celestial rishis likewise thought, "Excellent! Excellent! yet none of them said anything at all.
Then Lakṣmī, filled with devotion, summoned those brahmins;
grasping their feet, she said, "May you show me favor."
And thirty-six thousand dwellings are situated here;
may all of you reside in those which were fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Having promised "So be it," they remained with joyful minds;
they were abundant in wealth and grain, characterized by the attainment of their desires,
and fulfilled in all their wishes even without undertaking any laborious actions.
Having thus established those brahmins, she remained there and protected them;
meanwhile, Viṣṇu, devoted to the pleasure of the goddess Śrī, remained stationed in four forms.
When the marriage sacrifice had thus concluded, the sages said to him: "O Janārdana, where shall we perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna)?"
Having heard these words from the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī,
he released the pure water of the Jāhnavī into the midst of the Revā.
Upon seeing the water from Hari’s feet flowing out, those sages were filled with wonder, for they were well aware of its greatness.
Accompanied by Rudra, all the deities and sages likewise engaged in conversation, filled with wonder and shaking their heads.
The sages said:
"Tell us, O Śambhu, what is this sudden appearance of water here,
arising from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, which causes such great delusion?"
Īśvara said:
"O gods, I indeed know this water from Viṣṇu’s feet;
here, a bath surpasses even the concluding purificatory baths of ten horse-sacrifices."
"The Lord of Śrī is to be worshipped by you; from where will your purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) come?
Therefore, this has been quickly prepared for your sake."
O lords of the thirty gods, no one is able to describe the fruit that is obtained by bathing here; what further words could possibly exceed that?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, O bull of the Bharatas, all those gods, led by Maheśāna, performed their ablutions and departed as they had come.
Then all those brahmins returned to their own homes,
O great king, at the Devatīrtha which destroys all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Śrīpati," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
In the 195th chapter of the *Rukmiṇīkalyāṇa-vyākhyāna*,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is the greatness that has been proclaimed regarding the Devatīrtha?"
O Sage, what fruit arises for those who perform acts such as ritual bathing and giving?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O mighty-armed one, whatever holy places exist on earth that have been frequented by the gods and the hosts of sages were all meditated upon by Viṣṇu.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, all these have indeed come together as one at that sacred ford;
that meritorious Vaiṣṇava ford is known as Devatīrtha.
Kurukṣetra is supreme on earth, Tripuṣkara in the intermediate space, and Puruṣottama in heaven; the divine tīrtha is higher than the highest.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is no sacred ford equal to Devatīrtha, both in this world and the next; having reached it, a man shall never suffer.
The holy fords have been proclaimed by the gods; that man who performs his ablution here at Devatīrtha becomes as one who has bathed in all of them.
Having been told by them, "So be it," the gods and the hosts of sages, being well-pleased, worshipped the Lord of Śrī and returned each to his own abode.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing here in this sacred field during a solar eclipse, that same fruit one attains by bathing,
fasting according to the prescribed rite, and worshipping Śrīśa.
O King, whatever gifts of gold one bestows according to the prescribed rites during a solar eclipse, all of that yields infinite fruit.
Śatakratu has declared that the gift of land, the gift of a cow, the gift of gold, and the gift of a diamond yield infinite fruit.
Soma is indeed satisfied by the gift of clothing, Bhārgava by pearls,
Ravi by the gift of gold, and Dharmarāja by an infinite [gift].
The noble-minded Bṛhaspati has declared that whatever gift is given at a divine pilgrimage site by one endowed with faith yields infinite fruit.
O King, at Devatīrtha in Bhṛgukṣetra, which is superior to all other tīrthas,
a man who bathes in Devatīrtha and beholds Śrīpati—
O lord of men, by giving gifts to the foremost of the twice-born at Devatīrtha during a lunar eclipse, he uplifted a hundred lineages and attained the celestial realm.

Those men by whom food has been given to brahmins at a sacred ford for the sake of Hari shall partake of enjoyments both here and after death; so too for one who would perform the feeding of brahmins at a divine shrine dedicated to Hari.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having bathed at Devatīrtha with a restrained mind, a man or a woman attains all delight in the heavenly world.
He who, having observed the Ekādaśī fast with devotion, worships the Lord of Śrī, keeps a vigil at night, and lights a lamp with ghee; RKV_195.17 //
Having risen in the morning on the twelfth day, O descendant of Kuru, one should likewise duly worship a Brahmin couple in the waters of the Narmadā.
Having observed the vow, he rejoices in the imperishable world of Viṣṇu, provided with garments, ornaments, betel, flowers, incense, and ointments.
Whoever, having bathed and fasted on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), should worship Hari and perform a night vigil according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Śāstras; // RKV_195.20 //
He who worships the Lord of Śrī according to the ritual of the Pañcarātra shall not experience the painful torments inflicted by Dharmarāja.
Having duly received the Vaiṣṇava initiation (dīkṣā), which destroys sins, bestows heaven and liberation, and grants merit, enjoyment, and wealth; 195.22.
"O highly fortunate one, it bestows a kingdom, or sons, or good fortune; it grants a virtuous wife, or even devotion to Viṣṇu."
O descendant of Kuru, that man who worships the Lord of Śrī at that very Devatīrtha shall cross over the ocean of existence.
Or else, on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) at home, one should worship Viśvarūpa, or Samyaṅmūla Śrīpati, or even Nārāyaṇagiri.
O King, one who is full of devotion and endowed with faith [should worship] with milk, even with waters from sacred fords,
and with very fine, unwashed garments made of great silk.
With various incenses produced from the eyes [of plants], as well as with agallochum and sandalwood,
with guggulu mixed with clarified butter, and also with various kinds of food offerings.
O lord of men, Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should worship] with milk-rice and other offerings, or with milk,
along with very pure, increasing, and charming lamps made of flour.
Listen, O Bhārata, to how that man goes after having performed worship:
having become the one who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, he becomes the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
He who, with supreme devotion, [worships] the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī, transcends the worlds of the gods and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
One should behold Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, established in four ways;
through the diversion of dance and song, one is certainly liberated from sin.
He who, being self-restrained, daily beholds and worships Hari during the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) of the Lord in the morning, at midday, and likewise in the evening; RKV_195.32 //
Having indeed crossed over that difficult calamity, he shall never again encounter affliction;
it increases the lifespan and prosperity of men and even fulfills their eyesight.
The lustration rite (*nīrājana*) of Hari always removes even minor sins;
therefore, at the time of that lustration, whoever recites a hymn to Hari—
He is blessed who, with a serene inner self, offers into his hands the remains of the lustration rite (nīrājana) performed for Hari, the God of gods.
Having gathered [the powder], one should apply it with the eyes while cleansing the face;
this destroys eye diseases such as cataracts and makes the face radiant.
O best of men, for one who constantly maintains a lamp burning before the Lord of Śrī, it is sufficient for the destruction of all evils without exception. (RKV 195.37)
Having bathed in the holy waters of the Revā, the observer of the vow should give an additional gift;
by that act, he has given the earth consisting of seven continents, along with its oceans, forests, and rivers.
"Indeed, the earth has been circumambulated," Śaṅkara said;
"whoever hears this being recited, or even recites it themselves."
At that time, he, freed from sin, shall attain remembrance of Hari;
this [account] is conducive to fame, longevity, heaven, and is dear to the virtues of the ancestors.
One should cause the Brahmins to hear the majesty of the Lord of Śrī during the śrāddha rite;
by that [recitation], the ancestors shall be satiated with clarified butter and honey.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrīpati," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O lord of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Haṃsatīrtha.

Traversing a vehicle yoked with swans, possessing the splendor of the rising sun,
and enriched with all objects of desire, he is attended by throngs of apsarases.
Having there enjoyed all desired pleasures according to his wish,
he shall indeed be born with the memory of his former lives upon returning to the human state.
By means of renunciation, O Bhārata, one should abandon the body and attain liberation.
Thus has been told to you, O Pārtha, the fruit of Haṃsatīrtha,
which removes all sins, is meritorious, and destroys all suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Haṃsatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mūlasthāna Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

Being pursued by many men, O bull of the Bharatas,

they both went to Bhṛgukaccha on the banks of the Narmadā; having performed extremely difficult austerities, they attained supreme perfection.
O Pārtha, whoever bathes at that sacred ford and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods will be born handsome and fortunate wherever he may be.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Āśvina Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O Pārtha, is the supreme Sāvitrī-tīrtha,
where the highly fortunate Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, who is Sāvitrī? How is she worshipped by the wise? When pleased, what boon does she grant? Tell me this.

The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said: Padmā is presided over by the one seated upon the lotus-throne; she is the Yoginī of the Lotus, resembling the splendor of Sāvitrī, and for that reason she is called Sāvitrī.
Lotus-faced, lotus-colored, with eyes resembling lotus petals—
she should be meditated upon constantly by Brahmins and by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas according to the rule.
Indeed, out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, it [the Veda] was never [recited] by Śūdras;
for by reciting or retaining it, one certainly falls into hell.
"By the mere utterance of the Veda by Kṣatriyas who protect the Dharma, the tongue of this Śūdra must be cut out; such is the settled rule. (RKV 200.6)
A young girl, resembling the crescent moon, clad in red garments and anointed with red unguents,
should be meditated upon at dawn during the supreme conjunction of the twilight.
With high, full breasts, a beautiful face, and auspicious appearance,
she was adorned with every ornament and anointed with white garlands and unguents.
Clad in white garments and wearing a white sacred thread,
the midday twilight should be meditated upon as a young woman who bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Furthermore, O Pārtha, at dusk, Śvetā, with her white hair,
being well-disposed, protects one like a mother in a difficult wilderness.
But especially, O Indra among kings, is the supreme Sāvitrī-tīrtha;
having bathed and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) according to the rules with respect to the actions of mind, speech, and body.
One should burn away the many defects accumulated over seven lifetimes by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
one should sprinkle one's own body with the mantra beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
O best of kings, by reciting "āpo hi ṣṭhā" nine, six, and three times at that sacred ford, one is not defiled by the acceptance of gifts.
By reciting the three-verse *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while sipping water according to one's Veda— or even otherwise—
one shall not be stained by minor sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
For a Brahmin indeed performs the *tryāpaṃ* rite; he should perform three scrapings, but he who causes a fourth to be performed casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
And the mantra known as Drupada, which is found in the Vājasaneyaka Veda,
destroys all sins when recited once while submerged in water.
Having worshipped the Sun with the mantra "ud u tyam," one should recite the goddess Gāyatrī, who is pure and the mother of the Vedas.
The twice-born who recites the goddess Gāyatrī immediately after the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Brahmā.
The Gāyatrī destroys the sin acquired over ten lifetimes by being recited a hundred times, that committed in a previous life by a thousand times, and that of three ages (yugas) by ten thousand times.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if he knows only the essence of the Gāyatrī, is better than one who is unrestrained, though he may know all four Vedas, eat all things, and sell all things.
One who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever else he may perform, he shall not partake in its fruit.
That dull-witted Brāhmaṇa who does not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) shall be a Śūdra while still alive; once dead, he is reborn as a dog.
Having reached the Sāvitrītīrtha, the twice-born who recites the Sāvitrī mantra obtains the fruit of the three Vedas; of this there is no doubt.
O King, he who, having bathed, performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the sake of his ancestors for twelve years, his grandfathers remain satisfied.
Having reached the Sāvitrī-tīrtha, whoever brings about the end of their life shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
And when that time has fully elapsed, O King, he returns here to human birth, being born as a twice-born man learned in the four Vedas within a pure family.
Endowed with an abundance of wealth and grain, accompanied by sons and grandsons,
and liberated from disease and sorrow, he shall live for a hundred autumns.

Thus ends the two hundredth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Sāvitrītīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
[Chapter 201] Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O protector of the earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Devatīrtha,
where the highly fortunate gods, including Indra, attained perfection, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities—
whatever is performed there attains infinity through the power of the sacred ford.
Especially on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
there is that which is the foremost of all holy fords (tīrthas) and was inhabited by the gods in ancient times.
Having bathed on the thirteenth day and performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules,
and having worshipped the bull-bannered God established by the gods,
one is liberated from all sins and attains the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Devatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 202.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately following that is another unsurpassed holy place, Śikhitīrtha.
The fivefold abode is the preeminent among all sacred sites and is supreme.
Having performed austerities at that sacred site for the sake of a crest, the bearer of oblations (Agni),
having obtained a crest and become "The Crested" (Śikhin), established Śiva under the name Śikhā.
O King, on the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
one should go to that best of holy places and bathe in the waters of the Narmadā.
One should satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others with water mixed with sesame seeds;
having satisfied the sacrificial fire, one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa.
Then one should worship Śiva with perfumes, garlands, and incense;
having thus honored Maheśvara at the Śikhitīrtha according to this rite.
Surrounded by hosts of apsaras, being sung to by gandharvas, he indeed goes to the world of Rudra in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
One attains the destruction of enemies and becomes radiant on earth.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śikhitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 203.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, one should go to the unsurpassed Koṭitīrtha.
Where millions of highly fortunate great seers have attained perfection.
Having performed extensive austerities, the Ṛṣis established Śiva there,
as well as the goddess Koṭīśvarī and Cāmuṇḍā, the crusher of Mahiṣa.
O King, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
Śiva was installed by the sages after they had summoned ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
On that lunar day, when the asterism Hasta occurs— which destroys all sins—
one should go to that sacred ford and, being composed, perform a ritual bath.
By the offering of water with sesame seeds, one quickly rescues twenty-one generations of men from hell; how much more so, then, the man who performs a *śrāddha*?
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, and worship of the deities—
all these become ten million times more effective through association with that sacred place.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Koṭitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 204.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should then go to Bhṛgutīrtha, the unsurpassed king of holy places.
This [work] of the Grandfather is of great merit and destroys all sins.
In ancient times, for some particular reason, Brahmā performed the propitiation of Śambhu at that sacred ford for three hundred years.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For what purpose, O tiger among sages, did Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
worship Maheśvara, the God of gods, with great devotion?
The sustainer of the world and the teacher of the world is to be propitiated by all beings;
I wish to hear that which is to be heard—the supreme and great wonder.
Having heard the words of the Son of Dharma, Mārkaṇḍeya, the lord of sages,
related that ancient history and account of events.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of beings, in former times the Grandfather (Brahmā), desiring to approach his own daughter,
was cursed by the God of gods, who was overcome with wrath.
O Lotus-Seated One, your Vedas and your knowledge will perish;
you will become unworthy of honor by all the worlds, of this there is no doubt.
When the curse had been thus bestowed, Brahmā was then overwhelmed with grief;
having bathed on the northern bank of the Revā for three hundred years,
he propitiated the Lord of Gods, and Śaṅkara, being pleased, spoke to him.
"You shall become worthy of worship in the world on every festival day;
and I shall dwell here together with the gods and the ancestors."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From that time forward, that sacred ford attained renown from Pitāmaha (Brahmā);
it is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and unsurpassed among all holy places.
In that regard, specifically on the new moon day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, he who bathes and offers libations to the ancestors and the deities, [attains great merit].
O King, by means of a single offering of a rice-ball (piṇḍa) or even water mixed with sesame seeds, the ancestors remain satisfied for twelve years; there is no doubt about this.
But he who constantly offers the śrāddha when the sun has entered Virgo—
his ancestors, having attained satisfaction, leap about and laugh.
Whatever fruit is obtained by performing a śrāddha at all the ancestral pilgrimage sites (pitṛtīrtha), one attains that same fruit there on the new moon day (darśa); of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed at Paitāmaha and worshipping the Lord of Pārvatī, a person is liberated from major and minor sins; of this there is no doubt.
O King, for those men of purified soul who die at that sacred ford, there is undoubtedly a state from which there is no return from the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Paitāmaha Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 205.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Lord of the Earth, one should then go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
It is renowned by the name Kurkurī, which destroys all sins.
Whatever desire one prays for— be it cattle, sons, wealth, or the like— the goddess of the sacred ford, Kurkurī, the sovereign of the gods, grants each and every one of them.
The guardian of the field named Ḍhauṇḍheśa dwells there;
by performing his propitiation, whether it be a woman or even a man, [one attains success].
O Indra among kings, even by means of this salutation, misfortune shall come to an end;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth obtains excellent wealth.
In this manner, both woman and man obtain the highest desire through touching or beholding that sacred ford according to the prescribed ritual.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kurkurī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Lord of the Earth, go from there to that most beautiful,
meritorious holy site known as Daśakanyā, which removes all sins;
it was established by Mahādeva and bestows the fruits of all desires.
At that sacred ford, Mahādeva chose ten virtuous maidens from among the daughters of Brahmā and united them with him in marriage.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became renowned as Daśakanyā;
it is proclaimed to be merit-bestowing, a destroyer of all sins, and its fruit is inexhaustible.
At that sacred ford, the man who gives away a maiden well-adorned,
having given her according to his ability and properly decorated, attains [great merit].
O lord of men, those whose souls are purified by that merit arising from their gift dwell in the presence of Śiva for as many years as there are hairs on the body.
Then, after a long time, O lord of men, having attained a human birth here in this world which is so difficult to obtain, he shall become the master of ten million pieces of wealth.
Whoever bathes with devotion at that sacred ford and bestows gold upon a peaceful Brahmin, enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever [karma] was previously committed, whether verbal, mental, or born of action, all that goes to dissolution through the gift of gold, O Bhārata. (RKV 206.8)
A man, having given even as much gold as the tip of a hair at that sacred ford, goes to heaven upon death; there is no doubt about this.
There, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot and being honored by the Vidyādharas and Siddhas, he shall dwell for as long as the dissolution of all beings.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Daśakanyā Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 207.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In front of that is a purifying holy site (tīrtha) renowned as Svarṇabindu.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven, and after death, they do not undergo rebirth.
O Lord of the Earth, listen now to the fruit that is proclaimed for one who, having bathed at that sacred ford, gives gold to a Brahmin.
Of all jewels, gold is the supreme jewel;
born from the brilliance of fire, it is therefore the most excellent on earth.
He who bestows gold gives the entire earth— complete with its mountains, forests, groves, cities, and towns— just as if it were already given by him.
Whatever mental, verbal, or physical evil deed was committed in the past,
O Bhārata, all of that is swiftly destroyed by the gift of gold.
But he who, having given even as much gold as the tip of a hair at that sacred ford, dies there, goes to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
There, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot and being honored by the Vidyādharas and Siddhas, he shall dwell until the dissolution of all beings.
Then, when that time is complete, having attained an excellent human birth,
he is born as a twice-born man in a house possessing ten million gold pieces.
Freed from all diseases and honored in all worlds,
he shall live for more than a hundred years, renowned among the virtuous as a king.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Suvarṇabindu Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 208.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O protector of the earth, one should then go to that most beautiful tīrtha.
It is renowned throughout the three worlds as that which liberates one from debt to the ancestors.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, having satiated the ancestors and the deities,
and having given gifts, O best of kings, a man becomes free from his debts.
For all fathers desire a son for their own sake, thinking:
"This son will deliver us from the hell named Put. (RKV 208.3)
O dear one, the offering of funeral cakes and water is said to be the supreme debt;
for that is declared to be the debt owed to the ancestors, and beyond that is the debt to the gods.
The Agnihotra, as well as the sacrifices, the animal offerings, and the Ishtis—these are declared to be the debt to the gods; now hear that which pertains to humans.
Having made a promise to Brahmins, at sacred fords, or regarding works of temple construction, one should give those very things; such is the established rule of conduct.
"O son of Dharma, O Indra among kings, these three debts have been declared for sons; those who bathe in the Ṛṇamocana are indeed true sons."
For both those who have sons and those who do not are liberated from the three debts;
therefore, having reached this best of sacred sites, a son of self-restrained mind should perform libations for his ancestors, especially the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
If at that sacred site an oblation is offered, a gift is given, and the preceptor is gratified,
one enjoys inexhaustible fruit for seven births after death.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 209.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately following that, O Pārtha, is the excellent Puṣkalī Tīrtha.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a person indeed obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Then one should go to the holy site of Kṣamānātha, renowned throughout the three worlds,
frequented by Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
There dwells the Lord of Gods, Rudra himself, the Great Lord;
born with a great burden, he is known as Bhārabhūti.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of Brahmins, I wish to hear about the sacred ford renowned as Bhārabhūti, which is endowed with all virtues; for my curiosity is great.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of the Pāṇḍavas, listen to the origin of Bhārabhūti,
just as it was told in detail of old by the god Śambhu.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
he was renowned as Viṣṇuśarman and had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the Śāstras.
Forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, truthfulness, purity, fortitude, as well as knowledge, realization, and faith— all these are established in him.
O best of kings, those brahmins who possess such qualities indeed rescue their ancestors from falling into a terrible hell.
O best of kings, those brahmins who are greedy for sensory objects fall into the terrible Raurava hell, deluded by their own sins.

Those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who have desisted from killing living beings, and whose hands are restrained in receiving gifts— they are the Brahmins capable of delivering others across the ocean of existence.

Thus, endowed with a multitude of virtues, this Brāhmaṇa dwells on the bank of the Narmadā together with other Brāhmaṇas, sustaining his life by the practice of gleaning ears of grain and single grains.
Having recognized such a brahmin, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
assumed the form of a twice-born and went to his hermitage himself.
Seeing him reciting the *padapāṭha* and *kramapāṭha* together with the Brahmins, he saluted the learned man, who honored him in return with a welcome.
After a moment, the brahmin, filled with wonder, said to him:
"Tell me, boy, what is that? What desired thing shall I do for you?"
The boy said:
"O best of the twice-born, know me to have arrived as a seeker of knowledge;
if you grant me knowledge, then I shall remain in your house."
The Brahmin said:
"O boy, you belong to the most excellent lineage among all Brahmins;
how is it that the supreme gift among all gifts, knowledge, is being given?"
Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher or by means of abundant wealth;
furthermore, in this world, knowledge becomes fruitful through the pursuit of further knowledge.
The young student said:
"Just as other boys, having bathed, serve [their teachers] day and night, so too do I, together with the other students, perform service; of this there is no doubt."
Having said, "So be it," the lord of Brahmins continued to teach him day after day,
living together with his disciples while subsisting on the gleanings of grain he gathered.
Then, after a few days, the Lord was addressed by the young students:
"O student, perform the duties beginning with cooking, which have arrived in their proper sequence."
Having been told "So be it," the Lord of Gods went to Bhāragrāma;
after meditating upon all the lords of the forest, he spoke these words:
As long as the Brahmin does not arrive at the house with his young students,
so long must well-prepared food be kept ready out of sight.
Having spoken thus to them all, Maheśvara, assuming his universal form,
went there individually, disguised as a young brahmin student, for the sake of sport.
Seeing him arrived there separately, disguised in the dress of a young brahmin student,
they spoke harsh words to him in the presence of the mountain, saying, "Fie upon you!"
"Then all of us, our throats parched with hunger, shall go to the temple and attain satisfaction through the food prepared by you, a perfected one (siddha)."
O twice-born one, all that you have thought and done by coming here is in vain;
having made a false promise, you have now acted wrongly.
The boy said:
"O bulls among the twice-born, do not feel distress or regret for the sake of food; you shall come to my house when it has been prepared according to the proper rite."
The young Brahmin said:
"Whether our end comes at the close of this day, or whether it reaches completion day by day— this remains entirely uncertain."
"What you have cited as established is unestablished for us;
having seen that it is false, we shall go there, bind you, and cast you into the water."
The boy said: "O all you excellent twice-born ones here, together with your preceptors, listen!
Hear my invincible vow, upon hearing which wonder shall arise."
"If all this food in the teacher's hermitage were truly established [as such],
then you all must be bound by me and thrown into the waters of the Narmadā."
Or else, if the food is not prepared by you because of your stubborn persistence,
then while the Guru looks on, I must be bound and cast into the pool of the Narmadā.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," they all made a covenant in the presence of their guru;
then, having bathed according to the ritual for recitation, they departed for the assembly of spirits.
Seeing that the food and drink had expanded, they were filled with wonder;
O best of kings, having eaten the six-flavored meal and having offered oblations individually, they [proceeded].
Then that best of the twice-born, joyful and well-nourished, spoke these words:
"I am a granter of boons; choose a boon, my child, whatever pleases you."
O Brahmin, the Vedas with their limbs and sub-limbs, as well as various scriptures, shall manifest to you; let this be my boon for you.
Having prostrated, he sported at his pleasure together with the young students;
then, when the second day arrived, [he entered] the waters of the Narmadā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, they all went out for the sake of sport along with their preceptor;
then, having remembered the wager, they all spoke according to the prescribed rules.
Then the Lord, having bowed with palms joined in reverence, said to the preceptor: "O Master, today I shall cast into the water those young students who have failed to fulfill their vows."
O King, having heard those words of the god, those young students fled in the ten directions while their preceptor looked on. (RKV 209.40)
O Lord of Men, the god Vāyu, with the speed of the wind, plucked them all from every side and bound them together as a burden for all those young students.
"The Lord, who bestows both curses and favors, has cast them into the water as if they were in their own home";
then, seeing them in the waters of the Narmadā, he fell into despondency.
Then the preceptor said to the boy: "What is this rash act you have committed?
The mothers and fathers of these children, as well as their wives, are at home."
If those fools ask me, "Where have they gone?", I shall say this:
"O noble one, such being the case, if anyone were to die..."
Therefore, you ought to unite it with your own life;
for when those Brahmins have died, there is no certainty that the living person has died.
"When I am dead, there will be many instances of Brahmin-slaughter for you;
by the mere act of binding a twice-born man, hell becomes certain."
"O lowest of the twice-born, I do not know the destination you shall go after death.
When he had spoken thus, Maheśvara, the God of gods, smiled.
At the Bhārabhūteśvara Tīrtha, the Lord lifted the twice-born from the water;
having released the burden, the God then covered those twice-born ones.
A liṅga was installed there, renowned as Bhārabhūti;
indeed, upon seeing those dead twice-born ones, the sin of killing a Brahmin was cast off.
Having indeed seen those five hundred instances of Brahman-slaughter pass away,
the preceptor was then filled with wonder upon seeing those boys.
"No one else whatsoever could possess such power except for the Lord;
having realized this, the twice-born one prostrated before that God of gods."
O Supreme Lord, whatever I have said out of ignorance,
and whatever unpleasant thing I have done— all that must be forgiven by me, O Master.
The god said: "O Blessed One, you are my preceptor; you are my grandfather.
O Embryo of the Vedas, salutations be unto you; there is no transgression whatsoever."
The progenitor, the one who performs the initiation ceremony, the one who imparts knowledge,
the giver of food, and the protector from fear— these five are remembered as fathers.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the World, bowing down to Viṣṇuśarman,
went quickly from that sacred ford to Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth.
From that time forward, that sacred site became renowned as Bhārabhūti;
it is celebrated throughout all the worlds as the destroyer of great sins.
In that sacred place, I shall relate to you again a divine history that removes all sins; listen to it with one-pointed attention.
Long ago, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was a certain high-minded Vaiśya known as Sukeśa; his son was exceedingly righteous.
The large-eyed one, renowned as Somaśarman, having died,
made a certain poor son of a merchant his friend.
There was one renowned as Sudeva, skilled in all undertakings;
once, he considered entering into a business partnership with him.
"Friend, let us travel by sea on auspicious voyages,
taking with us a great quantity of merchandise for my commercial venture."
"We shall go to the further shore; our success shall be equal. Having thus consulted together regarding their desired goal as if with a formal counsel, they spoke.
Having taken all their travel provisions, the two of them boarded the salt ocean; having gone there and sold their excellent merchandise, they then stood before him.
Having obtained much gold and various kinds of jewels,
they brought that ship together and subsequently boarded it.
Having seen a boat filled with gold within the water at midnight, and having seen Somaśarman with his head placed upon [his father's] lap; 209.65.
Sahadeva reflected as he lay there, utterly trusting:
"He has fallen under the power of sleep, having indeed entrusted his very life-breaths to me."
"All this wealth and treasure, without exception, is dependent upon him;
he might go there and give me half of his excellence, or he might not. (RKV 209.67)
Having thus resolved in his mind, the wicked one, with a heart clouded by sinful thoughts, cast Somaśarman into the salt ocean.
Having crossed over by means of that raft and gone on, he took possession of that wealth;
then, after a few days, he was joined with the law of time (death).
Seized by the servants of Yama, he went to the terrible city of Yama;
he was led along that path where the sun blazes with heat.
Having divided himself twelvefold as if at the onset of universal dissolution,
he enters those places where there are extremely sharp thorns and most dreadful dogs.
Where there are great serpents with sharp fangs, tigers, and large wolves;
where there is scorching sand, hunger, thirst, and great darkness.
There is no talk of water, nor shade, nor any hermitage anywhere;
as long as food accompanied by water is being given, it is poison.
For those who fervently pray for shade, the fire blazes intensely;
being burned by it, they lament many times over again and again.
"O brother! O mother! O son!"—thus do they fall, unconscious, upon the road;
in such a manner is he led along the path by the servants of Yama.
Wherever Yama, the Lord of Gods and restrainer of creatures, resides,
the servants of Yama leave him at the gateway and report it.
"O Lord of Gods, having bound this betrayer of friends with a noose around his neck as he sits there, restrain him; understand what must follow."
Yama said:
"But never before have I seen the face of those who betray trust;
what punishment could there be for those wicked ones who are treacherous to their friends?"
"Expert sages have been appointed here for the purpose of investigation;
wherever they declare [a matter], cast it down there—let it not be further deliberated."
Having been told this, those swift-moving servants took him and,
having reported him there by the command of Yama, spoke to those lords of sages.
"O twice-born ones, by him his own friend was slain while asleep at night; he killed one who trusted him out of greed for wealth—what punishment shall there be for him? (RKV 209.81)
The sages said:
"We have never before seen the faces of those who slay their friends;
having placed him behind a curtain, let us hear what his destiny shall be."
Then, having deliberated upon those scriptures among themselves,
those bulls among brahmins summoned the messengers of Yama and said to them:
We have examined the treatises, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the Mīmāṃsā; and herein we have seen [the truth].

In the scriptures, an expiation is prescribed for the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the teacher’s wife; but for the ungrateful person, there is no expiation.
For those who kill women, those who kill their gurus, and those who slay children or Brahmins, an atonement has been prescribed in the scriptures; but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
Those sinners who break dikes, wells, and tanks, and those wicked people who cut down gardens and groves; // RKV_209.87 //
Those who set forest fires, those who are constantly harmful, those who misappropriate deposits, those who administer poison, and those who deceive their masters; // RKV_209.88 //
A woman who abandons her mother, father, and teachers; who brings harm to others; who is intent on deceiving her own husband; and who causes the destruction of her fetus—[is reborn as a jackal].
A woman who is devoid of discrimination, one who eats without having bathed, and likewise one who delights in eating twice a day on the day of Viṣṇu; RKV 209.90.
The destiny of those women has been seen, but not that of betrayers of trust— namely,
of men who betray their friends and commit treachery against them.
Their destination is not found even in the Vedas; what need is there to mention the Purāṇas?
Such being the case, when they are established in sin, no destination exists for them.
"We have heard that there is no other destination for one who kills a friend or betrays the trusting;
having led this betrayer of trust away from here, O messengers of Yama..."
For more than a hundred billion eons,
they shall dwell individually and separately in all the hells, numbering thirty koṭis.
"Let this betrayer of friends be cast out; let no further deliberation be made.
Having heard these words of theirs, the servants seized him.
Then they went there to cast him into those terrible hells;
indeed, taking him with them, they [cast him] into the dreadful hell known as Raurava.
They cast that most wicked man there; when he was thrown, a great cry arose from the beings dwelling in hell: "This evildoer must not be released! (RKV 209.97)
From the mere touch of this, the pain becomes a hundredfold,
just like the agony caused by swords, wooden stakes, and blazing fires.
What pure benefit is gained by touching it? Just as a good person comes to be held in low esteem through association with the wicked.
Just as the application of caustic to a wound is done immediately because of its proximity, let peace be made quickly; let [this being] be led away to another hell.
Having been addressed thus by them, they then went toward the impure place;
there those hell-beings were present, and as before, they too cried out.
Thus all those servants wander through the circles of hell;
yet even in hell, there is no place of rest for that evil-minded sinner.
Whenever that happened, they all took him and went into the presence of Yama; having reported everything that had been said by the men in hell, they said:
"Tell us, what can be done for one who has no place in hell?"
Yama said:
"O most sinful one, go indeed to the womb frequented by animals;
let him be cast into the animal womb for the duration of time prescribed by the sages."
When these words were spoken by the Restrainer of Creatures (Yama),
that wicked man went to the state of a worm, dwelling separately in various kinds of excrement.
Then, having undergone births as gadflies, mosquitoes, and those originating from ants,
and being abundant with lice and bedbugs, he attained the state of a bird.
Thereafter he attained the state of an immobile being, and after that, the state of a stone;
then [the states of] reptiles, pythons, boars, deer, and elephants.
Having entered the womb of a wolf, a dog, a donkey, or a camel; that of a village-born sow; that of a mule; and likewise that of a buffalo—RKV 209.108.
He indeed underwent these and many other wombs in succession;
having entered those various wombs, he became a beast of burden, a carrier of loads.
Once, in the house of that righteous and illustrious lord of the earth,
that best of kings, having seen that the full moon day of Kārttika had arrived, [acted].
Having summoned the family priest as well as many Brahmins, he said:
"One should not perform the Kārttikī festival at home; I have heard this repeatedly."
"O best of the twice-born, tell me where we shall go together:
he who observes the Kārttikī festival at home, devoid of ritual bathing, giving, and other such rites."
The Śruti declares that he falls outside the merit acquired over a year;
therefore, with every effort, one should resort to a sacred ford (tīrtha) endowed with all virtues.
"Let us go there together to bathe and to give according to our ability.
When these words had been spoken by the king, O best of the twice-born—
They said to the best of kings: "O most excellent of monarchs, on the northern bank of the Revā, there is a famous place of liberation known as Bhāreśvara."
"In that regard, let us all go [to him], which brings about the destruction of all sins.
Having been addressed thus, the king took abundant wealth.
Having prepared a cart, that beast of burden was yoked to it—
he who, having committed the murder of a friend, has entered the womb of a cow.
Thus he reached that supreme sacred ford on the bank of the Narmadā;
having gone there on the fourteenth day, he observed a fast.
Having gone to the bank of the Narmadā while recollecting the name of Rudra, let him take earth from a pure place with this mantra: RKV 209.119.
"You were lifted up by the boar Rudra, who possesses a hundred arms;
I too shall lift you up with progeny and through bondage."
Having thus brought that clay and placed it on the northern bank, he then beheld the sun and consecrated it with this mantra: RKV_209.121 //
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu;
O Clay, take away my sin accumulated over hundreds of millions of births.
Then, having thus entered the water, one should utter this mantra:
"O Narmadā of meritorious waters, your water originates from Śaṅkara."
"May it take away the sin accumulated by me today as I perform my bath.
Having bathed according to this rite and having satiated the ancestors and the deities, [he should proceed].
Afterwards, accompanied by offerings, he went to the temple,
meditating with devotion upon Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, as being present there.
He began the worship according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas.
O Goddess, it is said that there are four types of worship on Śivarātri.
Having bathed Śaṅkara with the five products of the cow during the first watch of the night,
the best of kings then performed the filling of the image with clarified butter.

Having duly offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, one should worship Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, with this *arghya* and this mantra: RKV_209.128: dhūpadīpanaivedyādyaṃ saṃkalpya ca yathāvidhi / arghyeṇānena deveśaṃ mantreṇānena śaṅkaram // RKV_209.128 //
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, Śambhu, the supreme cause!
Accept this *argha*, O God, and dispel the evil of saṃsāra.
Gold consecrated by mantras should be given according to one's means;
for Agni is all the gods, and gold originates from the consumer of oblations.
Therefore, all the deities shall be pleased by the gift of gold;
may Śaṅkara be pleased with the giver who bestows even half of that amount at all times.
By this rite, Śiva was worshipped by him during the first watch; then, during the second watch, he should perform worship again according to the previously mentioned procedure.
He bathed the Destroyer of Tripura with cow’s milk;
thereafter, the filling of the trident-bearing Lord’s linga was performed with rice grains.
Having performed the previously mentioned ritual, a pair of white garments was given;
for a pair of white garments is exceedingly dear to Śaṅkara.
Śambhu was indeed pleased by the gift from Śvetavāsas,
having seen that the third watch of the night had arrived, O best of kings.
Having bathed the deity with honey, one should perform the filling with sesame seeds and offer a drona of sesame seeds while reciting the mantra.
White sesame seeds, black sesame seeds—sesame seeds are the removers of all sins.
By the gift of one *droṇa* of sesame seeds, may my cycle of rebirth be severed.
By this procedure, the king, having passed the first watch of the night in worship and in diversion,
kept a vigil accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
Those who remained steadfast in Śiva during the vigil of the Three-eyed One on Śivarātri performed a worship of Śambhu that accomplishes great merit.
O Pārtha, those performers of sacrifices do not go to that destination which they have reached;
for whatever sins there may be, even those accumulated over ten million births, [they are all destroyed].
During the vigil for Hara and Keśava, as many moments as there are for men staying awake at night come to an end through that bathing.
O King, for those devoted to fasting and dwelling in the temple of the deity, the fruit of the horse sacrifice is certain at every twinkling of the eye.
Those who listen to the narrative of the Dharma and meditate upon Hara and Keśava shall attain a destination that cannot be reached even by a sacrifice involving much gold.
The lunar day of Śivarātri is meritorious, especially the full moon of Kārttika;
so too is the northern bank of the Revā, the shore known as Bhāreśvara.
"And how can one who remains awake with great suffering not cast off his sin?
Having thus kept vigil on Śivarātri, O lord of men, [he attained liberation].
At dawn, when the sky was clear, he went to the excellent bank of the Narmadā and bathed all those mounts, including the elephants and others.
"By those vehicles by which I went to the sacred ford and bathed, I shall cause them to bathe as well;
standing there in the midst, having bathed, the merchant emerged from his state as an animal."
He gave gifts on their behalf according to his capacity;
by that, the man is liberated from the fault incurred by the vehicle.
Otherwise, that gain made goes toward them;
having bathed him, the king then bathes himself according to the prescribed ritual.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule,
and having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, he should release a bull endowed with auspicious marks.
Having gone to the temple, he should then bathe the deity with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha),
then with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and thereafter with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, having anointed Śaṅkara with water containing all medicinal herbs, with pure water, and with fragrant sandalwood paste; RKV_209.152.
The fourth filling of the liṅga is performed with saffron mixed with camphor, various fragrances, and abundant, highly scented flowers.
The best of kings performed here the preliminary rite,
and afterwards he made the gift of a cow according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
O Dhenukā, you are of the form of Rudra, created by Rudra himself;
rescue me, who am falling into this bottomless cycle of existence.
Then, having adorned a cow, one should give her away according to this rite;
having asked forgiveness from the Lord of the Gods, one should feed many Brahmins.
One should honor them with six kinds of foods and edibles, as well as garments;
having worshipped them with various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), one should ask for their forgiveness.
Afterwards, he himself ate together with his retinue;
that lord of the earth stayed there for that very night.
O Lord of Men, while he was staying there, at the very depth of the night,
he heard a divine voice uttered from the sky.
The voice said:
"O King, for those evil-minded ones who have fallen here into this ocean of saṃsāra, the fruit [of their actions] is now equal throughout the world."
If it is said that the fruit arises there merely through proximity,
how could it be that which causes madness for the lineage of Śantanu?
"This ox in your house, which indeed bears an exceedingly heavy burden—
by him was committed the sin of murdering a friend and the betrayal of trust."
In a previous birth among thousands of past lives,
by means of the evil committed, one has established oneself in the hells.
Then, indeed, after passing through thousands of wombs and even among the animal realms, that evil-minded one reached the womb of a cow in your house.
And you have bathed him at this sacred ford on this occasion of the festival;
having seen the worship arranged by you, the rite of keeping vigil has been performed.
"O King, having become free from all taint by that act, he will cast off his body before you and today depart for heaven seated upon a celestial chariot."
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When this was spoken, the leader of the team fell down and was deprived of his life;
at that very moment, he was seen mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Having bowed down to that lord of kings, he spoke as if laughing:
Vṛṣa said:
"O best among the most excellent of kings, listen to the supreme majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha),
wherein even a man such as I is liberated from his sins."
"I have known in its entirety that there is no sinner equal to me."
Beyond this, what else could I do but further glorify sacred fords?
For you are my mother, you are my brother, and you are indeed my grandfather.
I must be forgiven; today I bow before you, for at whatever sacred ford those like me attain such a destination as this, I do not know what your own destination may be.
Having propitiated Maheśāna and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, [the sage said:
"O Lord, what is your destination? Please grant me permission to speak with you."
"Indeed, these hosts dwelling in heaven urge me on out of affection;
may it be well with you, I shall depart," saying this, he vanished in an instant.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When he had vanished from sight there, the king, filled with wonder,
returned to his own city while describing the incomparable majesty of that sacred ford.
For such is that sacred ford situated on the Narmadā;
it causes the destruction of all sins, destroys all suffering, and is supreme.
O Bhārata, minor sins are destroyed merely by bathing on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika for one who is devoted to fasting.
One should fill the liṅga in four ways; hear now the fruit of its merit:
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife.
The four great sins are destroyed by these four [practices];
he obtains the supreme fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
by giving gold at that sacred site, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice.
On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, as before,
one should fashion a lamp out of flour and thereby liberate all the ancestors.
In that regard, whatever gift is given, even if it is only as small as the tip of a hair, all of that has inexhaustible fruit; thus spoke Maheśvara.
O King, for those men of purified soul who die in Bhārabhūti, there is an irreversible destination, leading continuously to the world of Śiva.
Or else, for the sake of worldly conduct, he desires to conquer the world of mortals;
he is born into a pure family of Brahmins who know the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
Endowed with wealth and grain, possessed of Vedic knowledge,
and liberated from all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Furthermore, having reached that sacred ford, one shall indeed attain the imperishable state.
This merit-bestowing and sin-destroying account has been told to you, O best of kings;
now listen further to this great narrative of the Bhārata.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhārabhūti Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 210.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Immediately after that, O dear one, is the supreme Puṅkhila Tīrtha.
O Pārtha, in that sacred ford (tīrtha), Puṅkha attained perfection in ancient times.
The lordly Jāmadagnya, of great splendor and the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas,
performed extensive austerities on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
From that time forth, O lord of men, it became renowned as Puṅkhatīrtha;
and whoever bathes in that tīrtha and worships the Supreme Lord, [attains the highest goal].
Endowed with strength in this world, he shall attain liberation in the next;
by duly honoring the gods and the ancestors, he becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Whosoever, indeed, gives up his life at that sacred ford,
his destination is undoubtedly the world of Rudra from which there is no return.
Having bathed at that holy site, a person shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O King, whatever man feeds Brahmins at that sacred ford,
when one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Whoever worships the Bull-bannered Lord at that sacred site undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Puṅkhila Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 211.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
That which was performed by the God of Gods is a source of wonder for the world.
I shall relate all of that to you concerning those who dwell upon the banks of the Narmadā.
At the time when the śrāddha ceremony had arrived, the god, having become a leper and smeared with red perfumes and unguents, begged from the twice-born who were skilled in performing rites.
With limbs dripping from blisters, covered with flies and worms,
having diseased skin and a foul face, smelling of stench, he stumbles at every step.
Having gone to the Brahmin’s residence, he stumbled at the door and said this:
"O householder, today there is a meal with Brahmins! (RKV 211.4)
"I wish to perform [the rite] in your house, well-prepared along with these [materials].
Then, having seen that Brahmin, they were accompanied by the sacrificer.
As it flowed from all his limbs, they cried out, "Fie! Fie! "Go forth quickly, you foul-smelling one; depart swiftly from this house, O lowest of the twice-born! (RKV 211.6)
"Because it has been consecrated by your sight, this is unfit for consumption by anyone.
Having said, "It is even so; let it be thus," Maheśvara, the God of gods, [departed].
He went into the stainless sky while being watched by the best of the twice-born;
and when the god had vanished from sight, [the king], having bathed and sprinkled himself all over, [proceeded].
The twice-born and the kṣatriyas ate from their respective bowls,
yet wherever they looked, there were many worms.
Having seen this, they were all filled with wonder and asked, "What is this?
Then a certain virtuous and noble Brahmin spoke as follows:
There, in that assembly of many brahmins, the lord of yogis, out of suspicion, [thought]:
"The yogi who arrived here first is the Supreme Lord."

I consider this to be the sport of that [deity]; it is the fruit born of the rebuke of one who has been censured, and not of anyone else, according to the certainty of the scriptures regarding guests.
Having indeed worshipped the Supreme Self, one should especially honor a guest;
for he who does not honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a śrāddha [commits a fault].
Piśācas and rākṣasas will undoubtedly plunder that [offering] of his, whether it be handsome or ugly, dirty, or clad in soiled garments. (RKV 211.14)
"One should not discriminate between a lord of yogis and even a dog-cooker when they arrive as a guest.
Having heard those words of his, the assembly, led by the patron of the sacrifice, [acted accordingly].
The brahmins ran in every direction to search for the twice-born man;
meanwhile, he had somehow or other taken refuge in a dense forest.
"He has been seen! He has been seen!"—thus it was proclaimed, and so they all arrived;
then they beheld that brahmin standing motionless like a pillar.
Some cry out but do not move, and they do not even blink;
some wail piteously, while others offer hymns of praise.
O Three-eyed Lord of Gods, being constantly praised with pleasing words,
you ought to restore once more the lost food for all these brahmins, who are especially afflicted by hunger.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard those words of the brahmins,
the Lord, being pleased, spoke to them with supreme compassion.
"O beings of great power, since I am pleased, that very food has been prepared for you like nectar.
O Brahmins, eat it together with your kinsmen and servants, and worship my mandala constantly."
Thereafter, O Pārtha, is the auspicious abode of the trident-bearing God of gods,
renowned as Muṇḍina, which removes all sins;
it is especially significant on the full moon of Kārttika and is equal to the sacred site of Gayā.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Muṇḍitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 212.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now I shall further proclaim another great deed of the Lord.
By merely hearing it, one is swiftly liberated from all sins.
Having assumed the supreme form of a monk, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
went to a village consisting of a single hall, seeking alms while afflicted by hunger and thirst.
With hands raised holding a rosary, his body smeared with ashes,
the Lord of the Universe wields a throbbing trident and is adorned with matted locks and earrings.
Clad in a hide, possessing a massive body, and adorned with great serpents,
he was indeed sounding a beautiful hand-drum resembling a *ḍiṇḍima*.
