The Blessed One, skull in hand, surrounded by many children,
was in some places singing and laughing, and in others dancing and speaking.
In whichever house the Lord, by way of sport, places his drum,
O Pārtha, that house, overwhelmed by the weight, perishes right there.
Moving in this manner, the Lord, surrounded by many people and appearing both visible and invisible in form, went forth outside.
When people no longer saw him running here and there, they stood amazed; then Śambhu appeared, and they offered praise.
While they were thus praising Śaṅkara, the Lord of the worlds, with devotion,
the Blessed One appeared before them in the form of Ḍiṇḍi.
From that time forward, O King, the Lord of Gods is called Ḍiṇḍimeśvara;
by seeing him or touching him, one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ekaśālaḍiṇḍimeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 213.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall further relate another great deed of the Lord.
By merely hearing it, one is liberated from all sins.
O Bhārata, I shall tell you how Śambhu, though not a child, appeared in the form of a child and played with Āmalaka fruits together with the village boys.
O Pāṇḍava, all those stainless stones that had been thrown by the god were brought back at that very moment; thereafter, Hara threw them again.
Just as they go out in various directions and return from those directions individually,
so do they behold that stainless, supreme Lord, the ultimate reality.
And in the third [section] is the deed of the wise God of gods,
concerning the supreme station among all stations, the most excellent Āmaleśvara.
By merely honoring him, the supreme state is attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Āmaleśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 214.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now fully describe the great deed of the God, which is the fourth.
By merely hearing it, one is liberated from all sins.
Having become a wearer of a skull-topped staff and a necklace of bones,
he wandered the earth surrounded by piśācas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, ḍākinīs, and yoginīs.
Assuming a terrifying form and taking his seat upon a corpse,
he bestowed fearlessness upon the three worlds and performed extensive ascetic penance.
The Āṣāḍhī festival was established there, for which reason it became renowned by the name Āṣāḍhī;
thereafter, the supreme deity released his patched garment elsewhere.
From that time onwards, O Indra among kings, he is called Kantheśvara;
by the mere sight of him, one indeed obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The god wanders there again on the path by chance;
seeing him, the seller of meat was addressed by Hara:
"If, my good sir, you do not become angry with me now, force me to take up my linga; I will give you much wealth."
Thus addressed by the god, that merchant, deluded by greed,
mobilized his forces— the superior, the middling, and the inferior— before the Liṅga.
When all that had been well-accumulated over time had finally come to an end,
he beheld the tall, standing linga and was overcome with grief.
Having reduced him to pieces, that god, the Supreme Lord,
seeing that he was now free from fear, spoke these words with a smile:
"And my vow shall not be fulfilled if you depart as you intend; I shall give you wealth there once the linga has been completely filled."
The merchant said:
"O Supreme Lord, I am an unfortunate man who has failed to perform meritorious deeds;
having failed to do what is pleasing to you, I shall grieve for eternal years."
O Bhārata, having heard these words of that merchant's son,
Maheśvara remained there after bestowing inexhaustible wealth.
From that time forth, O Indra among kings, the Linga remained there, adorned as if by cranes,
for the sake of providing proof and out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world.
O Pārtha, this well-established [shrine] was built by the God for sport;
it is known as Devamārga and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
By seeing it or even by worshipping it, one is liberated from all sins.
But he who, having gone along the Devamārga, worships Balākeśvara after reaching Pañcāyatana, goes to the world of Rudra.
For those men of purified soul who die on the path of the gods,
there shall never again be a return from the world of Rudra.
O best of men, having heard with devotion the majesty of the Devamārga, one is liberated from all sins; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śrī Kapālatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 215.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Śṛṅgītīrtha, which bestows liberation upon all embodied beings.
O Indra among kings, for those who die there, the attainment of liberation occurs; of this there is no doubt.
By offering a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at that very place, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
purified by that merit, one attains the state of Gaṇeśvara.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śṛṅgī Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 216.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O delighter of kings, one should then go to the Aṣāḍhī Tīrtha.
There Maheśvara stands, having assumed a form that fulfills all desires.
This sacred ford, O King, is the best among all sacred fords throughout the four ages;
having bathed there, a man shall become an attendant of Rudra.
Whoever gives up their life at that sacred ford attains,
without doubt, a state from which there is no return, from the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Aṣāḍhī-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 217.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should go to the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, which is saluted by gods and asuras.
That sacred ford is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins.
Having become intent on fasting, with his senses and mind restrained,
one who bathes there according to the prescribed rite is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whoever, at that sacred site, should be intent on giving up their life with devotion,
will undoubtedly attain a state from which there is no return, from the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Eraṇḍī-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 218.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Lord of the Earth, one should then proceed to that most beautiful holy place (tīrtha).
It is known as Jamadagni, where Janārdana attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, how did Vāsudeva, the preceptor of the universe, become perfected while assuming a human form out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds?
O sinless one, I desire to hear all these deeds of the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, as they are recounted by you according to the proper method.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O great king, in former times there was a great lord of the Haihayas,
a king renowned as Kārtavīrya, who possessed a thousand arms.
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, he was the best among all wielders of weapons; having completed his studies and vows in the Vedas, he granted fearlessness to all living beings.
The illustrious king, the lord of Māhiṣmatī and commander of an akṣauhiṇī,
who possessed great strength, once went forth to hunt deer.
After many days, the immensely radiant Jamadagni reached the unsurpassed Bhṛgukaccha, where the ascetic remained.
Accompanied by Reṇukā, the illustrious one who grants fearlessness to all beings had a son, Rāma, the Lord who was Nārāyaṇa himself.
Endowed with all the virtues of a kṣatriya, he was a knower of Brahman and the best of brāhmaṇas;
he delighted his parents with supreme devotion as if they were the Supreme Reality itself.
Then, seeing Arjuna wandering on a hunt, the powerful Jamadagni approached him and invited him with the rites of hospitality.
Having said, "So be it," that king, together with his servants, army, and vehicles,
went to the holy hermitage of that high-souled seer.
At that very moment, it was perfected and endowed with supreme splendor;
seeing that there, the king experienced the utmost amazement.

As soon as he had arrived, the king, along with his servants and army, was fed excellent food by the Siddha Brāhmaṇa through his miraculous power; he then asked about the cause and the capacity for such a feat, wondering, "What is this?"
Having understood that power of the wish-fulfilling cow, he then said to the brahmin:
"O brahmin, give me as my sacrificial fee that excellent, sin-cleansing cow."
I give you a hundred times a hundred thousand, ten million, a hundred million, and even a billion cows adorned with ornaments.
Jamadagni said:
"O dear one, I will not give away this supreme Kāmadhenu for tens of thousands, millions, or even hundreds of millions; let her be taken back."
O descendant of Bharata, having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the lord of kings,
his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these words.
O defiler of the twice-born, since you act with such self-will even toward me,
I shall therefore take Surabhi from your house while you look on.
The twice-born said:
"Who indeed plays fearlessly with a furious great serpent,
even one whose gaze is death itself— he who would take away my cow?"

Having spoken thus, Jamadagni, seized with supreme rage, took up a great staff like a second Brahma-staff and said: RKV_218.20: "Having spoken thus, Jamadagni, seized with supreme rage, took up a great staff like a second Brahma-staff and said:"
"O lowest of the Kṣatriya clan, whatever power or splendor you possess,
let you lead away my cow immediately, along with your attendants, for your life is exhausted."
Having heard these cruel words, the Haihaya king, though surrounded by hundreds of followers,
ran across the surface of the earth and fell down, struck by the staff of Brahmā.
Then, by the lowing of the cow, thousands of dark-skinned beings were seen emerging, with swords, nooses, and axes in their hands.
From the tip of the nostrils and from the tips of the body hairs, the Kirātas and Māgadhas emerged;
and from the apertures within, they were born by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus, having struck one another and burning the Haihayas and Ṭaṅkaṇas,
they met their destruction along with the Brahmin through the splendor of Arjuna.
Having achieved victory in battle and slain that best of brahmins, Kārtavīrya,
deluded by the power of destiny, went to his own city rejoicing.
Then, having arrived later in haste after the enemy had departed, Rāma saw his mother weeping in the presence of his father.
Rāma said:
"By whom has this rash act been committed out of ignorance for his own destruction—
he who, desiring to kill my father, wishes to see Death here?"
Then, at Rāma’s words, she became distraught as if her life-force had departed; striking her belly with both hands, she spoke to him.
"Having come here together with other cruel kṣatriyas, my father was slain by that Arjuna, who is endowed with mighty arms."
Behold your father slain, O son, breathless and devoid of consciousness; having prepared him according to the prescribed rites, offer him libations as is fitting.
Having heard these words and having paid homage to his mother, he made a vow; hear that, O lord of men.
Having cleared the earth of the lineage of kṣatriya families twenty-one times,
and having bathed in their blood, I shall satiate your husband.
"Listen to my truth: having severed even the arms of that evil-minded Kārtavīrya with my axe, I shall drink his blood."
Having thus made this vow, the powerful son of Jamadagni,
overcome by great anger, then consecrated his father.
Overwhelmed with rage, Rāma went to the city of Māhiṣmatī;
having cut down that forest of arms and slain that lowest of Kṣatriyas, he departed.
He went forth to bring an end to the Kṣatriyas, surveying the earth with its seven continents, oceans, mountains, forests, and groves.
From east to the western quarter, and from south to north Kuru,
he created five pools of blood at Samantapañcaka.
Overwhelmed by rage, he offered libations to his ancestors with blood in those lakes of bloody water; so we have heard.
Then Ṛcīka and the others approached the bull among Brahmins and said to him,
"Forgive us," whereupon he desisted.
The region near those lakes of bloody waters,
which is known as Samaṃtapañcaka, is celebrated as a sacred place.
Having turned away from that ritual act, the son of Pāṇḍu, Rāma, whose soul is supremely devoted to dharma, addressed the ancestors: "This blood which has been shed by me..."
"May that which has been cast into these five sacred fords become the most excellent of all sacred fords.
Having said "So be it," all those ancestors vanished from sight.
Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, association with Rāma on the path of the gods destroys all the sins of men through both seeing him and touching him.
Even today, for the sake of providing proof to Reṇukā,
the ancestral deities are seen stationed in the path of the gods, bringing about the destruction of all sins.
O Indra among kings, at that sacred ford where the Narmadā meets the ocean,
men who establish a place of worship according to the prescribed rite are liberated from their sins.
O son of Kuntī, even the great ocean must not be touched with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
O best of kings, one should bathe there using this mantra.
"Salutations to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Lord of Waters!
O Lord of Gods, manifest your presence here in the salt-water ocean.
This is the mantra for touching [the water].
"Agni is the brilliance in the body, and Mṛḍayā is the seed; then Viṣṇu is the navel of immortality.
O Pāṇḍava, speaking this word of truth, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers.

O King of Kings, one should offer the *argha* oblation to the great ocean, combined with the five jewels and accompanied by fruits, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, while reciting this mantra: RKV 218.50.
"You are the treasury of all jewels, the source of the mine of all jewels;
O Lord, sovereign of all the foremost immortals, accept this water offering! Homage be to you!
Thus is the mantra for the water offering (*argha*).
"O Great Ocean, lift me up from the sins committed since birth!
O Treasure of Jewels, best of those who swell at the full moon, go now, having been worshipped!"—
this is the mantra for the dismissal.
Who else besides the god Sāgara is there for the opening of the gate of heaven?
There, extending as far as the ocean, lies that unsurpassed great sacred ford (mahātīrtha).
There the god was installed by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni;
there the gods, along with the gandharvas, sages, siddhas, and cāraṇas [reside].
Those men on earth who behold Virūpākṣa, the unsurpassed Jamadagni, and the goddess Reṇukā, worship them.
O King, having bathed there and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, men dwell for their desired time in that auspicious world, Priyavāsa.
Having bathed here, having given gifts, and having listened together with devotion, one shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage from the terrible hell. (RKV 218.57)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Jāmadagnya-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 219.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the supreme Koṭīśvara Tīrtha.
Where bathing and giving gifts shall all become ten millionfold in merit.
There, the gods along with the gandharvas and those stainless sages attained supreme perfection at Koṭitīrtha, a state difficult to find on earth.
And there, O King, Mahādeva Koṭīśvara was installed;
by beholding that Lord of the Gods of gods, one attains unsurpassed perfection.
O best of kings, whatever is performed at that sacred site, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all of it becomes ten millionfold in merit.
In that regard, whatever supreme sages dwell on the southern path,
having attained perfection or having died, they certainly go to the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka).
It is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that those preeminent bulls among sages who dwell on the northern bank of the Narmadā have previously gone to the world of the gods.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭitīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantyakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 220.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, one should go to the excellent Loṭaṇeśvara.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, it is the destroyer of all sins.
O King, at that very moment, all that sin accumulated over seven lifetimes is destroyed simply by the sight of the God of gods.
Whatever sin has been committed from childhood onwards, and whatever has been done in youth—
all that goes to dissolution by the sight of the God of gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Brahmin, you have indeed related in its entirety the great and wondrous account of Narmadā’s conduct, which destroys all sins throughout the worlds.
I wish to hear all about that one supreme holy place which bestows the fruit of all holy places; having shown compassion, please tell it to me quickly.
O best of beings, whatever questions are difficult to find within the three worlds,
all of them have been heard by me, together with my kinsmen, through your grace.
O best among all knowers of questions, having heard this one supreme question from you by your grace, I shall go there together with my kinsmen.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! For you who possess such an intellect, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to attain within the three worlds."
O bull among the Bharatas, that wise man who understands the proper time for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa at their respective times must act accordingly.
Therefore, I shall declare to you the auspicious answer to this question,
by hearing which men on earth are liberated from all sins.
The Narmadā is the best of rivers, auspicious and composed of all sacred fords;
its special excellence is said to lie at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
O best of kings, seeing Revā approaching, the great ocean bowed again to the goddess at the confluence with the Revā.
Having reflected in his mind, "Who indeed is this best of rivers? he recognized me, the supreme Revā, born from a *liṅga*, by reflecting in his mind.
Rolling forward, O dear one, the great ocean went to meet the Revā,
where the great river Narmadā enters the sea.
There, on the ocean, the *liṅga* of the God of gods arose;
from that *liṅga* emerged the highly fortunate Narmadā, the best among rivers.
Because she dissolved there into that *liṅga*, she is indeed most meritorious;
dwelling eternally on the Narmadā and always drinking the waters of the Narmadā,
he is initiated in all sacrifices and partakes of the Soma drink day after day.
That person who, having bathed at that confluence, worships Loṭaṇeśvara,
obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O King, whatever verbal or mental evil has been committed through action shall all go to dissolution upon reaching Loṭaṇeśvara.
O best of kings, listen to that which was specifically taught by Śaṅkara on the full moon day of Kārttika; it is the remover of all sins.
O best of kings, having seen that the full moon day of Kārttika has arrived, one should go there and,
having fasted on the fourteenth day, indeed bathe in the waters of the Narmadā.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods and performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules,
one should perform a vigil at night after having worshipped Loṭaṇeśvara.
His life is fruitful and his exertion is fruitful;
those others are undoubtedly like the lame—their birth is meaningless.
For those by whom Loṭaṇeśvara has not been seen with a one-pointed mind,
neither the state of a piśāca nor birth in a low womb shall ever occur in their family.
Having gone there to the confluence and performed his bath according to the prescribed rite,
he should likewise awaken [the deity] with meritorious songs and dances.
Then, seeing that the night has turned to dawn, one should bow to the great ocean,
take leave of it, and perform the ritual bath there according to the prescribed rules for bathing.
Oṃ, salutation to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutation to you, the Lord of the Tīrtha.
O God, O Ocean of salt water, grant me your presence.
This is the mantra of invocation.
"Agni is your brilliance, Mṛḍayā is your body, and Viṣṇu, the navel of immortality, is your seed.
Speaking these true words, O Pāṇḍava, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers.
This is the mantra for bathing.
Whatever sin a person has committed throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes,
they shall cast off that flood of evil by bathing once in the salt waters.
Otherwise, O best of the Kurus, this all-pervading great ocean, being of divine origin, should not be touched even by the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass by the gods.
"You are the foremost of all jewels, the source of all mines of jewels;
O Lord, sovereign of all the immortals, accept this water offering; homage be to you!
Thus is the mantra for the water offering (arghamantra).
Immediately after satisfying the ancestors, gods, and humans,
he emerged from the water onto its bank together with five eminent brahmins.
Having first performed the ritual installation according to the rules, one should subsequently perform the *śrāddha* with offerings corresponding to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Having honored them according to the rule, together with the Brahmins,
he should afterwards report all his good and evil deeds to them.
Having confessed whatever sin has been committed from childhood through old age and youth in the presence of those [elders], one should invite the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Whatever impurity I have committed from birth until now, starting from childhood—
all that has been confessed to the Brahmins while they remain in my presence.
Having spoken thus, he should thereafter roll on the ground before them and facing them;
and having obtained permission from those five, he should afterwards perform his bath.
And a funeral rite (śrāddha) for the ancestors should be performed according to the rules, O best of kings;
when this is done, O foremost of monarchs, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
But for anyone who, for the sake of inquiry, desires to know the self and whatever karma is auspicious or inauspicious— listen to this conclusion regarding it.
Having bathed in that great sacred ford, a man who rolls about there departs from sinful deeds; performing righteous deeds, he proceeds along the river.
Then, having realized that his evil deed was a sin accumulated in the past,
he should bathe in that best of sacred fords and give gifts according to the prescribed rule.
By worshipping Loṭaneśvara, one is liberated from all sins;
by going to Avakragamana, one is released from all transgressions.
Therefore, O best of kings, having understood this, men should bathe with every effort at that place where Hara is present.
Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rite, O protector of the earth, one should honor Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas for the pacification of all sins.
For such is that sacred ford (tīrtha), distinguished by its qualities, O best of kings;
listen with a one-pointed mind, O King, to the majesty of that tīrtha.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he who performs a śrāddha there, moved by a spirit of devotion toward his ancestors, [attains great merit].
He bestows gifts of cattle, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon the brahmins for sixty thousand years and one hundred crores of years.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he is honored in the heavenly world;
[he obtains] that fruit which results from bathing and giving gifts at all the sacred fords of the Narmadā.
One obtains that fruit at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean:
gold, silver, copper, gems, pearls, and ornaments.
By giving a bull, land, and grain there at that sacred site, the fruit is inexhaustible;
of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, there is no doubt in this regard.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to the meritorious fruit for that man who, at that sacred ford, gives up his life with devotion according to the prescribed rites.
Having sported for ten million years in the abode of Śiva,
that brahmin, learned in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, is born into a pure family.
Prosperous with sons and grandsons, endowed with wealth and grain,
and liberated from all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Whatever merit is gained by worshipping Somanātha during twelve pilgrimages under the conjunction of Kṛttikā on the full moon day of Kārttika, that same merit is obtained at Loṭaṇeśvara.
O Pārtha, one obtains that same merit from beholding Loṭaṇeśvara as one does from Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara.
The man who listens with devotion to this auspicious work as it is being recited,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Loṭaṇeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 221.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the southern bank of the Revā.
At a distance of two krośas from Mātṛtīrtha is a sacred site that is unsurpassed.
The meritorious Haṃseśvara, which destroys dejection,
was born in the lineage of Kaśyapa as a swan, the son of a daughter of Dakṣa.
In ancient times, he was born as the vehicle of Brahmā after performing great austerities; once, however, he fell into a state of agitation without following the instructions of the Creator.
Overpowered by the hosts of Śiva, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
he fled in all directions like one terrified at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, deprived of his authority.
When that bird did not quickly return even though summoned by Brahmā,
Brahmā then cursed him and indeed caused him to fall from his station.
Then, realizing that he had been cursed, the swan approached his grandfather in haste, prostrated himself, and spoke as follows:
The swan said:
"You ought not to curse one born from an animal womb;
for such is the very nature of animals that their minds are devoid of discernment."
Nevertheless, O Lord, I am a sinner in that I have abandoned my master;
however, O Grandfather, as the exceedingly fierce hosts of Śiva were rushing toward me,
I was suddenly overcome by fear and, trembling, fled, leaving him behind.
Even now, O Lord, I see only fear before me;
for that reason, though remembered by you, I did not come into your presence.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Even as he was speaking thus before the Creator, the swan—worshipped by the eyes, yet now deeply dejected—gasped for breath:
"O Lord, protect me, protect me! I am a sinner, a fool of dull intellect, fallen here before you."
You alone are the one God, the creator of this world; all these various things have been created by you alone.
That I was created by you as such—O Creator, this fault is truly yours alone.
There is no one other than you capable of either cursing or showing favor; to whom else shall I go for refuge?
O Father, protect me, your devotee, who has fallen from the duty of service, who has become like a slave, and who deserves only to be struck with slaps.
Knowledge and ignorance have emerged from you alone, as have merit and demerit, existence and non-existence, and day and night;
you ordain the manifold states of the world—into you, that one, I truly take refuge.
You are one, yet you possess many forms; through your manifold and wondrous single activity, you are both actionless and the performer of all actions. Therefore, I go to you for refuge.
Homage, homage to the most excellent one; homage, homage to the giver of boons. Homage to the Creator and the Ordainer; homage, homage to the refuge.
O Lord, how can this speech of mine, devoid of the syllables of training, offer praise?
What power or what understanding do I possess that I have spoken thus? Please forgive me.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While the swan was speaking thus, Brahmā, with a gracious mind, spoke:
"This very instruction has been given to you; do not fall into despair, O bird."
Purify yourself through austerity so that you may attain the end of the curse.
Perform service to the Revā by bathing in her and installing Maheśvara;
then, in a very short time, you shall reach your final abode.
And whatever fruit is obtained by performing many sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees,
as well as by the gift of ten million cows and gold, that same fruit is attained when Śiva is installed.
Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief of gold, or a violator of the Guru’s bed—
by installing Śiva on the bank of the Revā, one is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, having established Tryambaka on the bank of the Bharga river,
you, freed from all defects, shall go to the supreme state.
Thus addressed by Vidhi, that best of birds, delighted and satisfied,
said "So be it" and went quickly to the excellent bank of the Narmadā.
Having performed austerities for some time, he established Śaṅkara.
O best of the Bharatas, having worshipped the unsurpassed Haṃseśvara by his own name, that most excellent of birds attained the supreme abode.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having gone to that Haṃseśvara Tīrtha and bathed there, one should worship the Supreme Lord; he shall be completely liberated from all sins.
Praising the Lord with a one-pointed mind, one shall never fall into a state of wretchedness.
O best of kings, by giving a śrāddha, offering lamps, and feeding Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
O Pārtha, he who worships Śiva with devotion three times a day or once a day,
and gives a cow that has recently calved to an excellent brahmin,
is honored in the world of Śiva for sixty thousand years.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Haṃseśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 222.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go a distance of one krośa to the excellent Tīrtha called Tilāda.
In this regard, Jābāli attained purification by consuming sesame seeds.
One who abandons his father or mother, one who lusts after his brother’s wife, one who sells his son, a sinner, and one who acts with deceit toward his guru; RKV 222.2.
O Bhārata, wherever such a person, pervaded by faults, goes, there he receives reproach from the virtuous;
no one, even in assemblies, maintains association with him.
Thus, O King, at that time, the brahmin, filled with shame and not knowing how to proceed with his purification, fell into great anxiety.
He visited all the sacred fords and bathed in the Revā river as well.
Having reached the Aṇivāpa hermitage on the southern bank of the Narmadā,
O Pārtha, the ascetic Jābāli remained there, subsisting on sesame seeds.
Eating sesame seeds once a day, likewise eating at intervals of one day, eating every three, six, or twelve days, and likewise eating once every fortnight or month; RKV 222.7.
He also performed vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* with sesame seeds;
indeed, he gradually attained the status of a giver of sesame for seventy-two years.
As time passed, Īśvara became pleased with him;
he granted him purity pertaining to this world and the next, as well as residence in his own realm.
O bull of the Bharatas, that lord was installed by him under his own name,
and the deity also acquired the designation Tilādeśvara from the world.
From that time forward, that holy place became renowned as a destroyer of sins;
having bathed in that tīrtha on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, a man [attains the highest goal].
O Pārtha, likewise on the day of Hari, one should be devoted to fasting,
performing fire-oblations with sesame seeds, rubbing the body with sesame, bathing with sesame, and offering water with sesame.
Both the giver of sesame seeds and the consumer are liberated from various sins.
One who fills a linga with sesame seeds and gives a lamp with sesame oil attains the world of Rudra and purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
O best of kings, by the offering of sesame balls at a *śrāddha*,
even those ancestors who have followed improper occupations attain their desired destination.
Abiding in the heavenly world, those who have attained inexhaustible satisfaction through ancestral offerings (śrāddha) and the feeding of Brahmins rejoice for eternal years.
O King, by rescuing three families— the father's family, the mother's family, and likewise the wife's family— a man indeed leads them to heaven.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Tilādeśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 223.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Thereafter, O Pārtha, at a distance of one krośa, there is the supreme Vāsava Tīrtha."
Having stayed there for twelve years, he was established by the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these were the eight Vasus in ancient times.
Afflicted by their father’s curse, O Bhārata, they reached the Narmadā tīrtha and, with their senses restrained, practiced austerities in order to dwell in a womb.
O Indra among kings, while they were propitiating the supreme, imperishable Lord of Bhavānī for twelve years, Maheśvara then became pleased.
Pratyakṣa granted them their desired, supreme boon; then,
having established that Maheśvara under his own name,
the Vasus entered the sky and departed once Śaṅkara was pleased.
From that time forward, that sacred site became renowned by the name of Vāsava.
O Great King, whoever worships Śiva with devotion at that sacred site, and diligently offers a lamp along with whatever offerings they may have obtained— RKV_223.6 //
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or even every day according to one's ability,
he shall dwell in the presence of Śiva for eight thousand years.
Thereafter, he goes to the abode of Śiva and does not experience dwelling in a womb;
this may be accomplished with flowers, or even with sprouts, fruits, or grains.
One who worships the Lord Īśāna shall never encounter wretchedness;
liberated from all sorrow, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
O son of Kuntī, he who dwells for even a single day at Vāsava-īśvara shakes off a mass of sins and rejoices in heaven like the sun.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give garments as a sacrificial fee.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vāsaveśvara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 224.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Pārtha, then at a distance of one krośa is the supreme Koṭīśvara Tīrtha.
Whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, worship,
and so forth are performed there by men with devotion, all that shall become ten millionfold.
There, the gods along with the gandharvas, the ṛṣis, and the siddhas and cāraṇas, it is said,
go toward the ocean to behold the Narmadā.
O King, millions gathered at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean,
beholding the incomparable delight found in the meeting of the river and the sea.
Having bathed, established Śiva, and worshipped Maheśvara—who is named Koṭīśvara—according to the prescribed rite and with their own respective devotion; RKV_224.4 //
At Koṭītīrtha, supreme perfection was attained through the propitiation of Sarvatobhadra;
therefore, its merit is incomparable and the highest among all sacred fords.
O tiger among kings, whatever is performed at that sacred site, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, all of it becomes ten millionfold.
At that sacred ford, whatever supreme sages reside on the path attain the state of perfected immortality as well as the highest world of the ancestors.
Those who have taken refuge on the northern bank of the Narmadā and those on the southern—
my mind is certain that they have gone there to the world of the gods.
Having worshipped Maheśvara with bilva and arka flowers, with dhattūra, kuśa, and kāśa blossoms, as well as other seasonal flowers;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having propitiated Dhūrjaṭi according to the rules with various ritual services preceded by mantras, and with incense, lamps, offerings of food, and other oblations; RKV_224.10.
One attains the world of Śiva for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
a special merit is recorded for worship performed on the conjunction of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
And always, O best of kings, on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight,
one should worship Śiva and devotedly feed excellent Brahmins.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Koṭīśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 225.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, one should go a distance of one krośa to the supreme Alikātīrtha.
A woman named Alikā was a Gandharva-woman, immoral and crooked in her intentions.
Citrasena’s granddaughter went to the sage Vidyānanda;
she chose him, was accepted by him, and remained in his service for ten years.
For some other reason, she killed her husband while he was asleep;
having gone there, she reported [the matter] to her father, Ratnavallabha.
Abandoned by both father and mother, O King, and reviled by many, she said: "You are a killer of embryos! You are a killer of your husband! Do not show me your face! (RKV 225.4)
O most wicked woman, you who have slain a Brahmin, go away; depart from this house, forsaken.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, filled with grief and bewildered after being rebuked by those two,
she reached a certain other sacred ford and set her mind on abandoning her body.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having inquired of the Brāhmaṇas regarding sacred fords,
he heard of the sin-destroying tīrtha at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
There, O Pārtha, she performed austerities without food, having mastered her vows through the *kṛcchra*,
*atikṛcchra*, *pārāka*, *mahāsāṃtapana*, and other such penances.
He indeed emaciated his body through Cāndrāyaṇa and Brahmakūrca fasts;
thus, O King, one hundred and fifty years passed as he practiced asceticism.
Desiring her purification through the meditation on Śiva, worship, and other such practices,
Śiva— having understood her supreme resolve after a few days and being urged by Pārvatī— spoke to her with great satisfaction.
Īśvara said:
"Daughter, do not act rashly; you are now pure of body.
I am pleased today by your asceticism; choose a desired boon."
Alīkā said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if I am considered worthy of a boon,
grant supreme purification to me, who have been scorched by the fires of various sins."
For you are the protector of me who am protectorless; you alone are the teacher of the worlds. You are the deliverer of the wretched and the helpless, the refuge for all embodied beings.
The Lord said: "O blessed lady, you are one of pure body; do not grieve at all.
Having established me here under your own name, you shall thereafter go to heaven."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished right there; then Alikā also, out of devotion, bathed and installed Śaṅkara.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he attained a most exalted world,
as did his father and his mother.
O King, honored with affection by those kinsmen, Sālikā then ascended an excellent celestial chariot, adorned with divine garlands.
Having reached the world of Gaurī, he rejoices even today in her friendship;
from that time forth, O son of Pṛthā, it became renowned as Alikeśvara.
At that sacred ford, O Yudhiṣṭhira, whatever woman or man bathes and worships Mahādeva together with Umā with devotion, [attains the highest goal].
Freed from various evils, he attains the world of Śaṅkara,
along with whatever mental, verbal, and physical sins were previously committed.
All that [evil] goes to dissolution by always feeding the twice-born and by offering a lamp before the deity; one is never overcome by diseases.
O Indra among kings, by giving an incense burner, a celestial chariot, a bell, and a water-pot to the god, one shall attain the world of Śakra.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ālikeśvara Tīrtha at the Confluence of the Revā and the Ocean," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 226.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beyond that, at a distance of one krośa, is the meritorious holy site of Vimaleśvara.
Whereby, through bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, [one attains purification].
Having propitiated Vimaleśvara, whatever one may desire— that,
whether it be the attainment of heaven or anything else on earth according to one's wish— one shall obtain.
In ancient times, having slain Triśiras, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ,
Śatakratu attained supreme purity through the majesty of this sacred ford.
There, the brahmin Vedanidhi, having performed great austerities in the past,
became as stainless as the sun when his various stains of karma had been exhausted.
In former times, by the grace of Mahādeva, Bhānu, afflicted by the arrows of Love, [approached] Bhānumatī, his daughter, who was as pleasing to behold as the moon.
Because of that fault, he became afflicted with the disease of leprosy;
yet, by performing austerities here, he attained purity.
Delighted, he returned to his own abode with Mahādeva, who was pleased;
and in the same way, O Pārtha, did the sage Vibhāṇḍaka’s son in former times.
Having encountered the company of yogis in the forest as well as that of a king in the city,
the Supreme Self indeed incurs defilement from the fault of association with the passionate (rājasa).
Reflecting thus, he went to the confluence of the Revā and the ocean,
and having performed austerities for twelve years together with his wife Śāntā, he remained there.
By propitiating the god Tryambaka through the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances,
the sage also attained purity when Mahādeva was pleased.
O King, in ancient times, Śarva, impelled by Śarvāṇī in the Dāruvana forest,
indeed manifested his own stainless form through the enchantment of the wives of the sages.
Having reflected upon the supreme site at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean,
O Great King, he remained there and performed austerities together with Umā.
Since he was born from Vimalā, he is Vimaleśvara;
by that name he himself remained there, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
Then, having created Tilottamā, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds;
and the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), too, having created her, beheld her standing before him, most enchanting.
Overpowered by the force of his destiny, he became enamored of her;
yet, perceiving the faults therein, he took refuge on both banks of the Revā river.
Wandering among sacred fords, observing silence, bathing three times a day, and constantly remembering Śiva,
the royal sage Brahmā attained purity in a short time after bathing at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean and worshipping Śaṅkara.
In this way, many others as well— divine sages and the most excellent of kings— having abandoned the stain of faults there, became stainless.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, by bathing there and worshipping Śiva, you too, though already stainless, will attain supreme purity in an even more distinguished manner.
Having bathed there and having worshipped Maheśvara, a man or a woman,
liberated from the defects of sin, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O King, whoever observes a fast there and beholds Vimaleśvara on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on all festival occasions, [attains the highest merit].
Having abandoned the sins committed over seven lifetimes, one goes to the abode of Śiva;
by performing the *śrāddha* rite according to the prescribed rule, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beneficial to oneself at home— all that should be given to one possessed of virtue by him who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible:
gold, grain, garments, an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.
Having constructed a temple for the God according to one's ability, one shall become a sovereign on earth;
and one should satisfy the Supreme Lord with songs, dances, and sacred narratives.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Vimalēśvara Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 227.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
These have been recounted to you in brief, according to their importance.
O Pāṇḍava, it is not possible to state the number of sacred fords in detail.
This river Narmadā is pure, stainless, and renowned throughout the three worlds;
she is the best of rivers and the beloved of Mahādeva.
O King, he who constantly remembers the Narmadā in his mind quickly obtains the supreme fruit of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
"Those men who lack faith and those atheists who abide here fall into a terrible hell; thus spoke the Supreme Lord."
The Lord Maheśvara himself constantly frequents the Narmadā;
therefore, this river should be known as meritorious and the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
This Gaṅgā of Maheśvara, born from the body of Maheśvara,
is called the Southern Gaṅgā of Bhārata, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Jāhnavī is indeed Vaiṣṇavī Gaṅgā, and the Gaṅgā is Brāhmī Sarasvatī;
this [river] is Māheśvarī Gaṅgā, the Revā—of this there is no doubt.

"Just as the God, residing within a single person, assumes the state of the three forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, yet there is no actual division therein; even so, O Pārtha, do not conceive of a division among the triad of rivers."
For here, O Bhārata, there are crores and even lakhs,
as well as thousands of sacred fords situated on both banks of the Revā.
Who is capable of determining those [beings] situated between trees and in the sky, as well as those on water and on land— not even Vāgīśa or Maheśvara?
By remembering [the river], the sin produced in one birth is destroyed; by seeing her, that produced in three births; and by bathing in the Revā, the sin committed in seven births perishes.
By him the work of the gods has been accomplished, the sacred fires have been offered according to rule,
the four Vedas have been studied, and the Revā river has been plunged into.
O Pārtha, these sacred fords have been described by me to you according to their importance and in brief; it is not possible for me to hear or to speak of them in detail.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me of the ordinances, the restraints (yamas), and the observances (niyamas);
tell me what the rule is for undertaking the purpose of expiation (prāyaścitta).
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Well asked, O great king, regarding that which is beneficial for the world beyond. Listen with an attentive mind; I shall speak to you according to my knowledge.
One should perform steadfast deeds with this unstable body;
for the vital breaths will inevitably depart, like guests leaving.
One should extract the essence from what is insubstantial: generosity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, fame and merit from renown, and service to others from the body.
In this cauldron consisting of great delusion, Time cooks all beings with the fire of the sun, using day and night as fuel, and stirring with the ladles of months and seasons; such is the report.
Having understood what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scriptures, you ought to perform action here;
for there is neither this world nor the next, nor happiness, for one whose mind is consumed by doubt.
In regard to a mantra, a sacred ford, a brahmin, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a teacher—
whatever one’s conception is, such will be the accomplishment.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given in charity, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit either in this world or after death.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own desires,
attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
There are various means here for the purification of the human body;
yet there is no purification of one's own body equal to the service of sacred fords (tīrtha).
O King, for those who perform the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, or for a second time through the service of sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
when a man sets out with a sacred ford as his goal,
then the gods and the ancestors follow him as he travels through the sky.
Filled with supreme joy, those followers of his proceed after performing the *abhyudayika* śrāddha and taking leave of the deity.
Having taken up his religious observances and being permitted by the twice-born, he should go to his beloved kinsmen, as well as to Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara together with the lords of the Gaṇas.
Eating at a single sitting, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, truthfulness,
avoiding the food of others, and the avoidance of accepting gifts.
O best of kings, having avoided malice, deception, and the like,
and having assumed the guise of a virtuous man, he was adorned with humility.
He who is free from hypocrisy and egoism enjoys the fruit of pilgrimage;
he whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained.
O Indra among kings, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, and firm in his vows, enjoys the fruit of sacred pilgrimage through knowledge, austerity, and fame.
He who treats all beings as himself attains the fruit of pilgrimage;
shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule for all sacred sites.
Except for Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā,
[one should avoid] bathing, the worship of deities, and indeed the offering of funeral cakes at a śrāddha ceremony.
This is the rule for all sacred fords: one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability;
and this applies to whoever, with a restrained mind, goes there for the purpose of expiation.
I shall also declare its procedure; listen with a concentrated mind, O Pārtha:
eating but one meal a day, practicing celibacy, and abstaining from pungent and salty food.
Having bathed, one should visit sacred fords, eat sacrificial food or food from a single source,
and avoid conversation with the fallen as well as excessive speech.
One should avoid slander, the food of others, and association with the base;
one should go about barefoot, wearing two clean garments and remaining pure.
Having formed a resolution in his mind and having obtained the permission of the Brahmins, he should depart;
then, having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha) and bathed there, he should perform the worship of the gods.
If one who has committed an evil deed should feel remorse, he may be liberated from that karma by means of the Veda, a sacred ford, a deity, an astrologer, medicine, or a preceptor.
Whatever kind of meditative cultivation one possesses, such is the success that occurs;
this has been stated in the Purāṇas and also in the Smṛtis regarding the fruits of visiting sacred fords.

O bull among the Bharatas, having abandoned any doubt regarding the existence of explanatory passages (arthavāda), and having reflected upon what is taught in the scriptures, you should determine what is appropriate.
Indeed, for those who are unable to perform difficult penances with the body,
one should understand that there is no distinction among sacred sites and perform an expiation accordingly for the sake of purification.
Listen to that, O Great King, as it truly is regarding the Narmadā: a man should travel twenty-four yojanas [to reach it].
One obtains the auspicious fruit of twenty-four kṛcchra penances; beyond that, for each yojana, a quarter-kṛcchra is prescribed.
And within that [distance], O Great King, for one who should travel out of a desire for purification,
the wise know that there is an expiation for every yojana.
O Great King, having gone to the place called Praṇava, as well as to the confluence of the Revā and Urī, and likewise to Bhṛgukṣetra, that fruit is said to be twofold.
O best of kings, at the confluence of the celestial river and at Śūlabheda, the merit is double; likewise, it is one-quarter less at the confluence of the Karajā.
Likewise at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī and at the confluence of the Kapilā;
some say it is tripled at the confluence arising from the Kubjā and Revā.
And at Oṃkāra, O Great King, that too would be consistent;
likewise at the confluences of other rivers with the Revā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, they say that the fruit previously mentioned is indeed a *kṛcchra* and a half;
however, at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, one obtains three times that *kṛcchra*.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is said that at Śuklatīrtha, the *kṛcchra* penance is fourfold;
having traveled twenty-four *yojanas*, going from *yojana* to *yojana*, he who dwells there for a very long time, O best of men, [attains great merit].
He who is devoted to the practice of serving the Revā, endowed with pure intellect,
and free from hypocrisy and egoism, is liberated for the sake of purification.
Thus, O Pārtha, I have told you the characteristics of the purpose of expiation, as well as the procedure for the pilgrimage to the Revā; this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is a secret.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of sages, tell me the measurement of a yojana;
by knowing which, my mind may attain certainty as a cause for its purification.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O Pāṇḍava, I shall describe the measurement of a yojana,
as well as the specific hardships encountered during various journeys.
They say that eight horizontal barley grains or three vertical rice grains constitute the measure of a finger (aṅgula); twelve fingers make a span (vitasti).
Two *vitastis* constitute a *hasta*; four *hastas* are known as a *dhanus*.
That same measure is declared by those who know the distinctions to be a *daṇḍa*, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Two thousand bows make one *krośa*, and four *krośas* make one *yojana*.
This measurement of a *yojana* has been described to you, O bull among the Bharatas.

O best of kings, it has been stated that at a sacred ford (tīrtha) consisting of water, one who goes on a pilgrimage perceives the measure of the fruit earned by oneself; such is the fruit described for the Kṛcchra penance.
I shall tell you those specific details as they were previously stated in various places;
listen to that from me, O protector of the earth, for it is being told to one who possesses faith.
O King, whatever fruit— such as that of the *kṛcchra* penance— is proclaimed for a particular sacred ford (*tīrtha*),
one obtains even more than that fruit of the *kṛcchra* by fasting there.
By reciting [the mantra] there for a day, one obtains the fruit of a *kṛcchra* penance according to one's capacity;
having bathed there, beheld the renowned Lord of Devas, and worshipped him.
O Pārtha, a wise person who bows down obtains the fruit arising from the Kṛcchra penance;
at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one obtains the primary fruit from bathing and a second from fasting.
The third [stage] is through seeing and worshipping the renowned deity;
the fourth is by means of the yoga of recitation, day and night, according to one's physical capacity.
Indeed, the fifth [type of pilgrimage] should be considered as being at a distance from all sacred fords (tīrtha);
standing on the bank, one obtains a tenth part of the fruit within a distance of one yojana.
O Pārtha, no deliberation need be made here regarding the fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha) thus described.
O Pārtha, bathing in a great river accompanied by a fast,
even if it is within a yojana [of one's home], bestows upon men the fruit of the kṛcchra penance.
The small streams flow for six yojanas, and the minor rivers for twelve;
the great rivers flow for twenty-four yojanas, and those beyond them are even greater still.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Specific Narration of the Rules for Pilgrimage and Other Rites," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rāmāyaṇakathāvalī, Chapter 228.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
For one who goes on a pilgrimage for the sake of others, what is the fruit for whom?
O best of sages, O treasury of compassion, tell me: how much [is that]? 228.1.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, listen as I tell you about one who goes for the sake of another; hear how much fruit shall accrue from his undertaking of the pilgrimage and other rites.
O King, a person of the highest caste, out of greed for wealth and other motives,
must never perform the service of a lower caste, such as undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred sites and the like.
O Great King, one who is himself learned should personally perform a righteous deed,
either according to his physical capacity or through other means as the occasion demands.
A legal act should always, as a general rule, be performed by one of the same caste,
or else by sons, grandsons, and so forth, or by kinsmen born of the same lineage.
"For they say, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that the performance of dharma is the highest ordinance;
therefore, one should have it performed by those very people—neither by the most excellent nor by the lowliest."

It is my conviction that what is done by an inferior person will not be correct; moreover, even an excellent person, by acting for the sake of an inferior, may indeed fall into an evil state of existence.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for a sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.
Recitation, austerity, pilgrimage, renunciation, the practice of mantras,
and initiation for the propitiation of deities— these six lead to the downfall of women and Śūdras.
A wife whose husband is living certainly does not become a widow; she may perform all [rites].
While her husband is capable, she should do everything with his permission.

Having gone to a sacred ford or similar site for the sake of another, one obtains a sixteenth part of the fruit; and for one who goes to a sacred ford incidentally, half the fruit is traditionally taught.

Those who know the truth understand that by bathing at a sacred ford merely out of habit, one obtains only the fruit of the bath; they do not obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage as declared in the scriptures, which destroys all impurities.
And for the sake of one's father, paternal uncle, mother, maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, as well as brother, father-in-law, and son; RKV 228.13.

And also for the one who nourishes, for those beginning with "artha," as well as for the maternal grandmother, the teacher, the sister, the mother’s sister, the paternal aunt, the preceptor, and the instructor.
Having bathed for such purposes as these, a man shall himself obtain one-eighth [of the merit];
performing it directly on behalf of his parents, he shall obtain one-fourth.
The wise say that the fruit for a wife and a co-wife is equal when shared between them;
however, a man obtains one-sixth, one-third, one-fifth, and one-fourth of the fruit respectively from his sister’s son, his disciple, his brother’s son, and his own son.
Thus has this been told to you, O Pārtha, handed down through the sequence of tradition:
that which must be done for the sake of one's kin as a means of accomplishing dharma for the sake of others.
At the onset of the rainy season, all rivers are in their menses,
with the exception of the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, and the river Yamunā.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruit of Pilgrimage for the Sake of Others," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth Āvantya-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV Chapter 229.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has this Purāṇa, which is a compendium of dharma, been narrated to you, O King.
Just as it was proclaimed by Vāyu in the assembly of the gods out of devotion to Śiva.
There are sixty thousand and likewise sixty crores of sacred fords along the Narmadā, at every step, in its beginning, middle, and end.
The twelve-thousand-verse compendium which I heard in the past from the God of Gods as he was speaking, has now been recounted by me to you.
"O King, when questioned by you on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
I, while staying there, related all of that to you in brief."
Listen to the meritorious account of Narmadā and the fruit that belongs to it;
it is the same fruit that would be obtained through all the Vedas, together with their six auxiliary limbs and the methods of Pada and Krama recitation.
Therefore, by reciting or even merely hearing it, one shall obtain a much greater fruit than that which a performer of a sacrificial session (satra) receives after twelve years.
But by hearing the life-story of the Goddess, one obtains such a fruit as that merit which is gained by bathing in all the sacred fords, beginning with the ocean.
Indeed, that same fruit which comes from bathing once and likewise listening [to this] at the Narmadā is obtained through the auspicious account of the Narmadā from beginning to middle to end.
Hear now the fruit of merit for that man who listens with devotion:
having attained the abode of Śiva, he will be surrounded by the daughters of Rudra.
Having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices together with him;
this narrative of dharma is the most excellent among all scriptures.
Whether in a country, or a province, or even in a village or a city,
or in a house— wherever one of the four castes resides, O Bhārata.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva manifest, and he is the god Janārdana;
he is the threefold cause in the world and the supreme path of dharma.
O Pārtha, having heard from the mouth of the Lord this scripture, which is the teacher of the gods and the supreme cause of accomplishment, it has been proclaimed by me to you as well.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) there are on the southern and northern banks, those which are preeminent and highly meritorious have been specifically described.
By touching them, by seeing them, by reciting their names, and likewise by hearing them,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Whoever should constantly hear this ancient Purāṇa spoken by Śiva—
a Brāhmaṇa shall become possessed of Vedic knowledge, and a Kṣatriya shall be victorious.
A Vaiśya shall become a possessor of wealth, and a Śūdra shall indeed become a partaker of dharma;
by hearing this, a woman shall obtain good fortune, progeny, heaven, and wealth.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—
having heard the majesty of the Narmadā, they are cast out from sin.
One who betrays his kin, one who is ungrateful, one who betrays the trust of his master, a killer of cows, a giver of poison, and one who sells his own daughter; // RKV_229.19 //
Upon merely hearing these, O King, they are liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
But those who have cultivated their souls and listen to them constantly, O King, [attain even greater merit].
By honoring this, the gods and their gurus are honored by them;
Narmadā is honored by him, as is the Blessed Lord Maheśvara.
Therefore, with every effort, this scripture— which bestows fruit— should be worshipped with supreme devotion using perfumes, flowers, and ornaments.
Having had the entire auspicious narrative of Narmadā transcribed—
which is superior to all scriptures— he who gives it to a twice-born man, [attains the highest merit].
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing and giving gifts at all the sacred fords of the Narmadā, that same fruit a man attains; there is no doubt in this matter.
This Purāṇa, spoken by Rudra, bestows the fruit of great merit;
it grants heaven, grants sons, is auspicious, brings fame, and increases renown.
O Pārtha, it removes all sins and destroys suffering and bad dreams;
O King, for those who recite or hear it, it grants the fulfillment of all desires and goals.
May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may the worlds be free from disease;
may there be well-being for cows and Brahmins, and may righteousness be the refuge of those whose souls are devoted to dharma.
May Revā, who brings an end to hell, who possesses excellent tirthas, and who purifies the entire universe—
may Narmadā, the bestower of dharma and the giver of happiness, always be with you, O Pārtha.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Hearing of the Fruits of Reading, Listening to, and Giving Gifts Relating to the Revā-khaṇḍa," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa), within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira.
RKV Chapter 230.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the son of Pāṇḍu, the sage then ceased.
The wise son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who remembers seven kalpas, stood before him.
O best of men, just as it was proclaimed by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to the son of Pṛthā,
so has this entire, supreme majesty of the Revā been narrated to you.
This is the meritorious Revā, the best of rivers, the sole purifier of the universe;
born from the body of Rudra, she grants fearlessness to all beings.
The descendant of Bhṛgu spoke concerning the various distinctions between sacred fords and their confluences as far as the ocean of Oṃkāra, to the son of Dharma who was questioning him.
In brief, O sages, I shall likewise tell you:
there are sixty-seven thousand and sixty crores.
How and by whom could this be fully described here, even in hundreds of years?
Nevertheless, O best of sages, it has been told here just as it was told to the son of Pṛthā.
Beginning with the sacred site of Oṃkāra, I shall describe the auspicious series of holy places;
listen, O great sages, as it is being told in brief.
Having bowed to Soma and Maheśāna, having bowed to both Brahmā and Acyuta,
and to Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśāna, and the lotus-feet of the Goddess;
Having likewise seen all the former teachers who knew the unseen reality,
and having bowed to the goddess Narmadā, I shall now describe this series of sacred fords (tīrthas).
Oṃ, salutations to the one of universal form, to the syllable Oṃ, the self of all!
O twice-born ones, beginning with him, I shall proclaim the series of sacred sites (tīrthas) of Revā.
In this auspicious account of the sequence of Revā tīrthas narrated by Mārkaṇḍeya,
the chapter from the Purāṇa Saṃhitā is the description of Mārkaṇḍa’s hermitage.
Then follows the section on questions, the praise of the origin of the Narmadā,
and likewise the proclamation of the fifteen streams.
Likewise, there is the etymological explanation of his name, as well as the origin of the eons;
and similarly, there is the proclamation of the names of the twenty-one eons.
The characteristics of the seven [kalpas] experienced by Mārkaṇḍeya,
as well as the majesty of the Revā and likewise of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Likewise, the characteristic of dissolution and the origin of the syllable *oṃ*,
as well as the majesty of the *oṃ* syllable and the glorification of Amarakaṇṭaka.
And the Amareśvara Tīrtha, as well as the great Dāruvana,
the Dārukeśvara Tīrtha, and the Carukeśvara Tīrtha.
Likewise, there is Carukāsaṅgama, Tadvyadvatīpāteśvara,
the Pātāleśvara Tīrtha, and the one called Koṭiyajña.
There is the Varuṇeśvara Tīrtha and one hundred and eight Liṅgas;
beyond that are Siddheśvara, Yameśa, and Brahmeśvara.
O best of the twice-born, there are Sārasvata, Aṣṭarudra, Sāvitra, that which is known as Soma, the great holy ford Śivakhāta, and Rudrāvarta.
Brahmāvarta is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), and Sūryāvarta is even more excellent than that;
so too are Pippalāvarta-tīrtha and the confluence of the Pippalī.
The majesty of Amarakaṇṭaka, the confluence of the Kapilā,
the origin of Viśalyā, and the glorification of the mountain Bhṛgutuṅga.
The meritorious Viśalyāsaṅgama, the Karamardāsaṃgama,
the holy site of Karamardeśvara, and the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha.
The confluence of the Nīlagangā, the destruction of Tripura,
the glorification of sacred fords and gifts, and the Madhuka-tṛtīyā vow.
Then there is the Apsareśvara Tīrtha and the rite for casting off the body;
likewise, the Tīrtha named Jvāleśvara and the confluence of the Jvālā.
Śakratīrtha, Kuśāvarta, and likewise Haṃsatīrtha;
the tīrtha of Ambarīṣa, and likewise Mahākāleśvara.
The Mātṛkeśvara Tīrtha and the description of Bhṛgutuṅga;
therein, the majesty of Bhairava and the glorification of Capaleśvara.
The greatness of Caṇḍapāṇi, as well as the confluence of the Kāverī;
the Kubereśvara Tīrtha, and likewise the confluence of the Vārāhī.
The confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, the sacred ford of Caṇḍeśvara,
the meritorious confluence of the Eraṇḍī, and the excellent Eraṇḍeśvara.
O lords of sages, right there is the Pitṛtīrtha and the origin of Oṃkāra; [I shall describe] the majesty of the five liṅgas and of Oṃkāra.
The majesty of Koṭitīrtha, as well as the Kākahrada Tīrtha,
the Jambukeśvara Tīrtha, and thereafter the Sārasvata [Tīrtha].
Likewise, there is the confluence of the Kapilā, the holy site of Kapileśvara,
the Daityasūdana-tīrtha, the Cakratīrtha, and Vāmana.
The ancients knew a hundred thousand holy sites at the confluence of the Kapilā;
this is the characteristic of both heaven and hell as spoken by the sages.
The arrangement of the body, the description of the gift of cows,
the sacred ford of Aśokavanikā, and the description of Mataṅga’s hermitage.
And there is the Aśokeśvara Tīrtha, the excellent Mataṅgeśvara,
as well as the meritorious Mṛgavana and the Manoratha Tīrtha.
The confluence of the Aṅgāragartā, the supreme Aṅgāreśvara,
as well as the Meghavana Tīrtha and the recitation of the names of the Goddess.
Also the confluence with the Kubjā, the holy site of Kubjeśvara,
likewise the Bilvāmraka holy site, and beyond that, Pūrṇadvīpa.
Likewise, there is the meritorious confluence of the Hiraṇyagarbhā,
as well as the holy pilgrimage site named Dvīpeśvara and the sacred Yajñeśvara.
And there is the Māṇḍavya-hermitage-tīrtha, as well as the confluence of the Viśokā;
the tīrtha named Vāgīśvara, and the meritorious confluence of the Vāgu.
There is the Sahasrāvartaka tīrtha, as well as the Saugandhika;
and the confluence with the Sarasvatī, the supreme tīrtha known as Īśāna.
Then there is the Devatātraya-tīrtha and thereafter Śūlakhāta;
following that are Brahmoda, Śāṅkara, Saumya, and then Sārasvata.
And the Sahasrayajña-tīrtha, as well as Kapālamocana,
Āgneya, Aditīśa, and the supreme Vārāha-tīrtha.
Likewise, Devapatha, Tīrtha, [another] Tīrtha, Yajñasahasraka,
Śuklatīrtha, Dīptikeśa, Viṣṇutīrtha, and Yodhana.
O best of beings, [there are] Narmadeśvara-tīrtha, Varuṇeśa, Māruta,
Yogeśa, Rohiṇī-tīrtha, and Dāru-tīrtha.
Brahmāvarta, Pattreśa, Vāhna, and Saura are celebrated; as well as Meghanāda, Dārutīrtha, Devatīrtha, and Guhāśraya.
That supreme Kapilā-tīrtha is known as Narmadeśvara;
beyond that are Karañjeśa, Kuṇḍaleśa, and Pippalāda.
The Vimaleśvara Tīrtha, the confluence of the Puṣkariṇī,
the praise of Śūlabheda, and therein the valor of Andhaka.
The granting of consolation to the gods, likewise the subduing of Andhaka,
the origin of Śūlabheda, and the examination of the alms-bowl.
The praise of the virtue of giving, the manifestation of the power of Ṛṣiśṛṅga,
the heavenly rebirth of Dīrghatapas, and likewise the gestures of Bhānumatī.
The greatness arising from Śūlabheda, including the Śabara’s ascent to heaven, as well as the Kapileśvara Tīrtha; beyond that is the Mokṣatīrtha.
The confluence of the river of liberation and the holy site of Vimaleśvara,
as well as the Ulūka-tīrtha and the confluence of the Puṣkariṇī.
There is the Ādityeśvara Tīrtha, and the Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha;
there is the confluence of the Bhīmakulyā and the auspicious Bhīmeśvara Tīrtha.
And the Mārkaṇḍeśvara Tīrtha, as well as Pippaleśvara,
the Karoṭīśvara Tīrtha, and the auspicious Indreśvara Tīrtha.
Agastyeśa, Kumāreśa, the unsurpassed Vyāseśvara,
Vaidyanātha, Kedāra, and the one known as Ānandeśvara.
Mātṛtīrtha, Muṇḍeśa, Caura, and likewise Kāmeśvara; the confluence at Anuduhyā, indeed, and the holy site called Bhīmārjuna;
the holy site named Dharmeśvara, and Luṅkeśvara beyond that.
Then there is Dhanadatīrtha, Jaṭeśa, Maṅgaleśvara,
Kapileśvaratīrtha, and the excellent Gopāreśvara.
There is the place named Maṇināgeśvara, the confluence of the Maṇinadī river,
the Tilakeśvara Tīrtha, and beyond that, Gautameśa.
O lords of sages, in that very place, Mātṛtīrtha was spoken of by the Sage;
and after that, Śaṅkhacūḍa, Kedāra, and Pārāśara, according to the opinion of Parāśara.
Bhīmeśvara, Candreśa, the confluence of the Aśvavatī,
Bahvīśvara, Nāradeśa, Vaidyanātha, and Kapīśvara.
Kumbheśvara, Mārkaṇḍa, Rāmeśa, Lakṣmaṇeśvara,
Megheśvara, Matsyakeśa, and the one known as Apsarāhrada.
Dadhiskanda, Madhuskanda, Nandikeśa, and Vāruṇa;
likewise Pāvakeśvara-tīrtha and Kapileśvara.
The holy ford named Nārāyaṇa, the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha,
the supreme Caṇḍāditya Tīrtha, and the excellent Caṇḍikā Tīrtha.
The holy ford named Yamahāsāhvaya, as well as the auspicious Gaṅgeśvara,
the one known as Nandikeśvara, and the one called Naranārāyaṇa.
And Naleśvara, Mārkaṇḍa, and beyond that Śuklatīrtha;
Vyāseśvara is a supreme holy site, and likewise Siddheśvara is there.
Koṭitīrtha, Prabhātīrtha, the excellent Vāsukīśvara,
the confluence of the Karañjā, and the supreme Mārkaṇḍeśvara.
The holy ford named Koṭīśvara, as well as that called Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Kanakeśa, Manmatheśa, and the holy ford Anasūyaka.
The confluence of the Eraṇḍī is meritorious, as is the beautiful Mātṛtīrtha;
there is also the holy site known as Svarṇaśalākā, and likewise Ambikeśvara.
Karañjeśa, Bhārateśa, Nāgeśa, Mukuṭeśvara,
the Saubhāgyasundarī Tīrtha, and the excellent Dhanadeśvara.
Rohiṇya, Cakratīrtha, the one known as Uttareśvara,
Bhogeśvara, Kedāra, and beyond that, Niṣkalaṅka.
Mārkaṇḍa, Dhautapāpa, the Tīrtha Aṅgiraseśvara,
the meritorious Koṭavī-saṅgama, and Koṭitīrtha are indeed located there.
The supreme non-womb-born (ayonija) Tīrtha, the excellent Aṅgāreśvara,
and those known as Skānda, Nārmada, Brāhma, and Vālmīkeśvara.
Koṭitīrtha, Kapāleśa, Pāṇḍutīrtha, Trilocana,
Kapileśa, Kambukeśa, Prabhāsa, and Kohaneśvara.
Indreśa, Vālukeśa, Deveśa, and Śakra;
Nāgeśvara, Gautameśa, and the supreme Ahalyātīrtha.
Rāmeśvara, Mokṣatīrtha, as well as Kuśalaveśvara,
Narmadeśa, Kapardīśa, and thereafter Sāgareśa.
Dhauḥ-āditya is a supreme holy site, as is the holy site born from the lower womb;
there is also the Piṅgaleśvara-tīrtha and the unsurpassed Bhṛgvīśvara.
O virtuous ones, there are the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha, Koṭitīrtha,
Mārkaṇḍa, Brahmatīrtha, and the supreme Ādivārāha.
The holy site named Āśāpūra, as well as Kaubera, Māruta,
Varuṇeśa, Yameśa, Rāmeśa, and Karkaṭeśvara.
Śakreśa, Somatīrtha, and the unsurpassed Nandāhrada;
Vaiṣṇava Cakratīrtha, known as Rāma and Keśava.
Likewise, there is Rukmiṇītīrtha, the unsurpassed Śivatīrtha,
Jayavārāhatīrtha, and the tīrtha named Asmāhaka.
Then Aṅgāreśa, Siddheśa, and thereafter Tapeśvara;
again the one named Siddheśvara, and the Tīrtha Varuṇeśvara.
The meritorious Parāśareśvara, the unsurpassed Kusumeśa,
the Kuṇḍaleśvara Tīrtha, and likewise Kalakaleśvara.
The one known as Nyankuvārāha, the excellent Aṅkola Tīrtha,
the Śvetavārāha Tīrtha, Bhārgala, and the supreme Saura.
The holy ford of Huṅkārasvāmin, the beautiful Śuklatīrtha,
the confluence of the Madhumatī, and the Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha.
And there is the one named Narmadeśvara, the confluence of three rivers,
Anekeśvaratīrtha, and Śarabheśa, which is known as Mokṣa.
The confluence of the Kāverī is meritorious, as are the holy sites named Gopeśvara,
Mārkaṇḍeśa, Nāgeśa, and the confluence of the Udumbarī.
The holy site named Sāmbāditya, the confluence of the Udumbarī,
Siddheśvara, Mārkaṇḍa, and likewise that which was established by Siddheśvarī.
Gopeśa, Kapileśa, and the unsurpassed Vaidyanātha;
the holy site of Piṅgaleśvara and the great shrine of Saindhava.
Beyond that is the holy site named Bhūtīśvara, followed by Gaṅgāvāha;
then there is Gautameśvara Tīrtha and likewise Daśāśvamedhika.
Likewise, there is the meritorious Bhṛgutīrtha, the famous Saubhāgyasundarī,
Vṛṣakhāta, and right there Kedāra, which washes away all sins.
Likewise, there is the holy site known as Eraṇḍī, which is the confluence of Dhūteśvarī;
and the holy site of Kanakeśvarī, and after that, Jvāleśvara.
The sacred site called Śālagrāma, the unsurpassed Somanātha,
as well as the Uddīrṇavārāha and Candraprabhāsa tīrthas.
And the Dvādaśāditya-tīrtha, as well as the one named Siddheśvara,
the Kapileśvara-tīrtha, and likewise the auspicious Traivikrama.
The holy site named Viśvarūpa, likewise that created by Nārāyaṇa,
the Mūlaśrīpati-tīrtha, and the one known as Caulaśrīpati.
Devatīrtha, Haṃsatīrtha, and Prabhāsa, the most excellent tīrtha;
then Mūlasthāna, Kaṇṭheśa, and beyond that, Aṭṭahāsa.
There is the Bhūrbhuveśvara Tīrtha, as well as the famous Śūleśvarī; also the Sārasvata, Dārukeśa, and the excellent Tīrtha of the Aśvins.
The incomparable Sāvitrītīrtha, as well as Vālakhilyeśvara,
Narmadeśa, Mātṛtīrtha, and the unsurpassed Devatīrtha.
O best of sages, there are the Macchakeśvara Tīrtha, the beautiful Śikhi Tīrtha, and Koṭi Tīrtha; and there is the goddess Koṭīśvarī Mṛḍā.
There is the sacred ford named Paitāmaha, known as Māṇḍavyeśvara;
there is also Nārāyaṇeśa, and beyond that, Akrūreśa.
Devakhāta, Siddharudra, and the unsurpassed Vaidyanātha;
likewise Mātṛtīrtha, and thereafter Uttareśa.
Likewise, there is Narmadeśa, and again Mātṛtīrtha; as well as Kurarītīrtha, Ḍhauṇḍheśa, and Daśakanyaka.
They know Suvarṇabindutīrtha, which releases one from debt and sin,
as well as the Bhārabhūteśvara Tīrtha and Muṇḍīśvara.
Ekaśāla, Ḍiṇḍipāṇi, the supreme Tīrtha of the Apsarases,
Munyālaya, Mārkaṇḍa, and the one named after the deity Gaṇita.
They speak of the Āmaleśvara-tīrtha, as well as the Kantheśvara-tīrtha,
the Āṣāḍhī-tīrtha, and likewise the Śṛṅgī-tīrtha.
Bakeśvaratīrtha and likewise Kapāleśa,
