Mārkaṇḍa and Kapileśa, as well as the confluence of the Eraṇḍī.
Next is the Erandīdevatā Tīrtha, and beyond that the Rāma Tīrtha;
then the supreme Tīrtha of Jamadagni, and the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
O best of sages, there is the Loṭaneśvara Tīrtha, as well as the one named Luṅkeśa; and there is likewise a pool (kuṇḍa) excavated by Vṛṣara.
Likewise, there is the one named Haṃseśvara, Tilāda, and Vāsaveśvara;
as well as the Koṭīśvara Tīrtha and the supreme Alikātīrtha,
and the Vimaleśvara Tīrtha at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
Thus, O great sages, this meritorious series of sacred fords has been proclaimed by me;
this auspicious string of hymns to the fords is strung together upon the rope of the riverbanks.
Purified by the waters of the Narmadā and fashioned by Mārkaṇḍeya,
it was created here for the adornment of the virtuous and for the welfare of all the worlds.
This Dhāraṇī, which pacifies the darkness of calamities, should always be upheld by those seeking the Dharma;
by reciting it even once, one quickly destroys the evil committed during a day and night.

By reciting [the mantra] three times a day for one month before Śiva, one obtains the fruit of one month; for three months, that of three months; by reciting for one month, that of one year; and by reciting for one year, that of a hundred years.
Standing before the Brahmins while they are eating at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
one who recites this meritorious series of sacred fords (tīrthāvali) becomes a performer of a śrāddha at Gayā.
And by reciting this with faith before the gods at the time of worship,
one delights all the deities and purifies one's entire lineage.
Thus, O best of sages, I have described this meritorious series of pilgrimage sites situated on both banks of the Revā; likewise, O sinless ones, listen now [to what follows].

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Series of Tīrthas," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said:
In the same manner, O best of sages, I shall describe the clusters of sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
by which the previously mentioned garland of holy sites was woven together as one.
In former times, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who expands the bliss of the world of devotees and is auspicious, spoke this divided [account] to the inquiring Pārtha.
In whatever manner I shall describe here the clusters of sacred fords (tīrthas),
the Revā— born from the drinking of Śiva’s water— is indeed a meritorious wish-fulfilling creeper.
Blossoming with the flowers of the sacred fords arising from both its banks,
that auspicious river has indeed made the three worlds fragrant with the splendor of its meritorious scent.
The sage Mārkaṇḍeya, the best among the wise, was indeed a bee most skilled in savoring the taste of the nectar from those flowers.

The sage, the scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage, constantly wears upon his heart that meritorious flower garland, variegated with clusters from sacred fords. O best of sages, I shall describe the arrangement of its clusters.
Starting from Oṃkāra-tīrtha as far as the western ocean,
there are indeed thirty-five confluences of rivers that destroy all sins.
On the northern bank there are ten and one, and twenty-three on the southern;
the thirty-fifth is the most excellent, the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
O best of the twice-born, at the confluence where the two banks of the Revā meet, there are likewise four hundred renowned sacred sites (tīrthas).
There are three hundred and thirty-three Śiva-tīrthas;
I shall describe them to you individually, O virtuous ones—listen to them!
O lords of sages, among them there are ten Mārkaṇḍeśvara tīrthas;
here there are ten born of Āditya and nine indeed of Kapileśvara.
There are eight established by Soma, as many Narmadeśvaras,
eight Koṭitīrthas, and likewise seven Siddheśvaras.
There are exactly seven Nāgeśvaras on both banks of the Revā;
likewise, there are seven established by Vahni, as well as a group of seven Āvartas.
There are five Kedāreśvara tīrthas and five Pañcendrajā;
likewise, there are five Varuṇeśas and five Dhanadeśvaras.
There are exactly five Devatīrthas, four Yameśvaras,
four Vaidyanāthas, and four Vānareśvaras.
O lords of sages, there are as many tirthas of Aṅgāreśvara as there are;
there are four of Sārasvata and four of Dārukeśvara.
There are three Gautameśvara Tīrthas, three Rāmeśvaras,
three Kapāleśvara Tīrthas, and those created by Haṃsa.
The sage declared that there are exactly three pilgrimage sites for liberation, three indeed are the stainless lords, and exactly three are the pilgrimage sites of the thousand sacrifices.
Three Bhīmeśvaras are renowned, as are three Svarṇatīrthas;
two Dhautapāpas have been proclaimed, and likewise two Karañjeśas.
O twice-born ones, there are two Ṛṇamocana tīrthas, as well as two Skandeśvaras,
two Daśāśvamedha tīrthas, and two Nandī tīrthas.
Likewise, there are the two Manmatheśas, the two Bhṛgutīrthas,
the two Parāśareśvaras, and the two Ayonisaṃbhavas.
Two Vyāseśvaras are proclaimed, as well as two Pitṛtīrthas;
there are two Nandikeśvara Tīrthas, and two Gopeśvaras are remembered.
Likewise, there are two Māruteśas and two Jvāleśvaras are remembered;
as well as two meritorious Śuklatīrthas and two Apsareśas.
The descendant of Bhrigu likewise spoke of two Pippaleśvara Tīrthas, two known as Māṇḍavyeśvara, and two Dvīpeśvaras; similarly,
there are two Uttareśvara Tīrthas and two Aśokeśas.
There are two Yodhanapuras and two Rohiṇītīrthakas;
likewise, the Sage has related the famous account of the two Luṅkeśvaras.
O twice-born ones, one hundred and nineteen holy sites have been established individually in the clusters;
thus, two hundred and fourteen holy sites have been made in total.
O best of beings, listen as these Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava holy sites, as well as those of Brahmā and Śakti, are described to you in their proper order.
The sage declared that there are twenty-eight Vaiṣṇava tīrthas;
among them, O best of sages, there are exactly six Vārāha tīrthas.
The son of Mṛkaṇḍu previously declared that there are four *cakratīrtha*s, while the remaining eighteen are indeed presided over by Viṣṇu.
In that same manner, for the sake of spiritual perfection, Brahmā proclaimed seven sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
Among them, there are three sites of worship dedicated to Brahmā, and four others dedicated to Brahmā-Īśa;
these twenty-eight have been described by me according to their number and sequence.
This sacred account of Narmadā’s deeds, spoken by the sages, is incomparable, supremely purifying, and a destroyer of sins. RKV 231.31.
Sūta said:
Thus has the sequence of the Revā tīrthas been declared by me in brief,
according to how the sage Mārkaṇḍeya spoke it to Pārtha.
There are numerous minor holy sites within them that remain hidden;
O sinless ones, listen to where they are and what their extent is.
In all directions for a distance of two *krośas* from Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, surrounding the Oṃkāra-tīrtha, three and a half crores [of holy sites] are reckoned.
O best of the twice-born, there is one crore of sacred fords— both hidden and manifest—
distinctly gathered at the confluence of the Kapilā.
O best of sages, a sacred ford (tīrtha) extending for a hundred thousand [yojanas] is established at the confluence of the Aśokavanikā and the Śatamangāragartā.
Likewise, ten thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated at the confluence of the Kubjā,
and one hundred are established at the confluence of the Hiraṇyagarbhā.
Sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated at the confluence of the Viśokā,
and likewise, a thousand sacred fords are established at the confluence of the Vāgu.
One hundred [merits] at the confluence of the Sarasvatī, two hundred at Śuklatīrtha,
one thousand at the Viṣṇutīrthas, and ten thousand at Mahiṣmatī.
O twice-born ones, the sage declared that there are more than a hundred thousand holy sites at Śūlabheda,
and one thousand holy sites at Devagrāma.
In Luṅkeśvara, seven hundred and one holy sites (tīrthas) are situated;
at the confluence of the Maṇinadī, there are one hundred and eight holy sites;
and in Vaidyanātha, they know there to be one hundred and eight holy sites.
Thus, O twice-born ones, there are approximately one hundred and twenty-five thousand sacred fords at Kumbheśvara on the Tīrtha,
situated at the confluence of the Revā.
Furthermore, Mārkaṇḍeya stated that there would be even more than those,
numbering eighty-eight thousand islands inhabited by Vyāsa.
And at the confluence of the Karañjā, there are eleven thousand eight hundred [tīrthas] situated;
likewise, at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, there are one hundred and eight tīrthas.
At Dhūtapāpa, sixty-eight holy fords are situated;
the sage has declared that at Skandatīrtha there is the merit of one hundred holy fords.
Sixty-eight holy places (tīrthas) are situated at Kohaneśa,
and indeed one and a half crores of holy places are situated in Korilāpura.
He has declared that at the Rāma-Keśava-tīrtha there are more than a thousand [deities],
and indeed a thousand tīrthas reside at Asmāhaka.
O best of the twice-born, in ancient times Bhārgava recounted eight hundred thousand and two thousand sacred fords at Śuklatīrtha to the son of Pṛthā.
He stated that there are one hundred and eight confluences for each of the remaining rivers,
excluding the confluence of the Kāverī.
O Brahmins, five hundred [sages] likewise reside at the confluence of the Kāverī;
furthermore, the sage has declared a special distinction for these sacred sites on festival days.
For they say that the true place of liberation is that which is resorted to by the Ancient Puruṣa; and in the field of Bhṛgu, ten million holy fords (tīrthas) are situated together.
O best of sages, who indeed would be able to describe that which is more than sufficient [in merit],
which is declared to be the refuge of all immortals and likewise the refuge of all sacred fords?
Renowned throughout the three worlds and honored as a means for attaining spiritual success,
one hundred and eight sacred sites (tīrthas) are situated at Bhārabhūti.
At Akrūreśvara-tīrtha, one hundred tīrthas reside together;
and at Vimaleśvara-tīrtha, at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean,
the sage declared there to be more than ten times ten thousand tīrthas.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Enumeration of the Number of Tīrthas," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
RKV, Chapter 232.
Sūta said:
Thus, O brahmins, the supreme majesty of the Revā has been narrated to you.
Just as it was taught to Pārtha by Mārkaṇḍeya in the past.
Likewise, among those [places], the clusters of sacred fords (tīrthakadamba) have been declared by me according to their specific characteristics, primarily, in their respective numbers and sequence.
This sacred account of Narmadā’s deeds is incomparable, supreme in its power to remove sin, meritorious, and the majesty of the river as spoken by the sages.
O lords of sages, the wise son of Mṛkaṇḍu, a brahmin who followed [the river] for seven kalpas, was the most excellent knower of the supreme truth on the Narmadā.
Having previously visited all sacred fords and all rivers,
he beheld the Revā, born from the body of Śiva, who remembers many kalpas.
And saying "I am yours," he went for refuge to Śarvā, who was born of Śarva—
the supreme goddess, ageless and immortal, the destroyer of the Daityas.
Having bound his true love for that river of existence— the Ganges of becoming— which is endowed with great majesty and destroys worldly existence, he too became free from old age and death.
O virtuous ones, sixty thousand and sixty crores of sacred fords are established at every step along both banks of the Revā.
O lords of sages, although there are thousands of excellent holy sites existing everywhere around Sārita, I consider them not to equal even a fraction of the Revā.
O twice-born ones, all this that was asked has been told to you in its entirety—
that which Vāyu spoke to the sages after hearing it from the mouth of Maheśa.
In the same way, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, having experienced the entire river along with its sacred bathing places step by step, recounted that purifying account to the son of Pāṇḍu.
And all this meritorious account of the Narmadā, which is difficult to find in the three worlds, has been told in brief, O best of the twice-born.
What is the use of resorting to the waters of thousands of other rivers,
if the water of the Revā, which destroys all sins, is resorted to?
One who resorts to the waters of Mekalā attains eternal liberation.
In whatever manner a mortal pilgrim worships, whatever he desires, he certainly attains that— whether with faith or even without faith.
This is Brahmā, this is Hari, and this is the manifest Supreme Hara;
this is formless Brahman, this is absolute liberation—the water of the Narmadā.
Holy fords and rivers that yield the fruit of the heart roar only so long as, in the Kali age, they are not remembered by men who have found devotion to the Revā.
Surely, for the sake of the welfare of the world, Śiva has brought down from his own body this certain power in the form of a river— this Reva.
In the Kali age, sacrifices, forests, sacred fields, and the like roar loudly only so long as the glorification of the one named Narmadā is not performed.
The weight of people is calculated in terms of their asceticism, charity, vows, and so forth,
only as long as the river born of Bharga flows upon the earth.
Those who dwell on the northern bank are indeed the attendants of Rudra;
those who dwell on the southern bank go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Blessed are those excellent lands, in which regions the Narmadā—
the eternal destroyer of hell, created by Śarva— is ever present.
And those people who have performed meritorious deeds do not come to grief,
they who drink the meritorious water born from the river of the Lord of Pārvatī.
O twice-born ones, he who hears or recites this incomparable, purifying account of the Revā is liberated from all sins.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all the Vedas, together with their six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Pada and Krama recitations,
when heard and recited, the fruit from this [practice] shall be eightfold greater than that.
Whatever fruit one who performs a sacrificial session (*satra*) obtains over twelve years,
that same fruit one may obtain by hearing the life-story of Revā even once.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing in all the sacred fords, such as the oceans and others,
one obtains that same fruit by hearing the majesty of the Revā but once.
This sacred narrative is unsurpassed among all scriptures;
it may be recited in a region, a district, a city, or even in the midst of a village.
In whosever house this [text] written for all castes remains,
he is Brahmā, he is Śiva in person, and he is the Lord Janārdana.
This scripture, served by the gods, is the path to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
it is the teacher of teachers and the supreme cause of spiritual accomplishment.
Whoever should constantly hear this Purāṇa spoken by the gods,
a Brāhmaṇa shall become possessed of the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya shall be victorious.
A Vaiśya becomes wealthy, and a Śūdra indeed becomes a partaker of righteousness.
Upon hearing this, a woman shall obtain a lineage of good fortune,
as well as prosperity, happiness, residence in heaven, and rebirth in an excellent family.

One who distinguishes flavors [for personal gain], one who is ungrateful, one who betrays his master, one who deceives a friend, one who kills a cow, one who administers poison, and one who sells a daughter; RKV 232.34.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—
he who listens to the account of Narmadā and serves her for a year [is purified].
One who is liberated from all sins is born [again], of this there is no doubt;
[this applies even to] one who divides cooked food, one who cooks in vain, and one who reviles the gods and Brahmins.
One who slanders their guru, parents, virtuous people, or the king—even they, upon hearing this, are liberated from sins; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, those who have cultivated their selves constantly listen to this scripture and honor that scripture with garments and ornaments, as if it were the Narmadā river itself.
When this scripture is honored with flowers, fruits, sandalwood and other perfumes, and various kinds of food, the gods are thereby honored, as are the gurus.
In this world and in the next as well—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, with every effort, one should [honour them] with perfumes, garments, ornaments, and the like.
One should worship the reciter and the scripture itself with supreme devotion;
[the merit gained] by the recitation of the Vedas and by the maintenance of the *agnihotra* sacrifices—[that merit one gains by honoring them]. (RKV 232.41)
One obtains that fruit in the auspicious narrative of the Narmadā,
as well as the merit found at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and Puṣkara.
At Rudrāvarta, at Gayā, and especially at Vārāṇasī;
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Whatever merit arises for men at such sacred sites as these,
one obtains all that merit by hearing the narrative of the Narmadā.
The man who listens with devotion to the auspicious account of Narmadā’s deeds from beginning to middle to end— listen now to the great fruit thereof.
Having completed his residence in Śiva’s abode, surrounded by celestial maidens and having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices together with Śiva.
O best of beings, this meritorious exposition of the Dharma is unsurpassed among all expositions;
it should be recited even in the home of anyone belonging to the four castes.
I consider the house of one who would worship the book of the *Narmadācarita* to be blessed, as well as that householder and his entire lineage.
By him the Narmadā has been honored, as well as the Blessed Maheśvara;
likewise, when the reciter is honored, the gods and the sages are worshipped.
And having caused this entire, supreme narrative of Revā to be written down—
the ornament of all scriptures— he who gives it to a twice-born man [attains great merit].
Whatever fruit is obtained through bathing and giving gifts at all the sacred fords of the Narmadā, that same fruit a man attains; there is no doubt about this.
This Purāṇa, spoken by Rudra, bestows the fruit of great merit;
it grants heaven and sons, and is auspicious, conducive to fame, and increases one's renown.
It is righteous, conducive to long life, and incomparable; it destroys suffering and bad dreams, and bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims upon those who recite or even hear it.
For one who has bestowed this merit when the Purāṇa is recited by the twice-born,
their residence in the world of Śiva shall last for as many years as there are syllables in the Purāṇa.
Thus has this supreme account of the Narmadā been narrated, having been received from the mouth of Śarva as spoken by Pavana;
it was first properly related by the chief of Sūtas before the Kulapati of the sages, who is revered by the people of the three worlds.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Gift of the Revā-khaṇḍa Manuscript and Other Matters," marking the conclusion of the Revā-khaṇḍa within the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
